Drug-use offenders fall to 24.8% of Taiwan prison population
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:56:33 UTC
21:56:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — People imprisoned for drug use accounted for 24.8% of Taiwan’s prison population at the end of June, down from 35.1% in 2022, as the government increasingly used deferred prosecution and addiction treatment for less serious cases, per CNA.
The Ministry of Justice’s Agency of Corrections said the government’s New Generation Anti-Drug Strategy follows approaches used in other developed countries that emphasize case diversion, differentiated treatment and multiple forms of rehabilitation.
People involved in less serious drug-use cases who primarily require medical care may receive mandatory addiction treatment as a condition of deferred prosecution, allowing them to remain in the community. Those involved in violence, serious crimes or other offenses are more likely to enter correctional institutions, the agency said.
The approach aims to provide treatment suited to individual circumstances while reducing unnecessary incarceration, easing overcrowding and limiting contact between people imprisoned for drug use and drug dealers inside prisons.
The Justice Ministry’s anti-drug strategy for 2025 through 2028 has four goals: cutting drug supply and demand, reducing drug-related harm, supporting reintegration into society, and reducing recidivism. The government has allocated NT$15 billion (US$471 million) for the program, per the MOJ.
Since 2019, the agency has expanded its psychological and social-work staff and used interdisciplinary teams to connect prisoners with resources inside and outside correctional institutions, particularly those assessed as having a greater need for addiction treatment.
Research by the Judicial Academy’s Crime Prevention Research Center found that people who completed mandatory addiction treatment under deferred prosecution had a 66.3% lower risk of relapse than those who did not complete treatment, per CNA.
The agency said medical, psychological, social-work and community resources should be coordinated whether treatment takes place in the community or a correctional institution. Continued support after release is intended to help people reintegrate into society and avoid reoffending.

Yoseph Haddad rejects past support for Palestinian state after old interview resurfaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:56:32 UTC
21:56:32 KST

People of Israel member Yoseph Haddad rejected his past support for the establishment of a Palestinian state on Sunday after an old interview resurfaced showing him endorsing a two-state solution, triggering a new political dispute weeks before Israel’s election.
Journalist Mohammad Magadli circulated footage from an interview Haddad gave to Al-Arabiya more than five years ago, in which the Arab-Israeli public diplomacy activist said the eventual solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict should include a Palestinian state alongside Israel.
The comments stand in sharp contrast to the current platform of People of Israel, the right-wing party led by Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter, which has explicitly rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state. Haddad is running in the second slot on the party’s Knesset list.
In the old interview, Haddad argued that greater integration of Arab-Israelis into the country’s decision-making institutions could eventually help advance Israeli-Palestinian peace.
“The final solution is the State of Israel alongside the State of Palestine. Of course, this is something that has to happen. There is no denying it,” Haddad said in the interview.
Haddad, who joined Winter’s party in August and announced his ambition to become Israel’s public diplomacy minister, responded to the resurfaced video by saying his position had changed following the May 2021 riots during Operation Guardian of the Walls.
“When I saw the unity between Palestinians and Arabs from within who were setting mixed cities on fire, I changed my mind and understood that this was not the solution,” Haddad said.
He later expanded on his current position, saying that his shift regarding the Palestinians and the possibility of peace began during Guardian of the Walls.
“That was when I understood that there would be no peace with them and that they must not be given a state,” Haddad said. “As public diplomacy minister, I will expose the Palestinian lie to the world to make sure that no one remains who believes them and to finally kill the idea of a Palestinian state.”
People of Israel party leader Winter defends Haddad
People of Israel party leader Ofer Winter defended Haddad, calling him "my brother" and "the State of Israel's strongest public diplomacy fighter."
"I saw the things Yoseph Haddad said in past interviews before October 7," Winter said. "People write to me, go after him, remove him, throw Yoseph out, what hypocrisy, what a disgrace. You've lost the plot."
Winter also defended Haddad's character, saying, "A person who has done and continues to do so much for the State of Israel, who pays prices you would not believe for you, for us."
He argued that people should be able to change their views when circumstances change, particularly when they believe they are moving in the "right direction," and said he supported Haddad's shift in position.
"Friends, anyone who did not change his views after October 7 is ignorant and foolish," Winter said.
Winter also reaffirmed his party's opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state and reiterated a hardline position on Gaza, calling for a decisive victory, saying that "trucks will not enter Gaza," and pledging to ensure "voluntary migration."
Haddad's past statement used as political ammunition
Haddad’s political evolution quickly became ammunition for Winter’s rivals.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party attacked Winter and his slate, arguing that the resurfaced remarks exposed contradictions within the new right-wing party.
“Ofer Winter and his opposite,” the party said in a statement.
“Pro-conscription, but supports a draft-evasion government.
“Pro-‘responsibility,’ but supports the prime minister of October 7 and opposes a state commission of inquiry.
“Pro-‘settlement,’ but members of his party support a Palestinian state, and to this moment Winter has not even thought to call them to order or clarify the matter.”
Yashar accused Winter’s party of lacking “a value-based backbone and a path,” and claimed its objective was “to confuse the serving public and crawl into Netanyahu’s draft-evasion government.”
The attack follows previous criticism of Winter from Eisenkot’s camp. Eisenkot has argued that Winter’s positions contain contradictions, particularly because Winter has conditioned his participation in a future government on passage of a broad conscription law while remaining politically aligned with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Winter has publicly said that his party would not join a government unless legislation ending draft exemptions was passed first.
Show of support from Channel 14's Abuhatzira
The resurfaced interview also prompted an unusual intervention from inside Channel 14.
Yitzhak Abuhatzira, editor of Channel 14’s website, published an article defending Haddad and accusing Likud and Religious Zionist Party chairman Bezalel Smotrich of turning against a figure they had previously praised because he now posed an electoral threat.
“Just two months ago, the Right was furious when Eisenkot compared Yoseph Haddad to Mansour Abbas, and Netanyahu was still showering him with praise,” Abuhatzira wrote. “Now, when he threatens to take votes from them, Likud and Smotrich have already turned the public diplomacy hero into a target.”
“The Israeli political system proves once again: Values end where the mandates begin,” he added.
The dispute comes as People of Israel seeks to establish itself as an independent force on the Right. Likud officials have previously expressed concern that Winter and Haddad could draw votes from established right-wing parties, particularly if their slate hovers around the electoral threshold. Political sources have estimated that part of Winter’s support is coming directly from Likud voters.
Haddad, meanwhile, has increasingly emphasized a political platform that combines strong Israeli national identification with greater integration of Arab Israelis. In a recent interview, he described his goal as building an Arab-Israeli “partnership” rather than “coexistence,” while drawing firm political red lines following October 7. He has described that approach as central to his bid to enter the Knesset.
The old Al-Arabiya footage nevertheless gives Winter’s opponents a new line of attack as the campaign enters its final weeks, while Haddad maintains that the views expressed in the interview no longer represent his position.
One point worth flagging for the desk: a second video was being circulated later Sunday that Magadli reportedly said was recorded after Operation Guardian of the Walls, potentially challenging Haddad’s stated timeline for his change of position. I left that development out of the copy because it wasn't in your supplied material, and the available reporting had not yet established the recording date conclusively.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Iran-backed militias in Iraq determined to retain arms after US withdrawal - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:56:07 UTC
21:56:07 KST

The United States’ planned withdrawal from Iraq on Wednesday has been celebrated by Iraqi militias as an “incomplete victory,” emboldening them to continue to resist disarmament beyond the previous deadline, with the extension likely to be pushed back again, Dr. Ronen Zeidel, an Iraq specialist at the Moshe Dayan Center, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
With US forces fully withdrawn and Turkey expected to leave the strategic Bashiqa-Zilkan military base in northern Iraq by the end of 2026, Baghdad has projected a celebratory sense of “sovereignty” despite Iranian and Houthi military elements remaining unofficially present in the country. Iraqi militias have shared videos of themselves driving over American flags to demonstrate their sense of accomplishment.
With Iran maintaining a physical presence in Iraq, Zeidel said much of Washington’s remaining leverage over Baghdad would come through economic pressure, including potentially halting transfers from the Federal Reserve. Since 2003, Washington has held Iraq’s oil revenues, giving it significant leverage over Baghdad’s affairs and helping prevent Iraq from fully aligning with the Iranian axis.
If Washington concluded that Baghdad was not committed to disarming the militias or was testing the limits of its patience, Zeidel said the United States could threaten Iraq’s entire economy, though it has so far shown patience. Zeidel said that Baghdad is aware of such a threat, but insisted that there was still a “dilemma” over whether to risk military escalation against the Iran-backed groups.
The apparent reluctance to confront the militias, as shown by the deadline extension, and America’s withdrawal have resulted in a sense of confidence that will see the militias continue to resist and influence Iraqi legislation.
Iraq postpones militias' disarmament
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi announced on Thursday that the original September 30 deadline for militias to disarm would be pushed back to June 30. However, statements from the militias have indicated that they may disregard the extended timeline as well.
Kataeb Hezbollah military spokesman Jaafar Al-Husseini said Baghdad had not yet responded to the group’s negotiations to “regulate” its weapons.
As a result, “the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of,” he claimed.
Zeidel said the development was not surprising, noting that the militias would likely point to the continued presence of armed Kurdish groups in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region as an excuse for refusing to disarm, as well as continued American military flights over Iraq.
The militias would continue to “bluff” in negotiations, finding new ways to delay disarmament, Zeidel said, noting that their terminology had increasingly shifted away from disarmament and toward the “regulation” of weapons.
Any new “eruption,” whether a return to active conflict between the United States and Iran or an escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, would likely see the groups abandon all their commitments, he predicted, pointing to militia demands to retain missiles and drones capable of striking Israel and Saudi Arabia.
“They make a distinction between small arms or light arms and strategic arms. Under strategic arms, they include long-range missiles and long-range drones that can hit Saudi Arabia, Israel or any other country in the region. So they are ready to deliver some of the small arms, and probably some of the short-range drones, but not the strategic arms,” Zeidel said.
Beyond the issue of arms, Zeidel acknowledged that the US withdrawal had altered the psychological state of the groups. He noted that leaders aligned with the militias had pressured the cabinet to finally approve the new Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) law, controversial legislation that would formally recognize the Iranian-backed paramilitary network as a permanent national security institution.
Legislation to integrate the PMF into Iraq’s armed forces under a unified military hierarchy was pulled last year following both internal strife and pressure from Washington.
“It’s not going to be voted on this week, but it’s very close to being put on the agenda of the Iraqi Parliament, and they might have their way by having this law approved,” Zeidel warned.

Head of Yemen's presidential council announces military operations to retake territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:55:57 UTC
21:55:57 KST

The Saudi-backed head of Yemen's presidential council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced on Sunday the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory held by Iran-backed Houthis terrorists and restore state authority across the country.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
Regional and western officials had previously told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.
Saudi Arabia entered neighboring Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa.
A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.
Houthis continue to hold territory seized in ground offensive
Despite the preparations for a counteroffensive, the Houthis have so far maintained the initiative on the ground, weeks after seizing the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait in a lightning offensive down the coast that saw government forces collapse.
Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.
In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen's Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden, where the Saudi-backed Yemeni government is based.
Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen's third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.
Houthis seek control of mountains overlooking Bab el-Mandeb coastal area
It would also consolidate control of that flat coastal Bab el-Mandeb area by seizing the rugged mountains overlooking them in the western Taiz countryside, according to Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist from Taiz now working as a political analyst.
"This will help them protect their back in case of any operation against the coastline, and make recapturing those areas much more difficult," he said.
The city is important not just for its strategic location; Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.
Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

High Court to weigh direct Shin Bet protection over private security for Democrats chair Yair Golan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:55:56 UTC
21:55:56 KST

The High Court of Justice is scheduled to hear arguments Tuesday over whether intelligence monitoring and armed private guards are enough to protect Democrats chairman Yair Golan, or whether the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) must guard him directly during the final three weeks of the election campaign.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justices Ofer Grosskopf and Ruth Ronnen are scheduled to hear the petition at 1 p.m.
Golan and the Democrats petitioned the court last week (September 29), asking it to order immediate Shin Bet protection at least until the October 27 election results are published, and afterward according to an updated threat assessment.
The state responded Thursday that it had already begun implementing a new security framework for party leaders. It did not, however, commit to providing Golan with a Shin Bet close-protection detail.
The framework followed a top-secret decision adopted by the Ministerial Committee for Shin Bet Affairs on September 16, nearly two weeks before the petition was filed.
Following that decision, the Shin Bet reviewed the available intelligence and security measures and devised a response tailored to the threat facing each party leader, the state said.
The plan applies to party leaders contesting the election who are not ministers or members of Knesset and are not already protected because of a previous position. Relevant Shin Bet officials intend to contact Golan shortly, the state said.
Under the arrangements announced publicly by the agency, Shin Bet intelligence units will monitor threats against all party leaders and help build an updated picture of the danger surrounding each of them.
Democrats argues state responsible for protecting politicians
Party leaders who want physical protection will be able to hire private security companies whose guards may carry weapons even without specific intelligence pointing to a concrete threat. The Shin Bet will coordinate with those private teams and conduct periodic assessments to determine the appropriate level of protection.
The Democrats rejected that model when it was announced, arguing that the state was shifting responsibility for protecting threatened political leaders to private companies.
The dispute now before the court is whether the measures offered by the Shin Bet are sufficient, or whether the circumstances require direct Shin Bet protection.
Petition documents dozens of threats
According to the petition, the head of the Israel Police unit responsible for threatened individuals informed Golan’s office approximately a month before the filing that the threat level against him had been raised to four on a six-point scale.
The petition documents dozens of threats posted between July and late September, including calls to shoot or hang Golan and messages threatening members of his family.
It also says Golan’s name appeared in a death-threat letter attached to a brick thrown at Channel 12’s studios on July 27. According to the petition, he was the only party leader named as a target in the letter.
The petitioners said they made three written approaches seeking state protection. They sent letters dated August 25 and September 2 to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee and copied security and legal officials.
The party sent a third request directly to Shin Bet Director David Zini on September 22. It sought a response by September 27 and warned that the party would petition the High Court if it received no decision.
None of the three approaches had been answered by the time the Democrats filed the petition.
The state’s response indicates that officials had begun addressing the broader question of protecting party leaders before the petition. It does not say, however, that the September 16 decision or its practical implications had been communicated to Golan.
Under Section 7 of the Shin Bet Law, the agency must protect people designated by the government. Golan argues that the threats against him, his position as a party leader, and the public demands of an election campaign require state protection rather than reliance primarily on a privately hired company.
The petition also argues that leaving a threatened candidate without state protection restricts his ability to appear before voters and campaign on equal terms.
The state said the exact measures approved for party leaders are classified and can be presented to the judges only behind closed doors, without Golan or his lawyers present.
Grosskopf declined to order immediate protection when the petition was filed. He nevertheless wrote that “the respondents can be expected to keep the need to protect” Golan “under ongoing review, in accordance with the latest threat assessment in his case.”

Israeli spy Eli Cohen may have been buried near Damascus barracks, Syrian official claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:55:51 UTC
21:55:51 KST

Legendary Israeli spy Eli Cohen may have been buried near unidentified military barracks outside Damascus, Syrian security officer Saeed Jawish claimed in an interview with the Saudi-owned Al Majalla on Saturday.
Cohen, a Mossad agent best known for his work in Syria, operated under the alias Kamel Amin Thabet, posing as a wealthy Syrian businessman who had returned to Damascus after years in Argentina. His cover was ultimately blown in January 1965, when Syrian counterintelligence caught him transmitting messages to Israel. He was arrested, tried for espionage and publicly hanged in Damascus on May 18, 1965.
Jawish, who claims to have been involved in the operation that led to Cohen’s arrest, explained that he and five other Syrian officers heavily debated the matter of where to bury the spy the night before his execution.
“We said the Israelis would not let the matter go and would try to obtain his remains, so each of us began suggesting a place where he could be buried,” Jawish told Al Majalla.
According to Jawish, another Syrian official named Adnan Tayara suggested burying Cohen at the entrance to a military barracks that already had permanent security.
That way, Tayara had explained at the time, “the grave would not need special guarding.”
“There were several barracks, and I do not know which one was chosen,” Jawish said in the interview. “The person who knows is [Syrian Warrant Officer] Melhem Qassem, who attended the burial.”
Since Cohen’s execution, Syria has refused to return his remains, which have allegedly been buried multiple times to prevent Israel from finding and returning them.
Nearly a year ago, Saudi state-run news outlet Al-Hadath reported that Cohen’s remains could be returned to Israel in a deal with Syria.
The report followed the Mossad's seizure of 2,500 documents on Cohen. Additionally, Reuters reported at the time that Syria's leadership approved the handover of the remains to Israel in a bid to ease Israeli hostility and show goodwill to US President Donald Trump.
Israel seeks return of Jewish remains buried in Lebanon as part of prisoner talks
More recently, Hezbollah-linked Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Israel and Lebanon discussed what was referred to as a "civilian prisoner exchange deal" during recent negotiations, with Israeli officials raising the possibility of transferring the remains of Jews buried in Lebanese cemeteries to Israel.
According to the report, the issue was raised during discussions over Lebanese prisoners and detainees held by Israel. The discussions focused on individuals classified by Israel as civilians whose ties to Hezbollah were unclear, but who Israel said nevertheless posed a threat to IDF troops and were detained on those grounds.
The Israeli representatives specifically referred to what Al-Akhbar described as a significant number of remains buried in Jewish cemeteries in Beirut and Sidon.
The report came after Israel and Lebanon's recent round of talks in Rome, which a source speaking to The Jerusalem Post at the time described as "positive."
Shir Perets and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

GFCN finds inconsistencies in Telegraph investigation into Leipzig drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:50:09 UTC
21:50:09 KST

MOSCOW, October 4. /TASS/. The Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) has identified a number of inconsistencies in a joint investigation by Britain’s The Daily Telegraph and Germany’s Welt am Sonntag into an incident involving a drone detected at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
The association said its review of the report showed that the purported scoop relied largely on circumstantial evidence and logical assumptions. GFCN identified chronological falsification as one of the investigation’s key problems. At the beginning of the article, the incident is described as having occurred in "September," although the authors later say that the alleged reconnaissance was recorded on July 31 and that the drone collided with an aircraft "five days later."
Thus, according to the association, the text itself directly indicates that the actual incident occurred on August 5. Using "September" as a narrative anchor establishes in the media not the date of the incident itself but the start of the political campaign. This discrepancy indicates that the August incident was instrumentalized in the public sphere with a one-month delay, the association added.
A second fundamental gap in the investigation concerns the description of counterintelligence activities. In particular, the newspapers claim that German investigators had established suspect Oleg Levushkin’s links to the GRU by the time he entered the country, yet "he was not placed under surveillance." The authors also claim that he instructed a Belarusian intermediary, Andrey Korshakov, to launch the drone, but provide no information about his detention, questioning, or procedural status, which "turns him into a convenient ‘missing figure’ intended to conceal the inability to prove the suspect’s personal presence at the scene of the crime."
The Western newspapers’ report also claims that explosives were secretly brought into Germany via Turkey, Bulgaria, and Serbia. The fact-checking association noted that this version was unsupported by evidence and did not fit well with the description of the device itself.
The association also noted that the acute lack of facts was compensated for by aggressive visual argumentation. Readers are shown a collage that artificially places the suspect alongside the damaged drone and police officers, creating the false impression that his involvement in the incident has been proven. Footage of a burning parcel at a DHL warehouse in Britain further heightens the atmosphere.

Ukraine will begin deploying domestically produced small missiles by late October to counter Russian jet-powered strike drones, alongside expanding networks of automated gun turrets around the capital region, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced during a joint press briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukringrom, Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian defense enterprises have developed several types of specialized, lower-cost interceptor missiles engineered to neutralize high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with initial combat deployments anticipated during the second half of the month.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The small missile program – I will not state the name now, there are several types – we will evidently see results in the second half of this month. We expect to see results,” Zelensky said.
While the missiles are not yet in serial mass production, the president stated that manufacturing can be scaled up rapidly once operational performance is confirmed.
Zelensky noted that Ukrainian forces currently intercept roughly 50 to 60 percent of incoming turbojet Shahed drones, with combat aviation demonstrating the highest efficacy against high-velocity targets.
“Right now, high-quality interception of [jet UAVs] is about 50 percent, 55 percent, sometimes 60 percent – that is our aviation,” Zelensky said.
“F-16s are helping very significantly, and 20mm ammunition is working well.”
Ukraine Hits Russian Buk-M3, Drone Hub, and Bryansk EW Station
Automated defensive turrets in Kyiv
To reinforce ground-level interception networks, Zelensky announced that Ukrainian defense units have installed more than 12 automated counter-drone turrets across the capital, with plans to deploy eight additional systems in the surrounding Kyiv region.
The automated modules are configured to fire 50-caliber (12.7mm) ammunition to destroy incoming loitering munitions on terminal approach vectors. Zelensky explained that the installations form part of a layered, combined defense posture required to address Moscow’s evolving air assault doctrine.
“The Russians will now focus precisely on jet-powered drones and ballistics,” Zelensky observed. “Regarding mass strikes similar to what we are seeing now, I believe they will move toward quality rather than quantity, transitioning from conventional Shaheds to maximum utilization of jet variants.”
The technological adaptation arrives as Russian forces have increasingly paired high-speed loitering munitions with ballistic missile salvos to overwhelm mobile air defense fire teams and deplete inventories of high-end surface-to-air guided missiles.
Bilateral drone agreement
The technical announcements coincided with the formal conclusion of a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and Germany to deepen operational cooperation in counter-drone warfare, enabling German defense manufacturers to integrate Ukrainian combat lessons directly into joint production ventures.
Chancellor Merz emphasized that defense cooperation between Berlin and Kyiv functions as a reciprocal partnership, noting that German corporate representatives accompanying his delegation are studying Ukrainian battlefield adaptations while establishing joint high-tech industrial facilities.
Merz referenced a thwarted Russian-directed sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 as a clear demonstration of why counter-drone technologies are critical for Germany’s own domestic security.
Addressing Russian rhetoric, Merz stated that public threats issued by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs warning foreign diplomats of “mortal danger” in Kyiv did not influence his decision to visit the Ukrainian capital.
“Despite the threats that reached us from Moscow in recent days, I came today. Together with me came a colleague from the government, Federal Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche, a large delegation from my government, and a major economic delegation,” Merz said.
“This shows: we will not allow ourselves to be intimidated.”
The chancellor added that ongoing Russian drone attacks on the capital during his visit underscored Moscow’s conduct, reaffirming that Berlin’s solidarity remains steadfast on his second visit to Kyiv as head of government and fourth overall.
Diplomatic resilience
Merz’s presence in Kyiv follows public assurances from EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová, who confirmed that no EU member state embassy is preparing to evacuate the capital despite Moscow’s threats and infrastructure strikes.
Mathernová confirmed regular coordination with the diplomatic missions of 25 EU member states based in Kyiv, stating that both the EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission (EUAM) Ukraine remain fully operational.
The ambassador characterized Moscow’s escalatory statements as an attempt to compensate for military setbacks on the battlefield, echoing statements by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine that standard diplomatic protocols mandate prior notification and that zero relocation requests have been received.

Voting begins in Brazil’s presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:44:41 UTC
21:44:41 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 4. /TASS/. Voting in Brazil’s presidential election has begun. Polling stations opened on Sunday at 8:00 a.m. Brasilia time (2:00 p.m. Moscow time) and will close to voters at 5:00 p.m. (11:00 p.m. Moscow time). As in the previous election, voting is taking place simultaneously across the country. Thus, polling stations opened at 6:00 a.m. in the western part of Amazonas state and neighboring Acre, and at 7:00 a.m. in several other western states.
Brazilians will elect not only the country’s president for the next four years but also state governors, all members of the Chamber of Deputies, one-third of the Federal Senate, and members of state legislatures. The country’s Superior Electoral Court, which performs the functions of a central election commission, has registered 12 presidential candidates, while more than 158 mln Brazilians are eligible to vote.
The main presidential contest is between incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. According to the latest opinion polls, the two politicians are neck and neck, with each receiving 45-48% support in a potential runoff, while pollsters consider a first-round victory by either candidate unlikely.
The first preliminary results will begin to be released shortly after polling stations close. Thanks to Brazil’s electronic voting system, the final vote count is usually completed within a few hours. If none of the candidates for executive office receives more than 50% of valid votes, a runoff will be held on October 25.

No EU Embassies Leaving Kyiv Despite Russian Threats, Envoy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

No EU member state embassy is preparing to evacuate the Ukrainian capital despite Russian aerial bombardments and threats directed at foreign missions, EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová confirmed in an interview with state news agency Ukrinform.
Mathernová stated that she maintains continuous coordination with the diplomatic representations of 25 EU member states based in the capital, rejecting reports in foreign media alleging that Western embassies were preparing contingency withdrawals to western Ukraine or Poland.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I am not aware of any embassy that is leaving – and certainly not embassies of EU countries,” Mathernová told Ukrinform. “I do not know what sources The Guardian used, but I am not aware of any embassy currently leaving; quite the contrary.”
The ambassador confirmed that both the EU Delegation to Ukraine and the European Union Advisory Mission (EUAM) Ukraine, alongside national embassies representing EU member states, remain fully operational on the ground in Kyiv.
While security personnel continuously evaluate operational hazards, Mathernová emphasized that the latest public threats from Russia have not altered their operational posture.
Mathernová framed Moscow’s escalatory rhetoric as an attempt to compensate for military setbacks on the battlefield.
“I think [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s rhetoric is a consequence of the lack of success on the battlefield,” Mathernová observed.
Ukraine’s Science Under Fire: Russia Is Targeting Knowledge, People and the Future
“He is escalating rhetoric and threats – both regarding the civilian population and diplomats, and regarding EU countries. I believe this is a sign of frustration over failing in his strategic goals – to conquer Ukraine in a few weeks.”
Diplomatic coordination
Mathernová‘s public clarification directly addresses reporting published earlier in the week by The Guardian, which cited anonymous Western diplomats claiming that contingency plans were being drafted to relocate staff to the western city of Lviv or eastern Poland if the Kremlin began deliberately targeting foreign diplomatic compounds.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) previously refuted the report on Friday, with spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi noting that established international diplomatic conventions mandate formal notification to the host nation prior to any mission transfer, confirming that zero relocation requests had been received by Ukrainian authorities.
The ambassador’s comments also reinforce statements made by European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand, who dismissed threats issued on Saturday, Oct. 3, by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
In an official dispatch, Moscow had warned foreign citizens and accredited diplomats in Kyiv of “mortal danger,” pledging to sustain mass aerial strikes across the capital. Wigand reaffirmed that the EU would not be intimidated into reducing its diplomatic footprint or scaling back defense assistance.

Iran shines brighter in Nagoya with 19 gold medals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:40:19 UTC
21:40:19 KST

Iran shines brighter in Nagoya with 19 gold medals
TEHRAN - Iran’s delegation concluded its campaign at the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with an improved gold-medal tally compared with the previous edition in Hangzhou.
The Nagoya Asian Games came to an end with Iran finishing sixth in the overall medal standings after winning 19 gold, 18 silver and 15 bronze medals for a total of 52 medals.
Iran sent a delegation of 304 athletes to Nagoya, competing across 38 sports. The number of athletes was higher than at the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou.
Iran also climbed one place in the overall standings compared with the 2022 Asian Games, moving up to sixth. The country had previously finished sixth at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta as well.
Although Iran’s overall medal haul fell short of the 54 medals won at the Hangzhou Games, the number of gold medals increased significantly. Iran won 13 gold medals in Hangzhou, compared with 19 in Nagoya — an increase of six golds.
The performance of Iran’s women was another notable highlight of the Games. While Iranian women failed to win a gold medal in Hangzhou, they claimed three golds in Nagoya.
Overall, the Nagoya campaign marked a significant improvement in Iran’s performance at the top end of the medal table, with the delegation combining a higher gold-medal tally with a one-place rise in the overall standings.

The Strait of Hormuz is the main focus of Iran’s negotiations to end the war with the US, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Sunday.
"Securing the Strait of Hormuz, or restoring security to this waterway, requires specific steps from the American side,” Baqaei told a news briefing, as cited by the state-run IRNA news agency.
"This issue has been discussed many times, including stopping interference with Iranian commercial shipping, ending sanctions, and other interventionist measures," he added.
Baqaei said the latest US proposal to Iran to end the war was almost identical to previous proposals, adding that Washington continues to focus on the nuclear file.
"We will conduct the necessary investigations regarding some details and will also reflect our supplementary points to the other party," he noted.
The spokesman said Iran’s top leadership has not discussed allowing International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to return to the country.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic route for energy supplies. The US military later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Efforts to end the war have continued since a June framework deal, which seeks to pave the way for a final peace agreement covering navigation through the strategic waterway and Iran’s nuclear program

‘Russia is not our enemy’: Hundreds rally in Paris against Ukraine aid (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:39:38 UTC

‘Russia is not our enemy’: Hundreds rally in Paris against Ukraine aid (VIDEO)
Hundreds of anti-government protesters took to the streets of Paris on Saturday to rally against continued aid to Ukraine as part of a nationwide protest organized by former MEP Florian Philippot, who is running in France’s 2027 presidential election.
The protesters called on French President Emmanuel Macron to halt aid to Ukraine and pushed for France’s withdrawal from the EU and all supranational institutions, including NATO. Apart from Paris, the right-wing Les Patriotes party, led by Philippot, organized rallies in Aubiere, Annecy, Grenoble, Perigueux and Chaumont, highlighting issues such as fuel costs, freedom of expression and peace.
The demonstration comes after a series of mass protests has gripped France in recent weeks, with students taking to the streets alongside broader labor actions over wages, public spending, working conditions and the government’s budget plans.
Philippot, a prominent Eurosceptic, marched through Paris with supporters, who waved French flags, as well as banners reading “Russia is not our enemy,” and calling for France to stay out of the Ukraine conflict.
“We must leave NATO, we must stop funding the war in Ukraine and stop arming it as well,” he stressed. “Instead of putting money over there, it must be put into lowering taxes on petrol, for example, because people can’t take it anymore.”
A Philippot supporter argued that “war efforts don’t achieve much,” calling for greater spending on “hospitals, education, and a whole range of budgets that are humane.”
The nationwide unrest comes as the French government unveiled its proposed 2027 budget earlier this week, targeting €54 billion in measures to bring the budget deficit to 5% of GDP, including spending cuts and freezes affecting public services, pensions and social benefits.
Philippot tore up an EU flag in front of demonstrators, saying, “This blue-starred rag is not our flag and never will be. So today, we are obviously going to get rid of it, because our fight is to get out of this horror through Frexit.”
Earlier this week, the EU reiterated its commitment to the €90 billion ($101 billion) loan aimed at covering the Ukrainian government’s budgetary and military financing needs for 2026 and 2027.

MOSCOW, October 4. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army lost around 1,395 troops over the past day in operations by Russian battlegroups in the special military operation zone, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
According to the ministry, the Ukrainian army lost more than 235 troops in Battlegroup North’s area of responsibility, up to 225 in Battlegroup West’s area, up to 180 in Battlegroup South’s area, more than 435 in Battlegroup Center’s area, more than 290 in Battlegroup East’s area, and up to 30 in Battlegroup Dnepr’s area.
Russian forces also struck Ukrainian transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, as well as military equipment depots.
"Operational-tactical aircraft, strike drones, missile forces, and artillery of Russian Armed Forces battlegroups <…> struck Ukrainian transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, military equipment depots, drone storage sites, as well as temporary deployment sites of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 147 areas," the ministry said.
Russian forces destroyed a Ukrainian air target detection radar. "Operational-tactical aircraft, strike drones, missile forces, and artillery of Russian Armed Forces battlegroups destroyed an air target detection radar," the ministry said.

Bernie Sanders rallies for billionaire tax ahead of midterms

Breadcrumb
Bernie Sanders rallies for first-ever billionaire tax ahead of midterms
If a billionaire tax passes in California, it would be the first of its kind in the world, which advocates hope will give momentum for similar measures elsewhere.
On Saturday, one month ahead of the midterms, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and other progressives held a rally in San Francisco to advocate for Proposition 40, a measure that would impose a 5% wealth tax on billionaires, who account for a fraction of a percentage of the population, but who hold an estimated 45% of the state’s household wealth. The tax would go toward the healthcare of residents.
Opponents of Proposition 40 say that the measure risks pushing businesses and jobs out of the state.
“I say to California billionaires and billionaires all over this country: Show a little concern for your fellow Americans. You and your class have never ever had it so good, but you cannot have it all,” Sanders said to a cheering crowd.
“Instead of spending over $225 million on TV ads, we have a better idea. Start paying your fair share of taxes,” he said.
“Once California passes Proposition 40, trust me that will not be the end. We’ll enact a national wealth tax,” Sanders added. He likened the fight for a billionaire tax to the right for democracy, saying there can be democracy or extreme wealth inequality -- but not both.
The 85-year-old senator was met by a standing ovation and roaring applause as he took the stage at the Curran Theatre, an intricately designed French revivalist structure near the city’s downtown.
He was introduced by Representative Ro Khanna, whose district makes up a large swath of Silicon Valley (home to a high proportion of the state’s billionaires), and who is rumoured to be considering a 2028 presidential bid.
“We’re here to do something very important. It’s the first time in the history of the world that there is a billionaire tax on the ballot,” he told a cheering crowd. “The whole world, the whole nation, is watching. And you know what they’re asking us? They’re asking us: Will the Democratic Party stand with the donor class or are they gonna stand with the working class?”
He described Proposition 40 as a choice between 250 billionaires or giving poor children healthcare and keeping the jobs of 150,000 healthcare providers. He noted that the billionaires who oppose the tax are spending $200 million to oppose it. He called out politicians who oppose the tax. He also challenged his colleagues to call Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide.
Another headline speaker was Jane Kim, who is running for the state’s Insurance Commissioner, a position she describes as the most important job you’ve never heard of.
In her speech, she vowed to lower monthly premiums and develop a system in which insurance is used for protection rather than profit.
Audience members, many of whom were healthcare workers, held signs reading “Yes on 40, No-41-42, Save Lives, Tax Billionaires” and raised them in the air after speakers made rousing statements.
“We’re trying to hold the billionaires accountable. They have made millions off of regular people for years. This one-time five percent emergency tax will not even put a dent in what they are making,” Savonnda Blaylock, a healthcare worker, told The New Arab prior to the rally.
“They are still making trillions of dollars. Some of them are becoming trillionaires, whereas regular people can’t even afford basic needs like gas and food. We’re here to make sure voters know, that communities know, that we’re going to fight this to the very last day – November 3rd,” she said.
“I’m excited about all of us seeing Bernie, because he brings hope. His vision and the hope he brings is what we need right now to be able to bring this home,” she said.
Saturday’s rally was part of a multi-day tour across California by progressives to encourage voter turnout and advocate for Proposition 40.

Putin Hugged the Man Behind Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Program—OSINT Identifies Him
Ukrainian OSINT researchers have identified a senior executive at Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone as the man who presented the new jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones to Vladimir Putin during Russia’s Center-2026 military exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Evocation.info on October 3, the man seen briefing Putin was Ildar Tazutdinov, a senior executive at Alabuga, the Russian industrial complex involved in producing Iranian-designed Shahed-type attack drones.
The identification followed the publication of footage from the Chebarkulsky training ground in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, where Putin inspected new Russian weapons on October 2.
In the video, Tazutdinov described the capabilities of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 before concluding: “We are ready to continue striking the enemy in the same way. That concludes my report!” Putin then shook his hand and embraced him, according to footage analyzed by Evocation.info.
Interfax reported on October 2 that Putin had been shown both jet-powered Geran variants during his visit to the training ground. According to the presentation, the Geran-4 uses a jet engine allowing it to reach approximately 350 km/h, carry a 50-kilogram warhead, and operate at a range of around 750 to 800 kilometers.
The larger Geran-5 was described as having a speed of up to 450 km/h, a 90-kilogram warhead, and a maximum range of roughly 900 kilometers. Evocation.info identified Tazutdinov as one of the executives connected to Alabuga’s drone program.
His involvement with the facility has previously been documented by the US government. In February 2024, the US Treasury Department sanctioned Ildar Rashitovich Tazutdinov, identifying him at the time as Alabuga’s deputy director general of corporate affairs.
Treasury said he had been involved in the shipment and import of materials and disassembled Iranian UAVs to Russia in connection with drone production at Alabuga.
The US Treasury said Alabuga officials were involved in producing Iranian-designed UAVs, including the Shahed-136 and its Russian Geran-2 variant, as well as importing components from Iran for the program.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 represent newer jet-powered additions to Russia’s expanding family of long-range attack drones. Their higher speeds make interception more difficult than with earlier propeller-driven Shahed-type UAVs, prompting Ukraine to develop and deploy faster drone interceptors designed specifically to engage such targets.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence identified 20 pieces of foreign-made industrial equipment being used at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone to produce various Geran drone modifications, including machinery from China, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and Iran.

Few people thought I could win gold: Emami
TEHRAN - Iranian freestyle wrestler Yones Emami, competing in the 74kg weight class, spoke about the difficulty of the competition, the high level of his opponents and his determination to win gold after claiming the title at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya.
Emami, who also won gold at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, secured his second consecutive Asian Games title with another impressive performance.
“Everything went well and I was able to win the gold medal. I’m happy that I can return home with a gold medal, and I hope I have not disappointed my family, the federation or my dear people. It was really difficult, and few people thought I could win the gold medal, but thankfully I was able to achieve this success.”
“The level of the competition was really high. There were world champions and many highly regarded wrestlers in my weight class, and I faced all of them. I managed to defeat my opponents and win the gold medal.”
The Iranian champion also reflected on his victory over Olympic champion Razambek Zhamalov, a match that many observers had expected to be particularly challenging.
“The reality was that many people did not think I could beat Zhamalov. Even before the competition, some people were worried that I might have problems in the early rounds. But, I was able to manage the competition well from the very beginning and eventually win the gold medal.”
Emami also admitted that winning two consecutive Asian Games gold medals was not something he had previously imagined.
Asked about the feeling of winning his second Asian Games gold after his triumph in Hangzhou, he said: “I honestly hadn’t thought about winning two Asian Games gold medals. My entire focus was on these competitions in Nagoya. I wanted to be in the best possible condition, wrestle my best matches and ultimately win the gold medal.”

How the ‘G2’ effect of Trump-Xi summit is reverberating through Asia

Wang Xiangwei is a senior visiting scholar (2026-27) at the Rajawali Foundation Institute for Asia, Harvard Kennedy School, and a former editor-in-chief of the South China Morning Post. 
For American and Chinese people interested in the outcome of the latest summit between China’s President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, their conclusions could not be more different if they turn to the media and pundits for guidance.
Chinese state media spared no superlative, echoing the official description of the summit as: forging the right way for the major powers to get along and writing a new chapter in ties. OPEC+ Agrees to Keep November Oil Output Targets Steady
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
“The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
“Consequently, the oil market remains tight.”
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
OUTPUT HIKES HAVE BEEN LARGELY ON PAPER THIS YEAR
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members’ 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven hold their next meeting on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group called the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), which does not decide policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.

During the yellow level, trains will transport passengers between the banks of the Dnipro. At the red level, service on the above-ground section will be suspended.
In Kyiv, the green metro line will now operate during a yellow alert. Before passenger services began, trains made test runs in both directions. This was reported by the Kyiv City State Administration, according to UNN.

As of today, trains on the "green" line operate during an alert: during the yellow threat level, they carry passengers between the right and left banks of the Dnipro; if a red threat level is announced, service on the above-ground section is suspended

Ten stories of Ukraine’s defenders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:26:00 EEST
21:26:00 KST

From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
2026 has been a year of victories great and small for the Ukrainian military, and the whole country has celebrated along with them.
Nazar Daletskyi, a serviceman believed to have been killed three years ago – a funeral had even been held for him – came home alive from captivity.
Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander in the 475th Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), single-handedly evacuated two wounded soldiers in a civilian pickup truck as Russian drones circled overhead.
The National Guard awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to a woman for the first time – machine gunner Oleksandra Davydenko.
Ukraine's defence forces in the south reclaimed up to 435 sq km of territory. The 3rd Army Corps stunned the public with the successful Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast.
Ahead of Defenders' Day, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) looks back to 10 of this year's most interesting stories about our defenders. Read them all – you won't regret it!
"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
"Eighteen", a company commander in the Special Operations Forces (SOF), would normally have been expected to coordinate the evacuation from the command post. But when four of his soldiers were no longer able to walk independently after a battle and an encounter with an improvised explosive device, he went into the area himself.
"The guys all had leg wounds. There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk," Eighteen recalls.
It took 15 hours to carry the most seriously wounded soldier, Malyi (Little One), to the medics. The young man had severe injuries to his arm and abdomen and a ruptured liver.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on," Eighteen says.
As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the doctors, Eighteen went back for the body of his fallen comrade, Sava. The rescue operation took five days in all, and the soldiers covered more than 50 km. All but Sava survived.
This remarkable operation proved once again that even in the era of ground robots, those who operate on their own two feet still have the decisive say in battle.
"I thought about tightening the tourniquets and bleeding to death so I wouldn't suffer": how a badly wounded infantryman hunted by six drones was rescued
Herodotus is a private first class in the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade. After 18 months fighting in an assault unit, he miraculously survived being hunted down by six Russian drones.
Herodotus was alone in a wooded area. He had already lost a foot, and as he was being evacuated, a Russian drone destroyed the ground robot and mangled his other leg.
He crawled, hid from FPV drones, and even played "cat and mouse" with one of them around a dugout, moving in such a way as to stay out of the Russians' line of sight. His comrades watched him from a drone throughout, dropping water, painkillers and food and trying to find a way to get him out.
Eventually three soldiers came to retrieve him and carried him for about 2.5 km. Herodotus lost both legs, but he survived. He says that in his darkest moments he remembered that he had promised his family he would return.
"There, look at what I've got now instead of legs. Ta-da! What am I supposed to do now – cry? It's already happened... I'm alive, so everything should be all right. Life can be a complete pile of shit sometimes, but we'll get through it," he says cheerily.
"We accepted that we were going to die": the military anaesthesiologist who volunteered to go to the besieged Azovstal steelworks
In spring 2022, military anaesthetist Oleksandr Demchenko volunteered to fly to the besieged Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol by helicopter. He realised that it could be a one-way trip. He later learned that the helicopter was shot down on its return journey.
At Azovstal, Oleksandr operated on wounded soldiers in an underground hospital, in cold and damp conditions and with a dwindling supply of medicines: even amputations had to be performed under local anaesthetic.
After one airstrike, five floors of the building above the medics collapsed while hundreds of people were inside.
"We all accepted that we were going to die there, because, essentially, there were no other options," Oleksandr recalls. But he was lucky – he made it out of there.
He survived Azovstal, Russian captivity and the Olenivka prison camp. When he returned home, he went back to medicine.
"I returned to the profession because I love it. I genuinely love my work," he admits.
"I'd serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this": the nurse who swapped her uniform for combat fatigues
Before joining the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Tamila had worked as a nurse at a district hospital for 15 years. Then she swapped her uniform for combat fatigues, eventually becoming head of the medical station of the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade.
In autumn 2022, when the brigade was conducting a counteroffensive in Kherson Oblast, Tamila was constantly going out to evacuate the wounded.
"I provided first aid in the vehicle. I had to stop the bleeding from severed arms and legs, apply tourniquets and administer painkillers. The brigade was carrying out assault operations, and guys were dying both on the battlefield and in front of me," she recalls.
Once, two years later, she happened to meet a soldier whom she had once evacuated with a severed arm. He recognised her first: "You were the one who evacuated me back then. Thank you."
Tamila's first contract ended long ago and she could have left the military, but she stayed. She still goes out on evacuations sometimes, even though her current position does not require her to.
She says she is ready to serve for as long as necessary, as long as her 16-year-old son never has to follow in her footsteps.
"I've been in the Armed Forces of Ukraine for six years now, and they haven't been easy years for me – they've been really hard. Because war is the worst nightmare there can be. But I'm ready to serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this, as long as he never has to fight," Tamila admits.
"Several times we had enemy infantry jumping into our trenches": the company commander who spent 343 consecutive days on the front line
Three hundred and forty-three days is enough time to celebrate Christmas, New Year and Easter. But for company commander Oleksii, aka Botanik (Nerd), it was the length of time he spent at positions on the Orikhiv front without rotation.
About half of the soldiers in Botanik's company are over 50, and many suffer from chronic health problems. This makes normal rotations almost impossible, so they have to remain on the line of contact for long periods.
Oleksii's longest combat deployment took place in June 2025. The Russians would attack the Ukrainian positions using infantry fighting vehicles, motorcycles and quad bikes and on foot. When they managed to reach the trenches, machine gunners and drone operators would join the fighting. Evacuation crews collected the wounded under fire.
"I tried to make the fighters' time at the combat positions as bearable as possible. I made sure everyone had a chance to talk to their families every day – that helps a lot," the company commander says.
Oleksii finally left the line of contact on 8 March 2026 and immediately went on leave to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday. Then it was back to the front line.
"I see my primary role as a commander as minimising personnel losses – ideally ensuring there are none at all," he says.
Pastry chef by day, air defence operator by night: the woman from Bucha shooting down Russian drones
Liudmyla, from Bucha, isn't your typical volunteer. By day she makes exquisite cakes and pastries, but after dark, she protects the skies over Kyiv Oblast.
It all began in 2024, when an acquaintance told Liudmyla about the Bucha Witches – a women's unit of mobile air-defence fire groups established as part of the Bucha Volunteer Formation of the Territorial Community. Liudmyla couldn't stand idly by.
The first time she shot down a Russian Shahed drone, the adrenaline rush was overwhelming. Two years ago she knew almost nothing about the military – now she commands a mobile fire group.
Liudmyla does all this as a volunteer and receives no pay. After a night shift, she returns home, puts down her weapon, and gets back to making cakes.
"It can be difficult at times – exhausting night shifts and winter cold when your hands quite literally freeze to the machine gun – but I love this work. Now I see safety in a completely different way and always silently thank those who protect my sleep when I am off duty," the defender says.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
In March 2022, urological surgeon Dmytro Hetmanov was operating on wounded civilians in besieged Mariupol. The hardest moment came when a father carried in his wounded teenage son. The injury looked minor from the outside, but the boy's heart and blood vessels had been virtually torn apart. The boy could not be saved.
On 16 March, Dmytro decided to try to escape the city with his parents and neighbours. On the way, he saw the bombed-out Drama Theatre still smouldering. It took him a long time to get through the Russian checkpoints.
Two years later, Dmytro was working as a surgeon at the University Hospital in Katowice, Poland. He had a job and his life was gradually getting back on track, but thoughts of his homeland never left him.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life," he admitted.
Dmytro resigned and left Poland to return to Ukraine. He completed basic military training, signed a contract and joined the Unmanned Systems Forces. Six months later, he realised that he was missing surgery.
Now Dmytro is serving as a surgeon once again, this time with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. He deals with combat injuries, assists with amputations, and has even tried his hand at neurosurgery for the first time.
Although Dmytro's daughter lives in the United States and rarely sees her dad, he does not regret his decision to join the military.
"They actually listed me among the dead": Azov fighter Web on the Olenivka terrorist attack and rehabilitation after three years in captivity
Dmytro "Web" Tishchenko was listed among the dead after the Russian terrorist attack on the Olenivka prison camp. When he came to, he was lying in a pile of metal and concrete, with a punctured lung and a bleeding arm. He crawled out of the destroyed barracks by himself.
"We asked the Russians for at least some medical supplies, but all they brought us was a bag of army sheets. We tore the fabric into pieces and used them to dress our wounds," the Azov fighter recalls.
When he was finally taken to hospital, one of the Russians was surprised to hear his name called out: "You're alive? I'd already got a body bag ready for you."
Web was only 21 at the time of the terrorist attack on Olenivka. He became a soldier at 18, took part in the defence of Mariupol, was wounded in the leg, made it to Azovstal, and from there he was taken into Russian captivity.
Dmytro spent another two months in hospital after the attack, and then he was moved from one penal colony to another. He had to endure torture, cold, hunger, and being made to stand for hours on end.
Because of a shrapnel wound, his leg became so badly infected that the wound simply opened up. In order to be admitted to hospital and avoid losing the limb, he had to pretend to faint.
Dmytro spent almost three years in captivity. In April 2025, he was suddenly taken out of his cell, given clean clothes and driven to an unknown destination. It was a prisoner swap. Web came home on the eve of Easter – exactly when he had dreamed of returning.
Now Web is undergoing treatment for his injuries and the effects of captivity, while also helping other young soldiers who have returned from Russian captivity.
"Sometimes I forget I'm missing a leg": two Khartiia infantrymen who've returned to service after suffering severe injuries
Assault trooper "Bilyi" stepped on a mine 15-20 metres from his position. He applied a tourniquet himself and waited to be evacuated, but the team that set off to retrieve him was attacked by a drone. When dawn broke, he realised that help might not come in time, so he started crawling on his own.
Bilyi crawled for nearly a whole day before two reconnaissance soldiers found him. By then the tourniquet had been on his leg for about two days. Bilyi had realised immediately after the explosion that his leg would have to be amputated.
"Terry" went through a similar ordeal. During his third combat deployment, he stepped on a petal mine hidden in the grass.
"It didn't hurt, I didn't lose consciousness. I opened my eyes and saw these toes lying around. Only the heel was left. I thought, 'That's it. I've had my run,'" Terry recalls.
It took 25 hours to evacuate him. Along the way, the wounded man and the soldiers carrying him were pursued by Russian FPV drones. One drone missed them, but another exploded near the group, injuring all three of the soldiers who were carrying Terry. Despite their own injuries, however, they managed to carry him to shelter.
Both Terry and Bilyi had their legs amputated. Months of surgery, rehabilitation and prosthetic fittings lay ahead of them. Terry recalls that after receiving a temporary prosthesis, he started walking the very next day and soon left his crutches behind. Bilyi was also quick to learn how to use his prosthesis.
"After they cut off my leg, there were moments when I felt a bit down. Then I'd lie there and think: it's all good. I'm alive, I can eat and get around on my own, go to the toilet and have a shower – I can do all of that," Terry says.
Bilyi is equally convinced: "Life goes on. The main thing is that I'm alive."
Their service didn't end there. Less than a year after being wounded, Bilyi got a call from the company's senior sergeant, who offered him a new position. On 12 May, he rejoined the Khartiia Brigade. Terry later joined him.
The two former infantrymen began learning an entirely different role – they became ISTAR dispatchers at a command and observation post. Instead of going out on combat missions, they now monitor the battlefield through screens, work with reconnaissance personnel and drone operators, and pass on information about targets.
"If I sat at home, what would I do? At least this way I can help out here," Bilyi says.
For now, the Khartiia soldiers have no plans to return to civilian life.
Olena Barsukova

Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit

Germany has committed a comprehensive military and energy assistance package valued at more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukrinform, the newly allocated assistance package comprises roughly €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid focused on air defense, long-range strike capabilities, combat drones, and satellite communications, alongside approximately €350 million ($396 million) to reinforce Ukrainian power substations and emergency generation ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking during a joint press briefing in the capital, Zelensky stressed that the agreements combine emergency battlefield deliveries with sustainable industrial integration.
“There is a new support package for Ukraine – a comprehensive package of more than €1.3 billion,” Zelensky stated. “This is weapons that will help right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter – an important energy package. Naturally, we discussed the need for air defense, which is crucial at this time.”
In parallel with the emergency assistance, the two governments and corporate partners concluded 15 bilateral agreements and industrial documents valued at more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), focusing on long-term arms manufacturing, joint defense ventures on Ukrainian soil, and direct state orders for German industrial manufacturers.
Russia Launched 1,900 Drones and 25 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
“To date, we have 15 agreements and documents, and most of them concern security cooperation, manufacturing, corresponding procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine,” Zelensky said.
“The total weight of today’s agreements is more than €8.5 billion.”
Military breakdown, long-range systems, and winter energy aid
Details outlined by Chancellor Merz during the briefing confirmed that the €1 billion ($1.13 billion) military component prioritizes long-range standoff capabilities and advanced communications to allow Ukrainian forces to target Russian launch installations directly.
“We are launching another military support package worth around one billion euros,” Merz said, noting that Berlin will supply long-range strike weapons, combat drones, and satellite technologies.
“Regarding the details of the military support, I ask for understanding that we do not wish to disclose them in detail.”
Merz emphasized that German military assistance is concentrating on two foundational capabilities: expanding layered air defense and reinforcing space-based satellite communications to ensure Ukrainian units receive real-time operational data.
The chancellor added that German funding is accelerating serial assembly lines for newly developed interceptors engineered to neutralize jet-powered strike drones following recent technological breakthroughs.
Addressing the civilian heating sector, Merz announced approximately €350 million ($396 million) in targeted energy assistance to procure mobile generators, repair damaged electrical substations, and restore transmission infrastructure battered by Russian aerial strikes.
“We are facing what may be a very difficult winter. Moscow is deliberately targeting energy supply infrastructure – thermal power plants, substations, fuel stations, and railway infrastructure,” Merz said.
“The goal is entirely obvious: to break the morale of Ukrainians. Despite the attack that occurred this morning, I see here a determined people and a determined government.”
Industrial ventures and Berlin winter summit
A core component of the newly finalized accords is a dedicated bilateral agreement on joint counter-drone operations, established to counter Russia’s accelerating use of turbojet-powered loitering munitions against Ukrainian urban centers and power generation facilities.
The agreement aligns with Chancellor Merz’s pledge, announced upon his arrival in the capital, that Berlin intends to ensure the expedited transfer of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed specifically to defeat turbojet-powered Shahed drones directly from German production lines.
Merz traveled to Kyiv accompanied by German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche alongside a 10-member delegation of chief executives and senior managers representing Germany’s defense and energy industries.
The corporate representatives conducted working sessions with Ukrainian defense officials to advance collaborative assembly lines, technology transfers, and resilient industrial supply chains.
The industrial focus comes as German defense planners and corporate partners seek to deploy lower-cost interceptors capable of neutralizing fast-moving strike drones without depleting high-end surface-to-air missile stockpiles such as the IRIS-T or Patriot.
Looking ahead to multilateral diplomatic coordination, Merz announced that Germany intends to convene a high-level summit in Berlin this winter alongside France and the United Kingdom.
“Together with France and Great Britain, we want to hold a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin this winter, particularly to coordinate further assistance,” Merz confirmed, though specific calendar dates and formal agendas remain under development.
Academy of Sciences visit
Following their formal talks, Zelensky and Merz traveled together to inspect the site of a recent Russian drone strike on the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv.
The strike on the academic institution killed two people and injured seven others, causing severe structural damage to the historic scientific complex.
Zelensky stated that video records confirmed the facility was deliberately targeted by Russian loitering munitions, characterizing the strike as an intentional effort to destroy Ukrainian scientific infrastructure.
The joint inspection took place against the backdrop of recurrent air raid sirens and ongoing drone strikes across the capital on Sunday morning, which included a repeat strike that damaged the road deck of Kyiv’s North Bridge.
Zelensky commended the German chancellor for maintaining his itinerary and visiting the damaged research complex despite operational security warnings, describing the gesture as an important signal of personal and national solidarity from Berlin.
Merz’s visit follows statements delivered in Berlin on Sept. 29, in which the German leader identified territorial air defense as Ukraine’s “weakest point” ahead of the winter heating season, confirming that Germany is coordinating with EU partners to finalize additional military aid packages ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15–16.
