Iran urges UNESCO to help restore scientific infrastructure damaged in war
TEHRAN – The head of the National Committee for Management of Social Transformations (MOST) has called for UNESCO to play an effective role in safeguarding knowledge, ensuring uninterrupted access to learning, and rebuilding academic centers damaged during the US-Israeli imposed war against the country.
Highlighting the destructive impact of conflicts on educational institutions and human capacities, Seyyed Ziae Hashemi said the international community needs to pay close attention to these outcomes, IRNA reported.
The official made the remarks while addressing the extraordinary session of the Intergovernmental Council of MOST Program, which took place at UNESCO headquarters on October 1 in Paris; the official and the Secretary General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO, Hassan Fartousi, attended the session online.
Referring to the impacts of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and the damage inflicted on certain educational and scientific institutions, cultural heritage and civilian infrastructures, he called for UNESCO to utilize its capacities for rebuilding scientific and educational capacities, strengthening international cooperation, and supporting sustainable development.
“International responses must be tailored to the specific circumstances of each crisis, while simultaneously placing the fundamental principles of protecting human lives, safeguarding knowledge, and ensuring the continuity of learning at the heart of these efforts,” he added.
“The catastrophic dimensions of war in Gaza have inflicted irreparable damage on civilians, educational centers, cultural and scientific activities; the international bodies have to make it clear what they can do within the frameworks of BRIDGES and MOST to protect knowledge, sustain education and research,” he added.
The restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women was another issue raised by the official.
Fartousi, for his part, emphasized that science is not merely a driver of industry or technology, but an essential part of human life and a factor that enhances our understanding of the world. Access to knowledge, equal learning opportunities, and universal participation in research are fundamental rights in human society.
Referring to UNESCO’s approach to open science, he called for the establishment of specific mechanisms that prevents the monopolization of knowledge, ensure the free flow of knowledge, and strike a balance between supporting researchers and universal access to science.
Highlighting the challenges faced by researchers due to unilateral and coercive measures, the official noted that BRIDGES frame work needs to propose practical solutions to remove barriers to scientific cooperation, prevent concentration of knowledge and power, and consolidate the concept of knowledge as a shared heritage and asset of humanity.
The Intergovernmental Council (IGC) of the MOST Program was established by UNESCO Member States in 1994. It is composed of 35 Member States elected by the General Conference, whose representatives meet every two years to guide and oversee the planning and implementation of the MOST Program. The IGC defines the MOST Program’s broad priorities, reviews its activities and achievements, and helps strengthen the link between social and human sciences research and public policy.
Through its work, the IGC provides a platform for Member States to exchange on contemporary social transformations and to promote more inclusive, evidence-based policies aligned with national priorities.
Attacking universities is a “crossing of red lines”
In June, Minister of Science, Research and Technology, Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, said that attacking universities is a crossing of red lines, highlighting that many universities and educational centers in the country were targeted by the United States and Israel during the recent war.
When a university is targeted, in fact, one of the most authentic centers of culture and civilization is attacked, and the harm is directed at the entire scientific community of the world, msrt.ir quoted Simaei-Sarraf as saying.
The official made the remarks while addressing the tenth meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Education Ministers, which took place in Minsk, Belarus, on June 16. A delegation led by the science minister attended the meeting.
Elaborating on the US-Israeli military attacks on Iran, destruction, and assassinations of Iranian universities and scientists in the past year, he emphasized that universities should be safe havens for thought, dialogue, and hope, rather than victims of conflicts.
The official raised a question, asking participants, “Will the international community allow the most authentic centers of civilization to fall victim to violence?”, and urged the global scientific community and international organizations to adopt a clearer, more responsible, and decisive stance in defending the security of universities, scientists, and scientific centers.
Silence in the face of these aggressions will lead to constant violence against science and civilization, he added.

In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian fire engaged a modernized Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile system deployed near the settlement of Kuroshany. Russian Drone Strikes in Kherson and Chernihiv Injure 6
Ukrainian precision units also targeted Russian military telecommunications hubs deployed across three contested sectors in the Donetsk region, striking signal installations near the town of Hirnyk, the railway hub of Yasynuvata, and occupied Donetsk.
Concurrently in the occupied sector of the Luhansk region, Ukrainian long-range strikes hit military equipment repair and maintenance installations located in the vicinity of Vesela Tarasivka and the industrial center of Lysychansk.
Sustained campaign against rear logistics and air defense
The overnight operations mark the latest phase of a systematic Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian air defenses, drone infrastructure, and logistical chokepoints across occupied territories and adjacent Russian border regions.
On Oct. 2 and Oct. 3, Ukrainian forces conducted precision strikes against another drone preparation facility near Donetsk alongside a tactical military crossing over the Mokri Yaly River near Novoocheretuvate, severing a key supply conduit for Russian units in the southern Donetsk sector.
Across the border in Russia’s Belgorod region, Ukrainian strikes destroyed a Russian command post near Novaya Tavolzhanka and hit an equipment warehouse in Voznesenovka, while follow-on fire damaged a vehicle repair facility near Hromivka in occupied Kherson region.
Degrading Russian air surveillance and air defense batteries remains a central priority for Ukrainian long-range strike units.
In late September, Ukrainian forces conducted targeted strikes against two Russian mobile radar complexes in occupied Zaporizhzhia region, damaging an advanced 35N6 Kasta low-altitude detection radar near Chekhohrad and a Soviet-designed P-18 early-warning radar operating near Akymivka.

flydubai attacker may have shut down engines during 16,000-foot plunge, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:47:33 UTC
20:47:33 KST

At the height of the drama aboard the flydubai flight last Wednesday, after repeatedly striking the Indian captain, who used his remaining strength to activate the switch allowing the cockpit door to be opened, the Omani terrorist co-pilot realized his plan to crash the aircraft would fail. He then tried to bring the plane down in the Saudi desert, according to a new investigation by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera.
The report said the attacker disconnected the autopilot, took control of the aircraft and pushed the controls sharply forward. The plane lost 16,000 feet in less than a minute.
The investigation also raises a possibility not previously reported: that the attacker may have cut the fuel supply to the engines, effectively shutting them down.
Two captains who spoke with Corriere della Sera reached that conclusion after examining one of the videos documenting passengers’ efforts to stop the attacker. In the footage, emergency lights suddenly illuminate the passenger cabin, lighting designed to assist evacuation during an emergency or when an aircraft is on the ground. At cruising altitude, the report noted, they would not normally be activated.
According to the captains cited by the newspaper, those emergency lights can come on when a Boeing 737 loses its main electrical power source and switches to battery power. For that to happen, either the generators or the engines would have to be shut down.
Investigators will therefore need to determine whether the co-pilot moved the switches controlling fuel flow to the engines from the “Run” position to “Cutoff.”
Corriere della Sera said its investigation was based on passenger testimony, reports submitted to security authorities by the flight crew, accounts from people with knowledge of the incident, airport employees, air traffic controllers and data from several platforms. Videos recorded aboard the aircraft were analyzed by Boeing 737 captains who spoke with the newspaper.
Another detail disclosed in the report concerns the emergency code transmitted from the aircraft after additional pilots were summoned into the cockpit.
One of those pilots transmitted squawk code 7700, which signals a general emergency aboard a commercial aircraft without specifying the nature of the problem. Air traffic controllers initially did not understand what was happening.
Seven minutes later, the emergency code was changed to 7500, indicating suspected hijacking. By then, the aircraft was approaching Jordanian airspace, and controllers instructed it to turn back.
Seven minutes after that, air traffic control ordered the plane to continue to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, for an emergency landing.

MOSCOW, October 4. /TASS/. Seven leading OPEC+ countries adhering to voluntary oil production cuts - Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Oman, and Algeria - have decided to keep their existing oil production quotas unchanged in November, the organization said.

Australian law enforcement authorities have launched a broad security investigation into the country's links to Hamam al-Hamami, the copilot accused of trying to hijack and crash a flydubai aircraft bound for Israel, the BBC reported on Sunday.

The complex investigation is being carried out in cooperation with state police forces and the country's national security agency to trace his movements and activities in Australia.
The main focus of Australian counterterrorism officials, according to a report by ABC, is determining whether Hamami underwent ideological radicalization while in the country.
Sources familiar with the case said Hamam Hamami, identified as an Omani citizen, stayed in Australia on a student visa issued to him in 2014. He studied in the country from 2015 to 2017, when he left.
ABC also reported that authorities ultimately canceled his visa in 2019 after determining he was no longer enrolled in active academic studies and had failed to meet the conditions of his stay.
Hamami's identification as the copilot responsible for the attack was also reported by prominent international media outlets, including Reuters, CNN, and The New York Times.
The investigation into his past has taken on greater significance following the events of September 30. Hamami was arrested immediately after the emergency landing and is currently being questioned by Saudi authorities. On Saturday, the United Arab Emirates' attorney-general stated unequivocally that the incident constituted an attempted terrorist act.
Hamami's Australian connection and the apparent failure to prevent him from continuing his aviation career are now raising serious questions internationally, particularly following reports in US media that he had previously been removed from flight training with Oman Air because of substantiated concerns regarding his extremist views, but nevertheless later found his way back into the cockpit.
Hamami had over 2,000 social media posts showing his radicalization
A Telegraph investigation published on Sunday analyzed more than 2,000 posts from a social media account directly linked to Hamami, published between November 2021 and August 2022.
Using the name "Pilot Hamam al-Hamami," he described himself as a civilian pilot from Muscat and shared biographical details matching his known identity. His posts revealed a consistent and disturbing pattern of support for physical violence against women, homophobic violence, and sexual humiliation.
In one online exchange, Hamami wrote to a woman: "I would crush your head, wipe the floor with you, make an example of you so others would see and fear, and then divorce you."
In another post, he expressed support for Russia's invasion of Ukraine while linking it to a justification for violence against a woman. Responding to a discussion about a man who had hit a woman, the copilot wrote: "He gave her a preventive slap so she would redefine her boundaries, just as Russia slapped Ukraine to adjust its borders."
In the same discussion, he added that if a woman "even breathes" near the man, he should "crush her head."

Three questions Israelis must ask themselves before voting on October 27 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:44:04 UTC
20:44:04 KST

In preparation for the upcoming Israeli elections scheduled for October 27, I thought it would be worthwhile to ask the prime ministerial candidates whose chances at least put them in competition for the position what they see as the major problems facing Israel today and how they plan to address them.
One would think, of course, that providing this information to the electorate would be a given in any democratic society. However, in the polarized world in which we now live, politics seems to have been dumbed down to personal rather than ideological battles.
In an attempt to change the discourse, a colleague and I prepared an extensive questionnaire addressing three major subject areas: (a) how candidates structured their party lists and their associated campaigns; (b) what they perceive as the key challenges facing Israel; (c) their approaches to foreign policy issues, including reversing the effects of our having become a pariah state in the opinion of most of the world.
About six weeks ago, I sent the document in Hebrew to all the identified candidates except the current prime minister.
Sadly, but not unexpectedly, I received only one response, and that was from the Bennett/Lapid camp.
From the others, despite almost daily dispatches of my blogs and op-eds to all of them, nary a peep. Thankfully, I have thick skin and can handle rejection, although I’m not sure why they didn’t even offer the courtesy of a note saying they weren’t interested in responding.
Nevertheless, on September 29, I had an extended conversation with fellow Chicagoan Jeremy Saltan, an American-born Israeli political analyst, strategist, and former Knesset faction secretary, who is part of the B’Yachad party’s Knesset slate in the upcoming election. He was good enough to spend time with me by phone to discuss many of the points in the questionnaire.
As the reader can see the party’s entire platform at https://be-yahad.org.il/en/home-en, there is no need for me to repeat all of it here, but it can be summarized as follows:
Governance and institutional reform
Electoral reform: Imposing an eight-year term limit for the office of the prime minister. Constitution: Promoting a long-awaited constitution that will be rooted in two sections: (1) the Declaration of Independence as its preamble; and (2) a Basic Law: Legislation section clearly defining the process for the passing of, and judicial review of, Basic Laws, as well as the powers allocated to the three branches of government: executive, legislative, and judicial.
Educational reform: Recognition that the education system is broken and needs restructuring for the 21st century and beyond.
Starting salaries for teachers need to be raised, principals need to be given more autonomy, and the core curriculum (i.e., math, science, and English) needs to be taught in every school, including those in the haredi and Arab communities.
Further, expanding state-haredi (Mamlachti Haredi) schools that teach core subjects while allowing haredim to maintain their identity and way of life.
Sixty percent of the curriculum in all schools, including Mamlachti Haredi ones, will be composed of the common core subjects; 40% will be at the discretion of individual communities. Schools that don’t meet these requirements will not receive state funding.
State inquiry: Establish a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attack, to be launched on the new government’s first day.
National resilience: Fostering national unity, reducing political polarization, and restoring public trust in state institutions.
Civic duty and social policy
Universal conscription (“equality of burden”): Ensuring that all segments of society, including the ultra-Orthodox community, share the military, civic, and national service burden of the state.
For all sectors, receiving state benefits will depend on completing military or national service. The vision, when it comes to enlistment, education, and the workforce, is for all parts of society to be part of one shared Israeli story.
Cost of living: Prioritizing economic measures to lower both housing prices and the day-to-day cost of living, including slashing bureaucracy and import barriers, dismantling monopolies, and making it easier to build apartments and rent them long-term.
Security and foreign policy
An active security doctrine: Maintaining a firm, assertive security policy on all fronts, alongside deepening alliances with moderate elements in the region.
Conscripting the 20,000 soldiers that the IDF says it is short of today.
Declaring Qatar, with its present modus operandi, as an enemy state.
Zionist and democratic identity: Preserving Israel as a Jewish, democratic, and liberal state in the spirit of our founders.
Repairing Israel’s reputation: A full-court press to reestablish Israel’s diplomatic credibility worldwide, with special attention to strengthening ties with members of both political parties in the US, based on Naftali Bennett’s continued personal relationships with American politicians even after he ended his earlier term as prime minister.
For those specifically interested in the party’s slate, its list of candidates for the Knesset and associated biographies can be found here: https://be-yahad.org.il/en/team
Every voter can decide whether this is a platform with which he or she can identify. This is not an endorsement of any candidate but rather an effort to help all of us, the voting public, understand what issues the party in question sees as important.
But what of the others who did not respond? Do they not care enough to provide at least the basic data that every thinking voter should have access to?
Or is it that the English-speaking population here is perceived as unimportant? If that is an issue, it is easy to refute.
There are as many as 300,000 English-speaking voters in the electorate.
If they were to vote as a bloc, they would command seven Knesset seats.
While we don’t vote as a bloc, an abnormally high percentage of us do vote, so our influence is magnified beyond our absolute numbers.
It would certainly seem that we, along with the entire electorate, are owed a full exposition of the platform of every party that would like our vote.
October 27 will be a critical election, as it will decide what direction the country will take after a decade in which we experienced a mass health casualty event, three years of a seven-front war that continues, a year of seemingly nonstop demonstrations against judicial reform, which many saw as the end of democracy, and the emigration of 270,000 citizens (almost 3% of the population) in the last three years.
Any party that wants our votes needs to show that, at a minimum, it acknowledges the challenges it will face if elected and is prepared to meet them in the most productive way possible.
Those candidates who choose not to share their intentions simply do not deserve our votes.
The writer, a 42-year resident of Jerusalem, is a former national president of the Association of Americans and Canadians in Israel, a past chairman of the board of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and a board member of the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce.

Iran will not reopen Strait of Hormuz until its conditions from June are met, Ghalibaf says

The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until Iran meets seven conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday.
Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, with the US replying to this proposal last week via Qatari intermediaries.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met," Ghalibaf, who is Iran's top negotiator, was quoted as saying.
He said Washington "must understand that the period of dragging out the (diplomatic) process and dictating one-sided demands is over."
Iran says no nuclear discussions
An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had clarified its broad positions via mediators in response to the US, but that it still had additional points to communicate to Washington.
"The Americans' propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus in this stage is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and the return to security in this waterway requires clear steps from the US," Iran's Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.
He also denied Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its nuclear facilities in exchange for US sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions with Washington.
The circulated document outlines a seven-day trust-building period aimed at returning the two sides to an enhanced version of the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, including concrete steps on Iran's nuclear program, an official briefed on the talks said last week.
The disagreement centers on the sequencing of the steps rather than the components of the plan, the official added.
Warning from Araghchi
Qatar has been shuttling messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
The June memorandum of understanding led to a brief ceasefire and included provisions on the strait and Iran's nuclear program.
Separately, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran on Sunday that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy but warned that Iran was prepared to respond if the US again chose military action.
On Thursday, sources told Reuters that Iran was preparing a broader and more forceful response if Washington resumed large-scale military attacks.
“If they again move towards military solutions, we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves,” Araghchi said on Sunday.
Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news agency on Sunday that Iran would upgrade the range of its missiles.

IDF paratrooper Yosef Haguel, associated with famed 'Ballad for a Medic,' dies at 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:43:46 UTC
20:43:46 KST

Famed IDF paratrooper Yosef Haguel, who was associated with the song Balladah L’Hovesh (Ballad for a Medic), died on Saturday at the age of 80.
During the Six Day War, Haguel fought in Battalion 28 of the Paratroopers Brigade in the battle against the Jordanian Legion in east Jerusalem.
Haguel was seriously wounded in the battle, and the company medic, Shlomo Epstein, treated him under fire. When mortar shells were fired toward them, Epstein shielded Haguel with his body to protect him and was killed on the spot by a direct hit.
Epstein’s act of heroism inspired Yehoram Gaon to sing the song at the 1969 Israel Song Festival, where it won first place.
Who wrote 'Ballad for a Medic'?
The song was written by Dan Almagor and composed by Effi Netzer about 11 years before the Six Day War. It was reportedly not written about any specific incident, but resembled several real-life events.
Many bereaved parents found the song too sad to listen to, and asked that it not be played on the radio. Epstein’s parents eventually approached Netzer and asked him to help ensure that the song was not broadcast.
Despite this, Balladah L’Hovesh became one of Gaon’s most beloved songs, even though for several years it was not played on Israeli radio stations except on Remembrance Day.

Ofer Winter looked at the images from Jerusalem and was filled with anger. “I was appalled by that event,” the chairman of the Amcha Yisrael party said in an interview with ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. “It doesn’t represent ultra-Orthodox society, but it’s what makes the headlines and it’s the narrative dominating the public discourse. And he has a clear message for the ultra-Orthodox public.
“God willing, when I’m defense minister, this situation will change,” retired Brig. Gen. Winter pledged. “It’s time for the ultra-Orthodox to become a significant part of the IDF. Winter sees drafting ultra-Orthodox men into the IDF as his life’s mission.
“If we fail to significantly integrate ultra-Orthodox recruits into the military, I will have failed,” he said of a challenge that many capable people before him have tried to tackle. “I know the system. Winter believes he can succeed where all his predecessors failed. The controversy surrounding the ultra-Orthodox draft is, in his view, a symptom of the way the entire country is being run.
“Decisions aren’t made. There is no decisive action. To me, the most important word is ‘decisiveness.’ We’re still living under the same conception. “That may be why they’re afraid of us. Wherever Winter looks, he says, he sees restraint, weakness and a failure to achieve decisive results.

But that is precisely the ammunition being used in the “genocide” campaign against Israel around the world.
“We’re fighting in Gaza in an unintelligent way. The enemy in Gaza knew it couldn’t take on the IDF. So what did it do? It designed the entire fight around the urban environment to lure you into a trap so it could shout ‘genocide.’ Because the enemy knows that it isn’t the one that will stop you — the world will. And the world succeeded in stopping us. Listen to Netanyahu explaining to the world that we don’t kill civilians and that we take them into consideration. We fell into their trap.”
Shouting from the stands
Despite his criticism of government policy, Winter again reiterated his commitment that after the election his party will recommend Netanyahu for prime minister.
“We’re on the right, and to implement right-wing policies we have to be part of a right-wing government, period,” he explained. “We have no choice. Defeating the enemy and facilitating voluntary emigration from Gaza can only be achieved under a right-wing government. But we don’t want the same composition as the current government. The current government’s makeup is very bad for Israel. Another government like this must not be formed.”

EXPLAINER – How Bosnia elects its 3-member presidency and multiple parliaments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:38:35 UTC
20:38:35 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
Voters in Bosnia and Herzegovina headed to the polls Sunday to elect the country’s three-member presidency and representatives to a complex network of state, entity and cantonal institutions.
Around 3.4 million people are registered to vote in the general election, with polling stations scheduled to remain open from 7 am to 7 pm local time (0500 to 1700 GMT).
The vote is being held under the power-sharing system created by the Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
Here is how the electoral system works, who is seeking seats in the presidency and what is at stake.
 
How is Bosnia and Herzegovina governed?
Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of two largely autonomous entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.
The Federation is predominantly populated by Bosniaks and Croats, while Republika Srpska has a predominantly Serb population.
The country also includes the self-governing Brcko District, which formally belongs to both entities but operates under its own administration.
Each entity has its own government, parliament and extensive powers, while institutions at the state level are responsible for areas including foreign affairs, defense and international trade.
 
How is presidency elected?
Instead of a single president, Bosnia and Herzegovina has a three-member presidency comprising one Bosniak, one Croat and one Serb.
Voters registered in the Federation may vote for either the Bosniak or Croat member, but not both. Voters in Republika Srpska elect the Serb member.
The three members serve four-year terms and take turns chairing the presidency every eight months. Each member therefore serves as chair twice during a full term.
The system is intended to ensure that the three constituent peoples share power at the highest level of the state.
It also restricts voters’ choices according to their place of residence. Serbs living in the Federation cannot vote for the Serb member, while Bosniaks and Croats living in Republika Srpska cannot vote for their respective representatives.
Citizens who do not identify as one of the three constituent peoples are also excluded from standing for the presidency.
 
Who is running for Bosniak seat?
Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency, is seeking another term as the candidate of the Social Democratic Party.
Bakir Izetbegovic, leader of the Party of Democratic Action, is seeking to return to the presidency after previously serving two terms and losing to Becirovic in 2022.
Semir Efendic of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Fahrudin Radoncic of the Union for a Better Future are also contesting the Bosniak seat.
 
Who is running for Croat seat?
Darijana Filipovic is standing as the candidate of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
She faces Slaven Kovacevic of the Democratic Front and Zdenko Lucic, who is supported by a coalition of five Croat opposition parties.
 
Who is running for Serb seat?
Zeljka Cvijanovic, the incumbent Serb member of the presidency, is seeking a second term as the candidate of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats.
Her challengers are Marinko Bozovic of the Serb Democratic Party and Nebojsa Vukanovic of the List for Justice and Order.
 
What else are voters electing?
The election extends far beyond the presidency.
Voters are choosing members of the 42-seat House of Representatives, the directly elected chamber of the state parliament. Twenty-eight members are elected from the Federation and 14 from Republika Srpska.
The state parliament’s other chamber, the 15-member House of Peoples, is formed indirectly after the election and includes five Bosniak, five Croat and five Serb delegates.
Separate ballots are also being held for the parliaments of the Federation and Republika Srpska.
Voters in Republika Srpska are electing the entity’s president, while those in the Federation are choosing representatives to the assemblies of its 10 cantons.
In total, the election will help determine the composition of governments at the state, entity and cantonal levels.
Preliminary results are expected after polling stations close Sunday evening.

Sacred Sites of the Eastern Rhodopes: St John the Batist Monastery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:36:59 UTC
20:36:59 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
Article
Sacred Sites of the Eastern Rhodopes: St John the Batist Monastery
Sunday 4 October 2026 14:03
Sunday, 4 October 2026, 14:03
Saint John the Forerunner church in Kardzhali
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
Font size
Nestled in the heart of the Eastern Rhodopes, between the two banks of the Arda River, lies the southern Bulgarian city of Kardzhali. Its people bear different names, profess different faiths and follow different traditions. Yet, contrary to what one might expect, these differences do not divide them. Quite the opposite: diversity is one of the defining features of the region.
In a series of publications, Radio Bulgaria will introduce you to three of the sacred sites of the Eastern Rhodopes in Bulgaria: the Orthodox Church of St John the Baptist in Kardzhali, the wooden mosque near the village of Podkova, and the spiritual centre of Elmalý Baba Teke near the village of Bivolyane.
The first stop on our route is the medieval Church of St John the Forerunner, which once formed part of an important medieval monastic complex.
As soon as visitors enter the church, they are struck by the remarkable interplay of preserved medieval masonry, partially surviving frescoes and traces of later restoration. The sections of stonework and the surviving frescoes have been preserved in their original form. The church remains an active place of worship, while at the same time being a protected cultural heritage site, as our guide, Georgi Kyuchukov, explains:
Guide Lyubomir Kyuchukov
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
“Yoan Predtecha (John the Forerunner) was the name of the church in the Middle Ages as well. We know this thanks to an act of vandalism committed by a Bulgarian who visited the church at the time. Using a sharp instrument, he inscribed on one of the frescoes in Old Bulgarian: ‘I, Dobromir, wrote in the Holy Prodromos.’ This tells us that the man’s name was Dobromir, while the church in which he wrote was called ‘Prodromos’, a Greek word meaning ‘Forerunner’ or ‘Precursor’. This was one of the principal monasteries in the region of Ahridos, as the area corresponding to present-day Kardzhali was known in the Middle Ages.”
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
The monastery must have been a place of considerable importance in its day, and was probably quite wealthy as well, judging by the archaeological finds unearthed at the site. Several discoveries attest to the significance of this sacred foundation:
“The first was made in 1998, when restoration work on the monastery began,” Georgi Kyuchukov continues. “The people working inside came upon a tomb, probably that of the monastery’s founder. From the grave came the oldest ecclesiastical textile ever discovered in Europe. It is an epitrachelion, a liturgical vestment, embroidered entirely in gold. Most likely, it was the gold that enabled the textile to survive to the present day. The epitrachelion has been restored and will be displayed at the Historical Museum in Kardzhali once a display case with the appropriate climate-control conditions has been provided.
“Archaeologists estimate that such a burial would, at the time, have cost approximately as much as the construction of an entire medieval town.
The monastery complex "St John the Forerunner" in Kardzhali
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
“The second piece of evidence pointing to the importance of this monastery dates to 1206. That was the year when, for a brief period, the Byzantine Empire ceased to exist and the newly established Latin Empire took its place. In that same year, a campaign by Latin knights set out along the Arda River. Their objective was to relieve the knight Renier de Trit, who was besieged in the fortress of Stanimachos, present-day Asenovgrad, together with his troops. They were under siege by the Bulgarian forces of Tsar Kaloyan.
“Among those taking part in the campaign was the man who left us the greatest body of information about the history of the Latin Empire, Geoffrey of Villehardouin. He wrote: ‘Evening found us before the well-guarded castle of Monech.’ This is a fortress well known to lovers of scenic views in the Kardzhali area.
“According to these accounts, the Latin knights remained at the fortress for about a week. It was there that they received the news that their emperor, Baldwin, had been killed by the Bulgarian Tsar Kaloyan in Tarnovo. And it was in the vicinity of Monech, probably at the fortress of Vishegrad, which served as the administrative centre of the region, that the barons’ council convened. The council decided that the next emperor of the Latin Empire should be the leader of the campaign, Baldwin’s brother Henry.mnOf course, the coronation had to take place officially in Constantinople, which is why the campaign turned back in the opposite direction.
But the same Villehardouin describes a meeting between the newly elected Latin Emperor Henry and Boniface of Montferrat, King of Thessalonica, who had set out for the lands of Ahridos because, and this is the sentence that concerns us, he believed in the immeasurable riches of the monasteries here.”
Saint John the Forerunner monastery in Kardzhali
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
More fascinating stories about the medieval Monastery of St John the Baptist in Kardzhali can be discovered on site, in the church of the same name or at the city’s Historical Museum.
To conclude, it is worth noting that the old medieval church, restored between 1991 and 2001, now stands at the heart of a modern monastic complex, which includes a Sunday school and another church. The new church is called "Saint Sophia - Faith, Hope, Love".
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
From the beautiful courtyard of the monastery, a magnificent view opens out over the city and the so-called Water Mirror, a hydraulic engineering facility built to regulate the flow of the Arda River as it passes through Kardzhali.
View of Kardzhali from the yard of the Saint John the Forerunner monastery

Torrential rain and flooding leave 2 dead and 1 missing in Spain's Catalonia region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:36:00 UTC
20:36:00 KST

Spain floods: 2 dead as heavy rain hits Catalonia
October 4, 2026
Two people were reported dead on Sunday, with at least one person missing, after torrential rain triggered flooding in Spain's northeastern Catalonia region.
Authorities have warned of an "extreme danger" in parts of Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents in some areas urged to stay indoors.
What do we know about the victims?
One person died when a wall collapsed at a campsite in Tordera, north of Barcelona, while another drowned in a flooded garage in Montornes del Valles, Catalan firefighters said.
Emergency services were also searching for a missing person in Pineda de Mar, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) north of Barcelona.
Catalan regional leader Salvador Illa urged residents to exercise "the greatest caution" and follow instructions from emergency services.
How badly has Catalonia been hit?
More than 100 millimeters (3.9 inches) of rain fell overnight in numerous locations, according to Spain's AEMET weather agency.
Civil protection authorities sent alerts to people living near the Besos River warning of a risk of it bursting its banks. Residents were told to move to upper floors if flooding occurred.
Homes were flooded and vehicles submerged in towns near Barcelona, while local rail services were disrupted.
Emergency crews rescued people trapped in vehicles on flooded streets in Granollers and other communities.
Flights at Barcelona airport were also canceled or delayed, while shops closed early and sporting and cultural events were called off.
What is causing the extreme weather?
The storms are linked to a weather phenomenon known in Spain as a DANA, traditionally called a "gota fria," or "cold drop."
It occurs when cold air high in the atmosphere meets warm, moisture-laden air rising from the Mediterranean, producing intense thunderstorms.
Spain's geography can amplify the effect, as moist air from the Mediterranean is forced upwards by mountain ranges separating the coast from the country's elevated interior.
The latest flooding comes almost two years after catastrophic floods linked to a DANA killed 238 people in eastern Spain, mostly in Valencia, in October 2024.
A study published in 2026 found that human-caused climate change intensified the rainfall during that disaster.
The findings apply only to the 2024 Valencia floods, and a separate analysis would be needed to determine the influence of climate change on the latest flooding in Catalonia.

From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:30:00 EEST
20:30:00 KST

From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
2026 has been a year of victories great and small for the Ukrainian military, and the whole country has celebrated along with them.
Nazar Daletskyi, a serviceman believed to have been killed three years ago – a funeral had even been held for him – came home alive from captivity.
Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander in the 475th Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), single-handedly evacuated two wounded soldiers in a civilian pickup truck as Russian drones circled overhead.
The National Guard awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to a woman for the first time – machine gunner Oleksandra Davydenko.
Ukraine's defence forces in the south reclaimed up to 435 sq km of territory. The 3rd Army Corps stunned the public with the successful Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast.
Ahead of Defenders' Day, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) looks back to 10 of this year's most interesting stories about our defenders. Read them all – you won't regret it!
"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
"Eighteen", a company commander in the Special Operations Forces (SOF), would normally have been expected to coordinate the evacuation from the command post. But when four of his soldiers were no longer able to walk independently after a battle and an encounter with an improvised explosive device, he went into the area himself.
"The guys all had leg wounds. There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk," Eighteen recalls.
It took 15 hours to carry the most seriously wounded soldier, Malyi (Little One), to the medics. The young man had severe injuries to his arm and abdomen and a ruptured liver.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on," Eighteen says.
As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the doctors, Eighteen went back for the body of his fallen comrade, Sava. The rescue operation took five days in all, and the soldiers covered more than 50 km. All but Sava survived.
This remarkable operation proved once again that even in the era of ground robots, those who operate on their own two feet still have the decisive say in battle.
"I thought about tightening the tourniquets and bleeding to death so I wouldn't suffer": how a badly wounded infantryman hunted by six drones was rescued
Herodotus is a private first class in the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade. After 18 months fighting in an assault unit, he miraculously survived being hunted down by six Russian drones.
Herodotus was alone in a wooded area. He had already lost a foot, and as he was being evacuated, a Russian drone destroyed the ground robot and mangled his other leg.
He crawled, hid from FPV drones, and even played "cat and mouse" with one of them around a dugout, moving in such a way as to stay out of the Russians' line of sight. His comrades watched him from a drone throughout, dropping water, painkillers and food and trying to find a way to get him out.
Eventually three soldiers came to retrieve him and carried him for about 2.5 km. Herodotus lost both legs, but he survived. He says that in his darkest moments he remembered that he had promised his family he would return.
"There, look at what I've got now instead of legs. Ta-da! What am I supposed to do now – cry? It's already happened... I'm alive, so everything should be all right. Life can be a complete pile of shit sometimes, but we'll get through it," he says cheerily.
"We accepted that we were going to die": the military anaesthesiologist who volunteered to go to the besieged Azovstal steelworks
In spring 2022, military anaesthetist Oleksandr Demchenko volunteered to fly to the besieged Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol by helicopter. He realised that it could be a one-way trip. He later learned that the helicopter was shot down on its return journey.
At Azovstal, Oleksandr operated on wounded soldiers in an underground hospital, in cold and damp conditions and with a dwindling supply of medicines: even amputations had to be performed under local anaesthetic.
After one airstrike, five floors of the building above the medics collapsed while hundreds of people were inside.
"We all accepted that we were going to die there, because, essentially, there were no other options," Oleksandr recalls. But he was lucky – he made it out of there.
He survived Azovstal, Russian captivity and the Olenivka prison camp. When he returned home, he went back to medicine.
"I returned to the profession because I love it. I genuinely love my work," he admits.
"I'd serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this": the nurse who swapped her uniform for combat fatigues
Before joining the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Tamila had worked as a nurse at a district hospital for 15 years. Then she swapped her uniform for combat fatigues, eventually becoming head of the medical station of the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade.
In autumn 2022, when the brigade was conducting a counteroffensive in Kherson Oblast, Tamila was constantly going out to evacuate the wounded.
"I provided first aid in the vehicle. I had to stop the bleeding from severed arms and legs, apply tourniquets and administer painkillers. The brigade was carrying out assault operations, and guys were dying both on the battlefield and in front of me," she recalls.
Once, two years later, she happened to meet a soldier whom she had once evacuated with a severed arm. He recognised her first: "You were the one who evacuated me back then. Thank you."
Tamila's first contract ended long ago and she could have left the military, but she stayed. She still goes out on evacuations sometimes, even though her current position does not require her to.
She says she is ready to serve for as long as necessary, as long as her 16-year-old son never has to follow in her footsteps.
"I've been in the Armed Forces of Ukraine for six years now, and they haven't been easy years for me – they've been really hard. Because war is the worst nightmare there can be. But I'm ready to serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this, as long as he never has to fight," Tamila admits.
"Several times we had enemy infantry jumping into our trenches": the company commander who spent 343 consecutive days on the front line
Three hundred and forty-three days is enough time to celebrate Christmas, New Year and Easter. But for company commander Oleksii, aka Botanik (Nerd), it was the length of time he spent at positions on the Orikhiv front without rotation.
About half of the soldiers in Botanik's company are over 50, and many suffer from chronic health problems. This makes normal rotations almost impossible, so they have to remain on the line of contact for long periods.
Oleksii's longest combat deployment took place in June 2025. The Russians would attack the Ukrainian positions using infantry fighting vehicles, motorcycles and quad bikes and on foot. When they managed to reach the trenches, machine gunners and drone operators would join the fighting. Evacuation crews collected the wounded under fire.
"I tried to make the fighters' time at the combat positions as bearable as possible. I made sure everyone had a chance to talk to their families every day – that helps a lot," the company commander says.
Oleksii finally left the line of contact on 8 March 2026 and immediately went on leave to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday. Then it was back to the front line.
"I see my primary role as a commander as minimising personnel losses – ideally ensuring there are none at all," he says.
Pastry chef by day, air defence operator by night: the woman from Bucha shooting down Russian drones
Liudmyla, from Bucha, isn't your typical volunteer. By day she makes exquisite cakes and pastries, but after dark, she protects the skies over Kyiv Oblast.
It all began in 2024, when an acquaintance told Liudmyla about the Bucha Witches – a women's unit of mobile air-defence fire groups established as part of the Bucha Volunteer Formation of the Territorial Community. Liudmyla couldn't stand idly by.
The first time she shot down a Russian Shahed drone, the adrenaline rush was overwhelming. Two years ago she knew almost nothing about the military – now she commands a mobile fire group.
Liudmyla does all this as a volunteer and receives no pay. After a night shift, she returns home, puts down her weapon, and gets back to making cakes.
"It can be difficult at times – exhausting night shifts and winter cold when your hands quite literally freeze to the machine gun – but I love this work. Now I see safety in a completely different way and always silently thank those who protect my sleep when I am off duty," the defender says.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
In March 2022, urological surgeon Dmytro Hetmanov was operating on wounded civilians in besieged Mariupol. The hardest moment came when a father carried in his wounded teenage son. The injury looked minor from the outside, but the boy's heart and blood vessels had been virtually torn apart. The boy could not be saved.
On 16 March, Dmytro decided to try to escape the city with his parents and neighbours. On the way, he saw the bombed-out Drama Theatre still smouldering. It took him a long time to get through the Russian checkpoints.
Two years later, Dmytro was working as a surgeon at the University Hospital in Katowice, Poland. He had a job and his life was gradually getting back on track, but thoughts of his homeland never left him.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life," he admitted.
Dmytro resigned and left Poland to return to Ukraine. He completed basic military training, signed a contract and joined the Unmanned Systems Forces. Six months later, he realised that he was missing surgery.
Now Dmytro is serving as a surgeon once again, this time with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. He deals with combat injuries, assists with amputations, and has even tried his hand at neurosurgery for the first time.
Although Dmytro's daughter lives in the United States and rarely sees her dad, he does not regret his decision to join the military.
"They actually listed me among the dead": Azov fighter Web on the Olenivka terrorist attack and rehabilitation after three years in captivity
Dmytro "Web" Tishchenko was listed among the dead after the Russian terrorist attack on the Olenivka prison camp. When he came to, he was lying in a pile of metal and concrete, with a punctured lung and a bleeding arm. He crawled out of the destroyed barracks by himself.
"We asked the Russians for at least some medical supplies, but all they brought us was a bag of army sheets. We tore the fabric into pieces and used them to dress our wounds," the Azov fighter recalls.
When he was finally taken to hospital, one of the Russians was surprised to hear his name called out: "You're alive? I'd already got a body bag ready for you."
Web was only 21 at the time of the terrorist attack on Olenivka. He became a soldier at 18, took part in the defence of Mariupol, was wounded in the leg, made it to Azovstal, and from there he was taken into Russian captivity.
Dmytro spent another two months in hospital after the attack, and then he was moved from one penal colony to another. He had to endure torture, cold, hunger, and being made to stand for hours on end.
Because of a shrapnel wound, his leg became so badly infected that the wound simply opened up. In order to be admitted to hospital and avoid losing the limb, he had to pretend to faint.
Dmytro spent almost three years in captivity. In April 2025, he was suddenly taken out of his cell, given clean clothes and driven to an unknown destination. It was a prisoner swap. Web came home on the eve of Easter – exactly when he had dreamed of returning.
Now Web is undergoing treatment for his injuries and the effects of captivity, while also helping other young soldiers who have returned from Russian captivity.
"Sometimes I forget I'm missing a leg": two Khartiia infantrymen who've returned to service after suffering severe injuries
Assault trooper "Bilyi" stepped on a mine 15-20 metres from his position. He applied a tourniquet himself and waited to be evacuated, but the team that set off to retrieve him was attacked by a drone. When dawn broke, he realised that help might not come in time, so he started crawling on his own.
Bilyi crawled for nearly a whole day before two reconnaissance soldiers found him. By then the tourniquet had been on his leg for about two days. Bilyi had realised immediately after the explosion that his leg would have to be amputated.
"Terry" went through a similar ordeal. During his third combat deployment, he stepped on a petal mine hidden in the grass.
"It didn't hurt, I didn't lose consciousness. I opened my eyes and saw these toes lying around. Only the heel was left. I thought, 'That's it. I've had my run,'" Terry recalls.
It took 25 hours to evacuate him. Along the way, the wounded man and the soldiers carrying him were pursued by Russian FPV drones. One drone missed them, but another exploded near the group, injuring all three of the soldiers who were carrying Terry. Despite their own injuries, however, they managed to carry him to shelter.
Both Terry and Bilyi had their legs amputated. Months of surgery, rehabilitation and prosthetic fittings lay ahead of them. Terry recalls that after receiving a temporary prosthesis, he started walking the very next day and soon left his crutches behind. Bilyi was also quick to learn how to use his prosthesis.
"After they cut off my leg, there were moments when I felt a bit down. Then I'd lie there and think: it's all good. I'm alive, I can eat and get around on my own, go to the toilet and have a shower – I can do all of that," Terry says.
Bilyi is equally convinced: "Life goes on. The main thing is that I'm alive."
Their service didn't end there. Less than a year after being wounded, Bilyi got a call from the company's senior sergeant, who offered him a new position. On 12 May, he rejoined the Khartiia Brigade. Terry later joined him.
The two former infantrymen began learning an entirely different role – they became ISTAR dispatchers at a command and observation post. Instead of going out on combat missions, they now monitor the battlefield through screens, work with reconnaissance personnel and drone operators, and pass on information about targets.
"If I sat at home, what would I do? At least this way I can help out here," Bilyi says.
For now, the Khartiia soldiers have no plans to return to civilian life.

Voting in Brazil's 2026 presidential election has begun, with polls showing Lula and Bolsonaro nearly tied

Brazil votes in tight election between Lula and Bolsonaro
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026
Voting began in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeking a fourth non-consecutive term and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro seeking to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro.
Polls have predicted a tight race between the two leading candidates, with neither likely to win more than 50% of the vote to avoid a runoff that would take place on October 25.
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.
Lula vows to 'defeat the far-right'
The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."
Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.
Bolsonaro calls for 'change'
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.
The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
Brazil's 2022 election rematch
The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.
Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."
What happens next?
Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.
In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.
The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.
In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

Iran's team wins Intl. Olympiad on Astronomy, Astrophysics

Ukraine’s Science Under Fire: Russia Is Targeting Knowledge, People and the Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

Russia’s war in Ukraine has another dimension that is often overshadowed by daily reports of missile and drone attacks: the systematic destruction of Ukraine’s scientific infrastructure and human potential.
On Sept. 28, 2026, a Russian strike damaged the historic building of the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in central Kyiv. People were killed, wounded and reported missing. The deaths of scientist Valerii Kotenko and Natalia Bukalo, assistant to the academician Volodymyr Horbulin, were later confirmed. Horbulin himself was injured.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As of Oct. 1, 2026, at least 180 Ukrainian scientists killed during the Russian-Ukrainian war had been recorded in the public database of the “My Science” project. The list includes researchers, university lecturers, engineers and graduate students who died either at the front or as a result of Russian attacks.
“It’s frightening”
On the same day that Russia struck the science academy in Kyiv, a Russian attack also damaged the Dobrobut medical center on Antonovycha Street in Kyiv. The upper floors of the building, where the Dobrobut Academy operates, caught fire.
Nana Voitenko, a neuroscientist and rector of the Dobrobut Academy, wrote on Facebook after the attack:
“It’s frightening, but not fatal. We will rebuild. Education will not stop. We will partially move it online and partially to other locations.”
Kulbergs’ Pro-Ukraine Party Wins Latvian Election
For Voitenko, whose research focuses on the functions of the brain and nervous system at the molecular and cellular levels, continuing to work during the war is both a scientific and educational challenge. After the building was damaged, she took responsibility for maintaining the academy’s educational process while continuing her own research and supporting international partnerships.
Damage to nuclear research institute
According to the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, at 6:18 p.m. Kyiv time on Sept. 30, 2026, a Russian drone struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research, where Kyiv’s VVR-M research reactor is located.
The attack caused a fire, which was quickly extinguished. No one was injured. Investigators are conducting an investigation and assessing the damage.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine described the incident as an attack on a “peaceful nuclear facility that performs exclusively scientific and research functions.”
“[It] is yet another cynical disregard by Russia for internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety, as well as a war crime,” the regulator said.
Ukrainian science communicator, scientist and volunteer Anton Senenko wrote on Facebook after the Sept. 28 attack that Russia is doing so “because [it] can.”
“Today [Sept. 28, 2026] Russia has proved that science does not exist outside politics. Russian scientists are developing methods and technologies every day that allow them to kill Ukrainians as effectively as possible. Including their Ukrainian colleagues,” Senenko said.
“More than one scientific institute has already been destroyed. The strike on the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences is simply a signal: ‘We are killing everyone because we can.’ Sanctions against Russian science must be strengthened and expanded. There is a peaceful atom, but there is no peaceful Russian science,” he added.
Interrupting years of scientific research
Russian strikes are destroying laboratories, scientific equipment, unique collections and research environments built over decades.
On the night of July 2, 2026, a Russian drone attack caused significant damage to the O. V. Palladin Institute of Biochemistry of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in central Kyiv. One of the laboratory buildings sustained extensive damage. Its roof was destroyed and a fire broke out.
The flames, blast wave and water used to extinguish the fire damaged laboratories, equipment, reagents and biological collections.
Such attacks disrupt research that cannot simply be restarted by replacing a damaged building. They interrupt years of work by scientific teams and schools that have developed over decades, bringing together researchers of different generations, students, international partnerships, accumulated knowledge and expertise.
Yet Ukrainian scientists are already demonstrating that even a destroyed laboratory does not necessarily mean the end of scientific work.
The laboratory of Valeriia Trusova, a biophysicist, Doctor of Physical and Mathematical Sciences and professor at the Physics and Technology Faculty of V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University, was completely burned down in the first weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Trusova had been working with leading scientists around the world on major challenges in human health. Like hundreds of her colleagues across Ukraine, however, she continues to live and work in the country.
She continues her research and teaching in Kharkiv.
Science as part of Ukraine’s defense capacity
Following the strike on the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Anton Senenko pointed out that modern warfare increasingly depends on science and technology.
“Only knowledge and technology can provide a qualitative advantage, inflict maximum damage or, conversely, save lives,” he said.
Modern defense industries rely on both fundamental and applied research – physics, mathematics, materials science, chemistry, electronics, engineering and programming. Ukraine has strong scientific schools in all these fields.
Despite the destruction, Ukrainian scientists continue to work. Their resilience is already part of Ukraine’s wartime response.
But preserving that capacity will require more than resilience alone. It will require protecting researchers, rebuilding scientific infrastructure, replacing destroyed equipment and maintaining the conditions in which Ukrainian science can continue to generate knowledge – and turn it into the technologies and solutions the country needs to survive, defend itself, rebuild and shape its own future.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend a meeting in Riyadh on Monday of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee established under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, an alliance founded in August with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Türkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, National Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu will also attend the committee meeting in the Saudi capital.
At the meeting, Fidan is expected to share Türkiye's views on the institutionalisation of the alliance and steps to be taken in the coming days, as well as assessments of threats to peace and stability in the Middle East.
Fidan is also expected to express Türkiye's views on regional developments concerning the allies' collective security and note that the progress achieved in the alliance's work in the short time since it was founded is valuable from the perspective of establishing lasting stability in the region.
Solidarity with Saudi Arabia
The top Turkish diplomat is expected to reaffirm Türkiye's strong solidarity with and support for Saudi Arabia in the face of recent Houthi attacks and underline that provocative actions targeting holy sites are unacceptable.
Fidan is also expected to highlight the alliance's importance not only in developing a joint and effective response to existing threats but also in preventing regional crises.
He is set to stress that resolving disputes in the region through peaceful means remains a priority and that actions that could further escalate tensions should be avoided.
Fidan is also expected to reiterate the importance of ensuring freedom and security of navigation along international trade routes and draw attention to Israel's continued targeting of efforts to establish peace and stability in the region.
Mecca agreement for joint defence
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in Mecca on August 7.
The agreement reflects Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia's commitments to developing regional solutions to regional problems and their shared strategic vision focused on regional security and stability.
It aims to strengthen the security of the three countries through collective deterrence and defence.
A Strategic Political and Defence Committee made up of the foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of General Staff of the three countries was established to guide activities under the agreement.
The committee held its first meeting in Istanbul on August 31, hosted by Türkiye.
Foundational decisions were taken at the meeting, and technical work towards institutionalising the alliance was reviewed, including establishing the alliance's secretariat in Riyadh as soon as possible.
Retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood was nominated to serve as the alliance’s first secretary-general.

Brazilians began voting Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, ideological opposites who are each seen as having a shot at an outright victory.
