Bombs instead of ballots: How political terror took root in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:17:42 UTC
20:17:42 KST

Bombs instead of ballots: How political terror took root in Russia
Public thought in the Russian Empire was always inclined toward radicalism. Much like France, which had been shaken by revolutions since the late 18th century, Russia faced armed political violence for a prolonged period. In itself, there was nothing unique about the confrontation between the government and radicals. However, the activity, energy, ingenuity, and resilience of terrorist groups in Russia was unprecedented. Of course, Russian terrorists were not the first radicals in the world – consider the actions of Giuseppe Fieschi, who attempted to assassinate French King Louis Philippe I using a multi-barrel volley gun, or the Gunpowder Plot in Great Britain. However, in Russia, some underground movements persisted for decades, surviving various times and switching their political identity. Terrorists emerged in Russia during the era of Emperor Alexander II’s Great Reforms, and Alexander II himself fell prey to them. The entire history of the late Russian Empire unfolded in the shadow of the bomb.
The revolutionary movement in Russia was multifaceted and complex, and terrorism was merely a part of it. The terrorists were, of course, revolutionaries; but revolutionaries weren’t always terrorists. For example, Vladimir Lenin viewed terrorism with skepticism. The phrase attributed to him, “We shall take a different path,” became cliché in the Russian language, but hardly anyone remembers the context in which it was originally spoken. Lenin’s main idea was that a small, underground organization would not succeed, unlike a mass-based insurgent movement.
Today, however, we will speak of those who intended to bring down the empire using only bombs and revolvers.
The flip side of reforms
The initial actions of the terrorist movement gave the impression of an uprising in a madhouse.
Revolutionary terror in Russia emerged as an unexpected side effect of Alexander II’s Great Reforms. The Emperor had inherited the throne from his father – the hardline conservative Nicholas I, a man viewed as a martinet who tried to rule the country as if it were an infantry platoon. Convinced that Russia needed to be dragged out of its archaic state, Alexander launched sweeping reforms.
From his accession to the throne in 1855 until his assassination in 1881, the new Emperor continuously introduced changes that transformed the face of Russia almost beyond recognition. The Emancipation Reform granted freedom to millions of serfs whose condition was not much better than slavery. While this was his most famous reform, it was far from the only one. He reformed everything from the judicial system and military to local self-government and the legal code. Several monarchs in Russian history are known as ‘the Great’, but only one – Alexander II – is known as ‘the Liberator’.
From a broad perspective, the reforms were brilliant. But upon closer inspection, the situation was more complex. Alexander strove to cushion the inevitable shock experienced by a society undergoing such rapid change. While they were noble in intent, the reforms had many unpleasant side effects when put into practice.
For instance, Alexander sought to mitigate the impact of the sudden financial ruin of the landed aristocracy, who could no longer rely on the forced labor of the peasantry. Even after gaining personal freedom, peasants were required to make ‘redemption payments’ to the state (in installments) for the land allotments they received; the state, in turn, compensated landowners for the loss of their serfs. This imposed a heavy additional tax burden on the peasantry; meanwhile, the aristocrats (many of whom were not the smartest individuals) often squandered the money received from the government. Moreover, the nobility retained the best land, though it was now cultivated by hired laborers and tenant farmers rather than serfs.
Many of the social consequences of the reforms were unpleasant. For example, some impoverished nobles turned to crime. Cities saw a surge in prostitution driven by peasant women who had formerly been the mistresses of provincial landowners; this caught the police completely off guard. In short, even a reform as beneficial as the emancipation of the serfs had a wide range of unexpected consequences.
Some viewed the reforms as too drastic, while others considered them insufficient. For a long time, Alexander left the structure of the highest government bodies untouched. He remained the absolute monarch, and his word was law. He didn’t introduce anything resembling a parliament, and there was no constitution. Freedom of the press was also severely restricted by censorship.
It was only a matter of time before radicals emerged.
Freaks against the Empire
‘Raznochintsy’ (people of miscellaneous ranks) were the primary social base of the revolutionary movement. These individuals were neither nobles, merchants, nor peasants; they made their own living and were not in state service.
Usually, they were poor but rather well-educated – and often highly ambitious. A famous example is Rodion Raskolnikov from Dostoevsky’s novel ‘Crime and Punishment’. Another source of recruits for revolutionary circles was the impoverished nobility. Legitimate discussion groups were severely restricted at the time; consequently, would-be terrorists gathered at illicit meetings, lending their groups the aura of secret societies.
Some of these societies were quite harmless – essentially nothing more than ordinary, small discussion clubs. Others, however, embraced a bloodthirsty idealism. They championed utopian socialism as their social ideal, viewing mass uprisings as the means to achieve it. Yet they ran up against a dismal reality: Amid the emancipation from serfdom and rapid urban growth, the vast majority of Russian people were concerned with things like property, money, social standing, and in urban areas, education as a means of achieving social status.
But then, in 1866, an event occurred that foreshadowed ominous and dark times.
Dmitry Karakozov was a typical young man of the reform era. Born into a family of the petty nobility, he lacked financial means; after completing two years of university, he was expelled from the law department for being unable to pay his tuition. He worked as a low-level clerk with no career prospects, and enjoyed attending meetings organized by his cousin, who founded an organization aptly called ‘Hell’. People of similar social standing gathered there to discuss the textbook demands of young Russian radicals: the need to build schools and hospitals, educate the peasantry, and… assassinate the Tsar.
The last point was discussed very vigorously, but it was pure fantasy: The group fantasized about a clandestine terrorist organization with its own far-reaching intelligence network. Yet Karakozov turned out to be the only member of the group who took this ‘Dungeons & Emperors’ role-playing game seriously. At a certain point, he decided that there was no reason to wait any longer, bought a revolver, and set out to assassinate the emperor.
Security measures at the time were archaic. Emperor Alexander often walked the streets of St. Petersburg without any security. One can still stroll through the Summer Garden where Karakozov fired his shot. The place hasn’t changed much. Karakozov fired at the emperor but missed and was seized on the spot. Alexander was utterly astonished and thought the man was simply insane. Karakozov was hanged. The police arrested the entire underground group. In theory, they were all fierce radicals, but when one person took their blather at face value, they were no more prepared for it than for an invasion by Martians. Some members of the group were exiled to Siberia. Furthermore, censors closed down the publications read by Karakozov, deeming them politically unreliable. Even fellow revolutionaries were unimpressed by Karakozov’s actions. As for the peasants, they didn’t get why anyone would champion their cause in this manner. Of course, land was important, and redemption payments were burdensome – but what did shooting the Tsar have to do with it?
However, others soon followed in Karakozov’s footsteps. While Karakozov was from the impoverished nobility, another terrorist, Sergey Nechaev, was from a very different background. He was born into a destitute family that sacrificed everything to ensure that he received an education. Nechaev was a course auditor at the university. But he wasn’t just preoccupied with taking lecture notes; he drafted a document that served as a sort of charter for the revolutionary sect. It demanded total self-abnegation and absolute fanaticism from the revolutionaries. Nechaev’s writings abound with terms such as ‘annihilation’ and ‘extermination’. He meticulously compiled a list of individuals who had to be killed for the triumph of revolutionary socialism – some of them right away, others later; his planning would have impressed even the likes of Arya Stark.
While recruiting followers, Nechaev portrayed himself as the leader of a powerful underground movement, but this was a complete fabrication. He found a few people willing to listen to his misanthropic nonsense, but the organization was short-lived. When a student named Ivan Ivanov objected to one of Nechaev’s ‘brilliant’ ideas, Nechaev and a couple of friends lured him to a secluded spot and murdered him. Nechaev died in prison, and the story inspired Dostoevsky’s masterpiece, the novel ‘Demons’, which is based on the story of Nechaev and his group.
Aristocrats in the village
Nechaev and Karakozov had quite a few followers. For the time being, they set aside the idea of assassinating the emperor. Instead, a new concept took hold within the circles of young radicals. Many of them were decent people who sincerely sympathized with the common folk – people who worked relentlessly yet lived in poverty. From the desire to help and a sense of guilt toward those less educated and more burdened by life’s hardships emerged the ‘Going to the People’ populist movement. Initially, the main idea was for the activists (propagandists) to move to rural areas disguised as peasants and agitate for a general uprising.
Activists who attempted to spread the propaganda among urban workers (these were often peasants who had recently migrated to the cities) weren’t received well. However, they soon shifted to a more sensible approach: teaching workers literacy and skilled trades, and establishing mutual aid funds. In short, they ended up organizing a humanitarian initiative which had little to do with the revolution. The majority of the propagandists, however, headed for rural areas as planned; certain liberal-minded landowners allowed them to get started on their estates.
It is surprising that Russian TV has never produced a series based on this story. Young nobles and ‘raznochintsy’ would try to pass themselves off as peasants, traveling to villages and fairs to agitate for an uprising. They usually wrote their own propaganda literature, attempting to mimic the style of folk tales. Initially, their strategy resembled network marketing: If each agitator could recruit three peasants per month, and each peasant could recruit three others, at that rate, a nationwide uprising could be launched within a couple of years.
In practice, however, the speech, daily habits, and behavior of the propagandists bore no resemblance to those of actual peasants. Sure, the peasants disliked the flaws of the reforms. But the masquerade raised obvious questions, like: Who is this guy who claims to be a farmer but doesn’t know how to handle a scythe? Many of the revolutionaries looked like they had robbed a costume shop and were dressed as shepherds from a play.
Even when the revolutionaries spoke bluntly, the peasants had many questions. “Fine,” they said, “suppose we overthrow the Tsar and redistribute the landowners’ wealth. But if we rob them, what’s going to stop someone else from robbing us the same way?” The unfailing common sense of the peasants stupefied the propagandists.
And when the populists encountered Old Believers – adherents of an ultra-conservative branch of the Orthodox Church – things went even worse. For the Old Believers, continuous labor and Bible study were the highest good; consequently, they were prosperous and did not consider themselves oppressed. As for the atheistic propaganda, it was best not even to broach the subject with them.
Quite a few young revolutionaries, however, found themselves unexpectedly fond of the common people. Some even settled in the villages and – dropping all pretense – began working as doctors, teachers, veterinarians, or even blacksmiths and locksmiths. And they unexpectedly found themselves showered with people’s affection. They made many friends and settled in rural areas; in the country, a skilled doctor was treated almost like a local saint. The ‘downside’, of course, was that these individuals often lost their revolutionary zeal.
However, many of those who had ‘gone to the people’ returned to the cities with a new mindset.
Justice on the side of the terrorists
Meanwhile, darker moods were brewing within the revolutionary movement. Those who had been overzealous in spreading revolutionary propaganda were arrested and imprisoned. Among those who evaded the police was a young woman named Vera Zasulich. Her background was typical for a revolutionary: She came from an impoverished noble family, had a good education, an unprestigious job with no career prospects, and was infatuated with radical ideas.
In 1877, Dmitry Trepov, the governor-general of St. Petersburg, ordered a propagandist named Bogolyubov to be flogged for refusing to remove his hat in the presence of the official. Corporal punishment had been abolished, making Trepov’s action illegal; the incident caused a public outcry but was swept under the rug.
Feeling outraged by the injustice, Vera Zasulich bought a revolver (which was legal), secured an appointment with Trepov, and shot him. He was critically wounded but survived, and Zasulich was put on trial.
However, no one could have foreseen what happened in the courtroom. Trepov had behaved abominably, and it was foolish to shield him. But the government assumed that, in the eyes of the jury, the attempted murder would overshadow Trepov’s abuse of power. That might well have happened. However, the prosecution, convinced that the verdict was already in the bag, handled the case in a sloppy, incompetent manner.
Meanwhile, the defense attorney, Pyotr Alexandrov, played his hand brilliantly. He stressed the point that Trepov embodied brute, unpunished force, and this compelled Zasulich to act the way she did.
There was certainly an element of manipulation in his speech, but this was natural for a defense attorney doing his job. The prosecution, on the other hand, failed to do their job. Aleksandr Koni, the presiding judge – a highly experienced and respected jurist – shrugged off attempts to coerce him into playing along with the prosecution, implying that he was an honest judge who would not rig the proceedings merely because the outcome might displease the government. If the prosecution wants to win the case, it should handle it better!
And so, to thunderous applause, Vera Zasulich walked free from the courtroom, acquitted of all charges. From our standpoint, it is difficult not to have mixed feelings about her acquittal: After all, she had attempted murder. Yet the Russian Empire was governed by the rule of law to such an extent that, in a trial concerning a terrorist act, a jury could acquit the defendant and the government would comply.
‘Let justice be done, though the heavens fall’, the Latin legal maxim goes. Justice was done. And soon enough, the heavens did fall.
Radicals raise their heads
The government soon had to deal with the Zemlya i Volya (Land and Liberty) organization – the first truly radical group (from which another group, Narodnaya Volya, soon emerged, that directly carried out assassinations). The members of this group retained the frenzied fanaticism of Nechaev and Karakozov but were far more pragmatic. While they envisioned the same ideals of collectivism and socialism, they believed that the growth of the bourgeoisie and ongoing reforms might render a revolution unnecessary; consequently, they felt they had to act fast. A key tenet of their program was the “extermination of the most harmful or prominent figures within the government and, in general, the individuals who uphold the order we loathe.” The Going to the People movement had left them disillusioned, yet they chose to alter their tactics rather than the underlying concept.
Sergey Kravchinsky – one of the first propagandists of the Going to the People movement – stabbed the chief of the Gendarme Corps (the political police), Mezentsev, to death. A wave of attacks on officials ensued. These assaults typically involved revolvers or daggers: After delivering a couple of shots or blows, the terrorist would quickly flee, vanishing in the alleyways.
Many of these new terrorists had met during the Going to the People campaign and now formed fully fledged militant cells. Their numbers were small; the entire terrorist underground likely numbered no more than a few hundred people – including everyone who provided the slightest assistance. As to those who were directly prepared to carry out terrorist acts, there were only a few dozen people. Yet the Russian Empire lacked any counter-terrorism service; the police had no understanding of counter-terrorism, and top officials were quite negligent about their own security.
Here’s an example. In April 1879, Emperor Alexander II was taking a walk through St. Petersburg, accompanied by only one officer armed with a saber.
Near Palace Square, Aleksandr Solovyov (a member of the Land and Liberty movement) stepped out to confront him. The group’s previous assassination attempt had failed because the bullets had lodged in the bulky fur coat of the prosecutor who was the intended target. Mindful of that incident, Solovyov had purchased a massive bear-hunting revolver. On hearing the shots, the Emperor started running along the embankment in a zigzag pattern. Meanwhile, the recoil of the powerful weapon kept throwing off Solovyov’s aim. Ultimately, after five shots were fired, the Emperor’s bodyguard struck him down with his saber.
It soon emerged that Solovyov was not a lone madman like Karakozov; there was a whole organization behind him.
Narodnaya Volya: A plot to kill the Tsar
Terrorists from the Narodnaya Volya (People’s Will) organization were headed by two people from very different backgrounds. Andrey Zhelyabov was the son of serfs who had risen through the ranks thanks to his exceptional intellect and had become captivated by revolutionary socialism while attending a prestigious gymnasium. Sofya Perovskaya, by contrast, was the daughter of a wealthy and influential official; she broke with her father for the sake of her convictions. In fact, there were quite a few women in the movement; the terrorists disdained prejudices based on social class, gender, or anything else.
The movement launched a true hunt for Alexander II.
In the autumn of that same year, they attempted to blow up the Emperor’s train with dynamite. They rented a house near the tracks, dug a tunnel, and planted the explosives. However, the train didn’t arrive on schedule. It turned out that instead of the imperial carriage, they blew up a different train. Fortunately, the blast only destroyed a baggage car and no one was killed.
The next step was an attempt to assassinate the Tsar inside the royal residence, the Winter Palace. To this end, another terrorist, Stepan Khalturin, secured a job in the Winter Palace. Khalturin was a carpenter and found work in the palace using forged documents.
At the time, palace security was as inadequate as the personal security of Alexander II. Khalturin managed to smuggle 30 kilograms of dynamite into his tiny room, hiding the explosives beneath dirty laundry.
A blast! And… another failure for the terrorists: It turned out that Alexander had stepped into an adjacent room just moments before the blast. However, 11 guardsmen on duty were killed.
Despite the terrorist attacks, Alexander was preparing to initiate political reforms. Mikhail Loris-Melikov was working on the draft of a constitution. He was an aged aristocrat of Armenian descent who had served as both a military commander and a civil administrator during his career. Alexander greatly valued his administrative talents and interpersonal skills. Loris-Melikov combined two qualities: He was an official deeply embedded in the Russian establishment, yet also a man of moderate political views who was prepared to reform the political system without dismantling it – an approach that perfectly aligned with Alexander’s own outlook. Moreover, Loris-Melikov was developing a program to alleviate the plight of the peasantry; he intended to rectify the imbalances of the earlier reforms and bring to completion the work Alexander had begun.
All this sounded excellent, but time was running out. The terrorists hated the tsarist regime, and to them, Alexander embodied the very idea of autocracy.
The terrorists’ endgame
This time, Perovskaya and Zhelyabov planned a complex operation involving an entire group of terrorists. They meticulously studied the Tsar’s departure schedule from the Winter Palace. The new assassination attempt was to be carried out by several people armed with homemade dynamite hand bombs.
The police found and arrested Zhelyabov at a safe house. However, this setback only spurred Perovskaya on. The terrorists even planted a command-detonated mine along the Emperor’s usual route, and four volunteers were tasked with hurling homemade bombs as he passed in the carriage. In other words, the plan was multi-layered. The homemade devices lacked shrapnel; they were not like modern grenades. Yet they were powerful in their own right – with a blast force equivalent to up to 1.5 kilograms of TNT. Visually, they resembled simple tin cylinders.
On March 13, Alexander left the Winter Palace on official business. He inadvertently bypassed the mine that had been planted. However, Perovskaya had enough time to reposition the terrorists and lie in wait for the Emperor on his return journey.
In the middle of the day, on the embankment of the Catherine Canal, Nikolay Rysakov hurled a bomb at the carriage. The vehicle was wrecked, but Alexander was not even wounded. Rysakov was seized. A delivery boy was killed on the embankment, and two Cossack guards were wounded. A police colonel who arrived on the scene urged the Tsar to leave at once. But Alexander wanted to first say a few words to his wounded bodyguards – and also, to the terrorist.
That delay cost him his life.
Ignaty Grinevitsky managed to run up and hurl a bomb right at Alexander’s feet. The terrorist was critically wounded, and Alexander’s legs were shattered.
In a bizarre twist, another terrorist – Ivan Yemelyanov – helped carry the Emperor to the carriage; he assisted in seating him, all the while holding, in his other hand, a bomb that he never used.
By the time Alexander was brought to the palace, he had lost a lot of blood. Amid the chaos and panic, by the time a surgeon reached Alexander, the Emperor was already in a state of deep shock, and the blood loss was irreversible. There was no time for a transfusion, and amputation was pointless.
One of the high-ranking officials remarked to Loris-Melikov as he entered, “There it is – your constitution!”
At 3:35 PM, Alexander II passed away. His assassin died a few hours later.
Since the first bomber, Rysakov, had been captured alive and did not suffer serious injuries, he was immediately interrogated. The young terrorist cracked right away. Two days later, police stormed the apartment where terrorist Gesya Gelfman was hiding. A few hours later, an ambush team left at the apartment captured yet another terrorist. Within a few days, the core of the terrorist group was captured.
Interestingly, many people – even including Leo Tolstoy – appealed for clemency, urging that the terrorists not be sentenced to death.
However, the matter was already decided. Alexander II’s son, Emperor Alexander III, declared that he might have pardoned his own assassins, but not his father’s.
Five of the terrorists, including Zhelyabov, were hanged. Gesya Gelfman escaped execution because she was pregnant; she later died from postpartum complications.
Plans for constitutional reform were abandoned, and political reforms were derailed. Alexander III was far more conservative than his father, and the horrific death of Alexander II further convinced him that those who sought reforms were dangerous propagandists and assassins. The popular uprising anticipated by the terrorist group never happened.
Meanwhile, Russia was hurtling toward a new wave of terror.

Brazil votes in deeply polarised election pitting Lula against Bolsonaro
Close race expected as left-wing Lula seeks fourth non-consecutive term against right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro, son of convicted former president.
Polls have opened in Brazil’s presidential election, once again pitting left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against a right-wing candidate from the Bolsonaro family – Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
About 160 million registered voters are eligible to cast ballots in Sunday’s elections, which will elect lawmakers, governors and senators.
If no presidential candidate wins more than 50 percent of valid votes, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off on October 25.
Most opinion polls ahead of the vote showed a close contest, with Lula holding a marginal advantage over Bolsonaro that tightens further in a potential second round.
Flavio Bolsonaro voted in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, telling reports he wants to “free the Brazilian people”.
“Brazil needs change … it cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed,” he said, adding that he was confident of victory in the first round.
Lula, of the Workers’ Party, is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term. The 80-year-old, who previously served as president from 2003 to 2010, wants to continue his series of social programmes aimed at addressing inequality.
Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, has promised a hard stance on crime and insecurity. The 45-year-old has also pledged close collaboration with the United States under President Donald Trump.
His father is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence over his role in a coup plot following his election loss to Lula by 1.8 percentage points in 2022. The far-right leader’s conviction and that of several military officers raised questions about the strength of Brazilian democracy, reviving past traumas of the 21-year-long period during which Brazil was ruled by a US-backed military dictatorship.
Reporting from Sao Paulo, Al Jazeera’s Lucia Newman, said “the Brazilian president is on a collision course with Donald Trump, who is a vocal and ardent supporter of Lula’s longtime foe, Jair Bolsonaro”.
“That puts Brazil in the middle of a fierce competition between Washington and China for political, diplomatic, and economic dominance, especially since Brazil is a powerhouse on all these fronts,” Newman added.
The presidential election has been dominated by issues such as crime, insecurity and the high cost of living. Corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign.
A recent survey by Quaest says violence was cited as the biggest concern by 31 percent of respondents, followed by corruption (20 percent), economy (19 percent) and healthcare (12 percent).
“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means”, Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera.
He added that while Lula embodies the “consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship”, the Bolsonaro family argues that “the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive”.
With reporting by Brian Osgood

At least five people were killed and 30 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russian forces targeted Sumy Oblast with drones and glide bombs, local authorities said on Oct. 4.
Overnight, Russia launched 135 attack drones of various types, including 52 jet-powered drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 125 targets, including 123 Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other drones, as well as two Banderol loitering munitions, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at five locations, while debris from downed targets fell at five others.
In Sumy Oblast, at least three people were killed and 16 others injured in a series of Russian attacks, according to local authorities. On Oct. 4, a Russian drone attack on a warehouse storing medical supplies in Sumy killed a 52-year-old employee and injured three others, local authorities said.
Russian glide bomb attacks on Sumy and the surrounding area also injured 13 people, including a child. Apartment buildings, homes, and vehicles were damaged.
In Kharkiv Oblast, two people were killed and five others injured as Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and nine other settlements over the past day, local authorities said. Russia used multiple weapons, including FPV drones, Molniya drones, a Lancet drone, and a multiple-launch rocket system.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, three people were injured as Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks using drones, artillery, and a glide bomb, local authorities said. Two people were injured when a strike hit food warehouses in Pavlohrad and caused a fire, while a 34-year-old man was injured in the Nikopol district.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia district, Ivan Fedorov, co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council, said. Russian forces carried out 745 attacks against 47 settlements across the region over the past day.
In Kherson Oblast, two people were injured as Russian forces struck critical infrastructure and residential areas, regional authorities said.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were injured in Sloviansk in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kyiv, a Russian drone struck the Northern Bridge on the morning of Oct. 4, hitting the roadway, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The attack marked the fourth consecutive day that Russian forces targeted bridges across the Dnipro River in the capital.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 glide bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine over the past week, including more than 800 jet-powered drones.

Japan: US Marine arrested in Okinawa on suspicion of murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

20:15:00 KST

Japan: US Marine arrested in Okinawa on suspicion of murder
October 4, 2026
A United States Marine was arrested on suspicion of murder in Okinawa, Japan, police said Sunday, prompting an official protest from the Japanese government.
The 20-year-old lance corporal is suspected of robbing and murdering a 39-year-old woman in a hotel in Naha, the capital of Japan's most southernmost prefecture.
Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported that CCTV footage showed a foreign man entering a hotel room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and who voluntarily accompanied them to a local police station where he was arrested.
The suspect reportedly denies the charges.
What have Japanese officials said?
"The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable," said Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a statement as Tokyo registered an official protest with Washington.
"The government of Japan strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation with the investigation," she continued, also calling for "stricter discipline among US military personnel" and "thorough measures" to prevent a recurrence.
According to the local Asahi Shimbum newspaper, the brother of the victim said: "We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter."
The US Marine Corps confirmed that a serviceman assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station at Futenma, Okinawa, was in Japanese custody.
"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior," it said in a statement.
The US Ambassador to Japan, George Glass, said he had spoken with Japan's Foreign Ministry and Okinawa's governor, offering "sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues."
How many US Marines are in Okinawa — and why?
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, stationed in Japan. Most are based in Okinawa, which the US captured during the Second World War and held until 1972.
Located only 100 kilometers (60 miles) from Taiwan at the closest point, Okinawa is considered by both Tokyo and Washington to be key in deterring potential aggression from China in the region.
But the US presence regularly stirs resentment among local residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel, with crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run incidents and drunk-driving accidents.
"Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen," said Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, around 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Okinawa since 1972. In 2024, that number hit 80, the highest in 20 years.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine to seven years in prison after finding him guilty of choking and attempting to rape a young woman.
In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.

Quick hits: Ponga lights up the grand final as DCE seals the premiership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:13:57 UTC
20:13:57 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
NRL grand final quick hits: Kalyn Ponga shines, Daly Cherry-Evans finishes with another title
The Sydney Roosters prevailed in a classic grand final, holding off a spirited Newcastle Knights outfit who threatened to complete one of the great premiership wins.
In a match where the Roosters statistically dominated, but the Knights managed to lead in the second half, these were the key moments from the 2026 NRL grand final.
- Report: Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final
- Analysis: Newcastle's magic NRL premiership tilt ends in defeat, pride and honour
- Clive Churchill Medal: Tedesco wins best on ground
- Jai Arrow Tribute: Amy Shark leads grand final tribute
1. Early bomb hits the Spidercam wire
There are no shortage of camera angles in professional sport these days.
One of rugby league's favourite angles used by the Nine Network in its broadcasts is Spidercam, an overhead view of the action.
The camera is hoisted by high wires well above the action, but not high enough for a bomb from Sydney Roosters five-eighth Daly Cherry-Evans.
The Roosters' playmaker, in his final NRL match, hoisted an early kick that hit the cable holding Spidercam.
Newcastle Knights fullback Kalyn Ponga was cool under pressure as the trajectory of the footy quickly changed and plummeted to the turf.
Ponga adjusted well and caught the footy. A knock-on would have been a major controversy.
2. Teddy fumes as Ponga avoids sin-bin for high shot
Ponga was always going to be a central figure at Stadium Australia, and he was involved in an incident of some controversy midway through the first half.
The Knights captain may well have been lucky to not have been sent to the sin bin when his shoulder collected the head of Victor Radley in the tackle.
The Roosters were clearly unhappy with the tackle, with Naufahu Whyte scuffling with Jermaine McEwan.
But referee Adam Gee and the bunker opted against sending Ponga to the bin.
"If we're consistent with the rules, that's a shoulder to the head," Roosters captain James Tedesco was heard on the Nine broadcast telling Gee.
"It's been a sin bin all year."
It would prove to be a massive call.
3. From dislocated elbow to first GF try in five weeks
Francis Manuleleua dislocated his elbow in Newcastle's final home and away match on August 30.
Just 35 days later, the 22-year-old from Auckland scored the first try of the NRL grand final.
The Roosters seemed to have the better of the early momentum, but it was the Knights who scored first, with Manuleleua running through a huge gap to score under the posts.
The Roosters' defenders appeared to be focused on Ponga who was running wide, but a beautiful pass from Fletcher Sharpe hit Manuleleua in full stride for the opening score.
"It looked way too easy – didn't look like there was anything wrong … absolutely brilliant football, outstanding pass, but it all looked too easy for the Knights," two-time premiership winner Luke Lewis said on the ABC Sport call.
The Roosters would have felt hard done by. The Knights were able to get into an attacking position off the back of a penalty against prop Lindsay Collins for a head-high tackle.
Replays appeared to show Collins made contact with the chest and shoulder of Newcastle's Mat Croker, but ref Adam Gee ruled in favour of the Knights.
4. Ponga runs 95 metres as Knights fans go wild
If the Knights were going to win the grand final, Ponga needed to have a big impact.
He made a diving effort midway through the first half to knock the ball out of the grasp of Mark Nawaqanitawase, denying a certain Roosters try.
A few minutes later, Ponga produced a moment of individual brilliance.
He stood at marker near the right touchline, then sprinted across the field as the Roosters put up a kick to the opposite corner.
It was another Roosters' kick for Nawaqanitawase who tapped the ball back for a teammate.
But Ponga, who had just sprinted across the field, swooped on the bouncing ball and ran 95 metres in the opposite direction as Knights fans went wild at Stadium Australia.
Ponga was chased all the way by Cherry-Evans, but the Newcastle number one had enough speed, and just enough energy, to score and help the Knights take a 12-0 lead.
5. Nawaqanitawase with one more for the highlight reel
Few have made such an impact on the NRL in two seasons as Sydney Roosters winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.
The walking highlight reel has produced many memorable moments since joining the competition, with Sunday's NRL grand final the final chapter of his NRL career (for now) before he returns to rugby union.
Nawaqanitawase got the Roosters on the scoreboard in the grand final, showing off his soccer skills for the Tricolours' opening try.
As the ball bounced to him on the final play, Nawaqanitawase decided to kick the ball towards the in-goal.
It was not the smoothest display of soccer skills, coming off his right shin, then trapped under his right boot, before then being kicked forward with his left foot.
Nawaqanitawase was able to keep his feet, and sprinted to the goal-line to score a grand final try and get the Roosters back into the contest.
6. DCE shows his experience with a clutch field goal
No off-season switch was more high-profile than Daly Cherry-Evans leaving Manly for the Sydney Roosters.
But the former Queensland State of Origin captain had his decision vindicated by guiding the Roosters to the grand final.
And it was Cherry-Evans who put the Roosters in a match-winning position with 10 minutes to play.
Holding a six-point lead after second-half tries to Billy Smith and Nawaqanitawase, Cherry-Evans showed off his years of experience to slot a smartly taken field goal, giving the Roosters a vital seven-point lead.
How vital that one point would turn out to be.
7. Marzhew scores and Knights fall one-point short
The Newcastle Knights never gave up. They fought until the final second as they tried to become the first team since the 1930s to go from wooden-spoon to premiers.
Down by seven points with less than four minutes to play, the Knights showed a never-say-die attitude that will define their 2026 campaign.
Left winger Greg Marzhew broke two tackles to score in the corner, giving the Knights a glimmer of hope.
Sandon Smith, who was a Rooster before moving to the Knights, landed the most fantastic conversion from the sideline to reduce the deficit to just one point.
The Knights had two more uses with the ball, but could not get close enough to the Roosters' goal-line to snatch the premiership.

Latvia's pro-European ruling party wins election as populists gain ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:13:53 UTC
20:13:53 KST

With more than 99.9 per cent of votes counted, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' United List party was in the lead with 35.4 percent, according to state TV.
Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centre-right United List party has won the Baltic state's parliamentary election, preliminary results showed Sunday.
With more than 99.9 percent of votes counted, the United List led with 35.4 percent, according to state television.
In the 100-seat parliament, Kulbergs' United List party secured 42 seats, a record for the post-independence history of the former Soviet republic, local media reports.
The results point to a continued pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course for Latvia.
Kulbergs, who became prime minister only in May, said the result was higher than expected and matched the lead shown in exit polls. "That means people truly want change," he said, adding that this meant "economic growth" and "a future for (Latvia's) children."
His coalition, which pre-election polls had suggested would weaken, will not survive in its current form. One member looked set to lose its seats, and others fared worse than they had hoped.
Populist parties, however, also performed strongly, helped by support from Latvia's Russian-speaking minority, after a campaign dominated by fears over neighbouring Russia and the cost of living.
Security at the centre of the debate
More than four years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, security remains central to Latvian politics. A member of NATO and the European Union since 2004, this small Balkan state sees Russia as its main security threat and has sharply raised defence spending in response.
"Because we are the external border of Europe, we must have a strong economy... a strong border region," Kulbergs said. "That is the main task."
Rising living costs, low wages, a strained healthcare system and long-term population decline also featured prominently in campaign debates.
Most parties expected to enter parliament support both high military spending and continued aid to Kyiv. The exception is the Sovereign Power party, which opposes military aid to Ukraine and further increases in defence spending. Having campaigned on cost-of-living issues, it looked set to finish third.
However, it has been criticised as pro-Russian by its detractors, and most major parties have ruled out working with it.
Latvia First, a conservative party run by a property magnate often compared with US President Donald Trump, looked set for second place.
Both populist parties were seen as benefiting from changes in voting patterns among the Russian-speaking minority who make up a third of the population.
They had long rallied around the Harmony party, which is broadly seen as pro-Russia and was at one time the country's biggest party.
However, Harmony's support collapsed dramatically in the last election, held shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and it lost its parliamentary representation.

Russia to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelenskiy interview

The ministry said Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defence industry sites and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine.

Erdoğan says gov’t has roadmap to address fund turmoil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:12:47 UTC
20:12:47 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan spoke at an event on Oct. 3. (AA Photo)
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan assured investors on Oct. 3 that Türkiye’s economy can absorb the ongoing financial shocks, announcing a new roadmap to manage turbulence in the investment fund market.
“Let our citizens rest assured. The Turkish economy has the capacity to overcome this problem,” Erdoğan said at an event in the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa.
The crisis has shaken Türkiye’s financial markets and prompted authorities to investigate alleged irregularities involving investment funds. The Capital Markets Board (SPK) ordered the liquidation of 131 funds on Sept. 17, affecting more than 455,000 individual investors, according to figures reported by Turkish authorities.
“We are working to resolve the problem swiftly on the basis of justice and fairness, without allowing anyone’s rights to be violated,” Erdoğan said.
“Turkish capital markets will continue on their path much stronger. The ambitions of those seeking to sabotage Türkiye’s economic security to cover up their own wrongdoing will be thwarted.”
The SPK on Sept. 30 approved interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per eligible investor in funds established by Tera, Pusula, Atlas and Hedef portfolio management companies that are undergoing liquidation.
“We have convened our boards and determined our roadmap. Our first priority is to ensure that no harm comes to the Turkish economy. Anyone who has obtained unjust gains must answer to justice,” Erdoğan said.
“Let our nation trust and believe in us... Those who lay a hand on the nation’s assets will never get away with it. We will not allow this. We will never turn a blind eye to injustice, lawlessness or greed.”
The payments will be calculated based on each investor’s net investment amount. Investors with net investments below 1 million liras will receive the full amount, while payments for investors with net investments of 1 million liras or more will be capped at 1 million liras.
Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, held its second meeting on Oct. 2 to discuss the payment schedule for fund accounts and a draft amendment to the SPK.
The liquidation process will begin with money market funds, while other funds will be liquidated according to the number of investors involved.
Erdoğan also vowed those responsible for wrongdoing would be held accountable.
Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli, a key ally of Erdoğan, noted that the issue lies with how fund regulations are executed rather than the rules themselves.
“The lack of oversight and supervision lies at the heart of the issue,” Bahçeli said in a written statement.
He called for legal, administrative and structural measures to establish and maintain a financial system that investors can trust.

People in Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kiev regime for this. It is Zelensky who bears full personal and political responsibility for it.

It also cited a strike on residential areas in Belgorod that killed and wounded civilians and damaged apartment buildings, houses, and vehicles.

Following Russia’s retaliatory strikes, Ukraine no longer has a steelmaking industry, he added.

Iran says Hormuz to remain closed until US meets conditions

Unknown Publisher

11:11:30 UTC
20:11:30 KST

Iran says Hormuz to remain closed until US meets conditions
Iran’s Foreign Ministry says reopening the strait has been its main goal, while the US continues to focus on nuclear talks.
The Strait of Hormuz is going to remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker has said.
Iranian state-linked news agency Nournews, quoting Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, reported on Sunday that Washington made “some proposals through a mediator” days after the US replied to Iran’s diplomatic proposal.
The US should know “that the era of wasting time and dictating unilateral demands is over”, Ghalibaf said, adding Iran’s position remains “clear and definite”.
He emphasised that “the Strait of Hormuz will not open until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum are met”, and that Iran is “present on the military battlefield and will confront them with new surprises”.
He added that Iran was neither “excited” nor “intimidated” by the latest US proposals and would “both fight and negotiate”.
US President Donald Trump ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last week, hours after Iran put forward a roadmap to reopening the strait, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas is shipped during peacetime.
Last month, Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran in his speech on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also said Iran is “serious about finding diplomatic solutions just as we are serious about defending ourselves”.
Speaking to foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran, Araghchi said Iran had clearly explained its conditions for reopening the strait and that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy and accept its proposal.
However, Araghchi warned that if the US takes military action again, Iran is “more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves”.
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Tehran used the UNGA platform last month to provide world leaders with its position on ending the US-Israel war on Iran.
He said the US has continued to focus on nuclear talks, while reopening the strait has been Iran’s main goal.
“We are at this stage mainly focusing on the strait, and our principal concern is to reach a solution and to have peace and stability restored within this waterway,” Baghaei said.
The Strait of Hormuz has been largely blocked and disrupted for more than seven months, since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, driving one of the worst maritime shipping disruptions in decades.

‘Dignity was disregarded’: Kurdish journalist recounts alleged abuse at Turkish detention to 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:09:00 UTC
20:09:00 KST

Turkish authorities at the Kocaeli deportation center beat refugees, denied them access to basic hygiene facilities and, according to Kurdish journalist Zanyar Aziznezhad, used the threat of deportation to profit from and traffic refugees, he told The Jerusalem Post on Saturday as he recounted the year he spent there after fleeing political persecution in Iran.
Aziznezhad, who was recognized by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) as a political refugee in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, fled Iran in 2018 over fears of political persecution. From Iraq, he traveled to Turkey, where he remained for a year from 2023 to 2024, with the threat of deportation hanging over him despite the UNHCR’s recognition.
Arrested on July 4, 2023, Aziznezhad said he was first held overnight in a crowded room with 40 other people, without access to water, food, blankets, or basic hygiene supplies. He was then moved to a small room measuring just 12 square meters, designed to accommodate four people but housing 12.
“Human dignity was completely disregarded there, and we were allowed no personal belongings. We were only permitted twenty minutes outside per day, and during our detention, we were subjected to torture, beatings, and harassment,” he told the Post.
The discussion came after unconfirmed reports in Turkish and Israeli media, first published by i24NEWS, that Israel was considering filing a case against Turkey at the International Criminal Court over its treatment of Kurds and alleged funding of Hamas. Though the Foreign Ministry declined to comment to the Post on the reports, Aziznezhad said he would like to see Turkey face justice for its crimes.
Detainees had no proper shower facilities, had to bathe in toilets
Describing a typical day at the center, Aziznezhad said meals arrived irregularly and often consisted of bread thrown into rooms in garbage bags or on reused single-use trays. During his brief daily period outside, he said detainees could purchase items such as cigarettes, but at a 500% markup. Each detainee was limited to one cigarette a day, and he said those caught smoking more were beaten by guards.
Aziznezhad said he was personally beaten four or five times for purchasing more cigarettes and described how he was taken to an officer’s room roughly every 15 days, where he was pressured to sign a deportation form.
“Even though I had submitted complete documentation showing I could not safely return to Iran, they kept putting me under pressure,” he said. “There were security cameras in the hallways, but none inside the rooms. They would drag you back, beat you inside the room with four or five guards, and try to force you to sign that paper. I refused to sign and endured that torture for an entire year.”
He said detainees had no proper shower facilities and had to bathe inside the toilets, which were “extremely unsanitary,” leading him to develop skin conditions multiple times. Medical treatment, he said, was provided only if detainees signed deportation agreements or were “on the verge of death,” while each detainee received just one small bar of soap per week.
Since 2015, the EU has allocated billions of euros to support refugees and host communities in Turkey, including €6 billion through its Facility for Refugees in Turkey between 2016 and 2020 and a further €3 billion for 2021-2023, according to the European Commission.
An Amnesty International investigation, titled Europe’s Gatekeeper, warned at the time that the EU risked becoming complicit in human rights violations through its migration cooperation with Turkey. The report documented unlawful detention, beatings, denial of access to lawyers and families, and forced returns at Turkish detention centers, including facilities that received EU funding. Amnesty also called for independent monitoring of conditions and the use of EU funds at such facilities.
Though Aziznezhad confirmed that there were occasional visits from Sosyal Gelişim ve Dayanışma Derneği (ASAM), a Turkish NGO that provides humanitarian aid and legal support to asylum-seekers, he said that authorities were careful not to allow the group to see the rights abuses and that no other international organizations visited during his time in detention.
Aziznezhad said men and women were housed on separate floors and allowed just 20 minutes of outdoor exercise each day. Although the center allegedly had recreational facilities, he said he never saw them and that officials would select refugees to showcase during visits by ASAM, creating “a false impression that human rights were being respected.” In reality, he said, “refugees were being used for political and human trafficking.”
Trading human lives for profit
Asked about the human trafficking allegation, Aziznezhad said Turkish authorities had begun rounding up people they believed might attempt to reach Europe, including families who had lived and established businesses in Turkey for years. He alleged that detainees were systematically forced to sign deportation forms so Turkey could claim it was intercepting and deporting economic migrants, allowing it to receive funding from human rights organizations and the European Union.
“They were systematically forced to sign deportation forms. Turkey did this to secure funds from human rights organizations, particularly the European Union, by claiming they were capturing economic migrants and returning them to their home countries to prevent them from reaching Europe,” he said. “It made no difference whether you were a political refugee, a social asylum seeker, or part of the LGBTQ+ community. People who had lived peacefully in Turkey for a decade were arrested at their homes overnight, brought to the camp, and forced to sign deportation papers.”
Aziznezhad estimated that roughly 11 buses of detainees were deported each week during the year he spent at the center. He also alleged that detainees were required to pay for their own flights through the partially state-owned Turkish Airlines before being allowed to leave.
“This is why I call it a human trafficking scheme; they were trading human lives for profit,” he said.
Aziznezhad said the fear of being returned to Iran, along with his hope of seeing his wife and two children again, helped him endure the year of mistreatment. He also shared photos with The Post of a prayer bead he made from olive pits, which he said brought him some comfort.

Days after US forces left Iraq, photos circulated on social media showing Iranian-backed militias driving over American flags during an event in Iraq. PMF displays Hezbollah flags

The government of Iraq says it wants to rein in the militias and disarm them. However, it is having trouble getting to an agreement with the militias. Several militias refuse to disarm despite Iraqi gov't's demand

It’s not clear how the more extreme groups such as Kataib Hezbollah will be disarmed. They are very close to Iran’s IRGC. Iran wants to use Iraq as a frontline. It also uses Iraq as a base for attacks on Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and other countries. The militias have also targeted Israel and killed American service members in Jordan. They also attacked a key Saudi Arabian pipeline in September.
The trampling of the American flag by the militias is not new. However, the US will now focus on their activities now that it has left Iraq. Iraq is talking about “sovereignty.” It won’t be sovereign so long as Iran can use the militias in Iraq.

Israeli investigators believe FlyDubai alleged hijacker was likely lone wolf, sources say
The FlyDubai alleged attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to people familiar with the matter.
The investigation is still in full swing and all avenues are still being explored, the people familiar told CBS News.
The flight Wednesday from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain have said.
The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The co-pilot is currently in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing a second round of interrogation after first being questioned by Saudi authorities when the plane made its emergency landing. Israel has sent its own representatives to the UAE to participate in the investigation.
President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."
"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
Netanyahu told CBS News on Wednesday that the co-pilot's motives are still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, adding, "I think it looks like a suicide attempt."
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified, although multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News on Friday that his name is Hamam al Hamami.
Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.
At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.
Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.
The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.

NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said the global landscape was being shaped by a “radical repositioning” of the United States and the rise of China, while asserting that India has the potential to move rapidly up the global power hierarchy in the coming years.Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, Jaishankar said the US had “deliberately become a lonelier power” as part of a chosen change in its posture.“No one in the room would disagree with the fact that the landscape today is primarily marked by a radical repositioning of the United States. And that competition coexists with the complexity of interdependence,” he said.
On India’s prospects, Jaishankar said the country had “decades of high growth” ahead and a demographic profile capable of supporting that growth.
He also said India may not have to follow the traditional industrialisation path taken by earlier economies.“I would even argue, a world that is much more creative, where many new possibilities are there, so that we don't necessarily have to tread the earlier path of industrialization,” he said.
“The orthodox path will have to devise something much more contemporary for what awaits us,” he added.Jaishankar said countries currently classified as middle powers could follow different trajectories as the global order evolves.“Among the middle powers, some will peel off, some will stay put, some may drop down a bit,” he said.“That is the reality. That will be part of the evolution of the global order,” Jaishankar added.The Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi is being held on October 4 and 5, bringing together senior decision-makers and experts to discuss international security and foreign policy issues.

But the voice that rises alone often gets suppressed. ‘Satyagraha’ is an initiative to bring these voices together on a map. Bapu taught us this; truth is the greatest weapon. But an even greater weapon is standing together with truth in unity. If you’re also fighting against any injustice, share your story.
It will take two minutes,” the Congress leader said.“Your story will appear on the map. You’ll see who else is fighting like you. And I’ll do whatever I can, in Parliament, on the streets, by writing letters, standing with you wherever I’m needed, as the leader of the opposition; this is my responsibility,” he added.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Voting began across Brazil Sunday morning in general elections where nearly 159 million eligible voters are choosing the nation’s president as well as state governors, members of Congress, and state lawmakers.
The presidential race is led by incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party and Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party. They are among 12 candidates seeking the presidency, and the only competitors that have double-digit standings in the polls.
Polling stations opened at 8 am local time (1100GMT) and are scheduled to close at 5 pm.

The campaign has been marked by sharp political divisions, with top issues including public security, the economy, and foreign policy.
Brazil uses electronic voting machines nationwide, allowing official results to begin being released shortly after polls close.

Ethiopian government forces seize Tigray capital Mekelle as TPLF withdraws

Ethiopian government troops seize Tigray’s capital Mekelle
The group leading an armed Ethiopian opposition alliance says it has withdrawn from Mekelle, the capital of the northern region of Tigray, after an advance by government forces and allied fighters.
In a statement on social media late on Saturday, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) said it had “temporarily moved out of Mekelle” to “operate from somewhere else”.
The announcement came hours after Ethiopia’s federal army and pro-government fighters recaptured Mekelle’s main airport. A source close to the Tigray Peace Forces, a pro-government militia, told the Reuters news agency its fighters had entered Mekelle’s centre on Saturday afternoon, followed by the Ethiopian military.
A humanitarian source and a Mekelle resident who asked not to be named confirmed the city was under the control of government forces, Reuters reported on Sunday.
Separately, a humanitarian source also told the AFP news agency that staff on the ground said the TPLF had abandoned the regional capital. “Ethiopian federal forces and allied forces have reportedly been observed in Mekelle city … across various locations,” the source said.
Fighting broke out on September 23 after seven armed and political groups announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establishing an inclusive transitional administration.
The return of the hostilities followed the collapse of a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating war between the federal government and forces from Tigray.
The latest round of violence is also leading to fears of a wider war that draws in other countries in the region.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the opposition coalition.
Khartoum and Cairo have denied involvement. Eritrea, which fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army in the 2020-2022 war, severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia over the accusations.
On Saturday, the United States urged Ethiopia and Eritrea “to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors, exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation”.
In a statement, the US Department of State warned that the increasing tensions “have the potential to affect the entire region”.
The TPLF began as an armed movement against Ethiopia’s military government in the 1970s. It later became the dominant force in a coalition that governed Ethiopia for nearly three decades until 2018 when Abiy came into office.
Relations between Abiy’s government and the TPLF deteriorated until war broke out in November 2020. The fighting killed hundreds of thousands of people, forced millions from their homes and largely cut off Tigray from the rest of the world.

Court quashes block on mothers and children in Gaza joining families in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:00:28 UTC
20:00:28 KST

A decision by the Home Office to block mothers and children in Gaza from joining their families in the UK has been quashed by a court.
Families abroad who have had their applications approved to reunite with loved ones in the UK usually have to undergo biometric checks, including fingerprinting and facial images at a visa application centre. But the VAC in Gaza has been closed since October 2023 and it is difficult to get out of the territory.
The government has an unsafe journeys policy that offers some flexibility in this kind of situation, but has taken a more strict approach to families – often mothers with very young children – in Gaza who are hoping to reunite with husbands and fathers granted refugee status in the UK.
A judge in the immigration court known as the upper tribunal has found the home secretary acted unlawfully in the way the policy was applied to two families and has quashed the decision to block them.
Both are young mothers with five children between them aged seven and under, hoping to reunite with their husbands who have been granted refugee status in the UK. Both families are living in dire straits in tents in Gaza with insufficient food, no access to clean water, rodents, mosquitoes, bedbugs and the risk of snipers.
The Home Office says it is looking to appeal against the decision.
An estimated 250-300 people in Gaza who want to reunite with immediate family members who have been granted refugee status in the UK are similarly stranded. The Home Office says biometrics should be obtained before families travel. The Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate some of these families from Gaza so they can obtain biometrics in Jordan.
In her judgment, the judge, Fiona Lindsley, said the families were living in vulnerable structures in a war zone, malnourished, unwell and struggling psychologically with anxiety from their husbands and fathers in the UK that they willwould not survive much longer if they remained in Gaza.
“The best interests of these children should be the primary consideration, and it cannot be in their best interests to be afraid, undernourished and suffering from diseases of poverty and insanitary conditions without their fathers and no end in sight to that separation,” she said.
Decla Palmer, a solicitor at Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit who represents the families, said: “The Home Office is doing everything possible to delay and to defend its unlawful decisions, taking a policy position that blocks people in Gaza who are eligible to come to the UK from being able to do so.
“These families are completely broken – it is difficult to put into words the trauma they have faced and continue to endure. The mothers and children, trapped in Gaza, are suffering each and every day. The fathers, in the UK, are facing the prospect that they may never hold their children again. The Home Office is actively keeping these families apart, leaving them stranded in Gaza in grave danger.”
On Monday, the Home Office announced refugee resettlement routes including for Palestinian refugees and women from Afghanistan. However, this scheme processes only a few hundred applications each year. It is not known when the much larger refugee family reunion scheme will restart, after it was suspended in September 2025. The Refugee Council estimates that since then approximately 20,000 people have been denied family reunion. Initially, the government indicated that new refugee family reunion rules would be introduced in the spring of 2025, but the scheme remains suspended. Home Office sources have indicated that no further details will be announced about this safe and legal lifeline for refugees to reach the UK until 2027.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We will be looking to appeal this decision. Biometrics, including fingerprints and facial images, are a core part of the UK’s immigration system, and their enrolment at a UK overseas visa application centre is a standard requirement when making a visa application to come to the UK.
“The enrolment of biometrics enables comprehensive checks against UK and international immigration and criminal records to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls, or who are likely to breach UK laws if admitted.”
