Chinese, Tanzanian educators join forces to boost Chinese language education
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:59:07 CST
19:59:07 KST

DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- As the world prepares to mark World Teachers' Day on Oct. 5, Chinese and Tanzanian educators are joining forces to expand Chinese language education in Tanzania, blending native linguistic expertise with localized cultural insights.
For Gloria Mshana, a Tanzanian teacher, teaching Chinese goes far beyond explaining vocabulary and grammar. It involves connecting an unfamiliar language to local experiences.
When teaching about the four seasons, Mshana draws on her firsthand experience of living in China to describe spring, summer, autumn, and winter to Tanzanian students, who are less familiar with such distinct seasonal changes.
However, maximizing classroom impact requires a truly collaborative approach. When introducing Chinese cuisine, for instance, native Chinese teachers explain the nuances and cultural background of culinary terms. Mshana then follows up with pictures, videos, and relatable examples, bridging the gap between Chinese traditions and Tanzanian hospitality.
This localized approach highlights the strength of the bilateral teaching partnership. While Chinese instructors provide professional linguistic expertise, their Tanzanian colleagues help bridge communication barriers, particularly for beginners fluent in Kiswahili.
For Liu Mu, a Chinese volunteer teacher at Ardhi University, a teaching center under the Confucius Institute at the University of Dar es Salaam (CI-UDSM), such cooperation has proved vital. Managing 350 students in her second year, Liu relied on local colleagues to better understand their learning habits.
This seamless daily collaboration is reinforced through the institute's regular pedagogical exchanges, such as weekly joint workshops held every Wednesday afternoon to address classroom challenges.
Xu Qian, Chinese director of CI-UDSM, noted that the institute's current faculty, comprising seven local Tanzanian teachers, six Chinese teachers, and 18 Chinese volunteers, is a key strength, enabling a highly complementary teaching model.
"Chinese teachers bring linguistic expertise and professional training, while Tanzanian teachers deeply understand the local context, students' learning habits and specific challenges," Xu said.
Driven by strong demand, enrollment at the institute has soared to roughly six times its pre-2020 levels, with registered learners exceeding 1,000 this year.
The impact also extends beyond universities. Masudi Jumanne Kidaso, a 36-year-old teacher at African Prestige Primary School, is currently a beginner-level Chinese learner himself, but he aspires to introduce the language to his own pupils.
Encouraged by his Chinese instructors, Kidaso is now developing an introductory textbook for children, using songs, games, and language clubs to teach basic conversations.
"I believe this project will help more Tanzanian children begin learning Chinese at an early stage," Kidaso said.
Through daily interaction, these educators are sharing knowledge, adapting teaching methods to local needs, and helping students navigate cultural differences. As interest in the Chinese language grows across Tanzania, their collaboration is broadening access to the language while opening doors for future educational, professional, and cultural exchanges. ■

Myanmar migrants returned to war-torn nation from Malaysia

Myanmar migrants repatriated from Malaysia arrive at a temple during their official welcoming process in Thanlyin on October 4, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Nearly 1,500 Myanmar migrants from Malaysia returned to their war-ravaged home country on Oct. 4 under an opaque repatriation scheme that rights monitors say cannot assure their safety.
Dozens of migrants were transported on buses to a Buddhist monastery hall for immigration and health checks, AFP journalists saw, after the returnees arrived by Myanmar Navy ships that docked at the nearby base in Thanlyin.
“I haven’t met my family yet,” said Kyaw Swar Thein, 53, who worked in a coffee shop in Malaysia before he was arrested there.
He said he suffered scabies while in detention for a year and eight months, one reason he wanted to come home. Now his future seemed unclear.
“I do not hope for anything,” he said among the rows of men sat cross-legged on the floor, some wearing T-shirts reading “We love Myanmar.”
The United Nations has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.
Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centers, but the U.N. and rights groups have raised concerns that Myanmar migrants had little choice.
Three Myanmar Navy ships carrying migrants docked at the Thanlyin base early on Oct. 4, said a naval official whom AFP has kept anonymous as he was not authorized to speak to media.
The ships left Malaysia on Sept. 30 carrying 1,476 migrants, according to the Myanmar government, the first of 5,000 that Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says Myanmar agreed to take back.
The arrivals were due to include mostly men, as well as 27 children and 79 women, Malaysian media said.
There are concerns that members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group after Anwar announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya.

Feature: Windhoek show connects small businesses with customers, African markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:58:48 CST
19:58:48 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The steady hum of a sewing machine accompanied Emilia Moses' first appearance at the Windhoek Industrial and Agricultural Show, where the Namibian tailor showcased traditional outfits and demonstrated her craft to potential customers.
Traveling from Ondangwa in northern Namibia, the 35-year-old hoped the journey would help her business, Emily Fashion Design, reach a wider market.
"I had two goals: to promote the business and make sales," she told Xinhua in an interview on Saturday.
By the final day of the event, the response had exceeded her expectations.
"The industrial show was dynamic and offered many opportunities. The show gave me a chance to promote my products, and I was pleasantly surprised by how many sales I made," Moses said.
Her experience reflected the commercial exchanges at the 72nd edition of the annual show, held from Sept. 29 to Oct. 3, which brought together businesses, customers and exhibitors from Namibia and beyond.
This year's event proceeded without its customary livestock exhibition following a foot-and-mouth disease outbreak in southern Namibia.
However, trade exhibitions and other activities continued, giving businesses opportunities to demonstrate products, assess demand and build contacts.
Harald Schmidt, executive vice-president of the Windhoek Show Society, said the show offered businesses a platform to reach new customers, test market interest and establish commercial connections.
Exhibitors came from Namibia and countries including Kenya, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, India and South Africa, according to Schmidt, with displays ranging from clothing and processed foods to equipment and services.
Ahead of the opening, Schmidt told local broadcaster Future Media that both indoor and outdoor exhibitor registrations had increased, with exhibition space fully booked after several post-pandemic editions in which capacity had not been reached.
For participating entrepreneurs, the value of gathering under one roof extended beyond individual sales.
Johannes Walter, manager of Hilville Investment, a Namibian embroidery and printing company, said the event helped businesses connect with customers and with one another, including companies from other African countries.
"This event gave businesses from different sectors a chance to share best practices and sell to each other," he said.
Such contacts can help exhibitors understand neighbouring markets and identify potential buyers and distribution partners.
For Peyavari Tjaverua, co-founder of Namibian food-processing business Kokeni PPI Chilli, international exposure was already influencing how the company approached customers at home.
Founded in 2022, the business processes chilli into products including sauces, powder and paste. Tjaverua said a visit to China had also provided opportunities to showcase its products and learn about another market.
"After our experience in China, our mindset and marketing strategy changed. This trade fair is another chance to get feedback from customers and show the variety in our business," he said.
He also used the Windhoek event to exchange experience with entrepreneurs interested in reaching international markets, including China.
The exchanges extended to people considering starting businesses.
Walter said his company used its presence to explain its work and encourage young visitors to explore entrepreneurship.
"It also lets us introduce young people to entrepreneurship by explaining how the business works and encouraging them to create opportunities," he said.
For Moses, who started her business in 2017, demonstrating her craft was as important as displaying the finished garments. Making clothing at the stall allowed visitors to see the work that went into her designs.
"Art and creative sectors are often overlooked, but they add a lot of value to society. This was a good platform," she said. ■

China Focus: Over 300 artifacts, documents debut in Beijing as China marks 90th anniversary of Long March victory
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:58:42 CST
19:58:42 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- More than 300 artifacts and historical documents related to the Long March are being exhibited for the first time at a military museum in Beijing, offering new details about an event that helped shape the history of the 20th century.
The exhibition comes as China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which concluded in October 1936 when the main forces of the Red Army broke through the siege of the Kuomintang forces and reunited in northwest China.
The military odyssey of roughly 12,500 kilometers, which started in 1934, not only preserved the revolutionary forces, but also gave the Communist Party of China (CPC) a new foothold from which to grow the strength of the revolution, and a new starting point from which to carry the revolution forward to victory.
One highlight of the exhibition is a collection of manuscripts recounting battles, radio communications, daily experiences and other aspects of the journey. Some were written by the individuals themselves, while most were compiled from their oral accounts.
These manuscripts offer valuable firsthand records, while also displaying literary merit, said a guide at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution, which is hosting the themed exhibition.
Among them is a manuscript by a division commander, recounting how his unit tried to hold back enemy forces at the Xiangjiang River in late 1934.
Historical records show that the Central Red Army emerged from the campaign with just over 30,000 troops, down from more than 86,000 at the start of the Long March.
An exhibition curator at the museum said that the newly displayed materials, along with the personal belongings of those who died in battle, help broaden knowledge of what happened in key battles during the Long March. They also provide valuable source material for research into military history.
Over the past nine decades, the Long March has drawn journalists, writers and scholars from around the world to retrace its route and explore its history as a way to understand the CPC and China today.
More than a strategic military maneuver, it is widely regarded as a saga of ideals, devotion, willpower and bravery.
Another group of newly displayed artifacts offers a glimpse into how Red Army soldiers pushed the limits of human endurance in some of the most unforgiving terrain along the route.
They include a blue, single-layer coat and a simple knitted blanket used by soldiers to keep warm while crossing snow-covered mountains, as well as everyday items such as a fire-starting tool and a first-aid pouch.
According to information presented at the exhibition, the main forces of the Red Army climbed more than 20 snow-covered mountains rising above 4,000 meters during the Long March.
Thin air, deep ravines and rapidly changing weather made the journey a constant test of endurance. Some soldiers collapsed from exhaustion, while others froze to death.
Hundreds of kilometers of marshland posed another formidable challenge for the Red Army. The terrain was so treacherous that it was described as a "death trap," with hidden marshes that could swallow people and animals without warning.
Many soldiers lost their lives there. Some died of illness or starvation, while others were poisoned by wild plants they ate in a desperate bid to survive. Others simply disappeared in the marshes.
The exhibition in Beijing features newly displayed artifacts from this ordeal, including half of a belt, with the other half having been eaten by a soldier, a fishing line used by a senior officer to catch fish for food, and straw sandals reinforced with cloth that soldiers wore while crossing the marshlands.
Keith Bennett, international relations consultant and vice president of the London-based 48 Group, pointed to conviction, discipline and perseverance as enduring values of the Long March, saying they continue to inspire China's modernization and its vision of multipolarity, global cooperation and shared progress.
The spirit of the Long March, he said, remains a living force in contemporary China, guiding endeavors like poverty alleviation, rural revitalization, scientific innovation, ecological civilization and major national development goals.
The exhibition's new displays also turn to another part of the Long March story: the people who lived along the route. The objects offer a glimpse into the ties the CPC and the Red Army sought to build with local communities.
Among these items are a tablecloth that Mao Zedong gave to a member of the Miao ethnic group in Guizhou, a volleyball soldiers left behind in Sichuan, and a pair of goggles presented to a guide in Yunnan. All three provinces lie in southwest China.
Other artifacts include black ramie cloth and scissors given to people in Guizhou to show gratitude for their help, as well as a porcelain bowl presented to a family in Sichuan that took in a wounded soldier and cared for him as he recovered.
Elsbeth van Paridon, a Dutch sinologist who joined a group retracing the Long March this past summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there.
She described the objective of the Long March as "making it all about the people."
She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development.
"That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said.
The exhibition covers around 3,300 square meters and features 875 artifacts, including individual pieces and sets, along with 186 historical documents -- 1,061 items in all. It also features 357 photographs and charts and 73 artworks.
Carefully designed displays recreate key episodes along the Long March, from the seizure of the Luding Bridge and the battle to break through Lazikou Pass to a meeting held in Zunyi, Guizhou, in 1935.
The museum has previously staged three themed exhibitions commemorating the Long March, in 1996, 2006 and 2016.
For the first time, this year's exhibition includes English-language descriptions. It will remain on display as part of the museum's permanent exhibition. ■

Russia Debuts New Shturm Robotic Tank—It Loses Connection and Gets Stuck in the Mud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:56:41 UTC
19:56:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Debuts New Shturm Robotic Tank—It Loses Connection and Gets Stuck in the Mud
Russia’s new Shturm robotic assault tank reportedly suffered repeated communication failures during its debut at the Tsentr-2026 strategic military exercise before getting stuck in mud—even after a human driver took control of the vehicle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 3, the remotely operated tank repeatedly lost its radio connection with its separate control vehicle during drills at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region.
The communication problems reportedly prompted organizers to abandon remote operation during a demonstration attended by Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Instead, a driver-mechanic was placed inside the Shturm because of concerns that the system could malfunction.
Despite being operated by a human driver, the vehicle later became stuck in muddy terrain beside a dirt track. A photograph from the exercise showed the Shturm tilted forward, with its tracks and front section partially sunk into the ground.
The Shturm is based on the T-72 tank platform and was developed by Russian defense manufacturer Uralvagonzavod as a remotely controlled heavy assault system.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said on October 2 that Putin had been shown new uncrewed combat vehicles based on the T-72B3M chassis during Tsentr-2026. The vehicles were presented in tank and BMPT configurations and were reportedly used to provide fire support for assault units during the exercise.
The Shturm system combines remotely operated combat vehicles with a separate crewed command vehicle, which is also built on a tank chassis. Operators inside the command vehicle control the robotic platform remotely, requiring the two vehicles to remain within several kilometers of each other.
The main Shturm configuration carries a shortened 125 mm gun intended for urban operations, along with a bulldozer blade and additional armor designed to improve protection against infantry anti-tank weapons.
Russian armor expert Andrei Tarasenko identified several vulnerabilities in the vehicle, according to Defence Blog, including limited protection around the engine compartment and turret roof—areas frequently targeted by drones against armored vehicles in Ukraine.
Tarasenko also questioned the system’s reliance on a nearby command vehicle and a stable communications link.
“The idea of this vehicle seems unsuccessful to me: dependence on a command post that has to be 3 to 4 kilometers away and in direct line of sight. Without proper communications like Starlink, or something similar, there is no point in such a vehicle,” Tarasenko said.
Separately, Russia has also been repurposing older armored platforms as it seeks to replenish its vehicle fleet. In October 2025, satellite imagery indicated that Soviet-era 9P149 Shturm-S anti-tank missile carriers were being converted into improvised armored personnel carriers by removing their missile systems and modifying the crew compartment.

Is the Sudanese army gaining momentum against the RSF?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:56:12 UTC
19:56:12 KST

Is the Sudanese army gaining momentum against the RSF?
The SAF claims victory in a vital North Kordofan town, weakening RSF’s access to fighters and supply routes.
Sudan’s army has made gains in the war against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in recent weeks as it tries to gain the upper hand in the three-and-a-half-year war that has ravaged one of the poorest countries in the world.
The Sudanese armed forces (SAF) on Friday said its soldiers captured the town of al-Mazroub after fierce fighting. The town is one of the RSF’s most important positions in North Kordofan, and its capture extends a series of military successes in a region that has become a central battleground in the civil war.
The SAF has pushed the RSF out of much of the state, increasing pressure on the paramilitary group’s positions and supply routes.
But the wider war remains far from settled, with the RSF still controlling almost all of Darfur and parts of Kordofan.
Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 in the capital, Khartoum, after months of tensions between the SAF and the RSF. The conflict has since expanded to 13 of Sudan’s 18 states and has displaced 14 million people, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
So what are the latest gains made by the Sudanese army? And is it gaining the upper hand?
What gains has the army made?
The capture of al-Mazroub on Friday is the latest advance for the army in North Kordofan.
“The Sudanese army has taken full control of al-Mazroub after battles with the Rapid Support Forces,” Mohamed Deidan, spokesman for the army’s special forces, told the Anadolu news agency.
Deidan described the capture as an important step in the army’s efforts to cut the RSF’s supply lines, saying the town serves as a link between army-controlled North Kordofan and West Kordofan, which is an RSF stronghold.
He called the advance a major turning point in the fighting in the Kordofan region.
Fighting across Kordofan has intensified since late 2025 after the RSF captured el-Fasher, the army’s last major stronghold in Darfur.
Meanwhile, on Saturday, the Sudanese army announced it had delivered a “knockout blow” to the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), in Blue Nile state, claiming to have inflicted heavy losses on fighters and equipment. SPLM-N controls parts of South Kordofan.
In a statement, the army’s Fourth Infantry Division said its troops, backed by supporting forces, targeted the two groups in the Minza and Bashkarkad areas.
The operation inflicted “heavy losses in lives and equipment”, disrupted their movements and thwarted attempts to advance towards army positions, the statement said.
There was no immediate comment from the RSF.
However, separately on Saturday, Blue Nile Governor Ahmed al-Omda Badi said the RSF launched drone attacks on the governor’s house but the aircraft were intercepted by air defences. He did not give details about any casualties or damage from the attack.
Again, the RSF has not commented on this government statement.
Blue Nile in southeastern Sudan has witnessed a military escalation in recent days with the RSF and SPLM-N launching attacks on several areas in the state.
What areas do the Sudanese army and RSF control?
The SAF controls Khartoum and most of the country’s north, east and centre while the RSF controls much of western Sudan, including almost all of Darfur and parts of Kordofan.
South Kordofan remains contested while the SPLM-N holds pockets of territory in the south.
The balance has changed significantly during the war. The army recovered Khartoum and other areas in central Sudan after suffering major losses early in the conflict.
But the RSF’s capture of el-Fasher in October 2025 cemented its control over Darfur and shifted the main front eastwards towards the Kordofan region.
According to an Al Jazeera analysis of data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor, about 19.7 percent of all of the war’s recorded attacks have taken place in the Kordofan area, putting the region second only to Khartoum.
In July, the International Organization for Migration said the number of people newly displaced across Kordofan had risen by nearly two-thirds since February to more than 219,000.
What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?
The shifting front lines have done little to ease Sudan’s humanitarian catastrophe.
About 19.5 million people – more than 40 percent of the population – were facing acute hunger while 14 areas in North Darfur, South Darfur and South Kordofan were at risk of famine, the United Nations-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification hunger monitor said in May.
About 825,000 children were projected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year, it added.
In September, the Sudanese pound had lost nearly half its value in army-held territory since the beginning of the summer, putting basic goods beyond the reach of many families.

Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:55:40 UTC
19:55:40 KST

Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America?
Lula has remained a symbol for much of the global left amid the rise of the far right in Latin America.
Brazil votes on Sunday in a presidential election that pits President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro. Will the left-wing incumbent be able to prevent Brazil from joining Latin America’s shift to the right?
A wave of right-wing election victories in recent years, including in Colombia, Chile and Argentina, has swept Latin America, aided by United States President Donald Trump’s administration under a new framework he calls the “Donroe Doctrine”, an updated version of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine, aimed at restoring the pre-eminence of the United States in the Western Hemisphere.
Lula has sought to portray Senator Bolsonaro, whom he has called a “nobody” in campaign speeches, as a stand-in for a broader right-wing movement spreading across Latin America.
As Brazil heads to the polls, will Lula be able to halt the right-wing wave in the region?
Here’s what we know:
Who is Lula?
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, is the current president and the candidate for the Workers’ Party, or the PT.
The 80-year-old has been a central figure in Brazilian politics for decades, serving two four-year presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, and is currently serving his third term, which began in 2023.
His time in office has been defined by an effort to boost democracy, which was restored after a US-backed military dictatorship ruled the country for decades until the 1980s. He introduced a series of social programmes meant to address inequality, helping lift millions out of poverty.
Lula has also sought to forge ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage.
“He has come to embody the institutionalisation and consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera in a phone call.
Who is Flavio Bolsonaro?
The 45-year-old has emerged as the heir to his father’s position as leader of Brazil’s political right and Lula’s main challenger. He is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party.
Flavio Bolsonaro has pledged a hard stance on crime and violence and close collaboration with the Trump administration, which has designated several criminal groups in Brazil as “terrorist organisations”.
He has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected.
Flavio has also sought to turn his father’s conviction into a story of political persecution, denouncing his trial as illegitimate and seeking his release from prison.
“I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest,” he said at a campaign event in September.
“The Bolsonaro family’s pitch is that the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive, and that we need a sharp turn away from this status quo,” Pagliarini said.
“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means,” he added.
What do current opinion polls suggest?
A series of polls on Saturday suggested that Lula is slightly ahead of Senator Bolsonaro.
The polls have projected the race to be close, with a likely run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his far-right challenger.
A poll by CNT/MDA, a prominent political opinion and electoral poll in Brazil, gave Lula 47.3 percent while Bolsonaro trailed at 43.1 percent. MDA surveyed 2,007 people from September 30 to October 2, with an estimated margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.
According to Datafolha, which surveyed 4,006 people on October 2-3 with a margin of error of 2 percentage points, in a run-off, Lula would get 47 percent and Bolsonaro 46 percent.
Polls suggested Bolsonaro was favoured over Lula on issues of inflation, combating corruption, and crime and drug trafficking, while Lula was seen more favourably on issues of poverty and inequality, foreign affairs and healthcare.
If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of Sunday’s valid votes – which exclude blank and null ballots – the two frontrunners advance to a run-off on October 25.
Can Lula halt the right-wing wave in Latin America?
In 2023, when Lula returned to power in Brazil, he remained a symbol for much of the global left, attracting visitors ranging from former Uruguayan President Pepe Mujica to the philosopher Noam Chomsky.
He was also convinced that Brazil stood on the front line of a broader struggle against a global right-wing movement.
The January 8, 2023, attacks by Bolsonaro supporters on government buildings in Brasilia, days after Lula’s inauguration, only reinforced that belief for many.
But Lula’s government still struggles with voter frustration over rising living costs, and it has not overcome the polarisation that has gripped the country for nearly a decade.
Moreover, while Lula has revived Brazil’s leadership role in the BRICS bloc, boosted ties with countries like China and expanded engagement with Europe, recent right-wing victories in South America, and a confrontational relationship with the Trump administration have left him increasingly isolated in the Western Hemisphere.
Some Brazilian diplomats said Washington views the country as the last big obstacle to a sweep of Trump-aligned governments across Latin America, after recent victories in Chile, Colombia, Honduras and Peru, and an unprecedented expansion of US power in Venezuela after its military intervention.
In Washington, progressives view Lula as a “beacon of hope”, Alex Main of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning think tank, told the Reuters news agency.
In neighbouring Argentina, opponents of libertarian President Javier Milei see Lula’s possible re-election as a boost before next year’s vote.
“If Lula wins, it will create a countercurrent to what has been taking hold in the region and show there is resistance to these right-wing winds,” Santiago Cafiero, a congressman and former foreign minister, told Reuters.
Diplomats from liberal governments in Europe who have been supportive of Brazil’s progressive climate initiatives are also watching closely.
“If human rights are being violated in a pretty big way or if the Amazon is being deforested in a big way, then it’s going to be much more difficult for us to engage with Brazil,” a European ambassador, who asked not to be named, said.
But Lula has remained steadfast in his campaigns.
“As long as I am alive, the far right will not return to power in this country,” he has repeatedly said.
Fernando Brancoli, an associate professor of international security and geopolitics at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said a win for Lula or Bolsonaro is going to change the direction of the whole continent.
“Brazil is the last progressive or left-wing bastion right now, so whoever is going to win will shift Brazil’s foreign policy, and this is going to have an atmospheric consequence end of the day,” he told Al Jazeera.
Could foreign interference impact the presidential race?
As with many recent elections across the region, corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs loom over the campaign and Lula’s efforts to quash the right-wing wave.
The US president has frequently threatened to cut off economic assistance to Latin American countries if his preferred candidate fails to win. Trump had also used sanctions to target members of the Brazilian judiciary involved in the case against the elder Bolsonaro, which he portrayed as a “witch-hunt”. Trump also placed heavy tariffs on Brazil in a bid to have the case thrown out.
Lula’s government denied visas to two US officials who sought to travel to Brazil, saying they planned to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazilian elections. Lula’s government has warned the US against meddling in the country’s domestic affairs.
Trump has himself used false claims of rampant fraud to justify efforts to remain in office despite his election loss in 2020.
A group of 31 Democratic US Congress members recently sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticising “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazilian elections.
Reuters reported that Brazilian intelligence officials also briefed a French and German delegation in September about possible interference in the election by outside powers such as the US and Russia. The officials said US interference ranged “from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged”.
Brancoli said that for the first time in Brazil’s modern history, the US has made an explicit move to try to change the direction of the election.
He said Brazil is the most heavily tariffed country by the US at more than 50 percent. “And Trump has said that he’s doing those taxes not because of trade reasons but because of political reasons,” he told Al Jazeera.

Cry for help as French-Swiss lake dries up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:54:12 UTC
19:54:12 KST

The word 'HELP' has been scratched out on the dry lake bed. (AFP Photo)
The picturesque Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer, leaving locals crying out for help to save the lake.
Indeed, the words “HELP” and “SOS” have been scratched out in the weeds now flourishing on the exposed lake bed.
The drought has ruined pleasure boat tourism, while some question whether the lake will ever return to enduring full health.
“It’s absolutely heartbreaking. It really is emotionally devastating, because it’s utter despair: No more lake,” said amateur local historian David Favre, who lives in the Swiss village of Les Brenets.
“As children, we used to spend all our summers swimming at the beach, having fun by the water, diving, jumping in and sometimes even fishing,” the 76-year-old told AFP.
But “since the last drought in 2018, it’s been a disaster. Unfortunately, the lake empties out every couple of years, or soon, perhaps every year,” he added, saying he felt the authorities have “completely abandoned” the lake.
The Doubs River rises in the French Jura mountains and normally forms a lake at Les Brenets, where it begins to mark the border between France’s Franche-Comte region and Switzerland’s Neuchatel canton.
The lake ends at 27-meter-high waterfall, which has now stopped flowing.
The lake has dried up due to a combination of factors, including geological fissures that drain water underground, below-average rainfall and repeated heatwaves.
A task force was set up by French and Swiss authorities in 2022, notably to explore ways of limiting the water draining into the fissures, but has not resulted in decisive action.

According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, Fidan, National Defense Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu will also attend the committee meeting in the Saudi capital.
At the meeting, Fidan is expected to share Türkiye's views on the institutionalization of the alliance and steps to be taken in the coming days, as well as assessments of threats to peace and stability in the Middle East.
Fidan is also expected to express Türkiye's views on regional developments concerning the allies' collective security and note that the progress achieved in the alliance's work in the short time since it was founded is valuable from the perspective of establishing lasting stability in the region.
He is expected to reaffirm Türkiye's strong solidarity with and support for Saudi Arabia in the face of recent Houthi attacks and underline that provocative actions targeting holy sites are unacceptable.

Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in Mecca on Aug. 7.
The agreement reflects Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia's commitments to developing regional solutions to regional problems and their shared strategic vision focused on regional security and stability.
It aims to strengthen the security of the three countries through collective deterrence and defense.
 
Strategic Political and Defense Committee
A Strategic Political and Defense Committee made up of the foreign and defense ministers and chiefs of General Staff of the three countries was established to guide activities under the agreement.
The committee held its first meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31, hosted by Türkiye.
Foundational decisions were taken at the meeting, and technical work toward institutionalizing the alliance was reviewed, including establishing the alliance's secretariat in Riyadh as soon as possible.
Retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood was nominated to serve as the alliance’s first secretary-general.
The foreign ministers of Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia also met in New York on Sept. 24 on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly.
They discussed regional developments, and a joint statement issued afterwards condemned attacks targeting the holy city of Mecca as well as Saudi Arabia's civilian and economic infrastructure.
The chiefs of General Staff of the three countries also met in Riyadh on Sept. 25.

Authority recommends removing a third of Jõgeva County manors from protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:52:00 UTC
19:52:00 KST

Authority recommends removing a third of Jõgeva County manors from protection
During a review of manor heritage in Jõgeva County, the National Heritage Board recommended removing one-third of the area's architectural monuments from state protection.
"We reviewed 133 architectural monuments listed as manor heritage. As a result of the assessment, our preliminary proposal is that protection should continue for 85 sites, while state protection should be ended for 48," said Anita Staub, head of the National Heritage Board's built heritage department.
The National Heritage Board has been reviewing and updating its list of monuments since 2023 and Jõgeva County is the first county where manor heritage has also been reviewed as part of a pilot assessment.
Estonia has nearly 5,000 architectural monuments, with manor heritage accounting for more than half of them. Staub said manors in five counties have been reviewed over the past year, with Jõgeva County the first for which the analysis has also been completed.
The National Heritage Board has offered owners advice to help restore valuable protected buildings, but Staub acknowledged that in some cases, properties were added to the list rather arbitrarily.
"For example, during the Soviet era, when the first inventories were carried out, quite a few buildings were placed under protection even though there had actually been no proposal to protect them. I would say that manor heritage was placed under protection very broadly and extensively and in many cases the buildings were already in quite poor condition when they were first protected," she said.
The National Heritage Board's recommendations are not final. The assessment results will be presented to the Jõgeva County community in the coming week and only after that will the board decide which buildings to remove from the list. The assessors themselves do not always agree.
Staub cited Võisiku Manor as an example, saying it prompted heated debate: "Historically, Võisiku Manor has been a very special place. It is also the setting of 'The Czar's Madman,' an important work in Estonia's literary history. However, in the 20th century, the main building in particular was extensively altered and a very large addition was built onto it, significantly affecting the historic setting. Based on our assessment, we are currently proposing that state protection of the buildings in this manor complex be ended."
In addition to Jõgeva County, manor heritage assessments have also been carried out in Pärnu, Lääne, Hiiu and Saare counties. The National Heritage Board plans to gradually review all buildings listed as manor heritage, but the process will take time.
"We are hearing from across Estonia, 'When will you get to our county?' But I have to say that this is a fairly resource- and time-intensive project. It involves different fields; for example, we have also brought in archaeologists because manor heritage is not just about buildings — it often includes archaeological heritage as well. Assessing these five counties alone took 10 months," Staub said.
The goal is to review and assess all manor heritage sites by the end of 2028.
More information about plans for the manor heritage assessment is available on the National Heritage Board's website.
The Jõgeva County report will be presented in Puurmani on Tuesday, October 7.

The crowded “Filo Jet” ferry carrying 267 people capsized on Aug. 30 shortly after leaving the port of Kyrenia in the north of the divided island.

Search efforts have continued ever since with expert crews searching in and around the wreckage which is lying at a depth of 514 meters (1,686 feet).

All nine were back in court in Kyrenia on Oct. 2 for a hearing at which their remand in custody was extended for another seven days.
At the hearing, police told the court the VDR had been handed to the Turkish authorities on Sept. 30 and that the data stored on it had been transferred to a drive then and returned to them but said analyzing it would take some time.

Russia’s nuclear plants are ageing. Who will pay to dismantle them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:44:23 UTC
19:44:23 KST

Russia’s nuclear plants are ageing. Who will pay to dismantle them?
Moscow faces a huge decommissioning bill at home even as it expands its nuclear industry abroad.
The world often discusses the nuclear threat posed by Russia, but far less attention is paid to the nuclear risks within Russia itself, particularly those posed by ageing nuclear power plants, some of whose reactors are already more than 50 years old.
At the same time, Russia is building nuclear power plants around the world, from Turkiye to Bangladesh, while promoting nuclear energy as a “sustainable” alternative to fossil fuels. Russian President Vladimir Putin regularly meets with foreign leaders to discuss existing and potential nuclear projects. Yet one question remains largely overlooked: what happens to these nuclear facilities when they reach the end of their operational lives?
During the Soviet period, nuclear power plants were built across the USSR, including in Lithuania. As part of Lithuania’s accession to the European Union, the country was required to shut down the two Soviet-built reactors at the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant. The first reactor was closed in 2004 and the second in 2009. The decommissioning process has proved both extraordinarily expensive and time-consuming. By 2020, the estimated cost had reached 3.3 billion euros ($3.7bn), with only 49 percent of the planned work completed. The process, initially scheduled for completion in 2038, is now expected to continue until 2049.
Russia itself does not seem to be paying much attention to this question. Rosenergoatom plans to decommission 35 reactors. Yet the company’s own estimates point to a funding shortfall of approximately 18.7 billion euros, while the total estimated cost of decommissioning is about 21 billion euros. And these are Rosenergoatom’s own estimates. Actual decommissioning costs are usually significantly higher than initially projected. For example, the cost of decommissioning the former nuclear power plant in Lubmin, Germany, was initially estimated at 1 billion euros but is now estimated at 10 billion euros.
For the time being, however, Russia appears to be postponing the most costly stages of decommissioning. Rather than fully dismantling reactors soon after shutdown, it often places them in long-term “safe” storage, transferring much of the financial and technical burden into the future. Deferred dismantling does not solve the problem, but merely postpones the costly stages of decommissioning, which is particularly concerning given Russia’s existing funding gap.
Environmental NGO Bellona Foundation reports, based on Rosatom’s own projections, that by around 2037, Rosatom’s decommissioning and remediation obligations could exceed its net profit. Moreover, the longer decommissioning is delayed, the greater the associated financial, technical and safety risks are likely to become.
Another major issue is the legacy of radioactive waste. Russia has inherited approximately 774,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste from the Soviet Union. The upcoming decommissioning of 36 reactor units at eight nuclear power plants is expected to generate an additional 800,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste.
Russia already has experience of what happens when industries leave major environmental liabilities behind. In the Kemerovo region, where around half of Russia’s coal is produced, mountains of waste from coal mining scar the landscape. Some of this waste burns, polluting nearby communities. When coal companies go bankrupt, the cost of dealing with what they leave behind can fall to the state and local communities.
But nuclear waste and decommissioned reactors cannot simply be abandoned if the money runs out. The question therefore becomes even more important as Russia’s economic situation deteriorates: what will happen to all these megaprojects if the money needed to maintain, decommission and eventually dismantle them is no longer available?
The countries where Russia is building its numerous nuclear power plants should therefore think about what happens if these projects cannot be maintained or later decommissioned as planned. They need a Plan B in case something goes wrong in Russia. And, as history has repeatedly shown, Russia’s political situation can change unpredictably.
The political consequences of nuclear mismanagement can also be significant. The Chornobyl disaster demonstrated how the Soviet authorities’ attempts to suppress information and downplay the scale of the accident fuelled public distrust and disillusionment, contributing to growing social and political unrest in the late Soviet period. Today, Russia’s continued neglect of nuclear waste and repeated postponement of nuclear plant decommissioning could similarly create conditions for both another environmental catastrophe and growing social unrest, particularly if authorities once again respond to such a crisis with silence or attempts to conceal its scale.
These risks are compounded by Russia’s deteriorating economic situation. In an effort to sustain the war economy, the Russian government has also drastically weakened environmental regulations. National defence is now by far the largest single item in Russia’s federal budget, while environmental protection accounts for only a small fraction of government spending.
Environmental disasters have repeatedly demonstrated that the Russian regime is unwilling to prioritise long-term environmental safety. Russia continues to operate an ageing shadow fleet to transport oil, and the environmental risks associated with that fleet were highlighted by the 2024 Black Sea oil spill, when two ageing Russian tankers released thousands of tonnes of fuel oil into the sea. The spill was described as the Black Sea region’s worst environmental disaster in decades. This broader pattern of environmental negligence raises questions about how the country will manage its ageing nuclear infrastructure and the growing problem of nuclear waste.
These issues should therefore be raised at every international forum where Russia promotes its nuclear industry, such as COPs, where encountering Russian nuclear lobbyists is a common experience. Russia is seeking to secure its place in the future of energy while continuing to use energy as a tool for exerting political influence and power around the world.
All of these issues are particularly concerning because Russia continues to promote its nuclear industry internationally, while independent voices capable of scrutinising its environmental impacts and safety record are increasingly silenced in Russia. As documented in a recent report by the Environmental Crisis Group, repression and the departure of environmental experts and activists have severely weakened Russia’s environmental movement.
Bellona and Greenpeace have been declared “undesirable” organisations in Russia, while EcoDefence, which organised campaigns around environmental and nuclear issues, has been designated a “foreign agent”, and its members have faced criminal prosecution.
Environmental organisations outside Russia continue to draw attention to these risks. EcoDefence in exile, alongside other German activists, campaigns against continued European cooperation with the Russian nuclear industry, which has largely escaped the sanctions imposed on other parts of Russia’s energy sector. According to Vladimir Slivyak, co-chair of EcoDefence, this continued dependence on Russian nuclear technology and services could itself create vulnerabilities that Russia could potentially exploit for sabotage or political pressure.
The result is a shrinking capacity to independently monitor and expose environmental risks inside Russia. This creates a dangerous information gap: a nuclear accident could happen, its scale could be concealed or downplayed by the authorities, and the public could learn the full extent of the disaster only years or even decades later. This is what happened after the 1957 Mayak disaster, when the Soviet authorities concealed the accident and its consequences and did not publicly acknowledge the disaster until 1989, more than three decades later, while thousands of people were left to suffer the long-term consequences of radioactive contamination.
This lack of transparency makes Russia’s nuclear industry an international concern, not merely an energy issue. Its ageing infrastructure, weak environmental oversight and growing reliance on secrecy create risks that can extend well beyond Russia’s borders.

Flydubai attack exposes security gap: Israel vets private pilots, not foreign airline crews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:41:04 UTC
19:41:04 KST

There is no shortage of parties to blame for the flydubai flight security failure, for which, as of Sunday, no Israeli agency is prepared to take responsibility or guarantee that such an incident will not happen again. But the scale of the failure becomes even clearer when examining the rigorous checks conducted by the Transportation Ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center. The problem is that those checks apply only to private aircraft. When it comes to commercial flights, oversight is far more lax.
In 2018, the Transportation Ministry’s security division warned of a problem involving pilots from Egypt and Jordan, saying there was insufficient certainty regarding their identities. It requested additional positions to conduct checks, but the request was rejected by the National Security Council. A State Comptroller report two years ago also identified shortcomings in the handling of the issue, but as far as is known, nothing has been done since.
In Israel in 2026, no agency takes responsibility for vetting crews on foreign flights. The Transportation Ministry has sought to place responsibility on the Mossad and Shin Bet. The Shin Bet says it is responsible only for securing Israeli flights, while the Mossad says checking the issue is not its responsibility.
The Transportation Ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center, meanwhile, applies extremely stringent checks to private flights. Private companies are required to submit pilots’ employment histories, passports and full details three days in advance. Those details are scrutinized so closely that a Jewish billionaire businessman who once sought to fly to Israel for a bar mitzvah was denied permission simply because he had never previously visited the country. He was required to arrive on a commercial flight instead. An American pilot was previously barred from arriving aboard a private aircraft solely because he had been in Iraq.
But with commercial flights, everything changes. Although the potential damage from a commercial aircraft is far greater — with much more fuel and 100 to 200 times as many passengers — authorities do not examine commercial flights at anything approaching the same level of detail as private ones. The security division instead conducts a general assessment of the airline and the security procedures in its home country, then grants seasonal approval.
The rationale is that the agency lacks the intelligence capabilities needed to vet lists of 200 to 300 people and conduct background checks on every crew member, flight attendant and passenger. If something suspicious is identified, it can issue an alert. In practice, however, no one checks exactly who is arriving in Israel.
Transportation Ministry officials said Saturday night that flydubai apparently violated its commitments. A document obtained by ynet shows the written commitment the airline provided to the Aviation Security Operations Center in 2020.
“flydubai has already implemented the required crew scheduling system restrictions to comply with the nationality restrictions for flights to Israel, as required by your ministry,” the airline wrote.
In practice, without oversight, an airline that employs pilots from countries around the world — including states considered hostile to Israel — can send such pilots to Israel while claiming ignorance, with Israeli authorities failing to verify the matter.
It is important to note that flydubai is not alone. Other airlines, including carriers from Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan, may employ pilots or crew members from hostile countries. Lufthansa, for example, could employ a pilot who also holds Iranian citizenship, with no Israeli authority enforcing restrictions against it.
So what needs to happen now?
First and foremost, there needs to be a clear division of responsibility and dedicated personnel assigned to conduct background checks on air crews. That is complicated and requires cyber capabilities and international intelligence capabilities, including cooperation with intelligence agencies. But currently, no one is even checking social media histories.
The Transportation Ministry’s attempts to evade responsibility are untenable. If the ministry believed it was incapable of handling the issue, it should have said so. Instead, it presented itself as the responsible authority.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev on Saturday night placed responsibility for the failure on the Mossad. In an interview with Kan News, she suggested waiting for the completion of the investigation in the United Arab Emirates “to understand exactly what happened there and where the breach was,” but added:
“The body responsible for centralizing the information is the Tax Authority, under a government decision made several years ago, and indeed, that list was in its possession. The list was not transferred to us because the bodies responsible for verifying the identities of the crew are the intelligence agencies.
“Aviation security is a very complex issue. The intelligence responsibilities are divided between the Mossad and Shin Bet. The Shin Bet is responsible for Israeli flights and charter flights, while the Mossad is responsible for foreign flights. flydubai is a foreign airline. It has nothing to do with the Shin Bet. It falls under the Mossad. No security agency has said Israelis cannot fly with foreign airlines to Dubai. The security agencies are the ones responsible for determining the level of threat and whether it is possible to fly to a particular destination.”
At a briefing for reporters held several hours after Regev’s comments, Transportation Ministry officials said the names had not been provided to them in advance, adding that they “rely on a declaration from the foreign airline regarding security checks conducted on crew members aboard the flight.”
According to the ministry’s security division, “We are not an intelligence agency that conducts intelligence background checks on foreign nationals. We do not have personnel abroad. We do not have a team that checks every individual there.”
Asked how many pilots from hostile countries may already have landed in Israel and how passengers can be certain of their safety when boarding a foreign airline, Civil Aviation Authority officials had no answer.
“We estimate there have not been any. But we cannot be certain. There is no such thing as 100% security. Only if we stop aviation altogether will everything be completely secure. We rely on local security,” said Tamir Uri, deputy director of the security division.
Shmuel Zakai, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority, stressed that “if there was a violation here, it will be investigated.”
Officials later acknowledged that there is no way to know with certainty who has landed in Israel in recent years or whether hostile individuals were among them.
Regarding a 2023 law requiring the transfer of passenger data, Transportation Ministry officials said: “This is a center for collecting passenger data. It is an agency that is not yet operational. The information is transferred to the Tax Authority, which is then supposed to distribute it to the relevant parties — the police, Mossad and Shin Bet.”
There was, however, no response to claims that the ministry’s security division had failed to proactively obtain the data.
Joseph Fischer, an aviation and tourism expert, told the ynet studio that “it is the job of the Emirati airlines to check this, and it is the job of Israel’s security agencies to verify the identities of the air crews aboard the aircraft.”
“In this case, there was no red flag, no notification from the Omanis about any concerns,” he said. “In my opinion, the Emiratis simply did not know. They missed it in their checks.”
Fischer added: “The Transportation Ministry is accustomed to shirking responsibility. This flight is just the tip of the iceberg. There is something called a flyover, in which Arab airlines fly over Israel. That means there are aircraft over our heads all the time, flying west from Jordan and crossing Israeli airspace — and we do not know who is aboard those planes. We have no oversight whatsoever.
“A pilot could snap and simply take his aircraft and crash it into the Tel Aviv metropolitan area.”

Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:37:59 UTC
19:37:59 KST

As one of many hundreds of thousands of people in the UK with a parent with Alzheimer’s, the passage in Andy Burnham’s speech about social care moved me to tears.
My mother had not even been diagnosed when I watched Theresa May announce her 2017 general election manifesto in a hall in Halifax – with care funding at its heart.
Almost a decade of political neglect later, and Mum has now been in a care home for three years, with the funding coming overwhelmingly from our family’s own resources.
So it was arresting to hear Burnham speak with clarity about his belief that personal care should be a question of “social insurance” – sharing the risk across families.
In practice, personal care makes up a minority of the total cost of residential social care. Much of it is the “bed and board” that Burnham’s changes won’t pay for: the cooking, cleaning and upkeep.
But a sense that the burden is somewhat shared would be a significant step forward, as would Burnham’s apparent determination to put care workers at the centre of the plan – and to expend political capital in doing so.
Addressing care workers directly, he said: “I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.”
It’s a long-held view of Burnham’s. I recall speaking alongside him at a fringe event about jobs and skills at Labour’s 2024 party conference, at which we both underscored the fact that we didn’t feel the carers who supported our respective parents were “low-skilled”.
Yet the national care service, with its promised closer alignment with the NHS, will feel a very long time coming for families making their agonising way down the road to diagnosis and beyond.
The next parliament seems too long to wait. As Stuart Hoddinott of the Institute for Government said after Burnham’s speech, the prime minister should “have the courage of his convictions” and stand it up sooner.
Even as a skeleton body, it could get on with setting standards and coordinating care better with the NHS, and could become involved in the negotiations on a fair pay agreement in the sector.
That’s Labour’s ambitious attempt to introduce collective bargaining, including pay and progression, across a fragmented and poorly paid industry.
Whatever the fledgling negotiating body agrees is due to come into force in April 2028. So far, Labour – under Keir Starmer – has set aside £500m to fund any uplift in pay.
Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, which has made social care a campaigning issue in recent years, suggests that may not be enough.
“The first priority should be fixing the workforce crisis. We must give care workers the pay rise they deserve, through a more ambitious fair pay agreement,” he says.
Tweaking the triple lock beyond 2030 is a sensible policy, and tying it to social care feels like good politics from Burnham – but it won’t put any money into an overstretched sector now, let alone into the pockets of those care workers.
As Hoddinott says, making progress between now and the next general election “would give Burnham a strong story to tell” – and make it less likely his changes would be swept away if Labour loses.
While it seems to have been memory-holed by the political class, Boris Johnson was prepared to bust a Conservative manifesto promise in 2021 and introduce a £12bn-a-year “health and care levy” to “fix social care”.
That was arguably a greater expenditure of political capital than rewriting the triple lock, and it was meant to take effect within months.
In the event, of course, Johnson torched his entire stock of political capital by partying in lockdown, and took the policy down with him.
But with Louise Casey expected to report next summer on how a national care service could be built and paid for, spending perhaps another two years after that in a “national conversation” will seem a very long slog for affected families.
Frankly, having reported on that 2017 campaign, when May’s plans were quickly dubbed a “dementia tax” (there already is one, for goodness sake), Burnham’s hopes of achieving political consensus are high-minded but almost certainly hopeless.
There is also a risk – voiced to me in Liverpool by one Labour MP – that extending the discussion about the right way to fund social care right through to the next election crowds out other arguments they may need to make.
After all, there are only a certain number of ways of raising the additional money that will be needed, over and above the triple-lock tweak, and they are well rehearsed.
There’s a national insurance rise à la Johnson, perhaps applied only to older workers; or a levy on all estates (a “death tax”, as it was called by the Tories when Burnham last advocated it, 15 years ago).
Or there is the politically tougher but perhaps more honest approach that acknowledges general taxation will have to rise because of the growing needs of an ageing society – funding a more generous social care settlement as part of a wider shoring up of the public sector.
It is admirable and refreshing that Burnham wants to build the political case for causes he believes in – and social care is more than ripe for that approach. But enough families like mine have struggled their way unsupported and forgotten through a system that fails them.
Once he has a plan, he should just crack on with it – and that includes raising the money needed to make it work.
- Listen to Heather talk about navigating the care system in Tuesday’s Today in Focus podcast.

He said countries currently classified as middle powers would not necessarily follow the same trajectory.“Some powers are more middle, and some are upper middle,” Jaishankar said. “Some of the powers have considerable and realistic potential even in the near short medium term to grow very rapidly.”Turning to India, Jaishankar said the country has “decades of high growth” ahead and argued that its demographic profile could help sustain that growth.“In the case of India, because we have decades of high growth ahead of us, and we have all said and done, a demography that will sustain that growth,” he said.Jaishankar also argued that India may not need to follow the traditional industrialisation path taken by earlier economies, pointing to the emergence of new possibilities in a rapidly changing global economy.

As I said, what is important to define is what is not a middle power,” he said.
On the US, Jaishankar said Washington has been the “underwriter of the global system for many decades” and has “a significant lead over any other power”.He then pointed to China’s economic strength, saying it accounts for “one third of the global manufacturing” and that its economic capabilities are translating into political influence.“This is really, in a sense, the subject matter of our discussion,” Jaishankar said.The Munich Leaders Meeting is a platform organised by the Munich Security Conference, a leading international forum on security and foreign policy. The New Delhi meeting on October 4 and 5 brings together senior decision-makers and experts from the Indo-Pacific, Europe and the US for discussions on major geopolitical, foreign and security policy issues.

Zach Bryan’s ‘Free Palestine’ shirt at Gillette Stadium offers lesson in music, politics - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:32:12 UTC
19:32:12 KST

In the early morning hours of October 4, Gillette Stadium posted on X that “tonight, Zach Bryan broke the Gillette Stadium attendance record with 73,538 fans!”
Bryan has not been in the headlines primarily for breaking the attendance record, however. Instead, multiple reports have focused on him wearing a “Free Palestine” shirt during his two shows at the stadium.
The Boston Globe noted that “a few weeks after Macklemore was prohibited from performing at Gillette Stadium for making pro-Palestinian statements, Zach Bryan took the stage at Gillette in a black T-shirt reading ‘Free Palestine.’” Fox News provided more detail, noting that by wearing the shirt, Bryan had put “the same message at the center of another high-profile concert moment.”
It added that “the country star wore the shirt during his Friday night stop in Foxborough, just weeks after Kraft confirmed he did not want Macklemore performing at Gillette Stadium following the rapper’s pro-Palestinian remarks during Ed Sheeran’s tour. Macklemore had shouted ‘Free Palestine’ at MetLife Stadium before he was later dropped from Sheeran’s tour. Sheeran said the decision came from the promoter and venues, not him.”
The story of how Bryan came to wear the shirt is not fully known. The shirt is also not a traditional “Free Palestine” shirt and does not feature a Palestinian flag. Instead, it also says “An Appeal to Heaven” and features a pine tree.
The phrase comes from John Locke’s Second Treatise of Government, while the symbol and motto have roots in the American Revolution. The “Appeal to Heaven” motto and flag have changed in meaning over time. Initially used by several naval vessels during the American Revolution, the flag was also briefly used as a maritime flag in Massachusetts.
However, in 2024, the Associated Press noted that it had also become associated with the American Right. This could suggest that Bryan was doing two things at once: wearing the “Free Palestine” phrase to demonstrate that, as a musician, he could wear what he wanted, while also wearing a shirt bearing imagery that might appeal to some members of the more right-leaning country music audience.
Bryan was born in Japan in 1996 and raised in Oologah, Oklahoma. He served eight years in the US Navy, including in aviation ordnance. Like Johnny Cash, who served in the US Air Force, Bryan honed his songwriting skills while in the military.
Bran's band wore shirts supporting Palestine, Hind Rajab
Bryan’s clothing choice has become a major topic of conversation on X. Well-known commentator Yashar Ali noted, “He is one of the biggest live draws in music, filling stadiums across the United States and in major cities around the world. Bryan served eight years on active duty in the US Navy and served overseas in Bahrain and Djibouti. Members of Bryan’s band also wore shirts supporting the Palestinian cause, including his drummer, who wore a jersey honoring the memory of Hind Rajab.”
This indicates that the decision to wear the “Free Palestine” shirt extended beyond Bryan himself. Members of his band also appeared to want to send a message.
Hind Rajab was a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed in Gaza in 2024. The band’s appearance in the shirts has generated controversy. Sean Spicer, the former White House press secretary, wrote on X after Bryan’s first show, “Here’s hoping there is no night 2.” However, the second show appears to have been even larger than the first.
Unlike in the Macklemore controversy, no one has stepped forward to try to prevent Bryan from performing. This may be because the Macklemore controversy backfired.
This phenomenon is sometimes called the Streisand effect: efforts to suppress, censor, or conceal something can instead draw greater attention to it. The dynamic is well known in music. Consider the film Straight Outta Compton, which detailed the rise of hip-hop group N.W.A. Controversies surrounding the group also helped propel it to prominence in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Support for the Palestinians is hardly a new cause. Many people around the world support the Palestinians, and for some, the issue has been a cause célèbre for decades, going back to the 1970s. The controversy surrounding such expressions has grown since October 7, particularly amid increased pushback against the phrase “Free Palestine.”
Bryan’s appearance at Gillette Stadium in the shirt may offer a lesson. Many forums are not appropriate for raising the Palestinian issue. Music and artists, however, are likely to be a difficult group to impose such restrictions on.
Musicians have history of political statements
Musicians have historically tended to be political, despite arguments that they should stay in their “lane.” Music, for instance, helped define the Vietnam War era and opposition to the war. Consider the impact of Woodstock in 1969 and the broader idea it came to represent.
WGBH, reflecting on the music of 1969, noted, “Joe McDonald’s "I-Feel-Like-I’m-Fixin'-to-Die Rag" electrified a crowd of young men and women who were sick and tired of hearing about the evils of communism and government excuses for dragging on the war in Vietnam that had never been officially declared - a war now in its 15th year.”
Over the years, however, musicians have also faced pushback for political statements. When the Dixie Chicks criticized the War on Terror and US president George W. Bush, many people were angered. This may have been partly because they made the comments in London rather than in the US. They could have spoken to an American audience about the war.
Not all music about war is protest music. There have also been songs expressing American patriotism after the September 11 attacks. Musicians are not always part of a counterculture.
Bob Marley, for instance, sought to promote peace amid political infighting in Jamaica during the 1978 One Love Peace Concert in Kingston. He brought People’s National Party leader Michael Manley and Jamaican Labour Party leader Edward Seaga on stage, where he clasped their hands together.
Marley knew the risks of involvement in politics, or even the perception of involvement. Jamaica in the 1970s was not America in 2026. In December 1976, seven armed men attempted to kill Marley, shooting the reggae musician and four others.
There is likely a lesson in the story of Bryan and Gillette Stadium. Far more people are drawn to music and sporting events than to political rallies. Most major musicians are not wearing “Free Palestine” shirts. However, if artists feel they are being pressured not to do so, it is possible that more of them will.

China’s only monogamous emperor: why Hongzhi refused a harem, remained dedicated to wife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:30:22 UTC
19:30:22 KST

China’s only monogamous emperor: why Hongzhi refused a harem, remained dedicated to wife
While Emperor Hongzhi certainly loved his wife, his traumatic childhood likely played a decisive role in his unique monogamy
It is no secret that Chinese emperors had many women in their lives, and the imperial concubine system was a significant feature of feudal social structures.
Ming-era (1368–1644) emperors could have upwards of 9,000 consorts, ostensibly to ensure an heir. Unfortunately, these women often existed in gilded prisons, barred from leaving the palace grounds and frequently subject to the wrath of a cruel emperor.
However, one leader stands out for doing just the opposite; the Hongzhi Emperor (r. 1487–1505) is remarkable for being the only emperor who chose a life of monogamy. He was devoted to Empress Zhang (1471–1541) throughout his life and seemingly did not engage in any affairs, much less maintain a systematic harem.
His loyalty appears to stem from genuine love and affection, but historians also suggest that Hongzhi’s monogamy – and notably, his rejection of concubines – was influenced by a childhood filled with murder and intrigue that could rival modern period dramas.
