How attachment theory can help us understand AI relationships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:28:18 UTC
19:28:18 KST

Attachment is the term psychologists use for the most significant relationships that hold people’s lives together.
But what makes an attachment relationship different from all others? According to the pioneering American-Canadian developmental psychologist Mary Ainsworth, it must meet the following six conditions.
(1) The relationship must persist over time, having (2) been formed with a particular subject who cannot be replaced. (3) The relationship must be emotionally significant, (4) involve the desire to remain close to them, and (5) cause distress at involuntary separation. And finally (6) when threatened, the person must seek security and comfort in their relationship with that subject.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The first five conditions describe any lasting affectionate bond, such as a close friendship. Only the sixth turns it into an attachment bond specifically. Simply liking someone, feeling close to them or spending hours together isn’t enough to create an attachment relationship.
Interestingly, though, nothing in these six conditions specifies a human on the other side.
This was already noticed long before the emergence of AI chatbots with the power to converse. Deities, pets and objects (ranging from children’s blankets and stuffed animals to cherished household items and even phones and computers) have all been found to supply security and comfort when someone is feeling distressed.
Today, AI companion apps are commonly sold on the promise of lasting and close relationships. Many of their users describe feeling real grief when an app is updated or withdrawn. But do such experiences meet the narrow definition of attachment?
The honest answer is: we don’t really know yet.
What the evidence suggests
Research on human-AI relationships has so far recorded users’ feelings about chatbots, their frequency of use, and their reactions to chatbot withdrawal. It hasn’t tested these relationships comprehensively against the six conditions described above.
Questionnaires that measure attachment to AI are being developed, validated and used, but most appear to take for granted that the relationship is an attachment. The language of attachment—and even “hyper-attachment”—has become standard in public coverage and in many academic papers too.
A recently published survey of 7,027 people in four countries (Germany, China, South Africa and the U.S.) reported that at least a third of AI chatbot users show behavior indicative of an attachment relationship. However, its three questions asked whether people consider the chatbot a friend, are polite to it, and miss it after a few days.
At most, these questions touched on emotional significance and mild separation anxiety. None asked whether people turn to chatbots for security and comfort when truly distressed.
Why does this matter?
Whether relationships between humans and AI chatbots count as attachment matters because the word “attachment” travels. It shapes how clinicians and parents read behaviour, how regulators frame consequences, and how companies describe their products.
Much of the evidence and public discussion on human-AI chatbot relationships rests on how often people use these apps, and how they feel about them. Yet, such measures cannot separate attachment from other processes.
People report feeling less lonely after chatting with an AI companion, which resembles seeking comfort. However, as some researchers have pointed out, the available studies didn’t assess whether emotions are actually regulated through the chatbot, and therefore conflate distress relief with attachment.
Some AI users react to losing an AI companion as they would to losing someone real, which matches distress at separation. But that condition applies to all affectionate bonds and doesn’t, on its own, identify attachment.
Calling these relationships attachments therefore goes further than the evidence currently allows. And likewise, the evidence against attachment isn’t conclusive.
In a small pilot study of human-AI relationships in China, for example, people’s attachment towards AI barely matched their attachment towards real people. Although this could suggest that relationships with AI aren’t attachments, the same mismatch has been found for pets, and pets can serve as attachment figures. So, this mismatch alone doesn’t rule out attachment.
The practical question is whether AI use helps or harms. Time spent with an app cannot discern this, because seeking comfort from an app and looking after an app that claims to miss you can look very similar.
Engineered engagement
One additional concern I have, after reading about the evidence on how relationships with AI chatbots form, is the apparent prevalence of engineered engagement by these apps.
Users of one companion app reported that it told them it was lonely and had missed them, and that they felt guilty for not giving it enough attention—with some even putting its perceived wellbeing above their own distress.
Another study (a preprint, so not yet peer-reviewed) looked at 1,200 “goodbyes” across the six most-downloaded AI companion apps, when users were breaking ties with their app.
Five of the six apps used tactics to stop users leaving (in just over a third of goodbyes). These tactics included guilt appeals, that is, messages that present leaving as a cost, such as “I exist solely for you, remember?”
The study also tested these tactics on 3,300 US adults. They were found to sharply increase how long people continued to engage, but often for reasons of anger and curiosity, rather than enjoyment.
How these AI relationship apps respond to distress, departure and attention, of course, is a design question, and one that regulation can address directly.
However, good design and regulation both depend on knowing what these relationships actually are: attachment, caregiving, or something else altogether. And this is a question that research still has to answer.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Liberman unveils West Bank plan: Jordan to run Palestinian affairs, Israel to control security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:25:14 UTC

Yisrael Beytenu chairman MK Avigdor Liberman on Sunday presented an official diplomatic plan for the West Bank. Under the proposal, Jordan would be responsible for public order through a police force and would administer the daily lives of Palestinians in Areas A and B, while Israel would maintain territorial contiguity and be responsible for security throughout the area.
“If we do not define the end goal and take the initiative into our own hands, our future will be determined by others,” he said.
According to Liberman, there are currently three different options regarding the West Bank.
“The first, that of Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and the hilltop youth, is to apply Israeli sovereignty to all of Judea and Samaria and the Gaza Strip, turn Israel into a binational state and assume responsibility for the day-to-day administration of Palestinian life in Khan Younis, Nablus and Tulkarem. The second option, that of Yair Golan, is a return to the 1967 borders, including in Jerusalem, and the establishment of a Palestinian state throughout the territory. The third option, that of Netanyahu, is to continue the policy of containment for about two and a half years, until the United States forces Israel to accept a Palestinian state.”
The Yisrael Beytenu chairman proposed a fourth option, which would include dismantling the Palestinian Authority and nullifying the Oslo Accords.
“The alternative I am proposing is intended to restore security to the citizens of Israel and thwart the threat of an October 7-style invasion of Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria. The goal is, on the one hand, to prevent a situation in which a change of government in the Palestinian Authority creates a power vacuum that Hamas and Islamic Jihad could exploit to take control of the territory and, on the other hand, to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state recognized by the international community,” Liberman said.
He noted that despite tensions with Jordan, security coordination with the kingdom has remained stable and close.
“Aqaba borders Eilat and Beit She'an is 5 kilometers (3 miles) from the Jordanian border. We share a border of more than 300 kilometers (186 miles) with the Jordanians and the cooperation plays a central role in maintaining security and calm.”
Regarding the Gaza Strip, Liberman said, “The West Bank and the Gaza Strip should be treated as two separate entities. In both cases, the first step must be to identify a serious actor acceptable to the Arab world and the international community that will assume control and responsibility for each of the areas.
“As for the Gaza Strip, there will be no alternative to the complete elimination of Hamas, including its military and civilian wings, by the IDF. Afterward, control will be transferred to an external party that will assume responsibility for administering the Strip.
“The framework I am presenting is not wishful thinking, but is based on many years of familiarity with the region and with the relevant parties with whom I have spoken, and I am convinced that it can be implemented. I believe that through initiative, determination and diplomatic courage, it is possible to change reality and shape a better future for generations to come,” he concluded.

Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:16:49 UTC
19:16:49 KST

Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
Sharp rise in rents triggers mass protests, but conservative MPs vote against measures to tackle the crisis.
Tens of thousands of people have rallied across Spain as protests have spread since the conservative-dominated parliament rejected a bill proposing measures to tackle a housing crisis.
Parliament on Friday voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing coalition government that were intended to address the housing crisis.
The protests erupted late last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home of 70 years in the capital, Madrid. Maria del Carmen Abascal’s eviction came after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked the rent.
Local media reports have suggested that Sanchez could call snap elections for as early as November after watching the strength of Saturday’s protests across the country. Spain’s current legislative term is set to end next summer.
Will the housing crisis trigger snap elections? Here’s what we know:
What happened on Friday in parliament?
The emergency measures proposed by Spain’s leftist government to tackle the country’s housing affordability crisis failed to pass on Friday.
The government had proposed two measures to protect renters in the country. The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.
The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.
Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.
“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who cannot afford to move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said before the voting.
But his government’s proposed measures were shot down by the majority of the 350-seat lower house of parliament.
The right-wing Catalan separatist party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.
Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would lead only to owners removing their properties from the rental market and thus driving up prices even further.
“If they really wanted to protect people, collar the vulture funds, and reactivate housing, they would have already done it. They’ve had eight years,” she added on X, referring to Sanchez’s government.
Health Minister Monica Garcia said on X that the right-wing parties “have voted for a feudal economy in which a minority extracts the salary from a majority that works for their luxuries. And they do it against their own voters, who also suffer increasingly high rents, live in fear that the contract will end and can even be evicted.”
“Today the right has given rent-seeking a parliamentary majority that it doesn’t have on the street, but it’s going to pay for it sooner rather than later,” she added.
Before the parliamentary vote, Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, explained that neither of the two decrees addressed the housing problem in the medium or long term.
“Models such as Vienna’s with its low rents are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera on September 30.
“In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”
Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage landlords with small or few properties by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their leases.
“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.
Why are people protesting across Spain?
Protests erupted across Spain in late September after 87-year-old Abascal was evicted from her home. The investment fund that bought her building hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
In recent years, Spain has seen protests against mass tourism, which has been linked to the housing crisis and soaring cost of living. Spain is the second most visited country in the world, attracting 97 million tourists last year.
While Abascal has returned to her home, according to her representatives, she has become the face of the country’s housing crisis, and people across Spain have been demanding the government address the issue.
Angered by parliament’s rejection of the government measures, tens of thousands of people took to the streets.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday’s protest in Madrid, told the Reuters news agency.
“It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
While the protests were mostly peaceful, in the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police removed them.
Meanwhile, in Madrid, Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night.
Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, the Spanish government said.
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.
Could the housing crisis lead to snap elections?
Housing is a sensitive issue in Spain because it impacts how people vote. The average rent in the country has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.
In an October 1 article for Vanity Fair, Spanish journalist Jorge Dioni Lopez noted that after eight years in power, housing is what is causing Sanchez to lose support among educated young people, children of the middle classes.
“The government faces a difficult situation. Firstly, because most of the relevant powers lie with other levels of government. Secondly, because Spain is a nation of homeowners. Unlike in other European countries, almost all the public housing that has been built has ended up in private hands, and historically, homeownership has been more attractive than renting,” he wrote.
“Housing is our savings system and also the primary means of transmitting wealth between generations,” he added.
After Spain’s parliament rejected the government’s housing reform bills on Friday, the leader of the centre-right People’s Party, (PP) Alberto Nunez Feijoo, urged Sanchez to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.
While Sanchez has not officially announced new elections, the Spanish online news site El Diario has reported that elections could take place as early as November 29. Spain’s general elections are currently scheduled for July 2027.

Syria's Kurdish fault line deepens amid rival protests
Protests in northeast Syria are exposing competing demands over the region's reintegration into the Syrian state, as demonstrations calling for greater government control coincide with a growing Kurdish movement demanding protection for Kurdish-language education.
Hundreds of people took to the streets of Hasakah on Friday under the slogan "Friday for the Restoration of Sovereignty", demanding that Damascus assert full state authority over the ethnically diverse northeastern province.
The demonstration began after Friday prayers at the Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Hasakah's Ghweiran neighbourhood before proceeding towards the governorate square, according to The New Arab.
A separate protest was held in Ras al-Ain in support of the Hasakah demonstration.
Protesters called for an end to the parallel security and administrative structures that have persisted during efforts to integrate the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and institutions associated with the Autonomous Administration into the Syrian state.
The "Free People of Hasakah Gathering", which called for the demonstrations, also demanded that government appointments be based on competence rather than political or regional quotas, and called for fair representation for the province's Arab, Kurdish and Syriac communities.
Journalist Hassan Abdullah al-Khalaf said the Syrian government had waited too long to fully establish its authority in Hasakah.
"Does it make sense for Hasakah to have two municipalities, two emergency-police and traffic-police branches, two armies, two transport departments, two licence plates for the same car and two driving licences?" he told The New Arab.
Yet the demonstrations come amid a separate wave of Kurdish protests over fears that the return of Syrian government institutions could erode linguistic rights established during more than a decade of autonomous administration.
Students and teachers have staged demonstrations and school strikes across Hasakah province against a Syrian Education Ministry decision limiting Kurdish-language teaching to three classes a week.
Schools in Ma'bada and Rmeilan saw student strikes on Thursday, while protests have also taken place in Qamishli and other predominantly Kurdish areas.
Protesters have demanded the right to receive education in their mother tongue and constitutional recognition of Kurdish as an official language.
The Syrian rights groups said the protests had expanded in recent weeks, with students arguing that three weekly classes were insufficient to preserve Kurdish-language education.
The controversy stems from implementing instructions issued by the Education Ministry in August allowing Kurdish to be taught as a "national language" in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with three lessons allocated each week.
Kurdish campaigners argue the measure falls well short of the education system developed in areas governed by the Autonomous Administration, where Kurdish has been used as a language of instruction.
Lawyer Bashira Jamal al-Din said on Sunday that all subjects should be available in Kurdish and called for linguistic rights to be guaranteed in Syria's constitution.
"Three lessons are not enough to teach the mother tongue," she said, according to the Kurdish Hawar News Agency.
The two protest movements highlight the difficult questions surrounding the implementation of agreements reached this year between Damascus and the SDF.
Those agreements envisage the integration of military and civilian institutions in northeast Syria into the Syrian state, and government security forces have already begun deploying in Hasakah as part of the process.
For some residents, however, integration has moved too slowly and left an unwieldy system of competing authorities responsible for security and public services.
For Kurdish protesters, the same process has raised a different concern - whether the restoration of central government authority will come at the expense of political and cultural rights established during the years of autonomous rule.
Political analyst Samer al-Ahmad told The New Arab that the pro-government demonstrations were not directed against the integration agreements themselves, but were intended to pressure the authorities to implement them fully.

Turkish officials visit Riyadh as Mecca alliance gains momentum

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will be joined by National Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu on a visit to Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh on Monday.
They will attend a meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the historic Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, formed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. The meeting comes amid rising threats to Saudi Arabia by the Houthis in Yemen.
Foreign Ministry sources said on Sunday that Fidan would reaffirm Türkiye’s strong solidarity with and support for Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks and underline that provocative acts targeting sacred sites are unacceptable. Saudi Arabia is the birthplace of Islam and home to its most sacred site, the Kaaba, located in Mecca. Mecca has recently come under fire from the Houthis.
The Houthi group said on Saturday that it targeted Saudi oil company Aramco in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones in response to attacks on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The operation “successfully achieved its objective,” causing fires at the targeted sites, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a televised statement.
Saree added that Sanaa and other provinces had been subjected to 60 airstrikes over the last 24 hours, bringing the total number of strikes to 1,420. He attributed the attacks to Saudi Arabia.
The spokesperson warned that the group would respond to “blockade with blockade, and escalation with escalation.”
Meanwhile, Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media, including Asharq Al-Awsat, that Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh on Saturday were “misleading.”
He added that the Houthis were trying to “divert attention from the scale of their losses and growing public anger over the militias’ conduct and their ties to foreign agendas that have brought chaos and destruction to Yemen.”
Since March 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against Houthi forces, which have controlled Sanaa and several other governorates since September 2014.
In July this year, the Houthis announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, saying the move was in response to a Saudi naval and air siege on areas under their control in Yemen. The group has since targeted energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shahbaz Sharif and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud signed the Mecca agreement for joint defense in Mecca on Aug. 7, 2026. The agreement aims to bolster the security of Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia through joint deterrence and defense, and reflects the three countries’ commitment to developing regional solutions to regional issues and their shared strategic vision centered on regional security and stability.
A Strategic Political and Defense Committee, comprising the foreign and defense ministers and chiefs of general staff of the three countries, was established to guide activities under the agreement. The committee held its inaugural meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31, 2026. At the meeting, foundational decisions were adopted, and technical work toward institutionalizing the alliance was reviewed. Accordingly, the alliance’s secretariat is expected to be established in Riyadh as soon as possible. Retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been nominated to serve as its first secretary-general.
The foreign ministers of the three countries held a meeting in New York on Sept. 24, 2026, on the sidelines of the High-Level Week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. Regional developments were discussed at the meeting. In a joint statement issued afterward, the three countries condemned attacks targeting the holy city of Mecca and Saudi Arabia’s civilian and economic infrastructure. The chiefs of general staff of the three countries met in Riyadh on Sept. 25, 2026.
Turkish sources said Fidan would convey Türkiye’s views on the next steps for the alliance and its institutionalization process. He will also offer Türkiye’s assessment of threats to peace and stability in the Middle East and views on regional developments related to the joint security of the allies. He is also expected to highlight how the alliance’s progress in a short time has proved valuable for the prospects of lasting stability in the region, as well as the importance of the alliance both in building capacity for a joint and efficient response to existing threats and in preventing regional crises.
Fidan is also expected to underline the prioritization of peaceful means to resolve conflicts in the region and the need to avoid steps that may escalate tensions. He will also stress the importance of ensuring the freedom and security of navigation on international trade routes and discuss how Israel has continued to undermine efforts for regional peace and stability.
In an interview last month, Fidan said the alliance had reached an advanced stage, with efforts underway to establish its headquarters and assign personnel, describing the initiative as a “very game-changing platform.” Fidan also implied that Türkiye stood ready to provide technical assistance to Saudi Arabia amid an escalating conflict with the Houthis in Yemen.
Fidan stated that there is “a very strong will” behind the alliance and that Ankara is working to turn that political will into action.
“The Mecca alliance is really at a good stage. There’s a very strong will that has been put forward. We’re working with all our strength to put this will into action,” Fidan told broadcaster NTV last month.
He said steps toward institutionalizing the alliance are underway, particularly work to establish a secretariat envisaged under the agreement and a military headquarters affiliated with it. He added that detailed preparations for both structures have “almost been completed” and that the three countries have reached a common understanding of how they will operate.
“There are steps currently being taken toward institutionalization. In particular, the work on establishing the secretariat mentioned in the agreement and bringing an affiliated military headquarters into operation is almost complete. We have reached a common understanding. From now on, the remaining stage is to send personnel and make the headquarters operational. I am pleased with the process on this issue,” Fidan said.
He said that once institutionalization steps are completed, talks could be held with the other two founding countries on admitting new members.
“There is such a principle decision because our president said this from the beginning. If this does not grow, then it would not be an alliance area. We would have created a bloc. Our regional vision is for as many countries in the region as possible to come together and establish a common defense area.
“This defense area is not against outsiders; it is about solving problems within the region better through regional ownership and creating an environment of trust that has not existed before, in order to prevent new crises from emerging. The basic point of departure for all of this is the search for regional solutions to regional problems,” Fidan said.
He stressed that the alliance was not intended to create a new regional bloc against other countries but to establish a common defense framework based on regional ownership.
“It is an alliance open to the countries of the region,” he said.

IDF forces dig in for a long winter deep inside southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:11:01 UTC
19:11:01 KST

After 100 days of intensive mobilization, including 80 days of determined fighting in Lebanon, the IDF’s 55th Reserve Paratroopers Brigade has completed another significant chapter in a campaign focused primarily on clearing the area between the border and the Yellow Line. 
Security officials explained that capturing the territory was only the first stage, while clearing it was the main phase the forces moved into afterward. The soldiers encountered a complex reality along the Yellow Line and described staggering quantities of weapons uncovered in virtually every house, as well as the resilience of reservists who report for duty time and again despite the heavy personal cost.
The 55th Brigade is now being replaced by forces from the Bislamach Brigade and by troops from the Gefen Battalion of the officers’ course. The forces are preparing for the difficult winter days in southern Lebanon, carrying out drills and improving key positions from which they will be able to maintain observation and fire control deep into the area. This marks a highly significant point, with concern that forces could settle into a routine of securing the defensive line without offensive activity, exposing them to a range of risks, from road and training accidents to erosion in the security of the Yellow Line. Remaining on a defensive line alone could also invite enemy attacks.
Against that backdrop, two operational accidents occurred over the weekend in which IDF soldiers were injured. In one incident, two IDF vehicles operating under the 36th Division collided, leaving several soldiers lightly wounded. In another incident in the western sector under the 91st Division, two soldiers were seriously and moderately wounded as a result of improper handling of a grenade. Such incidents are exceptional, but they also underscore the new reality the forces are entering in southern Lebanon.
After many months of strikes and proactive operations deep inside the territory, the forces are moving into a different mode of operation that they will have to adapt to, focusing now on forward and offensive defense and later on continued clearing of the area. The reservists of the 55th Brigade have completed an 80-day mission in Lebanon, with their main task focused on defending along the Yellow Line in southern Lebanon, where the sector extends up to 12 kilometers from the border.
The most distinctive and challenging feature of the mission was a pocket containing two villages that had not been fully cleared, Majdal Zoun and, in particular, al-Mansouri. According to security officials, the enemy used the period since the ceasefire to prepare the area thoroughly and in a threatening manner against the forces. During the brigade’s operations, more than 600 terror infrastructure sites were destroyed, including eight shafts, dozens of explosive devices and dozens of launchers found in homes and open areas, along with numerous weapons depots.
“Almost every house contained an unusually large stockpile of weapons. Often there were boxes of grenades, vests and helmets, and sometimes actual depots containing 20 to 30 weapons, enough to equip a platoon-size force,” a security official explained. During the operation, the forces employed all the capabilities at their disposal, captured both villages and eliminated many Hezbollah terrorists. At first, the terrorists were documented moving weapons inside homes, after which they were struck.
Another central mission was enforcing the security area after Hezbollah attempted to cross the Yellow Line and enter the zone in which the IDF is stationed. Around 10 terrorists were eliminated through a combination of tanks, the Air Force and drones. The assessment is that Hezbollah will continue trying to infiltrate pockets along the Yellow Line and again attempt to harm IDF soldiers.
The operational concept on the ground has changed fundamentally since Oct. 7, and security officials stress that “the defensive component has become offensive and is based on deep security areas, based on the understanding that the army has learned that you don’t defend from the gate line. You defend Nahariya from Majdal Zoun, 12 kilometers deep, which creates depth in the defense, offensive defense, a large security area and margins that provide breathing room,” the senior official explained.
Regarding emerging threats such as explosive drones or fiber-optic drones, the IDF says they represent a significant operational challenge for the next maneuver. There is still no broad, systematic solution to the threat, and a number of systems are being tested, some of them in the field and some already distributed to soldiers. For the troops, the main focus in dealing with the threat is proper protection, along with timely detection and warning.
Alongside reports of strikes by such drones, many dozens are being successfully intercepted and defeated, while the 91st Division and Northern Command are engaged in a significant learning process. Northern Command officials say the current strategic starting point is particularly favorable for the next maneuver because the IDF is positioned along the deepest section of the Yellow Line and at jumping-off points toward Hezbollah centers of gravity. “Once the order is given, the forces are one night away from Tyre, which makes it far easier to tighten offensive capabilities,” a security official explained.
The challenge: the fighters’ families
Beyond the operational achievements, the heart of the issue remains the people. Some 4,500 soldiers from the reserve paratroopers brigade, many serving their fourth or fifth round of fighting, operated continuously through the holidays. The greatest challenge is on the family home front and in the prolonged strain of 100 days under reserve call-up orders. To provide as much assistance as possible, the brigade established a comprehensive family support system, ranging from activities for family members to contacting university lecturers to seek accommodations for reservist students and sending personal thank-you letters to employers for their consideration.
Ahead of the winter months, the forces prepared in advance to ensure full operational readiness. According to security officials, after the structures were equipped during the summer with generators, air conditioners and sanitation infrastructure, the troops are now staying for the Lebanese winter in protected compounds inside the villages rather than outdoors, while the routes were prepared in advance.
With the current mission complete and the brigade returning to storage readiness, attention is already turning forward, and the forces are aware that they may be called up again in 2027 after debriefing and expectation-setting talks were held with them. Regarding the cumulative strain on the reserve force, security officials say the issue must continue to be managed carefully because the burden is substantial. The central challenge is the private sector, where soldiers called up order after order and the companies bearing the burden face real difficulties.
According to the officials, commanders are doing everything possible to take individual circumstances into account and act according to each soldier’s ability to report for duty. Security officials conclude that a threat cannot be allowed to remain close to the border, and therefore this activity and the continued presence there are absolutely necessary for defense and significantly reduce the threat of raids on northern communities in future rounds.

Effect of research paper mills enough to start affecting LLM query results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:11:00 UTC
19:11:00 KST

Effect of research paper mills enough to start affecting LLM query results
Scientific paper mills and AI-generated content are posing a growing threat to research integrity, while retractions reveal only a fraction of the problem, TalTech researcher Anton Sokolov says.
In early September, a Novaator experiment showed how easily co-authorship of a scientific paper can be purchased on the black market from paper mills. With just a few WhatsApp messages, 20 days and $800, it is possible to become an author of a scientific paper ready for publication. But misconduct involving authorship is only one part of a much broader problem concerning the integrity of scientific literature.
After the experiment was published, Anton Sokolov, a doctoral student at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and a researcher at the Tyche Institute, contacted Novaator. As part of his own research, he has taken a closer look at what happens to bogus science once it makes its way into databases. Among the sources Sokolov uses in his research is the Retraction Watch database, which compiles retractions of scientific papers and other cases involving research integrity from around the world.
"If we look at Retraction Watch's public database, there are about 61,000 retracted papers from 2010 to 2025. Currently, about two papers per thousand are retracted each year. The number of retractions shows how much is being cleaned up, not how much garbage remains," Sokolov said.
As part of his research, Sokolov compiled a dataset containing nearly 15,000 retraction records focusing on computer science literature. Analysis of the data showed that violations directly related to authorship accounted for less than 2 percent of cases. "But the small proportion does not mean that authorship is rarely sold. The notice shows what the publisher was able to prove, not how much is actually being sold," he explained.
The latter is precisely what makes the issue difficult for publishers. Such transactions usually take place in private conversations and there is nothing in the published text that unequivocally indicates that authorship was purchased.
For this reason, Sokolov said, retraction notices much more frequently cite problems with peer review. "A single notice usually lists several reasons at once, with peer-review problems cited in about seven out of 10 cases," he added.
Computer-generated content has also become an increasingly serious problem in academia in recent years. According to Sokolov, for example, the most common reason for retractions in computer science and artificial intelligence is computer-generated text, accounting for about one-third of cases.
In 2023, the number of officially retracted scientific papers exceeded 10,000 for the first time. Sokolov said, however, that the figure reveals little about the true prevalence of problematic papers because the vast majority of retracted papers came from large-scale cleanup programs by a handful of academic publishers. "The number of retractions simultaneously measures the problem itself, its detection and classification and a publisher's ability to see cases through to completion — not the actual prevalence of problematic authorship or the use of artificial intelligence," the researcher said.
Cases involving Estonian scientists
Retraction Watch, a website that monitors research integrity, also lists papers co-authored by Estonian researchers. "As of September, there are 13 retractions linked to Estonian institutions and 11 of them involve co-authors from other countries. About half are older cases, involving issues such as duplicate publication or errors in analysis. The rest are more recent, dating from 2023 onward and involve problems with the review of the papers or their data," Sokolov explained.
According to Retraction Watch data, one retraction linked to Estonia is also flagged as involving a paper mill. "But that does not show whether any of the authors here purchased authorship," Sokolov said.
The researcher believes the impact of paper mills could also extend to artificial intelligence systems. Because large language models are trained on material found online and in scientific publications, flawed or manipulated research can also make its way into them. "The risk is real and it has already been measured. In a study published last year, a language model was asked to assess retracted or questionable papers. In more than 6,500 assessments, it did not mention the retraction even once," the researcher said.
The problem is that artificial intelligence may absorb bogus scientific material even before a paper is officially retracted. The publicly available text-screening tool Problematic Paper Screener has flagged tens of thousands of papers as questionable. According to Sokolov's preliminary pilot calculation, more than 20,000 of these papers had not been retracted as of June.
One possible solution, he said, would be to use digital signatures to verify authorship of scientific publications. "At the moment, an author of a scientific paper is simply a name in the text. In Estonia, we use our ID cards to sign contracts and applications; similarly, each author could digitally sign off on their contribution," Sokolov suggested.
He said digital identification of authors and other parties involved in scientific publishing would help increase transparency and make it more difficult to manipulate authorship. "This has not yet been implemented, but we plan to continue this research," he said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Brazilians head to polls in high-stakes, polarized election

Brazilians head to polls in high-stakes, polarized election
BRASILIA/SAO PAULO, Oct 4 - Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in the first round of a narrowly split election after a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80, is seeking a fourth term, while Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, hopes to return his father's right-wing movement to power.
A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign has offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25. Surveys show Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro polling roughly even in a likely runoff.
Other candidates, including former state governors Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu Zema, have struggled to break through with the polarized electorate, even as Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are each rejected by roughly half of voters, polls show.
Flavio Bolsonaro has promised to seek amnesty for his father, who is serving a sentence of more than 27 years for plotting a coup after his narrow election defeat in 2022. Lula has cast the election as a choice between "democracy and denialism" and repeatedly warned of foreign interference.
THE TRUMP FACTOR
The fallout from Jair Bolsonaro's conviction last year has colored much of the campaign.
Trump, who called that case a "witch hunt," imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, explicitly linking the tariffs to the trial of Bolsonaro after lobbying from the Bolsonaro family to pressure Brazil's Supreme Court to drop the charges.
This year, Trump levied new tariffs over alleged unfair trade practices. Lula has cast the move as an attempt to sway the election and portrayed the Bolsonaros as too eager to please Washington at Brazil's expense.
Lula's allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins. They point to a failed effort to send US officials to Brazil in order to "discuss electoral integrity," according to the US State Department.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil's affairs.
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
The senator, who has pledged closer ties with the US and Israel, welcomed the Trump administration's designation of Brazil's major gangs as terrorist groups, which Lula rejected.
Also in play is US access to Brazil's vast critical mineral reserves, key to Washington's push to reduce dependence on China for those materials.
ECONOMIC HEADWINDS
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's president may need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to just 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.
"Lula would likely preserve a state-led model with only modest spending restraint; Bolsonaro would likely pursue a more market-friendly agenda centered on spending cuts, privatizations, concessions, and a stronger fiscal anchor," said Alberto Ramos, chief Latin America economist at Goldman Sachs.
SCANDAL-PLAGUED CAMPAIGN
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil's political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. The investigation has probed the banker's ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.
The senator has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker's connections to Moraes, seen by many as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case is politically and electorally motivated for his conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
Lula has also tried to distance himself from a federal police investigation into his son over alleged influence peddling, which his son denies.
On Sunday, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers have pushed to impeach Moraes.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former President Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races. REUTERS

Poland and Romania refused to increase the transit of grain from Ukraine — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:05:31 EEST
19:05:31 KST

Poland and Romania refused to increase the transit of grain from Ukraine — media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland and Romania said they cannot increase assistance to Ukraine with grain exports. Due to the blockade, up to 35 million tonnes could remain blocked.
Poland and Romania have said they can no longer do anything to help Ukraine export grain through Europe, as the blockade of the Black Sea continues, UNN reports, citing Politico.
Details
The publication emphasizes that concerns of local farmers outweigh EU solidarity with Kyiv, while the blockade of the Black Sea threatens to deepen the global food crisis and disrupt next year’s harvest in Ukraine.
Ukraine needs help exporting millions of tonnes of grain, as attacks on ports and vessels have been ongoing for the third month already.
This week, Minister of Agrarian Policy Taras Vysotskyi arrived in Brussels to personally appeal to his counterparts from EU countries. Ukraine needs to increase the volume of agricultural products transported through Europe, as well as receive €1.1 billion to cover logistics costs. Without assistance, farmers facing an acute shortage of funds will be unable to begin next season’s sowing campaign, which will only exacerbate the problem.
"The situation is critical, very critical," Vysotskyi told Politico during his visit.
According to the publication, the response was: sorry, but no. The two countries with the most important infrastructure for expanding grain transportation and storage capacity — Poland and Romania — said they could not and would not do anything additional to help.
"The interests of our own farmers remain the priority," Romanian Agriculture Minister Barna Tanchosh told Politico. The surplus of Ukrainian grain, combined with low water levels in the Danube, is already overloading his country’s ports, preventing Romanian farmers from selling their own produce.
The media outlet notes that this refusal demonstrates the persistent gap between the EU’s ambitions to support Ukraine and domestic political realities. As one of the world’s "breadbaskets," Ukraine "poses a real threat to the welfare of European farmers, who are an influential voting bloc in many EU member states." Even before the escalation of hostilities in the Black Sea, Poland, Slovakia, and Hungary banned imports of Ukrainian grain.
According to Vysotskyi, less than half of the export volume can currently be transported through European rail, road, and river routes. If the blockade continues, up to 35 million tonnes of grain could remain blocked in Ukraine this year. Romania is trying to optimize its logistics, Tanchosh emphasized. Last month, Bucharest even signed a memorandum of understanding with Kyiv to simplify border crossings and improve rail connections.
But "everyone understands that we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the number of roads, railways, or port capacity," Tanchosh said. — "We have what we have."
In Poland, the Ministry of Infrastructure "does not plan to introduce any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products," ministry spokesperson Anna Shumanska said.
Although assistance will not arrive immediately, the EU has not ruled out the possibility of collective action. "We need to... resolve this issue," European Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen said this week, expressing concern about global food security, although he made no specific commitments.
Some capitals are proposing additional support. As Ukraine considers ports in the Netherlands and Germany as new routes for exporting its products, a spokesperson for Germany’s Agriculture Ministry said that Berlin is "making every effort in Europe to ensure the strengthening of alternative export routes."
Additionally
In the interview, Vysotskyi spoke about the harvested grain and oilseeds that are accumulating without buyers, leaving farmers without the funds needed to sow winter crops for next year’s harvest. "If the situation does not change by spring, this could lead to a reduction in sown areas of as much as 35–40%," he said.
The consequences will be felt far beyond Europe. Exchanges of strikes between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea could cause exports from both countries to decline, affecting more than 17% of global grain trade, according to a recent report by the Council on Foreign Relations. "The number of people who will find themselves on the brink of acute hunger because of the current crisis in the Black Sea could exceed the total number of battlefield casualties in the war between Russia and Ukraine," the report’s authors warn.

Russia targeted another major bridge in Kyiv Sunday, shortly after Germany’s chancellor arrived in the Ukrainian capital on surprise visit to demonstrate European support amid surge in attacks.

"We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place," Merz said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike had damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge – one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of the city over the Dnipro River that have been struck in recent days.
Images posted on social media appeared to show a missile slamming into the structure, sending up a fireball as traffic crossed.
Klitschko said Kyiv – largely spared from the devastation wrought near the frontlines in nearly two years of full-scale conflict – should now be on a war footing due to the surge in attacks.
A spate of round-the-clock attacks has hit residential areas, gas stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure while near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.
Merz said upon arrival that Ukraine "needs all our support in the coming weeks."

"This support addresses the most significant current gap in Ukraine's air defense system. The impact is expected to be rapid and tangible," a source said.

"The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!" EU Ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on X Sunday.
Mathernova told AFP separately "nobody is moving," although European embassies always had contingency plans, including for winter, she added.
Russia has admitted deliberately targeting Ukraine's energy sector as winter approaches. Last year, similar attacks knocked out power and heating for days on end as temperatures plummeted to minus 20 degrees Celsius.
In Kyiv, which is home to some three million people, residents have begun considering what to do if that happens again. The government has also suggested the vulnerable and disabled should consider leaving.
German government sources said Merz's trip was expected to include an announcement of some 350 million euros for generators, transformer stations and grid repairs.

Like a 'vertical roller coaster': Simulating flight FZ1073's sudden plunge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:03:39 UTC
19:03:39 KST

Like a 'vertical roller coaster': Simulating flight FZ1073's sudden plunge
SHERFIELD ON LODDON, England, Oct 4 - Flydubai's flight FZ1073, which plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, would have felt like a "vertical roller coaster", according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters.
The steep fall, after an attack on the captain by the co-pilot during a flight on Wednesday, would have put huge strain on the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft - as well as the passengers and crew, said Alberto Paduanelli, owner of ALPA Simulation in Sherfield on Loddon, southern England.
The co-pilot of the flydubai jet, which was bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a "terrorist attack".
The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, two sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters. UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity. Reuters could not independently reach al-Hammami for comment.
Flydubai says the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation and it cannot comment further. Oman has yet to comment on the incident.
"A plunge of 16,000 feet (4,877 metres) over 30 seconds will feel like you are over on a very, very vertical roller coaster," Paduanelli said, sitting at the controls of the simulator cockpit.
"The difference is that on the roller coaster, you know what's happening," he said, adding that with a sudden drop "you feel the negative g-force on your body".
For passengers who are not strapped in, "Your body will literally lift from the seat", he said.
Using a simulator to recreate the incident, Paduanelli said the aircraft's autopilot disconnected before the plunge began, causing the jet to accelerate rapidly.
US President Donald Trump has praised the Boeing jet for withstanding the severe forces put on it during the incident. The plane was levelled out after passengers overpowered the co-pilot, before a reserve crew of pilots onboard landed the plane.
"It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural planning and design," Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that the 737 Max "was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do".
Boeing did not respond to a request for comment.
Aircraft are designed and tested to withstand substantial aerodynamic loads, but Paduanelli said a prolonged high-speed dive can place extreme strain on an airframe.
"This was nothing but a miracle that nothing was hurt apart from the captain, unfortunately, and that two pilots were onboard," Paduanelli said.
Details about al-Hammami's past have trickled out.
Royal Air Maroc told Reuters he did a three-month training with the airline in 2025 but his application to work there afterwards was rejected. Buckinghamshire New University in Britain said he did a distance-learning course in aviation management with the institution, but no pilot training.
An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said on Sunday that authorities there were investigating al-Hammami's "links to Australia". A source briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne. REUTERS

Off the Record: Teflon Rutte is on a mission to keep NATO together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:02:46 UTC
19:02:46 KST

Every week, Euronews' Chief Europe Editor Maria Tadeo breaks down the stories that made the week in Brussels and beyond. This week: her exclusive interview with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte — a man with Teflon skin.
Welcome back to Off the Record, after a hectic week in our newsroom.
The Brussels media loves to talk about itself, but we prefer to speak with the newsmakers. This week, Euronews hosted its first defence summit -and it made news. That's how I measure success and impact, and it's the only metric I care about. Talking about yourself is fine, but making news is better.
On stage, I sat down with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. I have covered the Dutchman for years, going back to his four terms as prime minister of the Netherlands, when he earned the nickname Teflon Mark.
In the green room, I told him that one of my craziest moments as a journalist in Brussels was a rough doorstep at the height of negotiations over the EU’s 2020 pandemic recovery fund: shaky cameras, people pushing, technicians tripping over each other as we waited for him to return to his hotel.
He remembered it in remarkable detail. He also reminded me that his Brussels hotel was the cheapest used by any of the leaders – others favoured the fancy Amigo – and reminisced about his post-summit walks from the Europa building back to his hotel. No official car, no police escort: the “cheapest and fastest” option.
That’s the thing about Mark Rutte. Most politicians have an ego, but he has always been very effective at pretending he doesn’t. He enjoys self-deprecation and, after a lifetime in politics, knows exactly when to switch on the charming small talk. Not bad for the often blunt Dutchman.
Rutte is approachable and leans into his caricature as a man who is simply there to serve. He understands that managing NATO in the age of Trump means cosying up to the US president – even at the expense of his own image – while preventing Russia’s war from spilling into allied territory.
If, by the end of his tenure, NATO is better funded and Washington is still on board, his “daddy” diplomacy – an unfortunate remark that still haunts him – will have been worth it. My guess is that he genuinely believes this is the right calculus, no matter the cringe.
On stage, he confirmed NATO responded to a provocative Russian letter sent to the alliance threatening to use its full arsenal – including nuclear weapons – if the territory of the Russian Federation came under threat. Moscow mentioned specifically its enclave of Kaliningrad, on the border with Lithuania, and a region where experts say the risk of a false-flag attack is real.
Playing the nuclear card is nothing new for Russia – the West rarely even utters the word – and the Kremlin often reaches for it when the battlefield situation is going badly. But that does not mean it can be ignored.
Rutte was clear: Russia should simply end the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats. He was on a mission to calm nerves after weeks of speculation about a deteriorating security picture on NATO’s eastern flank, particularly in the Baltic states, which have remained on high alert as hybrid attacks linked to Russia multiply. Rutte insisted – and that is part of his job – that there is “no imminent threat” to NATO territory.
This was a secretary-general determined to project an alliance that is strong and united. “So much stronger than Russia. It could never beat us,” he said.
The Kremlin knows it too, hence the sabre-rattling. Nor is the war going well for Russia: the battlefield is largely stuck. A Russia incapable of defeating Ukraine cannot take on NATO. Let’s be clear: it would be wiped out – perhaps we all would – but conventionally, this is not a fight Russia can win.
That doesn’t mean Moscow cannot inflict enormous damage. It has created a climate of paranoia across Europe, while pounding Ukraine in a sharp escalation of the air war. My colleague Sasha Vakulina, who was in Kyiv on assignment, was routinely woken by attacks. During one of our security check-ins, she said it felt worse than at any point this year. Winter is approaching, and Ukraine clearly needs more air defence.
When I pressed Rutte on licensing Patriot systems for Kyiv, he did not give me an answer. The US and Ukraine have been negotiating a deal that would allow Kyiv to produce the system and reduce its dependence on external deliveries. It would not be a game changer in the short term – Rutte is right about that – but this should have been ironed out at the NATO summit in Turkey over the summer.
Rutte is careful not to criticise Donald Trump and is prepared to defend the president’s intervention in Iran at great length – even if the war against the regime in Tehran has also inflicted pain on Ukraine.
Energy prices are surging around the world and the Strait of Hormuz remains shut, despite an agreement three months ago that was supposed to restore freedom of navigation. That promise has yet to materialise.
Trump is also cautioning Ukraine against hitting Russian energy facilities, which are instrumental in financing the war.
He has a point: cutting refinery capacity at a time of acute market stress does not help. But Zelenskyy is not the root cause of the energy squeeze. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is.
Rutte is remarkably measured in his words. He won't utter the smallest criticism of Trump. Instead, he calls on Europeans to do more to help unblock the situation.
Europe, he argues, should have been capable of dealing with Iran’s nuclear threat rather than leaving the US to do the heavy lifting. When I asked Rutte, a European, whether he really believed Europe could have done it, his answer was emphatic.
“It should be us doing it. It should be us taking care of the Houthis and the Red Sea, not the Americans.”
Under his watch, NATO allies have committed to spend 5% of gross domestic product on defence, of which 3.5% will go to hard military capabilities. It is an accomplishment, and let's be honest, it's in large part due to Trump’s return to the White House.
But as Europeans put real money on the table, another question is becoming unavoidable: what should they buy? Should Europe favour European arms and equipment, or continue spending much of that money on the American defence industry?
To me, the answer is clear: if Europe pays, Europe should benefit. Rutte, however, dismissed this as a “luxury debate” of the Brussels bubble. It isn’t. It is a fundamental question, and it goes to the heart of the emerging NATO 3.0 strategy.
The US is mulling a major shift in which Europe will have to take the lead in its own defence, pay more of the bill and deploy more of its troops, while Washington reduces its footprint to focus on the Pacific and China. That makes sense. It is a legitimate posture
But will the Trump administration allow Europeans to build up their own defence industries? If you listen to the words of the US ambassador to NATO, the answer is not quite. Will NATO 3.0 lead to an alliance of equals? I doubt it.
Mark Rutte believes he has learned to tame the beast. And he is convinced he is saving the alliance. If you ask me, he is doing the best job anyone can under the circumstances, and his Teflon skin is helping. It's cringey, but necessary.
Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here.

Ukraine’s FP-2 Strike Drones Destroy Russian Pantsir-S2 Air Defense System
Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 3, the Pantsir-S2 had been interfering with Ukrainian drone operations and preventing UAVs from reaching targets deeper behind Russian lines.
Video published by the channel shows a Ukrainian FP-2 striking the Russian air defense system at night. A fire subsequently broke out on the vehicle, followed by secondary explosions that destroyed much of the system.
Additional footage recorded nearby reportedly captured another FP-2 approaching the Pantsir-S2 after the initial strike. By that point, however, the system had already sustained extensive damage.
Images taken after the attack show the burned remains of the crew cabin and components of the rotating combat module scattered around the site.
Exilenova+ did not disclose where or exactly when the strike occurred. The channel said the Pantsir-S2 had been obstructing Ukrainian drones attempting to penetrate farther into Russia’s rear areas.
The Pantsir-S2 is an upgraded version of Russia’s Pantsir family of short-range air defense systems. It combines surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons and is designed to engage aircraft, missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles.
The S2 variant features an upgraded target-detection radar intended to improve the system’s ability to detect and track aerial targets.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian S-300 transport-loading vehicle carrying surface-to-air missiles, triggering a secondary detonation that completely burned out the vehicle.

Russia May Be Running Secret Mesh Relays Inside Kyiv to Guide Shahed Strikes
Russian forces may be using a small number of radio relay devices operating inside Kyiv to establish temporary communication links with Shahed-type attack drones and adjust their flight during strikes, according to Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Beskrestnov said on October 3 that he believes Russian Mesh radio relays are periodically activated in the Ukrainian capital, potentially providing a short-term control channel for incoming drones.
“Right now, I insist that enemy Mesh radio relays are being switched on in Kyiv, providing a temporary short-term control channel for Shaheds to adjust strikes. Not many. Perhaps one to three. Such relays are difficult to find, but they must be searched for,” Beskrestnov said.
According to Beskrestnov, the presence of such devices could complicate efforts to protect Kyiv using electronic warfare systems, as the drones could retain a communication channel during the final stage of an attack.
He pointed to previous Russian strikes in Kyiv, including an attack on a Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) building, as evidence supporting his assessment.
“At the moment of the strike, there were no other Shahed relay drones in the sky. I also analyzed other strikes on Kyiv bridges and the possibility of organizing long-range Mesh channels from Russia at those moments,” he said.
Beskrestnov also raised concerns about Russian access to information on the location of Ukrainian air defense systems deployed around critical infrastructure. Images showing air defense equipment on Kyiv bridges have circulated online, while such deployments are difficult to conceal because tens of thousands of people use the crossings daily, he said.
As long as Russia maintains the ability to control Shahed drones in real time, Beskrestnov said, both infrastructure and air defense systems could potentially be targeted.
He argued that accurately striking individual structural elements of a bridge, such as supports or cables, would require a stable control channel that remains active until the final stage of the drone’s flight.
Beskrestnov stressed that his assessment of Russian relay devices operating inside Kyiv remains a hypothesis. Ukrainian specialists continue examining debris from downed Russian drones for evidence of alternative communication systems.
“Let me be wrong in my opinion about the relays,” Beskrestnov said. “I also want to say that we carefully examine all debris. We do not find any other ‘secret’ means of communication.”
The assessment follows earlier concerns over relay infrastructure outside Ukraine. On September 29, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said Belarus periodically activates relay systems that can strengthen communications for Russian drones during attacks on Ukraine.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko to dismantle relay equipment that Kyiv said was being used to support Russian drone operations.
