What’s going to happen in the midterm election? Find out here. (Maybe)
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Two of the country’s top political prognosticators see Democrats likely seizing the House and quite possibly the Senate.
- The guardrails Republicans were counting on to stem their November losses don’t seem to be holding.
There are few people, if any, who’ve tracked U.S. elections for longer or in greater depth than Charlie Cook.
Ever since 1984, when he started his eponymous political newsletter, Cook and his stellar crew of nonpartisan analysts have plumbed many thousands of races — for president, Congress, governor — following the money, sussing out the candidates, watching their ads and assaying the campaign landscape at a granular level.
Cook calls this midterm election the strangest he’s ever seen.
What appeared to be a fairly normal election for a president halfway through his term — a probable setback, as unhappy voters register their discontent — has the potential, Cook said, to turn into a disaster for Republicans. Big losses aren’t rare for the party in the White House. Democrats picked up 41 House seats in President Trump’s last midterm election, in 2018.
What’s unusual, Cook suggested, is the prospect of big Democratic gains when Republicans started out this election season with so many advantages. (And that was before the GOP set off on a gerrymandering jag at Trump’s behest.)
The four-seat gain Democrats need to win control once seemed all but out of reach. Odds are looking up, though the party still faces a tough path, with toss-up races in a half dozen (mostly red) states.
Roughly two-thirds of the Senate seats up in November are in states Trump carried in 2024. Five of the seven toss-up races are in states Trump won, several by double digits.
On the House side, Republicans maintain control by an exceedingly narrow margin, meaning there aren’t a lot of low-hanging districts for Democrats to aim for. As Cook rightly noted, “A party cannot lose a seat they don’t have.”
But Trump’s deteriorating approval rating, an unpopular war, persistent inflation and the president’s egotistical indulgences have jeopardized a number of GOP-held seats that normally would be automatic wins, including contests in such Republican strongholds as Alaska, Florida, Iowa, Ohio and even Texas.
“I’m not a meteorologist, but it’s kind of like three competing weather fronts collided,” Cook said. “One was Iran and gasoline, diesel prices going sky high ... Then there’s trade, tariffs, overall non-energy cost of living, tariff impact on farmers. And then the third is kind of the catch-all and it’s everything from ballrooms, reflecting pools, arches, vaccines, Medicaid cuts.”
We’ll get to predictions in a moment. (Patience, dear reader.)
First, let’s hear from Nathan Gonzales, another longtime election handicapper. He’s been tracking political contests nationwide for more than 25 years and edits and publishes Inside Elections — formerly the Rothenberg Political Report — another nonpartisan field guide to campaigns. Like Cook, he traffics in clear-eyed, dispassionate analysis, not partisan wish-casting or political spin.
Gonzales, too, sees a bad moon rising for Republicans.
Trump’s performance — his approval rating is flirting with record lows — “has inspired Democrats, turned off independents and created a group of apathetic Republicans,” Gonzales said, “and those are the ingredients for a good or great Democratic year.”
He noted Democrats don’t need a big wave to seize control of the House. A pickup of just three seats would flip the House, marking the seventh straight midterm election in which one chamber or the other changed partisan hands.
(For the record, there is no authoritative definition of a wave election, though it’s generally agreed the term applies to an election in which one party or the other gains a large and lopsided number of House and Senate seats.)
It’s beginning to feel a lot like 2006, Gonzales said.
“We had an unpopular Republican president, a war in the Middle East that drove up gas prices. Some members on Capitol Hill that were behaving badly,” Gonzales recalled. “I remember talking to Republicans after the fact and they admitted that, while they thought they had great research on Democratic candidates and they had a fundraising advantage, voters just didn’t care. Voters weren’t in the mood to listen to what they were saying about Democrats because they were so frustrated with what was going on with the status quo and the direction of the country.”
In that election, at the midpoint of President George W. Bush’s second term, Democrats gained six seats to take control of the Senate and netted 31 in the House, allowing the installation of Nancy Pelosi as the first female speaker in history. “A thumpin’,” Bush called it.
So, 2026.
Gonzales and his team of experts believe the House is most likely gone for Republicans, forecasting a Democratic gain of seven to 15 seats, unless the bottom falls out for the GOP and their losses climb much higher.
In the Senate, where Democrats need to pick up four seats to take control, Gonzales sees the chamber teetering on a knife’s edge, forecasting a Democratic gain of three to five seats.
“It’s too late to fundamentally change the trajectory of this election,” Gonzales said. “But if Republicans can boost Republican turnout, it might be enough to save the Senate.”
Stepping in for a complacent Congress, Democratic attorneys general are ready to fight efforts to undermine or overturn the Nov. 3 election. “We need to stay vigilant,” says Colorado’s Phil Weiser.
For his part, Cook agrees that Mike Johnson may be nearing the end of his speakership. The best-case scenario for the GOP would be keeping its losses to 25 House seats or less, Cook said, which is right around the average for midterm elections going back well over half a century.
“It starts getting into eyebrow-raising territory if it gets north of 35,” Cook said, “because that shouldn’t be possible with the few competitive districts we have now.”
As for the Senate, he suggested the best Republicans can hope for is a net loss of two seats, keeping the GOP barely in control. (A loss of three would mean a 50-50 split, leaving Vice President JD Vance poised to be the tiebreaker on close votes — and wouldn’t he love having to drop off the 2028 campaign trail to be on hand, just in case.)
Of course, there’s still an election to be held, votes to be cast and ballots to be counted.
Blue wave, tsunami or a pale sapphire puddle?
We’ll know in a little more than four weeks.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Sunday called for a thorough investigation into a series of hacking attacks at major banks and other financial institutions that led to data leaks, according to the Yonhap News Agency.
The country has recently witnessed hacking attacks targeting Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Shinhan Bank, compromising customer information.

Financial Services Commission Chairman Lee Eog-weon and Lee Chan-jin, governor of the Financial Supervisory Service, also convened for an emergency meeting to discuss the hackings with the heads of the affected firms.
"We have detected multiple security breaches across various sectors in a short span of time, not only at major commercial banks but also at savings banks and specialized credit finance firms," the FSC chief said at the meeting.
He said that while no sensitive information that could be used for unauthorized payments appeared to have been compromised, he urged the financial sector to maintain the "highest level of vigilance," warning that the leaked information could still be exploited for voice phishing or other scams.
He also did not rule out the possibility that AI tools were used in the hacking attacks.

“The war is not over. Planes carrying Zionists, Americans and other infidels fighting Islam are still circling the skies and can be struck, as happened on September 11 and September 30,” the article threatened.

“America and the Zionists have far more enemies today than they did in the past,” the article said. “Perhaps someone who does not believe in God will strike them, and his action will ultimately benefit Islam. The day will come when America’s evil empire will be destroyed.”
Despite the Al-Qaeda publication, no evidence has emerged that al-Hammami acted on orders from the terrorist organization or under the direction of any other outside party. Israeli security officials believe al-Hamami underwent a process of “Islamic radicalization” and acted on his own. However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump have both suggested that the co-pilot was directed by others.
From Syria to Australia to flydubai
Media reports provide a general picture of al-Hammami’s background. The Wall Street Journal reported that he grew up in Syria during the civil war that began in 2011, where his radicalization process apparently began.
According to Britain’s Guardian, the co-pilot later received a visa to Australia. A Sydney newspaper reported that he studied engineering in Melbourne for three years, until his visa was revoked.
He subsequently served as a pilot for Oman Air, although this has not been officially confirmed. After extremist materials were found in his possession, he was suspended from his position in 2024 and fired about a year later. He was hired by flydubai in early 2026.
ABC News reported that he is cooperating with investigators in the United Arab Emirates, where authorities have already declared the incident an act of terrorism. He testified that he had planned to crash the plane.
Investigation into Israel’s failure: 'There is no 100% security'
Whatever al-Hammami’s motives, the central question remains how a pilot holding Omani citizenship, whose background should have raised multiple red flags, was still allowed to fly to Israel. The agencies involved in conducting background checks on foreign crew members aboard flights to Israel are already blaming one another.
Prime Minister Netanyahu acknowledged that there had been a “loophole” that al-Hammami managed to exploit: A citizen of a country with no formal relations with Israel had been authorized to fly an aircraft into the country.
ynet has learned that investigators are examining whether al-Hammami had previously entered Israel as a pilot. That contradicts initial briefings immediately after the attempted attack, when Israeli officials denied that possibility. Transportation Ministry officials did not deny that al-Hammami may have flown to Israel before but said they currently have no information confirming it.
The Transportation Ministry, the body responsible for security checks, said it is not an intelligence agency and did not have the intelligence capabilities needed to vet the names of pilots and crew members on flights arriving in Israel.
Senior ministry officials said data on crew members arriving in Israel aboard foreign flights had not been retrieved or checked for about two years. Transportation Minister Miri Regev has already placed responsibility for the failure on the Mossad and the Israel Tax Authority.
During a briefing for reporters, the Civil Aviation Authority had no answer when asked how many pilots from hostile countries may already have landed in Israel and how passengers could be confident about boarding a foreign airline.
“We estimate there were none. But we have no certainty. There is no such thing as 100% security. Only if we shut down aviation entirely will everything be safe. We rely on local security.”

A new political storm is brewing for Erdogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:51:35 UTC
18:51:35 KST

A new political storm is brewing for Erdogan
Until recently, it seemed that a split within the main, long-established opposition party (founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the architect of modern Türkiye) would play into the hands of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Following a court ruling that removed Ozgur Ozel as the leader of the Republican People’s Party (CHP), his supporters broke away to form the Yeni Parti (New Party). The opposition suddenly found itself with two headquarters, two leaders, and a dispute over who rightfully owns its political legacy. However, September polls showed that a significant number of voters had followed Ozel. Yeni Parti took second place in surveys conducted by ASAL and GENAR. While it still has a long way to go to catch up with the ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Parti), the new movement can no longer be dismissed.
According to ASAL, if parliamentary elections were held, 33.8% of respondents would support AK Parti, while 23.6% would back Yeni Parti; that’s a gap of 10.2 percentage points. GENAR put support for the ruling party at 36.1% and Ozel’s party at 21.6%, recording a difference of 14.5 points. In both instances, AK Parti retained the top spot. Yet, for a political force established only in late July, the result is remarkable – especially considering that the CHP, under the leadership of Kemal Kilicdaroglu, garnered only about 6% in the same polls. The leadership of the party changed due to the court ruling, but judging by the surveys, the party failed to retain the bulk of its voter base.
To understand the origins of Yeni Parti, one must look back at the events of this spring. In May, a court annulled the results of the 2023 CHP congress – where Ozel had been elected chairman – and reinstated his predecessor, Kilicdaroglu. Ozel’s supporters viewed the ruling as interference in the affairs of the opposition. Turkish authorities deny allegations of pressuring the court and insist on the judiciary’s independence. The confrontation lasted several weeks until Ozel and 90 opposition MPs left the CHP. On July 24, they announced the formation of a new party. It immediately secured 91 parliamentary seats, becoming the largest opposition faction.
This demonstrates the unique nature of the current crisis. Yeni Parti emerged from a split within the opposition, yet it did not have to start from scratch. Ozel was supported by MPs, prominent politicians, and a portion of the organizational network that had worked for the CHP. He also retained the experience gained from the campaigns that delivered the opposition’s victory in the 2024 local elections. The new party allows the team to stay together and continue the fight, even though legal and political ties to the former party have been severed. For voters who supported Ozel prior to the court ruling, the shift to Yeni Parti appears logical.
At the same time, the September poll results also point to the party’s growth limitations. Erdogan’s AK Party maintains the lead in both polls, with a margin exceeding 14 points in the GENAR survey. It is too early for Erdogan’s supporters to speak of defeat, or for his opponents to anticipate an imminent change of power. However, the Turkish leader now faces a less favorable situation than might have emerged immediately after the CHP split. Erdogan’s main opponent did not just disappear along with his former party post, contrary to the predictions of many domestic experts. Ozel managed to shift the confrontation to a new arena and to quickly reclaim the role of parliamentary opposition leader.
The party’s future will depend on whether it can reach beyond the CHP’s traditional base of supporters. For now, the September figures can be interpreted either as a success for Ozel or as a redistribution of votes within the opposition. For example, a July study by GENAR put support for the CHP at 15.4% and for the then-nascent Yeni Parti at 14.5%. By September, the balance had shifted: Ozel’s party polled at 21.6%, while the CHP stood at 6.6%. These figures indicate voter migration between the two political forces. However, further polls and, ultimately, elections are necessary to confirm a sustained expansion of the opposition’s overall electoral base.
There is another issue that party ratings alone cannot resolve: Who will challenge Erdogan in the 2028 presidential election? Following the creation of Yeni Parti, Ozel reaffirmed his support for Ekrem Imamoglu – the mayor of Istanbul and a politician popular among Turkish youth – who is currently under arrest and facing legal proceedings. While Imamoglu remains a pivotal figure for opposition voters, his potential candidacy is complicated by a court case and the invalidation of his university degree, a requirement for presidential candidates. Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas is also mentioned as a potential contender. While Yeni Parti boasts a prominent leader and a parliamentary faction, it is unclear who will be the opposition’s presidential candidate. And in a presidential campaign, this choice could prove far more significant than monthly fluctuations in party ratings.
Another challenge is that the Turkish opposition extends beyond Ozel’s party. Kilicdaroglu’s CHP party remains in parliament, while the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the nationalist IYI Party led by Meral Aksener, and other forces also have their supporters. While all of them may oppose the incumbent president, they have different supporters and differing visions for the country’s future. Parliamentary elections allow each party to vie for its share of the vote; winning the presidency, however, requires an agreement capable of persuading the supporters of several parties to back a single candidate. The opposition already encountered this problem in 2023 – and ultimately suffered defeat.
Despite certain public fatigue regarding his long tenure, Erdogan retains significant political advantages. The ruling AK Party remains the leading party in the two abovementioned polls. Together with its ally, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP, or Grey Wolves), it commands a stable electoral base, and the president continues to set the agenda for national politics. It is too early to say that Erdogan is in serious trouble, as the AK Party retains the top position in both surveys. However, Ozel has managed to retain a significant portion of the opposition electorate following the split within the CHP. If Ozel manages to attract voters who did not previously support the CHP, Erdogan will face a formidable rival.
The economic situation adds further tension to the situation. In September, the Turkish market faced a crisis involving investment funds and a sharp drop in asset prices. Against this backdrop, Zeynel Emre, a representative of Yeni Parti, leveled accusations regarding stock market transactions against AK Party Deputy Chairperson Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband. Kaya requested to be relieved of her party duties pending the investigation. While the allegations still require verification, the political impact is already evident: The new party is striving to position itself not only as a defender of its own rights following the split within the CHP but also as a force capable of posing uncomfortable questions to the authorities.
Yeni Parti has also encountered another problem: a dispute over its name. Another political organization, the Yenilik Partisi (Innovation Party), declared that the Yeni Parti name is too similar to its own and appealed to the prosecutor’s office. The matter eventually reached the Constitutional Court. On September 29, the court granted Yeni Parti 30 days to prepare its objections. No final decision regarding the name has been reached yet.
Looking ahead, Turkish politics faces another pressing issue: the upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for 2028. The question of whether Erdogan can participate in the presidential race hinges on the timing of the election and constitutional regulations. An early vote called by parliament would allow him to run for another term, but such a decision requires a majority of 360 out of 600 deputies. The ruling bloc lacks the votes to resolve this matter unilaterally. Consequently, the outcome will depend not only on voter sentiment but also on negotiations between parties – including those currently on opposite sides of the political divide.
The latest surveys only show that following a painful rift within the opposition, Ozel has retained significant support. They do not reveal whether the Yeni Parti can catch up with the ruling AK Parti, find a presidential candidate acceptable to other forces, or bring about a change of power. For Erdogan, this means that he will have to monitor his new rival more closely. And for Ozel, it marks the beginning of a new phase in which he will have to transform his rapidly gained popularity into lasting political influence. Put together, these factors will determine the outcome of their standoff.

Costa’s coffee shops return to profit with iced drinks and matcha on the menu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:50:28 UTC
18:50:28 KST

Costa’s main coffee shop arm has returned to an operating profit after revamping its high street outlets and broadening its menu with iced drinks, matcha and fresher pastries.
The chain, which has 2,700 outlets in the UK and Ireland out of 4,000 globally, and employs about 20,000 people, also opened a net 50 new outlets in the UK last year – its first net increase in several years.
It plans a further 50 new UK outlets this year, including more drive-throughs and high street outlets.
Demand from younger consumers for decaffeinated coffee and other options is driving sales growth amid concerns about drinking caffeine in the afternoon, while there is heavy competition on classic coffees from companies such as Greggs, Gail’s, Caffè Nero and numerous smaller operators. Costa says it is now the largest seller of matcha via cafes in the UK.
The Costa Ltd arm made an operating profit of £20m in the year to 31 December 2025 after losses of £13.5m in 2024 and £5.8m the year before, according to accounts filed at Companies House. Revenues rose 5% to almost £1.3bn compared with 1% growth in 2024.
Philippe Schaillee, the chief executive of Costa, said the chain had experienced the strongest growth in visits in a decade.
Sipping a Velvetino, a low-calorie iced coffee popular with younger drinkers, Schaillee said: “The coffee shop is increasingly a destination for morning and afternoon. People not only want caffeine but iced herbal teas and those drinks that people will drink in the afternoon and evening.”
Showing off Costa’s new headquarters in St Albans, Hertfordshire, which will have space for 300 workers when it opens in January, he said it “really signals our confidence in the business”.
Costa plans to remodel about 250 stores a year after updating more than 1,200 of 1,700 company-owned outlets. That includes adding more digital self-order kiosks, which are already in 200 UK outlets.
The group is also selling more Podio office coffee machines, which launched in May and are intended to be “a barista in your office”.
Schaillee said Costa was already the UK’s third biggest brand in home coffee machines, and said the potential there was “limitless”.
Costa’s campaign to flag its strong performance comes after its owner, Coca-Cola, in February officially confirmed it had abandoned plans to sell the chain after bids failed to meet its expectations.
Coca-Cola had high hopes for Britain’s largest coffee chain when it bought it for £3.9bn in 2018 from Whitbread, the owner of Premier Inn hotels.
However, since then the chain has struggled in the face of rising costs, particularly the increase in coffee bean prices, and competition on UK high streets.
Schaillee said coffee production – and potentially prices – remained high and could be affected by the El Niño global climate phenomenon, which is affecting coffee and cocoa growers in Latin and South America. “We need to be prepared for that,” he said.

The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:46:48 UTC
18:46:48 KST

The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
A team of book enthusiasts in Gaza is trying to keep Palestine’s literary heritage alive amid a genocide.
Aya al-Shawa, 10, sits in sixth grade at a school in northern Gaza, holding a book she recently received and what is now one of her most treasured possessions.
Before it reached Aya’s hands, it had a difficult journey. It once sat on a bookshelf before an Israeli attack demolished the building it was housed in, leaving it buried beneath the rubble. Then one day someone recovered it, cleaned it, sorted its pages and repaired them. The book then found its way to a new reader.
Amid the widespread destruction in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, books – one of the most vulnerable of all items – have become a rare commodity.
About 98 percent of school buildings in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed or damaged, according to UNICEF.
With approximately 700,000 children in Gaza deprived of regular in-person education since the war began in October 2023, books have also become a vital way for children to reconnect with learning.
UNESCO has documented widespread damage to cultural sites and institutions in Gaza, including libraries. With a “ceasefire” in Gaza since October 2025, during which there has been a relative decrease in Israeli bombing, books have begun to take a second life.
Mohammed Saad, 54, from Beit Lahiya, has spent more than 35 years collecting books, and before the war, he estimated that he had between 50,000 and 100,000 titles in his library.
On December 7, 2023, the library was destroyed.
After being displaced 16 times in total, Saad returned to Beit Lahiya again to see what remained of his book collection. From the rubble of his home, he began to pull out the surviving books.
“I risked my life to save these books from beneath the rubble,” Saad said.
He managed to recover about 12,000 books from the rubble and moved what he could to Deir el-Balah, where he erected a tent and established a library called Athar, meaning “impact” but also relating to antiquities or historical relics.
From the tent, Saad and his son Mohammed began cleaning and repairing the thousands of books in their possession.
But Saad’s goal is not only to save the books from damage. He also wants them to reach people, particularly children.
The library now sees children coming every day, looking for stories that might help them find some escape from their hardships.
They buy some of them at symbolic prices ranging from 5 shekels to 15 shekels ($1.63-$4.89), given that books have become unaffordable for most families.
Giving children access to books is a key reason for saving them in the first place: to keep knowledge accessible and give them a path back to reading and learning despite war and displacement.
But the books Saad rescues still face other dangers. Inside the tent, there is little protection from the sun, heat, humidity and rain.
“I saved them from beneath the rubble and from the fire. Today, I cannot save them from the rain,” Saad said.
Elsewhere, Omar Hamad, 30, a displaced person from Beit Hanoon in northern Gaza, has also been searching for destroyed libraries for books.
He traced the locations of libraries in northern Gaza and Gaza City and contacted their owners. So far, Hamad says, he and his team have extricated some 3,000 books.
Not all of the books came from rubble. Some were donated by the families of people who were killed and had private libraries, while the team bought or reprinted others.
Among the books Omar rescued was The Catastrophe of Palestine, printed in 1956. He found it in the destroyed Islamic University of Gaza library, where books were scattered among the rubble.
Retrieving the book was only the beginning of his task.
Omar and his friend Ibrahim cleaned the books, removed dust and traces of rubble, sorted and arranged the pages, and tried to repair whatever they could.
When a book required more specialised restoration, he turned to Jameel Mikdad, 71, in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
Mikdad has worked in bookbinding and book repair for more than 45 years. His library and printing shop were destroyed during the war, but he continued working with limited resources, using his experience to rearrange pages, glue torn sections of the works, sew books and rebind them.
There is no single cost for repairing a book; it depends on the extent of the damage and the materials required. But the cost of materials has risen sharply.
Mikdad says a 3kg (6.6-pound) container of white glue cost 30-35 shekels ($9.78-11.48) before the war. Its price has now risen to 450-500 shekels ($146.74-163.05) due to Israel’s siege on Gaza and the damage caused by the war.
Repairing a damaged book can take two days to a week, depending on its condition. Sometimes the cost of repair can exceed the value of the book.
Not every book can be repaired. Omar says some of the books they found were 80 or 90 percent damaged and had to be left behind because they were no longer repairable or restorable.
At other times, they kept books that could no longer be read because bullet holes or fire damage made them witnesses to the genocide in Gaza.
“We took them with us so they could remain witnesses to this crime,” Omar said.
For the books that can be saved, Omar does not want them to remain on library shelves but to be distributed throughout a population known for their love of literature.
At the Phoenix Library, books are lent rather than sold. Readers can borrow one or two books a week after paying a refundable deposit of 50 shekels ($16.30). The library has books on literature, medicine, law, history, economics and science. There are also books for children and for students related to specialised fields of study.
Omar also organises initiatives to deliver books to students at schools, so they can be used once again for their original purpose: reading and learning.
Aya, 10, ends up with one such book: The Adventure of the Empty House by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.
She sees the novel as a way of continuing her education when schools, often taking the form of a crowded tent, struggle to resume their role in teaching children.
And so, the journey of the book is complete.
It began on a shelf in a home or library in Gaza before the building was levelled in one of Israel’s thousands of air raids. It then remained beneath the rubble for months before being rescued by a person who risked their life to rescue lost books. It was then passed on to a restoration expert who repaired and cleaned it. Finally, it ended up in the hands of a student who will continue to love learning and overcome Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Ultimately, the book survived destruction and returned to its first purpose: to be opened and read.

South Korea investigates data leaks following cyberattacks on banks
Kyiv • UNN
The President of South Korea ordered an investigation into data leaks at banks and government institutions. The regulator is strengthening cybersecurity due to possible AI attacks.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung ordered a thorough investigation into recent leaks of personal data at banks, financial companies and government institutions. Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
Lee Eog-won, chairman of South Korea’s Financial Services Commission, held an emergency meeting on October 4 with representatives of the financial industry, regulators and heads of institutions that may have been affected by cyberattacks.
According to available information, he urged the financial sector to respond to threats with the highest level of vigilance. Lee said the authorities could not rule out the use of artificial intelligence in the attacks. He proposed an approach involving “AI-protected AI attacks,” as well as updating the financial sector’s cybersecurity system.
The Sunday meeting followed similar talks on Friday, when the FSC said that Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and others had reported cyberattacks, while the Yonhap news agency reported that Hana Bank and Woori Bank had also been affected by breaches. The banks could not immediately be reached for comment on Sunday outside normal working hours. The financial regulator said the authorities had launched on-site investigations after Shinhan Bank reported a breach on September 30, and had since expanded the investigation to other reported incidents
Also, according to available data, the regulator instructed financial institutions to conduct comprehensive security checks, strengthen access controls, minimize external access to systems and enhance consumer protection measures.
It is also noted that attack methods, internet protocol addresses and other threat information will be rapidly shared throughout the industry to prevent further incidents
At the same time, regulators believe that the attacks may not have been directed at one specific institution, but rather involved the simultaneous scanning of several financial companies to search for vulnerabilities.

Russia struck Kyiv's Northern Bridge with a drone again on 4 October, the second hit on the crossing in two days, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The attack damaged a heating main and rerouted public transport, as overnight and morning strikes also hit Kyiv Oblast, Dnipro, and Sumy, where one person was killed.
Russia's air attacks on Ukrainian cities are daily, and in recent days they have hit a Kyiv school sheltering children and turned supermarkets into targets. Strikes on the crossings between the capital's two banks add another layer: they disrupt how millions of people move through the city every day.
A crater on the Northern Bridge, no hot water across the river
The drone hit the bridge's roadway, and videos posted by local channels showed a crater, Liga reported. The strike also damaged a heating main, cutting hot water in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district on the left bank, Klitschko wrote. Repair crews are working to restore it, he added.
Kyiv's transport operator Kyivpastrans cut trolleybus routes short of the river. Routes 29, 30, 31, and 47 now run from the left bank only to Darnytsia Square, and routes 29, 30, and 31 run from the right bank only to Pochaina metro station. Buses 21, 73, 101, and 114 run only to Darnytsia Square because the bridge is closed to traffic.
Russia first hit the Northern Bridge on 3 October, damaging its roadway and trolleybus lines. Two people were injured, and one of them was hospitalized, Klitschko said. A day earlier, repeated drone strikes hit the Southern Bridge and forced its closure. Overnight on 4 October, drone debris also fell on two locations in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, Klitschko reported.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
Ukraine's government has already begun work on earth dams and pontoon crossings in case the city's Dnipro bridges are knocked out, Restoration Minister Mykola Kalashnyk told Suspilne.
The strike came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv. Ukraine and Germany would reach important agreements during the visit, Zelenskyy said. This week alone, Russia launched more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 guided bombs, and 25 missiles at Ukraine, more than 800 of the drones jet-powered, he added.
135 drones overnight
Russia launched 135 attack drones at Ukraine overnight, 52 of them jet-powered Shaheds, Ukraine's Air Force reported. By 08:30, air defenses had downed or suppressed 123 drones and two Banderol or Dan-T missiles. Strikes hit five locations, and debris fell on five more.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian drones damaged six detached houses, a car, a church, a primary school, a café, and a medical facility in Boryspil Raion, the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said. No one was killed or injured.
Dnipro and Sumy
Russia attacked a communications company's building in central Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported.
"The whole street there is covered in broken glass, debris, and branches," Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov wrote, adding that nearby homes and schools escaped damage.
In Sumy, Russian drones struck an ordinary medical supplies warehouse and killed one person, Zelenskyy said. Strikes across the city injured seven people, two of them seriously, the Sumy city council said. The attack also damaged gas networks and left 70 apartments without gas.

Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus after an outcry over the school’s handling of a student’s rape allegations, the Ivy League school’s president has said.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman, who alleges she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has prompted outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life,” Kotlikoff said.
“At their best, these organisations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility.“
The university would seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of others”.
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times has reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But “we must do better”, Kotlikoff said. “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
He vowed that university officials would “be more transparent” about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but he did not detail specific initiatives that the university would take. “In the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our community to ask questions and hear directly from university leadership,” he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.

Russian MiG-29 jet and the Pantsir air defense meant to protect it both hit in Ukrainian strike on Kursk airfield

‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
Ukrainian officials are embezzling foreign financial aid, former Polish Prime Minister Leszek Miller has said, adding that Kiev’s backers are well aware of the corruption but prefer not to ask questions.
Speaking on the ‘Jankowski Kontra’ podcast on Polsat News on Saturday, Miller called for suspending aid to Ukraine until Kiev accounts for previously supplied weapons and funds.
“Nobody’s asking what happened to the 300 tanks we sent in the first phase. What happened to the heavy equipment, the lighter equipment... Nobody’s asking what happened to the billions of euros we donated. Mr. Zelensky simply comes and says, ‘Give it’, and we give it,” Miller stated.
Asked whether he suspected that funds transferred to Ukraine were being embezzled, Miller replied: “Of course, everyone knows it.”The veteran politician argued that Warsaw should demand an accounting of how its assistance has been used and halt further support if Kiev fails to provide one.
“This is a fundamental issue: I’ll lend you the money, but give me a report on what you did with the previous installment,” Miller stated. “Without that help, there is no Ukraine… But we are not a country that is overflowing with wealth… We have obligations to our own citizens, and we cannot simply throw away money and equipment indiscriminately.”
Poland has been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Russia, pouring billions into military, financial and humanitarian aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western supplies. Yet relations have increasingly soured over Kiev’s honoring of Ukrainian Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which UPA militants, linked to the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), killed at least 100,000 ethnic Poles.

In the aftermath, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
Relations have also been strained by mounting opposition to Ukrainian refugees. A July CBOS survey found that 52% of Poles now opposed accepting them, against 42% in favor – a sharp reversal from the overwhelming support seen after Kiev’s conflict with Moscow escalated in 2022. Tensions deepened earlier this month after a 31-year-old Ukrainian man stabbed five people at a Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, killing a priest.
Poland is also not alone in questioning funding for Kiev. Despite receiving billions in Western assistance over the past four years, Ukraine faces a severe cash squeeze and has been pressing European backers for more money. But a string of high-level graft scandals has heightened scrutiny in Brussels, the largest of which centers on an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Vladimir Zelensky.
Western-backed investigators have uncovered multiple other graft schemes involving Ukrainian officials, including one reported earlier this month in which they allegedly embezzled more than $3 million through the delivery of used Soviet-made metro cars donated by Poland.
Against that backdrop, the EU this week rebuffed Kiev’s bid to fast-track its latest €90 billion support loan, making clear that further funds depend on Ukraine delivering promised anti-corruption and governance reforms.

One Palestinian killed, 15 others wounded in Israel's Gaza truce violations

Hosni Nedim and Serdar Dincel
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
Archive
GAZA CITY, Palestine / ISTANBUL
The Israeli army's renewed attacks in the Gaza Strip killed a Palestinian and injured 15 others on Sunday, medical sources told Anadolu.
The attacks come despite a ceasefire deal that has been in place in the strip since Oct. 10, 2025.
One Palestinian was killed and 10 others injured in an Israeli airstrike targeting a vehicle in Al-Hawouz, central Gaza, south of Deir al-Balah, the sources said.
Five others were wounded, including one in critical condition, when Israeli shelling targeted an individual passing near the Engineers Syndicate headquarters in northwest Gaza City, they added.
Earlier on Sunday, Israeli artillery shelled eastern areas of the Al-Maghazi refugee camp and southern parts of the city of Khan Younis, according to eyewitnesses.
Witnesses said Israeli military vehicles also opened fire toward the southern and eastern areas of Khan Younis and the northern parts of Beit Lahia, while naval vessels fired toward the coastlines of Rafah and Gaza City.
The Israeli army also carried out large-scale demolitions of buildings and facilities in eastern Gaza City, local sources reported.
As of Saturday, Israeli violations of last year’s ceasefire agreement have killed at least 1,445 Palestinians and injured 5,072 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, also destroying about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.

Iran sitting volleyball target fifth straight gold in Nagoya: Bigdeli
TEHRAN - Iran’s men’s sitting volleyball team captain Sadegh Bigdeli is confident that Team Melli can extend their remarkable record by winning a fifth consecutive gold medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya.
Iran have won the sitting volleyball title at all four previous editions of the Asian Para Games, and Bigdeli says the team will travel to Nagoya determined to maintain that unbeaten record.
The national team have been going through a period of transition in recent months, with several changes gradually being made to the squad. Despite the changes, Bigdeli believes the team are in good shape ahead of the competition.
“The training camp before our departure went very well,” Bigdeli said in an exclusive interview. “The players arrived in good physical condition, and we used the camp to complete the final stages of our conditioning work and finalize our line-up for the tournament. Thankfully, everyone is fit and there are no injury concerns.”
Iran will hold one final training camp in Tehran before heading to Japan. The camp is scheduled to begin on Oct. 5 and will provide the coaching staff with an opportunity to work on the final details before the competition gets underway.
“The coaches will use this opportunity to go over the final tactical and technical points with the players. It is our last chance to prepare before travelling to Nagoya, and hopefully we can arrive at the Games at 100 percent.”
Asked about Iran’s strongest opponents in Nagoya, Bigdeli pointed to Kazakhstan as the team most capable of challenging the defending champions.
“We recently had a joint training camp with Iraq in Iran, and I have to say that their team have improved significantly compared with the past,” the Iran captain said. “But our main rivals are Kazakhstan. They are the bronze medalists from the World Championships and are a very strong team.”
“We are going to the Asian Para Games to win our fifth gold medal,” he said. “We hope to return home with the gold and make the people of Iran happy.”
For Iran, Nagoya represents more than just another tournament. The team will be seeking to preserve one of the most impressive records in Asian Para sport. With a changing squad, stronger opposition and the pressure that comes with being the defending champions, the challenge may be greater than in previous editions. But Bigdeli’s message is clear: Iran are going to Nagoya with one target — a fifth consecutive Asian Para Games title.

FlyDubai captain said he had “one more fight left in me” and opened cockpit door
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:37:12 UTC
18:37:12 KST

FlyDubai hero captain Smit Machchhar described to Israeli prime minister Benjanim Netanyahu how the attack started and how he managed to finally open the cockpit door after nearly losing his vision under the co-pilot’s repeated blows.
The FlyDubai hero captain revealed new details of his fight to save the passengers aboard flight FZ1073 in an emotional telephone conversation with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, released by his office on Saturday evening.
Captain Smit Machchhar told Netanyahu he felt he had “one more fight left” in him when in a critical state he reached for the cockpit door once again to save the 174 passengers and 6 crew members, while the co-pilot kept attacking him and putting the aircraft in a steep defence.
He described how the attack started saying that the co-pilot asked to pray in the cockpit which he did not consider an unusual request and “and out of respect for him, I didn’t look back.”
“A few minutes later, I felt a strong impact and thought something had happened to the plane. But then I was hit again and realized it was him. I opened the cockpit door once, but he closed it, and I fell to the floor,” the captain said.
Machchhar said his vision became badly blurred and he felt how the aircraft went into a steep descent. He tried to open the cockpit door once again, but the co-pilot kept closing it while passengers were trying to get in using the access code.
Netanyahu asked him if the door was closed with a pin mechanism and the captain answered that on the inside of the cockpit the door had a twist handle and that from the outside it could be opened with a code.
Machchhar remembered hearing the whooshing sound of the aircraft plunging downwards and the passengers screaming.
Realising what was happening, he told Netanyahu how he reached for the internal twist handle and with “a sharp, quick turn” managed to finally open the door, letting the passengers in who subdued the co-pilot and stabilised the plane.
The Israeli prime minister told him that he is a hero with “an unbelievable courage, inviting him and Indian prime minister Narendra Modi to light a celebratory flame on Israel’s next Independence Day, the highest honour usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
“You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel, and you are a hero of the entire world. I wish you a very speedy and complete recovery," Netanyahu told captain Machchhar.
Israeli Ambassador to the UAE Yossi Shelley was at his bedside during the call and together with Netanyahu invited Machchhar and his family to visit Israel as soon as he is able, to receive the embrace and love that the entire country wants to give him.
Dubai's Crown Prince and UAE Minister of Defence Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid also visited Machchhar in hospital hailing the captain’s bravery, stating that he “embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life.”
“From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. We are proud that he is part of our team, part of the story of our nation and part of what the UAE stands for a nation of compassion, a nation of peace and a nation of life,” Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed said.
In a new development on Sunday, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that the FlyDubai flight copilot, named by multiple media outlets as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, studied aviation at the UK-based Buckinghamshire New University.
The Telegraph said that during his time at the university, al-Hammami commented in social media posts that women should be “stomped on” and praised giving a woman a “pre-emptive slap.” He also appeared to praise Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Telegraph said.
The co-pilot used a crash axe against the captain and “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack”, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said on Saturday, while the UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash called the incident "a dangerous terrorist act".

Who are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered Flydubai flight 1073?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:36:47 UTC
18:36:47 KST

Who are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered Flydubai flight 1073?
A passenger on Flydubai flight 1073 has described the actions of on-duty crew members who rushed into the cockpit to stabilise and land the plane after the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe. The flight carrying 182 people en route to Israel was able to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
Who are the mystery pilots who stepped in to stabilise the Flydubai flight 1073 as it hurtled toward disaster?
As of Saturday, three days after the uniformed crew members rushed to the cockpit to steady the Israel-bound plane carrying 182 people after a sickening plummet, they still haven't been publicly identified. Flydubai has called them only on-duty crew members traveling on the plane. It’s not clear why the airline hasn't said more.
One passenger at the front of the plane, though, described the men’s actions in an interview with The Associated Press, giving one of the most detailed accounts of the yet-unsung heroes.
Read moreFlydubai hero pilot tells Modi 'I could not let all those people die'
“This is one of the miracles,” said Daniel Schlichter, who was seated in the second row.
“That not in every flight they bring two extra pilots. In this case, they brought them because they should have brought the plane back from Tel Aviv to Dubai, and this is the only reason they were there.” The practice is called deadheading.
The two men responded after screaming passengers discovered what was unfolding in the cockpit. They said the co-pilot was attacking the captain over and over, and blood was everywhere. The captain, while badly wounded, managed to unlock the cockpit door.
After a passenger grabbed the co-pilot and pulled him out, and others grappled with the man to subdue him, Schlichter said that one of the traveling pilots practically hurdled the scrum to enter the cockpit and seize the controls.
Read moreUAE investigators say Omani Flydubai co-pilot was planning 'terrorist' attack
“He was actually kind of jumping above the guys that were handling the terrorist, and he reached out to the pilot area and started to take over,” Schlichter said. “And then the other guy, the other pilot, joined in and they closed the door because they didn’t want anybody else to be there.”
Schlichter, like others, wasn’t sure where the two men had come from. But whoever the first one was, he moved very quickly.
“He acted really like a hero, taking over the plane and reacted like he understood exactly what is going on, and I think we owe him our lives not less than the other heroes that went on the flight,” Schlichter said.
Once the two entered the cockpit and closed the door, Schlichter wasn’t sure who did what inside. It took “quite a lot of minutes”, maybe 10 or more, to stabilise the plane after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
A mayday call was made as the men frantically sought a place to land.

Meanwhile, some of the frightened and wary passengers wondered about them and whether they could be trusted.
“After they managed to stabilise the airplane, actually they did not have any communication with us, and I have to tell you, I was worried about this,” Schlichter said.
He worried about an even worse situation – that the men might be “hijacking the plane into maybe Iran, or I don’t know where, because we’re actually not too far”.
But after about 45 minutes, he said, the pilots announced that they would be landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and everything was going to be OK.
With that, Schlichter said, he decided to trust them. And it turned out to be true.

UN: Ukraine Civilian Casualties Surge 55% in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

The United Nations (UN) has verified 15,280 civilian casualties in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026 as a result of Russian aggression, representing a 55 percent increase compared to the corresponding period in 2025, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk announced.
Addressing the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Türk stated that the war results in an average of more than 400 civilian casualties each week.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Despite relatively static front lines, Russian forces have systematically directed strikes against residential apartment blocks, educational facilities, medical clinics, commercial shops, and railway infrastructure.
Türk specifically highlighted Moscow’s expanding deployment of high-explosive guided aerial bombs across the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia regions. During the first eight months of the year, guided bomb strikes killed or wounded nearly 2,500 civilians, marking a 62 percent surge over the same period in 2025.
Characterizing Ukraine as a “laboratory of drone warfare,” the high commissioner appealed to the international community to halt the escalation.
Türk also expressed alarm over systematic bombardments targeting critical energy facilities and commercial enterprises, noting that strikes on food processing facilities have produced localized shortages of vegetables and dairy products across several provinces.
Russian Glide Bombs Strike Sumy Apartments, Injuring 7
In the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region, Türk reported that approximately 2,000 civilians remain trapped without adequate access to food supplies, potable water, electricity, or municipal gas networks under an ongoing military blockade.
Conflict-related sexual violence and detention abuse
Türk also condemned a “shocking level” of conflict-related sexual violence documented against civilians and prisoners of war, noting that Russian forces and security services bear responsibility for 89 percent of more than 1,000 verified cases.
The high commissioner’s findings align with a comprehensive UN monitoring report spanning the period from February 2022 through July 2026, which documented 1,004 cases of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine.
The report attributed 892 of those violations directly to Russian military personnel, law enforcement agencies, and the Federal Security Service (FSB).
According to verified UN records, the documented victims of Russian abuse include 725 men, 151 women, and 16 children, with female victims ranging in age from 4 to 82.
Male victims consist predominantly of captured Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees subjected to beatings, electric shocks, genital torture, forced nudity, and sexual violence in detention facilities. Women and children were primarily targeted in occupied Ukrainian territories.
The UN report also attributed 112 documented violations to Ukrainian authorities, primarily involving the mistreatment of Russian prisoners of war. The findings noted that Ukrainian authorities have maintained cooperation with international investigators and enacted preventive measures, though formal accountability efforts remain limited.
Foreign fighters and third-country recruitment
Addressing recruitment pipelines sustaining Moscow’s frontline manpower, Türk revealed that representatives from his office conducted interviews with foreign prisoners of war from 36 countries currently held in Ukrainian custody.
Numerous captured foreign fighters reported that they were deceived, coerced, or recruited under misleading pretenses before being funneled into Russian military formations.
The testimonies reflect an institutionalized recruitment drive by Russian authorities utilizing expedited citizenship schemes, administrative residency mechanisms, and commercial intermediaries across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia to replenish combat units without declaring a domestic nationwide mobilization.

Japan arrests US Marine on suspicion of murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:32:24 UTC
18:32:24 KST

A US Marine stationed on Japan's southern island of Okinawa was arrested on suspicion of the murder of a Japanese woman, police said on Sunday.
The suspect "killed the 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet on Saturday," a local police spokesperson told AFP.
US Ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan's foreign ministry and Okinawa's governor to offer "our sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues".
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the crime "exceptionally brutal and vicious" on X.
The government has urged the US "to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes," Takaichi said.
Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found the 20-year-old man, who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.
He reportedly denied the charges.
US military crimes strain ties with Japan
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
A series of crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drink-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa and have been a frequent thorn in relations between close security allies Japan and the US.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
In the same year, US Forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after a drunken US Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

Tanker hit in Hormuz as Iran warns no military solution to end war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

A tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, a British maritime agency said, hours after Tehran warned there was no military solution to the Middle East conflict and the key waterway would remain closed until its conditions were met.
Iran has sought to impose control over the vital shipping lane since the start of its war with the United States and Israel.
It has repeatedly targeted vessels in the waterway that it accuses of transiting without its authorization, while the United States has struck ships allegedly attempting to skirt a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
An "unknown projectile" struck the ship but the crew were unharmed, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said.
No environmental impact had been recorded from the attack, it added.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which about one fifth of the world's oil and gas transited before the war, remains a key sticking point in negotiations between Iran and the U.S.
The latest attack came just hours after Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Strait will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement are met, Iran's Nournews reported.
"The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said separately Sunday there was no military solution to his country's conflict with the United States, with talks on ending the war apparently at an impasse.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
After a U.S.-Israel campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war, Washington in recent weeks has dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure.
The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at providing a framework for a permanent resolution, but the deal collapsed, largely due to disagreements over Hormuz.
Iranian and U.S. officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Araghchi reiterated that a plan put forward by Tehran to resolve its dispute with Washington could lead to the Strait of Hormuz reopening within seven days if accepted.

Keurig Alta First-Look: No More Plastic K-Cups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Opinions on Keurig’s K-Cup System fall into two camps: fans who value the convenience of a quick java hit and coffee purists who sideline it as flavored water. I land somewhere in the middle: I grind my own beans and brew them through a reusable filter, but I let the machine do the rest. So, perhaps, I’m the customer that Keurig has in mind with its new Alta system.
The Alta is Keurig's first single-serve coffee maker that uses plastic- and aluminum-free coffee pods—finally launching after years of development. If Alta takes off, we are likely seeing the beginning of the end for the disposable K-Cup, which launched in 1998.
Whatever your thoughts are on how the perfect cup should be made, for nearly 50 million homes in the US (and not counting the many more in offices), Keurig is coffee. For almost 30 years, we’ve been trained to ditch the old drip-coffee maker for disposable single-serve pods. But now, Keurig wants us to leave (eventually) the K-Cup and embrace the AltaRounds pod, a compostable, compressed coffee round that works the same: Drop it into the machine, press a button or two, and out comes joe.
During a presentation in New York City, Phil Drapeau, Keurig’s senior vice president of Future Coffee Systems, said customers wanted more than brewed coffee. They wanted to make fancy espresso drinks, from simple cappuccinos to salted caramel concoctions I sampled at the event (PSL fans, rejoice). But to do so, Keurig needed to invent an entirely new system.
“We wouldn’t be able to do any of that with K-Cup,” Drapeau says. “It will fail. You have to brew it at the right temperature and extract. You can’t be constrained by the K-Cup system.”
Robot Barista
If the K-Cup was about bringing Dunkin’ home, then the Alta is about mimicking brewing third-wave coffee in the kitchen. Keurig looked at how coffeehouse baristas brew espresso, and how it can simplify the process by applying the K-Cup experience.
With the AltaRound, you don’t need to measure and grind beans, tamp, or adjust pressure and temperature. The round is covered with a plant-based seaweed wrap that ensures the coffee stays compressed and fresh. After you insert it, pick a drink via the touchscreen, and the machine punctures the AltaRound and applies 10 bars of pressure to extract the liquid. Spent AltaRounds are dumped into a container.
The first-gen Alta coffee machine is sleek but enormous. It would take the space of my existing Keurig, coffee grinder, and Breville Bambino, and then some more. On the plus side, it has a built-in milk frother for drinks like lattes—it’s a separate process (a Keurig rep told me someone successfully made latte art with it)—and a built-in K-Cup brewer too. Keurig says this lets users keep brewing coffee styles not yet available in the Alta or if they want something quick. (At launch, AltaRounds come in single espresso, double espresso, and regular coffee.)
The machine is wonderfully easy to use, but the process from inserting the AltaRound to drinking takes some time. It's still faster than using a traditional espresso maker, and you do get flavorful coffee with that must-have crema on the surface. A fellow journalist/coffee enthusiast didn’t find it special, but for a K-Cup drinker like me, it’s a game changer.
Keurig is offering a bundle in the US that includes the Alta brewer (in four color choices), four boxes of AltaRounds, and Flur glasses for $500. The preorder has already sold out, which suggests strong interest. There’s no announcement on when the Alta will be on sale en masse and exactly how much (likely also $500, but without the bundled extras), but a pack of eight AltaRounds will cost $10 to $11. (Stay tuned for our full review.) With that high price, it will be some time before the K-Cup dies (well, plastic never dies) and the Alta takes its place.
It’s no secret that Keurig has been exploring a revolution in coffee pods to replace the K-Cup, and has already been beta-testing a prototype in homes. Customers have also been asking for something environmentally friendly that’s compostable and free of plastics and aluminum. (Foil wrappers and cardboard are still used in AltaRounds packaging.)
The K-Cup has been exhausted in terms of innovation. Specialty coffee for the Keurig doesn’t taste great (Nespresso does it better), and Keurig hasn’t been able to innovate beyond the K-Cup’s original intention: basic brewed coffee.
Beyond sustainability, the Alta’s technology echoes issues that plagued the K-Cup. To tell the machine which pod you inserted and to adjust the right settings, each AltaRound has a QR code that the brewer scans. In the past, Keurig ran afoul with consumers and advocates when it tried to implement a printer-toner-style DRM that would have shut out third-party pod makers. For now, Alta users can choose AltaRounds flavors from Keurig and Peet’s, both owned by the same parent company. Will Keurig allow other makers into the Alta system down the road, as it eventually did with the K-Cup? Time will tell if this is the pod revolution we’ve been waiting for.

Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid
October 4, 2026
Polling began in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday, with around 3.4 million voters eligible to take part in the Balkan country's general election.
Citizens are electing officials across multiple tiers of government, including members of the multiethnic, tripartite presidency.
They will also choose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.
The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic slowdown, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and a long-drawn-out political gridlock, with the ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that links them.
The election will see adversary ethnic parties, the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH, pitted against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.
Polls close at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results expected to be released late Sunday.
What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?
The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and the two semi-autonomous entities.
Both entities are further split into several cantons and communities.
The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war which was triggered by the breakup of Yugoslavia.
Simmering ethnic tensions
Currently in Bosnia and Herzegovina's populace, around half are Muslim Bosniaks, while 31% are Orthodox Serb and 15% are Catholic Croat.
The country has been peaceful in recent years but its ethnonationalist parties have kept the divisions alive even as voters say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric and division.
Milorad Dodik not on the ballot but still dominant in Republika Srpska
In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remains the key figure despite not being on the ballot.
Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
Dodik-backed Savo Minic is running for the Republika Srpska's presidency.
Dodik wants close ties with Serbia and Russia. He has just returned from Moscow where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.
What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.
The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.
Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.
Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
EU ambitions
Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.
But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.

Thousands protest in Spain after housing relief rejected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:27:13 UTC
18:27:13 KST

Demonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday. Photograph: Juan Barbosa/Reuters
Tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through Madrid and several Spanish cities on Oct. 3 demanding affordable housing after lawmakers voted down government-proposed tenant relief measures.
The protests extended a week-long crisis ignited by the eviction of 87-year-old pensioner Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid apartment. The parliamentary defeat marks another setback for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, renewing pressure on his minority administration ahead of general elections scheduled for 2027.
Parliament rejected the legislative package on Oct. 2 after Catalan separatist party Junts joined the main opposition Popular Party and far-right Vox in opposing the measures. The rejected provisions included automatic renewals for rental contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants.
Government authorities estimated turnout in the capital at 70,000 people, while organizers placed the figure at 500,000. Demonstrators also staged rallies in Palma de Mallorca, Santander, Segovia, Toledo and Valencia, where police detained five individuals following clashes.
Hundreds of demonstrators continued occupying a tent camp established a week earlier in central Madrid. Police blocked far-right groups attempting to reach the site late Oct. 3 and detained three people, local media reported.
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants' Union organizing the mobilization, called for a nationwide general strike. Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged Sanchez to call early elections, saying the country cannot endure current conditions.
Housing costs remain a central concern across Spain, where average rents have almost doubled over the past decade and property purchase prices have risen roughly 90 percent. Housing advocates said Abascal lived in her flat for seven decades before an investment firm acquired the property and sought a 275 percent rent increase, though public backlash prompted an agreement permitting her return at a reduced rent.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs speaks after the first exit poll results of the parliamentary election were announced during an election night event of his centre-right United List party in Riga on October 3, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List has won the country’s parliamentary election by a wide margin, putting the pro-Ukraine leader in a strong position to remain in power.
With almost all votes counted following Saturday’s election, the center-right United List won around 35% of the vote — more than 20 percentage points ahead of the far-right Latvia First party, led by veteran politician Ainārs Šlesers, who opposes restrictive tariffs on Russia.
Preliminary results released on Sunday put United List on course for 42 of the 100 seats in the national parliament.
Advertisement
Despite the decisive victory — far stronger than pre-election polling suggested — Kulbergs will still need to negotiate with other parties to form a majority government.
Two partners in his outgoing coalition, the conservative National Alliance and center-right New Unity, cleared the 5% threshold and are set to return to parliament. They appear to have enough seats for a majority without the Union of Greens and Farmers, which fell below the threshold.
That gives Kulbergs a solid path to another pro-Ukraine coalition without having to seek support from Šlesers’ Latvia First, an option that had loomed over the election campaign, which was marked by high inflation, uncertainty around the troubled national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.
Kulbergs became prime minister in late May after his predecessor, Evika Siliņa, stood down following a backlash over stray Ukrainian drone strikes.
The final stretch of Latvia’s election campaign also spilled into Brussels last week, where Kulbergs initially opposed an EU deal to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc’s sanctions list.
Latvia ultimately abstained, allowing the broader sanctions regime to be extended after a compromise among EU countries.
