‘It’s glottophobia’: Brazilians in Portugal battle for linguistic recognition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:24 UTC
18:00:24 KST

Not long after she started studying to become a nurse in Portugal, Iracema Ferreira began bringing a dictionary to her classes as a retort to accusations she was speaking Brazilian, not Portuguese. “It was to show that those words are in the Portuguese language dictionary,” she said.
A Brazilian speech therapist, Ferreira moved to Portugal in 2020 and later heard from several colleagues from her home country that the process of getting a licence to work in the European country was a dead end. The 45-year-old soon abandoned the idea of continuing the career she had practised for a decade and switched to nursing instead.
The speech therapists’ struggle for recognition underlines what Brazilians say is a wider strand of prejudice still embedded into Portuguese society against the language variant of its former colony. “It’s glottophobia,” said Tanise Anhaia, president of the Brazilian Speech Therapists Association in Portugal (AFBP), using a term to mean linguistic discrimination.
Barely any Brazilians have been awarded a licence to practise as a speech therapist in Portugal since 2019, according to the AFBP, which was set up last year. One of the two exceptions is a woman whose lawyer argued his client’s rejection was “totally incomprehensible, illegal and unconstitutional” and got it overturned.
For many Brazilians in Portugal the struggle will not come as a surprise. People from the Latin American giant make up by far the largest migrant group, numbering more than 480,000, according to the Portuguese migration agency, AIMA. (According to the Brazilian foreign ministry, the population is larger, at 628,000 in 2025.)
However, as the size of the group increases, so do the reports of xenophobia. In 2022, the commission for equality and against racial discrimination reported that “Brazilian nationality” was the most common basis of discrimination in the complaints they received, forming 34% of all complaints.
In 2023 Statistics Portugal reported that 55% of Brazilians said that they had suffered discrimination, the biggest proportion in terms of nationality.
Last year a Portuguese man was arrested after posting a video in which he offered 500 euros for each “Brazilian head” delivered to him.
A Brazilian woman who lives in the Lisbon district, who asked to remain anonymous, told the Guardian she had seen her then eight-year-old being punched by another child and told: “That’s for Brazilians to learn that they have to go back to their land.” Earlier, at a school meeting, she remembered a teacher saying “the kids were speaking too ‘Brazilianised’” and that they would themselves receive speech therapy.
The popularity of Brazilian YouTubers is leading to more young people emulating the speech of their favourite stars, say parents and linguists. In the 1980s there was a similar panic in Portugal over the popularity of Brazilian soap operas, said Afrânio Barbosa, dean of the Centre for Letters and Arts at Brazil’s federal university of Rio de Janeiro.
“Every time a Brazilian cultural product spreads in Portugal there is such a reaction. And you hear the same sentences: ‘They are worsening the Portuguese language’,” said Barbosa. “These are social reactions due to a colonial symbolic projection of the language, as if its legitimacy lay in its geographical origin and not in the historical demographic identity of its speakers.”
Brazil and Portugal are part of the Community of Portuguese Speaking Countries, which has the “diffusion of the Portuguese language” as one of its goals. Yet the question of whether the variants in practice are different languages or not splits linguists. “It’s a very complex discussion,” said Renato Basso, a professor of linguistics at the federal university of São Carlos who studies the history of the Portuguese language.
“The Brazilian Portuguese spoken by people with a university degree from the urban centres and the European standard are relatively similar.”
In schools it’s important that everyone has access to a “standard norm”, added Basso. However, linguists point out that even within Brazil and Portugal, people end up speaking differently depending on where they live and their social circle.
“If you get stuck with the idea that there is only one version of a language, everything gets too complicated,” said Basso.
That seems to be exactly what speech therapists are being told, however. When Anhaia sat the test to get a licence in 2021, there was no linguist present, just a speech therapist, she recalled. At the end, the examiner told her: “I won’t approve you because you don’t speak European Portuguese.” Anhaia will sit the test again this year.
Margarita Correia, a Portuguese linguist, said the requirement was “absurd”. The body responsible for the licences, ACSS, said that some candidates lacked the knowledge to assess the Portuguese population and that their university degrees were not equivalent.
The ACSS declined to comment. The Portuguese Association of Speech Therapists said its members did not have the authority to comment.
Álvaro Filho, a Brazilian journalist and writer who has lived in Lisbon since 2016, assembled chronicles of life as a migrant for his new book Eu Não Falo Brasileiro (I Don’t Speak Brazilian). One of them is about his son, whose teacher said that “he would just pass the class if he spoke Portuguese”.
“It’s implicit that when they say you speak Brazilian it’s because they don’t recognise this Portuguese variant as an equal. It’s worse,” he said. “It might become an autonomous version, but it has to be our decision, from Brazil.”

Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down | Chi Onwurah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

Debates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.
As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.
But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to 30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.
Developers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple and Google to protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.
Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, as reported in the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per year to Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.
My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found that Apple and Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.
Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.
Its consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.
But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.
This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.
- Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee

Elusive ‘Geoneutrinos’ Are Building a New Map of Earth’s Volatile Interior
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
In a laboratory 2 kilometers underground, a crane lowers Matt Depatie, a detector technologist, through a hatch into a white-walled cavern filled with about 7,000 tons of ultrapure water that glows as blue as wiper fluid in the light. “Splashdown,” Depatie says over a radio as he steps into an inflatable raft waiting below.
Normally, the cavern is one of the darkest places on Earth, but today it is lit up for maintenance, offering us a rare chance to see inside. I peer through the hatch at Depatie as he paddles over to examine the submerged experiment. He’s inspecting a house-sized detector built to catch some of the most elusive particles known to physics: neutrinos.
This is the SNO+ neutrino experiment, buried deep within the Creighton mine at Snolab, an underground physics laboratory in Sudbury, Canada. SNO+ consists of an acrylic sphere lined with nearly 10,000 sensitive light detectors and filled with 780 tons of oily liquid scintillator, which flashes when lit up by energetic particles. The water around the device and the rock above it shield the detector from the glare of cosmic radiation, allowing the flickers of less common particle interactions to shine through.
Our whole journey down has been part of the crusade to maintain absolute darkness, even beyond the visible spectrum of light. As we descended the main shaft and walked through a rocky tunnel to the lab, our bodies and clothes collected minute amounts of radioactive radon dust. Before entering the main laboratory space, we tossed our mine clothes, showered, and changed into electric blue jumpsuits and hairnets to minimize the contamination we carried in with us. “The showers aren’t for you,” Depatie said as we changed, “they’re for the science.”
Such extremes are necessary when you’re trying to catch ghosts—in this case, ghosts that may help reveal the secrets of inaccessible regions deep within the Earth.
Neutrinos are the most abundant of all the particles that have mass. But that mass is tiny: just a millionth of the mass of an electron. With such little heft and a neutral electromagnetic charge, the particles hardly ever interact with other matter. Trillions of neutrinos—mostly those produced in the sun—pass through our bodies every second, yet after years of hunting them with detectors such as SNO+, researchers have captured only a few hundred thousand of their precious flashes.
Even more elusive—so much so that after decades of searching, scientists have detected only a few hundred of them—are geoneutrinos.
Geoneutrinos are produced in processes that heat the interior of the planet. This heat plays a major role in powering the flow of rocks in the mantle, which shapes everything from plate tectonics to Earth’s magnetic field. It comes from two main sources: heat left over from the planet’s formation, and heat produced by the decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the rocks of the mantle and crust. Without this second source, Earth would have long since cooled off and become a tectonically dead planet.
In counting geoneutrinos, physicists can get a direct measure of Earth’s vital heat-producing elements. “It’s the one thing we do that focuses on the Earth,” said Ryan Bayes, a particle astrophysicist at Queen’s University in Ontario who works on SNO+. “Everything else we do is more focused on what we receive from other places in the universe.”
The first detection of geoneutrinos, by an instrument in Japan called Kamland, was reported in 2005. In 2009, the Borexino detector in Italy reported catching several dozen more. In November 2025, SNO+ reported its first detection, bumping up the number of observed geoneutrinos by about 50.
What makes the detections at SNO+ special is the experiment’s location: These are the first geoneutrinos measured in the western hemisphere, offering a new perspective on Earth’s radioactive interior.
Major uncertainties remain in interpreting the results from these experiments, but researchers’ best estimates suggest that each site is measuring a different flux. “It could be that that’s the first hint that the mantle is not uniform,” said Mark Chen, a particle astrophysicist at Queen’s University and director of the SNO+ collaboration.
Geochemists have conventionally assumed that radioactive elements are distributed evenly throughout the mantle, because the flowing rock should mix everything together. But the measurements of geoneutrinos in different locations could hint that this is not the case.
The regions that seem to be producing the most geoneutrinos sit roughly above continent-size blobs of anomalously hot, dense material, known as large low-shear-velocity provinces, or LLSVPs, which seismologists have mapped on either side of the core. One is under Africa, the other under the Pacific Ocean. “There may be deep Earth structures in the mantle that are not understood,” Chen said. “It could be that [they] concentrate some kinds of elements.”
Neutrinos could one day offer new insight into the still mysterious origin of these deep structures and, more broadly, the patterns in the mantle that underlie many aspects of the Earth system. “It really would be a way to make a chemical map of the Earth’s interior,” said William McDonough, a geochemist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who has long been a leading voice in the search for geoneutrinos.
The outstanding question is whether the geoneutrino measurements reveal differences between the areas of mantle below each experiment, or if the imbalance originates in the way the different experiments count their geoneutrinos. Researchers across the board say there’s still so much uncertainty that it’s impossible to say.
“If we take it at face value, we could say maybe the western hemisphere has a lot more radioactive material in it than the eastern hemisphere,” McDonough said. But there are reasons to be wary of these estimates. “Are the Italians right? Are the Japanese right? Are they both right? Or is something wrong?” he said.
The uncertainties associated with each detector’s results come from the sorting process that physicists go through to identify geoneutrinos, Bayes said. “They don’t just show up and say, ‘Hi, I’m a geoneutrino.’”
Scientists must eliminate signals from particles with too much energy, particles with the wrong measure of a property called helicity, and particles that they expect to see flowing from nuclear reactors. They must also eliminate geoneutrinos coming from Earth’s crust, with the largest contribution coming from the area within a few hundred kilometers of the detector. When those other detections are subtracted from the total count, the geoneutrino signal from the mantle should be all that’s left.
In general terms, the geoneutrino flux from the mantle seems to be very high at Borexino and very low at Kamland, though the uncertainties are great. A detailed geological interpretation of the SNO+ results is still in the works, Chen said, but so far scientists see a “pretty in-between” mantle below Canada.
A particular challenge for SNO+ scientists is understanding the neutrinos coming from the detector’s surroundings, including a basin formed 1.8 billion years ago by a giant impactor. “There are lots of unknowns in this geological area,” said Virginia Strati, a researcher at the University of Ferrara in Italy who helped develop a local model of radioactivity for Snolab.
Uncertainty also comes from estimates of the total amount of radioactive material heating the mantle. The flux of geoneutrinos suggests that these elements could contribute anywhere from just a small percentage of its heat to half of it—a discrepancy equivalent to the output of tens of thousands of nuclear power plants.
Both sources of uncertainty make it even more difficult to detect any differences between the chemical makeup of particular sections of the mantle. The difference in the geoneutrino flux expected from various distributions of radioactive elements “is very small, and is hidden in these uncertainties,” Strati said.
The detection at SNO+ comes at an exciting moment for geoneutrino research: JUNO, another huge neutrino experiment currently collecting data in China, is expected to report its first geoneutrino flux later this year, adding a fourth and notably richer view. With more than 20,000 tons of scintillator, the experiment—buried under a mountain outside the city of Guangzhou — is so large that it is expected to detect more geoneutrinos in its first year than the combined output of Kamland, Borexino, and SNO+ over decades.
Clearer estimates of the geoneutrino flux at each experiment could come from more detailed geological data, as well as further geoneutrino counts at each site. However, McDonough says the best thing would be to build a neutrino detector at the bottom of the ocean. It’s an idea McDonough has championed for decades.
Such a detector would be far from continental rocks, which are rich in radioactive elements; oceanic crust is also thinner and more uniform. Crust-related uncertainties go down so much that “you are in mantle-only territory,” he said.
The idea of an ocean-bottom detector, estimated to cost hundreds of millions of dollars, has seen little take-up from government funders to date. But McDonough is hoping he can make something happen in China, which has given the green light to other big geoscience projects. “It’s very possible,” he said. Until then, physicists will keep paddling around for answers deep underground.

‘A Talent for Murder’: Patricia Highsmith deserved something nastier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

‘A Talent for Murder’: Patricia Highsmith deserved something nastier
Adapted from the stage play Switzerland, Anton Corbijn’s film A Talent For Murder turns Patricia Highsmith into a character in her own fiction. It is an affectionate, but too gentle a tribute to a writer whose work was rarely known for its affection.
Patricia Highsmith’s permanent resting place in Cimitero di Tegna, a small municipal cemetery in canton Ticino, does not call attention to itself. The American novelist – the author, most famously, of the “Ripliad” series, five psychological thrillers set in Europe centered on the slippery character of Tom Ripley – is discreetly interned in a bare marble columbarium. Visitors have chosen stones over flowers to pay their respects.
A Talent For Murder, which premiered recently at the 51st Toronto International Film Festival and one of the highlights of Zurich Film Festival in September, casts Helen Mirren as the fractious writer shortly before her death, opposite Alden Ehrenreich as Edward Ridgeway, a young American editor sent to Switzerland to extract one final instalment in the Tom Ripley series.
Adapted from Australian screenwriter Joanna Murray-Smith’s play Switzerland, the script takes no small amount of pleasure in the games of submission and domination between the domineering Highsmith and the anxious Ridgeway, who might have arrived a few months later and simply left a rock.
“Perhaps you saw my email…” Ridgeway says to Highsmith, who, in 1995, we’re told, communicated almost exclusively via the Swiss postal service. It is a typical kind of interaction between an eager arts worker and an older artist who has seen it all. Attempts to bridge such divides are central to A Talent For Murder.
Murray-Smith’s play has been transposed from page to stage to screen, and, paying a modern kind of homage to Highsmith’s Ripley, A Talent For Murdercourts questions of imitation versus transformation at every opportunity. As Edward Ridgeway learns, the line between imposter syndrome and fake-it-till-you-make-it is razor thin.
Interview with a vampire
Director Anton Corbijn steps into a long and illustrious line of Highsmith cinema. Purple Noon (1960), The American Friend (1977), and The Talented Mr. Ripley (1999) are three standout adaptations of the Ripliad, while Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train (1951, screenplay by Highsmith) and Carol (2015, based on a semi-autobiographical Highsmith novel, The Price of Salt) highlight the remarkable range of her work. Corbijn is no Hitchcock, but with A Talent for Murder he ambitiously reaches towards territory occupied by filmmakers such as René Clair or Anthony Minghella, even if he falls short.
After an awkward prologue on board a Swiss train, A Talent for Murder begins not with Highsmith, but rather an extended riff on Dracula (1897). Ridgeway takes the part of the young, naive North American arriving to sign a contract with the mysterious European in a remote location.
The film displays a curious commitment to this interlude, even having Ridgeway awaken with marks on his neck, with Highsmith-as-Nosferatu emerging as the obvious suspect. Although the extended allusion is swiftly abandoned, it immediately signals the film’s ambition – if not always its ability – to weave elements of pastiche into its storytelling.
After failing to shake off the indefatigable Ridgeway, Highsmith makes him an offer: if he can help her devise a suitably Highsmithian murder plot, she will sign on the dotted line. What follows is a film within the film, with Ehrenreich, stripped of his spectacles in Ridgeway’s imagination, recast as a Ripley stand-in ready to seduce the young heiress Clementine Balfour and murder the older relatives standing between him and her inheritance. Fiction, reality and fantasy soon begin to blur, intertwining throughout the film’s brisk 104-minute running time.
Vertigo, Cluedo, velcro
If viewers cannot help but compare Ehrenreich with his Ripley predecessors, or Corbijn’s postcard-perfect Ticino with the seedy sensuality of Mongibello, the fictional seaside village in Highsmith’s thriller The Talented Mr. Ripley, the film is extremely eager to work these gaps into its text. It needles the audience’s familiarity with earlier Ripley films while wringing what suspense it can from a familiar set of tropes.
When Ridgeway-as-Ripley must pass as an Ivy League man at a Balfour party, for instance, it is impossible not to watch Ehrenreich straining to fill the shoes of Matt Damon or Alain Delon. The result is a curious dual-layered tension that produces a distinctly postmodern vertigo. Such pleasures, however, cannot unfortunately substitute for genuine suspense.
>> The first Ripley adaptation (1960) was French, directed by René Clément and starring a young Alain Delon. Highsmith hated the moralist tweak in the end of the film. In her works, crime usually pays off.
Corbijn attempts to shift the postcard-sunny vision of Ticino into a darker register whenever the narrative slips into the film within the film. Yet even a violent seduction scene never quite escapes the feel of a game of Cluedo. The brisk match cuts that should keep tension taut too often resemble Velcro fastenings, lacking the precision they require. At the script level, a limp succession of twists fails to distract from an ending that is visible almost from the outset.
Ehrenreich must flick a switch between the film’s two narratives, while Mirren remains free to inhabit cantankerous grande dame mode throughout. Less generously, one might suspect that her abundance of audience-pleasing one-liners is among the chief reasons A Talent To Murder exists at all. “You’re a homo,” she taunts Ridgeway at one point, before the famously promiscuous lesbian adds, “I should know”, with an almost conspiratorial wink towards the audience.
>> The most recent (2024) filmic adaptation of The Talented Mr. Ripley is a Netflix production starring Andrew Scott:
Never meet your heroes
The film nevertheless blunts Highsmith’s sharpest edges in order to preserve its portrait of a difficult but brilliant artist. A throwaway remark about leaving New York to escape “the Blacks and the Jews” seems an obligatory nod to many prejudices that once led Highsmith to refer to the Holocaust the “semicaust.”
All the same, A Talent For Murder’s multi-layered exploration of imitation proves more fertile ground for reflection than for suspense, or for an honest characterisation of its main subject.
Acting and adaptation emerge as merely two more of Ripley’s games, where the difference between success and failure is little more than confidence. Somewhat awkwardly, and in one of the film’s best jokes, the same appears true of seduction and artistic ambition, as Mirren purrs in the ear of an unsettled Ehrenreich.
History is full of such missed encounters between generations. The renowned New York painter Duncan Hannah once recalled his excitement at meeting Lou Reed as a young man, only for the Velvet Underground singer to introduce himself by asking whether the artist would return to his hotel room and defecate in his mouth.
A Talent For Murder is nowhere near that nasty, which is unfortunate when dealing with a character as offensive as Highsmith. Faced with a difficult legacy, it would be unkind to say the film merely places a stone upon the author’s grave. It is, however, extremely careful not to disturb the dead.

Cranberry harvest booms in Estonia's bogs as pickers seek extra income
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Cranberry harvest booms in Estonia's bogs as pickers seek extra income
Estonia's bogs are full of cranberries this year, and there is no shortage of people eager to pick them. For some, it is a hobby; for others, a chance to earn extra money.
Cranberry pickers say the berries are good this year and plentiful. Even after making the long trip to the Emajõe‑Suursoo bog, you still meet many people who have also come to gather the large red berries.
Most pickers arrive by boat across Lake Peipus.
"Using a boat is convenient: if you pick a lot of cranberries, it's hard to carry them out of the bog. But with a boat, it's easy. The cranberries grow right near the water. You take a potato sack or a sugar sack, throw it into the boat, and haul it out. I think that's the main thing. And besides, boating is pure romance," said Tauno Laasik, initiator of the Peipsi Toit regional food network.
"It's much closer when you come by boat. If you go on foot, you have to walk almost two kilometers across the bog," said cranberry picker Jekaterina.
"For many, this is a hobby, but here at the edge of the bog there are quite a lot of people who pick cranberries to earn a bit of money for the winter. These are serious masters — they can pick 100 liters a day. Then they sell the berries to buyers and earn a decent amount as extra income for winter," Laasik added.
According to Kristel Vilbaste, who has studied cranberries for many years, more and more people prefer to sell their berries directly through social media rather than to collection points.
"I looked at the ads: prices range from €6 to €10. But some people don't notice that the price is listed per liter, not per kilogram. €6 per liter is almost €10 per kilogram. So you should pay close attention to what exactly you're buying. The berries are very good and tasty. We had a lot of rain this year, so they're juicy. And there was enough sun too," Vilbaste said.
She added that because of the large amount of water in the bogs this year, it's best to wear high rubber boots — and not forget a reflector, since berry picking often continues into the dark.

‘Bir Arada Yalnız,’ directed by Ali Vatansever (R), is the festival’s top winner, taking home the Best Film and Best Director awards. AA photo
The 33rd International Adana Golden Boll Film Festival has announced the winners of its National Feature Film Competition, with Ali Vatansever’s “Bir Arada Yalnız” taking home the Best Film and Best Director awards.
The awards ceremony was held at Çukurova University Congress Center. Hosted by Volkan Severcan and Jülide Ateş, the ceremony also commemorated prominent figures of Turkish cinema who died this year.
“Bir Arada Yalnız” won the Best Film and Best Director awards, while Fatih Al received the Best Actor award for his performance in the film. Hazar Ergüçlü was named Best Actress for her role in “Mutter: Bir Annenin Hatıra Defteri.”
Tunç Şahin’s “Canavar” received the Adana Audience Award, while Banu Sıvacı’s “Günyüzü” won the Yılmaz Güney Award. Miraç Atabey’s “Moda Evlilik” received the Kadir Beycioğlu Jury Special Award.

Özkan Karaköse received the Best Cinematography award for “Mutter: Bir Annenin Hatıra Defteri,” which also won Best Art Direction, and Ayhan Ergürsel won Best Editing.
Asena Hotamış and Süleyman Kadim Kabaali received the Best Supporting Actress and Best Supporting Actor awards, respectively, for “Günyüzü.” Ege Damatoğlu was named the Türkan Şoray Promising Young Actress for “Moda Evlilik,” while Onur Gözeten received the Promising Young Actor award for “Bir Arada Yalnız.”
The Film-Yön Best Director award was shared by Pınar Yorgancıoğlu for “Karanlıkta Islık Çalanlar” and Ali Vatansever for “Bir Arada Yalnız.” The SİYAD Cüneyt Cebenoyan Best Film award went to Nuri Cihan Özdoğan’s “Ölü Köpekler Isırmaz.”

Bosnia Votes with Wartime Divisions Still Sominating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:55:00 UTC
17:55:00 KST

Bosnia was heading to the polls on Sunday after a general election campaign dominated by parties that identify closely with the ethnic divisions of its 1990s war.
Voters will elect a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government, in a complex system that has held the partitioned country together since the 1995 peace deal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Its key race will be for the tripartite presidency, split between Bosnian Muslims or Bosniaks, and the Serb and Croat ethnic groups, with frontrunners pitting visions of a united country against greater autonomy for the Serb-run entity while Croats seek greater political representation.
But the major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric and division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told AFP.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla, ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
The US-brokered Dayton agreement ended the 1992-1995 conflict but entrenched divisions that often paralyse decision-making.
It divided Bosnia into two semi-autonomous entities -- the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS) and a Muslim-Croat federation -- linked by a weak central government.
After State Elections: Can Merz Keep His Job?
Serb strongman’s grip tested
On campaign posters and billboards in RS capital Banja Luka the face of the entity’s former president, Milorad Dodik, beams out.
He remains the central figure in the Serb entity despite not being on the ballot after being convicted for overstepping his powers and banned from the presidency for six years.
His regular separatist threats have led to repeated clashes with the central authorities and stymied hopes of political cooperation.
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country,” Dodik told the final rally of his SNSD party in Banja Luka late Friday.
Despite Dodik’s two decades of dominance in RS, researcher Adnan Cerimagic from the European Stability Initiative (ESI) told AFP that it was “not impossible” for opposition candidate Branko Blanusa to beat Dodik-backed Savo Minic in the race for RS presidency.
“Dodik and his colleagues cannot be sure that they will be able to ensure victory for their candidate,” Cerimagic said.
‘Never been worse’
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the European Union and NATO.
But Cerimagic said little had changed on that front in years.
“The ruling coalition at state level has made practically no positive progress since 2024, either on reforms or on bringing the country closer to the EU and NATO,” he said.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
For 29-year-old environmental activist Sara Tusevljak, the political deadlock is a key reason many young Bosnians leave the country.
“I know quite a few young people who have left Bosnia precisely for these reasons, because they felt that their state, those in power, had nothing to offer them to make them stay,” she said in East Sarajevo, which is in the RS.
“I feel that, in some ways, the situation has never been worse.”
The start of voting was delayed in dozens of polling stations over technical issues, as the country rolled out biometric identification and scanning technology for the first time.
Polls close at 7:00 pm (1700 GMT) and first results are expected late Sunday.

Voters are casting ballots today for the country’s three-person multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers in the national parliament as well as the heads of institutions of Bosnia’s two powerful regional “entities”.
It’s a complicated governance structure – set up in the 1995 peace agreement that ended the preceding three-year civil war.
While Bosnia is one of the poorest countries in Europe after that devasating war, it has remained peaceful.

My colleague Pjotr Sauer, the Guardian’s Russian affairs reporter in Kyiv this week, has described the onslaught of around-the-clock attacks we’re seeing on the Ukrainian capital:
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.
For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”
This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.
Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.
The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
Merz tours science academy targeted in Monday daytime strike
Some more pictures through as the visit unfolds – the leaders have also toured the site of the National Academy of Science which was struck in a daytime attack just on Monday. Two people were killed.
The 19th-century building, in the heart of Kyiv, stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings.
You can see Merz and his delegation assessing the damage and detritus outside the building.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, who greeted Merz at the station this morning, had this week accused Russia of cynicism for targeting a scientific institution during the working day.
“Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries of what it believes the world will tolerate. Every attack left without a strong response only encourages the next one,” he said.
On Saturday, Russia’s foreign ministry had issued the message saying it was carrying out “mass retaliatory strikes” on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, urging foreign nationals and diplomats to leave the country. It last issued a similar warning in May.
The Russians have increasingly been using ballistic missiles on Ukrainian cities in recent months – which are near impossible to defend against without Patriot interceptor missles. The US continues to ignore Ukraine’s desperate please for new stocks.
Meanwhile Ukraine since the summer has also escalated its drone strike campaign targeting Russian oil refineries and energy sites as well as Wildberries warehouses– the Russian equivalent of Amazon – bringing the war home to consumers.
This is the German chancellor’s second visit to Ukraine during his 18 months in office so far.
Merz is facing significant domestic pressure back home with record-low ratings and major losses against his party in three recent regional elections.
But along with the leaders of France, the UK and Poland, with whom he last travelled to Ukraine in May 2025, he has been among the most staunch of Ukraine supporters and has pushed to increase aid as well as work on defence co-operation with Zelenskyy’s government.
He is expected to announce in his visit today the release of €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for repairs in Ukraine’s energy sector – the sites of which have been heavily targeted by Russian strikes and need to be restored going into winter.
He is also expected to finalise a deal for drone production between German and Ukrainian manufacturers. He’s been accompanied by several German CEOs including from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems and other firms as well as his Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche.
In his X post this morning he’d repeated the pledge “You can count on us” adding: “Germany’s security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well.”
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy had also said that Ukraine would close a deal soon on the joint production of drones, missiles and their software with Germany.
Merz has met Ukraine’s President Voldymyr Zelenskyy at the main war memorial on the Maidan in Kyiv.
Both men lay tributes at the central site, which features thousands of Ukrainian flags and framed portraits of the soldiers who’ve been killed in the war that’s gone on for more than four-and-a-half years.
Attack on Kyiv as Merz arrives shows upsurge in Russian attacks on capital
The North Bridge – one of several connecting central historic Kyiv to the residential suburbs across the Dnipro river -was struck not long after the German chancellor’s arrival in the Ukrainian capital.
The incident has been confirmed by Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko this morning who wrote on Telegram: “Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene.”
There’s no word of casualties yet. Pictures and footage being shared online appears to show a missile slamming into the cable bridge and the resulting fireball explosion.
It follows strikes by the Russians on the South Bridge on Friday and Saturday, and several earlier this week that had shut three of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro.
Merz has arrived in the thick of it, as Kyiv, which was largely spared direct aerial strikes in the first years of the war has increasingly come under attack since April.
The Russians have launched strikes day and night, hitting schools, petrol strations, government buildings and churches as well as rails and communication infrastructure.
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, I’m Frances Mao.
We begin in Kyiv where one of Ukraine’s strongest European backers, the German chancellor Friedrich Merz, has arrived this morning in an unannounced visit.
Soon after his arrival, the Russians struck the city’s North Bridge, just a 20-minutes drive from the central railway station where Merz had pulled into.
Sirens have rung out across the city and smoke can still be seen rising from the Dnieper River bridge. Yesterday, Russian drones also struck another bridge, causing injuries; the Kremlin has stepped up attacks on the capital this year and Ukrainians say they are steeling for another autumn blitz ahead of a tough winter.

Brazil goes to polls in decisive election for future of Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:53:01 UTC
17:53:01 KST

Brazilians go to the polls on Sunday in the first round of a highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region.
The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt.
Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro.
The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.
Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region.
Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days, both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
“My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he is under house arrest and there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” said Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais, in Paraná state.
At the beginning of the year, polls suggested Bolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son.
The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator was caught on tape asking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund a film about his father, as well as speculation that Bolsonaro might strip the country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive.
For many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing high rejection rates despite strong social and economic indicators.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as a scandal involving supreme court justices, which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one.
Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote.
AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”.
“Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections and protect the Amazon would be seriously threatened if his son came to power,” she said.

Museums and archaeological sites to adopt new visitor system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:53:00 UTC
17:53:00 KST

Türkiye is modernizing its cultural heritage sites, with Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy confirming plans to install a next-generation visitor system at 216 locations by year-end 2026.
“With the new system, which we will implement with a domestic and national infrastructure, we will bring about a comprehensive transformation in many areas, from smart ticketing and digital visitor management to data security and new-generation museum applications,” Ersoy said.
According to a statement from the ministry, Ersoy received a delegation from Türk Telekom as part of efforts to create a new-generation visitor experience at museums and archaeological sites.
The meeting discussed the current status and implementation schedule of projects being carried out under a cooperation protocol signed between the Culture and Tourism Ministry and Türk Telekom.
Ersoy said in a post on his NSosyal account that they exchanged views on the implementation schedule and next steps for the project covering 216 museums and archaeological sites across Türkiye.
He said the project would bring cultural heritage together with the opportunities offered by technology and provide visitors with a faster, safer and higher-quality experience.
The project will establish an integrated digital structure covering areas ranging from ticket office operations and visitor services to data security and museum shops.
The new system will include smart ticketing, multichannel digital payments, artificial intelligence-supported data analytics, digital visitor management, audio guides, digital archiving, augmented reality and virtual reality applications.
Fiber infrastructure, widespread wireless internet systems and 5G integration will also be introduced to provide faster and more secure services to visitors. Strategic data related to cultural heritage will be stored on domestic infrastructure within Türkiye.
The digital transformation will also cover museum shops, cafeterias, sales areas and other visitor services, rather than being limited to entrance and ticketing systems.
Museum shops will offer products reflecting Türkiye’s cultural heritage, including traditional Turkish handicrafts, Turkish coffee and Turkish delight, Turkish carpets and traditional decorative arts. The ministry also aims to expand overseas sales of products supplied by artists certified as Intangible Cultural Heritage Bearers and traditional handicraft masters.
Under the new system, existing Müzekart cards that are still valid will remain unchanged. Once their validity expires, citizens will be able to use their Turkish identity cards as Müzekart.
After paying the Müzekart fee through e-Government or a mobile application, citizens will be able to enter museums and archaeological sites without waiting in line at ticket offices by having their identity cards scanned.

Iran FM says war has no military solution, Trump mulls strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:52:50 UTC
17:52:50 KST

Good morning and welcome to The New Arab's live coverage of the war in the region. Here are the top stories:
In Yemen, the Houthis have reportedly cut the vital Aden-Taiz road, operationally encircling the city, according to sources speaking with AFP.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that there is no military solution to the conflict, warning: "If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force."
US President Donald Trump is pondering an escalation of the war and is expected to decide on a move soon, saying, "the only question is, it'll either be the easy way or the hard way."
Now, onto our live coverage:
Yemen leader announces military operations against Houthis
The leader of Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Regional and Western officials had previously told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
Yemen's Houthis on Sunday cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden -- the interim capital of the internationally recognised government -- according to four security sources.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military confirmed Houthi control over the area and supply route, with the group effectively encircling Taiz city.
An Israeli airstrike has killed a Palestinian in the city of Khan Younis in Gaza, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa, which added that another person was seriously injured in the strike.
Iranian army says will increase the range of its missiles
Iran will upgrade the range of its missiles following the war with the US as American forces are now positioned as much as 1,000 km (621 miles) away from the Iranian coast, Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news on Sunday.
"During this war, we concluded that we absolutely must increase the range of our missiles, and we have now moved in that direction," he said.
How Israel is weaponising archaeology to annex the West Bank
In late September, Israeli troops raided the Tulkarem area and posted notices on the Banat Yaqub shrine in Irtah, south of the city.
The two-story building, with its Roman-era lower floor and Mamluk-era prayer room above, would now be under the control of the Israel Antiquities Authority.
The shrine and its grounds cover no more than 300 square meters, according to Suhail Salman of the Popular Campaign Against the Wall and Settlements, a Palestinian grassroots group, yet the notices claimed more than 10 dunams (about 2.5 acres) of surrounding land, taking in dozens of inhabited homes.
The shrine is the latest site in a campaign that uses heritage protection to seize land and override Palestinian jurisdiction, rights groups and archaeologists say.
From Silwan in East Jerusalem to Shiloh, Tel Rumeida in Hebron, and Sebastia near Nablus, excavations have arrived alongside roads, visitor centres, and restrictions on access that turn Palestinian land into settler-run tourist sites.
Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a very large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades.
The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.
The company's director general, Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar, said in a statement that the move could allow SOMO to take advantage of better sales and pricing opportunities.
Iraq's Oil Tanker Company is also working to buy and own specialised crude oil tankers to expand its fleet and strengthen its ability to compete with regional shipping companies, he added.
Iraq has previously secured Iranian permission for Iraqi oil tankers to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively closed during its conflict with the US.
Tanker hit by unknown projectile in Strait of Hormuz
A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Sunday, without specifying when the incident occurred.
The crew was safe and no environmental impact had been reported at the time the notice was issued, UKMTO added.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that there is no military solution to his country's conflict with the United States, with talks on ending the war apparently at an impasse.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors. "There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions."
The US aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush arrived in Thailand's resort island of Phuket on Sunday with about 4,800 personnel aboard for a rest-and-recreation break after six months supporting US operations in the Middle East.
For the last six months, the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier and its strike group supported Operation Epic Fury and the US naval blockade in the US Central Command area of responsibility to secure maritime security and stability in the Middle East, according to the US Navy.
Phuket is the first port call for the George H.W. Bush Carrier Strike Group since departing Norfolk, Virginia, and Mayport, Florida, in March, the US Navy said in a statement.
Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until conditions met
The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, Nournews reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying on Sunday, a few days after Tehran received Washington's reply to its diplomatic proposal.
“The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."

====================================================================================================

&quot;Dream Like a King&quot;: the seventh game as part of the &quot;Day with the Kings Team&quot; project took place in Ternopil
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:51:58 EEST
17:51:58 KST

"Dream Like a King": the seventh game as part of the "Day with the Kings Team" project took place in Ternopil
Kyiv • UNN
In Ternopil, 50 children played the seventh game of the "Day with the Kings Team" project with 11 Nyva footballers. The initiative supports children affected by the war.
On October 3, the seventh game as part of the social project "A Day with the Kings’ Team" by the Betking Foundation and its founder, Pavlo Zhurylo, took place in Ternopil. This time, 50 children and 11 professional footballers from the Niva Ternopil football club met on one pitch, UNN reports.
The match format is traditional for the project but unusual for professional football: a team of 50 children plays against 11 professional footballers. There is no distance between the professional athletes and the young players: they take to the pitch together, score goals, celebrate successful moments and simply enjoy football.
For the children, it is an opportunity to share a pitch with professional players and feel part of a real football match.
"I had been looking forward to this day, but I never thought we would play with footballers like this, for real. What I will remember most is the match and the fact that afterward we could talk to the players and get autographs. Now I want to train even more and one day play for a professional team too," said 11-year-old Sviatoslav Romanchuk.
Football that helps bring childhood back
"A Day with the Kings’ Team" was created specifically for children affected by the war. The participants include children of serving military personnel and fallen defenders, displaced children, as well as children from families that have experienced the consequences of Russian aggression.
The idea of the project is to give children, through sport, communication and positive emotions, an opportunity to leave their everyday worries beyond the football pitch for at least one day.
Before the match, the children trained together with professional footballers, and after the game they talked with them, took photographs, received autographs and were given presents.
"The war has taken many familiar things away from Ukrainian children, but it has not taken away their right to dream. That is why it is important for us to create moments when a child shares a pitch with professional footballers and sees that a big dream is not somewhere far away—it may be much closer than it seems. For some, this match will remain a vivid memory, while for others it will become an incentive to train, believe in their own abilities and not give up on their dream. It is for moments like these that we continue "A Day with the Kings’ Team," involve new football clubs and expand the project’s geography. We want as many Ukrainian children as possible to have this experience," said Betking Foundation founder Pavlo Zhurylo.
FC Niva also emphasizes that participating in the project gives the club an opportunity to be closer to children for whom football has already become a part of life.
"For our footballers, this is also a special match. On the pitch, you see not simply 50 children, but 50 young footballers who genuinely love this game. Perhaps for some of them, today’s meeting will become another incentive to continue training, work on themselves and dream of professional football. We are happy to be part of such a day and to see the children’s emotions firsthand," said Ivan Fedyk, head coach of FC Niva Ternopil.
From one match to a nationwide project
Ternopil became the next city on the map of "A Day with the Kings’ Team." Over the course of two years, the project has brought together more than 330 children from different cities across Ukraine.
Matches have taken place in Kyiv, Bucha, Rivne, Oleksandriia, Irpin and Uzhhorod. Professional football clubs joined the initiative and, for one day, became not athletes seen on screens and from the stands, but opponents and partners for the children on the football pitch.
The Betking Foundation plans to continue expanding the geography of "A Day with the Kings’ Team" and involving new football clubs in the project so that children from different regions of Ukraine can take part in such matches.
A Ukrainian project that has received international recognition
"A Day with the Kings’ Team" reached the final of the UN Global Compact competition "Partnership for Sustainable Development 2025."
In 2026, the project also received two Davos Communications Awards: gold in the "Best Sports or Entertainment Campaign" category and silver in the "Best Social Media Campaign" category.
For Betking Foundation, these distinctions represented international recognition of a Ukrainian social initiative that serves as a tool to support children and creates a space for them to communicate, gain new experiences, and dream.
About Betking Foundation
The Betking Foundation charity, founded by Pavlo Zhurylo and part of King Group, transforms social initiatives into real opportunities for children and young people. The foundation pays special attention to displaced children and those who have lost relatives due to the war, helping them through sports, education, and psychological support. 66% of Hong Kong’s 8-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, experts warn
Association finds 67 per cent of grade-one pupils already have insufficient hyperopic reserve, urging parents to start eye checks at age three
More than 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s eight-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, optometrists have predicted, citing a shrinking “hyperopic reserve” that normally helps delay nearsightedness.
The Hong Kong Association of Private Practice Optometrists released the findings on Sunday from a screening of more than 3,500 pupils at eight primary schools conducted between November and May, urging parents to begin comprehensive eye checks when children turned three.
The association found that 67 per cent of six-year-olds had less hyperopic reserve than the recommended standard of 0.75 dioptres (75 degrees), while 24 per cent were already short-sighted.

The Ankara State Opera and Ballet (ADOB) is preparing to meet audiences in the 2026-2027 season with a repertoire ranging from Mozart and Puccini to works by Turkish composers and modern dance productions.
ADOB Director Demet Gökalp told state-run Anadolu Agency that the institution reached around 110,000 audience members last season and aims to attract an even wider audience with productions spanning different genres in the new season.
Gökalp said they staged a busy program from October through the end of June last season, with performances not only at the Opera House but also at CSO Ada Ankara, museums and the Atatürk Cultural Center.
She said three key factors were taken into account when preparing the 2026-2027 repertoire: Audience expectations, the development of artists and support for Turkish composers.
“In selecting our repertoire, we prioritize the expectations of our audience, the development of our artists and supporting Turkish composers. We have shaped our new season with the aim of including Turkish works to encourage Turkish composers and support them in creating new works,” Gökalp said.
Gökalp said ADOB’s new season will open with Mozart’s “The Marriage of Figaro,” which was first staged in 1786. The opera will have its premiere at the Opera House on Oct. 3.
The new season will feature productions ranging from ballet and opera to modern dance and children’s shows. Gökalp said the ballet “Coppélia,” which was previously staged in Ankara but has not been part of the repertoire for a long time, will return to the stage.
Highlighting the importance they attach to Turkish works, Gökalp said the opera “Hekimoğlu,” with music by Tolga Taviş and a libretto by Bertan Rona, will be staged in Ankara on Dec. 12.
“Hekimoğlu” was previously staged by the Samsun State Opera and Ballet. “We will stage it in Ankara for the first time. I think it will be very good. We attach great importance to it,” Gökalp said.
HH Modern dance project ‘Alice in Wonderland’
Gökalp said the children’s repertoire would also be renewed, with the new production “Şekeronya” replacing “Barış Ormanı.”
She said a new modern dance project would be presented to audiences from the new year onward. “Alice in Wonderland” will be staged for the first time, with a foreign choreographer working on the production.
Gökalp said the operas “La Bohème” and “Lucia di Lammermoor,” which were carried over from last season, would also return, with a limited number of performances planned.
She added that the dance musical “Gangster” and the ballet “Harem,” which attracted strong demand in previous years, would continue to be staged this season.
Gökalp said some productions continuing from last season would be staged at the Atatürk Cultural Center to reach a larger audience. “Carmen” and “The Nutcracker” will be presented there.
“We have made new decisions to reach more audiences. These are major operations, but we are making the effort for our audience,” she said.
Gökalp said “The Nutcracker” would be staged in a larger venue because of strong demand, while “Carmen” would also go on tour in Denizli.
She emphasized that moving productions to different venues would allow them to reach a wider audience.
HH New Year’s concerts to be held at both Opera House and CSO
Gökalp said the concert program would continue in the new season, with New Year’s concerts being held at two different venues.
She said the absence of a New Year’s concert at CSO Ada Ankara last year had drawn criticism from audiences and that, following strong demand, a concert would be held at the Opera House on Dec. 30 and at the CSO Ada Ankara Main Hall on Jan. 4.
ADOB’s concerts at CSO’s Blue Hall will also continue. Gökalp said Friday concerts would generally feature the institution’s soloists.
She said the number of foyer concerts had been reduced because of the increase in the number of performances, while Saturday programs would feature more matinee and evening performances.
Gökalp also said ticket sales would begin earlier this season.
“Ticket sales will start earlier in the new season. In previous years, tickets went on sale 15 days in advance, but now sales will begin one month before the performances. I hope art lovers will follow the productions to be staged in the new season, and I recommend that those wishing to buy tickets for the limited number of performances act early,” she said.

Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:48:38 BST
17:48:38 KST

Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
- Published
Major bridges in Kyiv have been hit by Russian drone strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.
Two people were injured when the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was struck on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week.
The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv in a show of support against Russia's continuing full-scale invasion.
Russia's military said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions. It earlier said it had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops.
Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.
Other videos and pictures have emerged on social media showing a gaping hole in the middle of a traffic lane on the bridge.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit.
Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.
Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.
The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times.
"To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.
Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.
Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person.
Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.
Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.
As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.
Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.
"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."
Zelensky later said that a new aid package worth more than €1.3bn (£1.1bn; $1.5bn) had been agreed with Germany.
"These are weapons that will help [us] right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter," he said.
As Merz was visiting Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building badly damaged in a Russian drone attack earlier this week, fresh air alert sirens were heard across the city. Two people were killed in that drone attack.
Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.
He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."
Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.
The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.
Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.
Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"
German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".
Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.
Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

More than 120 anglers compete for longest pike at Lake Saadjärv
Pike anglers competed at Lake Saadjärv on Saturday. Pike are crafty fish and less experienced anglers may end up with no catch at all.
More than 120 anglers gathered at Lake Saadjärv under a warm, summery sun to compete in the traditional "Saadjärve Haug" spinning competition for the 15th time. As only boats with engines of up to 10 horsepower are permitted on the lake in the Vooremaa Landscape Conservation Area, the day's fishing proceeded at a leisurely pace.
"The five longest pike count toward the result, with a minimum length of 52 centimeters. The lengths of the five pike are added together to determine the final result. Saadjärv is deep and large, with very clear water, so fishing here is difficult. You need to know the right spots and previous experience also helps," organizer Mart Toots said.
A total of 55 boat crews took part in Saturday's fishing competition at Lake Saadjärv, all trying to catch the longest pike.
"The fish are very finicky. You have to work the lure to entice them and they're very difficult to catch. Generally, if the fish aren't biting, there's nothing you can do to make them bite," Ivo said.
"We use something called a live sonar. It's a device that's like ultrasound underwater. It shows you how the fish are swimming in real time," Marcus said.
"We haven't had a single bite so far. It's been very poor. There are plenty of fish. They're picky, though, and don't want to follow the lure, so you have to work really hard," Kalmer said.
"It could be better, but we're actually happy with the three we've caught. When we first started 10 years ago, we didn't catch anything here at all," Margus said.
Although the day's average catch was around 60 centimeters long, Venno Viirsalu landed the longest pike, measuring 80 centimeters. Edgar Vaht and Allar Kukk took the overall victory, however, with their five pike measuring a combined 324 centimeters.
