Operation Inherent Resolve: Reflecting on a Campaign that Shaped a Generation of RAF Personnel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:43:27 BST
17:43:27 KST

As Operation Inherent Resolve concludes in Iraq, it closes a chapter that has shaped a generation of Royal Air Force personnel.
For more than twelve years, Operation Shader, the UK's contribution to the Global Coalition's campaign against Daesh, (Operation Inherent Resolve) has seen thousands of RAF personnel serve across the Middle East. From the humanitarian airdrops over Mount Sinjar in 2014 to the final stages of the campaign against Daesh, the operation became a defining experience for many of those who wore uniform.
As the Coalition mission transitions, it is an opportunity to reflect on the people, partnerships and achievements behind one of the RAF's most enduring operational commitments of the modern era.
For Group Captain Paul Hanson OBE, Typhoon Commander Air Wing, the moment represents an important milestone.
“It marks an important day in our collective history – the end of Typhoon operations over Iraq," he said.
"Operation Shader, as an overall mission continues - but Typhoon's part over Iraq has concluded."
What began in August 2014 with RAF Hercules aircraft delivering humanitarian aid to civilians trapped on Mount Sinjar evolved into one of the RAF's most sustained operational commitments. Over the following years, RAF personnel deployed across the region in support of Coalition efforts to defeat Daesh.
"When I think back over the last twelve years, I don't immediately think of aircraft or numbers. I think about people. I think about the young personnel who joined the RAF, completed operational tours and are now leading squadrons and teams themselves. I think about the pilots, engineers, intelligence specialists, force protection personnel, logisticians and support staff who quietly delivered excellence day after day. Tens of thousands of us served from CAOCs (Combined Air Operations Centre) to FOBs (Forward Operating Base), Akrotiri to Baghdad, Erbil to Al Assad. For many of us, we are defined by Operation Inherent Resolve and our fight against Daesh."
Group Captain Paul Hanson OBE
Typhoon Commander Air Wing
The campaign also spanned a period of significant change for the RAF, with capabilities entering service, maturing on operations and, in some cases, completing their final deployments.
"During Shader, the RAF used and retired E-3D, Sentinel, Tornado GR4, Reaper and C130," Hanson noted.
"Typhoon came of age as a proper multi-role aircraft and Storm Shadow strike asset leading the fight against Daesh."
Looking back, Hanson believes one of the campaign's defining achievements was helping create the conditions for Iraqi-led security.
"Today routine Combat Air Operations have finished with Daesh reduced to a level within which the Iraqis can address without our persistent support," he said.
The transition reflects years of partnership, training and cooperation with Iraqi Security Forces, with responsibility for security now increasingly held by Iraqi institutions.
Behind every deployment stood families and support networks who shared the demands of operational service, often across multiple tours and many years of commitment.
Hanson also highlighted the campaign's wider impact.
"We have stayed the course, and delivered a resounding success," he said.
"We have been instrumental in the territorial defeat of a twisted theocracy which threatened to upturn the Middle East permanently."
"And in doing so we have kept the streets of Britain safer, playing a vital role in disrupting ISIS terrorism abroad."
The conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve marks an important milestone in the international campaign against Daesh and an opportunity to recognise the contribution of those who served.
"Operation Inherent Resolve will be remembered as a defining chapter in the RAF's modern history," Hanson reflected.
"The contribution made by those who served helped create the conditions for lasting security and delivered an enduring impact both in the region and at home in the UK."
While the military mission in Iraq has concluded, the UK's commitment to regional security continues. For the thousands of RAF personnel who served on Operation Shader, the campaign remains a defining chapter of service, professionalism and commitment over more than a decade of operations.

Finland investigates alleged war crime committed in Ukraine
Finland's National Bureau of Investigation is investigating an alleged war crime committed in Ukraine.
Source: Finnish public service media company Yle, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The police confirmed the information to Yle. Finnish law enforcement officials said the preliminary investigation began this year.
Yle notes that such a case is rare for Finnish law enforcement agencies.
The police are not currently disclosing details. In particular, they have not said when the crime may have occurred, who the victim is, or whether there are any suspects in the case.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finnish police collected evidence of alleged Russian war crimes. However, the police have not specified how they learned about this particular case.
The investigation launched this year remains the only case involving an alleged war crime in Ukraine currently being handled by the National Bureau of Investigation. Such cases are extremely rare in Finland.
Background:
- In August, the Helsinki Court of Appeal issued a ruling in a case concerning war crimes committed in Ukraine in 2014. It is currently the only such case to have reached a Finnish court. Russian national Voislav Torden was sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison.
- He was detained while attempting to enter Finland in 2023. A court refused to extradite him to Ukraine, citing poor conditions in Ukrainian prisons.

The EU will not scale back its support for Ukraine or alter the operations of its diplomatic presence in Kyiv in response to Russian warnings directed at foreign missions, European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand confirmed.

“This is not the first time Russia has issued such threats. It shows that the Kremlin is losing the war and losing self-control,” Wigand said.

The European Commission’s rebuff followed an official dispatch issued on Saturday, Oct. 3, by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, which warned foreign citizens and accredited diplomats in Kyiv of “mortal danger” and pledged to sustain mass aerial bombardments across the capital.
Defense procurement tranches and air defense transfers
Wigand underscored that rather than retreating under Kremlin pressure, European institutions are accelerating military and financial assistance programs to reinforce Ukrainian resilience ahead of the winter heating season.

Operation Vivaldi Liberates up to 140 Sq Km in Donbas
Concurrently, European capitals have approved the allocation of €6.6 billion ($7.5 billion) through the European Peace Facility (EPF) to reimburse member states for bilateral military assistance delivered to Ukrainian forces.
Strengthening Ukraine’s air and missile defense architecture remains the primary operational priority for European defense coordinators.
To bridge delivery timelines while defense manufacturers scale up serial assembly lines, the EU is evaluating mechanisms to transfer surface-to-air interceptors directly from European national military stockpiles to Ukraine, with inventories to be replenished subsequently using funds allocated under the Ukraine Support Loan.
In addition to defense financing, Brussels is finalizing what officials describe as the most extensive sanctions package against Russia to date.
The diplomatic move follows the EU’s enactment on Sept. 28 of targeted restrictive measures penalizing individuals and entities involved in the unlawful transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children.
Unbroken diplomatic presence

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine quickly dismissed claims of an impending withdrawal. The diplomatic exchanges unfold against an intensifying Russian aerial campaign aimed at degrading municipal utilities, transit infrastructure, and life-support networks across Kyiv.

Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:36:17 UTC
17:36:17 KST

Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
Voters cast their ballots for a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government.
Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a general election to choose new leaders at the national and regional levels, in a vote that could affect the country’s European Union membership bid.
On Saturday, about 3.4 million voters are choosing the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.
Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a United States-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.
The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric and division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla, ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former president, Milorad Dodik, told the final rally of his right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) in the entity’s capital Banja Luka late on Friday.
EU membership bid
In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
The EU granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska.
This general election is the first in the country in which new electronic tools are being used to scan ballot papers and carry out biometric fingerprint verification in a move to reduce fraud during the election.
Polls close at 7pm (17:00 GMT) and first results are expected later on Sunday.

How 'Zionism is racism' motion has split Green party
Aletha Adu
Aletha Adu is a Guardian political correspondent.
Splits in the Green party over the ‘Zionism is racism’ motion being debated today have gone right to the top of the party.
Green party co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said he would “absolutely” support the proposals, which would declare the Green party anti-Zionist and state that Zionism should be treated as a form of racism.
But his fellow deputy leader, Rachel Millward, has described the proposals in their unamended form as “problematic” and said she would not support them without changes intended to protect Jewish members.
Zack Polanski, who left on Friday afternoon to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has sought to steer a path between the competing sides.
Polanski, who is Jewish and describes himself as anti-Zionist, has angered some senior Green colleagues by backing amendments including protections intended to ensure Jewish members are not treated differently because they belong to institutions or synagogues that identify as Zionist.
Speaking to the Guardian shortly after his leader’s speech on Friday, Polanski said the debate over Zionism was “not my priority”. He has also sought to move the argument away from defining Zionism and towards what he regards as concrete action on Israel and Palestine.
The motion has attracted significant support among the party’s rapidly expanding membership. Ali said his support was rooted in the proposals’ references to genocide, ethnic cleansing and ethno-nationalism. He said:
It talks about genocide, it talks about ethnic cleansing, it talks about ethno-nationalism. Anyone who believes in that, I think that is a racist ideology.
Millward has taken a markedly different position, stressing that the proposals originated with members rather than the leadership. “This didn’t come from leadership, it’s not part of a strategic direction,” she said, adding that there were “a lot of different opinions” within the party.
Other senior Greens, including Caroline Lucas, the former leader, and Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, both former co-leaders, have also said they oppose the proposals. (See 8.42am.)
One senior Green, who declined to take a position before seeing the final wording and amendments, said they were proud that such a contentious proposal was being considered alongside 148 others, describing this as part of being a “mass movement party”.
They stressed that any vote would not necessarily represent the end of the party’s discussions on Zionism and Israel and Palestine.
Supporters hope the proposals could eventually make the Greens what some members describe as the “western world’s first major anti-Zionist party”.
The party’s Jewish membership is itself divided. Jewish Greens has declined to take an official position after surveying its members.
Of the 108 respondents who answered its question on political identity, 81% said they did not identify as Zionist. However, 53% agreed that passing the proposals could make discrimination against Jews within the Green party more likely, while 68% expressed concern about the potential impact on the party’s electoral prospects.

At the heart of The Right Way are a series of principles which will guide the next Conservative government:
-Wealth must be created before it can be distributed
-Freedom requires responsibility
-Rules need consequences or they will be flouted
-A government should be judged on what it achieves, not what it intended
-It should be strong where only the state can act, and restrained where people are better placed to decide for themselves
Like any author with a book to plug, Badenoch has been soliciting positive quotes from celebrity figures likely to praise it. In their news release, the Tories have published glowing endorsements for the document from three rightwing historians (Andrew Roberts, Niall Ferguson and Robert Tombs), the former Tory cabinet minister Peter Lilley, the political philosopher John Gray and the Times columnist Juliet Samuel.
Many of them implicitly or explicitly compare Badenoch to Margaret Thatcher. For example, this is from Roberts.
Kemi Badenoch has laid down the gauntlet with this concise, hard-hitting and well-researched book, with its unmistakeable echoes of Margaret Thatcher’s own personal set of beliefs. Underlying political philosophies have historically always mattered much more than mere day-to-day policy-making, because they show which politicians have a star to guide by, and thus the capacity for true statesmanship. With this book - clearly the product of profound thought - Ms Badenoch has set out the battle lines between the open, entrepreneurial economics of the future and Mr Burnham’s collectivist economics of the 1970s.
And this is from Lilley, who served in cabinet under Thatcher.
The Right Way is an immensely important document – as crucial as was Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach, as a stepping stone to government equipped to achieve national renewal.
Tories say lifting earnings cap for free childcare would cost £700m, funded by quango job cuts
In her interview on the BBC this morning, Kemi Badenoch played down the costs of her proposal to lift the earnings cap on parents eligible to claim free childcare. Asked if it was right that people earning more than £1m a year should benefit, she said the number of parents in this category with small children was negligible. (See 9.20am.)
Badenoch may be right about this, but that does not mean her policy is necessarily cheap. According to the Tories, it would cost £700m per year.
In a briefing, they point out that the free childcare policy can be worth as much as £20,000 per child in some areas.
This is how the Conservative party explains its costing.
The policy is estimated to cost £700 million per year, based on analysis from the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation of the cost of removing the cliff edge for free childcare hours. The policy announced today includes removing the cliff edge for tax-free childcare as well, meaning slightly higher costs than those cited by CenTax. (CenTax, Removing the £100,000 childcare cliff-edge: Impacts and cost of reform, 10 September 2026, link).
Other analysis has estimated that the behavioural response to the policy could be sufficient to actually make it net revenue neutral or even a small revenue raising policy. Modelling by the Centre for British Progress estimated that the policy could increase overall receipts by between £130m and £425m in 2029-30. We have cautiously taken a more conservative approach and assume a net fiscal cost. (Centre for British Progress, Rates and wrongs: fixing UK tax cliff edges and tapers, 25 March 2026, link).
The Tories say they would pay for this by cutting the number of officials working for quangos. The party is already committed to cutting the size of the civil service back down to what it was at the time of the Brexit vote in 2016, and it has already banked the money it would save from this. Now it says cutting quango staff numbers to 2016 levels would save £1.6bn by 2029-30. In line with the party’s “golden rule” for deficit reduction, half of this would go towards cutting debt, and the other half would fund the childcare pledge.

David Gauke says Badenoch wrong to say contributory principle makes ditching pensions triple lock unreasonable
In her interview with Laura Kuenssberg, Kemi Badenoch argued that it would be wrong to get rid of the current version of the pensions triple lock because pensioners had contributed to the welfare system. (See 9.43am.)
She has used this line before. In posts on social media yesterday, David Gauke, the former Tory justice secretary, explained why he thought this argument was bogus.
The “contribution” argument on the triple lock is a poor. For a start, it is very hard for anyone living during their working life not to meet the contributory requirements. And in any event, this entitles you to receive a pension, not to uprating under a specific formula.
Anyone paying taxes/“making a contribution” from 1980 to 2011 did so in a period when pensions rose in line with inflation. No one can claim that they “contributed” over this period in the expectation that the state pension would rise in accordance with the triple lock.
The benefits system does to a limited extent reward people who have contributed more to the system through national insurance. Some politicians have argued that the contributory principle should be beefed up. If this is what Kemi Badenoch favours, then ironically she is aligning herself with Keir Starmer, who briefly explored this idea when he was in opposition. Badenoch publishes The Right Way, 100-page guide to her political philosophy
Kemi Badenoch has published a 100-page guide to her political philosophy. It is called The Right Way, and it is in part modelled on a pamphlet published by the Tories soon after Margaret Thatcher became leader in the 1970s. That one was called The Right Approach and drafted by Keith Joseph.
In her foreword, Badenoch says that the 30,000-word booklet is not a policy document; it is a statement of principle.
She explains.
In February 2026, the former head of MI6, Sir Alex Younger, addressed the Conservative parliamentary party. When I interviewed him on stage, he started with a warning: once you are in government, there is no time to construct first principles. If you have not worked out how you think before the crises arrive, you end up reacting to them one by one.
This is where the last Conservative governments went wrong, before they went wrong about anything else. We do not intend to make this mistake again. The Right Way is our answer to the challenge the now late Sir Alex Younger posed.
Good government enters office knowing how it thinks. A manifesto full of suggested policies for current, visible problems is not enough. Many problems a government ends up dealing with are not known at the time of the election. What is essential for success is a settled way of approaching the problems nobody predicted, how to recognise trade-offs, what government should do itself, what it should leave alone, and how to decide when circumstances, and indeed the world, change.
In her interview with the Times yesterday, Kemi Badenoch said she regarded Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, as a “grumpy grandpa”.

Andy Burnham is the cheesy uncle. I think he’s the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes. And what am I? Someone else has to do that. It’s very difficult.
Pressed to give an answer, she replied:
They probably see me, you know, as the no-nonsense mum. No nonsense, [that’s] probably me.

I don’t have exact figures for you, but what we have seen is an explosion in the number of people who are claiming for low-level, conditions … ADHD, anxiety. People have worked out how to game the system. I don’t believe that that’s right.

I’ll give you I’ll give you one statistic, which I saw the other day; that the increase in disability claimants has been higher in the UK than it has been in Ukraine where they’re actually at war. That cannot be possible.

In her BBC interview, Badenoch rejected suggestions that the Tories were regaining their “nasty party” reputation under her leadership.

It’s the common sense party. That’s what we’re doing.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The education ministry’s K-12 Education Administration continues to promote language programs for children of new immigrants.
The program covers seven languages: Vietnamese, Indonesian, Tagalog, Thai, Khmer, Malay, and Burmese, according to the education ministry. Courses create immersive environments where students can acquire languages through interaction while developing a deeper understanding of different cultures, the ministry said.
Fourteen cities and counties held language camps in 2025: Yilan, Kinmen, Pingtung, Miaoli, Taoyuan, Kaohsiung, Keelung, Yunlin, New Taipei, Chiayi, Changhua, Taichung, Taitung, and Tainan. A total of 103 schools and 1,420 students participated.
By 2026, the K-12 Education Administration had provided about NT$15.8 million (US$496,514) in subsidies.
At participating schools, language instructors work with other teachers to design courses combining everyday conversation with food preparation, traditional children’s games, songs and dances, and festival-related activities, the education ministry said. Students develop their language skills and cultural understanding through hands-on learning and play.

Taiwan environment minister promotes urban forestry for climate adaptation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:33:31 UTC
17:33:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Environment Minister Peng Chi-ming (彭啓明) visited Taitung on Sunday to promote a national climate adaptation initiative that treats trees and urban forests as climate-resilience infrastructure rather than solely as landscaping.
Speaking at National Taitung University, Peng said Taiwan faces increasingly frequent high temperatures and extreme weather. The central government is working across ministries to expand the role of trees in cooling urban areas and improving living conditions, per UDN.
Peng said Taitung’s extensive forests and natural landscape make it well suited to expanding green infrastructure. He cited converting some school walls into green hedges and the “Green Point 100” initiative as ways to increase vegetation in populated areas and strengthen ecological corridors.
The ministry’s “Urban Forest Open Government” initiative calls for cooperation among central and local governments, businesses, schools, and communities. Its six strategies cover areas including climate data, tree management and maintenance, a circular economy, and public and corporate participation.
Under Green Point 100, the ministry plans to train community volunteers, connect civic groups with corporate ESG resources, and match volunteers with tree-care and adoption projects. The broader initiative emphasizes choosing suitable species and providing long-term care rather than simply counting the number of trees planted.
Peng also addressed the disposal of driftwood and pruned timber, a challenge in eastern Taiwan. He said the government would continue promoting wood-based power generation and recycling surplus timber as part of a shift from waste disposal toward life-cycle resource management, per UDN.
National Taitung University Vice President Hu Cho-chun (胡焯淳) said forests and lawns cover about 60% of the campus and that the university has incorporated sustainability into its administrative planning.
The meeting formed part of the government’s effort to establish a nationwide urban forestry system that reduces heat while providing ecological and social benefits.

Three weeks to election, Opposition turns to wavering Likud, moderate Right voters - analysis

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:33:04 UTC
17:33:04 KST

Three weeks before the election, parties in the opposition are focusing on voters who could still shift between camps, including moderate right-wing voters, wavering Likud supporters, those considering staying home, and voters reluctant to back parties hovering around the electoral threshold, senior bloc officials said on Sunday.
"Everything has been stuck for a month," senior figures in the opposition said. After weeks in which a significant part of the political battle was also being fought within the blocs themselves, parties are now looking for seats they can bring in from outside their own camp.
According to senior bloc officials, studies and data held by the bloc's parties show no significant movement between the political camps in recent weeks. One senior official said the bloc's potential seats are among the moderate Right, including voters who oppose haredi draft evasion.
Those officials believe that if movement does occur, it is likely to come closer to Election Day.
Against this backdrop, parties in the bloc have recently sought to stop using political ammunition against one another. Party leaders decided to postpone the debate over their candidate for prime minister until after the election and, until then, focus on expanding the bloc.
Yashar's "largest party" campaign, which had largely targeted competition within the bloc, has also been toned down. The division of labor among the parties, however, is still not a binding agreement. Opposition officials said not all the parties are satisfied with the arrangement and not all are following it.
Eisenkot targets 'soft Likud voters,' Yisrael Beytenu looks beyond bloc lines
According to Yashar officials, Gadi Eisenkot's party has identified a pool of some 200,000 "soft" Likud voters, an internal term for voters weighing Likud, abstaining, Ofer Winter's People of Israel party, other parties, or Yashar itself.
The officials stressed that Yashar does not expect all 200,000 votes to move to the party. Rather, they represent a pool of undecided voters from which the party hopes to draw support.
According to Yashar officials, the party is also concentrating efforts on traditional voters and the moderate religious-Zionist public. The party has set a target of winning roughly two additional seats from those groups and, according to its internal assessments, already has support equivalent to about one to one-and-a-half seats from the religious-Zionist community.
A dedicated campaign headquarters led by Matan Kahana, fifth on the party list, is operating in Gush Etzion, Efrat, Givat Shmuel, and Ariel, among other places.
Yisrael Beytenu officials said the party is also looking for votes beyond the bloc's boundaries. According to the officials, the party has mapped cities, neighborhoods, and even polling stations where Likud previously received strong support and is focusing its activity there.
The officials said the party can identify the cities, neighborhoods, and polling stations where Likud won its highest levels of support and is conducting targeted activity there. The groups being targeted include secular and ideologically right-wing voters, disappointed Likud supporters, and Russian-speaking voters who previously backed Likud.
For now, senior bloc officials said the data available to them still shows no sign of the movement from the Right they are waiting for.
One senior official assessed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would lose, but said the question for the bloc was whether it itself would manage to win. That was the official's political assessment, not a forecast of the election result.
According to bloc officials, their concern is the gap between opposition to Netanyahu and their ability to translate that opposition into voters crossing over from the rival camp.
Gantz, Blue and White not out of the race just yet
Benny Gantz is facing a different problem. Blue and White is consistently polling below the electoral threshold, and the party has now decided to appeal directly to voters who fear their ballots will be wasted.
Even before Gantz's public declaration, Blue and White officials said the decision had been made to remain in the race until the end. They said the party was confident it would not waste votes and was relying on internal polling.
On Saturday night, Gantz presented the figures he said underpinned the decision.
"According to our research, more than five seats' worth of voters want to vote Blue and White," he said.
He claimed that "fear of the electoral threshold is the only barrier."
Addressing undecided voters directly, he said: "If everyone who believes in our path votes, we will pass it by a wide margin."
Gantz also personally tied his name to the decision to remain in the race.
"When you see the ballot slip 'Blue and White led by Benny Gantz' at the polling station, you will know that we checked the data and we stand behind the decision to run. Your trust is sacred to me, and therefore your votes are safe."
He also invited journalists to examine the data.
"Come check us: Go over the data, and you will receive clear and transparent answers."
The five seats Gantz referred to are, according to him, a figure derived from Blue and White's internal research, not from polls published by the media.
The decision to remain in the race is also occupying the other parties in the bloc. As long as Blue and White remains below the electoral threshold in the Maariv poll, the possibility that votes cast for it will not count toward the distribution of Knesset seats remains part of the bloc's calculations.
Blue and White argues, based on its internal research, that its main problem is voters' fear of the electoral threshold. According to the party, some voters want to support Blue and White but refrain because they fear it will fail to cross the threshold.

Inside the ‘kill box’: The Yemenis who stayed behind in Houthi-held Mocha
Yemenis trapped in the Red Sea port city speak of deteriorating conditions there.
Nabil watched from his balcony as a column of displaced people passed by at dawn on September 10, hours before Houthi forces entered Mocha, a Yemeni city on the Red Sea.
“People were terrified. There was fear everywhere,” he said.
Nabil, a daily wage labourer in his 40s, did not join them. He still lives in Yakhtul, a village north of Mocha, alongside relatives, none of whom has left their homes.
“Displacement is humiliation and homelessness,” he said. “I haven’t done anything wrong, so I have nothing to be afraid of, and I don’t belong to any side.”
Weeks after the Houthis took Mocha from forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, thousands of civilians remain in the district. The Houthis – an armed group that has controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, since September 2014 – have fought the government for more than a decade in a civil war that has drawn in a Saudi-led military coalition. No one knows how many people remain in Mocha, but according to Yemen’s last census in 2004 the city had 62,500 residents.
The government has declared Mocha a military zone and alleged that the Houthis have forced residents to demonstrate in support of the group or join its ranks.
Residents interviewed by Al Jazeera did not describe forced demonstrations, but one who asked not to be identified because he feared for his safety said three of his neighbours have been recruited and armed by the Houthis. They are now on the front lines fighting against government forces.
“Today my wife heard from a woman who came to our house that a Houthi-armed pick-up truck had kept coming to their home, wanting to recruit her sons, but she refused,” he said. “I know these people. They are our neighbours. One of her sons even spoke to me about it himself.”
The truck left after she refused, he said.
A refuge emptied
Mocha’s port lies about 75km (45 miles) north of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint for Red Sea shipping that the Houthis have repeatedly targeted since late 2023.
After government-aligned forces recaptured Mocha in 2017, the city became a refuge for Yemenis fleeing Houthi-controlled territory.
That changed in early September when fighting moved down the coast and families fled towards Aden, Taiz and Lahij. Many had already escaped Houthi rule once before.
On the evening of September 10, the government declared Mocha and its surroundings a “kill box”, a strike zone, warning that any Houthi movement there would be met with available firepower. Attacks began the following day.
Now residents say that leaving Mocha is almost impossible. “After the kill box was declared, the government opened the old al-Barh road so people could leave,” said Fuad, a 27-year-old pharmacist.
“Some got out, some were prevented by the Houthis and some stayed home, fearing the hardship of displacement.”
The Houthis have imposed a nighttime curfew on the city. Prices have soared, and power cuts have grown frequent, Nabil said.
A cooking gas cylinder has more than doubled in price to about 20,000 rials ($13), and a 50kg (110lb) sack of flour has risen by 8,000 rials ($5).
“A day’s work barely covers petrol and lunch,” he said. “Children have stopped going to school.”
Classrooms remain largely empty. “Parents and students are afraid of shelling or of their sons being thrown onto the front lines,” said Mansour, a teacher at a government secondary school who could not afford to flee with his family of seven.
“I am a teacher. I have nothing to do with politics,” he said. “In the end, we only die once.”
For Umm Khaled, a woman in her 60s whose husband is disabled and bedridden, leaving Mocha was never an option. “Where would I flee to? Look at my situation,” she said.
Her son, who had supported the family by fishing, joined the government-aligned National Resistance Forces for a monthly salary of 1,000 Saudi riyals ($267). He fled with them as the Houthis advanced, leaving behind his wife and two children, aged 15 and nine, in her care.
“Now they have fled, and we are lost,” she said. The local grocer has stopped extending credit, and the family survives on a sack of flour distributed by an aid group before the takeover. “Someone brings a fish, someone brings a yogurt and the rest is up to God,” she added.
Hassan, a 40-year-old fisherman who supports nine people, said he could not afford to leave the city. A ride to nearby Taiz costs up to 200,000 rials ($128). “Where would I go when I don’t even have my daily bread?” he asked.
Attacks and collapsed healthcare
Civilians have also been killed in the “kill zone”.
Before dawn on September 22, the bombing of a house in Mocha killed six members of one family, according to Mahmoud al-Otmi, a journalist with Saudi-owned Al-Hadath news channel whose relatives died.
Houthi-run media blamed Saudi air strikes. Saudi Arabia has not commented publicly.
Colonel Abdulbaset al-Bahr, deputy head of moral guidance in the government’s Taiz military command, said the kill box targets Houthi fighters.
“The kill box is for killing the militia, not civilians,” he said. “The statement did not ask civilians to leave the kill box area. Rather it asked them to stay in their homes and keep away from the militia’s barracks, positions and military gatherings.”
Sultan Mahmoud, the government-appointed director of the Mocha district, said no route out of the city was entirely safe as he accused the Houthis of targeting civilians.
Healthcare has nearly collapsed. On the day Houthi forces entered the city, Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, said nearly all health facilities except Mocha General Hospital had stopped functioning. This was largely because staff had fled although about 30 health workers stayed behind, MSF told The National newspaper.
Residents said conditions in Mocha have since worsened.
“Doctors who were paid by organisations have stopped working because there are no salaries,” Nabil said. Fuad said the Houthis had placed hospitals under a security cordon and some medical equipment had been moved to Sanaa.
Aid has barely reached those who have stayed. Najib al-Saadi, head of the government’s executive unit for displacement camps, said his unit could not reach those in need.
“It is certain that there are families who could not flee because of poverty,” he said, accusing the Houthis of blocking humanitarian work. The International Committee of the Red Cross declined to comment.
In Yakhtul, Nabil said he would not leave, even if the fighting intensifies. “First, money is an obstacle,” he said. “And the house would be looted.”

The Swiss banker who sought the freedom of Patagonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

The Swiss banker who sought the freedom of Patagonia
From Switzerland’s financial centre to the Patagonian Steppe: how Swiss national Christoph Schär left the world of finance to build a new life as a sheep farmer in Argentina.
Shortly after 8am, on his way from Zurich to Langenthal, Christoph Schär stops off at a café in Lucerne’s Sursee, in central Switzerland. It is the morning after the football World Cup final. Argentina had fought for the title late into the night the previous evening – and lost.
Had Argentina won, Schär would probably have missed a huge party in his adopted home city of Buenos Aires. Now he is sitting in Switzerland, processing the defeat. “I watched the match at a public viewing event with my daughter Joséphine.”
His own personal disappointment is limited – Schär isn’t a big football fan. He says his daughter, on the other hand – who holds both Swiss and Argentine citizenship – was a little downhearted after the loss.
For the Schär family, Argentina means much more than just football. The country is part of a life that Christoph Schär, now 60, has built over years, and which has become his home. The former private banker and financial adviser is now an entrepreneur and sheep farmer, producing wool on the Patagonian Steppe with a flock of almost 10,000 Merino sheep.
Our series profiles Swiss men and women founding and building businesses abroad. Through their personal stories, we explore why they choose to pursue projects beyond Switzerland’s borders, the working conditions they encounter there, and the challenges and opportunities.
Through their life stories, this series also showcases how the Swiss Abroad community contributes to Switzerland’s economic, cultural, and political influence.
From banker to entrepreneur
Schär’s Swiss roots go back a long way. Records in the Lucerne State Archives show that his family can be traced back to 1342, when they were “continuously active as farmers”. He likes to say that farming is in his blood – even his grandmother ran a vegetable farm.
Nevertheless, he was initially drawn to the wider world and a “traditional” career. Schär studied in St Gallen, later worked at the Swiss Consulate General in New York, and then his career as a banker took off. Among other roles with a major Swiss bank, he managed a branch in Brazil. He eventually rose to the position of managing director.
But by his late 40s, he was becoming increasingly dissatisfied with his professional life. “It simply wasn’t fulfilling me anymore,” he says today. Schär was looking for a new challenge and more scope for his own ideas.
He is particularly critical of the pressure which, in his view, the Swiss education system places on children. Children in Zurich, for example, would give up playing musical instruments because the academic demands were so high, he says.
“In South America, I’m fascinated by the vastness, and with it comes a certain freedom,” he says, adding that there are fewer rules and, as a result, more opportunities to shape things for oneself.
His wife Clara – herself Argentine – has close ties to her home country. Her family has been farming there for five generations. Eventually, they both decided to also set up their own business, just as Schär’s father once did, but in the same line of work as Clara’s family. They set out to find a farm of their own.
More
Everything you need to know about the Swiss Abroad
A piece of Patagonia
In 2012, they found what they were looking for. During an economically and politically turbulent period in Argentina, they bought a farm in Patagonia. At first, Schär envisaged an idyllic weekend project.
Today, he has to laugh at that notion. “It was a mixture of naivety and romantic idealisation,” he says.
In 2016, the Schärs permanently relocated their main place of residence from Switzerland to Argentina. They rented a house in a suburb of Buenos Aires, near the German school, and rented out their house in Switzerland. They spend every spare minute at the “Campo”, as they call their farm in Patagonia.
Running a business in such a secluded location is challenging. The farm is situated in a very isolated spot. It’s a four-hour drive to the nearest airport and an hour to the nearest village. At first, there wasn’t a constant supply of electricity. Internet access has only been available since the Starlink satellite made it possible.
Schär says that, for a long time, Radio Chubut was one of the most important means of communication in the region, as various messages submitted to the station were read out once a week. Through this, he says he was able to advise his staff that “the bosses” were coming. To give notice of a spontaneous visit, on the other hand, he says, was virtually impossible.
Added to this is the natural environment: in winter, the snow regularly lies metres deep. Winds of up to 120km/h sweep through the steppe; they are too strong to install wind turbines, for example. This region is archaic and harsh, but that is precisely what makes it so fascinating and beautiful, says Schär. “A sheep either survives or dies in these conditions.”
The challenges of self-employment
The search for suitable staff is also proving more difficult than expected. Schär had imagined he could simply place an advert and recruit qualified people that way.
“Finding good people with the right attitude is the hardest thing of all,” Schär says. In Patagonia, he says everything depends on the shepherds and the manager, and you must be able to build a relationship of trust with them. Developing this mutual trust with the local population takes time, he says – on the one hand as a foreigner and, on the other, in his wife’s case, as a woman. In the heavily male-dominated world of livestock farming, this is a particular challenge, he says.
In addition to the climatic and staffing challenges, there are further risks, such as livestock theft. “There have been instances where hundreds of animals were stolen from the area in one go. At night, pumas or Patagonian foxes snatch sheep from the flocks,” he explains.
And then there’s the wool market. Schär doesn’t want to simply sell his wool at the prices set by established middlemen. In Argentina, a handful of large traders dominate the market.
When he tries to export his high-quality wool directly, he comes up against bureaucratic hurdles. He invests in sustainability certifications and battles his way through the regulations. “In the end, we were the first farm in Argentina to succeed in exporting directly to Uruguay,” he says proudly.
What’s easier in Argentina
At the same time, he wants to keep as much of the added value within the region as possible. The wool is to be washed, combed and spun locally. “Through the local processing chain, we can create jobs. Quite simply, that means more food and a brighter future for the local people,” he says.
The development of this remote region is an important part of the Schär family’s project. In this regard, Schär adheres to rules that, not least as a Swiss national, he considers self-evident: he pays wages on time, insures his staff against illness and accidents, and abides by the law.
Despite all these challenges, Schär does not feel that life in Argentina can simply be described as more complicated. For him, the uncertainty in particular also has a positive side. Not everything is regulated down to the smallest detail, he says, and there is a great deal of freedom.
“Uncertainty has always unleashed strength within me,” he says. For many problems, he says there is a pragmatic solution. “Nothing is impossible” – his father’s philosophy also accompanied him to Patagonia.
For him, the difference to Switzerland therefore is less about there being fewer problems in Argentina, and much more about how one deals with them.
A family business
Schär and his wife run the Campo together. He takes care of the company’s development, while Clara, a former McKinsey consultant, oversees the finances.
The children have also found their own paths in Argentina.
Their daughter Joséphine studied in Lausanne and Singapore and now works in Zurich. Pauline discovered her passion for polo in Argentina and, through strict discipline, made it into the ranks of Argentina’s top female players. Their son Jacques moved to Switzerland for his military service. He is now studying agronomy in Argentina.
For Schär, his children’s development is one of the reasons why he does not regret the move to Argentina. Despite a demanding education, they found plenty of scope here for sport, nature and their own interests. And – unlike what he had observed in Switzerland – they have never lost their joy in making music.
Today, Schär divides his time between the two worlds. He advises a select group of wealthy Brazilian clients while also working on expanding his business in Patagonia. His connection to Switzerland has never been severed and he returns regularly to take care of his affairs there. This summer, for example, he is clearing out his parents’ house in Langenthal. After that, he’ll be heading back to Argentina.
His journey is far from over. Schär has further projects he wants to realise in Argentina. Above all, however, he hopes that his children will one day take on a greater role in the business.

“Cultural Iran” book collection inspires new fusion of music, calligraphy and film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:23:57 UTC
17:23:57 KST

“Cultural Iran” book collection inspires new fusion of music, calligraphy and film
TEHRAN- Iranian composer and ney player Hamed Mokhtarani is collaborating with Professor Dariush Farhud, widely regarded as a pioneer of genetics in Iran, on a multidisciplinary artistic project inspired by the 15-volume “Cultural Iran” book collection.
The project seeks to translate the concepts and achievements presented in the extensive collection into a combination of orchestral music, calligraphy, and cinematic visual production.
The “Cultural Iran” book project was initiated in May 2007 under the direction and supervision of Farhud, with the participation of a group of researchers and collaborators. Over nearly two decades, the project has resulted in 15 volumes containing thousands of pages devoted to various aspects of Iran’s history, culture, art, civilization and literature.
Farhud, a prominent Iranian scientist and pioneer in the field of genetics, has devoted part of his cultural activities to compiling the collection. The central idea behind the project, according to its organizers, has been to make Iran’s historical and cultural heritage accessible to the general public regardless of their academic background or field of expertise.
The collection has therefore been developed with a comprehensive and research-based approach while seeking to remain accessible to a broad audience interested in Iranian culture.
As part of the new artistic collaboration, Mokhtarani has spent considerable time studying and researching the contents of all 15 volumes. He is now developing his personal interpretation of the intellectual and cultural world presented in “Cultural Iran” into an independent musical work.
The composition draws on orchestral and classical music and is being developed with a view to a symphonic performance. According to the project’s plan, the work is intended to be introduced as the official musical piece of “Cultural Iran.”
Rather than providing a direct musical narration of the books, the composition seeks to reflect concepts and ideas derived from the collection as a whole. The approach is intended to transform an extensive body of scholarly and cultural material into a nonverbal artistic language that can communicate with audiences beyond linguistic boundaries.
The project also includes a visual component. Mokhtarani is set to design and perform a calligraphy performance at a major historical site in Iran. During the performance, the English word “CULTURE” will be rendered through calligraphy alongside selected Persian poetry and literary texts related to Iranian culture.
The calligraphy performance and the musical composition will be brought together in a professionally produced film, employing a cinematic approach to visual storytelling.
The final stage of the collaboration is planned to include the unveiling of the musical work, calligraphic artwork and multimedia film at a special ceremony held in conjunction with the presentation of the “Cultural Iran” book collection.
Following the unveiling, the works are scheduled to be prepared for dissemination through Iranian and international media and other platforms.
The project brings together Farhud’s long-running research and cultural initiative with Mokhtarani’s contemporary multimedia approach to music and visual art. Through the combination of orchestral music, Persian calligraphy, and cinematic production, the collaborators aim to present themes drawn from Iran’s cultural heritage in an artistic format capable of reaching audiences inside and outside the country.

Israel says 1,318 security personnel killed in 3 years of conflicts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:23:34 CST
17:23:34 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- A total of 1,318 troops, security personnel and first responders have been killed since the start of Israel's three-year conflicts in the Middle East, the country's Defense Ministry said Sunday.
The ministry released the figures ahead of the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, in which 251 people were kidnapped and about 1,200 others were killed. In response, Israel launched a military campaign in the Gaza Strip that has since expanded to fighting across the region.
The death toll includes soldiers, police officers, Shin Bet internal security agents, prison service personnel, firefighters, rescue workers, local security coordinators and members of emergency response squads, according to the ministry.
The tally includes Israel's military operations since the Oct. 7 attack in Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq, as well as its operations against Iran and Houthi forces in Yemen.
Over the same period, Israel's military offensive in Gaza killed more than 74,228 Palestinians and wounded 175,188 others, the Gaza Health Ministry said Saturday. The UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East said about 82 percent of the structures -- about 200,000 buildings -- in Gaza have been damaged, with two-thirds of them destroyed.
In September 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel issued a report that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and called on Israel to immediately halt atrocities in the Palestinian enclave.
Beyond Gaza, the conflict has spread across the region. Lebanon's Health Ministry said in June that the cumulative death toll from Israeli attacks on Lebanon since March 2 had reached 4,057, with 12,121 people wounded.
In Iran, the official news agency IRNA, citing Iranian officials, reported in April that the death toll had reached 3,468, including 1,460 civilians, during a 40-day conflict against Israel and the United States.
In the occupied West Bank, violence has also intensified. According to UN figures, 1,122 Palestinians were killed there between Oct. 7, 2023, and July 24, 2026.
Israeli forces have also entered the buffer zone between Israel and Syria following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad's government. The area, a UN-monitored demilitarized zone established under the 1974 Disengagement Agreement between Israel and Syria, is intended to remain free of military forces.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity, a decision Israel rejected. ■

Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
Oct 4 - Ethiopian government forces and allied militias have regained control of the capital of Tigray, three sources told Reuters on Sunday, dealing a major setback to the opposition alliance that rules the northern region.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which leads the opposition alliance, said in a statement posted on Facebook it had retreated from the capital and that the regional government would be "temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else."
A source close to the pro-government militia, the Tigray Peace Forces, said its fighters entered the centre of Mekelle on Saturday afternoon, followed by the Ethiopian military. A humanitarian source and a Mekelle resident, who asked not to be named, confirmed the city was controlled by government forces.

Asian Games | OCA says challenges addressed as Asian Games new model proves viable
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:22:50 CST
17:22:50 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) acknowledged that the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games had faced various operational challenges, but said Sunday that the Games had ultimately provided athletes with the necessary conditions to compete and perform at their best.
"There is no Games without challenges," said Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, chair of the OCA Coordination Committee for the 2026 Asian Games, at a press conference on the final day of the Games. "The way we handled the challenges should be more important to highlight."
Ikram said the OCA had heard concerns and complaints over certain aspects of the Games' operations, but emphasized that the focus should remain on how such challenges were addressed and whether athletes were provided with the best possible conditions in terms of logistics and other services.
He said the OCA's priority was to put athletes at the center of its work and continue improving the assistance and facilities available to them. "This edition of Games was different. It was a different model," Ikram said, referring in particular to the decision not to build a traditional athletes' village.
The Aichi-Nagoya Games adopted a distributed accommodation model, with athletes staying in containers, cruise ships and hotels rather than in a purpose-built village. "It was difficult to understand when this model was proposed, but we now have a good practice. Maybe other Games will look at it," he said.
Ikram also highlighted security as an important feature of the Games, saying the OCA had sought to ensure safe conditions for athletes and other stakeholders throughout the event. He said the organization would continue to focus on improving conditions and services for athletes.
OCA Director General Husain Al Musallam, meanwhile, pointed to the performances achieved at the Games as evidence that athletes had been provided with a suitable competition environment.
"Numbers are facts," Al Musallam said, noting the large number of world and Asian records set during the Games. He stressed that athletes could not perform at their best without adequate support.
"The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep well. The athletes cannot perform if they don't have transportation. The athletes cannot perform if they don't have good health care. They cannot perform if they don't eat good," he said. "These achievements do not come without the best environment that the organizing committee created for the athletes."
Al Musallam said the distributed accommodation model could also help reduce the additional burden on host cities associated with constructing and maintaining a large athletes' village, provided that athletes' conditions and Games experience were not compromised.
He described the approach as a potentially successful model for future major sporting events, saying it could avoid leaving behind large facilities that might become "white elephants" after the Games.
The two officials praised the organizing committee, local authorities, volunteers and other partners for their contribution to the Games, saying their cooperation had been essential to addressing operational challenges.
The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which began on Sept. 19, will conclude on Sunday night after bringing together thousands of athletes from across Asia to compete in 43 disciplines. ■

U.S. Navy seeks help redesigning F-35 mission planning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:22:34 UTC
17:22:34 KST

- The U.S. Navy plans a five-year follow-on contract for engineering support to redesign the F-35's mission planning software, with an award expected around May 2027.
- Computer Systems Center Inc. holds the current contract, and a Navy forecast puts the follow-on at $50 million to $100 million.
The U.S. Navy is lining up a five-year engineering support contract for the redesign of the F-35’s mission planning software, the ground-based system pilots use to plan sorties and load data into the stealth fighter before takeoff.
The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division in China Lake, California, said in a sources sought notice published Oct. 2 that it intends to buy the work on an other-than-full-and-open-competition basis. The contract would cover systems engineering, analysis, subject matter expertise and program planning and management support for the F-35 Mission Planning Environment integrated product team, in support of the Mission Planning Environment redesign project.
The requirement is a follow-on to an existing contract held by Computer Systems Center Inc., a small business in Springfield, Virginia. The Navy said there have been no significant changes in scope, size or complexity from the current deal, which ends June 10, 2027.
Under the planned schedule, the U.S. Navy expects to release a final request for proposals around Jan. 25, 2027, and award the contract around May 20, 2027. The work would run from May 2027 through May 2032. The service plans a single-award indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract with cost-plus-fixed-fee labor, and estimates about 278,800 labor hours, close to the 280,050 hours on the current contract.
A Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division acquisition forecast published in January listed the follow-on as a sole-source requirement worth between $50 million and $100 million, with Top Secret clearance requirements.
The F-35’s Mission Planning Environment is the set of software tools squadron pilots and planners use on the ground to build a mission: routes, threats, targets, weapons and communications settings. The finished plan is then loaded into the jet. It sits within the F-35’s offboard mission support systems, the ground computers and software that support the aircraft outside the cockpit, alongside the ODIN logistics network that replaced the troubled ALIS system.
Lockheed Martin builds the F-35 and its mission planning hardware and software. The contract the U.S. Navy is now planning covers the government side of the effort: helping the program office define requirements, analyze the system’s architecture and manage the redesign. The program is called Advanced Requirements Characterization, Engineering and Representation, or ARCHER.
Computer Systems Center won the current contract in February 2023. That deal, worth up to $49.3 million, was competed through an electronic request for proposals, but drew only one offer. The company has supported F-35 mission planning work for the Naval Air Systems Command for several years.
The sources sought notice asks companies of all sizes to describe past work, management approach and staffing, and says the responses will help decide whether to set the contract aside for small businesses. The current contract was not a set-aside. Responses are due by 5 p.m. Pacific time on Oct. 17. The U.S. Navy does not plan to hold an industry day.

Kyiv now feels like a front-line city — but its resolve is holding, for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:20:55 UTC
17:20:55 KST

Kyiv now feels like a front-line city — but its resolve is holding, for now
Firefighters work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Francisco Seco)
For much of Russia's full-scale war, massive attacks on Kyiv came mainly at night. Residents learned, as much as possible, to organize their lives around them. They would sleep in hallways or bathrooms, check Telegram channels for updates in the dark, then emerge in the morning and go to work, cafes, concerts, or dinner.
That fragile division between wartime nights and relatively normal days is now disappearing. In recent weeks, Russia has increasingly launched jet-powered attack drones toward the capital around the clock, bringing air raid alerts, air defense fire, and explosions into the middle of workdays, commutes, and afternoons in the city. The Russian campaign, started in late August, has changed the rhythm of life in the Ukrainian capital.
"In this sense, Kyiv can already, to some extent, be called a frontline region."
The last days of September and the first of October were particularly intense, and Kyiv has barely had time to come up for air.
On Sept. 25, a Russian drone tore into a high-rise apartment building in the central Pecherskyi district, killing a 14-year-old boy. The next morning, Sept. 26, residents had already heard the air raid siren five times by 10 a.m. On Sept. 27, another attack stretched into a nine-hour alert.
On Sept. 28, Russian drones struck central Kyiv in broad daylight, killing two people and injuring 26. A building of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences, an institution behind many of the country's major scientific achievements, caught fire after a Russian attack. Videos showed people trying to escape through windows as smoke poured from inside.
The following night, Russian missiles and drones hit an educational facility, apartment buildings, a railway depot, data centers, and business centers.
By Sept. 30, Russia had struck again, this time targeting Kyiv's energy infrastructure, already weakened by repeated attacks during the previous cold season. In the afternoon, authorities announced emergency power shutdowns in the capital.
On Oct. 1, the attacks pushed further into Kyiv's daytime routine. A drone hit a school, and two others struck the Southern Bridge as cars and a metro train were crossing. The next day, bridge restrictions caused major traffic jams across the city, with some residents crossing the Dnipro on foot to get to work.
At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports. The highest number of injuries came on Sept. 25, when at least 59 people were wounded as drones caught residents in the middle of the working day.
By the end of this intense stretch, the city had disappeared beneath a dense gray haze. It was not mere autumn fog, but smoke from the prior attacks that had accumulated over Kyiv in the still air. Authorities urged residents to keep their windows closed.
Buildings faded into the gray, as temperatures were falling. Parts of the city were without electricity. After more than a week of continuous strikes, the city looked as exhausted as it felt, and winter had not even begun.
Front-line city
A shift is visible not only in Russia's attack frequency. Sociologists are starting to see Kyiv move closer, on certain indicators, to Ukraine's eastern regions much closer to the front line.
Oleksii Antypovych, director of Rating Group, a Ukrainian polling and sociological research organization, said Kyiv residents increasingly resemble people in the east on several indicators, including worsening health, loss of income, and damage or destruction of property.
"In this sense, Kyiv can already, to some extent, be called a frontline region," he said.
Antypovych described the prevailing mood not as panic, but as anxiety and uncertainty about security, the city's protection, and what comes next.
"Before, at least you could expect the worst to happen at night and, if you wanted, prepare for it. Now it just feels like a lottery."
A survey conducted from Aug. 21 to Sept. 10 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) found that 83% of Kyiv residents believed Ukraine should continue armed resistance even if Russia tried to deprive people of electricity, heating, and water during the winter.
"Kyiv had the highest share of people (compared to other surveyed regions) who supported continuing armed resistance under any circumstances," Anton Hrushetskyi, KIIS executive director, told the Kyiv Independent.
A separate KIIS survey conducted in late July and early August found that the share of Kyiv residents ready to endure the war for as long as necessary had risen from 61% to 69% since April.
That people in Kyiv continue to stay, work, and build their lives in the city suggests that they are adapting, Antypovych said.
These latest polls suggest Kyiv residents are defiant in the face of Russia's effort to exhaust the country and weaken its will to resist. Yet, the polls were conducted prior to the continuous pressure Russia subjected the capital to in the last week.
'Normal life has been a forgotten concept'
Daria Lisich, a 28-year-old poet, had lived in Kyiv for only three months when Russia's attacks intensified in late August. She lives on the top floor of a five-story building. Staying in Kyiv is partly about conserving what little energy she has left, she said, because another move feels even harder.
"Moving is a huge effort and a major change. I just want this to end or at least to get easier," she said.
For four consecutive days, Russia struck the area close to where she lived. On the fourth day, a strike landed right next to her home, prompting her to leave the city for a while.
"All of the strikes were nearby, but the last one was the closest — right next to my home, in the neighboring building. I was at home during all of them," Lisich said. "I couldn't even take a shower. I constantly had my phone next to me, tracking where it was flying."
She left Kyiv for Lviv for three weeks. Back in the capital, the attacks continued.
Semen Krishtal, a 27-year-old creative marketer, has thought about leaving Kyiv for years, and the latest attacks have only intensified them.
"I want to move to Odesa, but the situation there is even worse in winter than in Kyiv," he said.
He felt the new reality set in clearly on Sept. 28, when a Russian drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv.
Krishtal was riding a trolleybus along Shevchenko Boulevard with his headphones on, listening to Sophie's "Immaterial" — a bright, euphoric pop song about freedom and becoming whoever you want to be. The city had already been filled with alerts and explosions that day, so he kept turning the music up to drown out the noise.
"At night, it's medication and deep sleep. During the day, it's music at full volume," he said. "Just so my brain can function at something other than a critical level of anxiety, at least at a moderate one."
But reality broke through anyway when the sound of another explosion cut through the music in his headphones. Minutes later, police cars and ambulances began speeding past his trolleybus.
Krishtal got off and walked toward the National Academy of Sciences. By the time he reached the attack site, emergency crews were already unfolding ladders to reach people trapped inside the burning building. He stopped and watched the scene unfold.
"Normal life has been a forgotten concept in Kyiv for a long time," Krishtal said. "Before, at least you could expect the worst to happen at night and, if you wanted, prepare for it. Now it just feels like a lottery."

Elle Pütsepp: Minimum wage remains a crucial safeguard for low‑paid workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:20:00 UTC
17:20:00 KST

Elle Pütsepp: Minimum wage remains a crucial safeguard for low‑paid workers
Raising the minimum wage directly boosts the earnings of the lowest‑paid workers, giving full‑time employees a higher income and reducing their risk of in‑work poverty, writes Elle Pütsepp.
When we talk about the minimum wage, the discussion quickly turns to companies and how large a pay increase employers can afford. Rarely do we ask what the current minimum wage means for a person whose bank account shows roughly €865 on payday — and that is their entire income after a full month of full‑time work.
In the second quarter of 2026, the average gross monthly wage in accommodation and food services was €1,389, while Estonia's national average was €2,243. Thus, wages in that sector were just over 60 percent of the national average.
Since April 1, the national minimum wage has been €946 per month, or €5.67 per hour. Compared with the 2025 minimum of €886, this meant an additional €60 per month for a full‑time worker.
Let's assume a person earns €946 gross, uses the €700 basic exemption, and contributes 2 percent to the second pension pillar. After income tax, unemployment insurance, and pension contributions, the worker takes home about €865.
The tax reform that took effect at the beginning of the year did affect their wallet, but did not bring major change. Compared with last year's tax system, their net income increased by about €10 per month.
In the second quarter of 2026, Estonia's average gross monthly wage was €2,243, and for a person earning that amount, the removal of the tax hump had a much larger impact on their wallet. With a 2‑percent second‑pillar pension contribution, the net income of someone earning €2,243 gross increased by €154 per month compared with the 2025 tax system.
For this reason, the tax reform cannot be tied to the need to raise the minimum wage, nor can it be claimed that the national minimum wage is sufficient. Changing the basic exemption did increase net income, but may not have covered the rising cost of daily needs for the worker and their family. According to Eurostat, Estonia's minimum wage has the lowest purchasing power among EU countries.
According to the 2025 labor market survey by Palgainfo Agentuur, 29 percent of service‑sector workers earning up to €1,460 gross were considering changing jobs within six months. In the 2026 survey, 52 percent of workers in retail sales and customer service said their financial situation had worsened compared with the previous year.
Low pay also affects a worker's willingness to stay in their job and their loyalty to their employer. When a worker leaves, their tasks remain undone — shelves must be stocked, hotel rooms cleaned, and guests checked in. If a replacement is not found quickly, the workload is divided among those who remain. Increased workload for the same pay may in turn increase the desire of remaining employees to leave.
Raising the minimum wage directly increases the income of the lowest‑paid workers. If a worker's pay falls below the new minimum, it must be raised to at least the new level by law. This gives full‑time workers higher income and can reduce their risk of in‑work poverty.
Statistics also show the need. In 2024, 7.9 percent of wage earners and 10.1 percent of employed people in Estonia lived in relative poverty. Household structure further affects well‑being: 44.8 percent of single‑person households and 37.9 percent of households with one adult raising children lived in relative poverty.
Therefore, the risk of in‑work poverty depends not only on wages but also on household size, other family members' income, housing costs, and available benefits.
The minimum wage does not solve all livelihood problems, but it is an important safeguard for workers earning the lowest wages. Tax exemptions and benefits can help people cope, but they do not replace a decent wage.
In Estonia, the national minimum wage is negotiated by the Confederation of Trade Unions and the Employers' Confederation, whose mandate comes from law. In 2023, the confederations and the state signed a goodwill agreement setting a goal of raising the minimum wage to 50 percent of Estonia's average wage by 2028.
Negotiations for next year's minimum wage will begin soon. They will consider, among other things, the Bank of Estonia's autumn economic forecast, labor market conditions, and other economic indicators. The final minimum wage level will be determined during negotiations. The outcome directly affects thousands of Estonian workers, many of whom work in retail, food service, and accommodation.
--

Five Drones Breach Moldova in 15 Minutes as Explosions and Wreckage Reported Across Country
Five drones crossed Moldova’s airspace within just 15 minutes on the morning of October 3, as explosions were reported across several districts and authorities discovered drone wreckage at multiple locations. No casualties have been reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Moldova’s Ministry of Defense, the five unmanned aerial vehicles entered the country’s airspace between 7:45 a.m. and 8:00 a.m. during a large-scale Russian aerial attack on neighboring Ukraine. Moldova’s Air Operations Service continued monitoring the country’s airspace together with other authorities and international partners.
Residents reported explosions near several communities in the Căușeni, Ștefan Vodă, Anenii Noi, and Hîncești districts. Moldova’s Defense Ministry said blasts were heard outside Crocmaz, Delacău, Puhăceni, Bozieni, Dubovca, and Constantinovca, among other locations.
Police received a report at around 7:50 a.m. of an explosion outside the city of Căușeni, where residents saw thick smoke. Officers subsequently discovered drone fragments at the site.
Additional drone debris was discovered outside the village of Dubovca in Hîncești district and between the villages of Delacău and Puhăceni in Anenii Noi district.
Near Crocmaz in the Ștefan Vodă district, an explosion occurred in a vineyard close to an agricultural facility. The blast sparked a vegetation fire and damaged windows in the building. Police later confirmed that drone fragments had been found in the area. No injuries were reported.
Authorities later reported another debris site near Constantinovca in Căușeni district, where the explosion also started a vegetation fire.
Police and National Army teams were dispatched to investigate the incidents and secure the affected areas. Authorities urged residents not to approach, touch, or move unidentified objects or suspected drone fragments and instead contact emergency services by calling 112.
Moldova’s Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the violation of the country’s airspace, saying the five-drone incursion occurred amid Russia’s large-scale attacks against Ukraine.
“Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to generate concrete threats to our country and to the security of the entire region,” the ministry said.
Earlier, on September 30, Moldova recorded three airspace violations in a single day, including an unidentified airborne object that entered from Ukraine and crossed toward the Transnistria region. Authorities temporarily closed airspace over central Moldova before restoring flight operations later that evening.

How to recognize animal abuse and whom to report it to
Kyiv • UNN
Animals without food, water, medical treatment, or shelter may be suffering from abuse. This is punishable by up to 8 years of imprisonment.
On October 4, World Animal Day is observed around the world. The National Police of Ukraine explained what signs to look for to identify possible animal cruelty, reports UNN.
The police emphasized that cruelty is not only physical violence.
Pay attention if an animal:
- is left without food or drinking water;
- has wounds or signs of illness but is not provided with the necessary care;
- has no shelter from the heat or frost;
- is subjected to abuse, including for entertainment or the creation of content.
The police also emphasized that the cases listed are only some signs of possible cruelty. Situations that may pose a threat to an animal’s health or life should not be ignored. Cruelty to animals carries administrative or criminal liability. Depending on the circumstances and consequences for the animal, the punishment may range from a fine to eight years in prison.
If you witness possible cruelty to an animal, notify the police by calling 102 or 112. Police officers respond to such reports and establish the circumstances and the persons involved. There is no place for cruelty to animals in a humane society, and everyone’s concern and timely contacting of the police can save their lives
We would remind you
In the Obukhiv district of Kyiv region, the prosecutor’s office is investigating a case of mass cruelty to cats after 51 dead animals were discovered and another 39 were rescued from unsanitary conditions.
