Germany's Merz visits Kyiv as Russia strikes bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:13:00 UTC
17:13:00 KST

Germany's Merz visits Kyiv amid Russian strikes
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:
"We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."
Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from Germany's arms industry, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.
President Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."
Focus on ramping up drone production
During his visit, Merz was set to announce a new raft of measures to support Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion, including a further billion euros in German military aid, plus €350 million ($395 million) for energy sector repairs, according to German media reports.
The chancellor was also expected to unveil plans for the co-production of interceptor drones and long-range missiles both in Ukraine and Germany.
According to German government sources cited by the Reuters and dpa news agencies, arms production is expected to focus on the development and delivery of thousands of drones capable of intercepting the rapid, jet-powered drones increasingly being deployed by the Russian military against civilian infrastructure targets in Ukraine.
The production of missiles with a range of over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) is also expected to be ramped up, enhancing Ukraine's ability to strike military and logistical targets far beyond the frontline and inside Russia itself.
Merz was expected to emphasize how Germany also stands to benefit from the expanded cooperation, both in terms of its own defense against Russian hybrid activities and in terms of jobs and technology.
The chancellor was also expected to speak to President Zelenskyy about the progress of political reforms in Ukraine and the continuing battle against corruption.
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit
The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.
"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."
In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.
His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.
"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."
Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Khanskaya military airfield near the city of Maykop in Russia’s North Caucasus Republic of Adygea early Sunday morning, Oct. 4, sparking a large fire across the facility, open-source monitoring channels and satellite thermal tracking indicated.
Local residents reported that the drone assault began shortly after 1:00 a.m. local time and continued through the early morning hours, with regional monitoring channels reporting repeated drone passages and active air defense fire around Maykop.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Geolocation footage published on social media confirmed an active fire at the military airfield, situated approximately six kilometers outside Maykop and roughly 500 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Thermal anomalies at the airfield were independently corroborated by NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which detected high-temperature fire signatures across the operational perimeter of the air base.
The airfield serves as the home station for the Russian Aerospace Forces’ 272nd Training Aviation Base, formed after the disbandment of the 761st Training Aviation Regiment in 2009.
Beyond its training designation, Russian forces actively utilize the installation as an operational logistics, staging, and refueling facility to support tactical aviation units executing missile and glide bomb strikes against Ukrainian territory.
Vilnius Airport Closes as NATO Jets Scramble Over Suspected Drone
Satellite imagery of the airfield recorded in recent months showed multiple combat and support aircraft deployed at the facility, including Su-24 strike aircraft, Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35S multi-role fighters, L-39 jet trainers, Mi-8 utility helicopters, and military transport aircraft.
The installation was previously targeted by Ukrainian deep-strike operations in December.
Deep-strike campaign against Russian air and drone assets
The overnight strike against Khanskaya marks the second consecutive long-range engagement targeting major Russian aviation and launch infrastructure within a 24-hour window.
Early Saturday morning, Oct. 3, Ukrainian strike drones hit the Tsymbulovo droneport in Russia’s western Oryol region, sparking multiple fires across storage and launch facilities identified by open-source intelligence and NASA thermal sensors.
The Oryol complex functions as Moscow’s primary launch hub for high-speed, turbojet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 loitering munitions directed against Kyiv.
Satellite monitoring throughout September documented rapid construction at the Tsymbulovo base, including eight reinforced domed shelters, new paved launch ramps, and 14 hangars, alongside efforts to convert surface-level storage shelters into underground bunkers to withstand drone strikes.

Japan’s counterstrike missile goes on public display
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:11:35 UTC
17:11:35 KST

- Japan showed its Type 25 surface-to-ship missile launcher to local residents at Camp Kengun in Kumamoto on Oct. 3, the first public showing since deployment.
- The upgraded Type 12 missile has a reported range of about 1,000 km and is Japan's first weapon for its counterstrike capability.
Japan has put its longest-range missile system on public display for the first time since deployment, showing the Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile launcher to local residents at the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Camp Kengun in Kumamoto on Oct. 3.
Four vehicles, including the missile launcher and an ammunition carrier, were lined up inside the camp’s maintenance facility, Kyodo News reported. A company commander from the 5th Surface-to-Ship Missile Regiment, the unit that operates the system, briefed visitors on the equipment. About 80 people attended the morning session, taking photos and asking soldiers questions.
Photos from the event show the launcher, a heavy multi-axle truck, with its box-shaped launch canisters raised at an angle inside a hangar lined with shipping containers. The display was open to residents of Kumamoto city and people from elsewhere in Kumamoto Prefecture who work or study in the city, with participants applying in advance.
The Type 25 is an upgraded, ground-launched version of Japan’s Type 12 anti-ship missile, built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The original Type 12 has a range of about 200 km (125 miles). The new version can fly about 1,000 km (620 miles), Japanese media report, putting much of the East China Sea, parts of China’s coast and the Korean Peninsula within reach from Kyushu.
It is the first missile Japan has fielded to carry out what the government calls “counterstrike capability,” the ability to hit enemy bases and launch sites, which Tokyo adopted in its 2022 National Security Strategy. Japan’s Defense Ministry describes it as a stand-off weapon, meaning it can strike an invading force from beyond the range of that force’s own weapons.
The missile was deployed to Camp Kengun on March 31, the same day the ministry formally named it the Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile, or 25SSM. Before that deployment, the Defense Ministry showed the launcher only to a limited group that included Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura, Kumamoto Mayor Kazufumi Onishi and heads of local community councils. Residents had called for a showing open to the general public, Kyodo reported.
Camp Kengun sits in a residential area in the eastern part of Kumamoto city, on Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu, the closest of Japan’s main islands to the East China Sea and Taiwan.
The Type 25 surface-to-ship missile is one of two new long-range weapons Japan deployed this year. On the same day, the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force sent the Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile, a ballistic weapon with a gliding warhead, to Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture.
The Defense Ministry plans to add ship-launched and air-launched versions of the Type 25 missile on Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force destroyers and Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighters in fiscal 2027.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,540,700 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:08:12 UTC
17:08:12 KST

Russia has lost around 1,540,700 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 4.
The number includes 1,750 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,391 tanks, 25,483 armored combat vehicles, 157,258 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,686 artillery systems, 2,179 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,686 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,837 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Northrop to build GPS-free navigation for three navies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:05:16 UTC
17:05:16 KST

- Northrop Grumman received a $29.2 million contract, with options to $103.6 million, for low-rate initial production of the AN/WSN-12 inertial navigation system.
- Canada and Australia are funding 73% of the order through Foreign Military Sales, with the U.S. Navy paying the remaining 27%.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Northrop Grumman a $29.2 million contract for early production of the AN/WSN-12 inertial navigation system, a shipboard navigator that keeps track of a vessel’s position without GPS, with Canada and Australia paying for most of the order.
The contract covers low-rate initial production units and maintenance assistance modules, along with engineering support, integration and testing, the U.S. Department of War said. Options could raise its total value to $103.6 million. The contract was awarded Sept. 30.
Canada is paying 42% of the initial order and Australia 31%, through the Foreign Military Sales program. The U.S. Navy’s share is 27%. The notice does not say how many systems each country will receive or which ships they will go on.
The full $29.2 million was obligated at award: about $12.3 million from Canada, $9.2 million from Australia, $4.7 million in fiscal 2026 U.S. Navy procurement funds and $3.1 million in fiscal 2024 shipbuilding funds. The shipbuilding money suggests at least some of the U.S. systems are meant for ships under construction.
Most of the work, 90%, will be done at Northrop Grumman’s facility in Charlottesville, Virginia, with the rest in Baltimore. The base work runs to May 2030, and options would extend it to July 2032. Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the deal without competition, saying Northrop Grumman is the only source that can meet the requirement.
An inertial navigation system works out where a ship is, which way it is pointing and how fast it is moving by measuring its own motion with gyroscopes and accelerometers. Because it does not depend on outside signals, it keeps working when GPS is jammed or unavailable, and it feeds position and heading data to weapons, radars and other ship systems. Submarines rely on such systems heavily because they cannot receive GPS while submerged.
The WSN-12 replaces the Northrop Grumman-built AN/WSN-7, a ring laser gyro system based on technology from the late 1980s that is installed on nearly every U.S. Navy ship. The U.S. Navy plans to fit the new navigator to destroyers, cruisers, aircraft carriers and attack submarines. Northrop Grumman has said the WSN-12 is more precise than its predecessor and fits in the same space, allowing it to be swapped in without major changes.
The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman a production contract for the system’s core component, the AN/WSN-12 inertial sensor module, in June 2023, and later approved full-rate production of the module after lab testing.

RIYADH/DUBAI – Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays and downscaling of the futuristic development housing it.
The NEOM Stadium was billed as an elevated arena in a glitzy 160km steel-and-glass structure known as The Line, in turn part of the broader development known as NEOM.
NEOM was introduced about a decade ago as a centrepiece of de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030, an ambitious plan to diversify the economy and cut reliance on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of NEOM’s owner, the Public Investment Fund, confirmed in April that The Line was no longer a priority and said it was not vital before 2030, the original delivery target for its first phase. He denied that any projects had been cancelled.
However, according to two sources, plans to build the NEOM Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely.
NEOM and the Saudi government media office did not reply to requests for comment, while Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Sports redirected questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The Authority said “substantial delivery” of construction milestones for the event was already taking place, but did not address questions around the NEOM Stadium and costs. It shared images of some of the other stadiums under construction.
Riyadh developing 15 venues for 2034 World Cup
The 2034 World Cup is seen as a marquee event for Saudi Arabia, which under the Vision 2030 programme has invested heavily in sports via wealth fund PIF.
The tournament will be the first time a single nation hosts the expanded 48-team format.
Riyadh is working to build or renovate 15 venues across five cities, as well as dozens of training facilities.
MEED Projects, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform whose team of analysts tracks tenders and projects in the region, puts the total value of the projects at US$22.7 billion (S$29 billion), in data shared with Reuters.
According to MEED, NEOM’s stadium is expected to cost US$2.5 billion. It lists the projected 46,000-seat stadium in its data as “on hold”.
The stadium has no listed completion date, according to the data, which describes the remaining stadiums and facilities as being in various stages of development, with completion expected between 2026 and 2033.
Saudi Arabia is under increasing pressure from the Iran war, which has led to heavy disruptions to energy shipments and damage to critical infrastructure, with the kingdom facing attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis.
Last week, the Ministry of Finance said it expected a fiscal deficit in 2026 that was wider than previously projected and a real gross domestic product contraction of 3.6% following a drop in oil activities.
Pivot from giga-projects
The geographic distribution of the stadiums adds to the challenge of delivering the projects, a third source said.
That could further be compounded by some projects set to host stadiums being delayed or downsized, such as The Line or Riyadh’s New Murabba development, the source added.
In January, Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia had suspended construction of The Mukaab, a colossal cube-shaped skyscraper at the centre of the New Murabba.
In 2025, Reuters also reported that the PIF was pivoting from its focus on costly giga-projects to endeavours with more immediate financial returns, a strategy later articulated by Saudi officials.
Still, other projects for the World Cup are progressing.
The Aramco Stadium in the eastern city of Al Khobar is set to be completed by the end of 2026 and host its first game in January 2027, for which tickets are on sale.
Work on other planned stadiums is going ahead, a fourth source said. REUTERS

Funeral held at Gaza church for mother and daughter killed in Israeli strike

Maysa Abu Daoud and her daughter Mary al-Najjar were among five Palestinians killed in the attack that hit the ground floor of a building in the Remal neighbourhood on Saturday, in the latest Israeli violation of a United States-brokered “ceasefire” agreement with the Palestinian group Hamas.
In a statement, the patriarch extended his “heartfelt condolences” to the loved ones of the two women and to the Christian community in Gaza.
Their funeral took place on Saturday at Saint Porphyrius Church in Gaza City’s Old City.
The two women were Palestinian Christians from Gaza City who devoted their time to helping parishioners and displaced people sheltering at the Holy Family Church, according to Palestine’s Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs.
The committee’s chairman, Ramzi Khoury, described their deaths as a “painful loss” for their families, the church and its parishioners.
Mary’s son, 14-year-old Fouad al-Najjar, told the Anadolu news agency the strike hit the building at about 1:30am (22:30 GMT).
“My grandmother and my mother died. May God have mercy on them,” he said.
Al-Najjar appealed for an end to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, saying Palestinians were losing their loved ones every day.
“We are exhausted by this war and have endured so much,” he said. “For almost three years, we have been living through the same destruction, the same grief and the same war.”
Palestinian Lutheran pastor Munther Isaac, who serves in Ramallah and directs the Bethlehem Institute for Peace and Justice, wrote on X: “The genocide continues in Gaza.”
The Gaza Strip is home to fewer than 1,000 Christians. The community was already small before the war, and many of its members have been killed since then in attacks on their homes and churches throughout the war that began in October 2023.
On October 19, 2023, an attack on the Saint Porphyrius Church compound killed at least 18 people. Two months later, the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem said an Israeli sniper shot dead a woman and her daughter inside the Holy Family parish compound in Gaza.
An Israeli strike on the Holy Family Catholic Church compound on July 17, 2025 also killed three people and wounded others, including parish priest Father Gabriel Romanelli.
According to the Ministry of Health in Gaza, Israeli attacks have killed at least 74,228 people, including at least 1,445 since the start of the “ceasefire” in October 2025.

Welsh racing ban rehoming standoff sparks fears for greyhounds’ welfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:00:22 UTC
17:00:22 KST

Wales’s greyhound racing ban – a UK first – has run into difficulties regarding how and when to wind down the practice, potentially risking the animals’ welfare, a charity has warned.
The law, which received royal assent in April, includes a three-year window for the ban to come into effect and is overseen by a Welsh government working group, which includes racing industry representatives and animal health and welfare organisations.
Its first report, however, revealed an impasse: animal welfare groups want a phased approach to avoid caring for and rehoming hundreds of dogs in a short period of time, while industry representatives say phasing out racing is impractical.
While the Welsh government report recommended a 12-month wind-down period to support rehoming, it says it cannot mandate it, and at present there is no clear mechanism for resolving the standoff.
Claire James, the chief executive of Greyhound Rescue Wales, said: “If there is a hard stop, we and the other groups working to end greyhound racing will do whatever it takes. Our priority is making sure these animals are happy and healthy but the industry is still trying to maximise its profits.”
Wales’s sole greyhound racing venue, Valley Greyhounds Stadium near Caerphilly, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Greyhound racing began in the UK 100 years ago as a working-class pursuit that made going to the races accessible for people of all incomes but the industry has been in decline for some years: most tracks now mainly rely on online betting and streaming rights rather than physical ticket sales.
Animal welfare groups say the sport is inherently dangerous: according to data from the Greyhound Board of Great Britain (GBGB), between 2018 and 2023, 2,700 greyhounds died and more than 26,500 injuries were recorded. Greyhound racing careers are short; one study calculated an average of 14 months.
The recent closure of racetracks in Oxford and Swindon has led trainers to relocate to Valley Greyhounds, meaning greyhound racing in Wales has actually increased since the ban was passed. Approximately 360 dogs and 18 trainers are currently registered at Valley Greyhounds, which the Welsh government’s implementation report said could cost up to £2,800 each to rehome.
Nicola Jones, the head of rescue and rehoming at Greyhound Rescue Wales’s site in Ammanford in Carmarthenshire, said the charity currently took in two or three dogs a week, usually through a volunteer who mediates with trainers.
Two dogs, Merlin and Alvin, were dropped off during the Guardian’s visit; another, Dolly, had arrived a week ago but was still too timid to come out of her kennel.
“Most of those relationships are positive, but some animals do arrive with signs of mistreatment, and many need veterinary care for fractured legs and dental disease and socialising and behaviour training after a life in kennels,” she said.
The Senedd’s decision to prohibit racing was followed a day later by a similar ban in the Scottish parliament, although the sport was already facing extinction in Scotland as the country’s last track closed in 2024. Following the Welsh and Scottish votes, at least a dozen Labour MPs, including members of the all-party parliamentary group on animal welfare, urged former prime minister Keir Starmer to bring a ban into force in England.
But potential issues with the Welsh legislation were clear early on: civil servants advised the Welsh government last year it would be better to license greyhound owners rather than bring in an outright ban on racing because “insufficient evidence” had been gathered to justify outlawing it altogether.
September’s implementation group report found that the economic impact of the ban is “yet to be quantified”. Valley Greyhound Stadium reported £15m in projected income from streaming contracts over the next five years.
The ban’s detractors also claim ministers pressed ahead as part of a deal with the Welsh Liberal Democrats to get a budget deal passed. GBGB launched a legal challenge to the bill, claiming the consultation had been rushed, but the petition was rejected by the high court.
Abbie MacGregor, the corporate affairs director at GBGB, said: “It is the people who care for these greyhounds day to day who must now manage the consequences for each dog. GBGB and its industry partners will do that work because the dogs’ welfare comes first. The Welsh government must give them the time and certainty to do it properly.”
A Welsh government spokesperson said: “This is the first in a series of reports, with further updates to follow as detailed plans continue to be developed. The implementation group will continue to refine its recommendations and provide regular progress updates to ministers.”

Lack of inspections at fish slaughterhouses a ‘disgrace’, says Animal Equality UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:00:22 UTC
17:00:22 KST

Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses in England and Wales, it can be revealed.
Concerns within government about the way fish are slaughtered date back decades but all of the official bodies responsible for animal welfare and food standards in England and Wales said they do not undertake regular inspections.
When Animal Equality UK contacted the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), it referred the charity to the Fish Health Inspectorate (FHI). In response to a previous inquiry, the APHA had said it does not carry out mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses and suggested contacting the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Both the FSA and the FHI told Animal Equality UK that they did not carry out routine or mandatory inspections.
Abigail Penny, the executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Fish are thinking, feeling beings, capable of pain. It is a disgrace that not a single government agency will take responsibility for checking on their welfare at slaughter. This is a huge blindspot, and it leaves these animals all the more vulnerable behind closed doors.”
In 1996, the government’s expert advisory body, the Farm Animal Welfare Council – now called the Animal Welfare Committee – suggested there should be legislation governing the slaughter of farmed fish. The committee returned to the issue in 2014 and again in 2024. On the latter occasion it urged governments across the UK to legislate for fish to be stunned before slaughter, and for inspection systems to be put in place to enforce those standards.
In its Animal Welfare Strategy for England, published in December 2025, the government committed to introducing humane slaughter requirements for farmed fish but draft legislation has yet to be published.
Penny said: “For 30 years, people in power have known that farmed fish need legal protection when they are slaughtered, yet for 30 years decisionmakers have failed to act.”
She added: “The government promised to change the law, and we welcome that promise, but promises don’t protect animals. Every month of delay leaves millions of fish at risk of prolonged, painful deaths. Ministers must bring forward species-specific slaughter legislation now, backed by a proper inspection regime, so that what happens to these animals is no longer left to chance. It’s the least they deserve.”
Animal Equality UK estimates that about 7,742 tonnes of trout a year are killed in England and Wales. The British Trout Association says the UK has almost 290 trout farms, including hatcheries, concentrated in northern England, southern England and southern Scotland.
An APHA spokesperson said: “It is incorrect to suggest fish farms aren’t regulated or inspected by government bodies. APHA investigates reports of suspected cases of poor welfare at fish farms, and the Fish Health Inspectorate inspects them on behalf of the government. We do not hesitate to take further action if we find evidence of cruelty or neglect.”

5 dead in 3 weeks: are Indonesia’s whale strandings on the rise?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:00:14 UTC
17:00:14 KST

5 dead in 3 weeks: are Indonesia’s whale strandings on the rise?
Recent whale and whale shark deaths have raised concern in Indonesia, but experts cite ocean shifts, human activity and smartphone reporting
On September 25, a whale shark became stranded and died on a beach in Aceh province, just days after a decomposed whale carcass was discovered in a mangrove in Riau province. Another whale was found dead in West Java on September 21, just two days after a whale shark stranded and died in South Sulawesi. The latest incidents began on September 12, when a dead whale shark washed ashore in Bali.
The recent deaths reflect a longer-term rise in reported whale shark strandings across the archipelago. A 2025 study by the Elasmobranch Institute Indonesia and Konservasi Indonesia recorded fewer than 10 whale shark strandings per year from 2011 to 2019. From 2020 onwards, however, that average jumped to more than 22 cases a year.
Published in Scientific Reports, the study linked strandings to seasonal and oceanographic conditions – including sea-surface temperatures, wave height and marine productivity – particularly in areas affected by seasonal upwelling, an oceanic process where wind-driven currents pull cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the surface, drawing feeding marine life closer to coastlines. But researchers have said that increased smartphone use and social media reporting could account for much of the apparent rise.

Senior figures in the opposition say that, according to the data available to them, there has still been no significant movement of voters from the Right into their camp, even as they assess that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose the election without the bloc necessarily securing a majority to form a government.
One senior figure estimated that Netanyahu would lose, but said it was not certain the opposition could secure a majority to form a government. That is also the bloc's concern: that opposition to Netanyahu will not translate into voters moving over from the opposing political camp.
The most complicated battle over those votes is taking place around Ofer Winter. Political sources estimate that People of Israel is drawing more than two Knesset seats' worth of support originating from Likud, along with roughly another seat from Yisrael Beytenu.
These are assessments by those political sources regarding the origins of the party's support, not data from a publicly available poll.
According to the same political sources, some right-wing voters who had moved away from Netanyahu had previously shifted toward Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu.
They assess that since Winter entered the race, those voters have been presented with another option on the Right that does not require returning to Likud. One source estimated that Winter and People of Israel currently have a unique potential to move votes between the political camps.
Likud is monitoring the phenomenon and, for now, is continuing to apply pressure on Winter.
"For now, we're going at him with full force," a Likud source said.
Asked what Likud's latest checks regarding Winter had found, the source said he could not elaborate on the results of the party's most recent assessments.
However, according to political sources familiar with the details, Netanyahu's circle has no consensus on that approach.
Those sources said that Likud figures had told them the attacks on People of Israel were a mistake, and that, in the view of those Likud figures, the right-wing camp had grown significantly since the party established itself in the race.
The political sources also said those Likud figures told them that, from their perspective, People of Israel would be a partner in the right-wing camp after the election.
According to the same political sources familiar with the details, Likud figures also told them that the data they have on the issue remains unclear.
Attacks continue on Winter, People of Israel
For the time being, the attacks on Winter are continuing, even though, according to those sources, there is no consensus in Netanyahu's circle over the move.
Sources in Yashar said the party is also monitoring Winter. Party officials assessed that if Winter's voters come to believe he will not cross the electoral threshold, between half a Knesset seat and 0.7% of a seat's worth of his supporters could move to Eisenkot.
That is an internal Yashar assessment.
Winter's appearance above the electoral threshold in Maariv's latest poll now makes the scenario that assessment was based on harder to realize.
According to political sources, part of Winter's support comes from right-wing voters who have moved away from Netanyahu and whom both Yashar and Yisrael Beytenu are seeking to attract. Another portion consists of voters Likud is seeking to win back.
Likud discussing coalition, gov't compositions for after elections
Likud is already discussing the possible composition of the government after the election.
Gideon Sa'ar said in an appearance on Meet the Press that even if the bloc reaches 61 seats, he supports bringing additional parties into the government and expanding the coalition beyond the parties currently in the bloc.
Sa'ar's remarks are already raising the question of which potential partners outside the bloc could join such a government. From his perspective, even a 61-seat majority would not be a reason to settle for the existing composition.
Which parties Likud would seek to bring in, and whether those parties would be willing to join such a government, will become clear only after the election.
The issue of haredi military enlistment is also expected to accompany that political struggle.
Senior figures in the change bloc say opposition to exemptions from military service is one of the issues through which they hope to reach moderate right-wing voters.
The haredi parties, by contrast, are expected to make military enlistment legislation a central issue in any negotiations over forming a government.
For now, the change bloc has decided to postpone the question of its prime minister candidate until after the election.
Disagreements over the possible composition of the government and the identity of potential coalition partners have not disappeared, but with the remaining weeks of the campaign, figures in the bloc are trying to bring the discussion back to the numbers.
Senior figures in the change bloc say the situation has remained stuck for roughly a month. In their assessment, if there is significant movement of votes between the camps, it will come in the final weeks of the campaign.

Terrace in Haifa: Between Wadi Nisnas and Tuscany with a twist - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:59:08 UTC
16:59:08 KST

The view from the Terrace Restaurant at the Hotel Botanica in Haifa may be the most beautiful view of any restaurant in Israel. It sits at the foothills of the Baha’i Gardens, which are lit up at night, and sitting at a table on the outdoor terrace with that view was a real treat.
So was the food. My husband and I made the trek from Jerusalem to try this restaurant, led by chef Zico Hijab, and I’m so glad we did.
The menu describes the food as “Between Wadi Nisnas and Tuscany,” and the fish-and-dairy menu offered dishes with twists I had never tried before.
The outstanding dish of the night was cheese gnocchi and za’atar (NIS 82), gnocchi in a creamy sauce with fresh za’atar leaves, pine nuts, and a za’atar crumble.
The gnocchi, made in-house like almost everything here, was incredibly light; as the dish is called in Hebrew, “gnocchi clouds.” If you are anywhere near Haifa, it is worth coming here just for that dish. You can thank me later.
But I’m getting ahead of myself. We began the meal with cocktails – a Spain to Egypt for me (NIS 52) and a smoked whisky (NIS 52) for my husband. Mine was a pretty pink concoction of white wine, strawberries, and basil. Just delicious and so pretty.
Between Wadi Nisnas and Tuscany with a twist
Hijab designed the extensive menu when the restaurant opened just over a year ago. He likes adding a twist that often surprises the diner.
For example, arancini is a classic Italian dish that is usually a fried ball of risotto on tomato sauce. It is one of my favorite dishes. Here, the arancini (NIS 59) is square, stuffed with spinach and herbs, and served on saffron cream.
I’ve always wondered why arancini are almost always served in portions of three, making them a possible source of strife when a couple dines together. These were different from any arancini I’ve had, and I was still thinking about them three days later. And just guess who got the third piece!
Michal, the shift manager, recommended dishes that were out of the ordinary, and I was very grateful for her advice.
We didn’t even order a salad, but a large and very fresh salad arrived anyway – called Bustan (NIS 75), it had fakus cucumber (a special kind of cucumber grown mostly in the North), zucchini, arugula, grapes, sheep feta, almonds, and an arak vinaigrette.
Hijab said that Arab restaurants in Haifa used to start a meal with grapes and arak, and the salad was a play on that. It was fresh and different from most restaurant salads I’ve had.
We also tried tuna kadayif (NIS 70) – red tuna tartare with a spicy mayonnaise served on kadayif, pancakes usually served at Ramadan iftar dinners and stuffed with nuts or cheese. Here, the serving included two small pancakes, and the fish was fresh and just a little spicy.
For our main course, in addition to the gnocchi, we shared a fillet of sea bass on truffle mashed potatoes (NIS 119). It was such a large portion of fish with crispy skin that we didn’t come close to finishing it.
We also shared one dessert of cannoli, stuffed with pistachio cream (NIS 56).
Overall, I felt the prices were very fair for food of this quality.
Hotel proves beautiful, relaxing, with amazing views of the Baha'i Garden
THE BOTANICA, an upscale, Fattal Limited Edition hotel, is inspired by the nearby Baha’i Gardens, with plants and greenery throughout the common areas.
The hotel is spotless, and our room was large, with a huge balcony and amazing views of the Baha’i Gardens.
The rooftop pool is beautiful and relaxing, and there is a small gym. Each floor also has a fascinating art display well worth checking out.
The next morning, the hotel breakfast was one of the best I’ve ever been to in Israel. It was as if all of the standard salads and dishes had been kicked up a notch or two.
The cheese selection was huge, with at least a dozen different artisan cheeses. There was a full honeycomb dripping fresh honey. And let’s not forget the lox.
Along with standards like shakshuka, there were roasted vegetables and ravioli.
For dessert, there was kanafeh and a warm vanilla soufflé.
They also had fresh juices, including pomegranate juice, and excellent coffee.
Overall, just a lovely experience at both the hotel and the restaurant.

Trump’s friendship with Erdogan ignores Turkey’s hosting of Hamas - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:58:42 UTC
16:58:42 KST

US President Donald Trump considers Hamas to be the world’s enemy, referring to them as “terrorists” and “killers,” explicitly condemning their violent acts, attacks on civilians, and the holding of hostages.
So why does he call their host a friend, praising him as a strong leader whom he respects and a “fantastic guy?”
While Trump may secretly recognize the real danger of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, knowing that this loose cannon could wreak havoc on the Middle East if he so desired, his high esteem takes the expression, “keep your friends close and your enemies closer,” to a whole new level.
Because it’s one thing to pretend to like the man, but why lavish him with such admirable qualities when it’s clear to most people that Erdogan is an authoritarian despot who has been accused of forcibly seizing power in his own country by rigging elections in his favor?
If Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent assertion during his speech at the UN General Assembly, claiming that “Turkey is one of several nations, financing information against Israel and spreading antisemitism, while hosting Hamas terror chiefs” is true, then why would Trump’s perception of the man, when describing him in public, reflect such a completely different character, making him sound trustworthy, helpful, and even honorable?
Is it possible that Trump’s desire to build a good rapport with the Turkish leader has colored his ability to see the man for who he really is? Does Trump’s desire to be seen as a peacemaker extend to a ruler who jails journalists and political opponents, provides a safe haven for Islamic radicals, and permits honor killings of Turkish women to continue?
With charges of financial corruption, it is said that “Erdogan’s closest associates control large portions of the construction, energy, communications, financial services, and media sectors. This system of kleptocracy ensures that the best business opportunities go to the most loyal members of Erdogan’s party, or those with familial connections, and that any illegal activity or tax evasion goes unreported and unpunished.”
Accusations of bribery are rampant, with transparency and accountability nowhere to be found. So, where’s the commonality with a democratically-run superpower that prides itself on following the rule of law and seeking to ensure less intrusive government involvement in the lives of its citizens?
Maybe Trump is enamored by the flattery that he’s received from the Turkish leader, who knows just how important it is for the American president to hear how wonderful his efforts are in trying to broker peace in the Middle East.
Or does it have something to do with his NATO ties? Turkey has become adept at positioning itself as a major diplomatic mediator, whose influence has led to key security initiatives, including the use of NATO forces to undertake specific projects. That is not surprising, considering that Turkey maintains the second-largest military in all of NATO.
And while Erdogan may be doing his best to insert himself into world events, it’s hard to ignore the fact that he is closely aligned with the greatest enemies of Israel and Western civilization.
Those include Russia, Qatar, Venezuela, and Iran. Each of their leaders has cozied up to Erdogan, which was not difficult considering their many shared interests, such as the religion of Islam, geopolitical common goals, and a strong dislike of Israel.
Given America’s completely different value system, isn’t it odd that Trump would not see Turkey as being antithetical to all of his own political aspirations?
After all, how can hosting Hamas be seen as a positive on any level? When Turkey continues to classify the terrorists as “liberators or resistance fighters defending their land,” where does Trump find common ground with such a preposterous perspective?
Who is playing whom?
While Turkey may be doing its best to pull off a balancing act of appearing to be pro-Western, due to its strong dependence upon European trade, investment, and supply chains for its industry, there’s no ignoring the anti-West policies that are so obvious to the casual observer.
Between its authoritarian rule, eroding all forms of democracy, including its judiciary, and its well-known suppression of civil liberties, as well as monetary corruption to the point of money-laundering accusations, there is almost no resemblance between Turkey and its Western counterparts.
All this makes the average person wonder whether Trump is playing Erdogan or vice versa, because this is not a natural affinity based on mutually shared values and ethics.
Described as a “transactional, multipolar actor, hedging policy directly undermining Western strategic cohesion,” one can only conclude that Turkey is feigning friendship and goodwill for the sake of appearance, hoping that it can gain an advantageous position in its long-range quest for world influence.
Is it really wise, then, for Trump to vocally consider Erdogan a friend, a fantastic guy, and a strong leader, when there’s a strong likelihood that, at some point, the Turkish leader will show his true colors? How will Trump moderate his warm sentiments when that happens?
On many levels, it seems as if Trump is playing a dangerous game by falsely attributing good character to someone who obviously has malevolent future aspirations that will also benefit evil regimes and their associates.
If Trump is serious about forging real peace in the Middle East, he should distance himself from anyone who would represent a barbaric terror organization as liberators who are merely seeking to right an injustice.
Because such a characterization is not only a monstrous fabrication, but it promotes and advances a twisted and perverse distortion of history, which is then responsible for fomenting anti-Jewish and anti-Israel sentiment, turning bloodthirsty murderers into righteous actors.
No honest and forthright leader who truly hopes to effect a true and lasting peace can afford to turn a blind eye to such duplicitous dealings, no matter how hard he wants to maintain good relations with everyone.
At some point, there must be a genuine and forthright acknowledgement of good and evil as well as the admission that terrorism has no place in civilized societies.
While diplomacy can be a wonderful tool in advancing peace, it should never be used as an excuse to call evil good or vice versa, as in the case of Trump insisting that Erdogan is a friend!

No room to roam: The cost of a crowded planet for wild animals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:56:48 UTC
16:56:48 KST

Over the past fifty years, the average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent, according to WWF's Living Planet Report 2024. The report names loss and degradation of habitat as the most commonly reported threat, driven mainly by how the world grows its food.This finding raises a plain question. When animals lose the land, water and forest they depend on, what happens to them?A shrinking home, not a vanishing oneHabitat rarely disappears all at once. It is cut into pieces by farms, roads, canals, railway lines, power lines and growing towns. Each piece may still have trees and water, but it supports fewer animals than the original whole did.The 73 per cent figure also needs careful reading. It describes the average change across thousands of monitored populations. It does not mean that three-quarters of the world's animals are gone, or that three-quarters of species have disappeared. What it does show is a steady thinning, and the report describes such declines as an early warning of greater risk to species and ecosystems. The pressure it describes is gradual and widespread rather than the result of a single event, which is partly why it is easy to overlook. The report also notes that some populations have held steady or recovered where conservation has worked.
Not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life
“This is not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life,” said Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF.What changes for an animal that loses spaceThe effects usually arrive in a recognisable order. Food and water become harder to find, so animals travel farther to reach them. Their routes cross fields, highways and railway tracks. Animals with large ranges, such as elephants and big cats, are affected first, because they need the most room.Smaller populations face a slower problem. When forest patches are cut off from one another, animals cannot move between them to find mates. Over time a small, isolated group becomes more vulnerable to disease and to sudden shocks such as drought or fire. Wherever forest meets farmland or settlement, animals and people also meet more often, and not always safely.Elephants outside the fenceIndia's elephants show how this plays out. The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants, according to the last census in 2017. Most of them do not live inside protected areas. Government and press figures put the share outside reserves at about 80 per cent. That share matters for everything that follows. A herd that lives mostly outside reserves has no boundary between it and the land that people farm, travel across and build on.For these herds, a journey between feeding grounds can pass through paddy fields, village lanes, rail lines and overhead power cables. Official data tabled in Parliament in 2024 shows what that means. Over five years, the leading cause of unnatural elephant deaths was electrocution, ahead of train accidents, poaching and poisoning. Odisha, Assam, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu reported the largest numbers of electrocution deaths.
The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants
The government has taken some steps in response. It has identified and ground-validated about 150 elephant corridors, the routes herds use to move between forests. The Railways and Environment ministries have also formed a standing committee to reduce deaths on tracks.Tigers on islands of forestTigers tell a more hopeful story, with a warning attached. The 2022 estimate counted at least 3,682 tigers in India, a record, spread across 53 tiger reserves. These reserves are among the best protected forests in the country.But the same assessment shows the limits of protection. Roughly a third of the reserves need stronger protection, habitat restoration or more prey for the tigers to feed on. A few reserves in Mizoram, Nagaland and Jharkhand reported almost no tigers at all. Summaries of the report also describe many reserves as small islands of forest, joined to one another by a limited number of corridors. A reserve with a healthy tiger population can send young animals out in search of territory of their own, and many of them end up in unprotected land among farms and villages.The record count and the weak reserves belong in the same account. Protection works where it is applied well, and the gaps appear where it is not.Where Kaziranga endsKaziranga's protection does not stop at the park boundary, and a new proposal from the Assam government has put that line under debate. The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve with a site-specific zone of one to three kilometres. An ESZ is a regulatory buffer, declared by the environment ministry on a state's proposal. It is not an outright ban: depending on the notification, activities in it may be prohibited, regulated or permitted, and mining is among those most strictly restricted.
The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve
Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma says the 10-km limit applies only because Kaziranga has not yet been finally notified. He argues it brings populated areas such as Kaliabor, Doboka and Jakhalabandha under restrictions, and holds up civic projects like a proposed stadium in Bokakhat. The state says the park's boundary and its UNESCO World Heritage status will not change, and that the 10-km zone stays in force until a new one is notified. Some residents agree. Hundreds rallied in support of the proposal on August 18, saying the current limits get in the way of building homes and basic infrastructure.The opposition and conservationists are not convinced. Congress state president Gaurav Gogoi led a protest at the Kohora range and alleged that the change could give legal cover to mining. The state government rejects the charge. Conservationists such as Jadav Payeng and Kavita Ashok point to the annual floods, when rhinos, deer and elephants move to higher ground outside the park. A smaller zone, they warn, could cut off those routes.A 2025 conservation assessment notes that a smaller zone is not necessarily a weaker one if it is designed to protect the most sensitive areas. Whether it does will depend on the final notification, which will decide whether wildlife corridors, flood escape routes and wetlands fall inside the line.Wetlands and the quieter lossesSpace does not only mean forest. Globally, freshwater species have seen the steepest declines in the WWF report, and wetlands are often among the first places to be drained or built over.The report points to Chennai, where rapid urban growth has led to a large loss of wetland area. Wetlands shelter birds, fish and amphibians, and they also soak up floodwater for the city around them. When they go, wildlife loses a home and people lose a buffer.The cost to peopleWhen space runs out, people pay too. Government data tabled in Parliament showed that elephants killed 2,853 people in India over five years, with the highest toll in 2023. Many of these deaths happened in places where farms, villages and elephant routes overlap. The elephant deaths and the human deaths come from the same stretches of land, where both now depend on the same ground.The Environment Ministry has issued guidelines on managing human-elephant conflict, and it says compensation is provided for losses. These measures respond to the damage after it happens. They do not by themselves restore the space that animals have lost.Where space is being rebuiltSome efforts aim at the cause. West Bengal has begun a community programme called Gajamitra, or Friends of Elephants, in which local people take part in reducing conflict. Conservation scientists have also suggested low-cost methods for farmers, such as planting chillies, ginger or citrus around fields, which elephants tend to avoid, or placing beehives along field edges.The WWF report also records progress in India, where it says some wildlife populations have stabilised or recovered. It credits government initiatives, careful habitat management, scientific monitoring and community involvement. At the global level, the report calls for more effective conservation along with changes in food, energy and finance systems.
What the evidence points toThe picture from India and from the world is consistent. Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out, they wander into danger, they come into conflict with people, or they disappear from places they once held. Where land is protected, connected and shared with the people who live beside it, some populations hold their ground or recover.
Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out
India's own examples point in both directions: electrocutions and train deaths on one side, a record tiger count and recovering populations on the other. The difference lies largely in whether land is protected and linked together, and whether the people who live beside wildlife are part of the plan.The question on World Wildlife Day is how much room is left for wildlife, and who decides what happens to it.

Japan’s island-defense glide missile seen at Camp Fuji
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:56:26 UTC
16:56:26 KST

- New video shows Japan's Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher arriving, raising into firing position and withdrawing at Camp Fuji.
- Japan deployed the missile to Camp Fuji on March 31 and plans new units in Hokkaido and Kyushu during fiscal 2026.
New video from Camp Fuji shows Japan’s Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher driving onto a firing site, raising its missiles into launch position and packing up again, giving a rare look at how the country’s first domestically built long-range strike missile is operated.
The three-minute clip was posted on X by Japanese military photographer @yahou5, who described it as the full sequence from arrival through moving into firing posture to withdrawal. It shows a heavy 8×8 truck carrying two large missile canisters on its back. The post was tagged with Camp Fuji and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Fuji School, which runs the service’s artillery training.
Japan deployed the weapon to Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture on March 31, the same day the Defense Ministry gave it its official name. Developed as the Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile for island defense, it was redesignated the Type 25 HVGP, also known as 25HGP. The unit at Camp Fuji is the Field Artillery Training Unit, which is using the first systems to train crews and work out how the weapon will be used.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said at the time that the deployment, together with the Type 25 surface-to-ship missile sent to Camp Kengun in Kumamoto, was the first time domestically produced stand-off missiles had been delivered to Japanese military units. Stand-off weapons are meant to hit an enemy force from outside the range of its own weapons.
The HVGP works differently from a cruise missile. A rocket booster carries it to high altitude, where the warhead section separates and glides toward the target at very high speed, maneuvering on the way down. That combination of speed and an unpredictable flight path makes it harder to intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. Japanese outlet Jiji Press has described it as a type of hypersonic glide weapon, flying at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Defense Ministry says the current Block 1 version has a range of several hundred kilometers. Japanese media have reported figures of up to 900 km (560 miles). The ministry is developing longer-range versions, with a goal of 1,000 to 2,000 km, and a later Block 2 with a more advanced glide body is planned for the 2030s.
The launcher made its first public appearance at the Fuji Firepower Review, Japan’s largest annual live-fire demonstration, at the East Fuji Maneuver Area on June 7. There, it raised its two launch tubes upright to show its firing posture. No missile was fired.
Camp Fuji is only the first stop. The Defense Ministry plans to form new HVGP units at Camp Kamifurano in Hokkaido and Camp Ebino in Miyazaki Prefecture on Kyushu during fiscal 2026, which ends in March 2027.
The deployment has drawn attention from local officials. The ministry told the town of Oyama, home to Camp Fuji, that launch equipment would be stationed there, but it has declined to say whether warheads are kept at the base.

billion.

OPEC+ Set to Keep November Oil Output Targets Steady, Sources Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:53:24 UTC
16:53:24 KST

OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
“The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
“Consequently, the oil market remains tight.”
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
OUTPUT HIKES HAVE BEEN LARGELY ON PAPER THIS YEAR
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members’ 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven hold their next meeting on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group called the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), which does not decide policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.

New U.S. Army tank and fighting vehicles spotted during live-fire testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:50:36 UTC
16:50:36 KST

- Footage shared by U.S. Army CTO Alexander Miller shows the M1E3 Abrams tank and two XM30 infantry fighting vehicle prototypes firing live rounds.
- Miller also saw the Mobile Tactical Cannon and robots from Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury shooting down drones.
New footage shows the U.S. Army’s next-generation M1E3 Abrams tank and two prototypes competing to replace the Bradley infantry fighting vehicle firing live rounds, one of the first public looks at the vehicles in action.
The footage was shared on LinkedIn by Alexander Miller, chief technology officer to the U.S. Army chief of staff. Miller wrote that he went hands-on with the M1E3 pre-prototype, one of the XM30 offerings, the Mobile Tactical Cannon and some new optics, and watched robots from the U.S. Army’s Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury shoot down drones. He did not say where the event took place or name the units involved.
The M1E3 is the U.S. Army’s redesign of its main battle tank, launched in 2023 after the service cancelled a planned SEPv4 upgrade to the current Abrams. The first early prototype was unveiled at the Detroit Auto Show in January. It has an uncrewed turret with an autoloader, a three-person crew seated in the hull, digital controls and an open systems architecture meant to allow quick hardware and software updates. Four pre-prototypes built by Roush are due to reach the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, known as the Iron Horse brigade, at Fort Hood, Texas, later this year, with General Dynamics Land Systems delivering more.
The XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle competition pits General Dynamics Land Systems’ Wolf against American Rheinmetall’s Lynx-based design. Both companies delivered their first prototypes at the end of August and the start of September, and each is building eight. The two designs are headed to the same Iron Horse brigade for soldier testing, including a National Training Center rotation in spring 2027, and the U.S. Army could pick a winner after that.
The Mobile Tactical Cannon is the U.S. Army’s program to replace the towed M777 howitzer with a wheeled, self-propelled 155 mm gun that can fire and move quickly. In August, the service picked Hanwha Defense USA’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, ordering six prototypes with an option for 12 more.
Miller used the post to argue that cheap, numerous systems still matter alongside expensive ones.
“Mass still matters. Pretending that it doesn’t is risk blindness and academics. To take and hold land you need mass – affordable mass, with autonomy, mission planning at superhuman scale and speed, and execution at echelon,” said Alexander Miller, chief technology officer to the U.S. Army chief of staff.
“We should always make the first engagement with any adversary a trade for blood and steel. Their blood, our steel,” Miller said.
He also pointed to the networks behind the vehicles. Miller said the Next Generation Command and Control program provides the data platform for tools and applications, while the Integrated Battle Command System-Maneuver handles fire control and asset management for counter-drone sensors and weapons. Cheap, attritable drones flow to units from the Defense Innovation Unit’s Drone Dominance Program through a drone marketplace, he wrote.
Power is a growing problem for troops in the field, Miller added.
“Soldiers draw between 60-120W depending on their loadout. That’s nearly continuous. When you get to a squad you’re at almost a kW of draw – that’s before drone batteries,” Miller said.
He said mobile power that does not give away troops through visual, acoustic or infrared signatures is critical.
Operation Jailbreak is the U.S. Army’s push to make sensors, weapons and software from different companies work together, starting with counter-drone and air defense systems. Miller did not say which robots took part or what weapons they used against the drones.
The U.S. Army has not said when M1E3 testing with the Iron Horse brigade will begin or released results from the live-fire event.

Darren Lyn
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
The president of the US’ Cornell University on Saturday addressed allegations that a woman was gang raped on campus in 2024, calling the claims “deeply disturbing.”
The case at the Ivy League university in upstate New York returned to the spotlight last week after the local district attorney announced that a criminal investigation was being reopened to determine whether charges are warranted.
The video statement by university President Michael Kotlikoff came nearly a week after the announcement and after the university issued written statements responding to the renewed investigation.
“What happened to ‘Jane Doe’ in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come,” Kotlikoff said, using the US term for a person whose identity is being withheld. “My heart aches when I think of what she experienced.”
He said the case raised “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use” at the university.
“This has been one of the most difficult weeks in our history, and I know many of you are angry, saddened, and struggling,” he added.
 
- Civil suit filed over 2024 incident
The criminal investigation was reopened less than two weeks after Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16 against seven men she alleges raped her. All were members of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity, according to the lawsuit.
She told Cornell University Police about the alleged assault of Oct. 19-20, 2024, on that Nov. 8, according to New York television station WCBS.
“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” she said in an interview transcript cited by the station.
Local prosecutors declined to pursue criminal charges at the time, with Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten saying there was “insufficient evidence.”
 
- New investigation with special prosecutor
Kathy Hochul, the governor of New York state, this week removed Van Houten from the case and appointed a special prosecutor to lead the reopened investigation.
Kotlikoff backed the decision and said the handling of the original allegations raised questions about how the case was investigated.
“We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves,” he said.
“I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better. We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again.”
As the case draws national attention, Kotlikoff said Cornell is reviewing its response to sexual assault and considering additional measures to improve campus safety.
“Where we can do better, we will. That is our responsibility and is one I take personally,” he said.
“This is a defining moment in Cornell’s history. We must lead the way. We owe it to Jane Doe and survivors of assault to get this right, and we must keep each other safe.”

Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
RIGA, Oct 4 - Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.
With 97% of ballots counted after Saturday's election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3%, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament.
A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into Latvia.
Latvia's economy has underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and Kulbergs has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, political scientist Roberts Kits said.
"Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that he can do things differently, bring some fresh energy," he said.
"This means the responsibility is huge. People expect him to deliver, but the question remains whether he has the team to do it."
United List appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said.
PM PLEDGES TO MAINTAIN HARD LINE ON RUSSIA
Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow.
"Any economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, it can bring some extra money, but it's a weakness Russia might exploit," he told reporters at his party's headquarters on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of the win.
"It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result," Kulbergs said.
Voter turnout was 51.8%, down from 59.4% in 2022.
United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1%. Latvia First had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote.
Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7%, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9%.
Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised moreanti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defencespending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highestlevels in NATO.
His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid toUkraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues,particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority.
Although pro-Russian parties increased their representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to influence government policy.
Latvia's ethnic Russian minority is split between thosewho oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life, which many of them see asdiscriminatory.
Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwichedbetween the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, withEU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south. REUTERS

U.S. Air Force adds $12M for AI agents on doomsday plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:43:42 UTC
16:43:42 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $12.1 million to Scale AI's contract for agentic AI on the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, raising it to $44.3 million.
- The work runs through Nov. 5, 2027, with $5 million in fiscal 2026 research funds obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has added $12.1 million to a contract with Scale AI to develop artificial intelligence agents for the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, the new “doomsday plane” meant to keep U.S. leaders in command of the military, including nuclear forces, if ground command centers are destroyed.
The modification raises the total value of the San Francisco company’s contract from $32.2 million to $44.3 million, the U.S. Department of War said. The work will be done in San Francisco and is expected to run through Nov. 5, 2027. The U.S. Air Force obligated $5 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at award.
The notice does not say what tasks the AI agents will perform aboard the aircraft, whether they will run on the plane itself or on ground systems that support it, or how much human control will be built in.
Agentic AI goes a step beyond chatbots that answer questions. These systems can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, such as gathering and sorting information, drafting options or managing workflows, with people supervising or approving key decisions. On a command aircraft packed with communications gear and a battle staff, that could mean helping crews handle large volumes of messages and data during a crisis, though the U.S. Air Force has not described its plans.
The original contract was awarded earlier this year through the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Information Directorate in Rome, New York. The latest modification was issued by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts.
The E-4C will replace the E-4B Nightwatch, a fleet of four heavily modified Boeing 747-200s that first flew in the 1970s and serve as the National Airborne Operations Center. The aircraft are hardened against the effects of nuclear blasts and can be refueled in flight, allowing them to stay aloft for long periods while the president, defense secretary and senior commanders direct forces from the air.
Sierra Nevada Corp. won a $13 billion contract in April 2024 to build the replacement. The company bought used Boeing 747-8I airliners from Korean Air and is converting them in Dayton, Ohio, adding protection against radiation and electromagnetic pulse, new communications antennas, computers and mission systems. The first E-4C test aircraft flew on Aug. 7, 2025, and flight and ground testing is continuing through 2026 before mission equipment is installed. Deliveries are scheduled to finish by July 2036.
Scale AI, best known for labeling data used to train AI models, has become a major supplier of AI tools to the U.S. military. In March 2025, it won the Defense Innovation Unit’s Thunderforge project to bring AI agents into military planning and operations, working with Anduril and Microsoft. Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office raised the ceiling on another Scale AI agreement from $100 million to $500 million. Meta holds a minority stake in the company.

Nothing stolen, lights left on: Finland probes MPs’ home break-ins amid Russia tensions
