Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:42:40 UTC
16:42:40 KST

Finnish authorities are investigating a series of suspicious break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, incidents Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said could potentially be linked to a foreign power.
Parliament Speaker Jussi Halla-aho said lawmakers had been informed of a “significant” number of break-ins and signs of attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians, prompting an investigation.
“I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspicious cases known to us, but in any event it is a significant number,” Halla-aho told a news conference. He said the incidents appeared to have taken place over an extended period, with the first believed to have occurred about a year ago.
“At this stage, there is no information about the motive or who is responsible,” he said.
Asked whether a foreign power could be behind the suspected break-ins, Orpo said it was “entirely possible. It is certainly possible these days.”
“If someone is trying to undermine stability in Finland, our sense of security or, for example, our support for Ukraine, it achieves the opposite result,” he added. “It only strengthens our unity.”
The investigation was announced after Finnish newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported last week that members of parliament had been warned several days earlier about possible break-ins.
President Alexander Stubb said an “attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy.”
“It must not be allowed or accepted in any form,” he told reporters at a ceremony marking the launch of Finland’s new F-35 fighter jets in Rovaniemi in the country’s far north.
Most of the known incidents occurred in the Helsinki area and targeted politicians from different parties, both men and women.
Halla-aho said it was possible the intruders had deliberately left clear signs that they had been inside the homes. Finnish media reported cases in which doors were left open, lights were left on or objects were moved to make the intrusion obvious and unsettle the occupants.
One member of parliament reportedly returned home to find that someone had used the toilet and failed to flush.
Because the intruders apparently left without stealing anything or causing major damage, the incidents have raised suspicions that the objective may have been intimidation or psychological pressure against senior Finnish officials.
The investigation comes amid growing tension in northern Europe over fears of possible Russian military action against countries in the region, particularly the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, all former Soviet republics and now NATO members.
Finland, which maintained military neutrality for decades, joined NATO following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The move angered the Kremlin, particularly because Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia, the longest Russian border held by any EU or NATO country.
Meanwhile, Finland’s government and Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen survived two separate no-confidence votes in parliament on Friday following criticism from opposition parties over the minister’s visit to Israel.
The Social Democratic Party filed a no-confidence motion against the right-wing government, accusing it of inconsistency in its Middle East policy. A separate motion by the Greens, backed by the Left Alliance and the Social Democrats, targeted Häkkänen personally.
Häkkänen survived by a vote of 114 to 61, while the government won its vote by 93 to 62.
The criticism followed Häkkänen’s September visit to Lebanon and Israel. In Israel, he met Defense Minister Israel Katz, primarily to discuss purchases of Israeli military equipment, including the David’s Sling missile defense system.
Finland and Israel signed a deal for the system in November 2023 amid Finnish concerns over a possible future conflict with Russia. Opposition parties also criticized Häkkänen for not meeting Palestinian representatives during the trip.
“It is still unclear whether Minister Häkkänen raised Israel’s violations of international law” against the Palestinian population during his visit, the Social Democratic Party said last week.
Häkkänen defended the visit, saying it was essential to Finland’s security.

Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while South Korea's military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its capabilities, said it travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea announced Saturday that it had test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile, claiming the weapon can manoeuvre in flight to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
The launch comes as tensions between the two Koreas run high over landmine explosions along their border.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother oversaw the test. She called the missile "strategic", a term that suggests it is meant to carry nuclear warheads. She also claimed it can alter its trajectory at low altitudes and has unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities, which she said would make it extremely hard to intercept.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while the South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea claims new missile capabilities
According to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, the North Korean missile was fired early Saturday from the eastern coastal Wonsan area. Japan's Defense Ministry later put the distance at roughly 680 kilometres.
In her statement, Kim Yo Jong pointed to the gap between the two US allies' figures as proof that they could not follow the missile in flight.
"Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said. "There is no way to avoid this attack."
The launch followed a day after she mocked Seoul's demand that Pyongyang apologise for the 21 September landmine explosions. The blasts went off about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line and wounded three South Korean soldiers.
A joint inspection by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had planted the mines, and the command later found that Pyongyang had breached the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Seoul has also asked the North to stop fortifying the border with mines and anti-tank barriers. That work has sped up since Kim Jong Un dropped the goal of reconciliation in 2024 and branded Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo Jong, who may be the second most powerful person in Pyongyang, called Seoul's demands "utterly pathetic" on Friday and rejected any North Korean responsibility for the blasts, warning of retaliation if the South fires on troops working along the border.
Pyongyang's weapons tests are piling up
The Wonsan launch is the newest in a string of recent military displays, which also include missile tests, live-fire drills and the commissioning of a new warship. Kim Jong Un is showing off his expanding nuclear programme even as Washington urges a return to diplomacy.
Wonsan also hosted the Sept. 20 test of what state media described as a hypersonic missile system. It belongs to a family of weapons built to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan, including solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles first revealed in 2024.
South Korea's military said it had raised its surveillance level for further launches and was sharing information closely with Washington and Tokyo. The US Pacific Command said the launch "does not pose an immediate threat to American personnel or territory or to our allies."
Kim has mostly turned his back on diplomacy with the US and South Korea since his nuclear talks with President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. He has shifted his focus to Moscow, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons to back Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. After years of heavier testing, his arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles now includes long-range systems that could potentially reach the U.S. mainland and shorter-range ones that threaten South Korea and Japan.
In August, Trump scaled back a large joint exercise with South Korea, apparently hoping to restart talks.
North Korea has brushed off the overture, insisting that Washington first end its "hostile policy", a phrase Pyongyang uses to describe US-led sanctions and joint military drills with South Korea.

Saudi-led coalition dismisses ‘misleading’ Houthi claim of Riyadh attack
The Saudi-led coalition spokesman says the Yemeni armed group is ‘attempting to divert attention’ from its losses.
Saudi-backed Yemeni army says 700 Houthis killed in 24 hours
The Houthis’ claims that the Iran-allied armed group has targeted Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh are “misleading”, according to the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki’s remarks came on Saturday after the Houthis claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on an Aramco oil facility near Riyadh.
The group said the assault caused large fires as fighting between the Houthis and government forces intensifies in Yemen.
In remarks carried by Saudi media Asharq Al-Awsat late on Saturday, al-Maliki claimed that the Houthis are “attempting to divert attention from the scale of the losses and the growing public anger against them”.
‘Chaos and devastation’
The development comes after the Yemeni forces “executed 257 precision targeting operations” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities on Saturday, according to the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili.
He added that initial estimates indicate that the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels.
Meanwhile, al-Maliki said the Houthis’ “ties to external agendas” have brought “chaos and devastation to Yemen”, adding that “what the Houthis are facing in Taiz … drive them to seek illusory victories”.
Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing hundreds of thousands of people since then.
In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

Taipei mayoral candidates clash over framing of drug policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:37:40 UTC
16:37:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) have clashed over drug policy, despite both supporting existing needle-exchange and methadone programs.
The controversy intensified after Shen discussed international harm-reduction approaches, including community centers, clean needles, and methadone treatment. Chiang responded in a Facebook post Saturday that drug policy must maintain a clear distinction between drugs and medicine, per CNA.
Chiang clarified Sunday that he supports methadone treatment and clean-needle policies but opposes drug decriminalization and community centers that provide drugs. He also supports stronger action against drug smuggling, trafficking, manufacturing, and use, along with expanded anti-drug education.
Shen has argued that harm reduction should form part of a broader strategy combining prevention, treatment, and law enforcement. He noted that needle-exchange and methadone programs are already established public health measures in Taiwan.
Taiwan introduced its harm-reduction program after HIV infections rose sharply among people who inject drugs. The Centers for Disease Control began implementing needle-exchange and methadone treatment programs in 2005, after which new HIV infections among people who inject drugs declined sharply, per a health ministry press release.
CDC Director-General Lo Yi-chun (羅一鈞) cited a National Taiwan University College of Public Health study that estimated the two programs prevented 13,664 HIV diagnoses among people who inject drugs between 2005 and 2020. It projected that they would prevent another 10,821 diagnoses from 2021 through 2040.
The measures cost an estimated NT$21 billion (US$660 million) from 2005 through 2020 while saving about NT$404.1 billion in HIV-related medical costs, according to Lo. He said every NT$1 invested could save about NT$19 in medical costs and added that disease prevention should not be viewed through a partisan lens.
The dispute centers on how harm-reduction programs fit within broader drug policy and how candidates communicate the distinction between treatment and decriminalization.

====================================================================================================

Across China: From import replacement to global exporter, Chinese harvester maker sweetens sugarcane business
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:34:17 CST
16:34:17 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhang Yunlong
ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- "People say a woman fears marrying the wrong man, while a man fears choosing the wrong trade. I definitely chose the wrong trade," Zhang Changxian, 59, said with a laugh.
When Zhang began developing a sugarcane harvester in 2008, he expected challenges. He did not expect it would take eight years to bring the machine to market.
For years, the engineer-turned-entrepreneur and his team spent harvest seasons testing and redesigning prototypes in cane fields in Chongzuo, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. The city is about 1,600 km from his factory in Luoyang, central China's Henan Province.
During one field test, a steering linkage snapped in a muddy patch. In many others, the machine struggled with cane flattened by typhoons.
Today, machines made by his company, Luoyang Chenhan Agricultural Equipment Technology, account for about half of China's sugarcane harvester market by volume, the company says. They are also drawing buyers overseas, from Southeast Asia to Latin America.
The company's rise comes as China's sugar industry seeks to cut costs and improve competitiveness through mechanization.
China has long relied on imports to bridge a wide gap between domestic sugar output and demand. In the 2024/25 marketing year, the country produced about 11.2 million tonnes of sugar and consumed about 15.7 million tonnes, according to the Chinese Agriculture Outlook Committee under the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Imports totaled about 4.6 million tonnes.
According to Zhang, major sugar-exporting countries such as Brazil generally enjoy lower production costs, with large-scale mechanized farming being one of the key factors.
Rising labor costs have added to the pressure on China's sugar industry. When Zhang entered the industry in 2008, a worker could harvest about one tonne of cane a day for 25 to 30 yuan (3.7 to 4.5 U.S. dollars). Today, the same work can cost 180 to 250 yuan, he said, while harvested cane sells for around 500 yuan a tonne.
As labor costs climb, demand for mechanized harvesting has grown. One Chenhan harvester, Zhang said, can now cut more than 100 tonnes of cane a day, roughly the work of 100 laborers.
When Zhang started, nearly all harvesters in China were imported. His team decided to develop equipment tailored to local conditions. But building a domestic harvester proved far harder than many had expected.
Unlike in Brazil and Australia, where cane is often grown on large plantations, China's major sugarcane regions typically have sloping terrain, with smaller and more fragmented fields.
Many major agricultural machinery makers focused on larger markets for wheat, corn and rice equipment, while sugarcane harvesting was a niche segment with significant technical challenges. With no established supply chains or mature domestic components for sugarcane harvesters at the time, Zhang's team had to design and test many critical systems themselves.
Each year offered only a narrow testing window because cane is harvested in a specific season, so a design flaw found in the field often meant waiting another year for large-scale trials.
After nearly three years without a breakthrough, Zhang put the project on hold for a while. Experts, including his former mentor, advised him to give up, he recalled.
A turning point came in 2011 when the team resumed work and shifted from an earlier whole-stalk harvesting approach to a chopped-cane system better suited to Chinese field conditions.
"At times we nearly ran out of money," Zhang said. To keep going, he used money set aside for his daughter's education and later mortgaged property to fund development.
Chenhan completed its first harvester in 2015. The machine entered the market a year later and sold more than 30 units in 2016, rising to more than 150 the following year.
Overseas expansion began in 2019. The company has since exported machines to countries including Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Costa Rica and Venezuela. Exports account for about one-fifth of revenue and are growing steadily, Zhang said.
Many foreign buyers are drawn by lower prices and the company's willingness to customize equipment. Customers in the French overseas department of Reunion, for example, requested tracked harvesters able to work on volcanic soil. The company developed a specialized tracked machine to reduce ground pressure and optimized its cooling systems for the island's tropical climate.
Looking ahead, Zhang said the company is exploring smarter controls, hybrid power systems and lower fuel consumption.
"Many people told us Chinese companies couldn't make a sugarcane harvester," Zhang said, recalling the early doubts. "We made it, and now we're exporting it." ■

Report: Israel's Transportation Ministry warned foreign-flight security was 'too big' for its security division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:25:16 UTC
16:25:16 KST

In mid-2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unequivocally placed responsibility for the security of foreign airlines flying to Israel with the Transportation Ministry and its Security Division. Behind the scenes, however, officials in the division strongly opposed the move, arguing they lacked the necessary tools, authority and budget.
Despite those concerns, no one raised a formal alarm. Neither the security agencies nor the ministry’s Security Division intervened, and the division did not approach the security services for assistance.
According to a report aired Sunday morning by Army Radio, the Shin Bet relinquished responsibility for securing foreign flights in 2021, while the Transportation Ministry failed to assume that responsibility in practice. The State Comptroller reportedly pointed to the issue in a classified May 2024 report that remains under gag order.
The comptroller’s report prompted the security cabinet in May 2024 to order the National Security Council to establish a team with the Transportation Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet, Mossad and Finance Ministry to examine the security framework for civil aviation to Israel.
The National Security Council conducted a year-long review, during which disagreements emerged within the Transportation Ministry. The NSC and Shin Bet pushed for the ministry to assume responsibility, a position also supported by Civil Aviation Authority Director Shmuel Zakai.
But according to the Army Radio report, Transportation Ministry Security Division chief Avri Cohen argued in internal discussions that the responsibility was too heavy and that the issue was beyond the division’s capabilities, voicing his objections to Zakai.
“During the discussions, a scenario was raised in which all it would take was for a Syrian migrant who had moved to Britain to board a plane. He would look British, not Syrian, and we would not know,” a source familiar with the discussions was quoted as saying.
“There were major blowups, confrontations and strongly worded letters, but Regev, Director-General Ben Zaken and the head of the Civil Aviation Authority did not listen,” the source said.
In mid-2025, Netanyahu ultimately ruled that responsibility would be transferred to the Transportation Ministry and its Security Division.
A year and a half later, according to the report, no one has approached the security agencies to request assistance. The Shin Bet and Mossad, for their part, have not expanded their responsibilities or offered such assistance.

Ossoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:21:26 UTC
16:21:26 KST

Ossoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democratic favourite, is running for re-election in Georgia in the 2026 US midterms while Abdul El-Sayed is a Senate candidate in the battleground state of Michigan. The two Democrats have very different profiles and platforms, underscoring divergences within the party. They could also determine the party's future ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Top Republicans have had it in for Senator Jon Ossoff and Abdul El-Sayed, both Democratic candidates for the US Senate, for a while now. As the November 3 midterms approach, campaign battles get more stinging, bruising – and at times, amusing.
Ossoff, the incumbent senator from Georgia running for re-election, has long been in President Donald Trump’s sights. But the 37-year-old Democrat can give as good as he gets.
Just months after Trump called the Georgia Democrat “Senator Os(jerk!)off” in a Truth Social post, Ossoff hit home with a quip on the president’s zealous aide, Natalie Harp. While accusing Trump of not wanting to “do the job”, Ossoff remarked that the US president simply wants to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace".
Read more‘She’ll never leave me’: Who is Natalie Harp, Trump’s most devoted aide?
The Republican response came swift and hard, with White House communications staff labeling Ossoff a “lightweight”, “Jon Jackoff” and “the biggest cuck loser”, among other epithets.
El-Sayed, who is running in Michigan, has also been the target of virulent attacks. At the Republican midterm convention in Texas, Senator Ted Cruz accused El-Sayed, whose parents are Egyptian immigrants, of seeking to implement Sharia law. Hecklers in the crowd roared back, “He should be shot,” sparking headlines in the US press. Weeks later, Cruz was at it again. In an interview with a conservative radio show, the Texas senator warned of a “green-red alliance of Marxists and Islamists” who are “taking over” the Democratic party.
Two candidates, two states, one goal
In the 2026 US midterms, Ossoff and El-Sayed are both trying to defend Democratic seats in high-stakes races. The Georgia senator is running for re-election after serving his first term in the US senate. In Michigan, El-Sayed is running for the seat vacated by outgoing Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
The two candidates also happen to be running against two Mikes: Ossoff’s Republican opponent is Mike Collins, who currently holds a seat in the US House of Representatives. El-Sayed is taking on Mike Rogers, a former FBI agent, veteran and staunch Trump ally.
As Senate candidates, Ossoff and El-Sayed have very different profiles.
The Georgia politician is ahead in the polls and is viewed as a rising Democratic star, a potential “hot presidential possibility” for the 2028 White House race. Feisty, media savvy and with choirboy looks, Ossoff is the country’s youngest serving senator and the only Democrat in the chamber to be seeking re-election in a state Trump won in 2024. Within the party, Ossoff is viewed as a moderate Democrat, capable of appealing to a broad base of voters in one of America’s right-leaning southern states.
El-Sayed, on the other hand, has never held elected office. The 41-year-old physician and public health expert is considered a left-wing politician, part of a wave of progressive Democrats focused on affordability and state services.
But in a battleground state that is home to cities with major Muslim communities such as Dearborn, “the capital of Arab America”, his position on the Israeli-Palestinian crisis often overshadows his economic justice messaging – and grabs global headlines. El-Sayed narrowly won his party’s nomination in August after a nasty primary against his pro-Israel rival Haley Stevens that exposed bitter divides within the party. In a state that regularly sends Democrats to the US Senate, the Michigan race is considered a tossup.
Read moreDemocrat El-Sayed narrowly wins Michigan primary
They are two candidates running in different states, but both are critical to the common Democratic goal of attempting to wrest control of the Senate in the November elections. “They're both important states where Democrats have sometimes struggled, perhaps Georgia more than Michigan, but they’re both seen as important wins for Democrats," said Matt Duss from the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders, who is a leading progressive in the Democratic party.
"Obviously, Abdullah El-Sayed is an Arab Muslim who is taking a much more progressive populist approach. But Ossoff has been a leader on the issue of anti-corruption, which is a major issue in American politics, and particularly for the progressive left. So they've both been offering what will be really important arguments for the party going forward.”
Left or right or in-between
The 2026 midterm race has increased attention on a progressive, leftward trend in the Democratic party that has picked up steam since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Democratic Socialism – a largely anodyne political ideology in many parts of the world, but which has long been stigmatised in the private capital-driven USA – is now the subject of polls and headlines across the country.
In barely two weeks, for instance, a Gallup poll found that Socialism is more popular than ever, with 43 percent of Americans holding a positive view. But The New York Times, citing another poll, informed readers that roughly half of US voters view socialism unfavourably.
For many Democratic strategists, that means a "Socialist" label is not a problem in primary race, but broadening a Socialist candidate's appeal in a general election could remain a challenge.
“In some ways, these are more differences in tone and manner and style rather than in policy,” said Richard Johnson, a US politics and policy expert at Queen Mary University of London.
While Ossoff is widely viewed as a moderate, Johnson notes that, “what people call moderate Democrat today is not what people called a moderate Democrat 20 or 30 years ago. Twenty or 30 years ago, a moderate Democrat was much more to the right of a moderate Democrat today because the whole party has moved much more consistently to the left.”
‘About three letters’
The party’s leftward move has put the focus on the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a political group founded in 1982 that spent decades in obscurity before the 2016 presidential primary catapulted Sanders to national prominence before his defeat to Hillary Clinton. While Sanders calls himself a democratic socialist, the Vermont senator is not formally affiliated with DSA.
The group got a boost in 2018, when DSA member Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won the New York primary and went on to win a House of Representatives seat. A high-profile breakthrough came in late 2025 with the election of Zohran Mamdani as New York City mayor.
Since the DSA is a movement that aims to promote progressive issues and not a political party, it can be a source of messaging gymnastics and sometimes panic for Democrats on the campaign trail. In a CBS interview last week, Florida's Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon stressed that "this is not about three letters" amid Republican criticism of her DSA membership. Nixon was one of the big surprises of the 2026 Democratic primaries, when the African-American self-described “former single mama” overcame a vast fundraising disadvantage to defeat former military officer and fellow Florida Democrat Alex Vindman.
While most analysts place El-Sayed on the left of the political spectrum, the Michigan candidate is not a DSA member. “El-Sayed has made it clear that he is not a Socialist. He describes himself as a capitalist who understands capitalism, that’s where his critique of capitalism comes from. But still, he is arguing for many things that DSA argues for. So, however he may identify himself, there is a formation behind him that includes the DSA that sees his message as consistent with their broader agenda,” explained Duss.
US Mideast policy on the ticket
A distinctive feature of the 2026 midterms race is the prominence foreign policy has played on the campaign trail. That’s largely because Trump’s Iran war has seen an overlap of domestic and international issues.
“The Iran war is raising gas prices, impacting the global economy and the US economy. But it's also feeding into a longstanding sense among many American voters, both Democrat and Republican and Independent, that America has been wasting time, resources and energy on all of these wars, particularly in the Middle East,” said Duss.
“But in the Democratic side, especially, I think Gaza continues to be a very severe tension point between the progressive left and the conservative establishment,” he added, referring to Israel’s military onslaught on the Palestinian enclave after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
In Michigan, while El-Sayed’s platform is focused on providing healthcare and cost-of-living issues, the spotlight in the bitter primary race was on the two candidates’ positions on Israel.
His Democratic rival, Stevens, ran on a pro-Israel platform and raised a record $60 million, around half of which came from sources affiliated with pro-Israel lobby group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). El-Sayed criticised Stevens for taking AIPAC donations, calls Israeli military onslaught in Gaza a genocide and opposes unconditional US aid to Israel. Stevens supported continuing US aid to Israel without conditions.
“The Democratic party is changing quite a lot on this issue. The party used to be pretty much as pro-Israel as the Republican Party. Now many Democratic voters are much more sceptical on Israel. There are elements where you can see the grassroots moving the party in a direction that's different from where it has been in the last few decades,” said Johnson.
Following El-Sayed’s primary win, Michigan Democrats – including Stevens and establishment figures such as Senator Elissa Slotkin, who holds the state’s other seat in the chamber – have rallied behind their candidate in the race against Republican Mike Rogers.
But it’s been a tripwire issue. El-Sayed has had to downplay his relationship with leftwing influencer Hasan Piker, who campaigned with him during the primary. Barely weeks after his primary victory, the Democratic candidate apologised to the state’s Jewish Democratic caucus for comments he made after a synagogue attack in March.
The controversies have sparked debates over whether El-Sayed, who won the primary by just 15,000 votes, can sway undecided voters and an estimated 130,000 Jewish Americans who live in Michigan, 61% of whom identified with or leaned Democrat, according to a 2021 study.
It also fuels Republican attacks as they eye a crucial Senate seat in a battleground state. Shortly after El-Sayed was projected to win the August primary, Trump declared it was “great news” for the Republicans in a Truth Social post. “El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in this race with the Socialist,” Trump wrote. Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in the Senate race, released a statement claiming that after spending “years hunting terrorists” he was now “running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11”.
“There's been so much attention on El-Sayed being an observant Muslim and much of it is, unfortunately, very bigoted and inflammatory,” said Duss. “Going back to 9/11, there has been an unfortunate tendency to see Muslim Americans as a source of threat. I completely reject that. And I think many Americans reject that.”
‘An almighty battle’ within the party
Ossoff, whose father is Jewish, has managed to negotiate the minefield of the Mideast crisis in US politics relatively unscathed.
On the Senate floor, Ossoff has attempted a balancing act between supporting Israel’s right to defend itself while criticising the humanitarian impact of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Gaza policies.
Last year, for instance, Ossoff voted to block a proposed US arms export to the Israeli police. But he also voted against another resolution that would have blocked the sale of air-to-ground munitions to Israel. “Despite my opposition to Prime Minister Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza, I believe the United States must continue to support the Israeli people,” said Ossoff in a press statement. Both resolutions were introduced by Sanders and failed the floor vote.
“Georgia is a more conservative state [than Michigan], Senator Ossoff has a read on his own politics,” said Duss, while noting that Ossoff’s vote to block arms exports to the Israeli police “took some courage”. The former foreign policy adviser to Sanders admitted that, “Personally, I wish he would go farther. I think he can go farther, and I would expect that if he wants to play a role as a leader in the Democratic Party in the future, he is going to need to go farther.”
In terms of policy shifts, Johnson believes the 2026 midterms will have a limited impact even if the Democrats manage to take over Congress. “I think government shutdowns in the US will be more likely to happen. If they win, the Democrats will use bargaining over budgets basically to try to extract some policy concessions over Trump, perhaps on immigration or such issues. But I think these will be fairly modest policy changes,” he explained.
The real impact of the November elections, Johnson predicts, will be the Democratic bench or the likely party candidates the midterms propel into the 2028 presidential race.
If El-Sayed and Ossoff win their respective races, the two men could influence their party’s future trajectory, according to experts.
“If El-Sayed wins the Senate, I think he is well very well-positioned to play a major national role, perhaps not running for president right now, but he is a very skilled candidate, a very courageous voice. And the United States is changing,” said Duss.
While Ossoff has dismissed speculation about his presidential ambitions, analysts believe the Democratic “star of the south” could be a strong candidate for the 2028 White House race.
“If Jon Ossoff is going to become the next [presidential] nominee, I think he’ll have a hell of a fight on his hands because I think the left of the party is going to really want someone that they view as a less compromising figure politically,” said Johnson. “The next Democratic primary is likely to see an almighty battle between the moderates and the left of the party.”

Ukraine’s Energy Future: a UN Pilot Project Backed by Italy in Odesa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:18:00 UTC
16:18:00 KST

Odesa has been chosen as a testing ground for an important United Nations initiative to advance energy innovation in Ukraine. Led by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and financed by Italy, the new Pilot Decarbonization Office in Odesa explores how solar power and decentralized electricity generation can help cities withstand Russian attacks on energy infrastructure while laying the foundations for a greener recovery.
The choice also reflects the Italian government’s focus on Odesa and its region as a priority for assistance to Ukraine. Alongside support for cultural heritage and the restoration of buildings, energy resilience provides an essential foundation for the city’s recovery: reliable electricity keeps hospitals, schools, businesses and public services running.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         Carlo Formosa (Italian Ambassador), Hanna Zamazieieva (State Agency on Energy Efficiency of Ukraine), Pier Carlo Sandei (UNEP)(Photo courtesy UNEP)                             
In this interview for Kyiv Post, Pier Carlo Sandei, Head of UNEP in Kyiv, explains why Odesa was selected, what its solar potential could mean for other Ukrainian cities, and how Italian support can help turn initial assessments into lasting investment.
SOS - Ukraine’s Looming Dark Winter Demands Decisive Action
Kyiv Post: UNEP presented the results of the Italian-funded project on green and resilient energy in Odesa. What problem was it designed to solve?
Pier Carlo Sandei: The problem was created by the war, and this was since the very beginning of the war. Energy infrastructures were a target by the Russian Federation’s attacks. We had to solve short-term problems, but also long-term problems. You need to find quick solutions for the immediate and humanitarian needs, but you also need to have a rethinking of the energy mix of Ukraine for a full EU accession. So, the project was aiming at addressing both aspects.
The question was: What can we do quickly and what can the project unlock quickly as resources for energy crisis solution? And on the other side: How can we start looking not only at today and tomorrow, but also to next year, to the next 10 years?
So the project had both dimensions. And this is what we are trying to do with different components of the project, working on short term and long term. An example of short term in Odesa is the solar city simulator, because it tells you today where to install solar panels on every roof. And this is something that can be done in one week. I mean, if you have the money tomorrow, you can install the solar panels and be independent. This is a quick solution.
On the other side you can have a long-term solution, which is, for example, what we are doing in Odesa, as well, with this 30-megawatt solar power plant. It will take more time, but will also have a longer-term impact on the overall energy balance of the region and in Ukraine.
What are the most important lessons learned from the assessment work presented in the Odesa Regional Recovery Forum?
As refers to the Odesa components of the project, the first thing is that with only 5% of the roofs covered with solar panels, you can get 25% of the energy needs of the city. So, there’s enough sun and there are enough roofs to have enough electricity and a diversified and diffused energy distribution.
I’m not saying that the Russian Federation will not hit the roofs with salt water, but the damage would be much less than if it were a centralized power. These are the lessons learned, where decentralization is important to make sure that we can get resilience.
The second thing is that we have so far relied a lot on gas turbines and diesel generators, but these have, in the long term, a negative impact on the energy mix of the country, as well as on the environment and the economy, because diesel generators, with the price of diesel today, is becoming very expensive source of energy. With solar panels, you do the investment only once and then they keep on giving you free energy the rest of the time.
And again, these are a positive contribution to the future of Ukraine, while diesel generation and gas turbines are a negative addition to the future energy mix of Ukraine, because they will be still relying on fossil fuels and not going into right direction for the EU.
The audience in Odesa was impressed that their city will host such a pilot project, because it is very rarely chosen for this purpose. Why this decision and what can Odesa teach to other cities, like Kharkiv or Mykolaiv, involved in the project?
There are two aspects. First of all, there is a logistical issue. Odesa has a lot of sun, similar to Mykolaiv. There’s less sun in Kyiv, Rivne or Kharkiv. So, it’s easier to sell solar panels in Odesa than in the north of Ukraine, even though it is meaningful there, too.
The second thing: in Odesa we found a very proactive and responsive administration that has embarked on this project with enthusiasm. So this made it easier to work with Odesa than other parts of Ukraine.
Thirdly, of course, the Italian funding, with a special patronage of Italy for Odesa, allowed it to welcome the project.
Odesa’s energy infrastructure is regularly targeted by Russian attacks. How do you design solar, storage and backup power systems that can withstand this risk?
Well, this is the solar city simulator. You want to have a diffuse and decentralized production. So the worst case scenario is that they damage 50 solar panels, which means that the value of the drone is higher than the damage that they can make on the other side.
For this reason, you don’t want to have the 30-megawatt plant built now until it is also properly defended or until the situation changes in terms of safety. Because such a big power plant is easier target to shell. And at that point the damage would be bigger than the value of the attacks. So, it is exactly the right response to this risk.
Any international project has to pass through an assessment on corruption risks. How is this project protected with regard to corruption?
First of all, the project is managed by the UN and we have very strong safeguards and anti-corruption mechanisms. So, we are not working with financial transactions through local authorities. We work with other partners on the other side that we can control. I don’t think corruption should scare us from investing. It should force a stronger rule of law. If there is corruption, it doesn’t mean you should not do business in Ukraine.
And this is what we are doing in this project. We cannot run away because of corruption. We should fight corruption. And you should fight corruption not only by having safeguard mechanisms, but also by showing integrity, leading by example.
What about the rooftop solar assessment developed by the IRENA Solar City Simulator? How much rooftop potential did you find in Ukrainian cities? And which building types are the targets: municipal buildings, residential or commercial?
We cover the whole northern part of Odesa. So, it’s not a cherry-picking roof by roof. But we did the assessment for all the roofs of the city. Now we can tell you which ones are more productive and which are less productive. And the reason is also due to the shade, because if you have a high building next to you and you are in the shade, this building will produce less.
The analysis done on the whole territory of the city and it doesn’t distinguish between public or private or whatever. So you can go and check your own building and see how much electricity you can produce.
How does the clearing house mechanism works in practical terms, what problem does it solve for cities and investors?
When we started looking at energy projects, we saw that part of them are going to the Minister of Energy, parts of the project are going to the Minister of Territorial Community.
Some projects are going to the Minister of Environment because they are climate friendly. Others are going to the Ministry of Development. So, there is no single repository of all the energy projects happening in Ukraine.
So, if tomorrow a donor comes and says, I want to finance projects on energy, they would not be able to have one answer. They would need to go to five different ministers and sometimes even to the different oblasts. And this because of some legal obligations.
The law says that big energy projects are managed by the Minister of Energy. Small energy projects instead are dealt by the Ministry of Territorial Communities and the Minister of Development. Some are private investments, so they are not even fitting into that. Therefore, it’s difficult to facilitate the match between offer and demand, or needs and offer.
The idea would be if tomorrow somebody needs to say, okay, give me all the projects down below 10 megawatts, you would be able to have that. At the same time, if there is somebody who says, I’m willing to install solar panels, tell me where to go, they would be able to find out. At the moment, this is not happening.
The clearinghouse is about having one place where you know, what are all the possibilities are, and, on the other side, what the demand and needs are, so that it’s easier to match the two.
Italy financed this stage. What comes next? Who will pay for the implementation? Other donors, private capital or again the Italians?
Let’s say donation is including everything. Of course, we would need more funding. The AICS (Italian Agency for Cooperation and Development) is providing the finance, but also the political oversight from a G7 country. This also fits into the G7-plus initiative in support of energy for Ukraine.
We hope to show results in the short term, especially with private sector investments and Ukrainian investments, because there are resources in Ukraine for this. So it’s not only to wait for donors, but sometimes you need a small snowflake to start an avalanche.

Diplomatic path to ending war remains open: Iran FM Araghchi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:15:45 UTC
16:15:45 KST

Iran’s top diplomat made the remarks during a meeting with ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions in Iran on Sunday, stressing that the diplomatic path to ending war remains open.
Araghchi first pointed to Iran’s delegation attended at 81st UN General Assembly in New York last month, stating that Iranian delegation had a strong, influential and effective presence in New York this year.
Iran’s response to any military action will be stronger than before, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated.
Iran showed at the UN General Assembly that it has solutions for both war and peace, while efforts to isolate it have failed, he said, adding, “New US sanctions will achieve nothing. The US has failed both militarily and diplomatically.”
It has become clear to everyone that Iran remains as serious about diplomacy and finding a peaceful solution as it is about defending itself, he underlined.
“We remain firm and resolute in defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy. Should our enemies opt for a military confrontation, they will face a response far more forceful than in the past, whereas if they seek diplomatic avenues, we are prepared to reach an honorable solution through diplomatic channels.”
Araghchi then pointed to the expulsion of Iranian diplomats by the US in New York, emphasizing, “The claim made by the Americans that they expelled Iranian diplomats is truly bizarre. It demonstrated just how angry they were about the presence of the Iranian delegation.”
Referring to the meetings held with the Persian Gulf Arab states’ officials, Araghchi stated, "All of these meetings were held in a friendly atmosphere, and we have embarked on a new path for relations with these countries. Our brothers in the Persian Gulf are aligned with us, and a shared determination to establish stability—with the participation of the countries themselves—is being pursued."
Referring to the meetings held with European countries, he stated, "We hope the Europeans will reconsider their approach toward Iran. The NATO Secretary General’s admission regarding participation in a war against Iran was a grave matter. He [NATO chief] stated that over 5,000 fighter jets took off from bases in Europe, and we await an explanation from European countries. Our proposal to these nations is to engage in dialogue with Iran and avoid being drawn into any warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime."
“We hope the United States chooses the path of wisdom and rationality; however, should they pursue a military course, we are more prepared than ever. In the past, the US has lost in both war and diplomacy. Sanctions, too, are of no avail. There is no military or sanctions-based solution; only a diplomatic solution will prove effective and serve to end the aggression against Iran.”
The US claim that Iran’s delegation was expelled is absurd. The Iranian delegation traveled to and from the US as scheduled, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated.

Poland launches the world&apos;s first &quot;AbortOmat&quot;, where abortion pills can be obtained
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:14:00 EEST
16:14:00 KST

Poland launches the world's first "AbortOmat", where abortion pills can be obtained
Kyiv • UNN
A pink "AbortOmat" in Warsaw provides anonymous access to abortion pills using a six-digit code. The initiative circumvents Poland's strict restrictions.
"AbortOmat" in Warsaw offers a new way to challenge the restrictions in force in the country and provide women with fast and anonymous access to abortion pills, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
"AbortOmat" is called "the world's first vending machine for abortion pills." Polish activists introduced this new method of distribution as part of their efforts to circumvent the country's near-total abortion ban.
Painted pink and decorated with curtains featuring a "zebra" pattern, the Warsaw "AbortOmat," with its 22 compartments, allows women to quickly and anonymously obtain pills using a six-digit code. The service is designed for those who cannot or do not want to wait several days for delivery by mail (for example, in cases of an incomplete miscarriage or health complications), or who are afraid to receive such medication at home.
"Why not?" says Kinga Jelinska, director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team initiative; these two organizations launched the project this week.
"You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, or anything else and receive it practically the same day or the next day," she says. "Why not do the same with abortion pills, since in some cases the situation may be more urgent?"
The initiative emerged six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest the tightening of what was already Europe's strictest abortion legislation; those events became the largest demonstrations in the country since the fall of the communist regime. The 2023 protests are believed to have helped bring Donald Tusk to power, as he had promised to review the legislation during the first 100 days of his government.
Thousands of people in Poland call for easing abortion law24.07.24, 18:31 • 20412 views
Since then, according to Jelinska, there has been political stagnation. She recalled Prime Minister Tusk's words from last year: he said that there was "simply no majority" in parliament to change the laws and allow abortion up to the 12th week. Instead, Tusk hinted that his government would act differently, telling journalists that the authorities would not prosecute those who help arrange abortions. Although possessing or taking abortion pills is not illegal in Poland, providing these medications or helping someone obtain them is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
According to Jelinska, this locker is an unconventional way to circumvent such restrictions. "It is a kind of 'hack' of the law," she says. "The law prohibits transferring medications directly to another person. But here, a vending machine appears between people, making the question of legality much less clear-cut."
The locker is located in an abortion support center opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. The facility, the first of its kind in democratic Poland, offers a safe space where people can receive advice on abortion options or support while taking the medication.
The center's location—symbolically, opposite the Polish parliament building—has allowed activists to draw attention to the ongoing need for access to abortion services in Poland while also providing assistance to a wide range of people, Jelinska said. "The result exceeded our expectations."

"The law prohibits transferring medications directly to another person. But here, a vending machine appears between people, making the question of legality much less clear-cut."

The center’s location — symbolically, opposite the Polish parliament building — allowed activists to draw attention to the continuing need for access to abortion services in Poland, while also providing assistance to a wide range of people, Yelinska said. "The result exceeded our expectations."
At the same time, it also exposed the fact that few people among those in power were willing to stand up for them, she added. "What really surprised us — and this is indicative of the political situation — is that protests are taking place in front of the center: three, and sometimes even four, times a week."
Although fewer than a dozen people usually gather, protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their position known. This has raised activists’ fears that, because of the noise, neighbors may eventually demand that the center be relocated. "Neither the city authorities nor the police responded to this. And that disappointed us greatly," Yelinska said.
According to Yelinska, this is a vivid example of how such organizations increasingly feel abandoned by politicians — despite the fact that about 50,000 people in Poland sought help last year from the broader network of organizations defending the right to abortion. "I think access to abortion in Poland will be decided not by politicians, but by women and communities themselves," she said. "We cannot trust politicians to control our bodies."

Malaysia looks to Türkiye's tourism experience to deepen Muslim-friendly travel cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:10:02 UTC
16:10:02 KST

- Mohammad Faisal bin Abu Suaib Khan says he would like to see Malaysia adapt Türkiye’s transit tourism model to turn airport stopovers into future visits
- Cooperation could work both ways, he says, adds Malaysia offers Muslim-friendly tourism standards and recognition system
Malaysia is looking to Türkiye's experience in managing historical heritage and developing transit tourism as the two countries explore greater cooperation in Muslim-friendly travel, according to the head of Malaysia's Islamic Tourism Center.
Mohammad Faisal bin Abu Suaib Khan, director-general of the center, told Anadolu that Türkiye's experience in combining tourism with the preservation and commercial use of historical sites offers lessons for Malaysia.
"Türkiye has experience in managing heritage. The way you monetize historical monuments, and at the same time get the funding to upgrade, take care of and manage them, is very important because conservation is very costly," Faisal said.
"We can learn from the way you do business and, at the same time, how you conserve certain monuments and make them good tourist spots," he said.
Both Türkiye and Malaysia seek to expand their already significant tourism industries while tapping into the growing global Muslim travel market.
Türkiye generated $65.23 billion in tourism revenue in 2025, up 6.8% from the previous year, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute. Museums and archaeological sites recorded nearly 65.9 million visits in 2025, an increase of 6.8% year-on-year.
Malaysia welcomed 42.2 million international visitors in 2025, up from 38 million a year earlier, according to Tourism Malaysia, and is seeking to further expand the sector through its Visit Malaysia 2026 campaign.
 
Türkiye's transit tourism
Faisal said his own experience traveling through Istanbul demonstrated another Turkish tourism practice that Malaysia could potentially adapt.
During an about eight-hour layover in Istanbul while traveling to Kazan, Russia, he and a colleague were offered a city tour by Turkish Airlines.
"They brought us from the airport to the city, then on a cruise to see the historical monuments along the Bosphorus Strait, with a little bit of the historical story about every building and the historical part of the Golden Horn," he said.
The program also included a meal before the passengers returned to continue their journey.
"It was a very nice offer because they gave us a small, simple gift that made us want to come again," he said.
"The way they crafted the trip was like giving us a teaser, a very good teaser, so that we would come again and stay in Istanbul and enjoy more."
Faisal said he would like to see Malaysia develop a similar model for passengers spending long transit periods at Kuala Lumpur International Airport.
"I wish that we could do the same thing for tourists who are transiting through KLIA or KLIA2, so that we can bring them to Kuala Lumpur, let them enjoy it, and then they will come again," he said, referring to Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 1 and Terminal 2.
"This is something interesting for us to learn from Türkiye."
 
Cooperation can be both ways
Faisal stressed that cooperation would not be limited to Malaysia learning from Türkiye, saying Kuala Lumpur also has experience, particularly in establishing structured standards for Muslim-friendly tourism.
"We can learn from there, but, like I said, we can also share something," he said. "It can be bilateral – both ways."
Malaysia's Islamic Tourism Center, an agency under Malaysia's Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture, develops standards, research, training and capacity-building programs for Muslim-friendly tourism and hospitality.
"We focus on Muslim-friendly tourism and hospitality. We do the standards and also capacity building, training and research," Faisal said.
One of its key initiatives is the Muslim-Friendly Tourism and Hospitality Assurance and Recognition, which recognizes tourism businesses meeting specified requirements for serving Muslim travelers.
More than 500 businesses and services in Malaysia are registered as Muslim-friendly, including 73 hotels, 39 travel agencies, 11 spa centers and 390 tourist guides.
Faisal said Malaysia's experience with such standards could complement Türkiye's established tourism infrastructure.
"We have the Muslim-friendly assurance recognition, so people who go to Türkiye can find and have a trusted hotel that is Muslim-friendly," he said.
Türkiye already has a substantial Muslim-friendly tourism market, supported by its Islamic cultural heritage and widespread availability of halal food, mosques and accommodation catering to Muslim travelers.
"Türkiye has a very good Muslim and Islamic history, so it will be very easy for Türkiye to get enrolled in this program and, at the same time, reach the Muslim-friendly market," he said.
 
Expanding Muslim-friendly tourism beyond Muslim countries
Malaysia received 9.7 million Muslim visitors in 2025, with the figure targeted to reach 15.2 million by 2030, according to the center's data.
The recognition framework is expanding internationally, with the center developing cooperation in markets including Russia, Taiwan, Indonesia, South Korea and Brazil.
Faisal said Muslim-friendly standards could be particularly valuable in non-Muslim-majority countries, where travelers may have more difficulty identifying suitable hotels, restaurants and other services.
"For non-Muslim countries, we work with the halal certification bodies. Their product now is halal certification, so we add another product, which is the Muslim-Friendly Assurance Recognition," he said.
"They can offer a variety of hotels and halal restaurants. Instead of selling only one product, they can add Muslim-Friendly Assurance to hotels."
"The tourists who go to these non-Muslim countries can be happy because they know they have certain products. We give them assurance and, at the same time, provide the products they need and fulfill their needs," he said.
 
'We grow together because the market is the same'
Faisal said closer cooperation between Türkiye and Malaysia could also encourage travelers to combine the two destinations rather than viewing them as competitors for the Muslim tourism market.
"It can be two ways," Faisal said. "Certain people can come to Türkiye and then come to Malaysia, or someone going from Malaysia can stay in Türkiye before going to a third country."
"We also share and grow together because the market is the same. Instead of fighting for the market, we can grow together," he said.

A collection of new artworks focused on healing and resilience has been added to ANU – Museum of the Jewish People’s “October 7” exhibit as Israel marks the third anniversary of the massacre.
Curated by Michal Hominer and Carmit Blumenzon and featuring the work of 25 artists, the exhibit opened shortly after October 7, 2023, to document the events and the creative ways Israel attempted to cope with the loss.
Additionally displayed in the exhibit are the documentary work “Local Testimony for 2023” and a musical playlist consisting of Israeli songs that have become part of the war’s soundtrack.
Now, three new works by graduates of the WIZO Haifa School of Design have been added to the exhibit, detailing the search for resilience, creativity, and optimism now that all of the hostages are back in Israel.
These works include Tamara Kloss’s “Compassion Fatigue,” which comments on the thousands of commemorative stickers for the hostages and fallen soldiers since the outbreak of the war, Yael Lerner’s “I Saw a Dove,” a book illustrating the range of emotions evoked by the dove symbol, and Yehuda Feldmer’s “Shalom,” a visual study of the word “peace.”
Art as a way to heal, create hope
"Art is a great force that allows us to observe, to ease, perhaps to heal, and to create the beginning of hope,” said Col. (res.) Oded Revivi, ANU’s director general. “Three years after the October Sabbath, it is interesting to observe not only what was broken, but also the work that was born from the fracture.”
“The exhibition continues to change along with society, and the new works allow us to listen to additional voices and see how memory, personal and collective, is formed, reflects a national mindset, and in the aspiration also shapes a better future."
Dr. Orit Shaham Gober, the museum's chief curator, added, "Three years later, the work is no longer just in the first moment of reaction to the event. It allows us to observe, process, remember, and also allows us to build new hope."
"The works created during this period range between pain and the desire to search within it for the possibility of a new movement forward."

Kaimar Karu: AI risks are real, but they're not what you think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:03:00 UTC
16:03:00 KST

Kaimar Karu: AI risks are real, but they're not what you think
Rapid automation presents both opportunities and risks. Malicious actors have already begun using it. But it is these actors who commit crimes, not AI agents — software portrayed almost as mystical beings, Kaimar Karu writes.
News in recent weeks about AI and AI agents, statements and open letters from top politicians and public figures, the frantic drive to regulate everything, the recent "hacking" of Australian health data and so on have generated a considerable amount of public and political debate. Unfortunately, much of the public discourse on the subject is fairly problematic.
First, there are no rogue agents from OpenAI and Anthropic (and other companies providing LLMs, or large language models) roaming around, breaking into systems of their own accord and wreaking havoc. Framing the situation this way does not reflect reality. What we have instead are automated applications built by someone for a specific purpose, given insufficiently detailed instructions and constraints and carrying out the commands they have been given. Software. Capable software, certainly.
These applications have no morality of their own. They do not make ethical judgments or operate within the context of laws and societal rules. Various considerations and rules can be prescribed for these applications as soft constraints, but those boundaries have gaps because, due to the particular characteristics of the technology, the applications may not comply with all the requirements imposed on them.
If the task given to an application was (deliberately) described too broadly, its security measures were (deliberately) inadequate, its monitoring was (deliberately) inadequate, its reporting mechanisms were (deliberately) inadequate — or all of the above, combined with carelessness and disregard for best practices — then there is little point in casting an accusatory eye at the application that was launched.
The technology underlying these applications has no experience and no concept of legality or permissibility. The probabilistic nature inherent in it does not operate in the same way as what we have previously been accustomed to.
You can, for example, throw a ball for your Labrador and shout, "Fetch!" and then reasonably expect, though not know with 100 percent certainty, that the dog will probably jump over a low fence (rather than ram it down or set it on fire), swim across a shallow stream (rather than cut down the surrounding forest to build a bridge), dodge a child playing in its path (rather than trample the child) and bring back the ball you threw (rather than collect every ball thrown to other dogs within 10 square kilometers, because its owner obviously likes balls).
An AI agent, or automated application, by contrast, may, if it has access to the necessary tools, take steps in various situations resembling those described in parentheses because, based on its training material, weights and configuration, the application "concludes" that the very step that would seem absurd or dangerous to humans will help achieve the objective described in the task.
An AI agent does not behave like a human, or like an animal. Even the verb "behave" is clearly conditional here because we are talking about an application that performs operations rather than behaves. Because of the particular characteristics of the technology and the nature of human language (and the human mind), LLM-based applications have simply ended up in a role in which it is easy to treat them as conscious beings. Much as, in some religions of the past, the wind, sun, rain and thunder were treated as such.
In light of recent news, it should also be said that there was no "evil AI agent hack" of Australian healthcare information systems, despite how the situation was initially presented to the public.
There was an automated application that, based on what is known so far, either used an unexpected method to access public data (in which case the problem is an inadequately thought-out or documented healthcare system architecture) or exploited a security vulnerability to access confidential data (in which case the problem is inadequate prior security testing).
The situation is not fundamentally different from a citizen interested in data finding that data at an undisclosed but publicly accessible web address or from a cracker (or hacker, though that distinction requires a longer discussion) discovering a security vulnerability in a system.
There is, however, an important difference in the intensity with which such incidents will begin occurring in a world of AI agents and in the potentially dangerous impact those incidents may have.
In practical terms, every individual, group, company and country now has the ability to automate many tasks that previously would have taken a great deal of time or would not have been done at all because they would have required too much time and money. Some of these tasks may lead AI agents, or automated applications, down a path that a human would not have chosen — for example, one that violates the law. Though, of course, humans come in all kinds too.
In some cases, likely an increasing number of them, breaking the law is exactly what the person launching the application wants. Theft of personal data, theft of trade secrets, discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities in the systems of other countries' government agencies or critical service providers — all of this can now be done several orders of magnitude faster than before.
In none of these cases, however, is this an "AI agent did it" situation when it comes to responsibility. "The hammer did it" or "the ax did it"? No. Even if that hammer falls off scaffolding and hits someone on the head, someone first carelessly put the hammer there or installed the scaffolding badly. The hammer did not choose to fall.
Yes, AI agents are technologically far more complex than a hammer or an ax because a hammer generally does not strike things on its own and cannot order an ax to aim its blade. Behind every blow and every movement is a human being, directly and immediately.
With automated solutions, however, there is no longer a human being directly behind every individual step. Modern production lines perform a series of operations without human intervention. In fact, we are already familiar with this from the digital world, for example in data analysis and report generation. Even a formula in an Excel cell automatically performs calculations when the input data changes.
The difference with AI agents is significant, however, because we have never before had such readily accessible ways to tell automated solutions that, while completing a task, they may leave their environment when necessary, use various external tools and keep looking for ways to improve results until they succeed if those results happen to fall below the desired level.
Figuratively speaking, we can give an Excel formula the tools and capabilities — for example, by exploiting vulnerabilities in third-party systems — to start changing the trend in its input data in order to improve margins, bankrupting a competitor in the process or steering a competitor's CEO's self-driving car off the road and into a ravine. The report for the company's supervisory board may be delayed slightly, but the charts will look great.
Many of the risks discussed in connection with the use of artificial intelligence are real risks. Not all of them, however, because we still do not have superintelligence whose risks are also discussed in the same breath, and presidential decrees will not bring it into existence.
The way artificial intelligence risks are discussed, however, is at times absurd. Rapid automation presents both opportunities and risks. Malicious actors have already begun using it. But it is these actors who commit crimes, not AI agents — software portrayed almost as mystical beings.
In my view, new regulations governing development would not have a significant effect. The technology in question has already advanced to the point where further development can, if there is sufficient interest, take place covertly. Regulations governing its use would work to some extent, but they would affect only those seeking to avoid breaking the law, not those who misuse the technology.
Given the capabilities of this technology that are already known, as well as those that can currently only be glimpsed, it is also unlikely that countries with political systems and civil liberties somewhat different from ours and that seek to improve their international standing in competition among states would, first, go along with such regulations or, second, actually comply with them even if they appeared to do so.
The various percentages attached to scare stories and cited in support of regulation are pure fiction. "A 10 percent probability that ..." and "in 50 percent of future cases ..." remain inventions even when they are backed up with citations to pseudoscientific papers and studies that do not, in fact, support those inventions. We currently lack the ability to make such forecasts reliably. There is too much we do not know.
When considering predictions of all kinds, it is worth remembering that AI psychosis is already extremely widespread. Unlike some other dangerous technologies, artificial intelligence in particular has attracted a disturbingly large number of quasi-religious people, as well as people who do not appear troubled by the ethical dilemma of whether it makes sense to actively contribute to humanity's destruction. Any possible destruction, I emphasize, would not be brought about by an LLM application that suddenly became conscious and began to hate humanity, but by people using LLM applications.
Some people have fallen into the trap of misleading information simply out of ignorance, including, unfortunately, most politicians and public figures who speak on the subject because they do not know how to distinguish other people's falsehoods from facts. This group often tries to do what it believes is good, but unfortunately things turn out the way they always do. This group is primarily afraid and acts out of that fear.
There are also those who are not afraid at all. This group naively and hopefully believes all the marketing announcements, bogus studies and pseudoscientific papers and thinks that LLM-based applications either are already conscious or soon will be and that we are almost certainly already in AGI (Artificial General Intelligence, or general artificial intelligence) or even ASI (Artificial Super Intelligence, or artificial superintelligence) territory. I cannot say what motivates these people.
And then, of course, there are people whose income and future wealth depend directly on how many people believe in the supreme capabilities of LLM-based applications. Some of these people develop LLM technologies (and may also be preparing for an IPO), some have raised investors' money to fulfill promises that are proving far more difficult to deliver than expected, while others have found a subject about which other people (whether frightened or hopeful) know as little as they do, creating an opportunity to convert this exceptionally favorable energy into revenue. See also: snake oil salesmen, gold rush, NFTs.
If additional legislation may not deliver results, falling into the trap of LLM mania is surprisingly easy and the situation is being exploited by scammers, charlatans and bad actors ranging from small-time operators to those with an international reach, then what can we do?
The following is certainly not a definitive or comprehensive list of what might help in the current situation.
- We urgently need to make our digital solutions even more resilient because the volume, speed and systematic nature of attacks will, in the near future, be several orders of magnitude greater than what we have been accustomed to.
- More effective monitoring systems will help detect more of these attacks more quickly, so we need to invest even more in them as well.
- More broadly, we must assume that it may not be possible to prevent a successful attack or data breach, which means we must also have a plan for what comes afterward: how we restore operations, how we communicate and how we learn.
- To make better use of the opportunities offered by AI technologies ourselves, both as a country and as businesses, we need to build stronger frameworks for automation and continuously strengthen and improve them as we learn from experience.
- We must preserve the ability to continue experimenting, testing, hypothesizing and making mistakes, but we must create that opportunity and capability as safely as possible — so-called sandboxes in which, however, we do not actively ignore everything that information security professionals have discovered and addressed over the past several decades.
- With AI-based applications (including LLM-based applications), as well as the agreements and policies concerning them, we must keep people at the center of it all. Applications (and regulations) work for people, not the other way around. This is easy to forget and the desire for authoritarianism is already emerging very strongly in current debates, proving remarkably attractive across almost the entire political spectrum.
- To avoid, or at least reduce, tomorrow's problems, we need to devote even greater attention to education. While the ability to use AI technologies and applications is also very important, even more important are general analytical skills, the ability to recognize and respond to threats, the courage to say "no" and the courage to make informed choices. It is crucial that efforts to ensure and improve these capabilities reach every group in society.
Finally, neither individually nor collectively can we give in to cognitive laziness and surrender our thinking and creativity to machines simply because it seems easier or because someone in a position of authority said this is our future and that we should welcome the Brave New World with open arms, lest we be considered backward or even criminal.
Let history be a source of lessons for us on AI as well.
P.S. LLM (Large Language Model) applications are one subset of the AI world. LLM-based applications are not all-encompassing artificial intelligence. Nor are LLM-based applications Skynet, the Terminator, HAL, etc., familiar from books and movies. It is unlikely, not to say exceedingly unlikely, that LLM technology specifically is the path that will lead to the world of AGI/ASI and conscious AI. The very fact that LLMs are equated with AI in many discussions — and often not with present-day AI but with sci-fi AI — is itself a source of many of the social and political problems associated with AI.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski
