German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks to the press after meeting soldiers of the 1 German-Netherlands Corps on October 1, 2026 in Münster. | Hesham Elsherif/Getty Images
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv for a surprise one-day visit to showcase Berlin's support for Ukraine amid Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital that continued after the chancellor's arrival.
Merz, who is in Kyiv to deliver new military, financial and economic support pledges to Ukraine, is planning to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss support against Russia's escalating war, particularly in the sector of air defense and long-range offensive weapons, as well as peace initiatives.
A German official said that Berlin will provide Ukraine with a new military support package worth about €1 billion, which includes missiles and drones, as well as satellite technology to help striking military targets in Russia.
Advertisement
Germany will furthermore provide Ukraine with financial assistance for the mass-production of new drones to intercept Russia's particularly dangerous high-speed jet drones. Berlin will also provide generators, substations, and repair kits worth €350 million to make the Ukrainian grid more resilient against Russian attacks.
Ukraine is facing harsh Russian drone and missile attacks on its infrastructure, power and heating plants as well as other civilian targets, which are feared to further intensify this winter.
In contrast to previous visits from Western leaders, during which Moscow had largely refrained from attacks on the Ukrainian capital, air raid sirens could be heard in Kyiv during Merz's visit. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia's foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.
This is Merz's first bilateral visit to Kyiv and his second trip as chancellor, after travelling there in May 2025 visit alongside leaders from France, the U.K. and Poland.
“If we fail to stop Moscow, sooner or later the Russian war machine will turn against us", Merz said upon arrival in the Ukrainian capital, adding: “I will tell President Zelenskyy today, 'You can continue to count on our help.'”
During a speech in Münster, Germany, Merz warned that, “in a few weeks, the fifth winter of the war will begin”, which “likely be the hardest one yet.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz shakes hands with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the 36th NATO Heads of State and Government Summit in Ankara, on July 7, 2026. | Pool photo by Michael Kappeler/AFP via Getty Images
Ukrainians “are bracing themselves for intense ballistic missile attacks, for destroyed power plants and schools, and for damaged apartment buildings and churches. Ukraine must survive this winter, and I am convinced that it will. It can count on our help,” Merz added, highlighting German help such as new interception systems against jet drones or repairs for bombed power plants.
Merz and Zelenskyy held a call on Wednesday, which focused on convincing European and international allies like Japan to deliver more Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine as well as procuring fresh ammunition for Kyiv's F-16 fighter jets, which are efficient in downing Russian jet drones with their onboard cannon.
Last month, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that Germany would transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles from its own stocks to Ukraine, and called on other states to follow suit.
Following the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig in August, for which Germany blamed Russia, Berlin announced that its intelligence services would help Ukraine with supplying targeting data for long-distance strikes against Russia's military as well as its industrial base.
Advertisement
Merz has refused to supply Germany's prized Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine, despite calling for it when he was opposition leader. Yet his government delivered financial and technical assistance for the development of Ukraine's own long-range weapons. On Thursday, Zelenskyy announced the successful test of Ukraine's FP-7 ballistic tactical missile.
German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from Merz's center-right CDU party, joined the trip alongside representatives from a dozen German energy, chemical and drone manufacturing companies, which will participate in a German-Ukrainian economic forum in Kyiv on Sunday.
There are tensions between Merz and Zelenskyy when it comes to Ukraine's desire to swiftly join the European Union.
The German Chancellor has voiced skepticism that an EU accession would be possible in the coming years and instead proposed an “associated membership” that would grant Ukraine access to the EU's single market and an observer status in the Council of the EU, the European Commission and the European Parliament, but without any voting rights.
Merz's visit comes amid renewed attempts to seek a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who met with his Russia counterpart Sergei Lavrov in New York last weekend, has welcomed a U.S. invite for Vladimir Putin to the G20 leaders' summit in Miami in December, saying it could be a chance for serious negotiations.
However, so far “Russia’s leadership shows no real interest in putting an end to its deeply inhumane fantasies of subjugation and conquest,” Wadephul said on Friday. “It intends to continue the war against Ukraine.”

Stench, violence and sirens: how Ceuta became Europe’s migration nightmare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:19:07 UTC
14:19:07 KST

The moment you step off the ferry and leave the terminal in Ceuta, migrants approach from every direction. They are not asking for money. They point to their mouths or rub their stomachs. They are hungry. Within your first 20 minutes in the Spanish enclave on the North African coast, you encounter hundreds of them. 
At the end of July, an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 undocumented migrants entered, or invaded, depending on whom you ask, this city of 84,000 people. Most were men, most from Morocco, with a smaller number from sub-Saharan Africa. Most returned within a day. Between 8,000 and 12,000 remained, at least a quarter of them unaccompanied minors.
Groups of migrants are everywhere: on benches, in parks, along boulevards, in squares, courtyards, stairwells and playgrounds. They wander or stand around with nowhere to go, smartphones in their hands and blank expressions on their faces. Every few minutes, a fight seems to break out and local police move in. Sirens and helicopters provide the soundtrack to scenes that can feel almost dystopian. Spanish troops have been deployed to the enclave. Police and military vehicles, some armored, patrol the streets. Many migrants carry food, drink, tarps, bags, discarded materials, tires to use as pillows and palm fronds for makeshift shelters. The city’s only official reception center, built for 500 people, was already full before the influx. It now holds about 800 migrants, including 300 women, 180 girls and five pregnant women. Those turned away are left to fend for themselves. Many have cuts and scars on their arms and legs that have gone untreated. Some head toward El Príncipe, Ceuta’s impoverished, predominantly Muslim neighborhood, where they hope at least to find some sympathy.
Most have gravitated toward Playa del Trampolín, or Trampoline Beach, named for the migrants’ hope of using Ceuta as a springboard into Europe. Ceuta belongs to Spain and the European Union but is outside the Schengen Area’s passport-free travel zone, meaning reaching the enclave does not automatically open the way to mainland Europe. A sprawling makeshift settlement of at least 5,000 people has emerged between the N354 road and the sea. The stench of human waste and vomit hangs in the hot, still air. Stalls sell clothing, hygiene products and fish caught that morning. Drug dealers work openly. Bottles arranged in a rectangle mark out a prayer area. Most of the young men wear swimwear, sometimes with a shirt, often barefoot or in mismatched sandals. Some have dug shallow depressions into the ground and sleep packed into them, like communal graves for the living. They wash for long minutes under beach showers, scrubbing themselves without soap.
Behind the tent used by women and families is another fenced-off area. A minor who was raped is staying there, along with an older Moroccan migrant who was raped by seven men in the camp. Violence is everywhere, waiting to erupt, especially after dark. People fight over space, food and pride. Police and humanitarian volunteers leave around nightfall. During the day, aid workers distribute cups of noodles, white bread and water and provide places to charge phones. The Spanish government has installed three cellular antennas to improve Wi-Fi access. At night, however, the camp becomes largely lawless. To pass the time, men hold boxing, wrestling and makeshift weightlifting contests, using one another as weights.
At night on my hotel balcony, I wrote down the stories I had heard during the day: the escapes, the hours in the sea, bodies floating nearby, longing for parents, hunger, thirst and crime. On almost every piece of cardboard or paper they possessed, migrants had written the same word: Asilo, Spanish for asylum. Asilo, asilo, everywhere. All I could think was: Help, help.
A city transformed overnight
This weekend marked exactly two months since the mass influx, yet no one can say with certainty why it happened when it did or how it grew so quickly. There are mountains of speculation and conspiracy theories. What is beyond dispute is what happened to Ceuta and to the people who crossed into it. Residents describe a small, relatively tranquil city transformed overnight into a crisis with implications far beyond its borders. Migrants describe believing they had swum toward freedom and the promised continent, only to discover that nobody was waiting for them. Instead, many found people determined to send them back. Whenever a new shelter opens, migrants race in from the beach, forests and other improvised camps, desperate for a bed, privacy and shade. In Ceuta today, few commodities are more valuable than shade.
Spain has controlled Ceuta and Melilla, another enclave bordering Morocco, for centuries and retained them after Morocco gained independence in 1956. Morocco considers the territories occupied, and their borders have long been a source of friction. Spain relies heavily on Moroccan cooperation to curb migration, drug trafficking and terrorism. Morocco, meanwhile, has repeatedly been accused of using control over migration as leverage in disputes with Madrid.
Economic pressures are also immense. Half of Morocco’s population is under 35, according to the article’s figures, while unemployment among young people stands at about 35%. In Fnideq, the Moroccan town immediately across the border, average annual pay is about 4,800 euros. In Ceuta, it is 36,800 euros. Seventy-one percent of young Moroccans have expressed a desire to leave. In January, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez advanced a plan offering legal residency and work permits to hundreds of thousands of migrants who had entered Spain legally but remained after their visas expired. The aim was to bring people already working informally into the legal economy and tax system.
Then came July. Sánchez visited Algeria, Morocco’s bitter regional rival, for talks on strengthening relations and increasing gas purchases. Later that month, Spain’s Supreme Court issued a ruling restricting the immediate deportation of migrants who had not crossed a physical barrier without first receiving a hearing. That decision may have helped fuel the belief that reaching Ceuta by sea offered a route into Spain.
‘Half of Morocco would leave’
On July 30, King Mohammed VI marked the 27th anniversary of his accession to the Moroccan throne. As he spoke about economic prosperity, tens of thousands of young Moroccans were making their way toward Ceuta and Melilla by train, bus, taxi and hidden in trucks. Tens of thousands entered through the sea. Dozens drowned. When border police lost control, crossings also began over land. Europe watched with alarm, haunted by memories of the 2015 migration crisis. For the past decade, governments across the continent have tightened external borders, asylum procedures and deportation policies.
“A decade ago, when more than a million migrants came, every death, every body washed ashore, was headline news,” Ceuta resident Francesca González said. “We cried and mourned the tragedy. This time, 141 people died in two days, some of them babies and children, and nobody cares.” The influx hardened attitudes even in a city where roughly half the population has Moroccan roots. Shops closed their doors to migrants, sometimes refusing to sell them food or water even when they had money. Local groups armed with sticks tried to drive them from the city center. Police and soldiers pushed others back toward the border.
Gradually, a routine emerged: registrations, hearings and decisions. Unaccompanied minors are treated differently because they cannot simply be returned. “I will die before I go back to Morocco,” said Abu-Khaber Naji, 26, whom I met hiding in a forest in Ceuta.
The blame game began almost immediately. Residents accused Morocco, citing migrant testimony that Moroccan border guards had encouraged or directed people toward the crossing. Across Spain, Sánchez’s critics blamed his migration policies and his approach toward Rabat. Spanish intelligence officials said warnings of a mass crossing had been delivered in advance. Sánchez, meanwhile, accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation that led people to believe the border was open. Others blamed Donald Trump and ties among the United States, Israel and Morocco. Nearly everyone blamed social media.
‘They stole my freedom’
The European Union has poured 109 million euros into new reception centers and border reinforcement in Ceuta, particularly facilities for minors. “For years we begged them to invest more money here in education and especially health care, and they always told us there was no budget,” González said. “Suddenly there are tens of millions to build reception centers with new infrastructure.” She described accompanying her daughters to school because soldiers were stationed outside and said she now feels compelled to tell them to dress more modestly when they leave home.
“They invaded our home, they stole my freedom,” she said, blaming Sánchez for abandoning the city. “I will never forgive that son of a b***h for turning me into a bad person who closes her heart to hungry children. I know I had to do it, but I will have to live with the images of those children, with the sand on their faces and in their hair.” “What I want is Ceuta’s old soundtrack back,” she said, “the silence, the waves breaking on the shore. But I know that isn’t coming back soon.”
That anger has spread into politics. Alberto Pérez, another resident, said locals understand the demographic and economic case for immigration. “We’re not naive,” he said. “We know there is a birthrate problem and immigration strengthens the economy, fills labor shortages and increases tax payments. We understand that this is the only way forward. But we also understand that it changes our identity.” “We are willing to accept immigration if we have control over our borders,” he added. “What happened here in July broke that trust.”
Six hours in the sea
Anwar Saidi, 20, from Tangier, said rumors began circulating a day before the mass crossing. “WhatsApp and Facebook groups said the border was open to anyone who came by sea,” he said. “There was a lot of information: where to go, where to buy equipment, where to swim from.” Then came images of migrants supposedly already inside Ceuta, eating ice cream and flashing victory signs. “Only later did we understand it was staged, and smuggling gangs had paid locals to film it for TikTok,” he said.
Saidi abandoned work immediately. A friend brought along his younger brother. They climbed into the back of a truck with about 100 other people, got off near the border and entered the water. “It’s not a short swim, six or seven kilometers, six hours in the sea,” he said. “I know how to swim, but people who don’t know how grab you and pull you down. You’re in survival mode. Then you start seeing bodies floating beside you. More and more bodies. But there is no choice. You keep going.” His friend lost his younger brother in the water and still does not know what happened to him.
“When I reached the beach, it was the happiest moment of my life, but it lasted one second,” Saidi said. He fled soldiers, police and local gangs, then discovered he had nowhere to go. “My stomach growled for 48 hours. It was pain I can’t describe,” he said. “Before we came, we thought all we had to do was cross the border and continue to Barcelona, Madrid or Valencia. We didn’t know we needed special permission to leave here for mainland Spain.”
On Facebook, parents post photographs of children who left Morocco and vanished. Some may have drowned. Others are hiding in forests. “Sometimes they are only 10 or 12,” said local social worker Maria-Luisa Viadén. “Sometimes we find them and contact their families in Morocco, but the families say they don’t want them back. Everyone asks us where our heart is, but where is the parents’ heart?” Among those who attempted the crossing was Faten Ben Omar al-Azizi, a 26-year-old soccer player who drowned. The day officials came to inform her mother of her death, a letter also arrived approving her daughter’s visa application to Spain.
‘We have no faces’
The Supreme Court ruling had been widely misunderstood. Morocco is considered a safe country by the European Union, and adults arriving from there are generally not entitled to political asylum solely on that basis. Over time, violence in Ceuta also shifted. In the first days, according to accounts in the city, most force was used by police. Later, some migrants began fighting back with tear gas and Molotov cocktails and setting police and military vehicles on fire.
Desperation and uncertainty have fueled the clashes. Whenever authorities open a new organized shelter for around 900 people, migrants rush in from beaches, forests, cemeteries and beneath bridges, sometimes violently, hoping for a proper bed, sanitation, privacy and shade. Some arrived with money or credit cards loaded into Apple Pay. Smugglers take others by speedboat across the strait toward mainland Spain, charging between 12,000 and 14,000 euros per person.
Almost none of the migrants still in Ceuta have identification documents. Before crossing, many carried out what they call harraga, burning their passports. “I want to get to Germany and become a truck driver,” said Ashraf Yousfi. “If I had somewhere to return to, I wouldn’t have come.” “I’m only going back to Morocco dead,” he said. “Give me a Rolls-Royce and a palace in Morocco and I’m not going back. I have no work there.” “If they opened the borders, half of Morocco would leave,” he added. “Those who went back only did it to prepare for the next attempt.”
For Yousfi, Spain is so close that it is almost cruel. “Spain is a dream we can see in front of us,” he said. “We see people who were born and immediately won the lottery. But to them we are noise. We have no faces. Nobody asks why we came. They only ask: How do I keep you out?”
The wall and the dream
Questions continue to follow Sánchez. Opposition leaders openly ask why his government has been so cautious toward Morocco, pointing to reports that Moroccan intelligence used Pegasus spyware to penetrate his personal phone and may have obtained sensitive information.
During five days in Ceuta, I visited the border several times. It is among the most formidable barriers I have seen: kilometers of double walls, barbed wire, police, soldiers, border forces, watchtowers and electronic surveillance. Spain spends hundreds of millions of euros financing, training and equipping Morocco to police the other side.
I looked at that monster of concrete, iron and steel again and again, struck by the fact that human determination had defeated it. It is a border separating hope on one side from an almost primal fear of that hope on the other. When the two collide, the result is explosive: a humanitarian disaster, lifelong trauma, a city turned upside down, parents who do not know where their children are and 141 dead, including babies and children, buried in Ceuta’s Muslim cemetery.
They were willing to risk death rather than return to Morocco, willing to die for the hope of freedom.

Shooting and scoring: Iconic World Cup memories explained by Getty photographers

Whether on or off the pitch, many of the most memorable moments from FIFA World Cups have been captured by Getty. Here, some of the photographers behind those lenses share their thoughts about taking the best emotive images.
Competition by its nature leads to comparison but there is no title to play for in this piece. Instead, we've asked several Getty photographers to pick their favourite shots from the past five World Cup tournaments that best capture the beauty and emotion of effort, grace, victory and defeat.
Argentina v France: Final - FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022
"This photo was taken at least 30 minutes after the main trophy lift. All the Argentina fans and photographers are waiting for Messi to go over to acknowledge the fans. All the Getty Images photographers had a loose plan of what we’d capture, but luck also kicked in with this picture. This is the first moment he opened his arms with the biggest of smiles two metres in front of me, whilst I was looking up on a 24-70mm lens." Shaun Botterill.
France v Croatia: Final - 2018 FIFA World Cup Russia
"What makes this image special is not only the celebration itself, but the access and the atmosphere around it. Thanks to FIFA’s exclusive access, I was the only photographer allowed on the pitch after the celebrations, which gave me a very different perspective on the aftermath of the World Cup final.
"The fireworks had just finished and the rain had left smoke and haze hanging inside Luzhniki Stadium. As the light came through that haze, it created visible rays above Paul Pogba while he held the World Cup Trophy. The combination of the smoke, rain, light and the space around him helped give the image a stronger sense of atmosphere than a standard trophy celebration.
"Technically, I wanted to keep the frame wide enough to show the scale of the stadium, the crowd, the haze and the pitch. The access allowed me to stay low and close, but the wider composition lets the atmosphere become part of the story. For me, it feels less like a standard trophy picture and more like a surreal, emotional moment in the aftermath of France winning the 2018 FIFA World Cup." David Ramos
Italy v France: Final - FIFA World Cup 2006 Germany
"The picture came following the 2006 final after Italy won on penalties against France, where my colleague Shaun Botterill and I were in prime position for the cup presentation.
"I was shooting tighter on a 400mm concentrating on the Italian captain Fabio Cannavaro, and as the players went on a lap of honour they suddenly started to reach out and touch the trophy en masse. I quickly balanced on top of a metal barrier near the front row of seats for extra height and took the image. I remember other photographers pulling at my feet trying to reach my position on the barrier, but the moment was over in a flash. The confetti and pyrotechnic smoke also adds to the picture.
Trophy presentations can sometimes feel staged, but this felt like a more impulsive and natural way of a team coming together, bonding in their historic moment." Michael Steele
Netherlands v Spain: Final - FIFA World Cup 2010 South Africa
"There are moments in every FIFA World Cup that transcend the match itself and become part of football folklore. Nigel de Jong's challenge on Xabi Alonso in the 2010 FIFA World Cup Final is unquestionably one of them.
Positioned perfectly to capture the incident, this image freezes the exact moment De Jong's outstretched boot meets Alonso's chest, preserving one of the most controversial flashpoints in World Cup history. Shown only a yellow card by referee Howard Webb, the challenge immediately sparked debate, with many believing the Netherlands midfielder was fortunate to remain on the pitch. More than fifteen years later, the photograph remains one of the enduring visual symbols of South Africa 2010, a split second that encapsulated the tension, physicality and controversy of a fiercely contested final." Laurence Griffiths.
England v Belgium: Group G - FIFA World Cup 2018 Russia
“Occasionally we are allowed to work from the ‘catwalk’ of a stadium, up 80 or 100 metres above the field. Only a small group of people are allowed up there. It comes with a long process of approval, training courses, safety belts, helmets, sometimes even medical certificates, because you need to be able to work at height.
"The pressure is massive. You are standing above people’s heads, so if you drop even a single small thing, the reality is you could seriously hurt somebody. Everything you take up there has to have a double connection. Every camera, every lens, even your phone, has to be attached. You empty your pockets. You can’t take spare pieces, because everything could fall. But it is a mega opportunity.
"This was Belgium versus England, and a header with six players involved, which does not happen often and is hard to predict from above. I like it because it is a different football image, an angle you do not see every day. I am a big fan of the green grass and the clean background, but it is also about what goes into getting there. You are lucky if six players jump for one header and you can still see the faces, the action, body language, the white line and the colours. In the end, it all just came together.”Matthias Hangst
Argentina v France: Final - FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022
"The FIFA World Cup Final in Doha was my first World Cup final, and I knew I was witnessing history. Like everyone else on the pitch, I expected the defining image of the night to be Lionel Messi lifting the World Cup trophy. Before that moment, he walked past the trophy as he received the Golden Ball award as the tournament's best player. At this moment he turned and looked toward the photographers, managed to capture this frame. Is just a quiet and simple photo but still powerful." Maja Hitij

The eyes have it: Getty photographer Alex Pantling on capturing the world’s greatest footballers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:14:46 UTC
14:14:46 KST

Shooting and scoring: Photographer Alex Pantling on capturing the world’s greatest footballers
Getty photographer Alex Pantling reported on the FIFA World Cup 2026 and shared with European Lens his reflection on the experience along with some of his favourite shots from the tournament.
What does it take to photograph the greatest footballers on the planet, in action, on the world's biggest stage?
Getty photographer Alex Pantling has spent more than a decade capturing sport’s biggest moments, from FIFA World Cups and Champions League nights to Formula 1 and the Olympic Games. Along the way, he has photographed some of the most recognisable athletes in the world, including F1 racing driver Max Verstappen, footballers, Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Harry Kane, and 19-year-old superstar Lamine Yamal.
This summer’s World Cup gave him some of his most striking football images yet. As he told Euronews Culture, capturing those moments is less about luck than preparation meeting instinct: "You can plan, you can have ideas in your head, but you've got to react when those ideas change in the moment."
After this summer's unforgettable World Cup, we caught up with Pantling to discuss his path into photography, the challenges of working at the highest level of sport, and the stories behind some of his favourite images from the 2026 tournament.
Could you tell me briefly how you got into photography, and the path that led you to sports photography?
Alex Panning: I always knew I wanted to be involved in sport. Originally it was kind of a fluke, to be honest. At school I actually wanted to do architecture, but the way subjects were bracketed meant I couldn't do architecture and the sport-related subject I wanted at the same time. I also found out architecture was a seven-year course at university, which put me off a little.
Someone suggested photography, so I thought, I'll give that a go - which I know isn't the romantic story you're hoping for. But I gave it a go and absolutely loved it. Then I realised there was a job that combined my two passions: sport and photography.
So I pushed that further and went to university at Nottingham Trent. At the start of the course I wasn't really photographing sport yet - it was predominantly an art photography course, so I was doing still life, street photography, portraiture, that kind of thing.
In my second year, I had a tutor from Italy who'd been at Nottingham Trent in the same year as a colleague of mine, Julian Finney. She put me in touch with Julian, which led to work experience at Getty with another photographer, Michael Regan - one of our best football photographers. And from there, it led into a job with Getty.
How much of your work is careful planning, and how much is reacting in the moment?
You plan everything, but reacting is more important, because what you plan never actually happens - let's be honest. You might get to a game thinking you want to sit in a certain spot because of the light, or because you want to photograph a particular team attacking your side in the first half. Then the captains do the coin toss, they swap ends, or the rain comes - there are so many variables that change in football.
I think that's why I love it. You never work the same day twice as a football photographer, because no game is the same. I might shoot Chelsea versus Tottenham again this year, but it won't be the same as last year or the year before. You can plan, you can have ideas in your head, but you've got to react when those ideas change in the moment.
What changes when you're photographing a World Cup game versus a normal Premier League match?
It does feel very different. The Premier League is amazing - I might be a little biased being English, but I think it's the greatest football league in the world, and it's incredible that we get access to it weekly working in the UK. But when you get to FIFA, it's something really special.
It's not just the Argentinas, the Englands, the Frances - I was lucky enough to being doing Curaçao, smaller countries like this, which were almost as enjoyable because of how much it meant to them to be there, and to their fans. And I love that aspect. So yeah, in terms of how it changes: you're still doing the same job, but the emotion and the felling behind the pictures and games is completely different.
Do you still feel nervous before these big games? You're there to capture huge moments and big players - is there a sense of pressure?
Yeah, 100%. Take Messi, for example - I'm sure we'll come to that. You know he'll arguably be one of the greatest footballers to have ever lived, and in ten, twenty, thirty, forty years, people will look back on pictures of him playing. You've got the opportunity to take the pictures people are going to look at. I find that really exciting.
In terms of nerves - yes, they're always there. Getting the goal picture, the celebration, being in the right place. But it does get easier with time. I was lucky enough to shoot the final of the Qatar World Cup, arguably one of the greatest football matches ever. I was up in the stands, and I remember Messi scoring his first goal - the penalty - on my side of the pitch, and my hands were literally shaking, I was so nervous about missing the shot. I think that was because it was my first World Cup, and there was a lot of pressure on me to do a good job so I could hopefully cover more of these. I don't have that same nervousness now, though there are still elements of it.
So, let's take a closer look at some of your images you took from this year's World Cup. Your portrait of Austria's David Alaba in the tunnel is a very cinematic image - most of the frame is actually in darkness. What was the intention behind it?
We get such great access from FIFA at these events. We're allowed in the tunnel before the game as the players walk out, and that always makes for iconic pictures - the two teams lined up, the referees, the ball kids, the players locked in, wearing their tracksuits. Those pictures are a little busier, there's a lot going on, and that's good in its own way for documenting the moment.
But what I try to do - and I think a lot of my colleagues do too - is use the tunnel at half-time as an opportunity, rather than just before the game. This stadium, Kansas City Stadium, was probably my favourite to work in. The tunnel the players came out of was long and narrow, and at the end, rather than going straight up the stairs, it split: the home team went one way, the away team the other, with a wall in front. At night games, the floodlights cast a shaft of light straight onto the players' faces.
You have to be patient - there were plenty of games where I tried this shot and it didn't quite work out. On this occasion, David Alaba was waiting for some of his teammates to come back from the dressing room, and he took a moment, looking out into the light. It worked out as a really nice picture. I think the colours worked well too - the blue branding against the red kit.
Talk us through your image of Lionel Messi taking a corner.
Absolutely. When I first walked into the stadium, the architecture was fascinating - a lot of the American stadiums are, because they're so different from what we have in the UK, mainly due to their scale. What I loved about the Kansas City stadium specifically was that it had no roof, so a lot more light came in during the day, and the floodlights were more prominent. I knew the wider shots would work really well because of how beautiful the stadium was.
When we work for FIFA, we get exclusive access to shoot from behind the bench, right down at pitch level, without an LED board in front of us - unlike the photographers positioned elsewhere, who can't get as low an angle. Going into this game, I knew this was a shot I wanted. A corner isn't the most athletic thing a footballer does, but as a picture, it lets you get close to the player on a wide lens. As he brings his leg back, that's maybe one of the most athletic positions a footballer can be in. I took around 20 frames of him doing it, but the best one is where his leg is fully extended - a really nice body shape, with the lights right above his head.
The low angle makes him look almost heroic in the frame - like the technique directors use in film, shooting from below to give someone a sense of authority. Where you going for the same effect?
Exactly. The low angle makes a big difference. It was actually quite funny - there's not much space to work in down there. You've got the linesman, the player taking the corner. About 20 minutes before this, Argentina won a corner, and as Messi walked over to take it I thought, this is the moment. But another player joined him and they played it short, so I didn't get the shape I was after. Luckily, the second time, he put it into the box himself. But yes - the low angle makes a real difference. If I'd been standing, it wouldn't have had the same impact.
You also captured this striking image of Ronaldo leading Portugal out. What did you see in that scene that made you want to shoot it differently?
Yes - again, I'm grateful to FIFA for the access. As with the Messi picture, we're allowed tunnel access before the games. I walked into this tunnel about ten or fifteen minutes before the teams came out to warm up, knowing Ronaldo would lead the team out as captain - that was the shot I wanted.
But the light in this tunnel wasn't as good as some others, and there were a lot of stewards around, making it a bit messier for pictures. So I stepped outside and thought about what else I could do. I liked the lettering above the tunnel, and there was a sea of Portugal fans nearby, all clearly about to be on their phones trying to photograph Ronaldo - because that's what everyone was there for. I also noticed the photographers had LED boards pushed back, so they had to stay behind a certain line. I thought if I shot from behind that line, framing the photographers with their cameras and the fans with their phones, it would show that all the focus was on him.
There's a certain poignancy to your image of Lamine Yamal walking alone on the pitch
Yes - I think this was in the Los Angeles Stadium. There's just something about that stadium - I don't think I'd been anywhere quite like it. The architecture is incredible to work in, and the roof is translucent, so you don't get full sun, but you get these shafts of softer light, which can make for really nice pictures.
What's also interesting about this one: I think it was a round-of-16 or quarter-final match, and FIFA had just started using pyrotechnics before kick-off. After the anthems, flares or fireworks went off from inside the stadium, which created a kind of misty effect in the air - you can see that smokiness in the picture, and I think it adds a lot.
This was just after the anthems - the players had come over for a drink or electrolytes, whatever they take pre-match - and Yamal took a moment to himself. It worked out well that no other player was in frame; it almost looks like everyone's there just to watch him.
Spain celebrating with the trophy in the dressing room. What was it like being in the middle of that chaos, and how did you go about finding the picture?
I'll never forget this one. I was on the pitch before the players came back to the dressing room, and it was my job to get in there. We were hoping Spain would let us in, and thankfully they did. I tried to time it so I didn't miss too much of the action on the pitch - players with their families and so on - while still getting back in time.
I waited outside for ten or fifteen minutes until we got the nod from FIFA to let us inside. And it was absolutely amazing - David Raya and lots of others were spraying champagne all over the players, and me to be honest, the state of the camera was not ideal when I got back, but it was brilliant. There were pictures everywhere - players celebrating separately, then together. Nico Williams grabbed me at one point because he wanted to replicate Michael Jordan's famous shower photo with the trophy, so we went and did that. There was a lot going on. It was almost hard to know what to shoot, because every time you took one picture, you felt like you were missing another happening somewhere else - which is a rare situation for a photographer, to be honest.

Taiwan’s deterrence is becoming harder to unwind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:14:27 UTC
14:14:27 KST

While political theater dominated the September Trump-Xi summit, the Western Pacific security architecture is transforming.
Driven by military realities and a commitment to reciprocal deterrence, the post-summit landscape is shifting toward greater multilateral integration and resistance to asymmetric interference. Preserving stability across the First Island Chain will require a security matrix combining agile executive diplomacy, robust legislative anchors, and unprecedented regional burden-sharing.
Part I: The starting line
The zero-sum nature of cross-strait diplomacy spilled into the open on Sept. 25 during a joint visit by US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to the National Archives Museum.
A temporary display prepared for the visit included a Qing dynasty scroll and a brick from the Great Wall of China, while US officials had also planned to show the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco. The entire temporary display was removed following last-minute Chinese objections to the treaty.
Beijing’s objection centered on the treaty’s implications for Taiwan. Japan renounced its rights to Taiwan under the Treaty of San Francisco, but the document did not specify a recipient of sovereignty, providing a basis for the argument that Taiwan’s postwar status was left undetermined.
Rather than compromise over the display, officials cleared the foyer, leaving the two leaders to view standard copies of America’s founding documents. The episode demonstrated how even decades-old documents continue to shape the most sensitive questions in US-China relations.
Part II: The legislative firewall
With the pivotal US midterm elections only weeks away, the 119th Congress is seeking to reinforce the legal foundations of longstanding US commitments to Taiwan.
At the center of that effort is the pending Six Assurances to Taiwan Act, H.R. 3452 and S. 3208, which would formally codify the Reagan-era Six Assurances into US law.
The legislation would reinforce congressional oversight of any attempt to alter longstanding US policy. It would require presidential notification before actions such as pausing defensive arms sales to Taiwan, consulting Beijing over those sales, changing the US position on Taiwan’s sovereignty, or pressuring Taipei to negotiate with China.
It would also provide a 30-day congressional review period, extended to 60 days for proposals submitted during part of the congressional summer recess.
This effort coincides with pressure from Republican senators led by Mitch McConnell, who wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding the release of US$300 million (NT$9.4 billion) in Foreign Military Financing and US$1 billion in delayed Taiwan security funding.
Their concern is straightforward: uncertainty over US security assistance gives Beijing ammunition for what Taiwan calls “US skepticism theory” (疑美論).
Part III: The thickening web
China also faces a thickening web of regional democratic security partnerships.
At the UN General Assembly, foreign ministers and senior officials from several Indo-Pacific and European democracies reiterated opposition to unilateral changes to the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.
Diplomatic alignment is increasingly backed by structural integration.
Japan has eased restrictions on defense exports, while Australia has signed contracts for its first three upgraded Mogami-class frigates to be built in Japan. US Forces Japan is also transforming into a Joint Force Headquarters intended to improve integrated operations with Japan’s Self-Defense Forces.
Japan, meanwhile, is fielding US-made Tomahawk cruise missiles as part of its expanding stand-off defense capability.
To the south, the Japan-Philippines Reciprocal Access Agreement has entered into force, enabling deeper joint training and military cooperation. Japanese forces participated in the 2026 Balikatan exercises under the agreement.
Australia is reinforcing the same architecture. Eight Australian-supported infrastructure projects are underway across five Philippine military bases, increasing logistical capacity and supporting a larger Australian presence.
Taken together, these arrangements do not create a formal Indo-Pacific equivalent of NATO. They do, however, create overlapping layers of access, logistics, interoperability, and deterrence.
Part IV: The autonomous horizon
Beyond traditional hardware, emerging technologies will shape the next stage of strategic competition.
During the Washington summit, the United States and China agreed to continue dialogue on artificial intelligence and establish a mechanism for notifying one another about AI-related national security incidents. Yet major disagreements remain over how autonomous and advanced AI systems should ultimately be governed.
Taiwan is attempting to match international support with a substantial expansion of its own defense capabilities.
Its defense spending is rising sharply, while President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has pledged to bring defense expenditure, calculated according to NATO standards, to 5% of GDP by 2030.
Taipei is also converting greater spending into asymmetric capabilities. Military planners have identified a requirement for approximately 1,600 anti-ship missiles, combining US-made Harpoons with indigenous Hsiung Feng II and supersonic Hsiung Feng III systems.
In the unmanned domain, the privately funded Global UAV Academy is expanding training and cooperation with Taiwan’s Pacific allies, while Taipei is using drone diplomacy to deepen technological links with democratic partners.
Cybersecurity and information warfare are becoming equally important as Taiwan prepares for the Nov. 28 local elections. Authorities have already stepped up efforts against political deepfakes and other forms of AI-enabled manipulation.
These areas will be increasingly important as China combines conventional military pressure with cyber operations, information warfare, and United Front activity.
Part V: The coming geopolitical timeline
The interconnected trans-Pacific network now faces a dense sequence of political, military, and economic events through the end of the year.
Oct. 18–20: The 25th annual US-Taiwan Defense Industry Conference will take place at the Kingsmill Resort in Virginia, bringing together officials, defense industry representatives, and security specialists to discuss Taiwan’s threat environment, procurement, and defense cooperation.
The conference follows the Oct. 2 arrival of Taiwan’s first two new F-16V Block 70 fighters at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung after their journey through Hawaii and Guam. The arrival marks a long-awaited milestone in a procurement program that had suffered repeated delays.
Nov. 3: The US midterm elections will establish a new congressional balance of power in Washington, potentially altering the political environment surrounding Taiwan policy and US-China relations.
Nov. 18–19: The APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen will put Trump back on Xi’s home turf, where trade, technology restrictions, and strategic supply chains will again hang over bilateral diplomacy.
Nov. 28: Taiwan’s local elections will provide another test of the country’s ability to withstand disinformation, cyber interference, and other forms of gray-zone pressure.
Dec. 14–15: The United States will host the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Doral, Florida, giving Trump another opportunity to engage major Indo-Pacific and global partners as Washington weighs the future of its regional security commitments.
Jan. 10, 2027: The current US-China trade truce is scheduled to expire. Unless the two sides reach another arrangement, trade tensions over tariffs, technology, critical minerals, and supply chains could again intensify.
Part VI: Hard-power readiness
The post-summit environment demonstrates that long-term stability ultimately depends on military strength, national agency, and coordinated regional action.
Trump has pushed US allies and partners toward greater burden-sharing, but the durability of deterrence will also depend on the independent decisions of regional leaders.
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae have each committed their governments to expanding defense capacity and strengthening regional security cooperation.
The emerging network is therefore less a single alliance than an increasingly interconnected system of national capabilities, access agreements, logistics, procurement, and political commitments.
The political theater in Washington has concluded. The harder work of sustaining deterrence has begun.

Trump says Iran dropped nuclear weapon plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:09:28 UTC
14:09:28 KST

AA Photo
US President Donald Trump said on Oct. 3 Iran has virtually abandoned its drive to develop nuclear weapons because severe financial exhaustion and regional setbacks crippled Tehran's strategic leverage.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said Iranian authorities no longer possess the capability or ambition to produce an atomic bomb and are eager to negotiate a new settlement. "They have virtually given up any plans for nuclear weapons," he said.
Trump reiterated his position an Iranian nuclear weapon remains unacceptable, asserting earlier maximum pressure sanctions and subsequent economic isolation had drained Tehran's revenue before recent regional conflicts further weakened the government.
The remarks come as international observers continue to monitor Tehran's atomic program. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported earlier this year Iran had accumulated an enriched uranium stockpile with purity levels reaching 60 percent, just below the 90 percent threshold required for weapons-grade material.
Tehran has consistently maintained its atomic work remains exclusively civilian, focused on energy generation and medical research. The diplomatic dispute intensified in 2018 when the US unilaterally pulled out of the 2015 nuclear accord, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, before reimposing sweeping banking and oil sanctions on the Islamic republic.

U.S. peace negotiations with Russia could now involve multi-billion dollar Lukoil deal, NYT reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:09:13 UTC
14:09:13 KST

U.S. peace negotiations with Russia could now involve multi-billion dollar Lukoil deal, NYT reports
The Trump administration’s peace negotiations with the Kremlin have come to include discussions of a multi-billion dollar deal involving assets owned by Russian oil company Lukoil, the New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct. 3.
The newspaper reported that business executives with ties to U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are pursuing a potential deal involving Lukoil refineries, oil fields and gas stations around the world. The deal would require approval from both the U.S. government and the Kremlin, according to the report.
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the potential deal with Kushner and Witkoff during their visit to Moscow on Sept. 5, proposing it as a way to demonstrate to Russians that they could still do business with the United States, NYT reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The two envoys responded that they would work on the proposal, as a way to build good will with the Russians, according to the NYT report. Another benefit for the Americans is that global oil prices, which have skyrocketed following the U.S. war with Iran, could go down as a result of the deal, following sanctions against Lukoil assets potentially being lifted.
Lukoil is Russia's second-largest oil producer and one of the country's largest companies, accounting for 2% of global oil output. The corporation has been under U.S. sanctions since 2025, with the American government freezing its U.S.-based assets and threatening secondary penalties for foreign entities engaging with them.
“Given President Putin’s refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia’s two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin’s war machine,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an October 2025 press release,
The sanctions, the first such measures imposed by the second Trump administration, were designed to pressure Moscow into peace talks in Ukraine, as fossil fuel revenues play a key role in sustaining Russia's war efforts. The U.S. government then proceeded to issue a limited sanctions waiver on some of Lukoil’s foreign assets, which was extended earlier this year.
While the U.S. Senate recently passed a bill that would make it easier to impose sanctions on countries that subsidize Russia’s war economy, this new potential agreement could allow Lukoil’s assets to be relieved of sanctions, potentially increasing their value, according to NYT
In January, the Russian energy giant agreed to sell most of its foreign assets to the American investment firm Carlyle, Lukoil's press service announced on Jan. 29. But the deal remains subject to U.S. government approval
Apart from stakes in oil fields in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Africa, and elsewhere, Lukoil also operates three oil refineries in Europe and hundreds of gas stations worldwide, including in the U.S.
Swiss-based oil trader Gunvor initially sought the purchase of the company's foreign assets, but withdrew its bid in November after the U.S. Treasury Department described the trader as the "Kremlin's puppet."

Germany's Merz arrives in Kyiv to pledge more support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:07:00 UTC
14:07:00 KST

Germany's Merz visits Kyiv amid Russian strikes
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:
"We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."
Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from Germany's arms industry, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.
President Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."
Focus on ramping up drone production
During his visit, Merz was set to announce a new raft of measures to support Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion, including a further billion euros in German military aid, plus €350 million ($395 million) for energy sector repairs, according to German media reports.
The chancellor was also expected to unveil plans for the co-production of interceptor drones and long-range missiles both in Ukraine and Germany.
According to German government sources cited by the Reuters and dpa news agencies, arms production is expected to focus on the development and delivery of thousands of drones capable of intercepting the rapid, jet-powered drones increasingly being deployed by the Russian military against civilian infrastructure targets in Ukraine.
The production of missiles with a range of over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) is also expected to be ramped up, enhancing Ukraine's ability to strike military and logistical targets far beyond the frontline and inside Russia itself.
Merz was expected to emphasize how Germany also stands to benefit from the expanded cooperation, both in terms of its own defense against Russian hybrid activities and in terms of jobs and technology.
The chancellor was also expected to speak to President Zelenskyy about the progress of political reforms in Ukraine and the continuing battle against corruption.
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit
The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.
"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."
In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.
His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.
"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."
Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

Bosnia votes Sunday in election that could affect EU bid

Bosnia votes Sunday in election that could affect EU bid
SARAJEVO/BANJA LUKA, Oct 4 - Bosnians are voting on Sunday in elections that could affect their country's European Union membership bid and the influence that the United States and Russia seek over the small Balkan nation.
Voters are casting ballots for the country's central tripartite presidency and national parliament, alongside regional legislative races in its two federal entities.
Some polling stations had to be temporarily closed due to problems with the electronic voting system, Bosnia's Central Election Commission head Jovan Kalaba told reporters in Sarajevo. The commission redesigned ballots and introduced new biometric voter identification and electronic scanners it said were aimed at curbing voting fraud.
Voter frustration has grown over an economic slowdown, the slow pace of EU entry talks and a lingering political crisis in which ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities have repeatedly stalled decisions by the weak central government that links them.
Bosnia, which has struggled to recover from the bloody 1992-95 war, secured EU candidate status in December 2022 and the green light to open accession negotiations in 2024. Actual talks have not started because domestic political leaders have yet to enact core requirements such as bolstering judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.
Preliminary results are expected to be released by the election commission after polls close at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) on Sunday.
MOVING BEYOND DIVISIVE RHETORIC
The Bosnian war ended in 1995 with the US-brokered Dayton peace accord, which left the country split along ethnic lines into the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation — linked by the central government and tripartite presidency.
Many voters in the country of 3.4 million people say they want to move beyond the divisive rhetoric, but the politics appears stuck.
The vote pits rival ethnic parties — the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH — against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.
According to tracking platform Poliwave, the SDA holds a narrow national lead with 21.4%, followed by the SDP on 16.7%. In Republika Srpska, SNSD, the party run by secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, who wants close ties with Serbia and Russia and is at odds with the government in Sarajevo, is ahead with 34.2%.
"We are ... choosing those who can manage certain processes, build society, and make the Republika Srpska peaceful and stable," said Zeljka Cvijanovic, the SNSD candidate who is seeking a second term in the tripartite presidency.
If ethnically based parties prevail and continue their bickering within the central government, the body that would eventually officially join the EU, progress on accession is likely to stall further.
In the capital, Sarajevo, Ismar Garasljevic, a 51-year-old high school teacher, said: "More than 30 years after the war, the situation is still the same; we are talking about nationalism ... The same faces, the same story, constantly."
Kalaba said that voter turnout stood at 11.94% by 11 a.m. (0900 GMT), down from around 15% by the same time during elections in 2022.
Major powers have long sought influence over Bosnia. The EU is seeking to expand its membership across the Balkans, including Bosnia, but Russia is slowing it down, maintaining its support of the Republika Srpska.
The US has also sought influence and wants to push for a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas, run by a company with links to the Trump administration, but the EU warned that the company selection lacked competitive transparency.
Washington has also clashed with Brussels over the role of the international High Representative, who, under provisions of the Dayton accord, enforces the laws. REUTERS

Where is Europe’s greenest city? Eight finalists announced for 2028 and three are in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:02:48 UTC
14:02:48 KST

The finalists were judged in seven areas, including climate change resilience, waste management and how quickly they are cutting emissions.
Next week, eight European cities will find out whether their efforts to cut emissions and make room for nature are enough to win one of the EU’s top green titles.
The European Commission’s annual European Green Capital and Green Leaf Awards recognise cities making measurable environmental progress while improving quality of life for their residents.
This June, an independent panel whittled 27 eligible applicants down to eight finalists, judging them on everything from air and water quality to their biodiversity and efforts to cut emissions.
The winners will be announced next week on 8 October in Guimarães, Portugal, the 2026 Green Capital. They are selected more than a year in advance, giving cities time to prepare projects, events and public programmes they want to run during their title year.
Five are in the running for the Green Capital title: Aalborg in Denmark, Bielsko-Biała in Poland, Košice in Slovakia, Porto in Portugal and Zaragoza in Spain.
Another three – Benidorm and Chiclana de la Frontera in Spain, and Estarreja in Portugal – have been shortlisted for the Green Leaf awards for cities with smaller populations.
How are Europe’s greenest cities judged?
The EU launched the Green Capital Award to recognise cities that are making measurable progress on environmental problems and improving quality of life for their residents.
The main prize is open to cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants. Smaller cities with populations between 20,000 and 100,000 compete for the Green Leaf title.
The expert panel judged applicants in seven areas, including how clean their air and water are, how they protect nature and green space, how they manage waste and noise, how quickly they are cutting emissions and how they are preparing for threats such as extreme heat and flooding.
Each finalist has different strengths.
Zaragoza, for example, scored well for biodiversity and green space. The city is connecting parks, riverbanks, wetlands, street trees and surrounding natural areas into one network, designed to give wildlife more room to move and help reduce the risk of flooding.
Porto stood out for its water management, as well as its preparations for a hotter, less predictable climate. Over the past decade, the city has worked to restore the Rio Tinto riverbed and banks, built new parks that hold rainwater during downpours and begun reusing treated wastewater for agricultural irrigation and street cleaning.
The resort town of Benidorm, meanwhile, has earned praise for adding far more greenery to its built-up streets. Since 2012, it has expanded its public gardens from 350,000 square metres to more than 1.5 million and nearly quadrupled its number of trees. Today, 92 per cent of residents live within 300 metres of a public green space.
The finalists will present their plans to an international jury next week, on 7 and 8 October.
The Green Capital winner receives €600,000 to put environmental plans into practice, while Green Leaf winners can take home €200,000 for green projects and public activities.
How are European cities adapting to a hotter climate?
The changes being recognised by the EU are part of a paradigm shift visible in cities around Europe. As summers get hotter and weather patterns become more unpredictable, urban planners are giving more space back to trees, parks and water.
In Barcelona, for example, some streets have been closed to through traffic while others have been turned into parks and pedestrian areas.
Meanwhile, in Milan, the Bosco Verticale has provided a small but important example of ways cities can add greenery even where there’s little room for parks. The two residential towers feature more than 21,000 trees and shrubs on their terraces.
In Breda, the Netherlands, widespread civic involvement has transformed the city since the turn of the century. Concrete tiles have been replaced with grass, flower beds and trees. Homes and schools have added rooftop gardens.
Today, 60 per cent of the city is green space – part of more than a decade of work that helped Breda become the EU’s first National Park City in 2025.
The Green Cities Awards are not only a matter of adding plants to buildings or streets, though. Heilbronn, Germany, won the 2027 Green Capital title after scoring highly for its clean air and water, noise reduction policies and waste reduction, among other things.
When the jury meets next week, it will be judging how far the eight finalists have turned similar ideas into city-wide change.

Creamery De Zuivelarij from Berlare (East Flanders) has won the 2026 BioVLAM award. The cheese dairy impressed the jury with its organic versions of paneer and labneh, two international dairy specialities.
Cheese dairy De Zuivelarij wins BioVLAM 2026 award with organic paneer and labneh
Every year, the BioVLAM award recognises a Flemish organic entrepreneur who excels in innovation, a passion for organic produce and sustainability. The creamery received the award at the BioXpo organic trade fair in Groot-Bijgaarden (Flemish Brabant) last Monday.
David De Coster founded De Zuivelarij in 2014. Previously, he worked as a chef, both at home and abroad, and taught at a hotel management school.
He developed Berloumi, a Belgian grilled cheese, inspired by Cypriot halloumi.
In 2017, De Zuivelarij also began producing organic cheeses. Four of the company’s five products now have an organic variant. The company has now been awarded the BioVLAM prize on account of its organic variants of paneer, an Indian cheese, and labneh, a cheese popular in the Middle East.
Pig feed keeps production process sustainable
De Zuivelarij will act as an ambassador for the organic sector over the coming year.
“Of course, you hold out hope, but when I saw the other nominees, I was already feeling a bit less confident,” admits David De Coster. “They also have some excellent organic projects. I’m looking forward to taking on the role of ambassador for organic farming for a year.”
Organic cheese now accounts for around 20 per cent of De Zuivelarij’s turnover. One in five production days is devoted entirely to organic production.
The company is also committed to efficient and sustainable production in other areas. Leftover cheese whey is used as pig feed. In addition, heat from the production process is recovered to warm milk for the next production run.

The best place to retire abroad is no longer in Europe – but six of the top ten are
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

European destinations scored highly in a new global retirement ranking, with six countries among the top ten, as people looking to retire abroad weigh higher taxes against quality of life.
Uruguay has taken the top spot in a new global retirement ranking, overtaking last year’s leader, Portugal. But Europe remains the most represented region, with six countries in the top ten. The Americas hold three places, while Mauritius ranks second.
Global Citizen Solutions’ 2026 retirement index compares 46 retirement and passive-income residence programmes, assessing quality of life, travel freedom and routes to citizenship, taxation, application procedures and costs.
Europe’s strengths lie in its high living standards, strong passports and routes to citizenship, although higher taxes weigh on its scores. Spain, Portugal, Latvia, Andorra, Italy and Greece all make the top ten, with Portugal slipping to fifth this year.
Uruguay leads thanks to solid scores across all five categories, rather than coming first in any one of them. Mauritius follows, combining favourable taxation with good results elsewhere.
The report stresses that the right destination depends on each retiree’s priorities. Fewer than four points separate first and tenth place, making the leaders closely matched.
What are the major priorities for those retiring abroad?
Quality of life carries the most weight in the index, followed by mobility and citizenship, then taxation, application procedures and costs. The weighting reflects the priorities of a typical person retiring abroad, according to the report.
Europe performs strongly on quality of life and mobility but scores less well on taxation, with wide differences between its programmes. The Americas stand out for affordability and favourable taxation, while Mauritius leads Africa’s performance. In the Middle East, low taxes and fast processing are the main attractions. The United Arab Emirates, 19th overall, ranks first for preferential tax regimes. Spain, third overall, also scores strongly on mobility and options for moving with family members.
Strong passports and clear routes to citizenship help European and many Latin American programmes score highly. Gulf destinations offer favourable taxation and fast processing, but their retirement programmes provide no standard route to citizenship.
Europe’s top-performing programmes in the 2026 index
Europe’s ten highest-ranked international retirement programmes are those offered by Spain, Portugal, Latvia, Andorra, Italy, Greece, Austria, Albania, Cyprus and Malta. All ten rank in the top half of the index.
European programmes perform particularly well on quality of life and mobility. The trade-off is taxation. Spain, the best country in Europe to live abroad in retirement, ranks fifth in the world for quality of life and offers a smooth application process taking up to eight months. However, the country also ranks last out of 46 on tax, with worldwide taxation, regional wealth taxes and no special regime for visa holders.
Portugal ranks second in Europe. The country, which topped the global list in 2025, slipped to fifth place this year. This came as Portugal increased the number of years required for citizenship. In May, the requirement increased from five to ten years for most non-EU applicants.
The country has still secured a very high global ranking, helped by its position as one of the most affordable major European routes, with the income requirement set at €920 a month. Portugal also scores highly on mobility, but processing takes up to two years, and its 41st-place tax ranking may make it less attractive to retirees prioritising lower taxes.
The programmes that do perform well on tax, notably Malta, Andorra and Cyprus, often have other demanding requirements, including high income thresholds, large investments or slow processing. Several countries also offer opt-in regimes, such as the 7% flat tax on foreign pensions in Greece and southern Italy.
Processing times and costs vary widely: Latvia, third in Europe, offers processing times of two to four months and one of the lowest-cost programmes. By contrast, the process in Cyprus can take more than two years, but the country offers a 5% tax rate, subject to specific conditions.
Ireland ranks first for quality of life in the index. It combines an English-speaking environment with some of the strongest safety and environmental ratings.
Andorra posts the index’s best safety and environmental scores; it ranks third in the world for quality of life and offers low taxes, with income tax capped at 10% and no wealth or inheritance tax. It is also the most expensive programme in the entire index, requiring a €1 million local investment on top of substantial income.
Italy and Greece rank first and second globally for mobility and citizenship, respectively. They are also Europe’s fifth- and sixth-highest-ranked retirement destinations. Both offer options for lower taxation, but Greece’s monthly income requirement of €3,500 is one of the highest.
How much monthly income do you need to qualify?
Monthly income requirements vary widely, from less than €600 in Nicaragua to more than €9,000 in Bahrain. In Europe, a monthly income of less than €800 could be sufficient in Cyprus if other requirements are met, while in Andorra, monthly income has to be more than €4,500. For comparison, the amounts shown in the chart have been converted to euros, so they may fluctuate with exchange rates.
The qualifying sources of income are also important. In some cases, applicants must show foreign-sourced passive income or a pension; others accept savings or dividends. And while the income threshold may be relatively low, some routes also require savings, deposits, investments or other substantial upfront payments.
Cape Verde, Namibia, Chile, Zambia and Morocco are excluded from the chart because the report does not specify whether their income requirements are monthly. El Salvador is also excluded, as it gives separate thresholds for pensioners and people living on passive income. Income requirements in these countries vary between $825 and $1,800.
How quickly can you get a passport?
A route to citizenship is common, but not guaranteed. The report says 24 programmes offer naturalisation within five years and 17 within six to ten years. Andorra requires 20 years. Four — Malta, the UAE, Ireland and Bahrain — offer no standard route through retirement or passive-income visas.
The shortest timelines are in South America: around two years in Argentina and roughly three in Uruguay, Paraguay and some other countries.
However, 11 countries, including Austria, Andorra, the UAE and Malaysia, do not permit dual nationality, according to the report. Applicants may therefore have to give up their original citizenship. For those unwilling to do so, permanent residence may be the limit.
What other regions offer
The Americas stand out for affordability and favourable taxation. Brazil, Argentina and Chile also offer strong passports and relatively short routes to citizenship, adding to the region’s appeal.
Mauritius is Africa’s strongest performer. In the Middle East, the main attractions are low taxes and fast processing, although retirement routes offer no standard path to citizenship.
