Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian captain who was seriously wounded during the attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight to Israel, said his Omani co-pilot told him he wanted to pray shortly before attacking him from behind.
Machchhar recounted the attack in a conversation Saturday night with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying saying the co-pilot was praying behind him, and out of respect, he continued to look ahead.
"Suddenly, I took a very hard blow to the back of my head," Machchhar said. "My first thought was that there had been catastrophic damage to the plane, that something was wrong. But then the blows kept coming, one after another. That's when I realized it wasn't the aircraft – it was the other guy in the cockpit with me."
Machchhar said he tried to fight back, but the initial blows left him barely able to see. "My vision was almost completely gone," he said. "At that moment, I could also feel the plane diving."
He said he used what strength he had left to reach the cockpit door, but had to open it more than once after the co-pilot apparently slammed it shut again.
"I managed to open the door once, but I think he slammed it shut," Machchhar said. "Call it personal instinct or call it doing it for everyone else, but I did it knowing that if I didn't, I was going to die."
"I used every bit of strength I had left," he continued. "I just charged at the door and opened it. And fortunately, people were waiting there to rush back inside."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a conversation with the Indian pilot from the flight from Dubai, Captain Smit Machchhar: "You are a hero for Israel, India, and the entire world. I invite Prime Minister @NarendraModi and you to light a flame on Israeli Independence Day."
Show more
Passengers and crew members then entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker, while another flight crew aboard the plane took control and landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar also said he hoped to meet the medic who treated him aboard the plane, saying he believed the physician had saved his life.
Netanyahu praised Machchhar as "a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel" and invited him to light an Independence Day torch alongside Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Yossi Shelley, Israel's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, who was with Machchhar during the call, also invited the pilot and his family to the Prime Minister's Office.
The account came as new questions emerged over how the suspected attacker was able to serve on a flight to Israel. Haaretz reported Saturday that Israel had received the flight's crew and passenger list in advance.
According to Israeli security sources, the Transportation Ministry's security division and the Mossad are the bodies responsible for monitoring and screening foreign flight crews arriving in Israel and were supposed to review the list. Both are expected to receive the names of foreign crews and flag any concerns, according to security sources.
The Transportation Ministry's Security Division and the Mossad are the bodies responsible for monitoring and screening foreign flight crews arriving in Israel and were supposed to examine the list, security sources told Haaretz.
The sources said both bodies are supposed to receive lists of foreign flight crews arriving in Israel and issue warnings if there are suspicions about any of the crew members.
On the website of the Transportation Ministry's Security, Emergency and Cyber Division, it is stated that its role includes "directing security procedures for air transport services to, from and within Israel, ensuring they are free from terror threats, and among other things, security screening of foreign flights crossing/arriving in Israel."
Two security sources, however, said that while responsibility formally rests with the Transportation Ministry, it lacks the intelligence capabilities needed to carry out such screening independently. "The Transportation Ministry has no intelligence capabilities," one source said. "Those capabilities exist only in the Mossad or Shin Bet."
The Shin Bet said it is responsible for securing Israeli airlines and setting security guidelines at Ben-Gurion Airport, but not for foreign carriers.
Another security source said that under agreements between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, the Transportation Ministry's security division is responsible for ensuring that foreign flight crews do not include pilots from enemy states or countries hostile to Israel. If a name raises suspicion, the ministry is supposed to refer it to the Shin Bet or Mossad for further examination.
According to the source, that did not happen in this case. There is currently no law or formal procedure requiring the Shin Bet or Mossad to routinely use the foreign crew database, although the Shin Bet, as the body responsible for setting incoming-flight security procedures, is theoretically expected to ensure that those procedures are followed.

Space Popular creates carpet-covered gallery for Nieuwe Instituut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

Space Popular creates carpet-covered gallery for Nieuwe Instituut
Architecture and design studio Space Popular has completed a gallery space for the Nieuwe Instituut in Rotterdam, using a colourful gridded carpet to demarcate its collection.
Occupying a long, narrow volume within the museum, the Collection Gallery serves as a permanent space to exhibit the Nieuwe Instituut's physical and digital collection documenting the history of Dutch architecture.
The gallery, which is cloaked almost-entirely in soft furnishings, was designed by Space Popular to offer visitors a cosy alternative to the "bright minimalism" of a typical contemporary gallery.
"We wanted to create something opposite of the usual bright minimalism of gallery spaces and make something that would feel more like a club or a lounge," the studio told Dezeen.
"We wanted to create a space that people would spend more time in than they might usually do in a gallery."
"The darker tones and soft gradients invites visitors to slow down, take a seat and feel the softness of the carpet and the warmth of the colours," it added.
Working alongside graphic designer Mariana Lobão, Space Popular arranged the entire gallery across the gridded design of a digitally printed carpet.
The carpet's design is complete with both a 50 by 50 centimetre grid and coloured-coded portions, which organise the collection into five themed sections.
"Together we created a non linear and multi-visitor way to experience and interact with the five thematic stories the curatorial team at the Nieuwe Instituut had created," the studio explained.
Within each section, wooden podiums crafted by Rob den Dulk have been colour-coded and similarly finished with carpeted surfaces.
These are topped with glass cases, where the collection's physical models are on show. Other wooden cabinetry in the space serve as interactive screens for visitors.
Flanking the entire exhibition is a 40-metre-long concrete wall that doubles as a projection wall.
"The carpet frames the gallery as a soft, slower space, while its 50 by 50 cm grid organises everything within it," the studio explained.
"Every podium and collection object follows this grid. We feel there is a positive quality to all-encompassing geometries in space," it added.
The gallery by Space Popular will remain open at the Nieuwe Instituut until May 2029, with an evolving showcase intended to "reflect current events".
Previous interventions by the studio include a colourful installation at the MAXXI museum in Rome designed to reinterpret Aldo Rossi's architectural theories for the metaverse.
The photography is by Special Thanks Studios.

Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:20 UTC
14:00:20 KST

They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.
Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”
The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.
Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.
While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”
The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”
But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”
While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.
It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%.
EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China.
Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.
“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.
Figures released on Friday showed that British new car registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s Sealion 7 among the top sellers.
The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.
Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
.
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”
Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”
He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

Dante Mayfair, Claridge’s, London W1: ‘Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

Dante Mayfair, inside Claridge’s on Brook Street in London, has been created, the hotel’s management says, to become “the living room of Mayfair”. It’s a charming idea: pop in, have a cuppa or a bowl of pappardelle bolognese, or lie about on the fancy sofas wearing elasticated tracksuit bottoms and slurping soft-serve with s’mores. No, sorry, I’ve gone too far: it’s nowhere near that informal.
Still, like many well-used living rooms, this one has been rearranged, redecorated and repurposed many times over the years. I’ve eaten fancy-schmancy Simon Rogan dinners here when it was Fera, as well as his table experience at Aulis during which venture capitalist “foodies” bored the pants off me over a 12-course meal in the kitchen itself. I’ve stared unmoved at Daniel Humm’s New York-style pomp at the short-lived Davies and Brook, and have visited several times since Claridge’s took matters in-house in the shape of a rather anonymous ye olde British brasserie.
Now I’m here for Dante, and we’re back in New York again, this time in the hands of Linden Pride and Nathalie Hudson, with no named chef at all, although there’s absolutely definitely a man plinky-plonking his way through John Legend’s Ordinary People on the piano. Pride and Hudson are a husband-and-wife team from Sydney, Australia, who met at college, moved to New York and in 2015 bought Caffe Dante, an institution of a Greenwich Village coffee house that’s been open since 1915. By 2019, the place had been named the world’s best bar. The couple’s new space on Brook Street is a restaurant site in need of stability and comprehensible finery, as well as of caviar tarts with champagne pearls, shrimp cocktails and lobster linguine, and of caviar martinis and vintage or chocolate negronis.
If you like, you can enter via a small side door on Davies Street, but ignore that. The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance past the men in top hats – you need to feel like Paddington, a little bear in a big city just making it on your own. Take a right turn, hand in your coat at the beautiful little cloakroom, then quickly powder your nose in the vintage loos where nice ladies polish the sinks. Order a marmalade sandwich … sorry, I mean dover sole meunière or veal milanese. For this part of Mayfair, the prices are weirdly reasonable – a bowl of fazzoletti with pesto may be £27, but you should see how much they charge for pasta at Bacchanalia just down the road – and a mini martini is a tenner between 3pm and 5pm.
Dante is useful for client lunches or intimate tête-à-têtes when you want to be heard perfectly and don’t want to be constantly interrupted by the waiting staff. After all, no one needs a tomato and peach salad with marinated feta and freekeh explained to them, even though this one is very fresh, very nicely arranged and whispers more of California than of Italy. A large plate of San Daniele prosciutto comes with baked mozzarella, and the iceberg salad features very neatly dressed lettuce wedges. The pappardelle al ragu, or house bolognese, lacks depth and the pasta is a touch overcooked, but chicken alla diavola with green goddess dressing is earthy and fresh. Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not, but then this is Claridge’s, not Clacton seafront.
I do wonder, however, whether Dante’s most noteworthy offering is its “dessert cocktail” list, which is aimed squarely at that moment after the main course when customers wrinkle their noses at shelling out on “something sweet” but will happily carry on drinking. That’s when the rounds of honey bees (tequila, coffee liqueur, amontillado, raspberry, salted honey cream) are ordered. And wait, what? It comes with my own face printed on top of it!?! Dante has a piece of kit that stamps photographs on to the foam in edible ink, and I defy anyone not to be exhilarated by that – or to think that it’s not perfectly sensible to have a nonna’s alexander or a grasshopper afterwards. We wanted pudding, too, though, and the waiter asked if we fancied the sticky toffee doughnut with whisky flambé. Yes. Yes, please. Yes, I would like you to set fire to things. It goes up like a firework and is a sweet, sticky mess.
On this Tuesday lunchtime, Dante was probably the quietest place in Mayfair. A small, elegant wedding had taken over the side room, while a few hotel residents were eating burgers in the main room. Service was warm, slick, effusive and casual, and completely on it. The issue with a semi-casual restaurant inside Claridge’s is that the very name scares off the general public. But you could invite anyone here, and at any time; I’d use it for breakfasts and meet-ups. Dante is not a destination dinner, but it is, as promised, a living room. It won’t win prizes for its food, but it is friendly and handy as hell, which in Mayfair these days is exceptionally rare.
- Dante Mayfair Claridge’s, Brook Street, London W1, 020-7629 8860. Open all week, noon-9.30pm (10.30pm Thurs-Sat); breakfast 8-11am. From about £60 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

Where to celebrate Halloween 2026 in Europe: Spooky cities, haunted hotels and scary events
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:12 UTC
14:00:12 KST

Fancy a fright? These European destinations, hotels and Halloween events promise everything from Gothic legends to full-blown horror.
Halloween is nearly upon us, and the festival has become so popular that it’s nearly impossible to escape it throughout the entirety of October.
The month is peak spooky season, as temperatures drop across much of Europe and things start getting a bit darker and, in some cases, eerier.
If you’re a big fan of Halloween, there’s no shortage of things to do across the continent, from the best cities to experience the creepy vibes to haunted hotels and events, which will be over once November comes.
These are the best ways to get into the Halloween spirit, European-style this year.
Destinations
Transylvania, Romania
Starting, of course, with the most obvious destination, some might argue that a visit to Romania’s Transylvania region is the ultimate way to do Halloween.
It’s forever linked to Dracula and the imposing Bran Castle, but there’s far more to its spooky appeal, with atmospheric villages, medieval citadels, striking churches and more than 100 castles scattered across the region.
October is also the perfect time to see the beautiful autumn colours which fill the forests of the Carpathian Mountains and to explore Brașov, a beautiful city with plenty of atmosphere of its own.
Bruges, Belgium
Bruges may be known for its canals and romantic medieval streets, but come Halloween, the Belgian city takes a much darker turn.
Hear the story of the water ghost said to haunt the Lake of Love, or join a night-time tour through the city’s legends, myths and more sinister tales.
The Historium gets a spooky makeover too, with pumpkins, cobwebs and bats, and a Halloween Virtual Reality Experience. There’s also the Torture Museum, if you’re feeling brave enough.
Paris, France
Paris is more than just romance and lights – and has plenty of spooky sights to go with its usual glamour.
Start underground in the Catacombs, where the bones of some six million people line the dimly lit tunnels. Afterwards, wander through Père Lachaise Cemetery, where winding paths and elaborate tombs are the final resting place of figures including Oscar Wilde, Marcel Proust, Molière, and Édith Piaf.
There are countless themed parties throughout the city but, if you prefer a bit of light relief rather than gore, head to Disneyland Paris, which extends its park hours until 11 pm on the night itself.
Edinburgh, Scotland
Edinburgh’s dark history and atmospheric old town make it a natural fit for Halloween.
Each year, the Samhuinn Fire Festival brings the Scottish capital’s ancient Celtic traditions to life, with colourful costumes, fire performers and a lively procession through the cobbled streets.
It’s a dramatic way to mark the holiday, with plenty of local folklore thrown in.
Derry, Northern Ireland
Derry puts a more festive spin on Halloween, making it a good option for families and groups who want plenty of atmosphere without too many scares.
Each October, the city hosts Derry Halloween, billed as one of Europe’s biggest Halloween festivals, with light shows, acrobatic banshees and Celtic circus performers taking over the streets.
During the day, visitors can pick pumpkins or try a craft workshop, before live music and performances take over after dark.
Hotels
The Haunted Bedroom at Talliston, Great Dunmow, England
What was once a normal house in the Essex market town of Great Dunmow has been transformed into something far stranger.
Talliston House and Gardens is a maze of rooms, each designed to transport visitors to a different time and place, with elaborate details that make the property feel more like stepping into a story than visiting a home.
For a proper fright, book a stay in the Haunted Bedroom. It recreates the bedroom of a seven-year-old Edwardian child in unsettling detail, complete with old-fashioned toys, books and furniture.
Castello Dal Pozzo, Piedmont, Italy
Now a hotel, this Italian estate on the shores of Lake Maggiore has a tragic story that has given it a distinctly spooky reputation.
Set in its own hillside grounds, the property is a quick drive from Arona on the lake’s southwestern shore. Its ghostly tale dates back to 1467, when a young woman named Barbara fell in love with an army captain, Matteo.
The pair planned to elope, but Barbara’s father discovered their romance and locked her in the estate’s tower, while Matteo was sent into exile in France. Barbara never knew what had happened to him and died waiting for him to return.
According to local legend, she never quite left. Guests have reported seeing Barbara at the tower window, still watching and waiting for her lost love.
Ballygally Castle Hotel, Northern Ireland
Ballygally Castle has a ghostly tale dating back to the 1600s, when Lady Isabella Shaw, wife of the castle’s builder, is said to have died after being locked in a tower room.
Legend has it she either jumped or was pushed to her death, and her ghost is now said to haunt the castle.
Guests have reported knocking sounds, sudden cold spots and sightings of a woman in period dress, particularly around the tower stairs and Room 421, known as the Ghost Room. The four-star hotel embraces the story without overplaying it, with historical exhibits in the tower and Room 421 available to guests brave enough to request it.
The Haunted Chamber Apartment, York, England
Dating back more than 600 years, this atmospheric apartment feels like stepping straight into York’s spookier past. Overlooking York Minster, it is filled with original character, including timber panelling and historic details that give the property a suitably eerie feel.
The city itself adds to the spooky setting, with its winding medieval streets, ghost stories and centuries of dark history. Nearby, York Dungeons and the Halloween thrills of Hallowscream at York Maze offer plenty more scares after dark.
Hotel U Prince, Prague
Right on Prague’s atmospheric Old Town Square, Hotel U Prince combines luxury with centuries of history. The building’s foundations date back to the 12th century, giving it plenty of old-world character – and some suitably spooky stories.
Guests have reported unexplained noises, cold spots and shadowy figures in the corridors, while Prague’s Gothic architecture, alchemical legends and long history of ghost stories add to the eerie atmosphere.
After dark, the city’s winding streets and medieval buildings make the setting feel even more mysterious.
Events
Bran Castle Halloween Party, Transylvania, Romania
On 31 October, the legendary ‘Dracula's Castle’ in Bran hosts a Halloween party, combining a special night-time tour with interactive characters, horror screenings and a party in the Royal Park. The 2026 event includes DJs, costumes and theatrical touches, with festivities running until 4 am.
Bram Stoker Festival, Dublin, Ireland
Taking place from 23-26 October, the Bram Stoker Festival brings four days of Gothic-inspired events to venues across Dublin. Expect immersive outdoor theatre, dark storytelling and literary events celebrating the Dracula author, who was born here.
Tivoli Gardens Halloween, Copenhagen, Denmark
From 2 October to 1 November, Copenhagen’s historic Tivoli Gardens gets a spooky autumn makeover, with more than 20,000 pumpkins, atmospheric decorations and seasonal market stalls.
Families can also enjoy Halloween-themed rides and entertainment throughout the park
Halloween Horror Festival at Movie Park Germany, Bottrop, Germany
From September 26 to November 8, Movie Park Germany transforms into a full-blown horror experience, with more than 300 roaming monsters, terrifying scare zones and haunted mazes.
It’s aimed firmly at thrill-seekers, with plenty of jump scares and creepier attractions after sunset.
Halloween at Little Kook, Athens, Greece
October and Halloween is the best time of year to visit Little Kook in Athens. The fantasy-themed café goes all out for scary season, transforming its buildings and surrounding streets with elaborate seasonal decorations.
Expect giant pumpkins, skeletons, witches, ghosts and cobwebs spilling across colourful façades and balconies, creating theatrical street scenes that feel like a Halloween film set. Visit after dark, when the illuminated displays make this atmospheric corner of central Athens even more dramatic.

EU neighbors shun Kyiv’s plea to free trapped grain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

A driver looks at wheat being unloaded from the combine into a car during harvesting in a farm field near Malopolovetske village, some a hundred kilometers from Kyiv. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Domestic farmers’ worries are trumping EU solidarity with Kyiv as the Black Sea blockade threatens to fuel a global food crisis and stunt Ukraine’s next harvest.
Ukraine needs help getting millions of tons of grain exports out of the country, as attacks on ports and ships continue into a third month.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi came to Brussels this week to make a direct appeal to his EU counterparts. Ukraine needs to be able to move more farm products through Europe, as well as €1.1 billion to cover higher shipping costs. Without help, cash-strapped farmers won't be able to start planting for next season, compounding the problem.
Advertisement
"It's very, very critical," Vysotskyi told POLITICO during his visit.
The answer: Sorry, but no. Two of the countries with the most vital infrastructure for boosting shipping and storage capacity, Poland and Romania, said there is nothing more they can or will do to help.
“The interest for our own farmers remains a priority,” Barna Tánczos, Romania’s agriculture minister, told POLITICO. Excess Ukrainian grain, combined with low water levels on the Danube, is already overloading his country’s ports, preventing Romanian farmers from selling their own goods.
The rebuff illustrates a persistent gap between the EU’s ambitions to support Ukraine and domestic political realities. As one of the world’s breadbaskets, Ukraine poses a real threat to the livelihoods of European farmers, a powerful constituency in many member countries. Even before the latest eruption in Black Sea fighting, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary barred imports of Ukrainian grain.
Currently, less than half of the exports are able to get out through the European rail, road and river shipping routes, Vysotskyi said. Up to 35 million tons could end up being stuck in Ukraine this year if the blockade persists.
Romania is trying to optimize its logistics, Tánczos stressed. Last month, Bucharest even signed a memorandum of understanding to ease border crossings with Kyiv and boost rail links.
Advertisement
But “everybody knows we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the roads, railways and port capacity," Tánczos said. "It is what it is.”
In Poland, the infrastructure ministry “has no plans to introduce any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products,” spokesperson Anna Szumańska said in a statement.
Though help isn't coming immediately, the EU isn't ruling out a collective response. "We need ... to address this," Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen told reporters this week, citing concerns for global food security — though he made no commitments.
EU Commissioner for Agriculture, Christophe Hansen, speaks during an interview at the EU headquarters in Brussels on February 24, 2026. | John Thys/AFP via Getty Images
Some capitals are volunteering more support. As Ukraine eyes Dutch and German ports as new outlets, a German agriculture ministry spokesperson said Berlin “is making every effort in Europe to ensure that alternative export routes ... are strengthened.”
Spiraling to next season
In an interview, Vysotskyi described harvested grain and oilseeds piling up without a buyer — leaving farmers without the cash they need to plant winter seeds now for next year’s harvest. “If the situation stays like this till spring, it could mean the decrease of even 35-40% of the planted area,” he said.
The pain will be felt beyond Europe. As Russia and Ukraine trade bombs in the Black Sea, more than 17 percent of the world's traded grain could be affected by the drop in exports from both countries, according to a recent Council on Foreign Relations report. "The number of people driven into acute hunger by the current Black Sea crisis could exceed all recorded battlefield casualties in the Russia-Ukraine war," the report warns.
Advertisement
Yet the pain for European farmers — struggling with drought, heatwaves and spiking prices for fuel and fertilizer — is real too.
Iulia Blagu, a Romanian cereal farmer, described looking out at unharvested fields, "at the mercy of God and the climate," because the crops can't be stored or transported.
“And then you have this entire transit of Ukrainian cereals coming towards our country," she said. "I mean … how can we handle that?”

Lithuanian trio recreate painting stolen by Nazis and still held in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

A large-format painting by Lithuanian landscape master and watercolourist Jonas Buračas, Lithuania’s Gateway to the Seas, has been brought back to life. The painting was taken to Germany by the Nazis in July 1944 and subsequently disappeared.
“The story of the canvas being stolen is, I would say, a typical example of Nazi behaviour in the occupied territories,” said Romualdas Beniušis, a historian.
He worked together with Antanas Buračas, son of the late painter, as well as painter Rodionas Petrovas and Memelio Miesto real estate developers in the port city of Klaipėda to bring the painting back to life.
According to Beniušis, returning works of art to their rightful owners is a difficult problem to solve. Lithuanian institutions can point to only a handful of successful cases in this area. Unfortunately, Buračas’ painting is not among them.
In 1938, Buračas won a competition organised by the Klaipėda Chamber of Commerce and Industry to depict Lithuania’s maritime gateway to the world. The work was intended as a gift to the newly established Kaunas Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Crafts, designed by architect Vytautas Landsbergis-Žemkalnis.
Painter and watercolourist Buračas (1898–1977) was born in Sidariai, in the Radviliškis area in northern Lithuania.
He graduated from the Kaunas Art School and furthered his studies in Paris, Berlin and Riga. He became known for his depictions of Lithuania’s landscapes, towns, hillforts and architectural monuments, painted in a realistic style influenced by Impressionism and Pointillism.
From 1945 to 1951, he taught at the Kaunas Art School and the Kaunas Institute of Applied and Decorative Arts. From 1950, he devoted himself mainly to his creative work, leaving behind a significant collection of images of Lithuania’s landscapes and cultural heritage.
The renowned landscape painter worked “from nature”. During summers spent on the coast, he produced numerous works and watercolours.
“It seems the dimensions of the painting had been agreed in advance with the architect, and a place for it to be displayed had also been designated in the building. The canvas, approximately 2 metres high and 4 metres long, was the first of this size that Buračas had painted,” Beniušis says.
Buračas took up residence at a local guesthouse and got to work. After moving to Smiltynė, he made sketches and took photographs. This is documented in archival material left to his son, Antanas Buračas.
A prize of 5,000 litas was awarded for the work, with Buračas receiving 3,500. The organisers used the remaining money to cover the artist’s accommodation costs.
According to Beniušis, a photograph of the painting appeared in the Klaipėda newspaper Vakarai on September 16, 1938.
“Buračas depicted a panorama of Klaipėda’s port and city as seen from Smiltynė. Some of the landmarks no longer survive. For example, St John’s Church, which had a 75-metre-high tower with a clock. The artist painted the Reformed and Laukininkai churches, the Lietūkis warehouses and the Pilots’ Tower,” the local historian says.
In February 1939, the Kaunas Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Crafts celebrated the opening of its new premises. Buračas’ monumental work became a prominent part of the chamber’s interior.
After the Soviet occupation, the chamber was nationalised. “Buračas’s canvas was supposed to be transferred to the M K Čiurlionis Art Gallery, but for some reason it never reached the gallery,” Beniušis says.
After the Nazis occupied Lithuania, the official governor of the territory, Theodor Adrian von Renteln, set up his headquarters in the Chamber of Commerce building, while taking up residence in the house of industrialist Jonas Vailokaitis, a signatory of Lithuania’s February 16 Act of Independence, in Vienybės Square.
“Apparently, the ‘newcomers’ liked Buračas’s canvas depicting Klaipėda’s port and city – the Nazis considered it their own. So when they had to retreat in 1944, the painting was taken away along with other property looted in Lithuania,” the local historian says.
According to him, evidence of the work’s whereabouts in Frankfurt am Main was later recorded in several documents, including the 1981 catalogue Jonas Buračas’ Paintings and a book by Lithuanian émigré journalist and local historian Bronius Kviklys.
State showed no interest
The artist’s son, Antanas Buračas, tells LRT.lt that he became interested in the painting’s history after finding a description by art collector Vladas Žukas in his father’s archive.
The artist had told Žukas that he had personally seen German soldiers in 1944 cut the canvas from its frame, roll it up and load it onto a lorry parked in the courtyard of the Chamber of Commerce.
“It was later discovered that the theft had been carried out on the orders of Renteln, the general commissioner of Ostland,” the artist’s son adds.
In 1989, Antanas Buračas visited Chicago, where he spoke to fellow Lithuanians about the Sąjūdis movement and the aspirations of the Lithuanian people. There he met Bronius Kviklys, a prominent Lithuanian émigré journalist, ethnographer and historian.
Kviklys told his visitor that, after the war, while living in a displaced persons (DP) camp, he had seen the painting Lithuania’s Gateway to the Seas in a museum in Frankfurt am Main.
Antanas says he was more interested at the time in Kviklys’ other accounts and was focused on the affairs of Lithuania undergoing a national revival, so he did not remember the name of the museum. Kviklys died a year later.
When interest in the fate of the painting resurfaced in recent years, Antanas contacted Germany’s commission dealing with property confiscated by the Nazis. The commission replied that it would be happy to help search for the work, but that the artist’s son would have to provide proof of ownership.
“The owner was effectively the Kaunas Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Crafts. After 1940, I believe its property was nationalised by the Soviets and should have become state property. During the war, my father asked Paulius Galaunė [director of the M K Čiurlionis Art Gallery] to shelter the canvas somewhere.
“But the work was very inconvenient because of its size, so it was left without being hidden. I believe the current successor in title is the Lithuanian state, and the Culture Ministry should represent its interests,” Antanas Buračas says.
He and Beniušis approached the ministry, but heard no more about anyone taking decisive action.
‘Houston, we have a problem’
“As you know, I like getting involved in all sorts of adventures. And when an adventure begins... ‘Houston, we have a problem!’ The harsh reality stares you in the face,” says painter Rodionas Petrovas, who recreated Buračas’s painting.
He is neither a copyist nor a landscape painter nor a restorer – that is not his field. However, he realised that there might not be another professional in Klaipėda capable of recreating the painting with the necessary technical skill. So he accepted the offer.
Besides, Petrovas had experience working with architecture, which is also one of the themes of his work.
According to the artist, the hardest part was that only two black-and-white photographs of Buračas’ painting survive. It is very difficult to make out specific details in them.
Petrovas set out to find images of all the buildings depicted in the painting. In search of high-quality panoramic photographs, he visited museums, libraries and archives. He found Kęstutis Demereckas’s book, Klaipėda in Old Postcards, particularly helpful.
It was also necessary to understand the contrast between the tones in the original. “Then you can work out what colours the artist used,” Petrovas says. According to him, Buračas used vivid colours when he painted the work in the late 1930s. Petrovas himself opted for a more muted palette.
“I thought that, since I was partly creating a historical interpretation, I could allow myself to tone down the colours so that it would look like a work that has stood the test of time,” he says.
Petrovas has two theories to explain the mystery surrounding the painting’s high-altitude perspective.
According to one, the landscape painter viewed the panorama of Klaipėda from the Kurhaus, at the time the tallest building in Smiltynė, and gradually widened his field of view in his sketches. “That is no problem for a professional,” he says.
His other, “conspiratorial”, theory is linked to the fact that an airship flew to Klaipėda during the interwar period. Buračas may have used photographs taken from the airship.
In 2027, it will be 50 years since Buračas’ death, and the following year will mark 130 years since his birth. Is his son considering how these anniversaries might be commemorated?
“It is very gratifying that, just before these anniversaries, there has suddenly been some excitement about the great painting and its rediscovery. As a panorama, it has turned out to be not bad at all and has deserved this attention. I am very pleased about that,” says Antanas.

Bosnia general election 2026 explained in maps and charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
04:58:50 UTC
13:58:50 KST

Bosnia general election 2026 explained in maps and charts
Bosnians head to the polls on October 4. Here’s a quick guide to the voting process, candidates and what’s at stake.
Bosnians are heading to the polls to choose the next government at all three of the state, entity and canton levels. It may seem complicated, but for a country divided into two entities – the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, along with Brcko District – this is nothing new.
When do Bosnia’s elections take place?
The general elections are scheduled for Sunday, October 4. More than 3.4 million people are eligible to vote.
What’s different about this election?
This year, new election technology will be used. Voters will be identified using biometric devices, while ballot papers will be scanned rather than simply placed in ballot boxes.
The use of scanners, however, does not mean voting will be fully electronic. Votes will still be cast and recorded on paper, but verification and counting should be faster and more transparent, while voter identification should be more accurate.
Who is running for the Presidency?
Candidates for the Bosniak representative include current Presidency member Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), Bakir Izetbegovic of the Party of Democratic Action (SDA), Semir Efendic of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina (Stranka za BiH), and Fahrudin Radoncic of the Union for a Better Future of BiH (SBB).
Izetbegovic, the president of the centre-right SDA, the biggest Bosniak party in the country, is running for his third term after being defeated by Becirovic in 2022.
Three candidates will run for the Croat seat in the Presidency: Darijana Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH), Slaven Kovacevic of the Democratic Front (DF), and Zdenko Lucic, a candidate supported by a coalition of five Croat parties.
The current Serb member of the Presidency, Zeljka Cvijanovic from the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), is running for a second term. During her term on the country’s top state body, which began in November 2022, just a few months after Russia’s war in Ukraine started, she maintained close and continuous cooperation with Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin.
SNSD is led by Milorad Dodik, the former president of Republika Srpska, best known for his separatist moves and for challenging the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the decisions of former High Representative Christian Schmidt.
Cvijanovic will face Marinko Bozovic of the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) and Nebojsa Vukanovic of the List for Justice and Order.
Who else is on the ballot?
Voters will be choosing representatives for 14 governments, as well as members of the country’s three-member Presidency.
Each entity has its own president, assembly, prime minister and ministers. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is further divided into 10 cantons, each with its own government.
For all this to happen, the Central Election Commission (CIK), the main body responsible for overseeing the voting process, earlier said that 75 political parties and four independent candidates were registered and eligible to participate.
How are Presidency members chosen?
When registered voters go to the polls, they do not elect one president, but choose one of three members of the country’s collective head of state. They are the representatives of the three constituent peoples – Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs.
The Bosniak and Croat members are elected from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while the Serb member is elected from Republika Srpska.
This is because the majority of Bosniaks and Croats live in the Federation, while most Serbs live in Republika Srpska.
The election of the Croat member has weighed on Bosniak-Croat relations for years and has often been used as a reason for political blockades.
Parties gathered around the centre-right Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) are demanding changes to the Election Law, saying they want to prevent Bosniak voters from influencing the election of the Croat member of the Presidency.
But that would also require changes to the Constitution, which allows all citizens in the Federation to choose whether they want to vote for the Bosniak or the Croat member.
What about citizens who live outside their constituent group’s voting area?
A Serb living in the Federation, or a Bosniak or Croat living in Republika Srpska, who wants to run would not be able to do so, nor can they vote for those they consider to be their own representatives.
That is one of the many paradoxes of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s electoral system.
How is the state-level government chosen?
Citizens elect representatives to the Parliamentary Assembly, which consists of two houses.
Forty-two representatives will be elected to the House of Representatives.
Two-thirds are directly elected from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and one-third from Republika Srpska.
A quorum consists of a majority of all members elected to the House of Representatives.
The second chamber – the House of Peoples – has 15 delegates and is elected indirectly through the institutions. It consists of Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs – five from each group.
What happens with the entities?
The election of entity-level authorities works somewhat differently.
In Republika Srpska, citizens directly elect the National Assembly, as well as the entity president and vice presidents.
They do not directly elect the government – it is confirmed by the National Assembly.
In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, citizens directly elect the House of Representatives of the Federation Parliament and the cantonal assemblies.
Those cantonal assemblies then elect delegates to the Federation’s House of Peoples.
The president of the Federation, the entity government and the cantonal governments are formed after the elections, through parliamentary majorities and political agreements.
Why is it a challenge to form the government?
It is difficult not only because the electoral system is complex, but also because of the lack of agreement among representatives of the three different ethnic communities.
Frequent blockades and obstruction make decision-making difficult at all levels, even though many politicians invoke the politics of compromise.
Elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, therefore, are not only about who wins, but about whether a system designed to represent everyone can serve its citizens.
Why are the elections important?
New election technologies might reduce potential fraud, but much more will be needed for the country’s path towards the European Union.
The outcome of the election could unblock, or further slow down, the adoption of key laws needed for the country’s progress towards EU membership.
The EU granted Bosnia and Herzegovina candidate status in December 2022 and opened accession negotiations in 2024.
However, the country’s progress has since been assessed as very limited and slowed by political blockades.
These elections will also be a test for the ruling coalition, which promised to focus on social and economic issues amid the rising cost of living.
When are the results?
The first preliminary results are traditionally published by CIK late on election night, on October 4, and are updated every few hours.
In the days after the elections, CIK gradually enters votes from the remaining polling stations, mobile voting teams, as well as ballots received by mail and from diplomatic and consular missions.
The official results will be known no later than November 20.

China Focus: Int'l expeditions in China unlock secrets of Asia's longest cave
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:57:28 CST
13:57:28 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- For French caver Jean Bottazzi, caves never disappoint. In the vast underground maze of Shuanghe Cave in southwest China's Guizhou Province, even an unfinished mission can lead to an unexpected discovery, opening up whole new horizons.
Bottazzi has spent more than two decades exploring Shuanghe, witnessing its 25-year journey of international exploration. Situated in Suiyang County, it is the world's third-longest cave system and Asia's longest.
Since the first China-France joint exploration in 2001, the mapped cave system has expanded from several dozen kilometers of known passages to more than 480 kilometers.
The latest findings from the 25th international cave scientific expedition were announced last month in Suiyang. Another 41.8 kilometers were added to the mapped passages.
With the newly added length, the cave system now stretches 481.5 kilometers and reaches a vertical depth of 912 meters. It has 124 interconnected entrances.
For Bottazzi, as well as the scientists and explorers who have worked alongside him, the significance of Shuanghe Cave cannot be measured by its length alone.
It is also a vast natural archive that preserves clues to the evolution of species, the changing climate and the geological history of southwest China.
Researchers found nine additional individual giant panda fossils, mostly in newly explored passages, during the 25th international expedition this year, bringing the total number of individual giant panda fossils discovered in Shuanghe Cave to 61.
They also found two sites bearing clear giant panda claw marks. Wang Deyuan, an associate research fellow at the Guizhou Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Resources, said the marks and the structure of the cave passages offer clues to how some of the animals may have died.
The pandas apparently entered the cave and moved more than 10 meters inward before falling into a vertical shaft. They survived the initial fall and left claw marks as they tried to move on, but eventually fell into a deeper shaft and became trapped, Wang said.
The latest expedition also uncovered fossils of ancient animals. Among them, fossils of a giant tapir and a clouded leopard were found in Shuanghe Cave for the first time.
For Bottazzi, however, the fascination of cave exploration lies not only in what researchers find, but also in what they do not expect to find.
A recent expedition experience reminded Bottazzi once again why he fell in love with caves in the first place. The team had set out to connect several caves at the northern end of the Shuanghe Cave system, but the goal remained elusive.
However, the story didn't end there. As they groped their way forward, something entirely unexpected appeared before them -- an entire magnificent wall of gypsum crystals.
"Curiosity instantly rekindled a new thrill of exploration and unexpectedly opened up a new direction," Bottazzi recalled. "If we had focused only on our planned goal, we would never have met this surprise. Half disappointment, half satisfaction -- that is the true charm of cave exploration," he said.
The Shuanghe Cave also serves as an archive with hidden clues to ancient climate. Researchers have been conducting uranium-series dating of calcite deposits inside the cave, according to Bottazzi.
"As long as we can find calcite samples of different ages and combine them with isotope analysis, we can obtain a record of climate evolution from the present day all the way back a million years," Bottazzi said. "It is an extremely precious archive of paleoclimate."
The line of research made a breakthrough this year. Using the new uranium-lead isotope dating technique, the research team determined that some secondary carbonate deposits inside the cave are more than five million years old.
The finding significantly extends the chronological framework for the development of Shuanghe Cave and other large caves in the karst regions of southwest China.
The vast underground maze of Shuanghe Cave has not only yielded a string of discoveries that have captivated the scientific world, but also become a vivid example of international cooperation in cave research.
Asked how Chinese and foreign researchers share exploration data and cave maps, Bottazzi was unequivocal: "We work for science. All the data and cave maps are shared."
For Bottazzi, the cave has continued to captivate him so deeply that in recent years he settled in Shuanghe Village in Wenquan Township, Suiyang. Over the years, he has become such a familiar face in the village that locals affectionately call him "Lao Rang," or "Old Jean."
To Bottazzi, there are few better places than Shuanghe to explore the Earth's hidden treasures. The cave is a world of diverse landscapes, from underground rivers and vast chambers draped with waterfalls to completely dry fossil galleries.
"We are exploring as if inside a maze; you can never guess where the passage leads, and you have to keep thinking. For cave exploration, this is a wonderfully fascinating place," Bottazzi said. ■

A heated exchange over allegations of racist abuse involving Irish players brought the Republic of Ireland's soccer team's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's Nations League game against Israel to an abrupt end on Saturday, after Irish head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson clashed with Israeli journalists.
One journalist asked, “What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder... Just this week, one of them tried to kill 170 Israeli passengers, including 27 innocent children and thousands of others,” to which an Irish press officer said, “We are not doing any questions like this today. We are doing football questions.”
The coach refused to respond when a second journalist asked why Irish players "call our players monkeys during the [previous] match."
The microphone was then taken from the journalist immediately after the question, and Hallgrimsson left the room.
The upcoming match, scheduled to take place in Serbia after Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their first match in Hungary, is part of a series of controversial incidents between the two countries.
Boycotts and unsportsmanlike conduct
During the match in Hungary, the Irish team, which wore black armbands in protest of Israel, bowed their heads while the national anthem played and refused to shake hands with the opposing team's captain after the match.
According to UEFA rules, black armbands are reserved for universally recognized tragedies, periods of national mourning, or the passing of prominent football figures, and require prior approval from the soccer association.
The two teams are playing despite calls in Ireland to boycott the match. Despite the a vote confirming the team's decision to play and the Football Association of Ireland announcing that the match would indeed take place, backup goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu boycotted the match and did not participate.
"The player expressed his discomfort with participating in the match, after which there were another four hours of talks between the players, the coaching staff, and association leaders, and we heard a great many viewpoints," the FAI CEO David Courell said at a press conference.
Multiple protest marches, public meetings, demands from opposition politicians that the Irish government intervene to stop the games, and incessant social media pressure on Irish players had clearly contributed to internal divisions within the team.
The controversy and concurrent cancellation attempts are symbolic of the rift in relations between the two countries and are the result of tension stemming from public opinion in Ireland toward Israel and its policies during the war in Gaza.

Russia has reduced use of ballistic missiles ahead of winter – Dutch analyst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

Russia has reduced use of ballistic missiles ahead of winter – Dutch analyst
He expressed this opinion in an exclusive comment to Ukrinform. Bolder is a strategic analyst and defense expert at the Hague Center for Strategic Studies (HCSS) and a former lieutenant colonel in the Royal Netherlands Air Force.
Bolder said that Russia was currently escalating its attacks on Ukrainian territory and that these attacks were having a severe impact on the lives of ordinary Ukrainian civilians. He said this was horrific. According to the analyst, the main weapons Russia was currently using were the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones. Ukraine did not yet have a complete response to these drones, although it was making very active efforts to destroy them as well. The effectiveness of intercepting them was gradually increasing and had already exceeded 50%.
At the same time, Bolder noted that the number of ballistic missiles Russia was using was currently lower than before. In his view, this suggested that, as Ukraine did not yet have a real response to the jet-powered drones, Russia was refraining from using ballistic missiles and was likely saving them for further use during the winter.
He also drew attention to the development of Ukrainian ballistic missile capabilities. In his view, the creation of such systems could have a dual significance: in addition to providing Ukraine with the ability to strike Russian launchers, it would give the country a technological foundation for developing its own interceptor missiles.
At the same time, he identified the need to scale up production of such systems to sufficient volumes as the key challenge.
The analyst also warned of possible problems for Ukraine in winter. He said these could affect not only electricity supplies, as the country had a significant number of generators, but also the operation of water treatment and sewage systems, as well as electricity supplies to defense industry enterprises.
In his assessment, the intensification of strikes on civilian infrastructure could be linked to the situation on the battlefield, where Russian forces, he said, were suffering significant losses and had recently lost some territory.
Bolder said that a serious problem was that businesses were being left without electricity. He said that, in effect, Russia wanted to suffocate Ukraine and make the Ukrainian economic model unviable for a very long time so that Ukraine would eventually become exhausted. At the same time, he said, efforts were also being made to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine, leaving it with no choice but to accept Putin's demands. However, he noted that history showed this never worked that way: the more strongly one state attacked a people or another country, the more people rallied around their flag.

Tarek Chouiref
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
The Serbian Orthodox Church said on Saturday that Christians in Palestine face persecution and discrimination, warning against attempts to marginalize their historical presence.
In a letter to Palestinian official Ramzi Khouri, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije expressed solidarity with the Palestinian people, as well as concern on worsening conditions facing Christians and other residents in the region.
The church said the community was facing “suffering, persecution and discrimination,” stressing that the suffering of civilians regardless of their faith or background was incompatible with human dignity.
It urged the protection of Christian communities, noting that Christians have maintained a continuous presence in the region for more than 2,000 years and remain an integral part of its history and heritage.
The church also warned that excluding or marginalizing any religious or ethnic community risked damaging the region’s social and religious fabric, and urged respect for international law and religious rights.
Porfirije said the church would continue raising the protection of Christian communities and efforts for peace in the Middle East in meetings with political leaders and international institutions.
Khouri is a member of the Palestine Liberation Organization’s Executive Committee, and heads the Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine.
The Palestinian committee has repeatedly raised concerns about attacks on Christian communities and institutions in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, as well as restrictions affecting worship, education and access to religious sites.
The effect has also extended to the Gaza Strip, where five Palestinians were killed early Saturday, including four women, two of whom were Christians.

Russia’s top-grossing movie in September was ‘Twilight.’ Yes, the one from 2008.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
04:43:31 UTC
13:43:31 KST

The 2008 film “Twilight” was Russia’s highest-grossing movie in September, RBC reported. The first installment in the vampire saga stars Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart.
The film returned to Russian theaters on September 17 and has already grossed 340 million rubles. It outperformed new releases “Kak Ivan v skazku popal” (“How Ivan Ended Up in a Fairy Tale”), which earned 296 million rubles, and “Devyataya planeta” (“The Ninth Planet”), which took in 183 million.
This is the first time an older film has topped the monthly box office, according to data from the Russian Cinema Fund’s Unified Automated Information System (EAIS) cited by RBC. The system has tracked all Russian theatrical box office data since 2015.
Nearly half of those who saw “Twilight” during its rerelease in Russian theaters were 18 to 24 years old, Maria Shcherbal, director of the research firm Wanta Group, told RBC. “Word of mouth played a very big role here: in the second week, 36% of viewers heard about the film on social media, another 29% heard about it from friends and acquaintances, and one in five cited recommendations as one of their reasons for going to the movies,” she said.
All the remaining films in the “Twilight” saga will also return to Russian theaters from October to February.

Three years since Oct. 7: Israel reports 1,318 military and security deaths, 1,029 civilian deaths and over 87,000 civilian victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
04:38:16 UTC
13:38:16 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- Survivor Testimonies
- Three years later: More than 87,000 civilians recognized as victims since October 7th
Three years later: More than 87,000 civilians recognized as victims since October 7th
Figures released by Israel’s Defense Ministry and National Insurance ahead of October 7’s third anniversary show 1,318 military personnel and 1,029 civilians have died since the Hamas attack
Israel’s Defense Ministry and National Insurance Institute released figures Sunday detailing the deaths, injuries and bereavement recorded since October 7, 2023, ahead of the third anniversary of the Hamas massacre and the outbreak of war.
The Defense Ministry said 1,318 people had been added to Israel’s official count of fallen military and security personnel since the attack. Separately, the National Insurance Institute reported that 1,029 civilians had been killed in terrorist attacks during the same period, including 63 children and teenagers and 88 foreign nationals.
The Defense Ministry’s total includes 1,153 IDF fallen, among them 43 members of local emergency response teams, alongside 116 police officers, nine Shin Bet personnel, five Fire and Rescue Service personnel and 11 Israel Prison Service personnel.
It also includes 24 people who died from war-related disabilities.
More than 7,150 relatives joined the Defense Ministry’s circle of bereaved families: 2,143 parents, 355 widows, 880 orphans and 3,772 siblings. The ministry said the figures cover those who fell in Gaza, southern and northern Israel, Lebanon and the West Bank.
Civilian losses and lasting trauma
Of the 1,029 civilian victims reported by the National Insurance Institute, 668 were men and 361 were women. The 63 victims aged 18 and under included six children aged three or younger.
The institute said 87,286 civilians had been recognized as victims of hostilities since the start of the war.
Its figures included 34,878 people recognized on the basis of psychological harm, 3,171 for physical injuries and 2,355 for both physical and psychological injuries. Twenty-four victims were amputees.
The civilian deaths also left 1,216 people without a parent, including 345 children under 18. Another 300 people lost a spouse, 231 women and 69 men.
The institute recorded 1,204 bereaved parents, including 156 left with no surviving children, and 2,281 bereaved siblings.
Billions in assistance
The National Insurance Institute said it had paid approximately NIS 662 million (approximately $216 million) in assistance grants to 83,563 civilians affected by the October 7 attack.
It also reported paying more than NIS 5 billion ($1.63 billion) in housing grants to over 110,000 residents of northern and southern Israel who evacuated independently, and more than NIS 1.4 billion ($458 million) in return grants to approximately 110,000 people.
The Defense Ministry said it had expanded emotional support, financial assistance and memorial services for bereaved families over the past three years, recruiting additional social workers and hundreds of therapists.
Its services include hundreds of support groups, a network of approximately 500 volunteers and more than 1,000 individual support plans for orphans aged four to 21. A dedicated program also supports women who were pregnant when they lost their husbands.
The ministry said military funerals had been held at 282 cemeteries and military burial sections across Israel. More than 30 military cemeteries and burial sections have been expanded, with work underway to expand another 20. Three new cemeteries serving the Druze community were built in Yarka, Sajur and Jatt.
Aryeh Moalem, head of the ministry’s Families, Commemoration and Heritage Department, said Israel’s obligation to those who died extended to sustained care for their relatives.
Three years after the war began, he said, the department remained committed to preserving the memory of the fallen and ensuring their families would never have to face their loss alone.

NEW DELHI: Strain deepened within the Samajwadi Party-Congress alliance ahead of Uttar Pradesh polls, with SP MP Shiv Pal Singh Patel in an off-the-cuff remark claimed that Rahul Gandhi was "reluctant to contest the 2024 Lok Sabha election" from Amethi and chose Raebareli because he was "so scared".Patel, who represents Pratapgarh, also credited the SP-Congress alliance for the Congress's six Lok Sabha wins in Uttar Pradesh, arguing that the party would have drawn a blank in the state without SP's support.Speaking to news agency PTI, Patel said the SP leadership had to persuade Gandhi to contest from Raebareli after he appeared unwilling to fight from Amethi, the traditional Gandhi family constituency.
"Had there been no alliance (with the Samajwadi Party), they (Congress) wouldn't have won a single seat. It even reached a point where their top leader Rahul Gandhi was ready to give up his seat. He contested from elsewhere (Raebareli) instead of Amethi. He was so scared," he said.The leader futher added: "It was our national president who reassured and persuaded him, asking him to contest and warning that if he didn't, he (Akhilesh) would field his own candidate. Only then did Gandhi agree to contest. Otherwise, he was extremely reluctant to run for that traditional seat, the one said to belong to the Nehru family.
Gandhi only managed to win it because of that persuasion," he said.
Patel credits SP for Congress wins
Patel said SP voters backed Congress candidates in constituencies allotted to the Congress under the alliance arrangement."Every single vote from the Samajwadi Party went to the Congress wherever they were allotted seats. That is precisely how they managed to win those six seats," he said.The SP won 37 of Uttar Pradesh's 80 Lok Sabha seats in the 2024 elections, while Congress won six. The BJP won 33 seats, while the NDA's tally in the state stood at 36.Patel said the difference in the two parties' performances should be reflected in any future seat-sharing discussions."We secured 37 seats. We are far ahead of the Congress in every respect. They shouldn't ask for more than 50, and should feel happy. The Congress should cooperate, rather than making all sorts of absurd or negative remarks," Patel said.
SP MP dismisses Congress's caste strategy
Patel also criticised the Congress's reported caste strategy in Uttar Pradesh, including its appointment of a Brahmin as state Congress president and a Muslim as working president."This will not yield any benefit. Look, Dalits were with Mayawati, but they have now shifted to our side. They realised that there was no significant upliftment of Dalits during the Congress regime, and certainly none is happening under the BJP. Whereas, during the Samajwadi Party's tenure, everyone gets equal opportunities. Everyone gets an equal chance to progress; their children get a chance to receive an education."He added, "That is precisely why the party was named 'Samajwadi'. Our party operates based on the ideals of (Ram Manohar) Lohia-ji. Our party's objective is the welfare of all sections of society."The SP currently has 101 MLAs in the 403-member Uttar Pradesh Assembly, while Congress has two.Patel said the SP could benefit from continuing its alliance with Congress, but argued that the Congress would suffer more if it contested elections without its regional ally."If we proceed with an alliance, we will certainly benefit. Even if it doesn't happen, we won't have any significant loss. But for them, the tally will drop to zero. I can say this with confidence: if they don't contest as part of an alliance, they will end up with zero seats.
The public will realise they are fielding candidates solely to split votes. If they act as vote-spoilers, they will be reduced to zero," Patel said.
Congress hits back
Uttar Pradesh Congress spokesperson Anshu Awasthi pushed back against Patel's remarks and said the SP should rein in leaders making such statements."The Samajwadi Party must work to rein in leaders who make such statements. It is because of the INDIA bloc that he (Patel) has become an MP. He should know his limits and avoid making statements like these," Awasthi told PTI.

Police fire tear gas as housing protests sweep Spain (VIDEOS)
Tens of thousands of people have demonstrated across Spain to demand affordable rent and stronger protections for tenants amid a deepening housing crisis.
Average rent has almost doubled over the past decade, according to property website Idealista. On Friday, parliament narrowly rejected two emergency housing decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government.
Around 70,000 people marched through the streets of Madrid on Saturday to denounce the decision, according to the authorities, while organizers put the figure at half a million. Similar demonstrations took place across around 50 Spanish cities.
In the eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police, who fired rubber bullets and tear gas to disperse the crowds. Around 30 protesters breached the security perimeter around the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural complex, before officers removed them.
Protesters are demanding a 50% reduction in rent, open-ended rental contracts, and the expropriation of homes from investment firms they describe as “vulture funds.” Tenants’ Union spokesperson Valeria Racu said a general strike would be called following talks with labor unions.

Dutch writer: I was trying to show Netherlands what Ukraine is like just as war began
She said this in an exclusive interview with Ukrinform.
"It is an absolutely crazy situation – trying to introduce people to one of the largest countries in Europe precisely at the moment when it is at war," she said.
According to Weeda, people's understanding of Ukraine was very superficial, and their perceptions were often biased. And suddenly, they had to get to know Ukraine, but through the lens of war.
Weeda also noted that very strange stories or narratives can sometimes be heard in the Netherlands.
"For example, if we start with Crimea, there were Dutch RTL journalists there. Then there was a book that literally described how a Russian tank drove up to the gates of a Ukrainian military base. It showed everything that happened, but people simply did not read it. There have been many books and videos about Ukrainian history. But the Russian narrative is still there. It feels as though they really know how to 'flood the information space with shit' — with such a huge amount of propaganda, narratives about 'brotherly nations' and all kinds of other information that getting rid of this influence seems almost impossible," she added.
The writer says that people in the Netherlands still do not understand enough about how Russian propaganda works and too often see Russia as an "incomprehensible" country with a unique "Russian soul."
She stressed that there is still a need to explain what Ukraine is fighting for, that Ukraine is defending itself, and that Russia is the aggressor.
Dutch writer Lisa Weeda has Ukrainian roots. Her novel Aleksandra tells the story of her grandmother, who was deported by the Nazis from the Luhansk region to Germany for forced labor and whose love story later brought her to the Netherlands.
Weeda is involved in more than writing. In the Netherlands, she works to counter Russian propaganda, curates literary and artistic programs, and draws on her own experience to help European audiences better understand Ukraine.
