Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
Trump tells a rally in Ohio that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections.
US President Donald Trump has continued rallying for Republican candidates while visiting Ohio, proposing a defiant outlook on his party’s chances in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump told a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, claiming his Democratic opponents do not know what is happening.
Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, but the US president said Republicans would do better than critics expect.
“Just get out and vote,” Trump said as he rallied for US Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and other Republicans.
“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” he said.
Ohio’s Senate race
Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds, with Trump’s popularity falling in recent months as higher petrol prices and those for other staples persist amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Husted, a Republican in a competitive Ohio race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, hopes the president can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip midterm elections.
Trump garnered more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.
Ohio petrol prices increased 35 percent over the past year to $4.16 per gallon (3.8 litres) on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which compiles data on automobile travel. Trump’s trade policy with Canada has also led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3bn worth of Ohio exports, based on 2025 figures, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported.
Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday’s rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war “on our terms” and, in the interim, he is “showing people that I’m fighting for lower prices”.
Hot political issue
Trump extensively promoted his administration’s action on data centres, mainly those built for AI, during the rally, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Husted for an unsuccessful attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.
“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said, repeating his defence of data centres.
Data centres have become a hot political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.
The issue became especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centres to the Midwestern state as lieutenant governor.
The Republican-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats.
“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centres in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

Reports said the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and the Central Public Works Department were still looking for suitable space for the library.The proposed relocation has also raised concerns about ensuring proper facilities for the preservation of its extensive collection.
The Union ministry of housing and urban affairs, however, has rejected reports that the library has been left without space under the redevelopment plans.
"Contrary to a few reports, it is clarified that space for the Central Secretariat Library has been provided for in the Kartavya Path redevelopment plan. The necessary process for construction of the library is underway," the ministry wrote in a post on X.The ministry's statement indicates that a new location for the library has been included in the Kartavya Path redevelopment plan, although the Supreme Court is now set to examine the issue.

Interview: China partnership constructive in strengthening Africa's community resilience, development, says IFRC official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:06:29 CST
13:06:29 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Partnerships between China and African countries strengthen community resilience and build capacity for sustainable development over the long term, a humanitarian official has said.
"We see this engagement as constructive and look forward to further strengthening and expanding this cooperation into more areas," said Asha Mohammed, permanent representative of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) to the African Union and International Organizations.
Mohammed, who also heads the IFRC Delegation for Ethiopia and Djibouti, made the remarks in a recent interview with Xinhua on the sidelines of a seminar on resilient community building for Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies under the China-Africa Cooperation Framework in Beijing.
The two-week seminar in September, supported by the IFRC, was hosted by the Training Center of the Red Cross Society of China.
Twenty-six representatives from national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies from 19 African countries, along with representatives of the IFRC, attended lectures, field visits and interactive discussions during the seminar, exchanging experience and learning about China's practices in disaster risk reduction, community resilience and sustainable development.
"This training will allow participants to learn from China's experience as well as from one another," Mohammed said. "Participants will be able to use what they learn to develop solutions that respond to the needs of communities in their own countries."
In African countries, natural disasters are becoming more frequent and severe as a result of climate change. Crises are also becoming increasingly protracted, leaving communities with less time and fewer resources to recover between shocks. At the same time, people still need access to quality health care, education and livelihoods.
Therefore, Mohammed said, humanitarian response cannot be separated from longer-term development. "We need approaches that address the two together."
"Against this backdrop, training on community resilience is both timely and practical, helping participants explore how humanitarian response and development can be brought together to address Africa's challenges in a more sustainable way," she said.
Achieving durable development results is another key challenge. Communities may make significant progress, but a new disaster can quickly undermine those gains.
Early warning systems are an important part of preparedness, but warnings alone are not enough, Mohammed said, adding that the critical question is whether communities have the resources, capacity and leadership to turn early warnings into early action and reduce the impact of disasters.
"It means enabling communities not only to anticipate and prepare for shocks, but also to act on warnings, sustain development gains and recover more quickly when disasters occur," she said. "In that sense, the focus of the training on resilient communities is particularly timely and practical."
China has been actively engaged in capacity-building activities at the African Union level, including those focused on food security and community health systems, and has shared its valuable experiences, Mohammed said.
The cooperation goes beyond addressing immediate humanitarian needs to strengthening the capacity of African institutions and communities to sustain these efforts over the long term, she said.
"The training is a good example of that approach. By sharing knowledge and building local capacity, China's partnership can help strengthen Africa's own capacity for independent and sustainable development, which is aligned with the durable solution approach of the IFRC," Mohammed said. ■

Tennessee prisons chief steps down after botched execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
04:02:46 UTC
13:02:46 KST

Tennessee prisons chief steps down after botched execution
Tennessee’s prisons chief will step down following a failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike, Governor Bill Lee said on Saturday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, remains unconscious and on a ventilator after surviving a failed lethal injection with two doses of pentobarbital on September 30, according to her lawyers.
Lee announced the resignation of Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada after ordering an independent review of the botched execution.
“Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” Lee said in a statement.
“I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred,” Strada added.
The New York Times, citing outside medical experts, said Pike probably survived the procedure because the lethal drug leaked into tissue around the insertion sites instead of entering her bloodstream.
Her lawyers said Pike suffered chemical burns and blisters as the execution team made at least seven attempts to insert needles while trying to find a vein suitable for administering the drug. They previously warned that her medical history, including a blood-clotting condition, and small veins increased the risk that she would experience unnecessary pain.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder after she, her boyfriend, and another accomplice lured Slemmer, a fellow student, to an isolated area near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus, where Pike brutally beat her and cut her throat. Pike was 18 when she committed the crime.
The case was Tennessee’s second botched execution this year. In May, officials halted the execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers after repeatedly failing to establish intravenous access to administer pentobarbital.
Carruthers was returned to death row, and Lee subsequently granted him a one-year reprieve. The incident raised questions about Tennessee’s lethal-injection procedures months before Pike’s execution.

‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
04:00:17 UTC
13:00:17 KST

People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok.
On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop.
“We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.”
Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size.
“What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.”
In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business.
While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling.
The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations. “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.”
Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.”
The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.”
Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said.
Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.”
Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.”
Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.”

In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:48:00 UTC

Ethiopia government forces reclaim Tigray capital airport
October 4, 2026
Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.
Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.
"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.
The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.
Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.
Return to civil war?
Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.
The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.
The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.
The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.
Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.
The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.
Fears of wider regional unrest
The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region, with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.
For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.
Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.
The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.
Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea
The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."

Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Taiwan Army plans Land Sword II testing facilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
03:38:18 UTC
12:38:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army plans to commission the National Chung Shan Institute of Science and Technology to renovate aging munitions facilities and build facilities to test its inventory of Land Sword II missiles.
The Navy previously conducted the testing on the Army’s behalf but will be unable to continue doing so from 2028, according to Liberty Times.
The Army has allotted more than NT$259 million (US$8.14 million) for the project to avoid a gap in field air defense readiness. A military official said the project does not include the purchase of new missiles.
The funding will go toward installing precision temperature- and humidity-control systems, building facilities that meet ammunition safety standards, and procuring dedicated testing equipment, the official said, per Liberty Times.
The equipment will simulate radar signals and midcourse guidance commands and conduct full missile circuit tests, the official said. The Army will eventually be able to conduct routine missile inspections, functional tests, and service-life extension work independently at its own bases, Liberty Times reported.
The project marks a shift toward self-sufficiency in air defense logistics and maintenance, the official said.
The Land Sword II uses active radar guidance, and each launcher vehicle can carry four missiles. It can engage multiple targets in all directions and weather conditions and is highly mobile.

Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
Spokesman for Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government says the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh are ‘misleading’.
Yemen’s Houthis have said they attacked an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government intensifies.
In a statement posted on X on Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a “military operation with ballistic missiles and drones” that targeted Aramco in Riyadh.
He claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and “led to fires breaking out” at the site. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising near an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday.
Later on Saturday, Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media that the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh were “misleading”.
Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, said the attacks targeted “at least 260 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled 44 military vehicles”.
Late last month, the Houthis said they had attacked Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Red Sea port on Saudi Arabia’s west coast.
Saudi Arabia said at the time it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired towards Taif and Yanbu and reported no damage to Aramco sites.
Earlier this week, the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis attacked a power station in the Muslim holy city of Medina on Tuesday.
The fighting has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July.
In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since fighting restarted.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

Iran is delaying Hamas's request to renew financial support for the organization due to its disappointment with Hamas's inability to undermine overall security stability in the West Bank, KAN News reported on Tuesday evening.
A senior Hamas delegation visited Tehran in early September, according to the KAN report, which noted that the delegates met with senior Iranian officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf.
A Palestinian source told KAN that the Hamas delegation asked the Iranian regime representatives to renew its financial support, which had been frozen due to recent alleged "stress" on the budget.
Due to their "dissatisfaction" over Hamas's failure to influence the situation in the West Bank, Iran made no commitment to renew Hamas funding, the source told KAN.
IDF warns of rising West Bank tensions despite low terror levels, pushes for preventive operations
In mid-September, Israeli officials noted that despite the fact that West Bank terror levels were at the lowest point since 2011, Hamas headquarters in other locations (Turkey, Gaza, Iran, Qatar, Lebanon, and others) were likely to attempt to advance terror plots targeting Israelis and IDF soldiers.
The low level of terror activity is attributed to combined operations by the Judea and Samaria Division, commanded by Brig.-Gen. Kobi Heller, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police and Border Police.
Ahead of the recent Jewish holidays, the Judea and Samaria Division carried out extensive preventive operations, targeting not only suspects involved in terror activity but also incitement hubs, in an effort to minimize the potential for attacks in the area.
IDF reinforces West Bank amid growing tensions as settlers, Palestinians clash in villages
More recently, the IDF reinforced its West Bank division to a total of approximately 25 battalions amid growing tensions, violent confrontations between Israelis and Palestinians, and security establishment concerns over a wave of lone-wolf terrorism and organized terrorist infrastructure, as tens of thousands of Israeli hikers arrived in the area on September 27.
In addition, a divisional headquarters responsible for the Judea and Etzion regional brigades was deployed to the area.
Despite the reinforcements, military officials warned that the situation on the ground remained highly volatile. One of them told Walla that "all it would take is a friction incident between Palestinians and Israelis that spirals out of control, is caught on video, and ignites the area."
This comes amid several recent instances of settler violence in the West Bank.
Amit Bohbot contributed to this report.

What is fuelling French school protests?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
03:25:00 UTC
12:25:00 KST

What is fuelling French school protests?
- French high school students are protesting against teacher shortages, poor classroom conditions, and long school days, feeling they receive an inferior education.
- The movement started at a Paris suburb school and spread nationwide, amplified by social media sharing dramatic protest footage.
- The protests involve clashes with police, accusations of heavy-handed force, political tensions ahead of elections, and concerns over social inequality in education.
AI generated
PARIS – Protests by teenagers outside their schools have shaken France in recent days, with students blockading entrances to their institutions and security forces on occasion responding with tear gas.
The government has said that while the grievances may be legitimate, violence is not and has accused the hard-left of whipping up the movement.
Critics have meanwhile accused some police of heavy-handed force against protesters, who are legally still children.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested since Sept 28, according to the Interior Ministry, while about 735 educational establishments were affected on Oct 2, the education minister said.
While the weekend may see a lull, a major new day of protest is planned for Oct 6.
AFP looks at the origins of the movement.
Multiple grievances
The protests affect lycees, the schools where French teens have their last years of school aged from 15 to 18, the equivalent of high school in the United States and sixth form in Britain.
The students’ grievances are numerous, but chief among them are teacher absences, conditions in classrooms, overloaded school timetables and a school day that can be as long as 8am to 6pm, which some say is excessive.
“High-school students – particularly those from low-income neighbourhoods – feel they are receiving an inferior education,” said French sociologist Valerie Becquet.
Origin of the movement
The movement began two weeks ago on Sept 17 at the Saint-Exupery high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, in support of teachers striking over a lack of staff and resources.
It gained momentum, gradually spreading across the country over the last week.
Ironically, as tensions raged elsewhere in France, the situation at the Saint-Exupery high school returned to normal after educational authorities agreed to send additional staff, including a deputy principal and a nurse.
“Our grades were slipping. If we had not rallied now, it would have augured very badly for the future,” said student Abderrahmane, who expressed “enormous” pride at taking part in the inception of the movement.
Role of social media
The protests are being further fuelled by the spread of dramatic images and videos on online platforms, notably TikTok.
Students themselves hold up their phones to record scenes such as burning rubbish bins or police deploying tear gas. Numerous channels, seeking to boost their reach, spread this footage and edit together the most dramatic moments.
“With social media, they can offer a narrative different from the one presented in traditional media – a narrative that is not manufactured,” said sociologist Becquet.
Social inequality
France offers all students access to the lycee, but in reality there is a vast spectrum, ranging from vocational schools to elite institutions.
Despite numerous diversity initiatives, the latter remain dominated by students from white, affluent families with university-educated parents.
“There are glaring inequalities among different students and schools, and this is a real problem,” said Becquet.
Political exploitation
The protests have become a major issue of political tension just over half a year ahead of presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) of being behind the movement.
Senior LFI official Manuel Bompard has rejected the government’s accusations, saying it was “descending into conspiracy theories”.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon – who is currently polling at over 40% among 18- to 25-year-old voters – has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
Police response
Protesters have blockaded schools, set fire to bins and other objects and hurled projectiles at police.
But police have also moved to disperse some of the protesters, notably firing tear gas canisters, using rubber bullets and sometimes beating them with batons.
After students clashed with police on Sept 30 in Tours in central France, one wounded young man lost the use of his right eye, the city’s prosecutor said.
Numerous videos have gone viral showing alleged brutal conduct by security forces – such as a police officer placing his arm around the neck of a girl during her arrest.
But police have also been targets, notably an officer who was chased and beaten and kicked by a group of youths from a school in the eastern city of Belfort. AFP

More than 87,000 victims of hostile acts have been recognized since October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
03:21:38 UTC
12:21:38 KST

Civilians, soldiers, police officers, firefighters, parents, brothers, sisters and children: On the eve of the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, the Defense Ministry and the National Insurance Institute on Sunday published updated figures on those killed, including victims of hostilities and the wounded on the day of the attack and throughout the months of war.
The National Insurance Institute’s count refers only to civilians, including foreign nationals, and does not include members of the security forces or local civilian security squads. The Defense Ministry’s Department of Families, Commemoration and Heritage, meanwhile, publishes figures on those killed in Israel’s wars.
According to National Insurance Institute data, 778 civilians were murdered on the day of the massacre, and another 251 have been killed since then. In all, 1,029 people were murdered, not including members of the security forces and local security squads, who are recognized as fallen IDF personnel. Among those murdered were 63 children and teenagers under age 18.
The figures also have financial implications. Over the past three years, 87,286 victims of hostile acts have been added to the number of people handled by the National Insurance Institute, as distinct from members of the security forces, who are under the responsibility of the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department. Most were affected as a result of being present on October 7, while the rest were injured during the course of the war and in the operations Rising Lion and Roaring in Iran.
Of all those affected, about 43,000 applied to the National Insurance Institute to have disabilities recognized as resulting from hostile acts. The vast majority of applicants, about 40,000, had their disabilities recognized, while the remaining requests are currently being considered by medical committees.
Of those recognized, 34,878 were approved on psychological grounds, 3,171 for physical injuries and 2,355 for combined physical and psychological injuries.
In total, the National Insurance Institute has transferred more than 6 billion shekels to victims of October 7 and the war, including victims of hostile acts, bereaved families and families of hostages.
In addition to those payments, the institute issued various other grants, including reserve-duty compensation, grants for evacuees and payments to residents of northern and southern Israel who suffered financial harm because of the security situation.
Payments also were made to about 100,000 civilians placed on unpaid leave during Operation Rising Lion and nearly 200,000 civilians placed on unpaid leave during Operation Lion’s Roar. Unpaid-leave payments during the two operations totaled more than 2 billion shekels.
At the same time, the Defense Ministry’s Department of Families, Commemoration and Heritage expanded its operations, services and benefits for bereaved families during the war. Welfare workers, social workers, staff for the military commemoration unit and hundreds of emotional-support therapists were recruited to the department.
The military commemoration unit conducted funerals at 282 cemeteries and military burial sections across Israel and also arranged for the burial of fallen personnel abroad.

Live: Roosters and Broncos back at it in another NRLW grand final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
NRL grand final: Daly Cherry-Evans field goal wins Roosters premiership over Knights
The Sydney Roosters have held off a fast-finishing Newcastle to win 19-18 in a pulsating NRL grand final at Stadium Australia.
The Roosters seemed to have the premiership wrapped up late in the match, until Greg Marzhew scored a 76th-minute try down the Knights' left edge.
Sandon Smith converted from wide out, sending Knights' fans into a frenzy.
But the Roosters held on in the dying stages, with captain James Tedesco pulling off two kick receptions in a Clive Churchill Medal-winning performance to deny the Knights their first men's premiership in 25 years.
- Analysis: Newcastle's magic NRL premiership tilt ends in defeat, pride and honour
- Quick hits: Ponga lights up the grand final as DCE seals the premiership
- Clive Churchill Medal: Tedesco wins best on ground
- Jai Arrow Tribute: Amy Shark leads grand final tribute
The win completed a premiership double for the Roosters, with the club earlier winning their third NRLW title following a 30-6 thrashing of the Brisbane Broncos.
Daly Cherry-Evans was sent out a winner in his final NRL appearance, giving the 37-year-old a second premiership ring to go with the one he claimed with Manly in 2011.
Roosters coach Trent Robinson also added another premiership to his tally, the fourth of his decorated career at the Tricolours.
It was clear from the opening whistle Newcastle was going to enjoy the larger share of the crowd's support, with most neutral fans among the 80,814 spectators jumping on board the Knights' bandwagon.
They had reason to cheer when the Knights scored first in the 15th minute after Francis Manuleleua ran a brilliant angle off a Fletcher Sharpe short ball to cross for the opening try.
Smith landed the conversion to establish a 6-0 lead, before the Knights were given a life when the Roosters had a try disallowed 10 minutes later.
Mark Nawaqanitawase leapt high in the air to mark a Sam Walker kick in the right-hand corner, but the bunker ruled he knocked on as he attempted to ground the ball in the in-goal area.
The Knights built on their advantage in the 29th minute via the standout play of the first half, when captain Kalyn Ponga ran 95 metres to score his side's second converted try.
Nawaqanitawase had tapped back the ball in an aerial contest near the Knights' line, but it was pounced upon by Ponga, who proceeded to outsprint the Roosters' cover defence.
The Roosters showed no sign of panic, though, and Nawaqanitawase got them on the scoreboard with a trademark opportunist try five minutes shy of half-time.
Walker's conversion reduced the Knights' lead to 12-6, which they held through to the break.
The Knights' defence was under pressure early in the second half, as the Roosters launched a series of attacking raids.
The dam wall eventually burst in the 47th minute, with Billy Smith touching down despite the Knights' best efforts to hold the Roosters centre up over the goal line.
Walker added the extras to level scores, and he gave the Roosters the lead for the first time in the match following a 54th-minute penalty goal.
Nawaqanitawase's second try, scored midway through the second half, pushed the lead out to 18-12, before Cherry-Evans nailed a field goal with 11 minutes left in the contest.
It appeared the seven-point margin would see the Roosters through to full-time, prior to Marzhew's heroics setting up the grandstand finish.

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Rising prices, weak spending put Japan's policymakers in tight spot
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:16:58 CST
12:16:58 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- At a chain store in Tokyo, the Japanese capital, a notice announcing price adjustments on selected items is hard to miss.
These days, price hikes not only rank among the most talked-about topics in Japanese media but are also keenly felt in daily life, from household goods to food and from supermarkets to restaurants.
RISING PRICES, WEAK CONSUMPTION
According to a survey released by Japanese research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd., more than 3,000 food and beverage items in the country are set to go up in price in October, with the full-year tally for 2026 expected to top 20,000.
Data recently released by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) showed that the consumer price index excluding institutional factors rose 2.6 percent year on year in August, overshooting the central bank's 2 percent price stability target.
With prices climbing across the board, spending is showing signs of slowing.
Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's economy, was essentially flat in the second quarter.
As of July, inflation-adjusted household spending had declined year on year for eight consecutive months.
"Rising prices are eroding real purchasing power, and private consumption is likely to stagnate further going forward," said Taro Saito, an economist at NLI Research Institute.
Weak consumer demand is also weighing on corporate earnings. Shingo Ide, chief equity strategist at NLI Research Institute, noted that with costs broadly on the rise, companies that cannot pass them on to customers through higher prices will face sustained pressure on their profit margins, putting their businesses under considerable strain.
Large Japanese companies with strong pricing power still have some room to offset rising costs through price increases, but for the country's large number of small and medium-sized businesses, raising prices is far from easy.
Take ramen shops, a staple of Japan's dining scene. According to Tokyo Shoko Research, bankruptcies among ramen shops jumped 44.4 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, pushing the number of failures to a record high for the period.
Persistently rising costs for ingredients and utilities have forced many ramen shop owners to raise prices, yet with consumers growing more cautious about spending, higher prices risk driving customers away.
For many small restaurant operators in Japan, striking a balance between covering elevated costs and keeping customers coming through the door has become a headache.
LIMITED POLICY TOOLKIT
With rising prices eating into household purchasing power and business costs continuing to climb, Japan's economic policymakers face an increasingly stark dilemma.
On monetary policy, the BOJ finds itself in a bind. The risk that a weaker yen and inflated import costs will push prices up further has not gone away, giving the central bank reason to continue with its tightening cycle.
At the same time, with signs of softening consumption already emerging, raising interest rates too quickly could dampen economic activity.
Recent movements in the yen have added complexity to the BOJ's policy calculus. Even after joint intervention by Japan and the United States in the currency market, the yen has continued to face selling pressure.
A recent Reuters poll found that more than two-thirds of economists surveyed believe the joint intervention has had only a limited effect, merely postponing rather than resolving the deeper problems facing the yen. Against this backdrop, market expectations of a BOJ rate hike have gained noticeable momentum.
At its September policy meeting, the central bank raised its key interest rate to 1.25 percent. However, because the U.S. Federal Reserve also hiked its target federal funds rate, the interest rate gap between Japan and the United States narrowed only modestly, and the yen failed to sustain a meaningful rebound.
According to multiple Japanese media reports, U.S. President Donald Trump recently voiced concerns about the yen's weakness.
The BOJ, for its part, is keeping a close eye on the inflationary impact of a weaker currency.
"If the yen weakens further and economic indicators point to mounting price pressures, the likelihood of a BOJ rate hike in October will increase," said Eiji Maeda, president of Chibagin Research Institute and a former BOJ executive director.
Kyohei Morita, chief economist at Nomura Securities, said the fiscal policy of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government has pushed up inflation expectations, deepening market concerns that the BOJ is falling behind the curve.
On the fiscal side, the Takaichi government's strategy of "responsible and proactive" public finances is running up against the hard reality of limited fiscal space.
A Reuters poll found that 89 percent of economists surveyed expect the government's fiscal policy to drive the yen lower, with markets particularly focused on how measures such as a food tax cut and expanded investment will be funded.
Amid growing concerns over fiscal sustainability, the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond, a barometer of long-term interest rates, rose to as high as 3.115 percent at one stage on Sept. 25, its highest level since August 1996.
Japan's government debt has long been high relative to GDP, and as interest rates climb, that debt load is turning into a more immediate interest burden.
According to the Nikkei newspaper, the Ministry of Finance's budget request for fiscal 2027, which runs from April 2027 to March 2028, puts debt-servicing costs at 36.64 trillion yen (about 232 billion U.S. dollars), including 16.59 trillion yen in interest payments, both record highs.
Ultimately, Japan's current economic troubles go beyond a simple rise in prices. They stem from the interplay of shrinking household purchasing power, rising business costs and mounting fiscal pressure, each pulling against the others. When it comes to reconciling price stability, growth and debt control, Japan's policymakers have limited room to maneuver. ■

Police are seeking witnesses and dashcam footage from the area during the incidents and have urged anyone who saw suspicious people or vehicles to come forward.

Daylight saving time begins in parts of Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:16:43 CST
12:16:43 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Daylight saving time began in parts of Australia on Sunday, with clocks moving forward by one hour.
At 2:00 a.m. local standard time, clocks were advanced to 3:00 a.m. in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia.
The change means residents in those states and territories will have an extra hour of daylight in the evening during the warmer months.
Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory do not observe daylight saving time, leaving mainland Australia across five time zones.
Daylight saving in the participating states and territories runs from the first Sunday in October to the first Sunday in April. The current period will end on April 4, 2027, when clocks will be turned back by one hour.
Australia's different daylight saving arrangements mean the time difference between some states and territories changes during the summer months. ■

Defense Ministry: 1,318 Israeli security personnel killed across all fronts since October 7

Since the start of the Israel-Hamas War on October 7, 2023, 1,318 members of Israel's security forces have fallen in the conflict, according to data published by the Families, Commemoration, and Heritage Department of the Defense Ministry on Sunday.
The number includes fallen personnel from the IDF, Israel Police, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Fire and Rescue Services, security coordinators, and local response team members.
The numbers account for the fallen across all fronts, including the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and the West Bank.
Thousands have lost a family member to the war
More than 7,150 people have been officially recognized as relatives who lost someone in service since the start of the war, including 2,143 bereaved parents, 355 widows, and 880 orphans.
3,772 people lost a sibling in the war.
Despite the ceasefire that took effect in the Gaza Strip on October 10, 2025, a number of Israeli soldiers have been killed in incidents along the Yellow Line that delineates the buffer zone within the strip.
Two soldiers fell in a recent incident
Last week, two IDF soldiers were killed when a drone that they were operating landed and exploded within their military outpost in the northern Gaza Strip.
The soldiers, who were reservists serving as part of the 16th Brigade, were initially evacuated to Barzilai Medical Center in Ashkelon but were pronounced dead.
The two soldiers were Maj. (Res.) Nadav Kali, 24, from Har Halutz, and Maj. (Res.) Ofek Moalem, 23, from Jerusalem.

====================================================================================================

As elections loom, voters must choose the right pilot to navigate political turbulence - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
03:10:44 UTC
12:10:44 KST

When 166 Israeli passengers boarded a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, they did not imagine having to intervene to save their own lives from an attempted terrorist hijacker.
According to the ongoing investigation, the Omani co-pilot stabbed the captain and attempted to take control of the aircraft, sending the plane plunging thousands of feet before Israeli passengers – and the wounded captain – helped stop him.
The 174 passengers, including the 166 Israelis, had entrusted those in the cockpit to get them safely to their destination.
Instead, when the cockpit became the source of the danger, they had to take matters into their own hands – even shaking two pilots traveling among the passengers into action, as one passenger recounted in an interview with The Jerusalem Post’s editor-in-chief, Zvika Klein.
Israeli's political reality parallels flydubai incident
There is an uncomfortable parallel to Israel’s political reality as the country heads toward the October 27 election, as Israelis attempt to shake their leaders into action.
Israel’s political system has had its own trouble in the cockpit. For years, Israelis have watched their politics and security become consumed by foreign considerations, coalition survival, and internal squabbles.
Governments have been formed only to become trapped by the competing interests holding them together, while the state is left paralyzed and unable to deal with the challenges in front of it.
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israelis were sent to the polls five times in less than four years. Five elections were required before the political system finally produced a government that could command a stable enough parliamentary majority to govern.
The first election, in April 2019, ended without Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being able to form a coalition. The same happened after the September election.
In an attempt to break the deadlock, Benny Gantz then fractured his own Blue and White faction to enter a unity government with the prime minister. That government was supposed to end the political crisis.
Instead, it lasted only months before collapsing amid disputes over the state budget – and Israelis went back to the polls, forced to make the decisions their leaders could not.
The fourth election, in March 2021, did produce a government – but Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s diverse coalition lasted only a year before internal disagreements and defections brought it down.
Netanyahu returned to power at the end of 2022 with a government that appeared to have the parliamentary numbers to last.
October 7 exposed devastating failures in Israel's political, security establishments
Then October 7 happened.
The Hamas massacre exposed devastating failures across Israel’s political and security establishment. Despite an initial attempt at forging unity, the war that followed only deepened political divisions that had already been tearing at the country.
And nearly three years later, some of the most fundamental questions raised by October 7 remain unresolved.
There is still no state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed the massacre to happen. At the same time, the government has been repeatedly threatened by the issue of conscription of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men into the IDF – an issue that has taken on an entirely different weight since October 7 and the military’s manpower crisis.
The result has been another political crisis in which the survival of the coalition has become deeply intertwined with an issue that has divided Israeli society.
Israel’s political camps have increasingly pulled away from one another, with fewer areas of agreement and less willingness to compromise.
The result is a political system in which forming a government has become increasingly difficult, and keeping one together even harder.
Later this month, Israelis will again be asked to decide who they want leading the country.
And once again, politicians have left Israelis with a choice that is not simply about who gets the most seats, but whether the passengers can give the pilots a clear enough mandate to actually fly the plane.
This is the cycle Israel needs to break.
The passengers aboard the flydubai flight did not have the luxury of leaving the cockpit unresolved. They knew that if they did not take action to save their own lives, no one would.
Israeli voters will have their own chance to take control and choose who sits in the cockpit. After that, it will be up to the pilots to put their differences aside and form a coalition capable of keeping the plane on course.

====================================================================================================

Scientists uncover how the brain adds new information to an existing memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
03:00:51 UTC
12:00:51 KST

A joint study by three Spanish institutions shows how certain hippocampal neurons safeguard existing memories even as new information about events is stored.
Imagine, for example, a building site in your neighbourhood. The human brain can remember three key stages of it: the original state before the renovation, the construction work itself, and the final outcome once the project is completed. But how does it manage not to muddle those three memories?
The Institute of Neurosciences, a public research centre made up of CSIC and Miguel Hernández University, believes it has found this neurological mechanism in its new study published in the journal 'PLOS Biology' (source in Spanish).
The team at its Neuronal Network Plasticity laboratory thinks the brain uses a region of the hippocampus known as the dentate gyrus, which is dedicated to forming new memories. There, a specific type of neuron inhibits the activity of other cells to help integrate new experiences.
To test this idea, the researchers studied this inhibition process in mice, increasing or reducing it. "With lower-than-usual levels, their behaviour was more consistent with better memory retrieval and a more detailed recollection," explains Encarni Marcos, co-lead author of the study and head of this line of research at IN CSIC-UMH.
However, there are no fixed levels of inhibition that are always better or worse for preserving as much information as possible. The computational model the team used for the experiment showed that, with a lighter memory load, reduced inhibitory activity is beneficial, but that this is no longer the case once the amount of information rises sharply.
The study suggests that, depending on the type of memory, the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus may either favour the incorporation of new inputs or, conversely, hold an existing memory more firmly against new stimuli. It depends on the contextual importance, or what the team describes as task demands. "What we take from these results is that there is a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the mode of operation by using inhibition," Marcos concludes.

Unprecedented bluetongue outbreak hits British livestock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:49:51 UTC
11:49:51 KST

Unprecedented bluetongue outbreak hits British livestock
British livestock farmers are confronting an unprecedented spread of bluetongue, a virus carried by biting midges. Cases this season have exceeded the previous three seasons combined, according to UK government data updated on Saturday.
The UK has recorded 2,579 cases so far in the 2026-27 bluetongue season, which runs from July 1 to June 30 of next year, according to the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA). The government defines a case as a property where bluetongue has been confirmed.
In just three months, this season’s bluetongue outbreak has recorded more than four times as many cases as the previous three seasons combined.
The government recorded 348 cases in Great Britain in the 2025-26 season, 163 in 2024-25, and 126 in 2023-24.
The virus affects sheep, cattle, and other ruminants. Common signs include fever, lameness, mouth sores, and swelling of the head or tongue. Severe infections can cause a blue tongue, breathing problems, abortions, fetal deformities, stillbirths, and death. The virus does not infect people or pose a risk to food safety.
Bluetongue was first identified in Africa but has spread across southern, central, and northern Europe. Rising temperatures have helped expand the range and transmission season of the biting midges that carry the virus, according to the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH).
“Essentially the midges are active earlier and continue their activity until later in the year,” Dr. Christopher Sanders of the Pirbright Institute said in a WOAH publication on an earlier outbreak. “That means that the gap between transmission seasons is actually reduced, which may allow the virus to overwinter more easily.”
The bluetongue outbreak comes as livestock producers across the Atlantic are confronting another insect-borne threat.
The New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasitic fly eradicated from the US decades ago, re-emerged in the country in June. The federal and state authorities have since stepped up surveillance and imposed measures aimed at containing its spread. Canada has restricted imports of livestock and other susceptible animals from Texas and New Mexico, where screwworm cases have been detected.

White House forms task force to assess AI risks, opportunities: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:39:42 UTC
11:39:42 KST

Seyit Kurt
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
The White House has formed a task force to assess the risks and opportunities posed by artificial intelligence and examine the federal government's role in overseeing the rapidly developing technology, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
The "Super Intelligence Force," chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, will have 120 days to prepare its findings.
It will examine existing laws and potential steps Congress could take while working with the technology industry to identify risks and opportunities.
Its charter calls for developing plans to respond to threats posed by advanced AI, while avoiding regulations that could hinder innovation and competition.
The task force will also review how breaches, hacks, model jailbreaks and other AI-related incidents are reported to the government, and recommend ways to improve the federal response under existing authorities.
Its formation follows a White House meeting on Tuesday between President Donald Trump and technology executives, including OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Trump said that the heads of the largest US tech companies signed a "morally binding" agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence, including internal safety monitoring and independent external reviews of their systems.
Trump has emphasized maintaining US leadership in the technology while favoring voluntary industry safeguards as opposed to tighter government regulation.

Emily Damari, who was kidnapped on October 7, 2023, and survived Hamas captivity in Gaza, shared previously unreleased photos from her time as a hostage on Instagram on Saturday, marking three years since her abduction on the Hebrew calendar.
"Three years ago at this time on Simchat Torah I was deep, deep in the Gaza Strip," Damari wrote in her post.
She described her experience at Shifa Hospital in Gaza, seen in the pictures she posted shortly after her abduction, where she was treated for a gunshot wound in her hand and a shrapnel injury in her leg. Ultimately, Damari had two fingers amputated. She also had additional surgery on her hand after her release in early 2025.
"I'm in a disgusting room full of blood; there is a corpse on the floor next to me. A 'doctor' approaches and introduces himself as Dr. Hamas, [accompanied by] ten more monsters with Kalashnikovs [pointed] at my head," Damari wrote.
"People who know a little bit about medicine can understand from the pictures that the fact that I'm here today is a miracle," she added. "For four months, my leg continued to bleed...[I had stitches] meant to be removed after two weeks that stayed in my hand for a full year, and here I am."
In previous social media posts and media appearances, Damari has explained that her leg wound was improperly stitched, which is why it continued to bleed after initial treatment.
"When I woke up, ‘Dr. Hamas’ told me I had lost two fingers, and my leg wound was left open with only four stitches instead of sixteen,” she said in March 2025 after receiving corrective surgery on her hand.
Former Gaza hostage Emily Damari marries partner Dani Amit in Tel Aviv wedding celebration
In August, Damari married her partner, Israeli food influencer Danielle “Dani” Amit, in a wedding celebration in Tel Aviv.
The couple had gotten engaged in January 2026, one year after Damari was released from Hamas captivity.
"For 471 days, she was held in captivity," Damari's mother, Mandy, said during the celebration. "And during those endless days and nights, there were moments when the thought of standing here tonight, seeing my daughter alive, safe, happy, and standing beside the person she loves, would have been impossible to imagine."
The couple was joined by numerous other former hostages at the wedding, including Romi Gonen, Doron Steinbrecher, Liri Albag, Danielle Gilboa, Omer Shem Tov, Keith and Aviva Siegal, and Gali and Ziv Berman.
Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:19:09 UTC
11:19:09 KST

US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.
"The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high."
AI safety has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade.
Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with China on governing AI technology.
Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report.
External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said.

At least 15,000 civilian casualties documented in Ukraine in 2026, UN report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:17:32 UTC
11:17:32 KST

The UN Human Rights Office found that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025, High Commissioner Volker Turk told the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Oct. 2.
Turk’s office documented 15,280 civilians killed or injured during the first eight months of the year, as Russia has intensified attacks on civilian infrastructure in recent months. On the frontlines, the office found that nearly 2,500 civilians were killed or injured by Russian aerial glide bombs in the span of eight months, which is 62% more than last year.
"The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is growing and intensifying by the week, causing unfathomable pain to civilians, and threatening an even greater disaster across the entire region," Türk said.
Russian strikes on schools, medical centers, apartment buildings, railways and shops are leading to a growing number of civilian casualties, as people across Ukraine live in "constant dread," the UN office said in a summary of his remarks.
His office also outlined how a "sharp increase" of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial properties like supermarkets and food companies will continue to cause pain to civilians, who are forced to grapple with temporary shortages of dairy and food items as the winter months approach.
In his Geneva remarks, Turk urged "states with influence" over Russia to push for peace now, before the “tragedy becomes even worse.” He also criticized Russia’s leadership, who he said had created a militarized economy "that puts death and destruction ahead of healthcare and education."
In a response to the UN office’s findings, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha echoed Turk’s call for accountability, saying that the High Commissioner’s call to states with influence over Russia "must be acted upon."
"While Russia cannot achieve any of its goals on the frontline, it is killing and injuring more Ukrainian civilians," Sybiha said. "The principles of the UN Charter cannot survive as words alone while a country that illegally occupies the seat of a permanent member of the Security Council violates them day after day."
The UN office had also found “shocking” levels of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war, he said. Turk accused the Russian Federation of using such “abhorrent acts to torture, intimidate and coerce individuals and communities.”
According to the report, out of the 1,004 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence between February 2022 and July 2026 against civilians and prisoners of war (POWs), 89% were attributed to Russian forces. 11% of total verified cases were attributed to Ukrainian forces, with threats of sexual violence comprising almost half of these violations.
A summary of the report’s findings outlined that while the Ukrainian government has taken "concrete steps to prevent and address such violations," Russia has failed to do the same.
"This is just one terrible manifestation of the cruelty that has come to define this war,” Turk said, adding that “alongside peace, there must be accountability."
The High Commissioner elaborated that his office was also concerned about human rights violations against foreign nationals recruited by Russia to join the war effort. His office interviewed prisoners of war from 36 countries held by Ukraine, many of whom said they had been deceived into joining Russian forces.

Domestic breakthrough: South Pars Phase 11 reaches full 1 bcf/d output
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:14:29 UTC
11:14:29 KST

Domestic breakthrough: South Pars Phase 11 reaches full 1 bcf/d output
TEHRAN- Iran’s South Pars Phase 11 has reached a major milestone: after years of delays and the withdrawal of foreign partners such as France’s Total and China’s CNPC, the project has achieved its nominal production ceiling of 1 billion cubic feet per day at offshore position B, relying on domestic expertise.
The achievement is described as a leap in Persian Gulf gas production, a way to reduce energy imbalance, and a symbol of world-class Iranian engineering.
Phase 11 is strategically sensitive because it lies on the maritime border in the Persian Gulf.
The latest step was completion of technical operations on the final well at position B. Keyvan Tarighati, head of Phase 11 development, said drilling, completion and perforation of the 12th well are finished. After the well was lightened with nitrogen, test gas flow began and is monitored continuously. Following acidizing and pressure stabilization, the well will be connected to production at maximum capacity within days.
Tarighati called the entry of new wells a strategic step toward maximum extraction from the shared field, strengthening Iran’s position in regional energy diplomacy.
Hamidreza Saghafi, CEO of Petropars, said reaching 1 billion cubic feet per day at position B resulted from round-the-clock offshore drilling. With the 12th well added, gas extraction from platform B has risen to more than 28 million cubic meters per day. He described the production jump as concrete protection of national interests at the zero point of the Persian Gulf border and a way to control pressure decline in the shared reservoir. According to him, careful resource management allowed the team to overcome logistical complexity and bring the platform to full operation faster than initially forecast.
Comparative data show how rapid the development has been. In earlier periods, position B produced only about 400 million cubic feet per day, relying on the 12D jacket and a platform transferred from position 12C, with four wells in operation. During the past 17 months of intensive development, active wells tripled from four to twelve, and actual production is now near the record 1 billion cubic feet per day. More than 26,000 meters of specialized offshore drilling were completed in this period, bringing total drilling at the platform to about 50,000 meters. This added nearly 17 million cubic meters per day to the national gas supply, a figure expected to have a tangible effect on household and industrial consumption stability in the coming winter.
Development at position A has also advanced significantly. This platform will support the second part of gas extraction from Phase 11. At the start of the current period, it was in early construction: the offshore jacket was about 35 percent complete and the topside only about 4 percent. Today, a 4,000-ton jacket has been built, braced, transported and installed in its final Persian Gulf location after more than 700 meters of precise piling. The topside construction has reached about 50 percent despite difficult conditions.
Masoud Rezaei, an offshore structural engineering expert, called the rapid progress and the resolution of long-lead items an engineering feat under supply-chain restrictions. Plans call for the structure to be loaded out and installed at about 80 percent progress so the second part of Phase 11 can enter operation as soon as possible.
The record was achieved despite severe technical obstacles, international sanctions on equipment, security threats and tense maritime conditions. Project officials say that even during regional tensions, and at times when the contractor’s site for the position A topside was hit by projectiles, construction never stopped. Execution teams continued work while maintaining standards and safety principles. This resilience, they argue, shows that Iran’s oil and gas industry has reached a level of technical knowledge and durability that can withstand the strongest external pressures.
The future plan for position A is carefully set. After the topside is installed offshore, initial operation will begin with four to six wells. Gradually, as drilling rigs arrive, an average of one new well will be completed every four months. This phased drilling will continue for about three years until the platform’s nominal capacity is fully reached.
Petropars, which has carried out more than half of South Pars projects both onshore and offshore, has now turned Phase 11 from a symbol of years of uncertainty into a driver of sustainable national energy supply. Beyond production numbers, the project is presented as proof that Iranian specialists’ determination can overcome imposed limits, offering a model for other major national projects in the oil industry.

In brief
- The Australian Federal Police are investigating Australian links to the co-pilot of a flydubai flight last week.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) has confirmed it is investigating Australian links to the co-pilot of an Israel-bound flydubai flight accused of attacking the captain with an axe and attempting to seize the controls.
According to the ABC, the AFP's investigation is being run by the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, which is made up of the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO.
The ABC also reported that the co-pilot received a student visa in 2014 and became a student in Australia between 2015 and 2017. Following this period, he departed the country and, as is standard practice, his visa was cancelled in 2019 after he failed to enrol in another course.
The investigation will reportedly attempt to ascertain whether the man was radicalised during his time spent studying in Australia.
The UAE investigation
News that makes sense

The co-pilot was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country’s airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said Sunday.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the local investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit’s crash axe and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a "terrorist attack" on Thursday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him.
The new details raised questions about how thoroughly flydubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot's presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel's strict security protocols.
Israel has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman don’t have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security and 7 October security failures have been central issues.
Flydubai hired the co-pilot after Oman Air barred him
Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views.
The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline flydubai, the person said. It wasn't immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and didn’t go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalisation.
The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said the investigation, which hasn't concluded, hasn’t found any connections with militant groups, suggesting that the co-pilot acted on his own.
The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had travelled to Syria, with no details.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation,” but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel’s government.
A social media account was deleted the day of the flight
A flydubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged "there are many questions at this stage." There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
In a statement to The Associated Press (AP), Royal Air Maroc, Morocco's national carrier, said the co-pilot "completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment." There were no details.
Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, told the AP that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but "did not undertake any pilot training." There were no details on the timing.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared.
"In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks," he said.
Captain and passengers have described drama on board
Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.
The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarming sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the flight while passengers screamed.
In a phone call with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, the flight's captain, Smit Machchhar, said that before the attack, the co-pilot wanted to pray, and that he turned away out of respect. He said he felt a blow to the back of his head a few minutes later, and then the blows kept coming.
Netanyahu told Machchhar that he was amazed at his courage and his ability to stay cool under impossible conditions. “You saved so many souls. ... You saved the spirit of the world,” he said.
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was torn away, and aviation experts have marvelled that it didn't crash. Flydubai has said crew travelling on the plane helped to stabilise it and land. They haven't been publicly identified.
The captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE. The passengers, most of them Israeli, flew home later on Thursday on a separate plane, to cheers.
