Cornell University president Michael Kotlikoff said he was “deeply disturbed” by a student’s 2024 rape allegation that has drawn national outrage.
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” he said in a video message released on Oct 3, saying that the university must “do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe” from happening again.
Attorneys for a Jane Doe in September filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, its leaders, the Chi Phi fraternity, her sorority and seven men, saying that she was given drugs and alcohol and assaulted.
The men have largely remained silent. Lawyers for at least three of them have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing.
The university has defended aspects of its handling of the cases, while Kotlikoff acknowledged on Oct 3 that it could “do better”.
“There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make a greater effort to explain what we can, to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken and to be more transparent,” he said, acknowledging questions about the investigation and “distrust” in the community.
Next week, Cornell’s Board of Trustees will announce an independent review by an outside law firm to investigate all aspects of Cornell’s handling of the case, Kotlikoff said.
“We will not wait for the investigation or the review to be completed before we act,” he said. “The review should inform additional changes, not delay improvements already underway or ones we know we can make today.”
Cornell plans a “serious look” at fraternities and sororities, focusing on accountability, transparency and members’ responsibility to intervene when someone is at risk, Kotlikoff said.
He did not announce specific new restrictions on Greek life.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul criticised the university police and district attorney’s handling of the case and appointed New York Attorney-General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
James’s office will have the authority to prosecute offences and present evidence to a grand jury if warranted – a decision Kotlikoff said he supports.
He pledged the university’s “full support” for legislative efforts to change state sexual-assault laws and said Cornell eventually plans to use its research expertise to study sexual assault, trauma, intoxication and consent, and promote policies beyond its campus. BLOOMBERG

Cornell president vows 'serious look' at fraternities, sororities in wake of rape allegations
Oct 3 - Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus following an outcry over the school's handling of a student's rape allegations, the Ivy League school's president said on Saturday.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman, who alleges she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has sparked outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future. That includes "a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," Kotlikoff said.
"At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community," he said. "But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility."
The university will seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to "preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of others."
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But "we must do better," Kotlikoff said. "We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves."
He vowed that university officials would "be more transparent" about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but he did not detail specific initiatives that the university would take.
"In the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our community to ask questions and hear directly from university leadership," he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate. REUTERS

Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

11:00:00 KST

BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s largest opposition party wants to show it’s still on the electoral pitch during an annual gathering that kicks off Sunday.
Despite Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch consolidating her position and seeing improved personal ratings, the party is still far from its government heyday, and faces an ongoing challenge on the right from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK.
Here’s what POLITICO’s team of reporters will be watching for as the Conservatives gather in Birmingham.
Advertisement
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom
My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?
Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.
Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.
I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.
There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.
I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.
Advertisement
And, of course, I’d ask questions about a coalition. There is no love lost between the Tories and Reform but all recent polls suggest they would have to team up to have any chance of running a government. Will she pull any punches against Farage … or Restore Britain chief Rupert Lowe, whose vote-splitting might help her in the end?
Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber
I’ll be really interested to see how the party is positioning itself against what we know so far about Ed Miliband’s agenda as foreign secretary — so whether there’s any dissent over new sanctions introduced by Labour on Israeli E1 settlements.
Miliband has just begun to signal a potentially more conciliatory approach to China as an alternative locus of power and investment versus the U.S., so I’ll be looking at whether the Conservatives think this is a weak point where they can redouble attacks on Labour.
There’s also the question of artificial intelligence regulation and which camp the Tories are situating themselves in. Will they agree with the government on the need for a globally coordinated effort, or back U.S. President Donald Trump’s zero-regulation stance?
Finally, here’s a side plot: Are there any signs that former Home Secretary Priti Patel, traditionally a conference fan favorite, is actually doing anything in her new role in coordinating cooperation between the Tories and other parties internationally?
London Influence Reporter John Johnston
With little detail so far about Burnham’s plans for business, and many corporate execs pondering if Farage’s Reform has hit its peak, this Tory conference will be a vital opportunity for the party to try and show it is building back towards being a credible alternative.
Advertisement
Since the 2024 general election, many businesses and lobbying firms have sent only a skeleton staff to Tory conference. But I’ve heard that extra corporate passes and tickets to the standalone Business Day have been snapped up in the last few months. So, attendance may be healthier — even if most still won’t be splashing out on panel events or exhibition stands.
Business leaders remain skeptical about the prospect of an early general election. But as the official opposition, the Conservatives have the potential to help industry shine a spotlight on concerns and push issues up the political agenda if one comes. At last year’s conference, many public affairs pros felt the Tories lacked the ideas, unity and leadership to do that. My focus this year will be figuring out if that assessment has shifted.
Energy Reporter Abby Wallace
The Conservatives have come a long way from the party that, in government, enshrined net-zero targets in law. Badenoch has been clear about the direction she wants to take the party in: ditching legally-binding climate targets and drilling for more oil and gas in the North Sea.
The party’s leader has even suggested that former colleagues who still support the target will not be welcome back on the Tory benches. I’ll be looking out for whether that U-turn at the top has fully filtered through the party.
While energy bills have surged on the back of war in Iran, the party has been pressing Labour ministers to prioritize cutting costs in the system. For the Conservatives, that means ditching some support for renewables and a bigger role for gas and nuclear in the future. I’ll be keeping an ear on whether there is any pressure from the opposition for ministers to intervene ahead of what will be a difficult winter of price rises too.
The future of the North Sea, including looming decisions on Rosebank and Jackdaw, will no doubt spring up on the fringes — especially after the Conservatives clinched the Aberdeen South by-election following a campaign focused on oil and gas drilling.
Advertisement
Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers
Andrew Griffith will be stepping up this party conference, having been promoted to shadow chancellor earlier this year to replace his more mild-mannered colleague Mel Stride.
Griffith was a bigwig in business before he entered parliament, and as a former City minister, I’ll be watching whether he focuses his ire on the prospect of Labour raising bank taxes in the budget, which is now less than a month away.
Griffith will make his big speech on how to get Britain growing again at 2 p.m. Monday. Growth was the favored buzzword of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, and has been heartily adopted by her successor John Healey, although how to achieve it remains a challenge amid soaring debt and rising interest rates. I’m interested to see whether the Conservatives propose a solution.
Senior Technology Reporter Frank Hersey
This conference is a chance for Badenoch’s team to establish any sort of differentiation between Tory tech policy and that of the other parties. This has been getting harder as parties’ approaches have coalesced. Labour committed to a pro-growth agenda for AI under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer with planned regulatory reforms to match. Tory plans for a social media ban for under-16s were eventually (and reluctantly) grasped by Labour. The Tories were further hemmed in by Reform banking the low-tax, low-regulation space.
I’ll be looking to see if the party can get ahead in any policy areas or if it has to pick new ones to do so. Among all the parties, there’s perhaps most interest in what the Conservatives say on tech — as their policy ideas in this space are feeling overdue.
Senior Trade Reporter Sophie Inge
The fightback against Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with the EU is expected to continue in Birmingham, after Badenoch warned that Britain shouldn’t be “having arguments which started 10 years ago.”
Deputy Leader Alex Burghart has already pledged to “reverse” the Brexit reset, warning that plans for an agrifood deal with the bloc risk undermining the U.K.’s trading relationship with the U.S., among other countries.

Zimbabweans struggle to rebuild after fleeing xenophobia in South Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Zimbabweans struggle to rebuild after fleeing xenophobia in South Africa
Returnees face economic hardship and limited support as they try to rebuild in Zimbabwe.
Mutare, Zimbabwe – Samantha Chimbuya had built a life in South Africa after leaving Zimbabwe in 2019 in search of better opportunities.
She found work, could afford food and believed her two children had access to better education. She also had access to healthcare.
Then, she no longer felt safe.
As June 30 approached, a deadline set by anti-immigrant activists for undocumented migrants to leave South Africa, the 30-year-old packed her belongings and returned to Zimbabwe.
“It was not safe any more. They were raiding our homes, warning us to leave. It was scary,” Chimbuya told Al Jazeera.
Chimbuya was living in KwaZulu-Natal when anti-immigrant protests intensified. March and March, one of the groups behind the June 30 deadline, accused undocumented migrants of taking jobs and putting pressure on public services.
The deadline was not imposed by the South African government, which said June 30 would be a normal day and warned against intimidation and violence. But thousands of migrants left amid fears of unrest.
Some governments organised transport for citizens returning home. Chimbuya paid for her own journey to Hurungwe, in northern Zimbabwe.
By July 28, 116,670 Zimbabweans had returned from South Africa, according to Information Minister Zhemu Soda. Of those, 36,940 were assisted by the government, while 79,730 returned independently. A further 38,057 had registered for employment, Soda said.
Hard times in Zimbabwe
For Chimbuya, coming home meant confronting many of the economic difficulties that had pushed her to leave in the first place.
She has struggled to find work and now relies on family and friends for help. Her husband remains in South Africa, where she says he is also struggling.
She had hoped to receive a grant to start a small business but said she had not received one.
Reverend Useni Sibanda, executive director of the Zimbabwe Christian Alliance, said many returnees had spent years abroad and were coming home without jobs or adequate support.
Some had not invested in homes or property in Zimbabwe while they were away, he said, leaving them with little to fall back on.
“They are coming back to a country where there are no jobs and where the social support systems may not be enough to accommodate them,” Sibanda said.
The government says it is trying to help.
Local government Minister Daniel Garwe said authorities were screening and profiling returnees to identify their skills and needs. Reintegration centres were being established, while the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Schools was considering recruiting qualified teachers among those who had returned.
Garwe also said companies were being encouraged to employ skilled returnees and that vocational training and support for people wanting to start businesses were being considered.
For some, however, the skills they acquired in South Africa have offered a more immediate route to earning a living.
Rebuilding from scratch
Sidney Bunya, from Zvimba, northeast of Harare, left Zimbabwe in March 2020 because of economic hardship.
He moved first to Johannesburg, where he took various jobs, before settling in Port Elizabeth. There, a cousin introduced him to professional carpenters.
Bunya honed his skills and eventually secured large projects, specialising in roof trusses.
But in 2026, groups demanding permits began raiding his workplace. Bunya had only his passport, and employers became reluctant to hire him because of the harassment.
He bought carpentry tools, shipped them to Zimbabwe and left South Africa before the June 30 deadline.
Using his savings, he started a business at home. It now supports his family and employs five people.
“It was difficult to set up the business. But I am getting more jobs now,” Bunya said.
Motsi said churches had also partnered with local businesses to provide training in welding, carpentry and computer science.
Calls for longer-term support
Churches have been helping returnees with shelter, food and transport, but Ray Motsi, president of the Theological College of Zimbabwe, said the needs were overwhelming.
He criticised the government for not doing enough to support people returning after years abroad.
“We need a deliberate programme to reintegrate these people,” Motsi said, arguing that returnees needed more than transport home.
Rashweat Mukundu, a human rights activist in Harare, said the government should provide longer-term assistance, including small grants, agricultural inputs and machinery, to help people establish livelihoods.
The challenge, he said, was not simply getting Zimbabweans across the border but helping them remain economically secure once they arrived.
“I plan to open a grocery store, but funding is a challenge.”

Lula narrowly leads Flavio Bolsonaro in polls ahead of Brazil's presidential vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:43:08 UTC
10:43:08 KST

A series of major opinion polls published have placed Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva slightly ahead of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on the eve of Sunday's first-round presidential election, pointing towards an extraordinarily tight race in a likely second-round runoff between the leftist incumbent and his right-wing challenger.
Under Brazilian electoral regulations, if no presidential contender secures more than 50 percent of valid votes — a calculation that strictly excludes blank and null ballots — on Sunday, the two leading candidates will advance to a head-to-head runoff on October 25.
A nationwide survey conducted by the MDA Institute for the National Transport Confederation (CNT) placed Lula at 47.8 percent of valid votes, compared to 42.1 percent for Bolsonaro.
In a simulated second round, the CNT/MDA poll recorded Lula leading Bolsonaro by 47.3 percent to 43.1 percent.
The survey sampled 2,007 individuals between September 30, and October 2, carrying a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.
A separate survey from Datafolha recorded Lula securing 45% of valid votes in the first round against 42 percent for Bolsonaro, with Caiado at 4percent, Santos and Cury each at 3 percent, and Zema at 1 percent.
In a projected runoff, Datafolha placed Lula at 47 percent and Bolsonaro at 46 percent—a statistical tie within the survey's two-percentage-point margin of error.
Datafolha interviewed 4,006 respondents across October 2–3.
A tight battle
Meanwhile, a poll by Quaest showed the tightest opening round, placing Lula at 46 percent of valid votes to Bolsonaro's 45 percent, with Cury, Santos, and Caiado each registering 3 percent.
In a simulated second-round scenario, Quaest placed Bolsonaro slightly ahead at 44 percent to Lula's 42 percent.
The poll surveyed 3,702 individuals across October 2–3 and had a two-percentage-point margin of error.
Lula is locked in a tight battle against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
Brazil’s president is seeking a fourth and final term in office, warning voters that the country’s sovereignty is at stake amid pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Trump has not endorsed Flavio Bolsonaro, but has said he is "very closely" watching the Brazilian election.

Somalia will not accept Israeli presence in the country "under any circumstances," President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said.
In an interview with Al Jazeera to be broadcast on Sunday, excerpts of which were shared on the broadcaster's website, Mohamud said Israel plans to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, and that its real aim was to get closer to Gulf states and Iran.

Somaliland, the breakaway Somali region recognized by Israel last year, declared independence in 1991. Somalia, however, considers the region an integral part of its territory.

From Bazargan to Mersin: how Iran, Turkey plan to reach $30b in trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:36:43 UTC
10:36:43 KST

From Bazargan to Mersin: how Iran, Turkey plan to reach $30b in trade
TEHRAN- Iran and Turkey, aiming to increase trade to $30 billion, are pursuing the development of the Bazargan border, the launch of a fourth crossing, strengthening rail and road transport, and establishing a joint Khoy–Van–Mersin free zone.
According to the Mehr News Agency, while Iran and Turkey are pursuing the goal of bringing bilateral trade to $30 billion, the gap between current trade and this target cannot be filled merely by increasing exports and imports. Developing border crossings, reducing truck stops, strengthening rail and road transport, using Turkish ports, and creating new trade routes have now become an important part of the two countries’ plan to increase exchanges.
In this context, Turkey is not merely a neighboring consumer market for Iran; the country’s geographical location, access to Europe’s transport network, and the Mediterranean and Black Sea ports have increased its capacity as one of the routes connecting Iranian goods to more distant markets.
Dariush Vossoughi, Iran’s commercial attaché in Istanbul, also referring to this same capacity, has considered the development of trade relations with Turkey as going beyond increasing exports to its market, and has emphasized using Turkey’s transport and logistics capacities to access European and African markets.
According to announced statistics, the volume of Iran-Turkey trade in the year 1404 was about $19.2 billion; a figure that includes $6.8 billion in Iran’s exports to Turkey and $12.4 billion in imports from that country. Therefore, realizing the $30 billion target means increasing trade by about $10.8 billion compared with last year’s level.
In the first five months of the year 1405, Iran’s exports to Turkey were announced at $3.7 billion and imports from that country at $2.8 billion.
Therefore, reaching $30 billion from the current level requires changes in the trade and logistics capacities of the two countries, because increasing trade volume without removing border bottlenecks can merely lead to increased exchange time and cost.
Among existing infrastructure, the Bazargan border is considered the most important overland connection point between Iran and Turkey; a route that, in addition to bilateral trade, also covers part of the transit flow among Turkey, Europe, Iran, and Central Asian markets.
In recent months, increasing the capacity of this border has been on the two countries’ agenda. According to Iran Customs, in Mordad, the number of trucks crossing Bazargan reached more than 350 per day, and a target was set to increase this figure to 400. In this framework, coordinating work shifts, facilitating control processes, managing empty and transit trucks, and reducing unnecessary stops were put on the agenda.
This capacity increase has become more important as Bazargan Customs has faced significant growth in cargo volume in recent months. According to the director general of Bazargan Customs, from the beginning of the year to Mordad, about 190,000 tons of goods were exported via this route to Turkey, southern Persian Gulf countries, and India, a 40 percent increase compared with the same period last year. During the same period, about 150,000 tons of essential goods, medicine, bananas, and other imported goods entered and cleared through the Bazargan route, showing 250 percent growth.
Thus, the Bazargan issue is not limited to Iran-Turkey trade, and this border is becoming one of the important routes for moving goods in the regional network.
On the other side of the border, Turkey and Iran held a joint meeting in August to examine truck traffic problems and waiting times. The gradual increase in truck traffic, wider use of the TIR Carnet, and implementation of the electronic e-TIR system were among the solutions raised at this meeting.
In August, the International Road Transport Union also considered the Gürbulak–Bazargan route one of the region’s important road corridors; a route that connects Turkey and Europe through Iran to Central Asia and other Asian markets.
Therefore, each day of reduction in truck stop time is not merely a customs achievement; it directly affects transport costs, the predictability of delivery times, and the attractiveness of Iran’s route for transit.
Alongside increasing the capacity of existing crossings, the two countries are also seeking to increase the number of border crossing points. According to Iran’s commercial attaché in Istanbul, three main crossings between Iran and Turkey are currently active, and the issue of creating a fourth crossing in the Kuzeh Rash region has also been pursued in recent years. An initial agreement to create this crossing near Salmas has been proposed, and its goal is to increase trade capacity and reduce pressure on existing crossings.
Increasing the number of crossings matters because $30 billion in trade growth, if reliant on a few limited routes, could again lead to truck queues and higher logistics costs.
In this framework, the creation of a joint free zone among Khoy, Van, and Mersin is also being pursued; a plan that, if operationalized, could transform the two countries’ trade relationship from a merely border relationship into a broader logistics and production chain.
In September, the head of the Iran-Turkey Parliamentary Friendship Group announced that the proposal to create this free zone with Khoy as its center has been pursued and that the Iranian government’s approval for it has been obtained. Under this plan, the Khoy and Van route would continue and connect to Mersin, and the creation of economic hinterlands at the Razi border has also been deemed necessary to support this plan.
According to the plan to create a free zone centered on Khoy, the Khoy and Van route would continue and connect to Mersin, and the creation of economic hinterlands at the Razi border has also been deemed necessary to support this plan.
Also, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Zones has announced that necessary measures and coordination have been carried out by Iran to launch the joint Khoy-Turkey free zone, and continuing the work requires coordination with the Turkish side.
The importance of this plan lies in the fact that Khoy and the Razi border can be connected in a logistics chain to Van and then to Turkey’s transport network, making the access route for Iranian goods to Western ports and markets shorter and more diverse.
Another focus in developing trade relations is using the capacity of Turkish ports, including Mersin, Samsun, Trabzon, and Izmir. In this model, Turkey is not only a destination for Iranian goods; it can also be part of the chain for transferring goods to other markets. In particular, Mersin Port, in connection with the Iran-Turkey overland route, can play the role of a maritime hinterland for Iran’s trade with Mediterranean and European markets.
This issue has become more important as geopolitical developments and disruptions in some traditional trade routes have increased the importance of alternative and combined routes. In such conditions, connecting road, rail, and port can play as much a role in trade development as increasing border capacity itself.
According to this report, alongside existing capacities, Iran’s main issue in the Turkish market is not only increasing the value of exports; rather, it is increasing the share of Iranian goods in the Turkish market and using Turkey as a route to access third markets.
This matters because trade between the two countries still faces obstacles such as anti-dumping measures, quotas on some goods, higher tariffs and fees, and transit problems; obstacles that, even if transport capacity is available, can limit access of Iranian goods to the Turkish market.
On the other hand, trade development requires a more active presence of the private sector of the two countries. In recent years, thousands of companies with Iranian capital have operated in Turkey, and according to the representative of the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce in Tir, the number of companies with Iranian capital in Turkey has reached 7,288.
Accordingly, for Iran, Turkey can be both a destination market and a link in the chain of access to European and other regional markets. Therefore, the main challenge on the path to $30 billion in trade is not only “how much goods are exchanged”; rather, it is at what cost, at what speed, and through which routes goods can move between the two countries and markets beyond them.
At a meeting in Istanbul, in early July, ICCIMA head Samad Hassanzadeh met with Turkey-Iran Business Council (DEIK) and Iran-Turkey Joint Chamber officials. He highlighted over 200 investment opportunities prepared by ICCIMA for non-Iranian investors, inviting Turkish private-sector participation. He called Turkey Iran’s largest regional economic partner and key gateway to Europe, thanked Ankara for supporting Iran during the Sacred Defense, COVID-19, the 12-day war, and the recent imposed war, and condemned attacks that martyred Iranian leaders. He said official Iran-Turkey trade reached $23 billion this year despite war restrictions; the two presidents aim for $30 billion. He urged joint industrial towns in free zones and logistics/transit cooperation, especially petrochemicals and refining.
ICCIMA Vice President Qadir Ghiyafeh described five centuries of continuous ties and called the economies complementary, not rivals. He invited Turkish investment in mining, steel, petrochemicals, refining, energy, transport, logistics, ports, agriculture, food, tourism, pharmaceuticals, advanced technology, AI, and the digital economy. He backed technology transfer, joint R&D, knowledge-based firms, border-capacity expansion, rail/road/maritime links, and joint logistics centers. He called $30 billion achievable and $50 billion possible medium-term if banking, legal, customs, and transit obstacles are removed.
Mehrdad Saadat, head of the Iran-Turkey Joint Chamber, said preferential trade is outdated and proposed free trade. He noted Iran has almost no share of Turkey’s $400 billion imports despite capacity to export over $15 billion, and suggested a joint industrial town, local-currency trade, and allowing technology/infrastructure purchases under financial-transfer rules. He also proposed reciprocal chamber offices in Tehran and Istanbul.
On the Turkish side, Ferhat Dortkoshe said Turkey should not be only a transit corridor but a production/investment hub and bridge to Europe; Osman Aksoy hoped sanctions would be lifted and stressed trust and joint production. TIM head Ahmet Gulech said his assembly has 61 associations and 160,000 exporters/importers and urged direct B2B ties.
Other Iranian delegates stressed joint production for third markets, consortiums, and solving financial channels; Iranian assets in Turkey could serve as collateral. The overall message: $30–50 billion trade requires free trade, investment, logistics, and banking fixes.

Estonia beats Luxembourg to move into second place in Nations League group
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:34:04 CST
10:34:04 KST

TALLINN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Estonia defeated Luxembourg 1-0 at Tallinn's A. Le Coq Arena on Saturday to claim its first victory in the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League and strengthen its position in League C Group 4.
The victory lifted Estonia to five points from three matches and moved it into second place in the group, keeping the Baltic side firmly in contention for promotion.
Estonia had entered the match unbeaten but without a victory after opening its campaign with a 1-1 draw away to Iceland and a goalless draw in Bulgaria. Luxembourg, meanwhile, had three points from its opening two matches.
With three rounds remaining, Estonia's prospects will largely depend on its next match against group leader Iceland in Tallinn on Tuesday. It will then travel to Luxembourg on November 13 before completing the league phase at home against Bulgaria on November 16.
The group winner earns direct promotion to League B, while the runner-up enters the promotion play-offs, giving Estonia a realistic opportunity to move up from League C if it can maintain its current form. ■

Spain beats Czech Republic to continue winning start to Nations League
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:34:00 CST
10:34:00 KST

MADRID, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- World champion Spain maintained its 100 percent start to the UEFA Nations League on Saturday night thanks to a 3-1 win over the Czech Republic in Oviedo.
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente made nine changes from the team that won 4-1 at home to Croatia on Tuesday, with Ivan Fresneda and Roberto Fernandez both making their debuts, while Fran Garcia, Robin le Normand and Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya also returned to the team.
Despite the changes, the win was only in doubt for a handful of minutes from the moment Lamine Yamal opened the scoring in the fifth minute with a trademark curling shot into the corner of the Czech goal.
A flowing move minutes later almost saw Rodrigo Hernandez double Spain's lead, but with the Spaniards dominating the ball and playing almost entirely in the Czech half a second goal never looked far away.
Visiting goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky did well to deny Pedri after another swift Spain attack in the 32nd minute, but was helpless when the ball fell kindly for Rodrigo to net the second three minutes later.
Yamal saw another effort go across the face of goal before the break as Spain dominated and with the game seemingly under control De la Fuente took the opportunity to replace the Barcelona winger and Alex Baena with Victor Munoz and Yeremy Pino for the second half.
The changes saw Spain lose some midfield control, perhaps because Munoz and Pino stayed tight on the wings rather than moving inside as Baena and Yamal do. Just after Pino saw a shot drift just wide of the post with Fernandez inches away from a finish, the Czechs got back into things when Jiri Slama drilled a low shot across Raya to make it 2-1.
Raya got away with a bad mistake with just over 10 minutes left when he dropped a simple ball and Ryan Naderi fired into the Spain net only for the 'goal' to be ruled out for a prior foul on Le Normand.
Ladislav Krejci was sent off in the 85th minute and Mikel Merino made Spain's win safe in the last minute when he latched onto a loose ball following a swift break. ■

TEHRAN, October 4. /TASS/. Iran is aware of Russia’s proposals to transfer enriched uranium to Russia but will make its decisions based on its national interests, Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a briefing.
"We are in contact with Russia and have heard the proposal [to transfer highly enriched uranium], but I should note that ultimately we must make decisions based on our national interests," he said when asked why Iran had neither accepted nor rejected Moscow’s proposals.
Baghaei noted that Iran always holds consultations on its nuclear program with Russia and China as permanent members of the UN Security Council. "Whatever the developments, we will certainly coordinate our actions with both Russia and China," he added.
On October 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow’s proposal to transfer enriched uranium from Iran to Russia remained on the table.

MADRID, October 4. /TASS/. Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he does not expect Russia to attack Finland.

To become a dog-friendly city, Hong Kong needs dog literacy

To become a dog-friendly city, Hong Kong needs dog literacy
Education isn’t just for pet owners – it’s essential for anyone sharing public space, particularly after recent severe dog attacks
3-MIN READ3-MIN
7
 Listen
Ashleigh Tamblin is a strategic communications and creative consultant in Hong Kong. 
Since July, Hong Kong has permitted dogs in approved dining premises under a tightly regulated scheme. More than 2,200 restaurants applied, with more than 980 taking part within the first month. On the surface, these are straightforward changes to the rules around where dogs are allowed. But they reflect something more significant: a changing relationship between Hong Kong and the dogs who also call it home.
Small companion breeds are familiar in urban life, while larger dogs, local mixed breeds and strays can occupy a very different place in the public imagination. This difference matters because perceptions of dogs can shape how incidents are understood and addressed. Hong Kong is not suddenly becoming a dog-friendly city. It is beginning to work out what one might look like.
But that conversation has become more difficult after three recent incidents involving dogs. In August, a 60kg dog in Yuen Long attacked and killed two smaller dogs in separate incidents. Just a month before these incidents, the dog had been briefly detained by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) in connection with another dog attack. Its keeper was warned the dog had to be kept under proper control.

First underground preschool opens in Zaporizhzhia
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
“The first underground kindergarten has opened in Zaporizhzhia, near the front lines. Now, 115 children will be able to learn, play, and eat throughout the day in a safe environment,” the Prime Minister said.

1 / 9

As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine’s first underground kindergarten, “Mobil,” designed to accommodate 260 children, began operating in the Pisochna community of Kharkiv region at the start of the current school year.

Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia being investigated by security agencies after alleged cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:26:39 UTC
10:26:39 KST

Australian security agencies have launched an investigation after it emerged that the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound flight spent about two years in the country as a student.
Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625 feet (5,067 metres) in just over 30 seconds.
The United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general has said the co-pilot had used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national.
A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the following year.
He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said.
The Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country.
“The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said.
“An update will be provided at an appropriate time.”
US media outlets, including CNN, reported that a now-deleted LinkedIn profile said al-Hammami had studied engineering at an Australian university. Guardian Australia has not verified which university the co-pilot attended.
It came after a British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”
A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.
The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.

medvedev once again explained how Ukraine can achieve &quot;peace&quot;: surrender its territories and agree to Moscow&apos;s demands

medvedev once again explained how Ukraine can achieve "peace": surrender its territories and agree to Moscow's demands
Kyiv • UNN
medvedev demands neutrality, a change in policy, and the transfer of the occupied territories to Russia. In the event of refusal, he threatened to continue the war.
Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of the Russian Federation Dmitry Medvedev once again outlined Russia’s recipe for “lasting peace” for Ukraine. According to his version, Kyiv must agree to neutral and nuclear-free status, change its domestic policy, and recognize the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian. Medvedev said this in an interview with Iran’s state broadcaster, UNN reports.
Details
According to Medvedev, these demands are allegedly “well known,” but he decided to list them once again for the Iranian audience. He named Ukraine’s neutral and nuclear-free status as the first condition.
The Kremlin representative named Ukraine’s renunciation of the so-called “nationalist course” as the second demand. Medvedev also repeated Russia’s claims about an alleged “ban on the Russian language” and “everything Russian.”
He also suggested simply handing the territories over to Russia
The third point of Russia’s vision of “peace” was the transfer under the jurisdiction of the Russian Federation of the occupied territories of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions, which Moscow incorporated into its Constitution after the illegal annexation.
Medvedev said that Moscow was ready to obtain what it wanted through diplomatic means. At the same time, he immediately threatened to continue the war if Ukraine did not agree to Russia’s demands.
If this does not happen, we will do it by military means
Thus, the version of “lasting peace” voiced by Medvedev entails Ukraine fulfilling the key demands of the state that launched the full-scale invasion, including giving up part of its territory.

Teen arrested over flamethrower attack during student unrest in France (VIDEO)
French police have arrested a teenager on suspicion of using an aerosol can to direct a jet of flames at a woman’s face during student protests, which are sweeping the country.
The altercation was filmed on Thursday in the southern port city of Marseille, where protesters attacked public transport, torching at least one bus and a fire engine.
The victim, a social worker, told BFM TV that she was waiting for a bus when a crowd of young people approached and began vandalizing the bus stop. She said she tried to intervene, prompting one of the youths to use an aerosol can as an improvised flamethrower.
“I wasn’t expecting such violence. I thought I might get shoved… I didn’t expect kids to be so violent,” the woman said. “Fortunately, my face didn’t suffer injuries as serious as the images might suggest,” she added.

She suffered first-degree burns to her face, according to Le Parisien.
Police identified the suspect as a 15-year-old boy whose name has not been released.
The demonstrations began in late September over unfilled teaching posts at a high school in Creteil, near Paris, before spreading nationwide as students demanded better learning conditions, including more teachers, smaller classes, and repairs to deteriorating buildings. They have also called for increased funding for public schools.
More than 1,200 schools have been affected this week, and over 5,000 people have been arrested as the protests escalated into violence. National Police spokesperson Agathe Foucault said on Saturday that more than 600 police officers and gendarmes were injured. Paris Police Chief Patrice Faure described the unrest as “out of control.”
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Friday that 65 education staff, including 40 headteachers, were injured since the protests began. He also reported severe damage at more than 100 schools.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin has called for a firm criminal justice response, and where appropriate, for parents to be held civilly liable for damage caused by their children.
The government has also blamed the violence on the left-wing La France Insoumise party and “its far-left proxies.” The party has denied the allegation and urged students to refrain from violence.
Student unions have distanced themselves from the violence but called for further demonstrations on October 6, saying the government has yet to offer concrete measures addressing their concerns.
Louise Paternoster, a CGT education union representative in Seine-Saint-Denis, blamed staffing shortages on government cuts that eliminated 3,256 teaching positions nationwide in 2026.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget, unveiled on Thursday, would increase education funding by €1.2 billion ($1.35 billion) while eliminating another 1,588 teaching posts. Geffray has defended the planned reductions, citing falling student numbers.
The student unrest coincides with broader labor action across France, with unions staging strikes and demonstrations over wages, public spending, and the government’s budget plans.

Ancient Greek elegy dedicated to judge found in ancient Egyptian tomb sealed with protection spells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:25:02 UTC
10:25:02 KST

An ancient Greek funeral elegy stele was found within a pyramid-shaped mud-brick tomb in the Bir al-Shaghala archaeological site in the Dakhla Oasis, Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced in late August.
The tomb, which dates back to Egypt’s Roman period, was built for the burial of a man and his wife.
A 14-step staircase leads down into the tomb’s main entrance, made of sandstone and decorated with hieroglyphic inscriptions and writings, including protective funerary spells and other phrases.
The stone entrance is a unique to the Bir al-Shaghala necropolis, noted Mohamed Abdel Badie, Head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector at the Supreme Council of Antiquities.
It is crowned by an Egyptian cornice decorated with a winged sun disk and two cobras, followed by an architectural element in the form of a bundle of reeds.
The entrance’s upper lintel also bears a funerary scene previously unseen at the necropolis, depicting the seventh hour of the Book of Amduat, one of the ancient Egyptian books of the afterlife.
Inscriptions on both sides of the lintel include texts and scenes related to the tomb's owners. Additionally, the entrance was found sealed by a stone slab carved with the image of an Osirian form surrounded by a group of spells.
The entrance then leads into a mud-brick hall with a partially-collapsed vaulted ceiling, with two burial chambers branching off it to the right.
Funerary stele found affixed to tomb's wall
Archaeologists found the funerary stele affixed to the tomb’s southern wall. It is rectangular in shape and is topped with a gabled stone centered on the relief of a sun-disk.
Its 19-lines of ancient Greek text is written in red ink, dedicated to a person named "Pesikhtis," who, according to preliminary study, may have held the position of judge.
The elegy dates back to the late third and early fourth centuries BCE, and serves as evidence of a literary and cultural life in the region during the Roman period.
In addition to the stele, archaeologists also uncovered a sandstone offering table and purification basin, several pottery vessels, and a bronze coin with the portrait of the Roman Emperor Constantine within the tomb.
Director general of New Valley Antiquities Mohamed Ibrahim noted that there is evidence of the tomb having been reused at a later point, as the remains of mud-brick chapel and funerary shrine were found above the entrance.
The importance of the discovery lies in the tomb’s architecture, inscriptions, and funerary texts, explained Secretary-General of the Supreme Council of AntiquitiesHisham El-Leithy, providing important information about the funerary practices and life during the Roman period.
Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy echoed the sentiment, noting that the oases sites hold “important evidence… of the succession of civilizations Egypt has witnessed through the ages.”

Excavations near ancient Turkish port may have found Alexander the Great’s soldiers tombs - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:24:45 UTC
10:24:45 KST

Rescue excavations at the ancient city of Aigai’s (Aeolis) necropolis in Turkey may have uncovered the tombs of Alexander the Great’s soldiers, the Turkish state-run Andalou Agency (AA) reported earlier this week.
The excavations, coordinated by Turkey’s Culture and Tourism Ministry and carried out by the Adana Museum Directorate, have been focused on the area of the necropolis closest to the ancient city’s port.
According to AA, an initial survey of the necropolis identified at least 30 rock-cut tombs and chest-type graves scattered across the site. As of now, only 10 have been fully uncovered.
The tombs, AA described, are carved directly into the hillside and are complete with narrow corridors and staircases leading down to burial chambers where stone platforms mark where bodies used to be placed.
The chest-type tombs were finished with lime motar, reported AA, and a decorative rosette motifs is still visible on several of them.
Terracotta sarcophagi were also reportedly found at the necropolis site.
Associate Professor Faris Demir, who is directing the excavations, stated that the necropolis dates back to the Hellenistic period, between 323 and 31 BCE.
Demir added that it had remained in use throughout the Roman era, and that the damage visible on many of the tombs had likely accumulated from the Middle Ages onward.
The region surrounding Aigai is believed to be where Alexander the Great prepared for the Battle of Issus in 333 BCE, in which he defeated the Persian king Darius III.
It is known as Alexander's second great battle in his conquest of Asia
According to Demir, Aigai was founded by Macedonian soldiers for Alexander.
This, he stated, raised the possibility that some of the newly uncovered tombs may have belonged to this soldiers, but noted that further study is needed before a complete conclusion can be drawn.
In addition to the burial sites, archaeologists unearthed vessel fragments and tear bottles thought to be grave offerings.
After undergoing careful restoration and study, they are expected to eventually be displayed at the Adana Museum, according to AA.
Turkey places site of Alexander the Great’s first battle with Persians under historic protection
Earlier this year, Turkey officially registered one of Alexander the Great’s famed battlefields as a Historical Site.
“We have secured the site of the Battle of Granikos, a turning point that changed the course of world history,” Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy wrote in a mid-June on X/Twitter. “The Battlefield of Granikos, where Alexander the Great achieved his first major victory against the Persians and opened the doors to his campaign into Asia, has now been officially registered as a ‘Historical Site.’”
“I believe this important step, which will add value to Çanakkale's cultural heritage, will make significant contributions to historical science, cultural tourism, and the strengthening of our cultural routes,” Ersoy went on.
Archaeological and scientific surveys were carried out at the site ahead of the Çanakkale Regional Board for the Protection of Cultural Heritage’s decision in order to evaluate whether it met the criteria to be designated as a historic site.
Under the decision, both the battlefield and its surrounding areas have gained protected status.

Cornell president vows transparency amid outrage over fraternity rape case

Cornell president says university ‘must do better’ after gang rape allegations
Cornell University’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, has called the alleged 2024 gang rape of a student at a fraternity house “deeply disturbing”, pledging greater transparency amid mounting outrage over how the United States school handled the case.
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said in an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community on Saturday.
He characterised the past week as one of the most difficult in the New York-based university’s history and said it would weigh on the university for years to come. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanisation and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use,” he said.
The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 and has sued the university and seven former students.
Scrutiny over Cornell’s handling of the case intensified after New York Governor Kathy Hochul said newly released information had undermined her confidence in the local prosecutor, who initially declined to bring charges.
Hochul subsequently appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to take over the criminal investigation, saying she would “not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug”.
The case has also renewed scrutiny of the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving victims who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs, even if they later became too intoxicated to consent.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten had cited the legal provision in defending his original decision not to pursue charges. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to it.
At a student assembly hearing on Thursday, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
In Saturday’s video, Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s handling of the case and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”.
James’s appointment has placed the case under a prosecutor whose office has repeatedly clashed with President Donald Trump. She has separately described the case as “an active criminal investigation”.

AI generated

The task force will be led by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, who confirmed his role to the paper.
The role makes Clayton effectively the Trump administration’s new AI czar, a senior White House official told the Wall Street Journal.
“The President asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said, which is that we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first,” the Journal cited Clayton as saying.
Despite growing concerns about security risks posed by AI, President Donald Trump has spurned calls for new regulations.
Instead, he has prioritised keeping the US ahead of China and backed a voluntary framework involving outside safety audits and stronger internal controls.
“We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing,” the President said during a meeting with industry executives this week.
The task force has been named the “Super Intelligence Force”, Trump’s preferred name for AI, and will have 120 days to prepare the report, the report said.
Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticised prominent AI leaders’ warnings about existential risks posed by the technology as alarmist and unhelpful, calling on the industry to police itself and produce solutions.
“It is the people at the labs who have to accept responsibility, and I agree with that,” Bessent said in an Axios interview published Oct 3. “I think the labs have come around to that way of thinking, too.” BLOOMBERG

'He prayed before attack': Machchhar tells Netanyahu chilling flydubai cockpit ordeal

The pilot also recalled trying to open the cockpit door once, but said the co-pilot shut it again. He later found himself lying on the cockpit floor as he heard the aircraft moving rapidly and passengers screaming.
Flydubai pilot Captain Smit Machchhar spoke to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu where he described the incidents that unfolded inside the cockpit. He also described how he managed to open the cockpit door despite suffering repeated blows to his head. Netanyahu praised his courage and said he had "saved so many souls".Machchhar told Netanyahu that the flight had initially been normal. The co-pilot then wanted to play a game that he said many locals play. While Machchhar was looking towards the front of the aircraft, he suddenly felt a heavy blow to the back of his head.
Machchhar also told Netanyahu that the co-pilot had wanted to pray before the attack. He said he looked towards the front of the cockpit out of respect while the co-pilot prayed."...while he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back, and suddenly, after, I would say about four-five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head."My first thought was that there was a catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right," Machchhar said.He said the blows continued and he soon realised that the aircraft had not been damaged. Instead, the co-pilot was attacking him.
"And that's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me," he said.Machchhar said the initial blows left his vision severely blurred, making it difficult for him to understand what was happening. He then felt the aircraft sharply descending."My memory is still in bits and pieces right now," he told Netanyahu.The pilot also recalled trying to open the cockpit door once, but said the co-pilot shut it again. He later found himself lying on the cockpit floor as he heard the aircraft moving rapidly and passengers screaming.Machchhar said he then realised he had to make one final attempt to reach the door."And as I was telling the ambassador here, that I had that one last fight left in me that, you know, call it personal or call it for people," he said. "But let's say I did it that if I don't do it, I'm going to die."He said he pushed himself towards the door and managed to open it. Crew members and others outside then took control of the situation."And thankfully people were waiting to bounce back, took over the control and the rest is what you know, sir," Machchhar said.
'There is no pin'
Netanyahu asked Machchhar how he had managed to open the cockpit door when the co-pilot was preventing access.Machchhar explained that the door has a twist mechanism on the inside and can normally be opened from outside only using a code. His colleagues outside the cockpit were trying to enter the code, but the attacker was preventing the door from being opened."The only way to open the door was to reach the knob and like any other knob, just to twist it open and it opens on its own," Machchhar said."There is no pin, but yes, the door, it was, it was a short, quick twist, but the point was to reach to that point, to reach to that place."Once he reached the knob, Machchhar said he was able to twist it open.
Netanyahu invites Machchhar to Israel
Netanyahu repeatedly praised Machchhar during the conversation, calling him a hero of India, Israel and the world."I, frankly, I'm amazed at your courage, at your coolness of judgement under impossible conditions," Netanyahu said.He said Machchhar's actions had helped save lives and described the incident as an example of how courage could overcome violence."You're a hero of Israel. You're a hero of India. You're a hero of the entire world," Netanyahu said.The Israeli prime minister also said Machchhar would be welcomed in Israel and invited him and his family to visit.Netanyahu said he wanted Machchhar and PM Modi to light a celebratory flame at Israel's next Independence Day ceremony. He described the honour as one usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
"I really would like them to bear a celebratory flame. It's our highest honour that we give in our Independence Day. It's usually reserved for Israeli citizens," Netanyahu said."But I think here in this case, all the citizens of Israel will, will embrace you. They do now and they will then too."Machchhar thanked Netanyahu and said he looked forward to meeting him in Israel.Netanyahu ended the conversation by wishing the pilot a speedy recovery and saying his visit to Israel would be "memorable and historic".

Jim Chalmers flags savings package and downplays chance of cost-of-living relief
In short:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says a budget savings package will be delivered before the end of the year.
The prime minister had indicated this week that cost-of-living relief measures could be on the way for households.
What's next?
Mr Chalmers warned the cost of servicing government debt would rise by billions of dollars as borrowing costs around the world increase.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has vowed there will be more savings in the mid-year budget update but downplayed the prospect of more cost-of-living relief for Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had indicated this week help was on the way for households, but Mr Chalmers said the government was looking to run a "tight ship" because of sustained pressure on the budget.
He told Insiders a savings package would feature in the budget update, which is due in mid-December.
"One of the primary influencers on the mid-year update will be the need to find more savings,"
he said.
"There is very, very substantial and intensifying pressure, not just on our budget but on budgets around the world."
The treasurer said the package would be influenced by the inflation challenge and the "helpful and responsible role" the government "intend to play" to see that figure come down over time.
"So we can get real wages growing again and so some of this pressure can come off people," he said.
On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to a 15-year high.
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said she would not "play the blame game", but warned inflation "isn't all about the Middle East conflict".
On Sunday, Mr Chalmers said "no serious observer" would disagree the war in the Middle East was putting "very substantial" pressure on the Australian economy.
He said additional government spending had been concentrated in areas such as bulk billing, to ease pressure on family budgets.
The Coalition had argued the government was spending too much and had contributed to inflation.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson labelled Mr Chalmers a "disastrous treasurer" and called for him to step down.
"He's actively stoked inflation, and he's fundamentally undermined the success of this country," Mr Wilson said.
Mr Chalmers said the government was not actively considering another discount of the fuel excise discount.
Bond spike to add billions to budget bill
The treasurer also warned the cost of servicing government debt would rise by billions of dollars as borrowing costs around the world increased.
US government bonds were heavily sold off last month, in a sign investors were demanding higher returns to lend money.
Bonds are essentially IOUs issued by governments to borrow money and are bought and sold by large investment funds as well as individual investors.
The bond market is generally seen as safer than the share market, but big swings in bond prices can be an early warning sign of financial stress.
Mr Chalmers said the government's trillion-dollar debt burden would balloon as cheaper debt is paid off, and the government is forced to turn to new, more expensive borrowing options.
"This spike in borrowing costs in the major economies will also play out here," he said.
"The pressure will still come to Australia, unfortunately, and you'll see in the billions of dollars the magnitude of pressure, coming from those bond yields which are changing so quickly."

Serbian populist leader Vucic launches campaign for prime minister
Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic is seeking to extend his hold on power through a parliamentary vote.
Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has launched his campaign for prime minister ahead of a pivotal election on October 25.
Thousands of supporters of the populist politician packed the largest indoor arena in Belgrade on Saturday, as Vucic pledged a “comprehensive” victory in the upcoming parliamentary vote.
The snap election, which polls suggest could be tight between Vucic’s party and a group of candidates fielded by a student-led protest movement, was called before Vucic resigned as president on September 27, cutting short his second term by more than seven months.
Dozens of buses from across Serbia clogged streets around Belgrade Arena on Saturday, as supporters arrived at the rally in the capital carrying Serbian flags and banners bearing Vucic’s picture.
The event, televised by dozens of channels across Serbia, capped a week of Vucic touring towns and villages in an apparent bid to shore up his popularity, which has been shaken after almost two years of sustained antigovernment protests.
Vucic, on the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) ballot, has dominated Serbian politics as president or prime minister since 2014. Barred from seeking a third presidential term, he is now seeking to extend his hold on power through the parliamentary vote.
If the SNS wins a majority of seats, the parliament is expected to elect Vucic as prime minister.
Youth movement
The youth-backed movement that led the protests has demanded accountability for the November 1, 2024, train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad.
The movement’s quest for justice over the tragedy and against corruption has grown into a nationwide political force whose electoral arm, the Student List, will attempt to oust Vucic’s government.
The Student List includes university professors, teachers, experts and others from across the political spectrum. Vucic accused those behind the movement of seeking to “bring Serbia to a halt” and claimed, without providing evidence, that it is backed by unspecified foreign agents.
On Saturday, Vucic told his supporters: “Absent an intervention of some [foreign intelligence] service, we will defeat them. And they know that.”

There's division in the Greens. Can David Shoebridge unite the party?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
00:25:18 UTC
09:25:18 KST

IN BRIEF
- David Shoebridge's election as the Greens' new leader has caused a rift among prominent party-room members.
- Experts warn Shoebridge's vow to "beat down One Nation" won't be possible unless the party achieves greater unity.
David Shoebridge has been chosen as the Australian Greens' new leader in an unprecedented ballot that has caused friction within the party.
The 11-member party room in Sydney selected Shoebridge on Wednesday, two days after former leader Larissa Waters announced she was stepping away from the role, citing chronic kidney disease.
Shoebridge faced strong competition from former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi — who quit her role to run for top spot — and the party's Senate business manager Sarah Hanson-Young.
Shoebridge won seven votes to four against Faruqi after preferences, while Hanson-Young was eliminated after the first ballot with only two votes.
Steph Hodgins-May won six votes to five against Vanessa Bleyer for deputy leader in a race for which Senator Jordan Steele-John had also been nominated.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"God, politics can be brutal," Hanson-Young said in a video to social media on Thursday.
"Friendships made and lost, but it takes all types. We all care so deeply about the future of this country and the future of the planet."
She said the Greens have a serious challenge ahead of them to defeat the "radical right" and One Nation.
"Australians deserve an optimistic, caring and defiant progressive force, and I won't be backing down," she said.
"I'm sorry we couldn't pull it off this time, but buckle up because we've got a lot of work to do."
Hanson-Young's comments came a day after Faruqi hit back at her colleagues for electing Shoebridge, saying the party's grassroots members deserve a chance to participate in future leadership elections.
She wrote on social media that she was "disappointed" and shared "members' frustrations" that the vote was open only to the party's 11 parliamentarians.
Problems of profile and party division
Zareh Ghazarian, associate professor of politics and international relations at Monash University, told SBS News that Shoebridge's victory was "a bit surprising".
He said that the Greens had "two really high-profile candidates" in Faruqi and Hanson-Young and either "would have been able to win the leadership".
Ghazarian said Shoebridge will have to "lift his profile" and establish himself as a national leader, adding that, compared to his leadership rivals, "he hasn't been as strong in terms of profile".
Ghazarian also doesn't lend much credence to Shoebridge's denials that tensions are running high within the party.
He said the Greens have never experienced "such tension about the leadership as they have right now".
"There's a sense that there's a bit of division in the party and it's coming at a really difficult time for the Australian Greens."
Political science expert and associate of the Australian Politics Studies Centre Ian McAllister told SBS News that Shoebridge's leadership shouldn't affect the party's popularity.
"In terms of how leadership affects the Greens vote, it affects them a bit less than it does for major parties," he said.
"Whoever is leader, it's probably not going to be all that important in terms of attracting votes."
However, he said perceived division in the party will affect the Greens' popularity.
"If people perceive it to be divided, then they're less likely to vote for it. If it's not united, there's a whole series of consequences, like people arguing in public, or voters not being clear about what the party's policies are," McAllister said.
He said division affects parties like the Greens more than major parties because they "don't have the discipline of being a government or government-in-waiting".
Ghazarian believes the Greens' current tension "goes to the heart" of the party's identity crisis — its struggle between being an activist party that "works at a grassroots level" and a "traditional party" that is "pragmatic and political".
"This is really at the heart of this week's frustrations ... the idea that grassroots members should be involved but that opportunity was there for the party."
"It's going to come down to how David Shoebridge tries to be a leader that incorporates everyone and even those who weren't elected, who missed out on the leadership role — how does he work with them? That's going to be a real test."
Speaking after his victory, Shoebridge vowed to "beat down One Nation" and expose Labor's "failures", while also signalling that his party would place a greater focus on cost-of-living pressures.
Ghazarian said One Nation has "squeezed out the minor parties in the broader political debate" so the Greens will be challenged to "cut through and be on the front foot".
"They have signalled that they want to have a combative, activist style of politics which may potentially go some way to drawing attention," he said.
"But, at the same time, they also have to demonstrate that as a party they can actually do things in parliament.
"They've got the numbers, they've got significant numbers compared to One Nation, so they have to show they're doing something with those numbers."
The Greens have struggled to increase their level of support, according to recent polling, despite declining approval of both major parties and the rising popularity of One Nation.
McAllister said the Greens' vote has remained "pretty static" for more than two decades — with the party consistently attracting only "10 per cent of the first preference votes".
He believes the Greens would be debating whether to double down on what they're already doing or take advantage of the current volatility that's pushing voters toward One Nation and independents.
"They could capitalise on this volatility and cast a wider net in terms of attracting not just disaffected Labor voters, but also disaffected Liberals as well," he said.
At the 2025 election, the Greens lost three of their four seats and their leader, Adam Bandt. They later lost senator Dorinda Cox, who defected to Labor.
But the diminished party Shoebridge now leads has more leverage in parliament: it now holds the sole balance of power in the Senate on bills not supported by the Coalition.
