Flydubai security failure: Who was supposed to vet the crew, and how did the system fail?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
00:18:50 UTC
09:18:50 KST

It can already be said that the attempted attack on the flydubai flight occurred because the field was left completely unprotected. The evidence: all the bodies involved in vetting foreign crew members on flights to Israel are already blaming one another. Either way, the incident must be treated as a successful terrorist attack - with all that implies, and the division of responsibility for screening foreign crew members landing in Israel must be urgently redefined, after Omani pilot Hamam al-Hamami boarded a plane bound for Ben-Gurion Airport.
Formally, responsibility for the screening lies with the Transportation Ministry’s security division, the Aviation Security Operations Center, or ASOC. It is supposed to provide security approval for foreign airlines arriving in Israel. At the same time, the Shin Bet is responsible for securing Israeli airlines. But the Transportation Ministry says it is not an intelligence agency and did not have the intelligence tools needed to examine the names of pilots and crew members on flights arriving in Israel.
A law passed by the Knesset in 2023 requires all airlines to transfer to Israel the details of their passengers and crew members, as part of arrangements connected to the U.S. Visa Waiver Program. That database is transferred to the National Passenger Data Analysis Center, which operates under the Tax Authority — but the Mossad, Shin Bet and police insisted that they too have access to it for counterterrorism purposes, and the information is also available to the Transportation Ministry. The data provided on crew members includes identification details, citizenship and travel document information.
According to its official mandate, the Transportation Ministry’s security division is responsible for aviation security, and its duties explicitly include the “security assessment of foreign flights crossing or arriving in Israel.” The division also operates the Aviation Security Operations Center, which deals with coordinating the security aspects of aircraft arriving in Israel.
The Transportation Ministry is the body that grants seasonal approvals to airlines that commit to complying with all security regulations. Flydubai, an Emirati state-owned airline, pledged to Israel that it would comply with all the rules and send only pilots from countries that maintain diplomatic relations with Israel. That commitment was violated, but that does not absolve Israeli authorities of responsibility for the failure.
Although Flydubai sent an Omani pilot to Israel in violation of its commitments, the Transportation Ministry says it did not receive the passenger and crew list from the Tax Authority, while the Mossad also says it did not receive the list, even though it was available.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev placed responsibility on the Mossad, which did not obtain the list. The only Israeli body that actually received the list was the Tax Authority, but its focus is on identifying criminals and money launderers, not terrorists. The conduct of all the bodies involved and the incident as a whole suggest that Israel had not considered foreign pilots to be a potential source of danger and had not taken into account a scenario such as the September 11 attacks.
It later emerged that the state comptroller had indeed warned in the past of failures in the field, and nothing was done. In May 2024, State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman published a report on the security of international civil aviation to and from Israel. The audit examined outbound aviation from Ben-Gurion Airport, the security of Israeli aviation abroad and the security of foreign and private civilian aircraft entering Israeli airspace.
The comptroller recommended that the National Security Council conduct a staff review together with the Transportation Ministry, Finance Ministry, Israel Airports Authority, Shin Bet and police, and examine international aviation security in Israel “in all its aspects” — including foreign aviation entering the country. Despite the recommendation to regulate the division of responsibility among the bodies, the National Security Council, which was supposed to deal with the issue, did not do its job and no one took responsibility.
The Transportation Ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center knows, for example, how to rigorously inspect private flights arriving in Israel. Why could the same center not inspect commercial airlines in the same way? On the face of it, the explanation is that it lacks both intelligence capabilities and the manpower needed to examine the large number of pilots and crew members arriving in Israel.
Either way, the state will have to establish a commission of inquiry and quickly bring order to the field — before a major disaster occurs that cannot be prevented at the last moment, as happened on the flydubai flight.
'Transportation Ministry did not pull the data for two years'
What can be said with certainty is that the passenger and crew list for flydubai flight FZ 1073 was transferred to Israel before takeoff, including the details of the Omani pilot. The Tax Authority confirmed that the full list was sent and received in accordance with the mechanism established under the Passenger Data Law.
However, according to several senior officials, the Transportation Ministry did not retrieve or examine data on crew members arriving on foreign flights to Israel for about two years.
That means the current incident was not necessarily the first time a crew member from a country that does not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel arrived in the country without that information being flagged to the officials responsible for conducting the flight’s security assessment.
At the center of the examination is the Transportation Ministry’s security division, whose official responsibilities include, among other things, the “security assessment of foreign flights crossing or arriving in Israel,” issuing security directives to airlines and conducting security assessments of transportation professionals, including those in the aviation sector.
The Aviation Security Operations Center also operates under the division. The division is headed by Avraham Cohen, alongside deputy security division director Tamir Uri. The question now is where the failure occurred and who was responsible for disregarding critical information about the identity of the foreign airline’s pilot — information that could have determined the fate of everyone on the flight.
Officials familiar with the details say crew data was not retrieved from the database for examination by the relevant official at the Transportation Ministry. Nor did the security agencies systematically examine the data that had been transferred.
As a result, even though the co-pilot’s citizenship was included in the information transferred to Israel, it did not trigger further scrutiny.
That is significant because the co-pilot’s citizenship was not a detail that should have become known only after the incident. The law requires airlines to provide Israel with data on passengers and crew members on flights entering, leaving or passing through the country.
The information includes, among other things, name, date of birth, sex, citizenship, passport number and the country that issued it.
The mechanism was established under the Law on Powers for the Collection and Analysis of Passenger Data, approved by the Knesset in 2023 and entering into force in April of that year. The law established the National Passenger Data Analysis Center and defined the permitted uses of the information, including preventing and thwarting terrorism and securing civil aviation.
The law also defines how access is divided among the various bodies. The Transportation Ministry, Tax Authority, Population Authority and Health Ministry may approach the center and conduct a query or assessment of information in the database. The Shin Bet, Mossad and police are permitted to establish branches of the database within their own organizations.
In the case of the flydubai flight, the Tax Authority confirmed receipt of the list, including the details of all crew members. The Mossad also had access to the data but did not check the list in a way that would have flagged the co-pilot’s citizenship.
It is important to distinguish between a security agency having access to the database and being required to manually check every passenger and crew list. The law allows the Mossad to establish a branch of the database, but it does not stipulate that every list must be individually reviewed by the agency.
Regev: 'The Mossad is responsible for foreign flights'
The gap now exposed concerns not only the existence of the information, but the way the various bodies are supposed to use it. As part of the review, the relevant authorities will have to examine how responsibilities are divided among the Transportation Ministry, the passenger data center and the security agencies, what instructions were issued for checking flight crew data and how extensively the database has been used since the law took effect.
If it emerges that crew members from countries that do not have relations with Israel arrived during this period without that information being examined, authorities will have to investigate the scale of the phenomenon, not only the flydubai case.
At the same time, the security establishment and Transportation Ministry will have to decide whether changes are needed in how crew data is checked and in which cases cross-checking or further examination is required.
Ultimately, the review will have to determine where the gap arose between the information transferred to Israel and the information that reached the body supposed to use it, and whether this was an isolated failure or a problem in the existing mechanism.
Regev already on Thursday night placed responsibility for the failure on the Mossad. In an interview with Kan News, she suggested waiting for the investigation in the UAE to be completed “to understand exactly what happened there and where the breach was,” but added: “The body responsible for centralizing the information is the Tax Authority, under a government decision made several years ago, and the list was indeed in its possession. The list was not transferred to us because the bodies that are supposed to carry out the identity checks on the crew are the intelligence agencies.
“Aviation security is a very complex issue. The entire intelligence field is divided between the Mossad and the Shin Bet. The Shin Bet is responsible for Israeli flights and charter flights, and the Mossad is responsible for foreign flights. Flydubai is a foreign company, it has nothing to do with the Shin Bet, it is connected to the Mossad. No security body said Israelis cannot fly on foreign airlines to Dubai. The bodies that are supposed to say what the threat level is and whether it is possible to fly to that destination are the security agencies.”
'There is no 100% in security'
At a briefing for reporters held several hours after Regev’s remarks, Transportation Ministry officials said the names had not been transferred to them in advance and that they “rely on a declaration by the foreign airline regarding security checks carried out on flight crew members.”
According to the ministry’s security division: “We are not an intelligence agency that checks the intelligence background of foreign individuals. We do not have forces abroad, and we do not have a team that checks every person there.”
Asked how many pilots from hostile countries had already landed in Israel and how passengers could be sure they were safe when boarding a foreign airline, the Civil Aviation Authority had no answer.
“We estimate there were none. But we have no certainty. There is no 100% in security. Only if we stop aviation entirely will everything be safe. We rely on local security,” it said.
Civil Aviation Authority director Shmuel Zakai stressed: “If there was a violation here, it will be investigated.”
Officials later said it was impossible to know with certainty who had landed in Israel in recent years and whether hostile individuals may have been among them.
Regarding the 2023 law requiring the transfer of data, Transportation Ministry officials said: “This is a center for collecting passenger data. It is a body that is not yet operational. The information is transferred to the Tax Authority, and from there it is supposed to be distributed to relevant parties — the police, Mossad and Shin Bet.”
However, they did not address claims that the ministry’s security division had not proactively retrieved the data.

War in Ukraine leaves over 15,000 civilians dead or injured in first eight months of 2026, UN reports
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
03:15:00 EEST
09:15:00 KST

War in Ukraine leaves over 15,000 civilians dead or injured in first eight months of 2026, UN reports
The United Nations has verified that more than 15,000 civilians in Ukraine were killed or injured as a result of Russian aggression during the first eight months of 2026.
Source: Volker Türk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
Details: Speaking at a meeting of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Türk said his Office had verified that 15,280 civilians had been killed or injured during the first eight months of 2026. This amounts to more than 400 people per week on average, 55% more than during the same period in 2025.
Türk stressed that the front line has changed very little, but Russian forces have systematically attacked residential buildings, schools, hospitals, railways and shops.
Nearly 2,500 civilians were killed or injured solely as a result of Russia's use of guided aerial bombs in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia oblasts during the first eight months of this year, 62% more than during the same period in 2025.
"The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is growing and intensifying by the week," Türk said.
He also reported a "shocking levels of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war". Of more than 1,000 documented cases, Russia was responsible for 89%. Most victims are men held in detention. Women and children have been victimised predominantly in occupied territories.
"This is just one terrible manifestation of the cruelty that has come to define this war. Alongside peace, there must be accountability," he stressed.
The high commissioner also called Ukraine "a laboratory for drone warfare" and urged the world to stop the bloodshed caused by these weapons.
Among other problems, Türk highlighted the intensification of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial facilities. Strikes on the food industry have already caused shortages of vegetables and dairy products in some regions of Ukraine.
Around 2,000 people remain trapped in the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, living without food, water, electricity or gas.
He urged the Russian leadership to "consider what this war is doing to their own society", which, he said, "puts death and destruction ahead of healthcare and education".
The high commissioner also expressed concern about the involvement of mercenaries from third countries in the war. Staff from his Office interviewed prisoners of war from 36 countries held by Ukraine, and many said they had been deceived into joining the Russian forces.
Background: In September, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine published a report stating that at least 372 civilians had been killed and another 2,349 injured in Ukraine in August 2026 alone. This month saw the second-highest number of civilian casualties in 2026 after July, when 448 people were killed and more than 2,600 injured.

North Korea launches ballistic missile over 700 kilometers as hostilities heat up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
00:12:09 UTC
09:12:09 KST

North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, its latest missile launch this year, which came a day after it rejected Seoul's accusation that its mines wounded soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at around 6:30 a.m. on Saturday and flew more than 700 kilometers (434 miles), the South Korean military said in a statement. Seoul and Washington were analyzing the test for details, it added.
Japan's coast guard, in an emailed statement citing the Japanese defense ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea's military said it has raised its monitoring of any further missile tests and will share intelligence with the US and Japan.
The South Korean presidential office's national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation after the missile launch, the office said in a statement.
North Korea tested missiles at least 10 times this year, ramps up hostility
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Pyongyang has sometimes said it was testing new types of weapons systems. Some of the tests have come after North Korea protested joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
The launch came after Pyongyang's Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone, a heavily fortified area between the two Koreas.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4-km-wide (2.5-mile) border that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.
The missile test may be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister's statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research center on North Korean affairs. North Korea may also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has sharply ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its "primary foe."

Emirati airline flydubai reportedly hired Omani national pilot Hamam al Hamami without conducting a background check with the Omani government, sources told CBS on Saturday.
Al Hamami was the co-pilot responsible for the attempted hijacking of flydubai flight FZ1073 to Tel Aviv on Wednesday; he stabbed the other pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, and nearly caused the plane to crash before several of the Israeli passengers and off-duty crew members managed to take control of the situation.
The Omani government had been monitoring al-Hamami during his tenure with Oman Air - the airline where he had previously worked - and discovered that he had visited extremist websites, according to the CBS report. This led to his being moved from a pilot position to an office role at the company, prompting his resignation and eventual move to flydubai.
At one point, sources told CBS, al-Hamami posted a video of El Al planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al-Qaeda leader who was killed in a 2022 US drone strike.
Al-Hamami lived outside Oman for most of his life, CBS's sources also noted, adding that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani. His dual citizenship may be the reason he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv, the sources said.
The Omani government has not confirmed his nationality, per the CBS report.
Flydubai pilot attempts terror hijacking of flight to Tel Aviv, foiled by Israeli passengers
One hundred and seventy-four Israeli passengers were returned to Ben-Gurion Airport Tuesday evening after a stunning series of events in which multiple passengers helped restrain an Omani hijacker-pilot who attempted to crash the airplane earlier in the day.
The passengers were initially on a flydubai commercial passenger aircraft flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, but then the pilot-hijacker, who was the deputy pilot for the flight, stabbed the lead pilot and tried to crash the aircraft before as many as four passengers wounded him and tied him up.
Israeli dentist provided life-saving care to Indian pilot after stabbing
An additional flight crew member on board was then able to handle landing the plane in Saudi Arabia, though the original pilot, a native of India, was in critical condition, having been stabbed repeatedly by the Omani pilot.
One of the Israeli passengers was a medical professional who helped stem the bleeding of the Indian pilot, who was reportedly in stable condition in Saudi Arabia.
Some of the passengers who managed to restore control of the plane credited the Indian pilot for opening the cockpit for them even after he had been stabbed, so that they could provide assistance.

Baseball in Israel gets a boost from Jerusalem’s passionate baseball mom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
00:12:05 UTC
09:12:05 KST

Basketball and soccer are the two most popular sports in Israel by a long shot. If Callie Mitchell, an American-born Jerusalem resident, Evangelical Christian, and mother of four with boundless energy, has anything to do with it, baseball may soon be creeping up on those sports.
Thanks to her knowledge of and passion for the sport affectionately known as America’s Pastime, baseball’s popularity is already growing in Jerusalem and in the Holy Land.
“There is much more interest in baseball than people realize,” Mitchell tells In Jerusalem. “Baseball has the potential to be associated with Israel.”
Mitchell has been connected to the sport in Israel, first as a baseball mom for many years, and now as the Jerusalem regional director for the Israel Association of Baseball (IAB) and director of the Jerusalem Lions Baseball nonprofit.
In these capacities, she has helped introduce baseball to Jerusalem residents from age five through adult. She is involved with many of the day-to-day nuts-and-bolts issues of running a baseball program in Israel, and she has big plans for its continued growth.
Can baseball become Israel's pastime?
Mitchell says that, in 2023-2024, fewer than 30 participants were in the Jerusalem league which tried to field four teams. One of her sons had been playing for 11 years, since the age of four, so she had a unique window into baseball in Jerusalem and Israel.
All it took was one meeting for Mitchell to quickly go from parent observer to active leader of Jerusalem baseball.
“At the end of the 2023/24 season, I was invited by the director and coaches to what I thought would be a bigger meeting. It was actually just them, and the director informed me that he was stepping down. He said, ‘It’s you!’” She quickly learned that two of four coaches would not be returning and that she would need to rebuild the staff and the youth and adult leagues.
Mitchell playfully shares about when she started in her new role: “I came in as a mom who had been in the program. I asked, ‘What did I feel was missing these past 10 years?’” She recounts starting with improved communication, a social media presence, and transparency.
“We had 12 baseballs when I took over. I wanted the parents to see that their fees went to what their kids were doing!”
Mitchell immediately sought to increase funding to purchase additional equipment. Through crowdfunding and later more systematic fundraising, she acquired four batting helmets for each of six teams: “It was as simple as putting my heart into it and caring – like a garden that needs tending and weeding.”
Mitchell’s efforts are paying off. Last year, 75 people participated in Jerusalem baseball, and recently, over 90 people attended an open house. She expects 20 more people to sign up this year.
Mitchell has not only expanded numbers but also pathways to baseball, offering opportunities for new players as well as for those with a great deal of experience.
One key to her success has been listening to the parents. As an example, some parents reported that they signed up their children for baseball without realizing most games would involve travel outside Jerusalem, to places such as Efrat, Gezer, Beit Shemesh, and at times Tel Aviv and Ra’anana.
“I try to listen to people and see what they want and take their ideas seriously. I keep a list of their suggestions. I take feedback seriously,” she explains.
Mitchell now dreams of building a field and training facility in Jerusalem: “It will have an adult regulation field, Little League fields, an indoor training facility with batting cages, a weight room, and a space for infield practice.”
She envisions the complex hosting international tournaments where participants and their families can visit Jerusalem attractions such as the Old City and Hezekiah’s Tunnel. “Jerusalem is a great destination for international tournaments!”
'Baseball has been life from the womb'
Mitchell also imagines a day when players who grow up playing baseball in Israel could play college baseball in the United States, get drafted to Major League Baseball, and then return to Israel to continue giving back to baseball in Israel.
She is more than just a dreamer. She is a doer with passion and impeccable, lifelong baseball credentials that provide her with tools and connections to help her realize her Israel baseball goals. She elaborates on her somewhat hard-to-believe baseball credentials.
She cannot even remember her first baseball game or baseball memory. “Baseball has been life from the womb. It was always home for me!”
She reports, “I went to a baseball game every day of my life, from the day I was born to the day I moved to Israel (in 2009).”
Mitchell humbly shares that nine of her relatives – many with the surname Narron, including her father, Jerry Narron – have played and coached in the major leagues in the past 90 years!
“The first was my great-great-uncle, Sam Narron, drafted by Branch Rickey!” she shares, referring to the baseball executive and manager who broke Major League Baseball’s color barrier by signing Jackie Robinson in 1945.
Even Mitchell’s small talk is laced with baseball references.
She nonchalantly mentions that “Bob Boone [former MLB catcher, manager, and four-time All-Star] and the Boone brothers were my friends,” and she recounts hanging out with young A-Rod, Alex Rodriguez, when he played for the Texas Rangers from 2001 to 2003 – when her dad, a longtime Rangers coach, was appointed interim manager in 2001.
Mitchell and her four younger siblings spent their childhood summers on the road with various MLB teams, and she recalls how thrilling it was to overhear her father on the phone with general managers as she grew up.
Mitchell admires her father, who she says has been a highly respected role model on and off the field: “My dad had a 51-year career, and everyone respected his character.”
Narron was an MLB catcher for three teams from 1979 to 1987. In his first season, he was backup catcher to Thurman Munson and became starting catcher the day after he died in a plane crash in August 1979. Three months later, Narron was traded to the Seattle Mariners, until being released in March 1982.
The California Angels signed Narron, and he spent a few seasons in the minor leagues. The Angels released him in April 1987; the Mariners signed him again, then released him.
Narron retired as a player in 1989 and coached for and managed several teams, including the Orioles, Red Sox, White Sox, Rangers, and Reds. He also served as third base coach for Team Israel at the 2017 World Baseball Classic and as a coach at the 2023 World Baseball Classic.
Mitchell is particularly proud of her dad’s connection to Israel and to baseball in the Holy Land.
“He really loves Israel because of his own faith,” notes Mitchell. Like her father, she is deeply religious. “One of the biggest moments of his career was coaching in Israel.”
Yet, he always maintained his humble, respectful nature. “If there were an Israeli or Jew who needed his spot [on Team Israel], he would have stepped down.”
Her dad’s connections in the baseball world have already helped Callie in her work with baseball in Jerusalem. When she took over as director, Mitchell says, “I started the season with less than 12 balls until boxes arrived as a donation from my dad. He also gave us a set of catcher’s gear. He helped me get started.”
Jerry Narron also came through after Callie’s storage shed was flooded. Jerry’s dear friend Paul Goldschmidt, a first baseman and former teammate on the Arizona Diamondbacks, covered the cost of a new shed.
WHILE MITCHELL spends a lot of time setting up systems, dealing with logistics, and even using her architectural training to devise plans for a new baseball complex, she stresses that “the kids are the main focus of the IAB right now.”
At the same time, she hasn’t lost sight of the importance of getting young Israeli players to the next level: “We are really focusing on baseball in Israel. We want to make Israel baseball Israeli again, so local guys can play on the national team and represent Israel.”
For Mitchell, the journey to feeling more like an insider in Israel has not always been easy. In certain ways, she is “between” communities: “Since I’m not Jewish, I sometimes feel like I’m on the outside watching all the cool kids at a party.”
Most of Mitchell’s close friendships have been within the strong, present Evangelical Christian community in Israel, yet many of her experiences differ from theirs. “Most of them are here on visas, but I’m an Israeli citizen.”
Her children plan to serve in the IDF, following in their father’s footsteps.
Fortunately, Mitchell feels baseball has helped her feel more like an insider.
“Taking on the regional director position for Jerusalem baseball has made Israel home for me in a new way. Rather than life here feeling so foreign from my background, everything has finally converged. The baseball community has provided so many friendships and helped me to feel Israeli and like I belong.”
Mitchell is pleased that she has had so much support along the way. “The IAB president, Ari Varon, has been a huge source of encouragement to me. He’s helped me see that the value I bring to IAB is more than the proximity I have to Major League Baseball. It’s how baseball shaped me as a person.
“One time, I said something about how baseball is my second language. He lightheartedly corrected, ‘It’s actually your first language.’ I really appreciate that he values my perspective on baseball and also how baseball influenced my worldview. It’s been an honor to work with him this past year.”
The admiration is mutual. Varon says that “Callie Mitchel brings an incredible combination of energy, vision, and, most importantly, the ability to turn ideas into action. She is the engine of baseball development in Jerusalem and represents the standard we want our regional directors across Israel to aspire to.
“She is building from the ground up – bringing the youngest children into the game, developing players through every age and level, strengthening the Jerusalem Lions community, and creating a pathway toward high-level baseball.
“And she is thinking generations ahead, including a vision for a baseball stadium in Jerusalem that could stand proudly alongside professional facilities anywhere in the world. She isn’t simply growing a baseball program; she is building the future of baseball in Israel’s capital.”
Despite her successes, Mitchell continues to aim even higher – sometimes taking away from the credit she deserves. She paraphrases US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, who often points out that Israel has more Americans living abroad than any other country in the world (approximately 700,000 people). Mitchell adds, “We have Americans but not baseball!”
Mitchell is certainly doing her part, and she acknowledges that her efforts are “bearing fruit.” There is potential for ongoing growth.
Mitchell even sees baseball as a useful tool for promoting aliyah among American Jews. She says that “all olim bring something” from their country of origin to Israel: “American Jews bring a lot – education, and often wealth. They can also bring baseball into the country.”
She concludes, “The presence of baseball in Israel will help anchor American olim to Israel and maybe even draw them to come! It is like the Field of Dreams – if you build it, they will come!”

Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election
Latest polls suggest Lula’s lead over Bolsonaro is narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro have wrapped up their election campaigns, each voicing confidence in victory ahead of Sunday’s tightly contested first-round presidential vote.
Lula, 80, closed his re-election bid on Saturday with a march through Sao Paulo, Brazil’s economic powerhouse, drawing what his campaign called a record crowd for a closing rally.
“Tomorrow, we’re going to win the elections in the first round,” he told supporters, describing Sunday’s vote as a choice between “democracy and barbarism” and promising to “defeat the far right”.
He has also framed the election as a test of Brazil’s sovereignty, warning against “meddling” by Washington.
Bolsonaro led a motorcycle caravan through towns in Sao Paulo state, echoing the campaign style of his father, before rallying later in Rio de Janeiro. “I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round,” he said.
The 45-year-old is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The former leader, 71, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro was photographed at his rally holding a portrait of his father.
Trump has not formally endorsed Bolsonaro but has said he is watching the election “very closely”, a level of US interest that has become a flashpoint in the campaign.
Lula’s supporters have seized on it as evidence Washington is trying to meddle in the elections, while some Bolsonaro supporters, frustrated by the cost of living, say they would welcome US pressure if it helped force change at home.
Polls released on Saturday suggested Lula was still ahead but his lead was narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Such a result would send the race to a run-off on October 25 between the two frontrunners, a contest polls suggest would also be close.
It is a far tighter race than Lula’s last victory in 2022, when he beat the elder Bolsonaro by less than two percentage points.
Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign has faced scrutiny over a film-funding scandal. Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation over financing for Dark Horse, a biopic about his father, bankrolled by a jailed banker tied to one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals.
Brazil’s Supreme Court authorised federal police in April to investigate whether Flavio Bolsonaro made defamatory statements about Lula.
Bolsonaro has pledged to seek his father’s release from prison if elected, and has echoed his father’s unsubstantiated claims questioning the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system, which analysts say could be laying the groundwork to contest the result if he loses.
Beyond the presidency, Brazil’s nearly 160 million registered voters will also choose lawmakers, governors and senators on Sunday.
Right-wing candidates have gained ground in Latin America in recent months.

What is celebrated on October 4 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:53:03 EEST
08:53:03 KST

What is celebrated on October 4 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 4, the world celebrates World Animal Day and begins UN World Space Week. Lesotho celebrates its independence, and the faithful honor the saints.
On October 4, the world observes World Animal Day and begins World Space Week under the auspices of the UN, while the African state of Lesotho celebrates Independence Day. According to the new-style church calendar, the Holy Martyr Quadratus, one of the Seventy Apostles, is commemorated, and the finding of the relics of Saint Demetrius of Rostov is remembered; according to the old style, the Holy Martyr Hierotheus, Bishop of Athens, is commemorated, UNN writes.
World Animal Day
Established in 1925 on the initiative of German writer and conservationist Heinrich Zimmermann and officially approved in 1931 at the International Congress of Supporters of the Nature Protection Movement in Florence. The date was chosen in honor of the feast day of Saint Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals in the Catholic tradition. The observance aims to mobilize society to preserve endangered species, ensure humane conditions for keeping domestic and wild animals, combat cruelty, and develop environmentally responsible coexistence between humans and the animal world.
World Space Week
An official annual global UN event established by the General Assembly in 1999 (Resolution 54/68), held from October 4 to 10. October 4 was chosen to commemorate the launch of the first artificial Earth satellite, "Sputnik 1," in 1957, which opened the space age for humanity. The event promotes space science and technology, highlights the contribution of the aerospace sector to improving living conditions on Earth and monitoring the climate, and encourages young people to pursue science and technology education.
Lesotho Independence Day
The main national holiday of the Kingdom of Lesotho, commemorating the proclamation of sovereignty and the end of the British protectorate of Basutoland on October 4, 1966. The country gained full political independence as a constitutional monarchy under King Moshoeshoe II, and the holiday is marked by ceremonial parades in the capital, Maseru, traditional dances, and cultural events.
The Day of Remembrance of the Holy Martyr Quadratus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the Holy Martyr Quadratus, one of the Seventy Apostles, who preached Christianity in Athens and Magnesia in the 2nd century and wrote one of the earliest apologies (defenses) of the Christian faith for Emperor Hadrian. On this day, they also remember the finding of the relics of Saint Demetrius, a prominent Ukrainian church figure, theologian, writer, and author of the extensive collection of saints’ lives, "Chet’i-Minei."
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the Holy Martyr Hierotheus, Bishop of Athens—one of the members of the Athenian Areopagus, converted to Christianity by the Apostle Paul and ordained by him as Bishop of Athens in the 1st century. According to tradition, Saint Hierotheus was present at the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos, became renowned for his prayerful inspiration, and suffered martyrdom for his faith.

Great white sharks are increasingly swimming toward Canada&apos;s shores, and scientists have explained what is drawing them north
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Great white sharks are increasingly swimming toward Canada's shores, and scientists have explained what is drawing them north
Kyiv • UNN
Warming waters and the recovery of the seal population have increased the food supply for sharks off Canada's coast. Scientists are not recording a sharp increase in their numbers.
Great white sharks are appearing increasingly often off Canada's Atlantic coast, particularly near Nova Scotia. Researchers attribute this to the growing amount of available prey and changes in the marine ecosystem, BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
One such "visitor" was a nearly 4.2-meter-long great white shark nicknamed Contender. Just a few months ago, it was off Florida, but as the waters warmed, it headed north to Canada.
Over the past several decades, the seal population off the coasts of the United States and Canada has recovered significantly—they are one of the great white shark's favorite prey. At the same time, as the waters warm, more and more fish species are moving north.
Sharks are finding more and more food
Over the past 30 years, surface waters near Nova Scotia have warmed by approximately 1.5°C, while temperatures near the seabed have risen by approximately 3°C. More fish attract seals, which in turn attract great white sharks.
There are many food options for them in Nova Scotia. It is a fairly healthy marine ecosystem with many large animals they can feed on—seals and tuna
He does not believe that the overall population of great white sharks has increased sharply. Instead, individual sharks have begun visiting Canadian waters more frequently, remembering food-rich areas and returning to them.
As the number of sightings grows, so does the likelihood of encounters with people. In September, a great white shark attacked a diver off the coast of Quebec, but his injuries were not life-threatening. Experts emphasize that the risk of an attack remains very low.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton was chosen as the Trump administration's new AI czar, leading its response to artificial intelligence amid growing concerns about the risks of this rapidly evolving technology.
Clayton will lead a new White House task force, which will have 120 days to research and report on AI's risks and opportunities, and offer recommendations on the federal government's responsibilities regarding the new technology.
The group will be called the "Super Intelligence Force," or SI — the term President Donald Trump prefers over AI.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump said in a Truth Social post Sunday.
In addition to Clayton, the task force will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson; the Defense Department's Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer, Emil Michael; and Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management. The task force will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, the president said.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on Clayton's new role Saturday.
In September, Trump said in a Truth Social post that he would create a new "AI Force" to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said the post, which also announced plans to hire an AI czar.
"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" the president added.
Clayton is a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission and U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. The Senate confirmed him in July as DNI, giving him authority over 18 U.S. intelligence agencies.
The announcement comes days after AI industry leaders met with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House. The AI developers signed onto an agreement of voluntary safety standards that Trump said was "morally binding."
Despite dire warnings from within the industry and calls from AI leaders Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for federal guardrails on frontier AI models, Trump has so far opposed regulation.
In the same September post, Trump suggested AI fears were a hoax and blamed "Radical Left Dumocrats."
Venture capitalist David Sacks had previously served as AI and crypto czar under Trump, but in March said that his time as a special government employee had ended. Sacks is co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, a federal advisory committee made up of outside experts on technology, scientific research and innovation policy.

A 600-year-old hand cannon that could fire arrows and bullets has been found in South Korea
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:36:43 EEST
08:36:43 KST

A 600-year-old hand cannon that could fire arrows and bullets has been found in South Korea
Kyiv • UNN
The bronze hand cannon was made in 1377 or 1437. The inscription indicates that it may have been produced by the state.
In South Korea, researchers identified a bronze weapon found on Mount Geumseong as a hwanja hwathon — a handheld gunpowder firearm that could have been used to fire arrows or bullets. It was made about 600 years ago, ZME Science reports, according to UNN.
Details
The weapon was discovered back in 2023 in the southwest of the country, but it became known about only now. It is approximately 23 cm long and weighs about 900 g.
An engraving bearing the weapon’s name, its weight, and details of the production supervisor and craftsman, as well as a partially erased date, has survived on the handle. By comparing the inscription with historical documents, researchers concluded that the gun may have been made in 1377 or 1437.
A rare weapon from a transitional era
It comes from a decisive transitional period between the late Goryeo Dynasty and the early Joseon Dynasty, when physical artifacts of firearms were extremely rare
Another symbol was found on the muzzle, which may have been an inventory or production number. According to researchers, this could indicate that the weapon was made as part of organized state production.
The discovery provides scientists with rare material evidence of how early gunpowder weapons developed on the Korean Peninsula.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ centrist United List party is projected to win the greatest number of seats in the Latvian parliament with 35% support, exit polling commissioned by public broadcaster LSM showed on Oct. 3.
Votes are still being counted, with final results expected in the early hours of Oct. 4. The vote for the 100-member unicameral parliament — the Saeima — will be the second since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a war in which Latvia threw its full support behind Kyiv.
Latvians took to the polls on Oct. 3 to decide what their parliament will look like for the next four years. Affordability and security concerns have been top political issues in the Baltic country which shares a border with Russia and is home to a large Russian-speaking minority.
The election marked a test for Kulbergs, who has been prime minister since May. His predecessor, Evika Silina, was forced to resign following a political crisis triggered by a Ukrainian drone incursion into Latvian airspace. This led to a government collapse and paved the way for a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs.
Throughout his term, Kulbergs has expressed unwavering support for Ukraine, and Latvia has sharply increased defense spending since 2022, reaching 5% of GDP.
"Ukraine’s security is linked to the security of Europe as a whole, including Latvia," he said in a state visit to Ukraine in August.
Warnings from Western officials over an escalating hybrid threat from Russia is of particular concern to Latvia, an EU and NATO member which shares a border with both Russia and Belarus. Latvia is a key part of NATO’s Baltic defense structure on its Eastern flank.
While Latvia has said it sees no sign of an imminent conventional Russian attack, the Russia-Ukraine war has already spilled over into Latvian airspace, with several stray drones shot down by NATO planes.
The majority of Latvia’s electoral parties are pro-Ukraine, despite a third of the country speaking Russian as their first language.
If, as the exit polls suggest, United List wins 35% support, the party would still have to form a coalition government to achieve a majority.
The exit polls suggest the populist Latvia First party is expected to come in second with 11.3% support, followed close by the social democrat Progressive party with 11.1% of the vote. The Russia-friendly Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance is projected to win 10.8% of the vote, making it the fourth biggest party in the legislature.
Sovereign Power is the only political party in Latvia which opposes military aid to Ukraine.
The Latvian State Security Service (VDD) said that it was employing enhanced security measures to get ahead of potential Russian election interference, according to LSM on Sept 28. But no significant systematic interference had been detected, the VDD said.

Britain scraps heavily criticised plans to curb jury trials after backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:08:29 UTC
08:08:29 KST

Britain scraps heavily criticised plans to curb jury trials after backlash
- Britain has scrapped plans to limit jury trials for less serious crimes, responding to strong criticism from lawyers and politicians.
- The decision addresses concerns over defendants' rights but includes increasing magistrates' sentencing powers, which some fear could worsen court delays.
- The backlog of jury trials in England and Wales remains high, with nearly 81,000 cases pending, causing long waits for victims and defendants.
AI generated
LONDON - Britain will scrap plans to remove the historic right to trial by jury for defendants in less serious criminal cases, the government announced on Oct 4, in response to sustained criticism of the proposals by many lawyers and politicians.
The decision by Andy Burnham, who became prime minister in July, to drop his predecessor Keir Starmer's policy comes as hundreds of prisoners were released early to stop prisons becoming full, in just one element of a criminal justice crisis.
Plans to curb jury trials for cases where a jail sentence was likely to be less than three years would be abandoned, the Ministry of Justice said, which was broadly welcomed by the Criminal Bar Association and other groups.
But lawyers raised concerns over the MoJ's decision to increase sentencing powers for magistrates – who hear trials for more minor offences without a jury – and the removal of defendants' right to elect trial by jury.
"I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course," Justice Secretary Alex Norris said.
CBA chair Andrew Thomas thanked the government for "listening to the evidence and reaching the right verdict", though he said "a severe threat to our trial by jury remains".
The Bar Council's chair Kirsty Brimelow agreed, saying that giving magistrates greater powers when the backlog in magistrates' courts is increasing could be counterproductive.
Victims waiting for years for justice
The current backlog of cases awaiting trial by jury in Crown Courts in England and Wales was nearly 81,000 at the end of June, almost double the figure in 2020, and victims, defendants and witnesses often wait years for cases to come to trial.
Starmer's justice minister David Lammy in 2025 said reducing jury trials would speed up justice, but met a furious backlash from lawyers who said it curtailed the fundamental right of defendants to be tried by a jury of their peers.
Critics also argued that years of neglect and under-investment by successive governments, rather than jury trials, were the root cause of delays, while the head of England's judiciary raised "grave security concerns" for judges.
The MoJ said it would maintain plans that complex fraud trials could be heard by a judge alone, which has long been mooted to avoid jurors sitting on months-long cases, though a government-commissioned review in 2026 rejected the idea. REUTERS

Debris from missing medical plane found, US coastguard says
Six people were on board the Canadian-registered air ambulance jet travelling from Bermuda to Boston.
The United States coastguard has found debris from an air ambulance off the shore of Massachusetts’s Nantucket Island.
The US Federal Aviation Administration told the coastguard early on Saturday that it had lost contact with a Gulfstream jet travelling from Bermuda to Boston.
Several hours later, the coastguard said in a statement that it “located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft”.
The coastguard said that one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday for six people who were on board.
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers on board when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade International airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport.
Canada’s Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said in a social media post that four Canadians were on the plane.
“We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue,” MacKinnon wrote.
The other two people on board were Bermudian nationals, the coastguard said.
The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, departed Bermuda at 12:41am local time (03:41 GMT), according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware.
The plane was flying at 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) for much of the flight before descending 13,000ft (3,960 metres) in about two minutes shortly before flight controllers lost contact, data showed.
Last communication
Air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net offered a glimpse of the flight’s final communications before it went missing.
“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.
The pilot’s transmission could not be heard in the recording. The controller later confirmed the pilot was declaring an emergency just before losing contact with the plane.
The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram.
“We are praying that all six people will be found safe,” he wrote.
Latitude Air Ambulance is based in Ontario, Canada, and provides medical evacuation services. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) have introduced the Supporting Providers of English Language Learning (SPELL) Act to help address the national multilingual teacher shortage by increasing loan forgiveness from $5,000 to $17,500 for teachers of English learners (ELs). Representatives Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.-13) and Raúl M. Grijalva (D-Ariz.-07) introduced companion legislation in the House of Representatives.
Currently, if a highly-qualified teacher has been employed for five consecutive years in a low-income school, they are eligible for up to $5,000 of student loan forgiveness. Certain teachers who go into high demand subjects are eligible for an increased benefit of $17,500 of student loan forgiveness. Recognizing the growing EL teacher shortage, the SPELL Act adds EL teachers to this high demand category, making them eligible for additional debt relief.
Click here to find EL Teacher Education Programs that will Qualify for Loan Forgiveness
“Educating students learning English requires specialized instruction and unique teacher strategies,” said Senator Padilla. “Yet, we are facing a devastating shortage of teachers with the skills needed to support these students. By lessening the financial burden, we can help incentivize a greater number of passionate, and highly qualified teachers to enter and stay in the classroom.”
“Every student deserves a fair chance to succeed and thrive at school; teachers of English Learners are essential to making that possible,” said Senator Kim. “In the face of nationwide teacher shortages and attacks on critical education programs, this legislation would make it possible for more to answer the call to serve in our schools and to help generations of students along the way.”
“English Learners are among the fastest-growing groups of students in the country, especially in California, and it is crucial that they have qualified, passionate teachers in their classrooms,” said Senator Schiff. “The SPELL Act will encourage more prospective English teachers to pursue that path by ensuring the same loan forgiveness standards as math, science, and special education teachers. I am proud to join Senator Padilla in this effort, and I will continue to work with him to ensure that California’s students and teachers are in a position to succeed.”
The Department of Education has reported that 32 states have a shortage of teachers for EL students, making them unable to meet students’ needs and resulting in a discouraging academic achievement gap for this growing population. The cost of teacher preparation programs can be an obstacle for many to enter the profession, but data shows an association between teachers’ preparation level and their teaching effectiveness and retention. Research demonstrates that loan forgiveness programs are successful at encouraging teachers to take positions in fields and at locations where they are most needed, and forgiveness programs also help to support retention.
Specifically, the bill would provide up to $17,500 in loan forgiveness for teachers of ELs, bilingual students, and/or dual language immersion students. This matches the same level of enhanced forgiveness available to math, science, and special education teachers.
The SPELL Act is endorsed by organizations including TESOL, AFT, UnidosUS, and the California Community Colleges.
“At a time when the Trump administration seems intent on attacking English language learners, public school educators continue to fulfill their mission to serve each and every child who comes through their classroom door,” commented AFT President Randi Weingarten. “ELL teachers have dedicated their lives to helping kids, but student debt and the cost of living are dragging them down. The Supporting Providers of English Language Learning Act would allow ELL teachers to qualify for the highest level of Teacher Loan Forgiveness so they can pursue their careers free from the specter of permanent student debt.”
“To prepare students to succeed in school and beyond, they should have access early on to bilingual educators who understand their language, culture, and learning needs. Yet schools across the country continue to face shortages of bilingual and English learner teachers,” pointed out Carmen M. Feliciano, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy, UnidosUS. “The SPELL Act is a commonsense investment in strengthening that workforce by expanding student loan relief for educators who dedicate their careers to serving English learners and students in bilingual and dual-language programs. UnidosUS applauds Senator Padilla for championing this legislation and helping remove financial barriers to entering and remaining in the teaching profession. By investing in these educators, we are investing in the success of millions of English learners and in a stronger, more representative teacher workforce.”
Padilla also joined Senator Ben Ray Lujan (D-N.M) in reintroducing the Loan Forgiveness for Educators Act, legislation that would expand and modernize the federal loan forgiveness program for educators. This legislation would help address educator shortages and increase children’s access to a diverse and well-prepared educator workforce by strengthening the federal Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF) Program. In June, Padilla led Senate colleagues in condemning the Trump Administration’s attacks on English learners and the dissolution of the Department of Education’s Office of English Language Acquisition (OELA).

Ministers drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:01:11 UTC
08:01:11 KST

Ministers have scrapped plans that would have slashed the number of jury trials in England and Wales and replaced them with a judge sitting alone.
The proposals had sparked a fierce backlash from lawyers, who have welcomed the U-turn. But the victims’ commissioner expressed concern about the abandonment of measures drawn up by the then justice secretary, David Lammy, under Keir Starmer’s government, to tackle the record backlog in the courts.
There are almost 81,000 cases in the crown courts – with the number projected to hit 100,000 without the now-ditched changes – leaving victims and defendants waiting years for justice. The Ministry of Justice is selling the U-turn as a quicker way to address the problem, by saving the time it would take to set up a new judge-only crown court bench division.
The justice secretary, Alex Norris, said: “This government inherited criminal courts on the brink of collapse, with victims waiting years for their day in court. I remain committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice for those who so desperately need it. But I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the crown court and have made the decision to change course.
“This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.
“Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment.”
Lammy’s proposals came after a government-commissioned review by the former judge, Sir Brian Leveson, who recommended taking away the right to jury trial from thousands of defendants to prevent the criminal justice system from collapsing.
But critics, including Geoffrey Robertson, founding head of Doughty Street Chambers, where Starmer, Lammy and the attorney general, Richard Hermer KC, spent part of their professional careers, accused Labour of abandoning a centuries-old right and claiming that it would not reduce the backlog substantively. Some Labour MPs also opposed the move.
Legislation would have removed jury trials for defendants who were likely to receive a sentence of up to three years.
Ministers have not abandoned judge-only trials altogether, but they will only be for a small number of especially lengthy and technical fraud cases where the judge decides a jury trial is not appropriate.
The government will also retain Lammy’s plans to take away the right of a defendant charged with an “either way” offence to decide whether they will be tried by a jury in the crown court or magistrates. Instead those decisions will be in the hands of magistrates.
And the planned increase in magistrates’ sentencing powers – from the current 12 months maximum to 18 months, with an option to extend to two years – will still go ahead.
Kirsty Brimelow, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales, welcomed the new government’s “swift action” but said: “We underline that it is a dangerous experiment to increase sentencing powers of magistrates and remove the right to elect from defendants at a time when prisons are at capacity and the backlog of cases is accelerating in the magistrates courts.
She added: “We know that women, black people, mixed race people and older people elect jury trials more often than other groups and this proposal risks deepening existing disparities and exacerbating distrust in the justice system from minoritised communities.”
The Law Society of England and Wales and the Criminal Bar Association also welcomed the change of heart while expressing concern about pushing more cases to magistrates. The former additionally called for more investment, including in legal aid.
The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said: “Victims are entitled to ask whether what remains will be enough to meet the challenge [of delivering swifter justice]. “Indeed, they are being asked to place their faith in a plan that ministers themselves previously argued would not be.
“The lessons from the prisons crisis should be clear: postponing difficult decisions rarely solves problems. More often, it simply stores them up for the future.
“Victims need hope. They need to know this is genuine reform that matches the scale of the challenge: reform that will alleviate their prolonged suffering, rather than an easy compromise that delivers only marginal improvements today while leaving both the justice system, and the victims who rely on it, vulnerable tomorrow.”
The courts minister, Sarah Sackman KC, said other steps to tackle the backlog could include using AI to help list cases, more virtual hearings and ensuring defendants arrive to court on time.

Yemen's armed forces aligned with the internationally recognised government have launched strikes against Houthi targets across the capital Sanaa and the group's northern stronghold of Saada.
A spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces confirmed on Saturday that military units are striking "vital targets", without providing further operational details regarding specific facilities or casualties.
Earlier, the Houthi-run Al Masirah television network reported an attack on Sanaa, which it attributed to Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh offered no immediate confirmation or statement regarding the broadcaster's claim.
Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
Two AFP correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city.
In Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh.
Regional spillover
Also on Saturday, Yemeni army said it has killed at least 700 Houthi fighters in 257 operations across several fronts.
In a statement on social media, military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said government forces carried out the operations using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and rocket launchers.
The operations covered Sanaa, Midi, Baqim and fronts in Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda and Lahj, with the main operational effort concentrated on Taiz fronts, he added.
Targets included command and control centers, troop concentrations, combat buildups and reserves, weapons and ammunition depots, and military supply routes and transport.
According to preliminary battlefield estimates, the operations "neutralised at least 700" Houthi members and destroyed strategic and high-value military targets, along with 170 combat vehicles and assets, the spokesman said.
Direct conflict between the Houthis and internationally recognized government forces largely paused under a 2022 truce agreement.
However, armed clashes have resumed sharply as a direct spillover from the wider military confrontation between Iran and the United States.
Hostilities erupted anew this year after Houthi authorities declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July, launching cross-border attacks on Saudi territory and commercial shipping lanes.
Concurrently, Houthis seized significant territorial advancements along Yemen's strategic Red Sea coastline.
In response, Saudi Arabia has mounted retaliatory air strikes across Yemen, providing backing to government ground forces fighting to push back Houthi advances.

Insurance companies want policyholders to pay 10% of health claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:51:58 UTC
07:51:58 KST

The proposal, being considered by the General Insurance Council, would pair the change with common hospital empanelment and a formal mechanism for settling disputes between insurers and hospitals.
MUMBAI: Non-life insurers are considering a 10% co-payment by policyholders on retail health policies from Jan 1, 2027, with the patient's contribution capped at Rs 5 lakh per claim. In return, customers would pay lower annual premiums.The proposal, being considered by the General Insurance Council, would pair the change with common hospital empanelment and a formal mechanism for settling disputes between insurers and hospitals. The arrangement would require even those with comprehensive health insurance to keep funds for medical emergencies, as they would have to pay 10% of admissible inpatient hospitalisation costs, including those arising from accidents, whether claims are settled through cashless procedure or reimbursement.
Outpatient claims would remain outside scheme
The proposal covers retail indemnity products, retail-under-group policies, indemnity components of combi products, internal migrations and portability business. Outpatient claims would remain outside the scheme.Co-payment cannot be waived, reduced or modified through riders or endorsements, and the customer’s 10% contribution cannot be recovered from another health insurance policy.“The choice between a cheaper policy with a deductible and a full-compensation policy should rest with the insured.
People buy insurance to be indemnified for their costs. It would be unfair to customers willing to pay a higher premium for a higher sum insured to still bear part of the cost, and this could discourage them from buying high-value policies,” said Shreeraj Deshpande, a health insurance expert who earlier headed operations at a general insurer. While the industry is seeking to address what it sees as cost distortions in healthcare, some fear a mandatory requirement could be anti-competitive. “If the industry collectively decides that no one will offer a full-compensation policy, it might catch the attention of the Competition Commission,” said an industry executive.The logic behind the measure is that hospitals may order additional diagnostic tests, recommend procedures and extend hospital stays when patients have comprehensive insurance cover. Higher-category rooms can also increase total bills because doctors’ fees and procedure charges are often linked to room tariffs.
With insurance covering the full bill, patients may have less incentive to question charges or choose lower-cost hospitals.“This behaviour (overbilling and provider-induced demand) stems from the perception that insurance-backed patients are less price-sensitive, leading to inflated healthcare costs,” a council note said.The proposal also calls for common hospital empanelment, outcome-based contracts and a payor-provider grievance forum. GI Council plans standard empanelment across more than 4,300 hospitals to set benchmark tariffs and curb arbitrary billing, while linking contracts to clinical and procedure-wise outcomes.

“Oil is coming down. Oil is right now lower, and it's been lower than it was under the Biden administration, and they did nothing about the fact that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House to attend a rally in the state of Ohio.
“By the way, Iran, as you know, has virtually given up any plans of a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Iran has long denied accusations by the US and Israel that it seeks to develop nuclear weapons, a position reiterated by President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit last month to New York for the UN General Assembly.
Pezeshkian said Tehran is not seeking nuclear weapons because of a religious prohibition, and offered to dilute its enriched uranium stockpiles under international verification.
Iran, however, has maintained that it will not compromise on its peaceful civilian nuclear program or make structural concessions unless the US lifts economic sanctions.

Resource security key as global economy faces uncertainty: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

2026-10-03
22:19:22 UTC

The remarks assume significance amid global economic uncertainties triggered by US tariffs and conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, which have disrupted global supply chains and resulted in higher prices of key commodities.
NEW DELHI: Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Saturday said that amid uncertainty, “now a standing condition” of the global economy, national security requires structural autonomy in strategic inputs, as strategic resource security sits at the centre of macroeconomic policy.Besides, she argued for private investment to lead the cycle, including in research and innovation and skilling to prepare people for a changing world of work, while asserting that global financial architecture should reflect where growth was coming from.“We need to keep building resilience as we go along; it’s not a one-time exercise. The coming years call for preparation, and India approaches them from strength,” she said at Kautilya Economic Conclave.
The remarks assume significance amid global economic uncertainties triggered by US tariffs and conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, which have disrupted global supply chains and resulted in higher prices of key commodities.“A price shock can be cushioned with monetary and fiscal tools. But a quantity shock tests buffer stocks and the reach of delivery systems and therefore the capacity of the state itself,” she added.
Sitharaman said supply chains optimised for cost alone carry hidden fragility. To replace fragile single-source dependencies with domestic operational depth, the government has launched programmes focused on critical minerals and rare earths, semiconductors and small modular nuclear reactors.She said for India, resilience means building upon the structural foundations laid over the past decade such as entrepreneurial growth, focusing on efficient last-mile delivery, infrastructure creation and managing prices, essential supplies and external pressures. “The test of the coming years will again be partly invisible: the shocks India absorbs without disruption to households and enterprises.”The evidence of resilience lies in the counterfactual, in the outcomes that did not materialise, such as an inflation spiral that did not take hold, queues that did not form at the fuel outlets, banking stress that did not surface and a fiscal correction that was never forced. “These counterfactuals deserve as much attention from economists as the headline growth rate,” she added.
Talking about open, predictable and rule-based global economic relationships, Sitharaman said nations should engage with one another through dialogue and negotiated agreements, rather than allowing geopolitical differences to become barriers to trade and investment.

Red eyes, claws, and a mouth with three lips: Scientists discover two new species of sea spiders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:14:20 EEST
07:14:20 KST

Red eyes, claws, and a mouth with three lips: Scientists discover two new species of sea spiders
Kyiv • UNN
Two new species of sea spiders have been discovered in the Salish Sea, one of which has red eyes, claws, and three lips. Researchers do not rule out further discoveries.
Scientists have discovered two new species of sea spiders that had not been described in this region for nearly 100 years. One of them has red eyes, claws for capturing prey, and a triangular mouth with three lips covered in sensory hairs, LRT reports, citing the University of British Columbia, writes UNN.
Details
The new species were found in the Salish Sea between Canada and the United States. The specimens were collected during dives to depths of up to 18 meters from September 2023 to August 2024.
One of the new species was named Callipallene pilosuspedes. In addition to its red eyes and unusual mouth, its legs are covered with long, curved spines. Scientists even observed the spider using specialized limbs to "wash its face."
They can have up to 12 legs and breathe through their skin
Sea spiders appeared about 500 million years ago and are relatives of scorpions and horseshoe crabs. Some species have up to 12 legs, while their size ranges from less than 1 cm to more than 70 cm.
Some small sea spiders live as parasites on larger animals and suck fluids from them. The spiders themselves breathe through their skin, while males carry the offspring, attaching the eggs to their bodies.
The second species discovered was named Tanystylum kiixin. Researchers repeatedly found tiny parasites on its body, prompting one of the scientists to describe the spider as a kind of "ecosystem within an ecosystem."
Both species have already been added to a global database. Researchers believe that other marine creatures still unknown to science may remain in the area.

Hormuz blocked, but Gulf crude shipments at pre-war level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:13:59 UTC
07:13:59 KST

Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.
Disruptions to energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz notwithstanding, crude shipments from the West Asian Gulf region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels as countries cut dependence on oil tankers to navigate through the choked strait. According to maritime intelligence and research firm Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude left the region between Sept 1 and 28, matching the prewar average. During the peak of the West Asia war in March, the average was 10.5 mbd.
While 83% of the region’s crude crossed Hormuz before the war, 40% was exported in Sept through pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE without crossing the key chokepoint.Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.Belostrino said more than 70% of the crude that crossed the Strait of Hormuz in Aug changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman.
Crude via other routes made up the difference
Confirmed crude crossings were still more than a quarter below the pre-war level, but volumes moving through alternative routes had more than doubled and made up almost exactly the difference. Saudi pushed more crude through the east-west pipeline to Yanbu, with loadings rising from 0.8 mbd before the war to 4.3 mbd in June. UAE sent crude through the Abu Dhabi crude oil pipeline to Fujairah, where loadings rose from 1.1 mbd to 2.7 mbd.
325 million barrels released from oil reserves: IEA
The International Energy Agency said member countries had released 325 million barrels of oil and oil products from strategic reserves, out of 400 million barrels pledged in March.

Japan is considering transferring Patriot missiles to Ukraine, but there is an important caveat
