Japan is considering transferring Patriot missiles to Ukraine, but there is an important caveat
Kyiv • UNN
Tokyo is considering transferring Patriot missiles, likely PAC-3 CRI, to Ukraine. To do so, Japan needs to overcome legislative restrictions on arms exports.
Japan is considering transferring surface-to-air missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine, although it is not yet known exactly which type of munition is involved. Instead of the modern PAC-3 MSE, Kyiv may receive the older PAC-3 CRI, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
The possibility of transferring the missiles was announced by former Japanese Defense Minister and member of parliament Itsunori Onodera. The main obstacle remains restrictions under Japanese legislation concerning arms exports, which have been gradually eased in recent years.
Japan has 24 Patriot fire units and is one of the largest operators of these systems in the world. In addition, the country has localized production of modern PAC-3 MSE missiles.
Which missiles could Ukraine receive
Japan's armed forces operate PAC-3 MSE, older PAC-3 CRI, and PAC-2 GEM missiles. Defense Express suggests that Tokyo may transfer PAC-3 CRI missiles to Ukraine, keeping the newer PAC-3 MSE for its own needs.
PAC-3 CRI missiles are intended, in particular, to intercept ballistic targets. The newer PAC-3 MSE missiles have better maneuverability and approximately 50% greater range thanks to an upgraded engine.
PAC-2 GEM missiles also remain in Japanese storage facilities. They are less effective against ballistic targets but can be used against aircraft and cruise missiles.
It is currently unknown exactly which missiles Japan will ultimately agree to transfer to Ukraine and when this might happen. For the deliveries, Tokyo must also resolve legislative restrictions on arms exports.

US remains 'hell-bent' on preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, says Hegseth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:09:38 UTC
07:09:38 KST

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned Iran that US President Donald Trump remains determined to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, cautioning that Tehran must choose between relinquishing its nuclear ambitions and facing further American action.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Hegseth also declined to confirm whether the United States intends to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the region, saying his responsibility is to ensure that Trump retains the widest possible range of military options.
Asked directly whether three aircraft carriers would be deployed, Hegseth replied: “It’s a fair question, but I will never answer it.”
“I’d say maximizing the decision space for the commander in chief at any point is my job, while also recognizing the way we balance global demands as a force with global responsibilities,” he explained.
“So the president’s going to have options. Let’s put it that way, and I’ll leave it there.”
‘Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon’
Hegseth delivered his strongest warning when asked to clarify the administration’s message to Tehran.
“Well, the message is very simple: Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
“President Trump is hell-bent and determined to ensure that they do not. They will not. If they want to blink and think that he doesn’t mean it, it would be to their detriment.”
He added that Iran had reached a decision point.
“So now’s a moment where they can decide to give it up the way that they should, without any leverage that they have, or it may have to happen the hard way.”
Earlier in the exchange, Hegseth was asked whether he expected military operations to conclude before the end of the year. He declined to commit to a timetable, deferring the decision to Trump.
He nevertheless contrasted the administration’s approach with previous American military campaigns that, he said, had continued for years or decades without clearly defined objectives or an identifiable end state.
“As we’ve stated from the beginning, Iran will never have a nuclear bomb. Full stop. That is a vital national interest of the United States of America,” Hegseth said, citing Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.
He stressed that Trump would not allow operations to continue unnecessarily, arguing that the administration understands its mission and has the capabilities required to accomplish it.
Hegseth acknowledges Iranian efforts to rebuild missile capabilities
Asked whether Washington had evidence that Iran was attempting to reconstitute its missile capabilities and launchers, Hegseth said the United States was monitoring developments in real time.
He acknowledged that Tehran would attempt to rebuild its military infrastructure but maintained that the damage inflicted during Operation Epic Fury had severely complicated those efforts.
“Think of it this way, their Raytheons, their Boeings, their Lockheeds, their Northrop Grummans are what was destroyed in Epic Fury,” he said, referring to the Iranian equivalents of major American defense manufacturers.
“So they’re going to attempt to reconstitute, and they’re a terror state. So they’re going to always attempt to reconstitute, but when you’ve been so destroyed and degraded the way that they have, it’s a very slow process, a very frustrating process, and we see that, and we understand that.”
Hegseth argued that the extent of the damage to Iran’s defense industrial base, economy, and ability to rebuild would continue to constrain Tehran’s military options.
‘They don’t control the Strait of Hormuz, we do’
The defense secretary also emphasized American control over the Strait of Hormuz, describing the US blockade as a central component of Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.
“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it. We do,” Hegseth said.
“Our blockade has been ironclad, and we’re running almost at pre-war levels every single night through that,” he added, referring to maritime throughput.
Hegseth asserted that Iran’s naval and air capabilities had been so extensively degraded that it could no longer effectively challenge American dominance over the strategic waterway.
“It’s pretty tough for them to control the Strait of Hormuz when they don’t have a navy. They don’t have fast boats, and they’ve got no air force,” he said.
“And then we’ve done such incredible damage to their ability to see and sense the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. We dominate it in both an asymmetric and a conventional sense.”
He added that Washington was capable of maintaining the blockade for as long as necessary and adapting its implementation according to operational requirements.
“The longer we hold the blockade, and we can hold it as long as we need to. Trust me, we can adapt that as necessary,” he said, arguing that the pressure would further restrict Tehran’s remaining options.
Asked whether the conflict could ultimately have a military solution, Hegseth said it could be resolved in multiple ways and maintained that Trump had repeatedly offered Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement through negotiations.
“The president has given Iran every opportunity to do it at the table,” he said.
However, he reiterated that the combination of American military strikes and the continuing blockade had left Washington in a strong position.
“Iran ought to make the right choice. If they don’t, the president’s going to have all the options he needs on the table,” Hegseth concluded.

Indians live longer than Pakistanis, lag Bangladeshis, says WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:02:50 UTC
07:02:50 KST

The logic behind the measure is that hospitals may order additional diagnostic tests, recommend procedures and extend hospital stays when patients have comprehensive insurance cover.
NEW DELHI: Indians can expect to live longer than their counterparts in Pakistan, but have shorter lives than people in Bangladesh, the US and Canada, according to the latest World Health Organization estimates.India's life expectancy at birth was 71 years in 2023, compared with 68.2 years in Pakistan, 72.7 years in Bangladesh, 78.5 years in the US and 81.4 years in Canada. But living longer does not necessarily mean living more years in good health. India's healthy life expectancy was 60.6 years in 2023, compared with 60.5 in 2019. It had fallen to 58.4 years in 2021 before recovering to 60.2 years in 2022. The figures are part of WHO's Global Health Estimates, released Friday, covering life expectancy, healthy life expectancy, causes of death and disease burden from 2000 to 2023. WHO said global life expectancy recovered close to pre-pandemic levels, while healthy life expectancy has recovered more slowly.
In 2 years from 2021, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan: WHO
For India, the difference is particularly visible over the pandemic years. Life expectancy fell from 70.5 years in 2019 to 68.1 years in 2021 before rising to 70.5 years in 2022 and 71 years in 2023. In just two years, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan.Healthy life expectancy, however, recovered by only 2.2 years, from 58.4 years in 2021 to 60.6 years in 2023, leaving it just 0.1 year above the 2019 level.
The gap is also visible among older Indians. At age 60, a person could expect another 18.8 years of life in 2023, compared with 18.4 years in 2019. But 13.7 of those years were expected to be lived in full health, up from 13.4 years in 2019.India’s disease profile has changed sharply. Communicable diseases, such as tuberculosis and diarrhoeal infections, can spread from person to person, while non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as heart disease, stroke and diabetes, are generally long-term conditions.In 2000, communicable diseases accounted for nearly 62% of the combined death rate from the country’s 10 leading causes, while NCDs accounted for 34%. By 2023, the pattern had reversed, with NCDs accounting for nearly 75% and communicable diseases 16% of the combined death rate from the top 10 causes. The rest was from injuries.
The shift is evident in the leading causes. In 2000, tuberculosis and diarrhoeal diseases topped the list, with 92.4 and 87.8 deaths per 100,000 population. By 2023, ischaemic heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stroke and diabetes were among the leading causes, with rates of 138.5, 83.19, 74.8 and 49.01, respectively. Yet infectious diseases remain a significant burden, with diarrhoeal diseases, tuberculosis and lower respiratory infections still among India’s top 10 causes of death in 2023.Globally, the shift towards chronic diseases is also pronounced. NCDs accounted for 74% of deaths in 2023, up from 58% in 2000, while eight of the world’s 10 leading causes of death were NCDs. Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, almost back to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019, while healthy life expectancy stood at 62.8 years, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

====================================================================================================

Americans often fail to notice when Democrats and Republicans are moving in the same direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:00:25 UTC
07:00:25 KST

Informing people about how the political attitudes of opposing parties are moving in the same direction over time might help reduce partisan hostility. New research published in Political Psychology suggests that people frequently fail to notice how much support for certain social issues has grown within both parties. When people read about these shared trajectories of opinion change without being reminded of the current gap between parties, they tend to expect more future common ground and report slightly warmer feelings toward their political opponents.
To understand how political divides operate, psychologists often look at descriptive social norms, which are individuals’ perceptions of what other people believe or do. In politics, perceptions of these norms are frequently distorted. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicated that both Democrats and Republicans overestimate how much the opposing party dislikes them. When people assume their political opponents hold extreme or hostile views, it often drives further polarization.
Researchers often try to correct these false assumptions by presenting static norms, which describe the current level of support for a specific issue within a group. However, static norms only capture a single moment in time. Dynamic norms, on the other hand, describe how a group’s beliefs or behaviors are changing over time. A 2017 study found that showing people a trend is growing in popularity can persuade them to adopt new behaviors, even if current support is relatively low.
Applying this idea to politics requires overcoming another layer of misperception. A 2022 study indicated that Americans often misjudge how public opinion has shifted over decades, usually overestimating how much attitudes have changed, especially in a liberal direction. The authors of the new study set out to test whether correcting misperceptions about these trends could soften partisan hostility. How such a message is framed may matter: a 2021 paper argued that describing partisan divisions can make division seem like the norm and inadvertently deepen polarization.
The research was led by Trystan Loustau, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at Boston College. “A lot of research shows that Democrats and Republicans have distorted perceptions of one another, and that these misperceptions can make political divisions seem larger than they really are,” Loustau told PsyPost. “But most of that work focuses on a snapshot of the present: what Democrats or Republicans believe right now. We were interested in whether people also misperceive change: even when members of both parties are moving in the same direction on an issue, do people recognize that convergence?”
“That seemed especially important because the direction people think society is moving may shape how they imagine its future,” Loustau explained. “If you believe the two parties are becoming increasingly divided, you might respond very differently to political opponents than if you believe there are areas where they are gradually finding more common ground.”
In the first study, 368 Democrats and Republicans estimated current support and changes in support for 12 social issues on which support had actually risen in both parties. The researchers found that participants systematically underestimated attitude change. Only about half of the estimates accurately recognized that support for these issues was increasing. They also underestimated current levels of support by about 12 points for Democrats and 20 points for Republicans.
Misperceptions were especially pronounced when evaluating Republicans. Only about 25 percent of Democrats’ estimates and 44 percent of Republicans’ estimates regarding Republican attitude changes were accurate, compared to 77 percent and 66 percent accuracy for Democratic attitude changes. This finding is in tension with the 2022 study: here, participants often missed real increases in support for progressive positions, especially among Republicans. The authors suggest people may expect Democrats, but not Republicans, to move left.
In addition, the researchers found a correlation between recognizing these trends and intergroup attitudes. For every additional 10 percent of estimates that correctly identified change in the opposing party, participants felt about 3 points warmer toward that party on a 0-to-100 scale. This association held after accounting for accuracy about current support, which itself was unrelated to warmth.
“Political disagreement is real, but our perceptions of it are not always accurate,” Loustau pointed out. “We may be particularly bad at noticing when attitudes are changing.”
To see if correcting these misperceptions could help, the researchers randomly assigned 1,187 partisans to a dynamic norm condition, a static norm condition, or a control condition featuring apolitical topics. The dynamic norm message provided both the past and current levels of partisan support alongside the percentage-point increases over time. The static norm message only provided current support levels.
The results indicated that the dynamic norm group expected more future common ground between parties than the control group. Combining the current support levels with the trend data did not produce broader positive changes in attitudes toward the outparty, meaning the opposing party, such as warmth or expectations of belonging. The authors suggest that presenting the current levels of support alongside the trend may have inadvertently reminded participants of the existing gaps between the parties.
For the third study, the team refined the intervention using a new sample of 1,154 participants. This time, the dynamic norm condition isolated the trend information by completely removing references to current levels of partisan support. The message focused solely on how support had grown within each party over time. Participants were randomly assigned to read the refined message, the original combined message from the second study, the static message, or the control material.
The refined message increased expected common ground and expected future feelings of belonging with the outparty. People who read it reported outparty warmth of about 32.5 on a 100-point scale, compared to 25.9 in the control group, and also rated members of the other party more positively. The researchers noted that a recent review of 77 depolarization interventions found an average gain of about 5.4 points in outparty warmth, making the refined message’s 6.6-point difference comparable to that average.
The refined message was the only one to outperform the control condition on all four of these measures. On warmth and positive evaluations, however, it did not statistically outperform the original combined message or the static message, and the static message also raised warmth relative to control. No version of the message changed how much people saw the other party as overlapping with themselves.
“What surprised me most was how much the way we presented the same information mattered,” Loustau said. “It was a useful reminder that more information is not necessarily better: emphasizing how far apart the parties remain may overshadow evidence that they are moving in the same direction.”
He added, “The broader takeaway is that focusing exclusively on today’s partisan divisions can obscure meaningful ways in which public opinion is changing.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that showing partisans how much their core personal values overlap increased perceived similarity, strengthened beliefs that compromise is possible, and made people more hopeful. That study focused on present-day overlap in values, whereas the new study focused on how opinions on specific issues have shifted over time.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The sample was an online group of participants rather than a nationally representative one, and outcomes were measured right after reading the messages, with no follow-up.
The study also relied on real statistics for issues that were primarily progressive in nature, so it is not known whether these effects would hold for conservative policies or in different political contexts. Using real polling data also meant the researchers could not test larger shifts in opinion, and many of the real changes they presented were modest.
“The effects on attitudes toward the opposing party were small, and I think it is important to be clear about that,” Loustau noted. “A brief informational message is not going to eliminate partisan polarization. At the same time, polarization is a large, persistent social problem, so even small changes produced by a relatively minimal intervention can be informative, particularly because the intervention consisted simply of changing which accurate information about public opinion people saw.”
“I would view the findings less as evidence for a single solution to polarization and more as evidence that people’s expectations about where political groups are headed can influence how they think about those groups in the present,” he observed.
It is also possible that emphasizing negative trajectories could have the opposite effect. Messages highlighting increasing disagreement or polarization might inadvertently increase hostility. Future research could explore whether this kind of dynamic messaging works for other intergroup conflicts, such as those involving race or religion, and whether the observed changes in attitude persist over longer periods of time.
“Long term, I’m interested in what happens when we encourage people to think about political differences in a more future-oriented way,” Loustau said. “Rather than focusing only on how different we are right now, I want to understand what changes when people recognize both their own and others’ capacity to change. That shared capacity may itself be a form of common ground, opening space to imagine not just what society currently looks like, but what we want our relationships and world to look like in the future.”
The study, “Partisans misperceive and are influenced by dynamic norms,” was authored by Trystan Loustau, Ashley Fabrizio, Liane Young, Jordan Wylie, and Stylianos Syropoulos.

Details

The search-and-rescue operation is under way in the waters near Nantucket Island in Massachusetts. U.S. Coast Guard aircraft and maritime crews have been involved.
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board is also collecting information about the incident. There is currently no information about the fate of the 6 people on board.

Unknown Publisher

05:56:12 CST
06:56:12 KST

ATHENS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- The growing presence of Chinese car brands has been showcased at AUTO ATHINA 2026, an international auto show that began Saturday in the Greek capital of Athens.
The auto show, which runs from Oct. 3 to 11 at the Metropolitan Expo in Athens, features 52 brands, the largest number in the show's history. More than a dozen Chinese brands are among the exhibitors.
Chinese cars are drawing attention in Greece for their competitive prices and technological features, according to dealers and visitors to the auto show.
Thomas Kouris, a visitor to the BYD booth, said the cars' high quality, competitive prices and electric vehicle(EV) subsidies had prompted him to take a closer look at Chinese brands.
For Nikos Ioannou, a visitor to the Chery booth, the driving experience was important. He said Chinese cars offered reliable performance, good driving dynamics and competitive prices.
"They are very good cars. They turn well, brake well, ride well, have a lot of technology, and offer incredible prices," he said.
The growing presence of Chinese automakers, which have begun entering the Greek market in recent years, is also reflected in statistics.
Chinese brands accounted for nearly 10 percent of new passenger car registrations in Greece in the first eight months of 2026, according to data from the Association of Motor Vehicle Importers-Representatives (AMVIR).
BYD has registered more than 6,000 electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles in Greece since entering the market in March 2024, with registrations up by 47 pct in the first eight months of 2026 from the same period last year, Yiannis Kakouris, public relations manager for BYD at Greek dealer Sfakianakis Group, told Xinhua.
At Chery's booth, George Spanos, CEO of Greek dealer Spanos SA, said Chery had achieved strong retail sales in September, with the Tiggo 4 hybrid among its leading models.
The growth comes amid a broader shift in consumer demand toward EV, according to an analysis by AMVIR based on new-car registration data from the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT).
Hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) remained dominant, accounting for 57.7 percent of new-car registrations in the January-August period, compared with 49.2 percent a year earlier.
Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) accounted for 6.7 percent of new-car registrations, up 1.4 percentage points from the same period last year, while plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) accounted for 6.3 percent. Gasoline-powered cars accounted for 24 percent, down 8.4 percentage points year-on-year.
That market mix has also created opportunities for Chinese manufacturers, many of which have entered Greece with hybrid models alongside fully electric vehicles.
"The trend is toward new-technology vehicles that definitely have a battery and an electric motor. However, hybrids are still more popular," Spanos said.
"Chinese cars are now embraced by Greek consumers," he added. ■

Students from Germany's Burg Chinese Chorus and Yunnan University Secondary School performed a selection of Chinese songs at the concert, drawing warm applause from an audience of around 200.
The Burg Chinese Chorus is a non-profit organization that runs a "Learn Chinese by Singing" program for young people in Germany. Combining language learning with music and exchange activities, the group works to promote people-to-people ties between the two countries.
Olaf Millmann, chairman of the Burg Chinese Chorus association, said in his speech that learning through singing offers young Germans an accessible way to take their first steps in Chinese.
"A song can spark curiosity and make people want to understand more," Millmann said. "That curiosity can then create the motivation to continue learning the language and to get to know the people who speak it."
For 18-year-old chorus member Nikolaos Topoulos, that interest in Chinese has grown steadily since he began studying the language about two years ago. He told Xinhua that joining the chorus had helped him improve his vocabulary and spoken Chinese a lot. "I really like Chinese and want to keep learning it."
In July, he traveled to China with the chorus, visiting Beijing, Kunming and other cities. He said he was impressed by China's vastness, vitality and the warmth of its people. "Wherever we went, people were very friendly and welcoming," he said, adding that he plans to apply to China's Sichuan University after graduating from high school.
Zhang Yungang, leader of the chorus, told Xinhua that the "Learn Chinese by Singing" program has been running for more than a decade, introducing many young Germans to the Chinese language. Some have later studied in China or pursued careers related to China-Germany business and cultural exchanges.
"When they sing together, their hearts come together," Zhang said, adding that more than a decade of experience has strengthened his belief in music as a way to sustain youth exchanges between the two countries. ■

Greece, Bulgaria sign protocol for return of cultural artefacts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:55:20 CST
06:55:20 KST

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev (1st L) and other officials welcome the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, who ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, at the airport in Sofia, Bulgaria, Oct. 3, 2026. Greece and Bulgaria signed a protocol Saturday on the reciprocal handover of cultural artefacts, under which 48 Greek artefacts will return from Bulgaria, while Greece will hand over to Bulgaria the remains identified as those of medieval Bulgarian ruler Tsar Samuel, Greek national broadcaster ERT reported. After the handover ceremony in Greece, the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, who ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, arrived in Bulgarian capital of Sofia on Saturday. (Photo by Bulgarian Government Information Service/Xinhua)
ATHENS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Greece and Bulgaria signed a protocol Saturday on the reciprocal handover of cultural artefacts, under which 48 Greek artefacts will return from Bulgaria, while Greece will hand over to Bulgaria the remains identified as those of medieval Bulgarian ruler Tsar Samuel, Greek national broadcaster ERT reported.
The protocol was signed by the two countries' culture ministers at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki, northern Greece, in the presence of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev.
The 48 artefacts are being displayed at the museum until Nov. 5, 2026, after which they will be returned to their institutions of origin: the Monastery of Panagia Eikosifoinissa, the Monastery of Timios Prodromos in Serres, and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita.
After the handover ceremony in Greece, the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, who ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, arrived in Bulgarian capital of Sofia on Saturday.
The remains were discovered in 1965 during archaeological excavations at the Basilica of St. Achillius in Prespa in northern Greece and have since been kept at the Museum of Byzantine Culture. The Prespa area was a center of Tsar Samuel's rule in the late 10th century, and the basilica is believed to have been built by him as a major religious center.
The two countries also agreed to continue talks on identifying other historical objects of mutual interest that could be included in a future agreement. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: Why G7 agrees to release fuel reserves, how helpful will it be?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:55:19 CST
06:55:19 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Group of Seven (G7) leaders agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an action coordinated through the International Energy Agency (IEA), as surging fuel prices, disrupted refined-product supplies and threatened U.S. export restrictions added pressure on global energy markets.
Under the agreement, the 100 million barrels will be released over four months, starting immediately, with a substantial amount of diesel to be frontloaded within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners.
The G7 did not specify how much of the total would be diesel or crude oil, or how many individual countries would contribute. It said further diesel releases could be considered if necessary.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said Friday that around 325 million barrels have so far been released under the collective action announced in March, representing more than 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged, the largest move of its kind in the agency's history.
The group also agreed to coordinate refinery maintenance to avoid simultaneous shutdowns, temporarily raise refinery utilization where possible and encourage countries with significant refining capacity to increase production, particularly of diesel.
Pressure has been acute in global fuel markets, particularly diesel, as two major sources of diesel and gasoil supply have been hit at the same time.
Net diesel and gasoil exports from Gulf countries averaged just slightly more than a quarter of pre-U.S.-Iran war levels, as flows through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely constrained, according to the IEA.
Birol also said that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have added to the pressure on diesel supplies, pushing up prices.
Europe has felt the strain acutely. The European Commission said Friday that diesel prices had doubled since the end of February when the U.S.-Iran war started, contributing to what it described as an "affordability crisis."
EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday that the bloc had paid more than 100 billion euros (about 113.3 billion U.S. dollars) extra for fossil fuel imports since the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, without receiving additional energy.
The decision also followed mounting transatlantic friction over how to respond.
The Trump administration had pressed European governments to draw down more emergency diesel stocks and warned that restrictions on U.S. diesel exports could follow if Europe did not act.
The threat carried weight for Europe. The European Commission said last week that the United States accounted for around half of EU diesel imports in August, making the bloc highly exposed to any disruption in U.S. supplies.
Hours before the G7 agreement, the Commission publicly rejected the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban, saying such a move would benefit neither side and undermine trust in the United States as a reliable partner.
The eventual G7 agreement combined coordinated reserve releases with a commitment to refrain from restricting energy exports among members, a move later welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Analysts say the release could provide meaningful short-term relief, particularly if large diesel volumes reach the market quickly.
Alan Gelder, senior vice president for refining, chemicals and oil markets at Wood Mackenzie, estimated that a major diesel stock release could lower wholesale prices by 20 to 30 U.S. dollars per barrel.
But the effect may prove temporary. Gelder said further stock releases essentially buy time while global diesel supply remains below demand and inventories continue to be drawn down, adding that the EU continues to be vulnerable to the export policies of others such as the United States.
Ultimately, the longer-term stability of prices will depend on the restoration of refined-product flows from the Middle East. But with the U.S.-Iran conflict proving difficult to resolve, a swift return to more stable flows may remain out of reach. ■

Does a new plague epidemic threaten the world because of the case in Russia, and how dangerous is the disease today?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
00:38:06 EEST
06:38:06 KST

Does a new plague epidemic threaten the world because of the case in Russia, and how dangerous is the disease today?
Kyiv • UNN
A suspected case of pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast claimed the life of a laboratory technician, and around 200 contacts were isolated. The WHO considers a global epidemic unlikely.
Reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Russia's Irkutsk Region, where a 28-year-old employee of a plague-control institute died and about 200 of her contacts were isolated, have raised concerns about the possible spread of the dangerous infection. However, modern plague, despite its high risk, no longer poses the same global threat as it did during historic pandemics, since it can be effectively treated with antibiotics, the WHO reports, UNN writes.
Details
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The disease has not disappeared: natural foci exist in various parts of the world, while the largest number of cases in recent years have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.
The pneumonic form of plague is considered the most dangerous. Unlike the much more common bubonic form, it can be transmitted directly from person to person through respiratory particles. Without treatment, pneumonic plague is almost always fatal, and the patient's condition can deteriorate extremely quickly.
Could plague cause an epidemic like the one in the Middle Ages again?
Theoretically, yes. The WHO emphasizes that pneumonic plague, due to its ability to spread between people, can cause serious outbreaks. However, the situation is fundamentally different from the time of the "Black Death," which claimed tens of millions of lives in the 14th century.
Today, plague is treated with antibiotics. The most important thing is to establish the diagnosis and begin therapy as early as possible. According to the WHO, when detected and treated promptly, the chances of recovery from pneumonic plague are high. At the same time, without treatment, it can lead to death within just 18–24 hours after symptoms appear.
People who have had close contact with a patient suffering from pneumonic plague are given a preventive course of antibiotics. The patient is isolated, while medical workers use personal protective equipment. The CDC notes that transmission usually requires close contact with an infected person and their respiratory droplets.
Therefore, based on the information currently available, there are no grounds to speak of a threat of a global epidemic because of the events in the Irkutsk Region. It is much more important to determine whether there have been any new infections among the contacts and how quickly they were isolated and preventive treatment was initiated.
What happened in Russia
According to Russian media, 28-year-old Darya Shipilova worked as a laboratory technician at the Irkutsk plague-control institute. On September 25, she allegedly broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, after which she became ill. The woman was hospitalized, and she died during the night of October 2.
A drug that may prevent Ebola infection is being tested in Congo03.10.26, 20:08 • 4986 views
After that, about 200 people who may have had contact with her were identified. According to media reports, 189 people were hospitalized for observation, while the Shelekhov District Hospital was placed under quarantine. Anti-epidemic measures were launched in the region.
At the same time, much uncertainty remains surrounding the situation. As of the time the first reports appeared, Russian federal authorities had not released complete information about the circumstances of the infection or the results of examinations of the contacts. Therefore, it is still too early to conclude that there has been a full-scale plague outbreak based solely on reports of a laboratory technician's death and the quarantine.
The scale of isolating contacts in such a situation does not itself mean that all of them are infected. In the case of pneumonic plague, the rapid identification of contacts, their medical observation, preventive antibiotics, and the isolation of possible patients are standard measures intended to prevent an epidemic from developing.

Former IDF negotiator says Israel could have ended Gaza war, freed hostages a year earlier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:36:07 UTC
06:36:07 KST

Maj.-Gen. (res.) Nitzan Alon, who headed the IDF's hostage and missing persons directorate during the war, said Friday that Israel could have ended the war in Gaza and returned the hostages significantly earlier, possibly as much as a year before the intense fighting ultimately ended, Walla reported on Saturday.
Alon said different decisions could have saved thousands of lives on both sides and that some of the hostages who were killed or murdered in captivity might have returned alive to their families.
He made the remarks during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy panel titled "Three Years After October 7: A Bridge or a Chasm Between the Peoples?"
During the discussion, moderated by David Makovsky and featuring Israeli, Palestinian, and American experts, Alon was asked about the decisions that prolonged the war and whether an opportunity to return the hostages earlier had been missed.
'We missed the opportunity. The war was too long'
"I think we could have reached this point much earlier, perhaps a year earlier, without significantly harming the other strategic objectives of the war," Alon said.
"We could have achieved the same strategic accomplishments in terms of damaging Hamas's military strength, and in terms of many other security issues, much earlier. Perhaps we would have brought back alive some of the hostages who were killed or murdered during captivity," he said. "We missed that opportunity. The war was too long."
Alon stressed that he was not attempting to analyze Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal motivations.
"I'm not a psychologist who can know exactly what is going on in the prime minister's mind," he said, adding that political leaders are influenced by strategic and ideological considerations, political constraints, and personal matters, and that it was impossible to determine which factor had been decisive.
Still, he said, "I'm fairly certain that we could and should have shortened the war, brought back all the hostages, perhaps a year earlier, moved forward, and maybe saved thousands of lives on both sides. It is likely that some of the hostages who were killed or murdered in Gaza could also have returned alive to their families."
Alon was later asked about the tension between the war's two objectives, destroying Hamas and returning the hostages. He acknowledged that there had been significant tension between them, but argued that, in retrospect, the strategic achievements obtained after two years of intense fighting were not materially different from those that could have been achieved earlier.
He said the agreement reached in October 2025 was slightly better than an arrangement that could have been reached several months earlier, but not from a strategic standpoint. He noted that even after the war, Hamas remained in power and continued to control Gaza's population, although it no longer controlled more than half of the territory of the Gaza Strip.
'Not leadership based on slogans such as total victory'
In another part of the discussion, Alon addressed the October 7 failure and the leadership's conduct during the war.
"On October 7, there was of course a severe intelligence and military failure, alongside a mistaken and catastrophic conception by the political leadership," he said.
Alon said that while the government struggled to manage the war, Israeli society demonstrated initiative, solidarity, and mutual responsibility. He said meeting members of the public and thousands of Israelis who worked on behalf of the hostages and their families gave him personal strength during the difficult period in which he headed the directorate.
He contrasted what he viewed as the positive qualities of Israeli society with sharp criticism of the country's leadership.
"Israel needs leadership that takes responsibility as it is and offers hope. Not leadership that relies on slogans such as 'total victory,' but leadership that presents realistic and balanced plans for dealing with our security, economic, and social challenges."
Alon added that despite manifestations of extremism in Israeli society, the war had also revealed extraordinary civilian strengths.
"We definitely need different leadership, which will take these wonderful people forward with a realistic approach," he said.
Changing security doctrine: Buffer zones and military freedom of action
Alon also addressed the profound change that October 7 brought to Israeli attitudes toward the Palestinians and the prospects for a diplomatic agreement.
He said many Israelis had developed a deep loss of trust in the Palestinian side, in the two-state solution, and in the very possibility of reaching an agreement. The fact that the Hamas attack was carried out inside the June 4, 1967, lines, rather than only in connection with the dispute over territories captured that year, deepened the sense that the conflict extended beyond the question of borders.
He added that the brutality of the massacre, its documentation on social media, and the kidnapping of women, children, and elderly people deepened the trauma and made it more difficult for many Israelis to distinguish between Hamas and the broader Palestinian population, or to feel empathy for suffering on the other side.
Security thinking had changed as well, Alon said. The current approach relies on establishing buffer zones not only in Gaza but also in Lebanon and Syria, while demanding full military freedom of action, including extensive destruction of neighborhoods and villages within those buffer zones.
Nevertheless, Alon expressed hope that after Israel's elections, scheduled for October 27, a deeper understanding would emerge regarding the limitations of military force.
"I believe that over time there will be a deeper understanding of the limitations of the use of force, alongside recognition that diplomatic measures and nonmilitary solutions are necessary to deal with our national security problems," he said.
In closing, Alon pointed to diplomatic possibilities involving Lebanon and Syria as an opportunity for regional change. Progress in those arenas, he said, could be the first step toward creating renewed optimism regarding the broader Israeli-Arab conflict.

Pardes Hanna-Karkur offers new food scene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:35:27 UTC
06:35:27 KST

I’ve lived in Israel for almost 40 years, and as far as I can remember, I’ve never been to Pardes Hanna-Karkur. I knew it had a reputation as a kind of hippie mecca but had no idea it was also a food destination.
With just 50,000 people and no hotels (although one is in the planning stage), it is surprising how extensive the food scene is.
“Pardes Hanna is a colorful community, and that is an advantage for us,” Eyal Kogan, the deputy mayor of Pardes Hanna-Karkur, told The Jerusalem Post. “We already have at least 30 restaurants, and it’s going to get bigger and bigger.”
The city offers a range of restaurants, from casual to chef-driven. Some are kosher with a kashrut certificate, others are kosher without a certificate, and a few are non-kosher. All of the restaurants I visited were kosher with a teudah.
We started our morning at Bagels, a food truck behind the Sonol gas station, owned by 26-year-old Eitan Vallach. He originally opened the bagel truck in Kibbutz Hagoshrim in the summer of 2025. After the war with Lebanon expanded, he moved south and ended up here.
Eitan's food truck imports its bagels from New York
What’s unique about his food truck is that Eitan imports the bagels from New York. They come 80% baked, and he finishes them here. As a former New Yorker, I can attest that the bagels were excellent. They also have great tuna salad and several other dishes. Definitely worth a stop.
We stepped into the Being Wellness Center, which is basically like a WeWork but with a sauna, ice bath, and smoothie bar. Wonder if you can do a Zoom from an ice bath?
Our next stop was Café Hatzvi, where everyone who wasn’t at the Being Wellness Center seemed to be, all of them pecking away at laptops. There is a large outdoor area, and the menu is vegetarian/vegan.
We tried two vegan smoothies: a viral blue one made with spirulina and a banana-cocoa-mango mix that I preferred over the blue one, even though the color was prettier.
Lentil hummus vs chickpea hummus
One of the more interesting dishes was lentil hummus, which tasted very different from chickpea hummus. We didn’t want to eat too much because we still had two more stops ahead of us.
Next was Hersheleh’s bistro, a chef-run restaurant run by three siblings and often visited by Israeli celebrities like Eden Hason and Hanan Ben Ari. The food is unique and creative, including raw fish dishes like tuna tartare, bruschetta, and fatayer, a Palestinian dish made from pockets of dough stuffed with spinach and cheese. Really outstanding food and presentation.
Our last stop was Pasta Loco, run by a husband-and-wife team, and tucked into a small strip mall. A laundry line runs through the center of the small restaurant, where Chef Gilad Vazana and his wife Adi make customers feel like family. Gilad and Adi have spent a lot of time in Italy, and it shows.
I love surprises and was happy to taste the Pasta Loco Surprise, which basically means whatever Gilad feels like serving you. In this case, it was inky black tortellini (the secret is zinc mixed into the dough) with black garlic served on a cream garlic confit with butter and pecorino. Just wow!
There was also one of the best pizzas I’ve had in Israel.
“We have a community, not customers,” Gilad told me. “I go to their bar mitzvahs and weddings. I want people to feel like I’m hosting them in my home.”

- A sexually suggestive ad from Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton has drawn millions of views — and condemnation from allies on the right and Democrats.
- The spot urges a woman to vote for Hilton, who says its provocative humor is meant to reach Californians open to change despite his party affiliation.
- The backlash comes as Hilton trails Democratic front-runner Xavier Becerra, while some conservatives who called the ad “grotesque” say they still support him.
A provocative, sexually suggestive ad by GOP gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton is drawing heat from his fellow Republicans while drawing millions of viewers online.
Two young women sit on a bed, with an LGBTQ+ flag in the background, with one urging the other to try a new experience.
“I can’t believe I’m doing this,” one woman says, and the other replies. “Don’t be nervous. It’s not that bad ... Just try it. Look, give me your hand. Close your eyes, and I’ll do all the work.”
She leads the hesitant woman’s hand to mark her ballot for Hilton rather than Democrat Xavier Becerra, the front-runner in the race, and says, “Now lick it,” referring to the mail ballot envelope.
Fellow Republicans as well as several Democrats denounced Hilton over the messaging.
Two members of Hilton’s GOP “Golden Ticket” on the Nov. 3 ballot lashed out about the ad’s content.
“I emphatically denounce the use of young women as a political tool,” Michael Gates, the Republican candidate for attorney general who has frequently appeared alongside Hilton at campaign events, wrote on X. “California families deserve better, and as AG, I will fight every day to protect our girls, young women, and parental rights.”
Sonja Shaw, who is running to be the next state superintendent of schools, castigated Hilton, the state Republican party and its chairwoman for promoting the ad, which had been viewed by nearly 5 million people as of Saturday afternoon.
“Shame on you ... for reposting and cheering this creepy, weird, disturbing garbage,” Shaw wrote on X. “This is a clear example of exactly why good people are walking away from the Republican Party. As a mother and someone who has fought to protect the innocence of children, this crosses a line. We have lost our way. Embarrassing.”
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), an openly gay member of Congress, and state Democratic Party chairman Rusty Hicks also condemned the ad.
“This is a bizarre and desperate ad from a person who has attacked the LGBTQ+ community and stands with Donald Trump,” Garcia said. “Hilton is losing and more interested in AI slop than actually talking about issues Californians care about.”
Hilton acknowledged the ad has provoked strong reactions, but it underscored the foundation of his campaign — that many Californians may be put off by his party affiliation but want change given the state’s myriad problems, such as growing unaffordability, that have taken place under a Democratic lock of every statewide office and the state Legislature.
“We’re just saying, you know, just try it,” he said in an interview. “It’s a provocative and humorous way of making a point, right? Which often the best communication does.”
He also said the ad does not conflict with his beliefs about restrictions on gender-affirming care and on youth sports because those would only apply to people who are not adults.
A spokesman for Becerra, who led Hilton 58% to 33% in a recent UC Berkeley/Los Angeles Times poll, was gleeful about the rift the ad was creating among Republicans.
“MAGA is melting down over Steve Hilton’s creepy ad because they’re finally seeing him for the sellout he really is, willing to abandon his own twisted values to get ahead,” said Jonathan Underland.
As Californians prepare to elect a new governor in November, the top concern they want the new leader to prioritize is reducing the state’s entrenched high cost of living, according to a new poll.
However, some conservatives who were dismayed by the message stood by Hilton’s side.
Pastor Jack Hibbs of Calvary Chapel Chino Hills, a Christian nationalist, called the ad “grotesque” and said it promoted lesbianism among young women, on a Facebook Live post Saturday. However, he said he still supports Hilton over Becerra. He did not respond to requests for comment.
Hilton is scheduled to speak on Monday to a chapter of the Log Cabin Republicans, an LGBTQ group, at a brewery in Palm Desert. The organization did not respond to requests for comment.
Former California GOP chairwoman Jessica Millan Patterson said that while the ad wasn’t for her, she understood the campaign’s desire to expand its reach to different voters.
“Does the ad speak to me? No. He’s not going after my vote. He already has my vote. He’s trying to think of new and creative ways to make people who wouldn’t normally feel like voting for a Republican feel safe to do so,” she said. “He’s going out of his comfort zone and going for people that wouldn’t normally feel comfortable voting for him.”
Californian Fred Karger, who made history in 2012 as the first openly gay person to run for president, had mixed views about the ad, calling it shrewd yet hypocritical. And he questioned its effectiveness.
“The audience that he’s targeting there — the hipster, young hipster, lesbian audience — probably has a 1% chance of voting for him,” Karger said. “So it’s kind of a long shot. But it is a clever ad.”

Baby bonuses fail to address the fear of falling behind
In highly competitive societies like Hong Kong and Singapore, subsidies and parental leave can’t overcome the cultural pressure keeping young couples from starting families
When one of my seniors from medical school was pregnant during her surgical residency, she planned the exact date of her C-section so she could complete her training on time. When I asked why she didn’t consider taking maternity leave to recuperate afterwards, she said she couldn’t bring herself to lag behind her peers. “I didn’t want motherhood to slow me down,” she said.
In medicine, it is common for women to delay childbearing until after their early career years, often into their mid-thirties or later. When I speak to friends in professional careers such as law, accounting and consulting, they echo a similar sentiment.

Comando may be tiny, but Mexico’s national guard is giving him a very big role.
Outfitted with miniature goggles, a fitted tactical vest, a helmet and even a petite head-mounted camera, the 7kg (15lb) chihuahua has become the most unusual – and smallest – canine member of the force.
Officers said the 13-month-old pup is being trained not just as a crowd-pleasing mascot but for search-and-rescue work as well.
Diminutive Comando, who stands 21cm (8in) tall, looks nothing like the powerful dogs usually associated with military or police units.
During a training session in Mexico City last week, the little dog scampered up stairs and over obstacles while a much larger, fully trained canine named Roko looked on.
Lt Debora Hernandez said Comando challenges two stereotypes: that only big dogs can serve in the national guard, and that a military-style force cannot build a warmer connection with the public. His presence, she said, reminds people that “beneath the uniform, we are human beings”.
The force adopted Comando about six months ago in the northern state of Chihuahua, which inspired the breed’s name, after his elderly owners became unable to care for him. Comando now appears at civic ceremonies, school events and community outreach programs.
Comando is an outlier in a national guard canine force of about 350 dogs, most of them traditional working breeds such as German shepherds and labrador retrievers.
Chihuahuas, known for their large, upright ears, big personalities and expressive eyes, may be alert and energetic, but they are rarely seen as candidates for serious operational work.
Comando has already appeared in Mexico’s Independence Day parade and has inspired his own animated likeness and a growing crop of memes on social media.

Ukraine’s bomber drones, ones that dropped ground robots in its recent Donetsk counteroffensive, are getting 2.4-kilogram jammer to shield them from FPVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:26:50 UTC
06:26:50 KST

A Ukrainian firm is testing a jammer light enough to ride on a heavy bomber drone and shield it from the enemy FPVs that hunt it. Aura-Ukraine has begun final tests of the system, called Aura 3K mini, the Dignitas Fund, a charity developing it with the manufacturer, Oboronka reports.
The bombers it is built to protect have become some of Ukraine's most valued drones. In the Donetsk operation last month, heavy bombers dropped kamikaze ground robots more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines. The same weapon has been fitted with guided bombs that strike at long range with high precision.
At the same time, heavy bombers are large, making them prime targets for Russia. Keeping them in the air, and out of enemy hands, is the point of the new shield.
Two jammers cover 360 degrees
Aura 3K mini wraps the drone in a spherical, 360-degree cover using two broadband jammers, the fund says. Two emitters, not one, close the blind angles a single jammer would leave.
They work across the 2.1 to 2.8 GHz band, enough to disrupt FPV drones without cutting the bomber's own Starlink link. The whole device weighs about 2.4 kilograms.
"Radiation-pattern tests start on the front line in the coming days," the fund's press service says, and if they succeed, the system is set for serial production.
The fund moves to automate it
The next step is to make the jammer smarter, the fund says. It wants an auto-on function that fires only when a threat is detected, so the bomber does not give away its position with constant emission.
The team also plans to adapt Aura 3K mini to Vampire-type bombers, the heavy night drones that Russian troops nickname "Baba Yaga". That would widen the shield's reach across more of Ukraine's bomber fleet.
Russia hunts the Baba Yaga
The nickname points to a fairytale Slavic witch who flies by night. The real thing has been hard for Russia to counter: in 2024, a Ukrainian night bomber was often impossible to jam and, by one account, could be destroyed only with a flamethrower. By 2025, Russia was offering its soldiers 10 days' leave for capturing a Baba Yaga it could not build itself.

Rev Mariann Edgar Budde, the Episcopal bishop of Washington DC who gained national attention when she called on Donald Trump to “have mercy” on the country’s immigrants and LGBTQ+ community after his second inauguration, is resigning.
Budde shared in her resignation letter that she will be leaving her post on 3 June 2028 after the consecration and ordination of the new diocesan bishop.
“I write today because I have discerned, in consultation with diocesan leadership and the Presiding Bishop’s office, that it is time to begin preparing for the election of your next bishop. I have not come to this decision lightly or alone, and it will not be easy to say goodbye to the diocese I love,” her letter said.
Next week, the standing committee will outline the steps required, which include the appointment of two committees to undertake this work, the letter added.
Budde, 66, is the first woman to serve as the spiritual leader of the Episcopal diocese of Washington. She has been leading the diocese since her election to the role in 2011. Before that, she served as the rector of St John’s Episcopal church in Minneapolis for 18 years.
She made headlines for urging Trump during her sermon to show mercy to “gay, lesbian and transgender children” from all political backgrounds, some of whom, she said, “fear for their lives”.
Trump demanded an apology in a post shared on social media.
“She brought her church into the World of politics in a very ungracious way. She was nasty in tone, and not compelling or smart,” the president said.
“Apart from her inappropriate statements, the service was a very boring and uninspiring one. She is not very good at her job! She and her church owe the public an apology!”
It was not the first time Budde had called out and clashed with Trump.
During Trump’s first term, she published an opinion piece in the New York Times, expressing outrage over Trump’s appearance in front of St John’s Episcopal holding up a Bible for a photo after federal officers had used force to clear a crowd of peaceful protesters demonstrating against the police killing of George Floyd the previous week.
Budde wrote that Trump had “used sacred symbols to cloak himself in the mantle of spiritual authority, while espousing positions antithetical to the Bible that he held in his hands”.
Looking towards the future of the Episcopal diocese of Washington, Budde wrote, she is committed to ensuring a strong and healthy transition for her successor.
“Alongside the diocesan staff and leadership bodies, I will do everything in my power to ensure that the diocese is as strong and healthy as possible for this leadership transition. I am praying for all involved, and especially for the one God is preparing to serve as the tenth bishop of the Diocese of Washington,” Budde concluded.

‘Which homeland?’ American Jews do not have to choose between Israel and US - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:17:59 UTC
06:17:59 KST

As America celebrated its Bicentennial on July 4, 1976, my father called me over to the television. I was outside enjoying the local fireworks, so I was surprised that he would interrupt the fun on such a special night.
Putting his arm around me, he pointed at the screen. “Look.”
I expected to see fireworks over Boston Harbor. Instead, the news was focused on a word I could not pronounce, let alone understand: Entebbe.
My father explained that an airplane carrying many Israelis and Jews had been hijacked, that the hostages were being held in Uganda, and that Israel had undertaken a courageous mission to rescue them. We watched prime minister Yitzhak Rabin welcome the hostages home as blue and white flags waved in the background.
With tears pooling in his eyes, my father said, “This is why we have a homeland.”
As an eight-year-old, I did not fully understand what had happened, but my father’s impassioned message etched itself into my soul and helped shape my Jewish identity.
Over the past 50 years, I have returned to that moment many times. Only recently did I recognize the question I never thought to ask him that night:
Which homeland?
I know that my father meant Israel. But 50 years later, I hear his words differently.
Israel and America occupy distinct but deeply connected places in the modern Jewish story. Israel is the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people, representing Jewish sovereignty, peoplehood, and return. Its strength made the improbable rescue at Entebbe possible.
America, meanwhile, became a civic home for generations of Jews, offering something historically extraordinary: a haven from persecution and the possibility of becoming full participants in society while remaining distinctly Jewish.
These are not equivalent forms of belonging in the public square, but neither must they be competing ones. A strong Israel and a confident American Jewish community are not rival projects. Like Babylon and Jerusalem centuries ago, each is essential to the future of the Jewish people, and each places responsibilities upon those who call it home.
That unresolved question, what it means to belong deeply to the Jewish people while participating fully in American life, inspired Rabbi Menachem Creditor, scholar-in-residence at UJA-Federation of New York, and me to co-edit American Torah at 250. This collection of original sermons and Torah reflections for the weekly portions of 5787 marks the 250th anniversary of the United States.
The volume invites Jewish communities to encounter the American story through Torah, and Torah through the experience of American democracy. The overarching theme examines what America has made possible for Jews and other minorities while asking what its unfinished experiment in self-government requires of us.
That question has become more urgent since October 7. The massacre, the suffering of the hostages, the ensuing war, and the alarming normalization of antisemitism have shaken the sense of security long enjoyed by many American Jews.
The blurring of anti-Zionism and antisemitism has demonstrated how readily attacks on Israel’s legitimacy become attacks on Jewish history, American Jewish identity, and our belonging in the public square and the halls of government.
American Jewry has created an extraordinary network of synagogues, schools, scholarship, philanthropy, advocacy, and public leadership with global significance. It is a vital center of Jewish religious, intellectual, educational, and communal life. Its strength matters to Israel, just as Israel’s strength matters to Jews throughout the world.
The contributors to American Torah at 250 represent different movements, communities, and political perspectives. They do not speak with one voice, nor should they. Jewish tradition has never demanded uniformity of thought. Our sacred literature preserves disagreement because the search for wisdom is strengthened by multiple voices wrestling seriously with enduring questions.
Throughout the collection, rabbis, educators, and thought leaders examine freedom and responsibility, covenant and the Constitution, justice and religious liberty, pluralism and public trust, memory and hope. They ask how Jews can participate fully in American civic life without surrendering our particular commitments, including our bond with Israel and the Jewish people.
These are not questions separate from Torah. They are Torah questions.
Torah asks what it means to build a society worthy of our highest values. Jewish tradition teaches that disagreement need not destroy community, that power carries obligations, that the rule of law is the bedrock of a just society, and that human beings are responsible for one another.
American Jewish experience
For Israeli readers, America’s 250th anniversary may seem like a distant national commemoration. Yet America’s democratic ideals, global influence, and relationship with Israel have profoundly shaped modern Jewish history.
Understanding America’s promises, tensions, and unfinished work is essential to understanding the largest Jewish community outside Israel and the relationship between the two great centers of contemporary Jewish life.
Fifty years after that July 4 night, I can still see my father pointing toward the television and hear his voice: “This is why we have a homeland.”
Today, I understand that I inherited more than one story of home from my parents. Each has shaped me and carries obligations. And each has sustained the Jewish people in different ways.
As we prepare to read the Torah again, American Torah at 250 invites us to examine the rights, responsibilities, and reasons for hope embedded in the American Jewish experience.
Perhaps the question before us as Jews is not simply where we belong. It is what our belonging asks of us. As Pirkei Avot reminds us, “Turn it over and turn it over; it’s all in there.”
The writer is a civic educator and the executive director of Civic Spirit, a nonpartisan organization that provides training in civic education to Jewish, Catholic, and Christian day schools to prepare students to be informed and engaged members of American democracy. He is the 2026 recipient of The Covenant Foundation Award for Excellence in Jewish Education.

‘It has to pass’: Green Party members give their take on the Zionism is Racism motion
Members of the Green Party voiced strong opinions on the upcoming Zionism is racism motion at the annual conference in Brighton, with some saying they would struggle to remain members if it did not pass.
The motion, set to be voted on Sunday, calls for the party to define Zionism as a racist, settler‑colonial ideology and declare itself against it.
While the motion drew a record number of co-proposers and was endorsed by the likes of Greta Thunberg, concerns have been raised about key demands.
"If you want a homeland, then therefore you're taking somebody's land for it based on identity; that is racism, so yes, Zionism is racism. Of course, I want the motion to go through," Green Party member Alex Blower told The New Arab.
"If we're going to fight against settlements, and we're going to fight against genocide and apartheid, the same way as this country did back in the 80s against South Africa, which we recognise as a racist ideology, we have to recognise this as the racist ideology it is," Blower continued.
"Look at what [Zionism is] doing, look at what it's done, there is no manifestation of this ideology that does not involve the suffering, the subjugation, of other people seen as lesser than those who want the land."
Zoë Garbett, the newly elected mayor of Hackney in London, explained that she wanted to separate the concept from the question of whether Zionism is racism from the motion.
"I think it's been quite clear that we can say…that the acts that we see taking place in Palestine are clearly racist and clearly taken from a political ideology that is racist, and I think that's clear," Zoë Garbett told The New Arab.
While she agrees with the concept of Zionism being racism, the mayor wanted to leave the motion to the conference floor.
Many expressed optimism that the motion would pass.
"I think it's an important one we need to be having as a conversation in this country," member Humza Egal told The New Arab.
"Sometimes things go your way, sometimes they don't go your way. But I think from the overwhelming support for the motion, and how it's been put together, I think it will pass."
Green Party member Keith Garrett agreed with the sentiment, saying the motion was the main reason he went to Brighton. “[The motion] should totally pass. I mean it has to pass for the Green Party to have a position on this," he said.
When asked how he would feel if the motion failed, Garrett said he believes he would struggle to remain a member of the Green Party.
"I think it's that serious. We need to take a stand on what's happening across the world," Garrett explained. "I think a lot of it is essentially just giving determination to the Palestinian people."
"So, we have essentially forced a solution that wasn't theirs onto them. So now we need to help them and the people who are still in Israel work out a solution together."
Meanwhile, Garbett said she recognised the connection many may have to the issue, referring to the Green Party's strong stance towards Palestine, adding that "it would be a shame" if the motion causes divisions within the party.
However, for others, whether the motion fails or passes will not be the "be all or end all".
"We are already an anti-Zionist party… there's not really any disagreement about the need for Palestinian liberation within the party," member Eugene McCarthy told The New Arab.
"Ethnonationalism is racism, and Zionism is ethnonationalism. I don't think you need a motion to say that."
