The G7 Is Releasing Emergency Fuel Reserves. How Much Will It Help Americans?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:13:51 UTC
04:13:51 KST

The Group of Seven (G7) countries said Friday that the nations would release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming months, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel. The move comes amid a global shortage largely attributed to slowdowns of the passage of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
A joint statement from the G7 nations—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.—confirmed that the International Energy Agency (IEA) will coordinate the release over the next four months.
It calls the move a part of “decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies” amid record-high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran and the recent escalation of fighting between Russia and Ukraine.
Read More: Once Again, Energy Is Power
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Friday. “The process will begin immediately.”
In talks leading up to the announcement on Friday, Trump had been pushing European partners for the release, citing high fuel prices for Americans. Last month, the Trump Administration threatened to temporarily suspend its exports of diesel—earning immediate backlash from countries that rely on it, including Canada, Mexico, and much of Europe.
European leaders and oil executives at the time said that such a ban would be disastrous for long-term oil flow. For that reason, experts believe the threat helped pressure those nations to release their fuel reserves.
The agreement could offer some relief for Americans even if the released diesel stays in Europe, because Europe buys some of its diesel from the U.S. Releasing European reserves could ease competition for U.S. diesel and potentially reduce prices for American buyers.
This is especially critical as the cost of Brent crude oil sits at $102 per barrel as of Oct. 3 and on-highway diesel hit a high of $6.529 per gallon as of last month, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
But how much relief consumers will actually see—and how quickly—will depend on what type of fuel is released, how much reaches the market and when, and whether supply disruptions persist.
What is actually being added to the market?
Although the G7 shared how much fuel it would release, it did not specify the full breakdown of the release by fuel type. Its statement did say, however, that there will be a “frontloaded” and substantial release of diesel fuel within the first 20 days.
While crude oil must be refined into products like gasoline before consumers can use it, diesel is already a finished fuel. That means a diesel release could address the immediate shortage more directly.
The planned release could help ease shortages of both crude oil and refined fuels, with supplies disrupted by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
The supply of crude oil has been heavily disrupted this year after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes that ignited a war with Iran in February. In response, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in March. More recent negotiations to end the war have largely failed to address differing opinions on ownership and control over the Strait. This has critically restricted the passage of oil-carrying vessels through the waterway, with daily shipping traffic in the single digits last month, down from pre-war averages of roughly 138 to 140 daily transits.
Diesel, meanwhile, is essential to U.S. transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing: Most goods, food, and manufacturing supplies across the country are transported by heavy-duty trucks and trains running on diesel engines. The war in Iran has driven diesel prices up and lowered supply, but Russia and Ukraine’s targeting of one another’s energy infrastructure has further exacerbated the issue.
While the U.S. in particular does not heavily rely on Russian diesel, America is vulnerable to the volatility caused by Russia removing it from the global market. Trump has claimed outright that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian oil infrastructure is to blame for diesel shortages.
What could Americans feel, and when?
Jason Bordoff, founding director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, says it’s difficult to predict the consumer impact given the scarce details shared so far.
“It makes a big difference if the release is in the next two weeks or if it's four months from now,” Bordoff says.
“I think if we saw some announcement tomorrow from Germany or France that gave concrete, specific numbers for a substantial amount—50 million barrels or so—of diesel, then it could have a real impact if this release actually happens in a timely fashion,” Bordoff says.
At the same time, Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, cautions that American consumers may see limited benefits.
“Releasing diesel could make a difference on price, especially in tight markets in Europe,” Colgan says. “But American consumers are unlikely to see much of a price drop from this policy move unless the diesel share of that 100 million barrels is very large.”
With a timely release of diesel, Bordoff predicts that Americans could see a drop by as much as 25 cents per gallon after a few weeks—but, he adds, the markets seem pretty unsure that that will actually happen.
And market perception is central to whether or not prices drop in the short term.
“I think they’re saying: Show me the barrels, so I have confidence this is real, and it's going to happen quickly,” he says.
David Bieri, an economist and associate professor of urban affairs and planning at Virginia Tech, tells TIME that international interventions like this help “signal” to markets that governments are a credible safety net in prolonged periods of uncertainty.
“That's the main mechanism, because they want to influence market sentiment,” Bieri says. “Then, futures markets begin to price more optimistically, and then eventually the hope is that prices will come down.”
The effect Bieri is describing has already begun: The price of diesel futures in the United States fell 8% on Friday morning, a sign of more optimism in the market.
Bordoff adds that they are also, in part, a response to Trump dropping his threat of a diesel export ban—a threat that was lifted as a condition of the G7 agreement.
The release itself may not impact the markets “an awful lot,” Bieri says, given the broader context of the war with Iran.
“In fact, consumers might not necessarily notice it, ever. That's how insignificant the quantity itself is,” he says of the 100 million barrels. “But it's the importance of the cooperative signal that hopefully will make things better this fall.”
Bieri also cautions that any savings could take time to reach consumers, as carriers and other distributors may use lower fuel costs to rebuild their margins.
“[They] have been bleeding on increased fuel costs,” he says. “This is going to be, if anything, a welcome reprieve for their profit margins, and they're not going to pass that on immediately to consumers.”
What happens if the supply gap is still there when releases taper off?
This October announcement is not the first of its kind: Following the initial market shock of the war in Iran, IEA member countries announced a 400-million-barrel release in March—80% of which has already been released. Notably, the latest announcement did not clearly establish how much of the forthcoming release would be additional to earlier commitments.
In March, the IEA said that the majority of the barrel release would be crude oil; however, reports show that Europe has primarily contributed refined oil, like diesel—which could suggest more of the same in this latest round.
In either event, such fuel releases are just a matter of sticking a bandage over the larger issue of two unresolved wars and continued global energy disruption, says Bordoff.
“We're going to continue to have oil, gasoline, and diesel price shocks until that conflict comes to some sort of resolution, and energy flows can get going again,” he says. “Inventories, and stocks and other schemes like waiving state fuel taxes or something can help on the margin for temporary disruptions, but at some point this isn't temporary anymore.”
Michael Noel, economist at Texas Tech University, agrees with Bordoff, telling TIME that “unless something dramatic happens to end the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, the supply shortage will persist.”
Negotiations between Iranian leadership and the Trump Administration have stalled multiple times in the last six months. Trump said on Sept. 9 that he expected a resolution to come after the midterm elections, which take place in the U.S. on Nov. 3.
“I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer,” he said last month. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”
Axios reported, however, that senior Trump Administration officials met at Camp David to discuss the war on Friday. The talks come as the U.S. last week added economic pressure in the region with a series of sanctions aiming to curtail funding streams and stymy industrial lifelines for Iran.
Experts argue that the fuel crisis and volatility exposes the need for the U.S. to adapt to a changing energy ecosystem. Notably, Colgan says that would include “the national security advantages of clean technologies like EVs, batteries, and renewable energy.”

The rating of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has reached 30 percent nationwide for the first time, while support for the conservative bloc of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the Christian Social Union (CSU) has fallen to a record low. This is shown by the results of a survey conducted by the INSA polling institute for the Bild newspaper, reports UNN.
Details
Over the past week, support for the CDU/CSU across Germany fell by one percentage point to 18 percent
Compared with the previous week, support for the AfD increased by one percentage point. Thus, in the survey conducted for Bild, the far right is 12 percentage points ahead of the bloc of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The rating of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), which forms the governing coalition together with the CDU/CSU, has not changed since last week and stands at 14 percent. The opposition party Alliance 90/The Greens has the same level of support, but its rating fell by one percentage point over the week. The Left Party remains at 10 percent. The left-populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) and the Free Democratic Party (FDP) each received 4 percent in the survey, remaining below the electoral threshold.

Bulgaria suffered its first-ever defeat to Iceland, losing 3-0 in Reykjavik in the Nations League on Saturday, in a result that added another unwanted record to the national team's campaign.
The loss came after Bulgaria had recently been beaten by Luxembourg for the first time. The Reykjavik match was Atanas Ribarski's first in charge of the national team. He is also set to lead the side in its return fixture against Luxembourg. Ribarski took over after Aleksandar Dimitrov resigned following a 0-0 draw with Estonia in Plovdiv.

Bulgaria remains bottom of the group with one point from three matches. The team is due to play away against Luxembourg in three days, with Ribarski in charge. The match is expected to be his last as head coach.

‘There’s a lot of silence’: have we created a new ‘Lonely Generation’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:00:07 UTC
04:00:07 KST

In September, a Reddit user identifying themselves as a 25-year-old man turned to the r/ForeverAlone subreddit with a question: How do you deal with touch starvation? “It’s becoming obvious to me that I’ll probably be alone forever,” he wrote. He used to be worried about missing out on sex, but now he just misses hugs. Cuddles.
“I don’t have many friends and none with that kind of physical relationship. I don’t really hug family either anymore. Some days, I feel so desperate for a hug with someone I love.”
On another thread, a user identifying as a 20-year-old woman took to the platform to ask if anyone else had experienced university as one of the loneliest times in their lives. “I eat lunch alone, go to class, drive home, study, and repeat,” the user wrote. “Evenings and weekends are the hardest because I crave social connection, but there’s no one to go out with or even talk to.”
Another user, on another subreddit thread, expressed that they had tried to ease their unwanted solitude, but failed. “The loneliness is unbearable,” they wrote. “Is anyone else experiencing this” No question mark. No full stop.
The answer is yes.
Around the world, young people, according to the 2025 World Health Organization Social Connection Commission report, “feel the loneliest”. Between 17 and 21% of 13-to-29-year-olds report feeling lonely, a greater proportion than any other age group, the report found. Another study, based on a survey of more than 1 million young people from 38 countries, found that youth loneliness had increased in many regions between 2002 and 2022. From Germany to Australia to the UK, studies are showing an uptick in loneliness and social isolation among teenagers and young adults.
That much of the world has produced a generation in which so many regularly feel unable to meet their needs for social connection is a curiosity which has propelled years of work for Dr Michelle Lim.
The act of learning to be one human among many has always been a lonely, discombobulating exercise in parts, she says. But in her new book, The Lonely Generation, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist examines exactly what has happened over this century to make many young people even lonelier.
In short, she writes, “It must be said that the nature of childhood has changed dramatically over the past few decades.”
The list of aggravating factors Lim identifies is long: our hyper-competitive education culture, digital technology, the long tail of Covid (“they’re grieving”), the shift towards smaller families, the decline of third spaces, the high cost of living, hybrid working, hybrid learning, the decline of religion, and the rise of automation which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human. Young people, she argues, are being offered fewer and fewer opportunities to form meaningful connections.
“What I fear is social atrophy,” she writes. “People are getting used to being alone.”
‘Being very busy didn’t protect me’
Lim is one of the world’s pre-eminent loneliness scholars. Alongside her work as a psychologist and researcher, she leads the University of Sydney’s School of Public Health’s Social Health and Wellbeing Group, is CEO of the Australian Ending Loneliness Together campaign, is on a loneliness advisory panel to the World Health Organization and in 2020 cofounded and led the Global Initiative on Loneliness and Connection, which has since expanded to six continents.
In The Lonely Generation, she seeks to dispel myths around loneliness and expound on its many individual and societal consequences. But it is in diagnosing the cause of the “crisis” levels of youth loneliness that she spends the most time. And the first among the culprits she identifies is education.
“The current education systems are built to prioritise academic excellence from children and adolescents,” she writes. And this focus entails “hidden costs”.
After-school tutoring, high-stakes testing and well-intentioned enrolments in extensive extracurricular activities are the hallmarks of a 21st-century education. Lim says that parents tell her: “If I stop, then [my child] will fall behind and I’m not doing the best job I can.”
However, children need rest, free play and empty time in order to practise organic social interactions, says Lim – interactions which are essential to developing their fledgling social skills and a sense of identity outside their family.
“The more time you spend studying, it will come at the expense of [other] important skills,” she says. “We run the risk of raising them to be academically strong, but not socially well-equipped to manage the challenges of adulthood.”
The idea resonates with Usha Makkena, a 22-year-old student at university in Sydney.
“I think when you’re growing up with school, extracurricular activities and then later study and work, a lot of your time can become very structured and goal-oriented,” she says. “Something I realise as I’ve gotten older is that meaningful connection often develops in quite unstructured and almost unproductive times.
“And for me, being very busy certainly didn’t protect me from loneliness.”
Makkena, who is now a national reference group member for Australian youth mental health charity headspace, first started experiencing loneliness in her late teens, around her last year of high school. She did a lot of extracurricular activities and had an active social life, but she had a persistent feeling of disconnection. “What I was missing wasn’t necessarily having more people around me, but that deeper sense of feeling understood and genuinely connected to people.”
Her life did not have the contours of a lonely life. “And I think that can make it harder to recognise,” she says. “When you look at your life and you see all this happening, sometimes it makes you think ‘I shouldn’t be lonely.’”
Awkward anyway
At the high-rise campus of the University of Technology Sydney, in the centre of the city, students wander through chatting in pairs, threes. Some, solo, walk or sit with earbuds in and eyes fixed on their phones. Across the flight of stairs in the foyer of the main building are cast the words “MAKE NEW CONNECTIONS”.
Nenyasha Dongo has struggled to do as the stairs advise.
The Zimbabwean 18-year-old was excited to move to Sydney for her studies. She is a friendly person. She doesn’t want for a huge group of friends, or for parties. Three good friends would do it. But at the end of a day of classes where she didn’t really establish relationships with peers, she would return home to where every one of her five housemates were either out or had retreated to their bedrooms. “There’s a lot of silence,” she says.
“When I do get home, the loneliness,” she shakes her head. She would watch movies and TikTok to fill time until she could call family or friends back home. She carried on like this for six months. “You just have to get used to it.”
Dongo sits with Mihindi Pathinyake at a table in the sun outside a campus cafe. Around them, students and staff mill in and out. Often what the pair describe might have been a situation transplanted from university halls decades ago; the trepidatious step into a lecture hall, scanning to see who might be open to a greeting by a stranger, watching the one big group of old high school friends chat together in the front row, wondering whether the person you just spoke to might like you, might be interested in hanging out one day.
“Just to be clear, young people are just generally awkward,” laughs Lim. “They’re really awkward.”
And the transition from school to university, vocational training or work has always been an inflection point for loneliness, Lim says. Individual young people leave their highly structured environment of high school, with a set cast of characters with whom they are familiar and enter a new world populated by new – and often a vastly greater mass of – people. It is also a time when, often, the desire for a great deal of social interaction and a volume of connection is at its highest. Add to this their prefrontal cortex is still developing and adolescence has yet more years to run its course, the period can be one of flux, confusion, self-questioning and, of course, loneliness.
But this awkward rite of passage is now charged in a new way, says Lim. “Our young people in this generation are living in a world that is very different.”
‘Digital is not the enemy’
“You meet new people every day,” says Pathinayake, an exceedingly bright-eyed 20-year-old student from Sri Lanka. But she describes a new social script to developing friendships in 21st century adolescence and young adulthood.
“They take your Instagram and then you never talk to them again.”
Due to the hybrid online-real life attendance structure to many tutorials and lectures which has proliferated since Covid, it can be difficult to be sure that you may run into the same people with the frequency needed to establish organic connection.
“Sometimes following someone or reacting to something that they post can almost be a substitute for reaching out, even though those interactions don’t meet the same need,” says Makkena over a video call in late September. “And then there’s also that element of comparison.
“For me, when I was already feeling lonely, constantly seeing other people’s friendship groups or social lives could sometimes create the impression that everybody else had found their people and I somehow hadn’t.”
She is, however, wary of narratives which pit technology as the silent assassin of social connection. “It also helped me maintain relationships.”
“Social media has not been an entirely negative development”, writes Lim. While the professor is concerned about the dopamine hit from social media blunting the rewards we feel from other interactions and that, for people who are already lonely, it can embed an aversion to real-life connection, her own research has shown it can fortify young people living in communities that don’t accept them, or help others to learn about the world. “Digital use is not the enemy.”
However, she openly imagines (not happily) a future in which her own daughter might tell her that her best friend is an AI avatar. It does not feel like a big leap from what she already sees in her clinical practice, where she might be helping a young person navigate problems in their romantic relationship only to realise they have never met their boyfriend or girlfriend in real life. “It’s really common,” she says.
These virtual relationships, whether remote between human beings on separate continents or between human and AI avatar, are lower in the friction typical of in-person relationships, and entirely absent of touch.
“Humans are hard,” says Lim. “But that’s actually the beauty of relationships as well. We are being challenged, we are being pushed. Our ability to think more diversely, be empathetic are challenged by other humans.”
“Do we run the risk of getting de-socialised with real humans?”
The ‘loneliness loop’
Anxieties about the decline of social fabric and interaction – particularly for young people – have abounded for decades. Telephones and televisions were derided for their antisocial powers long before the term the “antisocial century” was coined by US writer Derek Thompson.
“But there is a sense of feeling unsafe right now, generally, whether it’s political safety around the world, or the lack of community,” says Lim. “It affects the way we see our relationships, the way we relate to people, what we choose to do.”
Lim writes about the “loneliness loop” – a particularly nasty trap for young people – by which experiencing loneliness causes the lonely person to perceive social interaction as more threatening, and so they retreat, reduce their social interaction and in doing so become more lonely.
But there is a bigger, community-wide loop too. We have settled, she writes, into a social disconnection crisis.
In The Lonely Generation, Lim imagines a world where social interaction becomes something like exercise has become today: something we once did as part of daily life, but which now we need to make a concerted effort to schedule in our diaries.
“We already see this,” says Lim. Paid-for services coming on to the market as apps or activities in order to facilitate human interaction and combat loneliness. Lim herself receives “so many” requests to endorse different offerings.
“People are capitalising on that,” she says. “This is not to say that they are not a good thing, but I think that it’s really reflective of the erosion of other kinds of social life that we once had.”
Loneliness, particularly youth loneliness, writes Lim, is a signal. A sign that we need to reassess our social world. “There is an ‘us’ problem here.
“People just go, ‘well, it’s not my responsibility’. But the problem is, actually everyone’s responsible,” she says.
“If everyone says that, then we are going to be living in a world, and raising kids in a world, where healthy social connection is ‘a nice to have’.”

The moment I knew: As a reality TV contestant, I was allowed one 15-minute call a week. Even at 3am, Chris would always pick up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:00:06 UTC
04:00:06 KST

At 29 I had lost my career in hospitality because of Covid and decided to throw my hat in the ring as a contestant on MasterChef Australia. By the time I was eliminated in 2021, restaurants still weren’t open and I didn’t know what to do with my life. My lease was coming to an end in Melbourne and I wasn’t doing well with the lockdowns and people recognising me from TV. So I decided to retreat to my father’s place in Adelaide for a while.
By early 2022 I was dating a guy but, after a few months, he ghosted me suddenly.
One sunny autumn weekend as I was miserably assembling some flatpack furniture at Dad’s, I realised I had to get out of the house. I got on Grindr and this lovely guy, Chris, fresh from England, started messaging me.
I’d lived in the UK in my early 20s and I knew how hard it was to make friends in a new city. Still processing the shock ghosting, I invited Chris for a drink – just as mates – so neither of us had to be lonely on such a beautiful day. He said he couldn’t imagine anything better.
We met at Brighton beach and had a beer. What followed was one of the most wonderful and unexpected dates of my life. It went for nine hours! We chatted and chatted, not wanting it to end. I wasn’t anticipating any chemistry but it was there, and we spent the night together.
The next day I took him on a tour of Adelaide’s wine regions and then sent him on his way. He was only in town for two days, en route to his new life in Sydney. I didn’t think I’d ever see him again.
But we stayed in touch as he settled into the harbour city. One thing led to another and, by May, little more than a month after we’d met, we both wound up in Melbourne. Chris had been offered a job and I had always planned to return at some point. So without ever having discussed the details, or even admitting to ourselves we’d caught real feelings, we’d moved to the same city and became a sort-of-couple, while still keeping things casual.
In July I was scheduled to be on this reality show, The Challenge, that was filming in Argentina. The show had a Survivor/Big Brother vibe and I didn’t think I was going to do very well. I figured I’d be eliminated within a week but, much to my surprise, I turned out to be quite the Challenge beast and made it all the way to the final.
We were only allowed one 15-minute video call a week and in that month I used 53 of my 60 allotted minutes talking to Chris.
I’m not a person who likes to show vulnerability but the demands of the show broke me in ways I wasn’t expecting. Being filmed 24/7 and doing all these insane challenges put my mental health on a knife’s edge. We weren’t even “official” but Chris would pick up the phone at 3am and just be there for me. No games, no bullshit: he was my support when I needed someone the most.
In the final week of the competition we were given time to write a letter to someone in our life. I wrote to Chris and all my feelings came flooding out. I told him I was falling for him and that if he ever read this letter it meant I was no longer just falling. I was, for sure, in love. I tucked it away and made my way back to Melbourne to recover.
Once home it became clearer that the reality TV filming had taken a real toll on my mental health and the network started paying for my therapy. Chris was with me all the way.
A few months later I gave him the letter. And he told me he loved me too. I didn’t know it at the time but those weekly therapy sessions were a blessing in disguise: they really set me up to be the best partner I could be for Chris.
When I lived in the UK, my dream was to find the love of my life and stay there for ever. Chris had his own ideas about what his time in Australia would look like – and they definitely did not include meeting his future husband in the first week!
We might not have got what we thought we wanted from our big solo adventures but in a roundabout way we have both found exactly what we were looking for. We’re engaged and plan to move back to England together next year.

Whales on Australia’s ‘humpback highway’ are at growing risk of injury from boat and propellor strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:00:06 UTC
04:00:06 KST

Gruesome images of adult and juvenile humpback whales along Australia’s east coast with slash and gouge injuries from boat and propeller strikes highlight what experts say is a growing problem, as the population booms 60 years after the ban on whaling.
Missing tail parts, deep red lacerations and shocking injuries to the spine of a whale calf can be clearly seen on the images, gathered by WWF Australia and shared with the Guardian.
One image of fresh and broad cuts on the back of a calf was taken last month in Hervey Bay in Queensland, where many mothers choose to bring their calves for rest and shelter on the long migration down to Antarctica.
The atmosphere on the town’s whale-watching boats is often one of heightened excitement and elation, as the majestic mammals come to the surface, says Isabel Taylor, a senior naturalist with the Pacific Whale Foundation’s whale-watching tours.
Last month, Taylor saw two mothers with calves come to the surface, but all was not well with one pair.
“The others were very surface active and putting on a show, but this other mum and calf were more reserved,” she says.
Clearly visible on the calf’s back were slash marks from a boat propeller. “The mood on the boat changed a bit,” says Taylor.
“We get people from all over the world and some say it’s the best day of their lives. So to have this on the other end of the spectrum was quite profound.”
Another image taken in June by drone off Sydney’s Bondi beach shows a humpback with lacerations and exposed red flesh that appear to have been caused by repeated sweeps of a propeller blade.
An image from 2024 shows a female humpback off the coast of southern New South Wales that has become known as “bladerunner” because of a highly distinctive sequence of deep slashes from a propeller blade on her back and tail thought to have been sustained more than 20 years ago.
“These images really bring home the physical and direct impact we’re having on these animals, especially on animals that size,” says Dr Raphael Mayaud, a marine ecologist at Griffith University and a member of an expert group advising the International Whaling Commission (IWC) on vessel strikes.
Rebecca Dunlop, an associate professor and humpback expert at the University of Queensland, says most of the images showed injuries to the back and rear of the whales, “suggesting they are surfacing as the boat propeller goes past and over their back”.
“When migrating humpbacks travel and surface like clockwork they don’t seem to be able to change their dive and travel behaviour to avoid an intercept pathway – this could be due to a boat approaching the intercept point at speed where they just don’t have the time to make an avoidance decision,” Dunlop says
Conservation success story
The IWC banned humpback whaling in the southern hemisphere in 1963 – after numbers had already crashed.
Soviet whalers continued to hunt them in the Southern Ocean until the early 1970s. Estimates from the 1960s put their numbers off the east coast of Australia at less than 300.
But as the threat of the harpoon was progressively removed, the population rebounded. One study based on observations of whales suggested that by 2004 the east coast humpbacks numbered 7,800.
It is seen by many conservationists as one of the planet’s great wildlife recovery stories.
By 2015, their numbers had more than trebled to 25,500. Estimates now suggest between 40,000 and 50,000 whales are migrating up and down the coast each year. Some modelling has suggested numbers will peak and plateau this year.
Dunlop and Mayaud both observe that, as populations have increased alongside the rise in popularity of boating and water recreation, the numbers of vessel strikes have also likely increased.
One in 10 Australians have a boat licence and of the more than 970,000 registered boats, more than half a million are in Queensland and New South Wales.
But it is difficult to know how many collisions there are with both large and smaller boats, experts say.
The IWC says that globally, “most collisions go unseen and unreported”. On Friday, it passed a resolution to work with all parties around the world to reduce “vessel strikes” which, the meeting agreed, was a “priority concern” for the commission.
Chris Johnson, the WWF’s global lead on initiatives to protect whales, who was at the meeting, says it is an important step for the IWC.
“Humpbacks have been one of the great conservation success stories. But along Australia’s humpback highway, there’s growing risk for them to be hit by vessels,” he says.
“Those strikes [in the images] would have been incredibly painful. We can see the evidence, but we have a black hole of information.”
Experts say cutting speed limits for all vessels moving along migration routes, and making boats and ships more aware of the riskiest places and times of the year, would help.
In California, for example, Johnson says shipping companies compete with each other to win high grades on public scorecards that assess how well they stick to speed limits during high-risk periods for whale strikes.
In San Francisco Bay, AI-assisted whale-spotting cameras are being trialled to give captains more notice about whales in their path.
While Australian law in theory requires that collisions with protected species like humpbacks be reported, Mayaud says most are either undetected or are never documented.
“The big thing is that a strike doesn’t have to kill a whale to have a serious impact,” he says.
“If a whale loses part of its fluke [tail] it may still survive, but swimming is likely to become less efficient and more energetically costly. That can then have knock-on effects on things like migration, feeding, body condition and potentially reproduction.
“There’s also the immediate trauma – the pain, blood loss, infection – and then the possibility the animal is carrying the effects of that injury for years afterwards.
“So I think the welfare issue is really about both the initial injury and the longer-term energetic and physical consequences for animals that survive.”

Ex-PM says Russia’s Putin cannot admit ‘mistake’ over Ukraine war
- Former Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Kasyanov said Putin realises invading Ukraine was a mistake but refuses to admit it and continues the war, confident of winning a war of attrition.
- Kasyanov warned of a harsh winter for Ukraine and urged the West to unite, apply psychological pressure on the Kremlin, and supply Patriot missile systems to defend against Russian strikes.
- Despite fear and tension in Russia's ruling class and society, Kasyanov sees no revolt yet but warns that large military mobilisations could spark protests; he described Putin as a calculating provocateur seeking respect, not open war with Europe.
AI generated
PARIS - Despite growing economic trouble and rising unease among ordinary Russians and the elite, President Vladimir Putin is not ready to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, his former prime minister said on Oct 3.
Speaking to AFP in an interview, Mikhail Kasyanov, Russia’s prime minister from 2000 to 2004, said he believed his former boss understood he had made a mistake by invading Ukraine in 2022 but would persist with the course he had set.
“He made a mistake that he cannot bring himself to admit,” Kasyanov, 68, said in Paris.
“He believed the reports from his security services that Ukraine was weak.”
The former prime minister said he was not convinced the war would end in 2027, adding that Putin was buoyed by high oil prices resulting from the US-Iran conflict and by disagreements between the United States and Europe over how to deal with the Kremlin on Ukraine.
“Putin is, of course, rubbing his hands with glee,” Kasyanov said.
“He clearly believes he can continue the war without making any concessions. And he is convinced that he is winning a war of attrition against Ukraine.”
He warned that the coming winter could be particularly brutal for Ukraine, urging Western countries to apply “psychological pressure on the Kremlin” by closing ranks, and urgently supply Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors to protect skies from intensifying Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Putin, a former KGB agent who turns 74 on Oct 7, has insisted that millions of Russians support Moscow’s war. In September, his ruling party won a record supermajority in elections that critics said were tightly controlled, with Putin portraying the vote as a show of support for the hostilities.
‘Sense of fatalism’
Kasyanov, who left Russia in 2022, lives in exile in Riga. In 2023, Moscow designated him a “foreign agent”, a term reminiscent of the Soviet-era label “enemy of the people”.
The Kremlin critic said he remained in contact with some members of Russia’s ruling elite.
“Fear reigns there – I am talking about the ruling class.
“Everyone wants the war to end. An overwhelming majority does,” he said.
“The difference lies in what kind of ending people want: some want the war to end in victory, some want it to end in Putin’s defeat, and others simply want it to stop, regardless of the outcome.”
Among ordinary Russians, Kasyanov said he saw “no grounds for a revolt”, despite mounting war casualties and rising food prices.
“Russians have lived with high inflation for the past 30 years,” he said. “They have grown accustomed to putting up with it.”
But a new wave of large-scale military mobilisations could trigger street protests, he added.
Speaking on the sidelines of a conference organised by the Paris-based association Russie-Libertes for anti-Putin exiles, Kasyanov said Russia had become “practically totalitarian” over the past few years.
“There is a sense of fatalism, hostility toward one another, and serious tension in society,” he said. “People are retreating into their own families, while negative feelings towards one another grow.”
After being dismissed by Putin, Kasyanov joined the opposition and became one of the Kremlin’s most vocal critics. Like many others, the start and duration of the war were a shock for him. Kasyanov told AFP in 2022 that the war could last about two years.
‘Calculating cynic’
After the Kremlin chief on Oct 1 said Russia would consider using “all types of weapons” if its exclave of Kaliningrad were attacked, Kasyanov said Western countries should not be intimidated by Putin’s sabre-rattling.
“The West’s and Europeans’ biggest mistake is that they are too afraid of Putin. He is not as strong as he appears,” Kasyanov told a packed audience in Paris.
“Putin fears the nuclear button more than many Europeans do.”
Kasyanov suggested that Putin wants foreigners to believe that “he is a psychopath” when in reality he is simply a “highly calculating cynic”.
“And he is raising the stakes in the game.”
Kasyanov said that with an increase in “hybrid attacks” Putin was provoking the West into taking measures that he could then exploit.
“He is a provocateur,” he added. “The only modus operandi he understands is the one he learned at the KGB academy. He told me that himself.”
But, Kasyanov said, he did not believe Putin was preparing for open war with Europe.
“What Putin wants is respect. He wants to force all of Europe to give it to him.” AFP

Breadcrumb
Egyptian journalists stage sit-in over detention of six reporters
Dozens of Egyptian journalists staged a sit-in in Cairo on Saturday, calling for the release of six reporters detained earlier this week in what rights groups say is the most serious blow to independent media in years.
The detained journalists made up the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, an independent media platform known for fact-checking and investigative reporting.
Journalists gathered at the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate, whose general assembly declared itself in permanent session and announced an open-ended sit-in at the syndicate's headquarters until its council meets on Monday to decide on further action.
"The danger is not limited to these journalists. It affects all independent journalists," local journalist Mostafa Bassiouny told AFP at the sit-in.
"There is a real threat to the already very narrow spaces for independent journalism," he said.
Security forces arrested the six journalists in raids across several Egyptian governorates between Monday and Tuesday, according to rights groups and the outlet's management.
Lawyers and rights advocates say the journalists were held without their whereabouts being immediately disclosed to families or legal representatives.
Saturday's rally followed several days of mounting criticism from international press freedom and human rights organisations.
More than 80 regional and international organisations, including Human Rights Watch, Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and called for the journalists' immediate release.
"Dismantling an entire newsroom in a matter of hours without warning or cause sends a chilling message to all journalists working in Egypt," said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch.
Egyptian authorities have defended the arrests. In a statement, the Interior Ministry accused the six journalists of belonging to a media network linked to the banned Muslim Brotherhood and of "publishing false news" with funding from abroad.
Officials said legal measures had been taken against them.
Matsadaash, whose name means "Don't Believe It" in Arabic, rejected the allegations.
Egypt has long faced criticism from press freedom organisations over restrictions on media activity.
According to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, the latest arrests bring the number of journalists in Egypt detained in connection with their work to 26.

The key features Australian homes may have in the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:39:56 UTC
03:39:56 KST

How Australians see future home life: More space to WFH and affordable access to energy
If you were to plan what your home life would be like in the future, what would be on your wish list?
A fridge always stocked with treats? An expensive electric vehicle in the garage?
Or would you settle for somewhere quiet to take meetings when you're working from home?
Researchers from Monash University, over a period of three years, have sought to understand what we want from our homes in the years to come.
The Foresights for Future Australian Home Life report included 49 participants from a range of backgrounds across the country.
"We're trying to understand how people will live in their homes, and what the implications will be for how they use energy," lead researcher Professor Sarah Pink says.
Multipurpose rooms
Participants were combining office zones with other parts of their homes, scheduling work and childcare around each other.
"They saw it as an opportunity often to do more than one thing at once," Professor Pink says.
So what could this mean when people are building new houses in the future?
University of Sydney associate professor of building science Jungsoo Kim says new homes could include more adaptable rooms or zones that provide visual and acoustic separation when needed.
"As well as good daylight, ventilation, thermal comfort, and access to power," he says.
"Some people need visual and acoustic privacy for concentration, meetings, or confidential conversations, while others may work effectively in shared, open areas.
"In smaller homes, flexible spaces that combine living and working functions may be more practical than a dedicated office.
"Movable screens, curtains, compact furniture, good storage, and task lighting can help create separation without requiring an additional room."
Working from home areas
Half of the households surveyed had one member working from home at least once a week.
Here is what some said about working from home.
It's so much easier when you work from home. You don't have to worry about traffic being terrible to get you to work. You don't have to worry about the train deciding to cancel … I also have a disability, so public transport's not viable for me a lot of the time.
The flexibility … [of] being able to drop the kids off, pick the kids up if you need to duck out or be here for an electrician to do something in the other room you can be here. You don't have to reschedule your whole life to do that. I can still keep working.
"You find people imagining their next home would have more space so that they could have a dedicated working-from-home room," Professor Pink says.
But that doesn't necessarily have to mean bigger houses, Dr Kim says.
"Instead, people may prioritise homes that use space more efficiently, with flexible areas or some spatial separation to support working alongside other household activities."
'Bloody expensive' EVs
Australians' relationship to their homes and cars is changing, as the energy transition shifts how electricity is generated and delivered across the network, according to the researchers.
An electric vehicle (EV) is being sold every 100 seconds in Australia and EVs are projected to make up almost one-quarter of all new car sales this year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.
But one-quarter of the survey participants felt they couldn't afford the costs associated with owning EVs from purchasing to maintaining and installing chargers.
Only 4 per cent of those earning less than $40,000 a year said they were currently using or intended to own an EV, compared to 22 per cent of people earning more than $241,000 a year.
It also found about one-third of households that owned or planned to purchase an EV or plug-in hybrid wanted affordable charging options, such as solar power or off-peak electricity tariffs.
Here is what some study participants said about EVs.
I think it's a great idea but they're so bloody expensive. Like who can afford to buy a brand new electric car? I'd love to but financially, it's just out of reach.
We would love to charge at home. We don't want to go outside and wait for hours. It's better to … if we have that, we'll get it charged at home.
I feel like saying Canberra is the Tesla town … People here may be able to afford electric cars, but I don't know, well, I can't, but how are people going to afford these new technologies?
Cheaper access to energy transitions
One in three homes in Australia has rooftop solar, with about 300,000 systems being installed annually.
The survey found adoption increased with income, with households earning under $80,000 more likely to report having no intention of installing solar.
It also found some participants felt excluded from the energy transition, such as the purchase of EVs and solar infrastructure, because these purchases felt targeted to more affluent groups.
"The cost-of-living crisis is an important dimension [in the energy transition]," Professor Pink says.
"One of our participants imagined themselves possibly living in their car in the future, [rather than] being able to purchase an electric vehicle."

"I had that one last fight left in me," Machchhar told the prime minister. "If I don't do it, I'm going to die... and just went for the door and opened the door."
Machchhar said the ordeal began when his co-pilot said he wanted to pray, which the captain noted was "not out of the ordinary."
The captain said he looked away "out of respect" when he suddenly felt a "big blow to the back of my head."
"My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft," he said. "But then, after that, the blows kept coming, one after the other, and that's when I realized that it's not the aircraft; it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me."
Machchhar: Co-pilot attempted to keep cockpit door shut during attack
Despite Machchhar's attempts to stop him, he said the aircraft pitched sharply downward as his vision rapidly faded, noting that he managed to open the cockpit door several times even though his co-pilot kept closing it.
"My colleagues from outside were trying to pitch in the code (to open the door), but the guy was not allowing them to open the code," the captain explained. "Once I had my hand on the knob, I guess I twisted it, and I opened it."
"I remember I was lying down on the cockpit floor, and I felt the aircraft and the whooshing sound and people screaming," he recalled. "Thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back, took over the controls, and the rest is what you know, sir."
Netanyahu invites Machchhar to join Indian PM Modi at Independence Day torch lighting
Netanyahu told Machchhar how he admired his "courage" and "coolness of judgment under impossible conditions," inviting the captain to light a torch alongside Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Israel's next Independence Day celebration.
"It's usually reserved for Israeli citizens, but I think here in this case, all the citizens of Israel will embrace you," he told Machchhar.
The prime minister thanked Machchhar for his "remarkable" actions, saying that he "saved the spirit of the world."
"You're a hero of Israel, you're a hero of India, you're a hero of the entire world," he told the captain. "I can tell you that people here (in Israel) will welcome you with open arms."
Captain Machchhar told Netanyahu that he would appreciate the chance to meet the Israeli dentist who saved his life onboard the aircraft immediately following the co-pilot's attack.
Israel ambassador to UAE meets Machchhar in Dubai
Israeli Ambassador to the UAE Yossi Shelley became the first Israeli to meet Machchhar in person on Saturday, with the pilot rejecting the idea that he should be described as a hero, saying that in the critical moments of the incident, he simply understood he had to act.
Shelley lauded the captain for his bravery before formally inviting Machchhar to visit Israel as soon as he is able, telling him that he would be welcomed with the appreciation and embrace of Israelis across the country.

New Tel Aviv exhibition shows never-before-seen private work from six Israeli artists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:38:32 UTC
03:38:32 KST

Three pairs of artists stand at the center of Something to Hold On To, which opened recently at the Genia Schreiber University Art Gallery at Tel Aviv University.
They are Hedwig Grossman and Rudi Lehmann, who came from Germany in 1933; Siona Shimshi and Jachin Hirsch, born in Tel Aviv in the 1930s; and Menashe Kadishman and Igael Tumarkin, who studied with Lehmann in the 1950s and wrote to him for decades.
What hangs on the walls is what they kept about one another – letters, diaries, sketchbooks, and photographs from the Ziffer House Archive: Documentation and Research Center of Israeli Visual Arts, now on public view for the first time.
The exhibition title, Something to Hold On To, came out of a conversation between the two curators during the Israel-Hamas War. Hila Cooper, who curated the show with Roni Kochavi, noted that when they began working on the exhibition, there were still hostages being held in Gaza.
New exhibition shows never-before-seen private work from six Israeli artists
“We tried to talk about what we were feeling at that time and what had become important to us in such a turbulent and difficult period.” For Cooper, it was the closeness of relationships, the support that family or friends gave each other.
“I was also swept into the ‘baby boom’ of the war, and there was my third child, the little one who is now in kindergarten. He was with me right from the moment we started working on the exhibition, and he was really my something to hold on to.”
'Thanks to those who chose not to throw them'
The title has a second meaning. “We work with archival materials,” Cooper said. “These collections exist today because somebody held on to these materials. The photographs, letters, sketches, work processes, correspondence between artists, drawings that artists gave one another. It survived and reached us, and today it is an important document, thanks to those who chose not to throw them.”
Grossman and Lehmann are the pair of artists to whom Cooper feels personally connected. “Hedwig Grossman is considered the mother of the artistic ceramics field in Israel, and Rudi Lehmann was a sculptor. She was Jewish, but he was not. They were born in Germany, and they came in the aliyah before the war. He was swept into the Zionist story following Hedwig, who was part of the Zionist movement in Germany. Here they really built an artistic hub over the years.”
“She was known as a rigid woman, very pedantic,” Cooper said. But what the drawers held was different. “When we dived into the materials, we felt we were really discovering a woman,” she noted. “Suddenly, when you see the materials in the archive, you meet a much softer and more romantic side of her. It is the personal materials that allow you to understand the professional practice in a different context.”
Shimshi and Hirsch, a generation later, left a different kind of record. Hirsch was a photographer and a documentarian, and his camera was trained on his partner. “She was his constant subject and muse,” Cooper said. There is plenty of evidence in the exhibition: photographs of her in New York in the early 1960s, at the Williams House in Eilat in 1965, in Paris, and asleep, taken over the years – even when she was older.
Kadishman and Tumarkin came into the show through the back door, out of other people’s archives. “We found that both of them had a central presence in the collections, both in Hedwig and Rudi’s and in Siona and Jachin’s, because Rudi was Kadishman and Tumarkin’s teacher,” Cooper said. “We saw how they stayed in touch with him for years, for decades, how they exchanged letters, and how they valued him. It is not something to be taken for granted, to stay in touch with your teacher from the very beginning of the road and to keep it up for decades.”
The exhibition feels like a 'rabbit hole'
Kadishman also put it into pictures. In the letters he sent to Lehmann and Grossman, he drew himself as a figure smaller than the great Lehmann, holding a little flower, a motif Lehmann had used in his early portraits. It was Kadishman’s homage to his teacher.
Tumarkin and Lehmann also shared a language. “Both of them came from Germany, and there was the matter of the language,” Cooper said. “I say this carefully, but Tumarkin saw in Rudi some kind of father figure. He sent him letters later on, and you see that he wanted Rudi to appreciate him.”
Editing all of this into a single exhibition was the hard part; the collections run to tens of thousands of items. It is work she calls Sisyphean and loves. “You can go in there and never come out, like a rabbit hole,” she said.
Something to Hold On To, Genia Schreiber University Art Gallery, 64 Haim Levanon St., TAU, next to Gate 7. Curators: Roni Kochavi and Hila Cooper. Runs through the end of January 2027. Free entry. Tue. and Fri., 10 a.m.-2 p.m.; Wed., 10 a.m.-4 p.m.; Thurs., 10 a.m.-7 p.m.

====================================================================================================

Jerusalem Biennale turns trauma and pain into art, healing, and hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:38:23 UTC
03:38:23 KST

As the offspring of a Holocaust survivor, I try to stay clear of comparisons between the most cataclysmic chapter in Jewish history and any of the – sadly, all too many – other disasters that have befallen us right through our timeline.
But it must be said that Oct. 7 comes close, and has left deep scar tissue and open emotional wounds that may never fully heal.
That is where art can come in and lend a recuperative or, at the very least, soothing hand.
There are historical, corporeal facts on the ground that support that supposition in the form, for example, of the astoundingly rich cultural life Jews led when incarcerated behind forbidding walls in the Warsaw Ghetto. Despite the desperate existential plight in which the inmates found themselves, they defiantly clung to a spiritually enriched way of life, and maintained their humanity for as long as they possibly could, engaging in theatrical and musical entertainment for fearful people starved of physical sustenance.
These days Israel finds itself largely politically-culturally incarcerated by members of the global political arena who impose and promote boycotts of anything that smacks of Israeli content. That strays far beyond political and military parameters and affects our artists, who simply want to keep creating and spread their rich expressive word as far and as wide as they can.
But while the number of foreign artists and institutions, across all areas of cultural endeavor, willing to come over here or even collaborate with their Israeli counterparts elsewhere continues to be depressingly negligible, our own homegrown artists maintain the good fight, keeping tabs on their muses and producing the quality, inspiring, heartwarming, spiritually uplifting goods time and time again.
That much is clear from the rollout of the current Jerusalem Biennale, which opened for business last week – postponed from May due to Iranian-Israeli shenanigans – and is due to run at all manner of museum, gallery, and ad hoc display spaces across the city through to mid-November. The breadth of styles, chromatic presentations, ideas, viewpoints and emotional undercurrents is mightily impressive.
Feeding off the bad vibes
Biennale founder Rami Ozeri believes that is part and parcel of the quotidian artistic condition, as well as a direct result of our ongoing predicament.
“The situation actually generates two contrasting things,” he posits.
“First, it detaches us from a lot of connections and friendships and institutions around the world. Those connections are enriching. When they exist, they help creativity. It is not good to be disconnected.”
Clearly, but Ozeri also sees the benefits of the sizable challenges faced by the Israeli artistic community.
“The intensity of our reality, and the pain we feel every single day, and the very significant things that have been happening here in the past few years, provide a very fertile platform for art.”
That sounds suspiciously similar to the age-old cliché of artists having to suffer for their art.
Setting hackneyed adages aside, Ozeri says the fruits of paying one’s dues, whether by choice or imposition, are being unfurled for our viewing and sensorial pleasure in the multi-exhibition program.
That, he notes, is reflected in the choice of the titular banner for the biennale’s seventh edition. There is a clear spiritual element to the logistical mix.
“I think that is what the title, ‘Mima’amakim’ [from the depths or, as the official non-Hebrew moniker has it, De Profundis], is trying to encapsulate. It starts from prayer. They say that when prayer comes from a low, deep place, it is more powerful and meaningful.”
The same, he argues, goes for the creative process. “When art comes from a sense of being satiated, from quietness, it is very limited. When art is spawned by trauma, by a wound, by struggle and pain, that is art which has a lot of power.”
Unfortunately, we have plenty of all those elements to draw on.
That, Ozeri feels, more than makes up for almost blanket worldwide exclusion.
“Despite the disconnection from international ties, we manage to create excellent art. Israeli artists are rising to new heights, de profundis, from the depths. Their works are very charged with meaning. They have a lot of strength that comes from our reality.”
Drawing from the depths
The event header comes from the opening verse of Psalm 130: “Out of the depths I cry to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice.”
That plaintive heavenward appeal is, naturally, a close fit for our present state of affairs. There is no escaping the trauma of Oct. 7, or our continuing unresolved security issues.
Ozeri is as painfully aware of all that as the rest of us, and it was clear to him, from the outset, that it would filter through the logistical and artistic choices made in the lead-up to the biennale.
“When we chose the theme, we still had hostages in Gaza; there were people being killed there. There was a lot of pain and trauma.”
The current edition of the biennale addresses that and tries to offer some light and hope amid the darkness and sorrow.
“De profundis is designed to try to generate some movement, to recognize the fact that we are down there in the depths. But this is about ‘out of the depths,’ to set us in motion towards healing and improvement of our quality of life.”
Light is generally not in ready supply the deeper you dig into solid substances or through emotional strata. There is, however, an abundance of illumination in the program centerpiece – “Or Chozer: An Active Vision.” Or Chozer translates as “Reflected Light” and references a Kabbalistic concept whereby humankind returns divine light to its celestial origin, after having shared its benefits.
The exhibition opened last week at the former home of the National Library of Israel, on the Givat Ram campus of the Hebrew University, specifically on the first floor of the celebrated cavernous, currently disused edifice.
The hall in question houses the monumental stained-glass window triptych created by Mordechai Ardon over 40 years ago. The three-parter’s official title is “Isaiah’s Vision of Eternal Peace,” otherwise known simply as the Ardon Windows.
As the biblical reference infers, there is so much to the substantial creation that was once frequently passed and, no doubt, intermittently observed and admired by then library users. And there is much to draw on, aesthetically, stylistically, and culturally.
The windows sport sumptuous colors – predominantly red, blue, and white – with a whole host of surreal and symbolic shapes and forms that suggest manifold lines of thought and inspiration. Jewish mysticism is well and truly in there, and the hues Ardon used almost knock you off your feet.
Harmony in art
“Or Chozer” is curated by Dr. David Sperber and artist Porat Salomon. The pairing of a reform rabbi – Sperber – and a settler, as Sperber put it, is in itself quite a declaration of harmonious intent.
“Putting us together goes against the standard grain of a religious man and a secular one,” Salomon notes. “We are, as it were, at different ends of the religious spectrum. But we haven’t spent even one moment discussing that.”
And they haven’t come to blows? I jokingly interjected. “We came close to it,” Salomon shot back in a witty touché.
That seamless flow, says Sperber, is at the core of the whole event.
“That is important in the context of the Jerusalem Biennale. There are people who think it is a biennale of Jewish art and, therefore, a religious project. I have been a part of the biennale since the beginning, and I can say that is not true. This is a biennale which brings everything together and somewhat challenges the divisions [between religiously observant and secular Jews].”
The coalescence of seemingly contrasting philosophies and lifestyles is central to the Ardon triptych, and the contemporary items Salomon and Sperber have physically and conceptually wedded with the veteran work address that, as well as, inevitably, that fateful day almost three years ago now, when our faith in the safety of our homeland was brutally shattered.
“Oct. 7 is undeniably at the core of this exhibition,” says Sperber. That, and violent altercations in general.
“The triptych talks about the [utopian] vision of Isaiah: ‘and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore.’ That is in the Ardon Windows. I don’t know if, at this time, we can even consider a situation like that.”
Still, one can dream. “Perhaps we should think about that,” Sperber continues. “That is what the [contemporary] works express vis-à-vis the windows.”
One current-day contribution to that intriguing philosophical and conceptual dialogue is the “Isaiah Is Waiting” set of sketches by US-born Jerusalemite multidisciplinary artist Andi Arnovitz.
It is a highly emotive series that evokes all sorts of heightened feelings and sensations, offering a string of snapshots from a storyboard of the tortuously interminable captivity of our hostages, and the war, in Gaza.
There is an image of pianist Alon Ohel returning to Israel after over two years in a Hamas tunnel, one of a decimated Gazan neighborhood, and another of a house on Kibbutz Be’eri reduced to rubble.
Perhaps the most recognizable and painful of the 11 sketches shows the parents of hostage Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Jon and Rachel, after their son was murdered almost a year after his abduction.
Visitors to the former National Library building will be drawn – corporeally – into the thick of the emotional mix evoked by the method of making visual contact with the Arnovitz works.
“There is a View-Master close to the windows, and people will be able to see the pictures by looking through the viewfinder,” Salomon explains.
The interface of a toy used by kids worldwide to get a 3D look at Disney characters and other similarly entertaining content, and the aftermath of the horrors of the violence that erupted down South three years ago, he says, spawns an oxymoronic fusion designed to grab us by the heartstrings.
“The sketches capture difficult moments of trauma and memories from that time,” says Salomon.
“Isaiah Is Waiting” also feeds off the Ardon centerpiece in a direct, elemental way.
“The light that illuminates the sketches in the View-Master comes from the windows,” he adds.
Glimmers of better things
to come
Ariane Littman’s installation also gets its visual and ideational nutrition from the triptych.
Over the past three-and-a-half decades, the Swiss-born Jerusalemite multidisciplinary artist has gained a reputation for her no-punches-pulled output, particularly since Oct. 7.
Her layout at the former National Library building takes the feral line to expressing her thoughts and feelings about where we are at these days, comprising receptacles of various shapes and substances and a maze of bandage-like material, all suffused with a sanguine-tinted liquid. No prizes for guessing the inference there.
“The cloth drips blood, and all juxtaposed with the very red section of the windows,” Sperber explains.
That sounds highly dramatic and dystopian, but there is hope of better things to come in there, too.
“It is very red at that spot in the Ardon work, but there is also the prophetic vision of Isaiah, with the healing element.”
Sperber says Littman gained some spiritual encouragement from her project. “It was her way to cope with reality here, to accommodate her own pain.”
That sounds like the quintessential site-specific effort, fueled by both the spirit and aesthetics of the host windows.
There is more soul-seeking in a video creation by internationally renowned artist Sigalit Landau, who has drawn on the Dead Sea for inspiration for many years now.
“She has been engaging with the Dead Sea for so long,” Salomon notes. “That is her ‘excavation site’ from which she gleans all the power of her art.”
The footage she shot at the lowest point on the face of the Earth shows a static figure standing on a revolving islet in the briny body of water. It is a Sisyphean scene, with the character not making any progress toward some unknown destination.
“I see Sigalit’s oeuvre in the context of the fate of the Israelis and the Jewish people. In the past she called that the ‘infinite solution.’”
That automatically and intentionally triggers thoughts of the Nazis’ “Final Solution.”
Belu-Simion Fainaru, whose global profile continues to rocket and is currently representing Israel at the Venice Biennale, has a somewhat cryptic item in “Or Chozer,” in the form of an alternative neon exit sign.
“It shows the words ‘yihyeh tov’ (things will be OK). That may mean things really will work out. But we all know the Israeli expression ‘yihyeh tov’ and what it may imply,” Salomon says with more than a touch of dark humor. “We say that, often, when we don’t actually know things will turn out in our favor.”
As ever, time will tell.
Other items in the expansive “Or Chozer” spread include a video work by French-born Israeli artist Yosef-Joseph Dadoune, shot in the Louvre, and a very large oil painting by Hanita Ilan, winner of last year’s prestigious Rappaport Prize, which approaches historical material about Jerusalem through a contemplative look at a particular moment in the city’s development, comprising snippets of information, photographs, archival documents, and testimonies.
Arab-Israeli artist Asad Azi bridges the ethnic-religious divide with a pair of paintings with a leitmotif of an Arab riding a donkey, which many visitors will, no doubt, associate with the coming of the Jewish Messiah.
Israeli-Arab artist and actress Raida Adon also features in the biennale hub.
“We are showing a simple and beautiful video work she created when she was still a student at Bezalel,” says Salomon. “I think she was the first Palestinian artist to have a large exhibition at the Israel Museum. She is seen walking through the Via Dolorosa, in the Old City of Jerusalem, with a cutout of a house on her head. That is, of course, a house with no foundations, and is similar to the wall in the Ardon Windows.”
That makes for a neat seamless fit.
“That work is another example of asking questions vis-à-vis the [prophetic] vision. It raises thoughts about home, and where that exists.”
An abundance of questions and issues is on display across no fewer than 42 exhibitions, at 21 venues, in the largest biennale to date.
Other shows to watch out for include Ilan’s collection at Hamiffal, and South African-born Pamela Silver’s rich “Undercurrents” rollout at the Mormon University, with a retrospective of watercolors and monotypes created over the past 25 years.
Over at the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum, Yehudit Sasportas premieres a video-and-sound installation, and there are contributions from some 80 artists from abroad dotted around town.
Our security and political issues may be a tough burden to bear, and we may be getting a resounding cold shoulder from many cultural bodies and personalities around the globe, but it doesn’t look like anyone or anything is going to stop our talented artists from having their say, come what may.

Former Israeli fighter pilot killed in light plane crash in northern Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:38:21 UTC
03:38:21 KST

Eran Peleg, a 75-year-old former Israeli Air Force fighter pilot from Kfar Saba, was killed Friday when a light aircraft crashed near Kafr Qara in northern Israel’s Wadi Ara region.
A 33-year-old man who was piloting the aircraft was also injured. The two had taken off from the Megiddo airfield before a malfunction occurred and the aircraft crashed. The circumstances of the accident are under investigation by police and the aviation safety investigation authority.
The aircraft crashed in an open area and caught fire. The blaze spread to a nearby wooded area and toward homes in Kafr Qara before firefighters brought it under control. The aircraft was completely destroyed by the fire.
The Magen David Adom emergency service said it received a report of the crash at 9:12 a.m. Friday. The injured pilot, who suffered burns to his limbs, was rescued from the aircraft and taken to Rambam Health Care Campus in Haifa.
His condition was initially described as serious, but the hospital later said that after he was examined in its trauma unit, his condition was assessed as moderate.
Peleg was a former Israeli Air Force fighter pilot who held the rank of lieutenant colonel in the reserves. He later entered the technology sector and also worked as a flight instructor at the Sky Aviation flight school.
In a 2020 interview with Yedioth Tikshoret journalist Mirit Kushnir-Strumza, Peleg spoke about a venture he had founded with Iyad Bader, an Arkia pilot, aimed at bringing the high-tech industry to Hurfeish, a Druze village in northern Israel.
The two had met about 12 years earlier at the Megiddo Aviation flight school, where Peleg, an expert in computers, information systems and model-driven software engineering, served as chief instructor. Bader joined the school after completing his military service, earned a civilian pilot’s license and later became a commercial pilot.
In 2020, they founded Metafor, a company specializing in model-driven development. Its technology allowed users to simulate planned processes using flowcharts. At the time, its customers included Israel Aerospace Industries, the Israeli Air Force and Mobileye.
The company employed seven people, most of them software and computer engineers, and established its office in central Hurfeish.
Peleg served as CEO and oversaw development and marketing, while Bader managed business development and fundraising. Their goal went beyond building a technology company: They wanted to create high-tech employment opportunities for residents of Hurfeish and the surrounding region.
“In Israel today, traveling to Tel Aviv to demonstrate against the Nation-State Law is a waste of time, but establishing a high-tech company in the village, close to home, is exactly the revolution the Druze need to make,” Peleg said in the 2020 interview, referring to the controversial 2018 law that defines Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people.
“Among the members of my family and that of Iyad, my partner in the venture, there are engineers and Ph.D.s,” he said. “At a meeting, we explained our product. They asked questions, discussed it together and argued a little. It was clear to everyone that if our venture succeeds, it will remain in Hurfeish and dramatically change the reality here.”
Peleg said at the time that his relationship with Bader had developed over many years.
“When they asked me to become chief instructor at Megiddo, I drove to Iyad’s home, and he helped me prepare materials and implement ideas,” Peleg said. “Our cooperation was excellent, both professionally and personally, and helped the school grow. Later our paths separated, and two years ago he called and said it was time to do something and bring high-tech to Hurfeish using the technology I had developed.”
The venture was intended in part to allow engineers and other residents of the region to work close to home rather than commute to Israel’s central high-tech hubs.
“I used to live in Kfar Vradim and had to travel regularly to Tel Aviv for work. It’s far,” Peleg said. “If I and the technology I developed can contribute something, I’ll gladly do it and establish a company that will make children in Hurfeish start thinking about high-tech.”
Peleg said one of the company’s employees had already received job offers with higher salaries but chose to remain with the venture.
“The principle is important to him just as it is important to me, and my part in this story is to succeed in establishing the software company in Hurfeish,” he said.
At the time, Peleg said the venture had begun attracting customers and had signed agreements with two marketing companies in Japan and India. He stressed that even if the startup were eventually acquired, he wanted its operations to remain in Hurfeish.
“Even if there is an exit, the company will continue to grow here, provide employment and allow people to work in the periphery and fulfill their potential,” Peleg said. “It gives me tremendous satisfaction, and I have all the energy in the world to invest whatever is needed to get where we want to go.”

It has no legal force — the Foreign Ministry responds to Russia’s “international manhunt” for Ukrainian officials
Kyiv • UNN
The Foreign Ministry stated that Russia’s placing Ukrainian officials on a wanted list has no legal force. The ministry reminded of the ICC arrest warrants for Putin, Shoigu and Gerasimov.
The latest decisions by the Investigative Committee and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation to place a number of current and former Ukrainian officials on the wanted list have no legal force whatsoever. This was reported by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, writes UNN.
Details
The foreign ministry emphasized that such steps by the aggressor state are adopted unilaterally, are null and void in any jurisdiction, and do not give rise to international legal consequences. On their own, they cannot serve as grounds for an international search or detention.
Any use of international police cooperation mechanisms must comply with the Interpol Constitution, Article 3 of which prohibits the organization from intervening in matters of a political or military nature
Additional information
Instead, the ministry reminded the public of the actual decisions by international and Ukrainian authorities concerning crimes committed as a result of Russian aggression:
-  On March 17, 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children; 
-  On June 24, 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Sergei Shoigu and Valery Gerasimov over strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. 
In addition, the Ukrainian prosecutor's office is investigating international crimes committed by representatives of the Russian leadership. The Foreign Ministry emphasized that Russia's attempts to create a false "mirror" picture are doomed to fail, and that justice for Russian criminals is inevitable.
Reminder
On October 2 the Russian Investigative Committee announced that Reznikov, Fedorov, Ivashchenko, and Brovdi were wanted. They were charged in absentia with a number of crimes.

As Russia expands attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine prepares to hit Moscow’s oil industry harder in response
