Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:30:36 UTC
03:30:36 KST

Ukraine will intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanded campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with Reuters on 3 October.
Russia has increased attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, hitting energy and telecommunications infrastructure, roads, railways, and bridges across the Dnipro. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would respond by targeting the Russian energy infrastructure that helps finance the war.
Russia expands attacks on Kyiv
Russian forces have broadened their strikes on infrastructure in and around Kyiv in recent weeks, with attacks increasingly affecting systems that support civilian life.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents indicating that Russian authorities had approved a broader policy for targeting infrastructure, including logistics, roads, schools, and hospitals. He said the goal is to put pressure on residents to leave Kyiv and other major cities.
Russia has also begun targeting bridges across the Dnipro, which connect the eastern and western parts of the capital.
Ukraine targets Russia’s war economy
Ukraine plans to keep striking Russian oil refineries because they generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war effort, Zelenskyy said.
The policy puts Kyiv at odds with US President Donald Trump, who has urged Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, arguing that such strikes contribute to higher global diesel prices.
Zelenskyy said he sees no indication that Moscow is prepared for either peace talks or an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.
Ukraine prepares for a new wave of air attacks
Ukraine is also preparing for intensified Russian attacks on its energy system over the winter. Ukrainian officials say Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles for a new campaign against electricity and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has also expanded its use of fast jet-powered Geran drones, launching dozens each day since the summer.
Ukrainian F-16s and MiG aircraft are intercepting around 60% of these drones, according to Zelenskyy, but ammunition for their 20 mm cannons is running low. Ukraine is increasing the use of electronic warfare and expects a first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles designed to counter the jet-powered drones later in October.
Ukraine is developing five interceptor drone models to counter Russian Shaheds. Two have already undergone testing, with Zelenskyy putting their current interception rate at around 30%.
Ukraine expands its strike capabilities
Ukraine is also expanding its long-range strike capabilities. It has used its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time, with a range of about 250 kilometers, while work continues on the longer-range FP-9.
At the same time, Kyiv is working with European partners to secure additional funding for its defense needs. Ukraine has found financing to order drones for early 2027 and is working to close a $27 billion gap in this year’s defense budget through its own resources, bilateral assistance, and financing linked to the EU’s €90 billion loan package.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s ability to sustain its defense and expand its strike capabilities will remain central as Russia prepares for another winter campaign.

Brazil's Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro wrap up campaigns on eve of tight vote

2026-10-03

03:30:15 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro have a final chance on Saturday to sway voters at rallies in crucial São Paulo before a tight election marked by scandals and personal attacks.
Millions of Brazilians will vote on Sunday in an election dominated by two rivals: the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former leader Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated four years ago.
The two stand on opposite sides of the political spectrum, with clashing views on issues ranging from how to tackle organised crime to what kind of relationship Latin America's largest country should have with the Trump administration.
The 80-year-old left-wing veteran Lula da Silva is running for a fourth and final term, warning voters that Brazil's sovereignty is at stake under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The Brazilian leader has repeatedly urged the United States not to interfere in Brazil's elections.
Last year, Washington slapped 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing, among other reasons, the trial of Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally.
Earlier this year, the US imposed another round of tariffs, alleging unfair trading practices despite running a trade surplus, and designated Brazil's biggest drug-trafficking gangs as foreign terrorist organisations shortly after Senator Bolsonaro visited the White House.
Lula has opposed both measures.
The left-wing candidate has made the defence of Brazilian sovereignty one of the main themes of his campaign. In the days leading up to the vote, his team released a Portuguese version of Bad Bunny's song "Lo que le pasó a Hawaii", which recalls the US colonisation of Hawaii as an example of what to avoid.
Flávio Bolsonaro campaigns on security and fiscal austerity
Lula da Silva is locked in a tight race with right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of Trump who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup d'état after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
After criss-crossing Brazil in recent weeks, the candidates are making final preparations for closing rallies to be held in São Paulo (Lula da Silva) and Rio de Janeiro (Flávio Bolsonaro).
Lula will hold his final rally in the megacity of São Paulo, with slogans on T-shirts and banners reading "Lula president again" and "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".
Flávio Bolsonaro, for his part, took part in a bikers' rally about 400 km away in the state of São Paulo and is ending the day with a final one in Rio de Janeiro. His rallies have featured huge US flags and giant inflatable balloons of Trump, who does not back the senator but says he is following the Brazilian election "very closely".
Jair Bolsonaro's son has campaigned on a platform of hardline security policies and fiscal austerity, branding Lula "incompetent" and highlighting the high cost of living.
If he wins the election, Flávio Bolsonaro will place Brazil in the group of Latin American countries, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Peru, that have swung to the right in recent votes and elected Trump-friendly governments.
Bitter campaign marked by scandals and insults
It has been a bruising campaign in a deeply divided nation. In a highly polarised Brazil, the candidates' policies and pledges have been overshadowed by a torrent of scandals and personal attacks as they fight for the attention of every undecided voter.
During the campaign it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption linked to the funding of the biopic "Dark Horse" about his father, financed by jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro.
Vorcaro himself is under investigation in one of the country's biggest financial scandals, which has implicated many figures in power. The affair also triggered a public row at the Supreme Federal Court, in which some judges were linked to Vorcaro.
A massive online campaign by both sides has seen the rivals seize on every gaffe, accusation and rumour, quickly turning them into slick videos or AI-generated images shared on social media.
For this 4 October election, twelve candidates are standing in the presidential race, but only Lula and Bolsonaro are seen as having a real chance of becoming Brazil's next head of state. The country's nearly 160 million registered voters will also be choosing members of parliament, governors and some senators, as well as the president.
According to opinion polls, neither candidate is set to win outright in Sunday's first round. The two are neck and neck and a second round, scheduled for 25 October, is more than likely.

Is it safe to charge your phone overnight?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Is it safe to charge your phone overnight?
It's bedtime. You set your alarm, notice your phone is down to 23 per cent battery, plug it in beside the bed and go to sleep.
By the morning, it's been connected to the charger for some seven to eight hours — much longer than it needed to reach 100 per cent, especially if it's on a fast charger.
You may have a vague recollection this could be bad for your phone's battery. The chemistry that makes lithium-ion batteries rechargeable has a limited shelf life, and it's shortened by repeated charge-discharge cycles.
In the past, the advice has been simple: don't leave your phone charging overnight and avoid bringing the battery up to 100 per cent to preserve its life span, ideally keeping it between 20 and 80 per cent.
In principle, that advice is still sound because the fundamental chemistry of the battery inside your phone hasn't changed. Regularly draining it to 0 per cent and then filling it up to 100 per cent will shorten its life span.
However, modern phones have improved battery health management and charging controls. As a result, the answer to whether it's OK to leave your phone plugged in overnight has become more nuanced in recent years.
Better charging controls
Rather than simply telling people not to charge overnight, modern phones can increasingly manage what happens to the battery during those night-time hours.
Apple has offered optimised battery charging since 2019. This feature learns a user's daily charging routine and delays charging beyond a certain percentage when the phone is expected to remain connected for an extended period.
Samsung and Google Pixel phones both offer a similar feature. Pixel phones have "adaptive charging", which also learns charging habits and slows charging overnight, aiming to reach 100 per cent shortly before you normally unplug the phone.
Samsung phones have "sleep time protection", which stops charging at about 80 per cent while you sleep and adjusts charging to reach 100 per cent just before you wake.
With the new iPhone 17, Apple has also introduced adaptive power mode, which learns typical battery consumption and anticipates when the user might run low, then adjusts power use to help the battery last through the day.
Setting charging limits
So what about charging only to 80 per cent? Reducing time spent at a high state of charge can help manage battery wear. But manufacturers themselves no longer treat 80 per cent as the only choice.
Samsung allows users of their most recent phones to set up battery protection that caps charging at a percentage of their choice: 80 per cent, 85 per cent, 90 per cent or 95 per cent.
Apple's iPhone 15 and later have a similar feature, allowing users to choose between 80 and 100 per cent in 5 per cent increments. The phone can even recommend a particular limit based on the user's charging habits.
Instead of using adaptive charging, Google Pixel 6a and later devices can simply be set to a limit of 80 per cent, an option that's ideal for people who usually finish their day with some charge remaining.
Ultimately, not charging your phone fully is a trade-off between reducing battery wear over the longer term and having more charge available day-to-day.
If 80 per cent comfortably gets you through the day, a lower limit will make sense. If you're travelling or facing a long day away from a charger, you may want to use more of the battery's capacity.
Even if you do choose a lower charging limit, your phone may occasionally charge itself to 100 per cent so the device's battery readings remain correct.
Whatever you do, avoid heat
While all these new charging features can prolong the life of the battery, they don't really address another important factor: heat.
The chemicals in lithium-ion batteries are sensitive to high temperatures and will degrade over time if stored in hot conditions, especially if they're also being charged at the same time.
Phones themselves increasingly respond to heat too, with charging limitations kicking in when the device detects high temperatures.
The general advice here hasn't changed. Always keep your phone away from excessive heat, including leaving it in a hot car or in direct sunlight.
If charging at bedtime, make sure you're not tucking your phone under a pillow or other bedding that could trap heat and risk overheating the device.
So, can you charge your phone overnight?
For most people using a modern smartphone, the answer is yes. The phone manages charging automatically, and you don't need to wake in the middle of the night to unplug your phone at exactly 80 per cent.
Instead, check what your phone offers and use optimised, adaptive or sleep-aware charging if it suits your routine. Consider a lower charge limit if you don't need 100 per cent every day. Above all, avoid excessive heat.
Even though phone batteries still aren't immune to aging, we now have more options to try to prolong their lives with smart charging features — so it's a good idea to check your settings and let the technology do some of the work.
This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

Steve Reich's infinite loops influenced David Bowie and Radiohead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

A beginner’s guide to minimalism in music from Steve Reich all the way to Radiohead
You may never have listened to Steve Reich or Philip Glass, but if you're under 90, chances are your musical tastes have been influenced by them.
Emerging from New York's experimental counterculture in the 1960s, minimalist composers and artists such as Philip Glass, Steve Reich, La Monte Young and Yoko Ono pushed the boundaries of what music could be.
Their ideas would go on to reshape the musical landscape far beyond their experimental circles.
The movement's fingerprints can be heard everywhere: in Brian Eno's ambient albums, Kraftwerk's electronic grooves, Radiohead's atmospheric soundscapes, and the film scores of Max Richter and Hans Zimmer.
To mark Steve Reich's 90th birthday on October 3, ABC Classic explores what minimalist music is, why it became one of the most influential musical movements of the past century, and where you might already be hearing it in everyday life.
What is minimalist music?
"Minimalist music is often harmonically static, or if it does change, it changes incredibly slowly," explains ABC Classic presenter Ed Le Brocq.
Loading...
Emerging as a reaction against the increasingly complex music of the 1950s, minimalism sought to "return to the purity of a single sound", Le Brocq says.
According to Le Brocq, the seeds of minimalism were sown in the late 19th century with music such as French composer Erik Satie's Vexations and Furniture Music.
"Vexations comprises a short musical phrase repeated [840] times, and a complete performance can last nearly a day," he says.
The most influential minimalist composers also drew inspiration from jazz.
"John Coltrane was a great influence on [composers like] Terry Riley, Steve Reich, La Monte Young and Philip Glass," Le Brocq says.
Minimalism was also shaped by influences beyond Western classical music traditions.
"La Monte Young and Terry Riley were both students of an Indian classical musician, Pandit Pran Nath."
In essence, minimalist music is "simplicity in one direction, which allows complexity in other directions".
Some works were so simple that they blurred the line between music and performance art.
What does it sound like?
Sometimes, minimalist music can be just two notes sustained for minutes on end, such as La Monte Young's Composition 1960 No. 7, according to Le Brocq.
Sometimes it's a sustained chord, as in Yves Klein's Monotone Symphony.
In the case of John Cage's 4′33″, it's silence.
More commonly, however, minimalist music is built around repeating musical patterns that evolve gradually over time.
These "infinite loops" can be heard in Reich's Piano Phase, Arvo Pärt's Spiegel im Spiegel and Philip Glass's Etudes and Metamorphosis.
Loading...
Pianist and composer Sally Whitwell, who has recorded and frequently performed Reich and Glass's music, describes the harmonic changes as "almost glacial", with patterns slowly shifting into something new.
But don't mistake simplicity for ease.
Whitwell says performing minimalist music is technically demanding.
"You have to always be extremely aware of where you are as a performer," she says.
What's special about minimalist music?
While some minimalist music can seem deceptively simple, Le Brocq says the point is to allow listeners to "hear more and more things just from a simple sound."
Whitwell remembers attending Philip Glass's four-hour opera Einstein on the Beach, which became her favourite opera.
"It's like sitting inside some kind of giant magical '70s analogue synthesiser," she says.
"There wasn't even a narrative, but I was just crying because it was so beautiful."
Whitwell says the opera's power comes from the way each elements come together.
"Every element, the music, the dance, the acting, the spoken word, the design, all of it together forms a complete work. None of those elements is really more important than any other."
For Le Brocq, Steve Reich's contribution to minimalism was equally transformative.
"Reich is so important because of his development of phase music," Le Brocq explains.
"Reich takes simple cells of sound and creates a new universe of music through his use of repetition to reveal new patterns in the music."
Le Brocq points to Reich's Different Trains as "one of the most moving and significant works of our time."
"He uses recordings of Holocaust survivors, takes their speech and turns it into musical phrases, then creates loops to form a tapestry of sound."
Loading...
How did minimalism influence popular music?
By the 1970s, minimalist ideas, including repetition, loops and gradual musical change, had already moved beyond experimental music circles into ambient and electronic genres.
"Brian Eno was heavily influenced by the minimalist movement in the 1970s," Le Brocq says.
Eno's 1978 album Music for Airports, often credited with helping define the ambient genre, uses layers of tape loops of different lengths to create a continuous soundscape that is "as ignorable as it is interesting".
"Everything from micro beats to synth-pop and that kind of thing is very rooted in loops," Whitwell says.
The minimalist fingerprint, particularly that of Steve Reich, can also be heard in David Bowie's "Weeping Wall" from his 1977 album Low and Radiohead's "Let Down" from the 1997 album OK Computer.
In some cases, the worlds of minimalism, avant-garde art and popular music overlapped directly.
Yoko Ono, a classically trained musician and a leading figure in New York's avant-garde scene in the 1960s, met her future husband, John Lennon, while assisting composer John Cage with his Notations project.
How did minimalism influence film music?
Minimalism's influence is perhaps most obvious today in film and television music.
Le Brocq describes composers such as Max Richter and Hans Zimmer as part of a direct line from Philip Glass and Steve Reich.
They use simple musical cells, gradual harmonic shifts and layered textures to create music that feels rooted in the minimalist tradition.
Zimmer's score for Christopher Nolan's Interstellar is perhaps one of the best examples of minimalist film music.
Richter's On the Nature of Daylight, featured in films including Arrival and Hamnet, has become one of the most recognisable descendants of the movement.
Richter and fellow composer Ludovico Einaudi are also among the most-streamed contemporary classical composers on Spotify.
Listen to Infinite Loops, a four-part audio series presented by Ed Le Brocq, every Saturday at 5pm throughout October and available on ABC Listen.

Electrification offers an off-ramp from fossil fuels, but there is a hook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

The Iran war is turbocharging electrification, but 'arteries of the clean energy age' are missing
At what would be his last Climate Summit as UN secretary-general, António Guterres took to the stage with characteristic gravitas.
"We are the first generation with the tools to end the fossil fuel age, and the last who can avert climate catastrophe," the 77-year-old told the audience in September.
"Let us use them well."
One tool, fast becoming the buzzword of global climate talks, is electrification.
COP31 host Türkiye will push for a voluntary pledge at the November conference to meet 35 per cent of global energy demand with electricity by 2035, up from 23 per cent today.
That would mean replacing fuels like gas and petrol with electricity across the transport sector and in homes, businesses and industry.
"We now have a strong common understanding of the urgency of the climate crisis," COP31 president Murat Kurum told the United Nations General Assembly in September.
"A significant part of the technologies we need is already available. The key question before us today is, how to put these solutions into practice, into real life?"
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has done some of the work for them, with a dedicated report on electrification that reveals an energy revolution is already taking place.
Solar PV and wind together are now the largest sources of growth in global electricity generation, overtaking coal and gas to meet over half of new electricity demand.
Electric vehicle sales have increased 40-fold since 2015, and dramatically falling costs have driven new stationary battery storage additions, which made up almost 120 gigawatts (GW) in 2025, the equivalent of more than 100 coal-fired power stations.
But if there was interest in electrification before, it has been turbocharged by another kind of crisis.
"Perhaps the most prominent reason is that it's an energy security strategy," said Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University.
"Especially Europe, but also many of the Asian economies rely heavily on imports, and electrification allows them to use domestically generated electricity instead."
The Iran war has left countries reeling from fuel shocks and volatility.
A proposal to ban diesel exports in the United States is now prompting calls for rationing, as the war looks set to stretch on into next year.
"The last serious energy crises were in the 1970s and only in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine," Professor Rosenow said.
"We've really seen supply-side constraints when it comes to fossil fuels.
"I think that really pushed electrification on top of the agenda."
Since March, about 25 countries have introduced structural policies to boost electrification.
Indonesia is making gas-powered motorbikes electric, while policies in Ethiopia have grown its EV fleet to more than 15 times what it was three years ago.
Australia is expanding a public EV kerbside charging program and has electrification incentives for both households and industry, while the Netherlands is replacing gas boilers with heat pumps.
China, which accounted for more than 60 per cent of the global increase in electricity demand from 2015 to 2025, is now electrifying heavy trucks and inland cargo ships.
"So, we're seeing projects not just in Europe, in the US, in China, but we're also seeing them in places like Thailand, for example, or India, so this is really something that is getting traction," Professor Rosenow said.
"Even under Trump, in the US, heat pumps now outsell gas furnaces and continue to do so."
If disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are adding to the momentum behind electrification, the IEA wants to run with it.
Given 55 per cent of energy-related carbon dioxide emissions come from sectors that can be electrified, including residences, industry and transportation, it argues there are significant climate benefits of converting that energy to clean sources.
The agency says electrification would cut the world's energy import bills by more than $US500 billion ($720 billion) every year, and because electricity is more efficient, switching to it as a supply source could roughly halve the global primary energy demand.
"COP31 comes at a crucial time," the IEA's executive director Fatih Birol told the UN during Climate Week.
"Because … the energy security objectives and the clean energy objectives are closely aligned.
"I have never seen that they are so aligned in the past."
Increased urgency as planet warms
The promise of a solution couldn't come soon enough.
August was the hottest month on record, and damage to human health, food security and water supplies is already evident.
The UN has predicted the planet will exceed 1.5 degrees of pre-industrial warming within the decade, with temperatures rising to at least 1.8 degrees.
Scientists have repeatedly warned that exceeding that threshold will lead to extreme weather, ecosystem loss, and submersion of small island states like Tuvalu.
Cities, infrastructure and economies are all vulnerable to the effects of warming, with the potential for irreversible changes to ice sheets, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest.
Grid bottlenecks grow
But if electrification promises a way to avert the climate crisis, there's a way to go before we get there.
Despite a decline over the past decade, coal remains the largest source of electricity.
And any efforts to replace it with low-emissions electricity sources run up against another problem: the grid.
Wind and solar farms are being deployed faster than the infrastructure needed to connect and move that electricity, like high-voltage transmission lines.
"The fact that we now have record growth in renewables and that we have record numbers when it comes to sales of EVs means that we have to build out the grid faster," Professor Rosenow said.
The IEA estimates more than 80 million kilometres of grid infrastructure, roughly equivalent to the entire global grid, will need to be added or refurbished by 2040.
"That's not an indicator that the transition is failing," Professor Rosenow said.
"We can build a bigger grid. The question is, how fast can we do it?"
The mismatch means more than 2,500 gigawatts of renewable energy projects, nearly twice the entire US's electricity generation capacity, are currently stalled in grid-connection queues worldwide.
In response, the UN has launched a grid acceleration initiative to increase investment in electricity infrastructure and, in Mr Guterres's words, to help "build the arteries of the clean energy age".
The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) estimates that investment in the grid will need to double, to about $US1 trillion a year, to meet that demand.
"The crisis is accelerating, but so are the solutions," the secretary-general said during Climate Week.
Türkiye won't meet its own target
Beyond highlighting the grid's constraints, Mr Guterres also used his platform to call on "every country to develop a credible road map to transition away from fossil fuels, with clear timelines".
He said it was "defying science, economics and common sense" that fossil fuel expansion would continue.
The US, no longer a party to the Paris Agreement that underpins COP31 negotiations, now leads the world in proposed gas-fired developments, much of which will be used to power data centres.
But the secretary-general's message could also have been directed at the countries leading COP31.
Data analysts from the global Climate Action Tracker group estimate Türkiye will fail to reach its electrification target by 2035, and analysts point out that the country's "renewable generation has largely supplemented, rather than displaced, fossil fuels".
"Türkiye is also investing heavily in oil and fossil gas exploration, overtaking Germany in 2024 as the largest producer of coal-fired electricity in Europe," the Climate Action Tracker analysts found.
In Australia, which will lead negotiations for COP31, the Climate Council has counted 16 new or expanded coal mines approved since 2023.
The NSW Independent Planning Commission has just approved the largest coal expansion in the state's history in the Hunter Valley, which will cause more than 800 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions over the next two decades.
As of 2026, nearly half of all electricity generation still comes from coal.
A spokesman for the Commonwealth's climate change minister, Chris Bowen, did not respond directly to questions about whether the country was on track to meet its 2035 climate targets.
Instead, they pointed to publicly available electrification incentives.
Professor Rosenow said the drive for global electrification was still a cause for hope.
"I would say it's a fork in the road for the energy discussion, where I think we're really talking about a fundamental reorganisation of the entire energy system here," he said.
"If we stand any chance of really bending the emissions curve down, then I think it is electrification because of these vast efficiency gains, and because we figured out how to actually generate clean electricity now at a pretty low economic cost.
"That is, to me, a reason why I'm quite hopeful."

What to know about the renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray

Ethiopian federal forces had entered the Tigray state capital on Saturday, a humanitarian source told AFP, after residents reported that the region's rebels had abandoned the city.
Fighting erupted on September 23 in northern Ethiopia as the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks into neighbouring states, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020-2022 civil war.
But federal forces and pro-government militias have pushed them back in recent days and were heading north towards the regional capital, Mekelle.
"Ethiopian federal forces and allied forces have reportedly been observed in Mekelle city... across various locations," a humanitarian source said told AFP late Saturday, citing reports from staff on the ground.
Earlier, a journalist in the city told AFP that "TPLF militants and leaders are leaving Mekelle".
He said government offices and police stations had been left without security personnel.
The journalist could not be reached for more details, as telecommunications networks have been severely disrupted in Tigray since hostilities, making the few bits of information that emerge difficult to verify.
Regional summit
"I am concerned that government and public property could be exposed to looting because there are no security forces in the city," a local resident said.
"Lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life. I want us to quickly return to law and order," added another resident.
Neither the spokesperson for the Ethiopian National Defence Forces nor that of federal Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has responded to AFP's requests for comment.
A diplomatic source told AFP that a mini-summit on Sunday would bring together the presidents of Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, as well as the head of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), Abdel Fattah al-Burhane, in Alamein, Egypt, on the sidelines of an African Business Forum.
The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year.
In a video message on Thursday, its leader Debretsion Gebremichael implied the TPLF would continue guerrilla-style attacks as they did when Mekelle fell to government forces in 2020.
Their insurgent campaign ultimately led to the TPLF retaking the city in mid-2021.
"We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose," Debretsion said.
Regional tensions
The conflict has triggered a breakdown in Ethiopia's relations with Eritrea and Egypt, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebels.
Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara on Thursday, while Eritrea responded that it would "sever all diplomatic ties".
Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to its coastline.
The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea".
Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat without explanation, prompting a reciprocal move by Cairo.
Counter-offensive
The rebels initially made advances in neighbouring Afar and Amhara states, working alongside local militias.
But they were pushed back this week, and the government launched a counter-offensive into Tigrayan territory along three axes towards Mekelle, according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.
There were reports that Mekelle's airport, on the southern approach to the city, had fallen to a pro-government militia on Friday.
But social media accounts are difficult to verify, media access is heavily restricted and there have been significant communications blackouts.
Earlier, a humanitarian source told AFP on condition of anonymity that the TPLF had been entirely pushed out of Afar.
The TPLF ruled all of Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, when it was marginalised with the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region.
The tensions led to a civil war from 2020 to 2022 - one of the deadliest in the world in recent times - that left more than 600,000 dead, according to the African Union.
The Pretoria peace agreement of 2022, brokered by African institutions and Washington, maintained an uneasy calm until last year, but was never fully implemented.

Latvia election: Pro-Ukraine PM Kulbergs set to retain power after historic victory for his United List party
Unknown

Latvia: PM's party wins biggest vote since independence
Published October 3, 2026last updated October 4, 2026
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election.
The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition.
What do the results show?
With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the left-leaning Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said.
Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones.
An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.
Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.
Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence in 1991.
The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, was dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns
Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.
Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.
Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.
Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.
Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.
German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace
Nevertheless, no parties proposed any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.
Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets were deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

The confirmation came in excerpts from Tebboune’s interview with local media outlets that was broadcast on Saturday ahead of its full release.

Ukraine Will Hit Russian Refineries in Response to Moscow's ‘New Doctrine’ of Airstrikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:01:54 UTC
03:01:54 KST

Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi,” had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict — Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The U.S. leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It's not fair just to normalize,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the U.S. has proposed resuming trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defenses have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones are too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft — F-16s and MiGs — to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions — including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it should receive its first shipment of small, cheap air defense missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defense chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We'll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile — the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to quickly finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, ‘Where is my FP-9?’” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defense budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance, and using “money credits” from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelensky said.

Hormone therapy before frozen embryo transfer is tied to larger babies but not to differences in early childhood IQ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:00:15 UTC
03:00:15 KST

Children conceived through frozen embryo transfers prepared with hormone replacement therapy tend to score about the same on early childhood intelligence tests as those conceived using natural cycle protocols. The hormone method was, however, linked to a higher rate of unusually large babies and more admissions to newborn care units. The research was published in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology.
Assisted reproductive technology provides medical procedures to help people achieve pregnancy, and advancements in freezing techniques have made frozen embryo transfer increasingly common. In this procedure, an embryo created in a laboratory is frozen, thawed at a later date, and then placed into the mother’s uterus. Preparing the lining of the uterus to receive the embryo is a necessary step. The timing must align closely so that the uterus is ready when the embryo is introduced.
For women who have regular menstrual periods, doctors generally use one of two methods to prepare the uterus. The natural cycle method relies on the woman’s own hormonal cycle to naturally thicken the uterine lining. Medical staff monitor this cycle, sometimes use an injection to trigger ovulation, and then provide a supplemental progesterone-like drug to support early pregnancy.
In contrast, the hormone replacement therapy method lacks natural ovulation. Instead, patients take external hormones, specifically estrogen and progesterone, to artificially build up the lining and prepare it for the embryo.
While hormone replacement therapy is widely used, it relies on adding estrogen from medication, which alters the mother’s internal hormone levels. Prior studies provide evidence that being exposed to unusually high levels of estrogen during early pregnancy might be linked to changes in an offspring’s brain development.
The research, led by Xiaomeng Shi, Minyue Tang, and Yimin Zhu of Zhejiang University, aimed to compare the cognitive function of children conceived through these two different uterine preparation methods. By analyzing past intelligence assessments of children between three and six years old, an age range the authors note is too young for puberty to affect the results, the researchers hoped to provide better guidance for patients choosing an embryo transfer protocol.
The research team looked at medical records and follow-up assessments from a reproductive center in China. Out of 1,538 recruited families, 790 children born from single, non-twin pregnancies met the criteria and made the final sample. These children were born to mothers who had regular menstrual cycles and underwent frozen, early-stage embryo transfers between 2004 and 2017.
Blastocyst transfers, which involve embryos developed a few days longer in the laboratory, were excluded from the analysis. Out of the included children, 434 were conceived using the natural cycle method, and 356 were conceived using the hormone replacement therapy method.
At the follow-up visits, trained assessors evaluated the children’s cognitive function using a standardized intelligence test adapted for Chinese children. The test measured verbal intelligence through tasks like vocabulary and comprehension, and performance intelligence using mazes, block design, and a matching task. Together, these scores provided a full-scale intelligence quotient, or IQ. To reduce bias, the assessors did not know which embryo transfer method each child’s mother had used.
The researchers also gathered extensive medical data to account for variables that might influence a child’s intelligence. In their statistical model, they adjusted for the year of transfer, the parents’ ages and body mass index, a measure of weight relative to height. They also accounted for the fertilization method, how long the embryo was frozen, uterine lining thickness, the mother’s estrogen level, length of pregnancy, and newborn unit admissions.
The results indicated that the cognitive function of children born after hormone replacement therapy was similar to that of children born after the natural cycle method. The researchers found no statistically significant differences in verbal intelligence, performance intelligence, or full-scale IQ scores between the two groups. After adjustment, the hormone group’s full-scale IQ averaged about two points lower, a gap that fell just short of statistical significance. The results argue against a large difference but cannot rule out a small one.
Rates of what the researchers defined as intellectual disability, an IQ below 80, were similar regardless of how the mother’s uterus was prepared. This threshold is higher than the usual clinical cutoff of about 70. After adjustment, the hormone group scored slightly higher on the vocabulary subtest. The authors did not correct for running many comparisons and describe these secondary results as exploratory, so this single difference may reflect chance.
The scientists also broke the data down by the child’s sex and by the specific fertilization method used. They looked at sex because biological differences can sometimes lead to different sensitivities to the environment inside the womb. They looked at the fertilization method, separating standard in vitro fertilization from intracytoplasmic sperm injection, in which a single sperm is injected directly into an egg.
Earlier studies disagree on whether this injection procedure is tied to cognitive differences. In all of these smaller groups, the researchers still found no statistically significant differences in IQ scores between the two uterine preparation protocols.
The authors propose that estrogen levels in the hormone therapy group may fall below the levels tied to cognitive problems in earlier research, though the study did not test this directly. The typical level in the hormone group, measured in the mother’s blood shortly before the transfer, was about a third higher than in the natural cycle group. However, levels varied much more widely, and about a quarter of mothers in the hormone group had levels more than four times the typical natural cycle level.
Looking at the birth records, the study noted that babies in the hormone therapy group had a higher chance of being born unusually large for their gestational age, meaning heavier than 90 percent of babies born at the same point in pregnancy. Specifically, 22.2 percent of the babies in the hormone group were classified as large, compared to 15.2 percent in the natural cycle group. The babies in the hormone group also had a higher rate of admission to newborn care units, at 14.6 percent versus 9.0 percent for the natural cycle group. The major reasons for these newborn care unit admissions included jaundice, respiratory system diseases, and preterm birth.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because the study looked back at past medical records rather than randomly assigning patients to a protocol, unmeasured factors such as the parents’ lifestyle, family socioeconomic status, or the child’s early educational environment might influence the results. The timeline of treatments was also not evenly distributed, with hormone therapy becoming much more common in the later years of the study period. The analysis adjusted for transfer year, but changes in clinical and laboratory practice over that period could still affect the comparison.
There is also a chance of over-adjustment in the statistical model. By controlling for factors like estrogen levels and length of pregnancy, which are part of the pathway being studied or possible downstream effects, the model could potentially hide a real effect. The unadjusted results also showed no statistically significant differences, so the main conclusion does not depend entirely on these adjustments.
Additionally, the findings may not apply to blastocyst transfers, which are now common in modern clinics, or to women who do not ovulate regularly. Finally, the children were followed only up to age six. Future studies could track cognitive abilities into the teenage years to see if any subtle differences emerge over time.
The study, “Cognitive function in offspring born after frozen embryo transfer following hormone replacement therapy cycles versus natural cycles: a retrospective cohort study,” was authored by Xiaomeng Shi, Xiaojing Wu, Aqiong Xie, Shuangying Liu, Xiaoqian Zhou, Yingzhi Yang, Minyue Tang, and Yimin Zhu.

The Nvidia Shield TV Is 7 Years Old. It Just Got a $100 Price Hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

How was an Omani pilot flagged for extremism cleared to fly to Israel? The failures and hard questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:57:23 UTC
02:57:23 KST

The flydubai flight that could have ended in catastrophe ultimately landed safely in Saudi Arabia. But as more details emerge about Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, accused of attacking the captain and trying to seize control of the Israel-bound jet, questions are mounting over the security failures that allowed him to be assigned to the flight in the first place.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, has formally described Wednesday’s incident as an attempted “terrorist act.” Authorities say al-Hammami attacked the captain with a crash ax kept in the cockpit and tried to take control as the aircraft plunged sharply. Passengers and others aboard subdued him, and the plane, carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Investigators are still examining his motives and whether anyone else was involved.
These are the central questions surrounding the apparent security breakdown:
How was an Omani pilot allowed to fly to Israel?
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acknowledged in an interview with Fox News this week that there had been a security “loophole” that the alleged attacker was able to exploit: A citizen of Oman, a country that does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel, had been cleared to pilot a flight there.
Early in the Israeli review, the Transportation Ministry considered whether the co-pilot might hold a second citizenship, which could have explained how an Omani national was assigned to an Israel-bound flight. That possibility was subsequently ruled out, according to reports, which say al-Hammami holds no additional citizenship.
Airlines flying to Israel are required to submit information on passengers and crew in advance under a 2023 Israeli law establishing a national passenger data analysis system. The system receives identifying and travel information, including nationality and travel document details.
The crew list was apparently submitted and cleared. But information that has emerged since the attack suggests the potential breakdown went far beyond his nationality.
How did Israel not know he had been grounded over extremism concerns?
Al-Hammami had already been barred from flying by Oman Air in 2024 after being identified as a security risk over concerns that he had adopted extremist views, according to officials familiar with the investigation. Officials told ABC News that extremist material was found in his possession while he was training as a co-pilot, after which he was removed from flying duties.
Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya reported that al-Hammami had become radicalized during time spent in Syria, saying he spent much of his time outside Oman, particularly in Syria. A source quoted in the report said Omani authorities became aware of his extremist views and that his mother is Syrian.
The Wall Street Journal reported that it remains unclear whether information about those concerns was subsequently passed to flydubai before the airline hired him earlier this year.
Royal Air Maroc, meanwhile, said al-Hammami underwent three months of training with the Moroccan airline but was not hired. That means two airlines — Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc — had declined to employ him as a pilot before he joined flydubai, without Israeli authorities apparently being aware of that history.
How did flydubai hire him despite his background?
A Gulf diplomat told The Associated Press that al-Hammami underwent standard security screening before he was hired, but the checks appear to have focused on whether he had a criminal record rather than digging more deeply into his background and potential signs of radicalization.
A person familiar with the investigation separately told AP that al-Hammami had been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns about extremist views.
According to the Gulf diplomat, intelligence agencies from four countries in the region are examining the co-pilot’s motives with assistance from the United States and other Western countries.
The investigation remains incomplete and has so far found no connection between al-Hammami and a terrorist organization, raising the possibility that he acted alone. An Israeli investigative team is already in the UAE, where al-Hammami was transferred after initially being detained in Saudi Arabia. 
Why didn’t the Shin Bet demand a halt to flights from the UAE?
Shin Bet chief David Zini had warned for months that he considered security arrangements on flights from the United Arab Emirates inadequate. In the weeks before the attack, the domestic security agency had also been at odds with Israeli airlines after barring them from flying to the UAE over security concerns.
Zini’s warnings primarily concerned Israeli airlines, whose overseas security arrangements fall under the Shin Bet’s purview. Flydubai is a foreign carrier and therefore is not directly supervised by the agency in the same way.
For years, the Shin Bet has provided professional security guidance for Israeli airlines operating overseas, while foreign carriers entering Israel are subject to a different system of licensing, oversight and security.
Still, Zini’s warnings have taken on new significance after the flydubai attack. According to officials familiar with the issue, the Shin Bet’s concern centered on security standards for flights departing the UAE for Israel, where security arrangements for foreign airlines may be less extensive.
The assessment is that stricter security measures could likely have prevented an incident like the one aboard the flydubai flight. Despite the warnings, however, Zini did not demand a suspension of all flights from the UAE.
Why is there no blacklist of pilots flagged for radicalization?
At this stage, the various Israeli authorities involved appear to be disputing where responsibility lies.
The Shin Bet says its direct responsibility extends to Israeli airlines. But the attack raises a broader question: Who is responsible for identifying a potential threat posed by a foreign pilot flying hundreds of Israelis into the country?
It also points to a potential gap in information-sharing among airlines and governments.
In 2023, as part of legislation connected to Israel’s entry into the U.S. Visa Waiver Program, the Knesset passed a law requiring airlines to provide advance passenger and crew information for flights entering, leaving or passing through Israel.
The National Center for Passenger Data Analysis was established within the Israel Tax Authority, with privacy safeguards. But the law explicitly permits the information to be used to identify, prevent and investigate terrorism and for aviation security. Among the agencies authorized to access information are the Shin Bet, Mossad, Israel Police and Transportation Ministry.
Much of the attention surrounding such systems naturally focuses on passengers. The flydubai case raises the question of whether pilots and other crew members are being scrutinized sufficiently as well.
The incident is likely to prompt a broader review of security for foreign airlines flying to Israel and the security establishment’s responsibility for protecting Israeli passengers traveling on them. Israel has previously imposed restrictions on foreign airlines when it considered security arrangements in their home countries inadequate.
And if al-Hammami had indeed been barred from flying in Oman over extremism concerns, another question remains: Why was no international warning issued, and why is there no system for flagging pilots removed from flying duties because of suspected radicalization?
Why wasn’t the pilot’s background — or at least his nationality — flagged?
Airlines are required to provide Israel with passenger and crew data in advance through the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis, which operates under the Tax Authority. Information supplied about crew members includes identifying details, citizenship and travel document information.
The center does not operate solely for the Tax Authority. Under the 2023 law, information can be made available to various government bodies according to their statutory authority, including the Transportation Ministry, Shin Bet, Mossad and police. 
The Transportation Ministry has stressed that it is not responsible for conducting intelligence background checks on foreign pilots and does not possess the intelligence capabilities of Israel’s security agencies.
Its formal responsibilities, however, make the picture more complicated. The ministry’s Security Division is responsible for aviation security, including security assessment of foreign flights entering or passing through Israel. It also operates an aviation security operations center that coordinates security matters involving aircraft arriving in the country.
There is an important distinction between conducting an intelligence background investigation of an individual — a task that falls to security and intelligence agencies — and conducting a security assessment of a foreign flight.
The Transportation Ministry is not necessarily expected to use intelligence tools to investigate every foreign pilot itself. But it does bear formal responsibility for security assessments of foreign flights.
The question, therefore, is who was supposed to take information already available in Israeli systems — in this case, the co-pilot’s identity and Omani citizenship — and determine whether he met the relevant conditions for flying to Israel.
Who will investigate the failure?
If it emerges that information about al-Hammami was available to Israeli authorities but none of the responsible agencies identified the problem in time, investigators will have to determine exactly where the chain broke down: with the airline, in the transfer of information, during screening or in coordination among government bodies.
In that case, examining flydubai’s conduct alone would not be enough. Israeli procedures and directives, as well as how different agencies use the information they receive, would also need scrutiny.
That question is particularly significant because the Transportation Ministry itself is among the bodies examining the incident. If its Security Division is responsible for security assessments of foreign flights, any review would also have to examine the division’s own conduct and its coordination with security agencies and the passenger data system.
The Shin Bet and other security agencies would similarly have to examine their roles and their coordination with the Transportation Ministry.
That raises the possibility of an external, overarching review capable of examining all the agencies involved rather than leaving each body to investigate itself.
Why wasn’t more done after the state comptroller’s report?
Questions about how responsibility for aviation security is divided among Israeli agencies predate the flydubai attack.
In May 2024, then-state comptroller Matanyahu Englman published findings from a systemic audit of international civil aviation security to and from Israel. Conducted between April 2022 and June 2023, the audit examined international aviation departing Ben Gurion Airport, security for Israeli aviation overseas and security arrangements for foreign and private civilian aircraft entering Israeli airspace.
The review involved the Shin Bet, Transportation Ministry, Israel Airports Authority and National Security Council, among other bodies. Much of the chapter remained classified for national security reasons.
In the publicly released portion, the comptroller recommended that the National Security Council conduct a comprehensive review with the Transportation Ministry, Finance Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet and police covering “the entire spectrum” of Israeli civil aviation security, including foreign aviation entering the country.
The comptroller also noted that some government and security Cabinet decisions governing aviation security dated back to the 1970s and recommended examining whether they remained relevant. He called for clearer arrangements governing responsibility and resources to ensure comprehensive oversight and urged the prime minister, transportation minister and finance minister to formulate an overall aviation security policy.
The public portion of the report did not specifically address flights from the UAE, nor did it identify the failure now under scrutiny. But its recommendation to clarify responsibility among the various agencies has gained renewed significance following the attack and the dispute over who should have identified the security gap.
Meanwhile, lawmakers Efrat Rayten, Ram Ben Barak, Chili Tropper and Oded Forer have asked Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee Chairman Boaz Bismuth to convene an urgent hearing with the Shin Bet chief over reports that security concerns involving UAE flights had been raised before the attack.
In their request, the lawmakers said the actions of passengers and crew prevented a major disaster and called for an examination of Israel’s aviation security system and the decisions made before the incident.

Police deployed around Cairo journalists' syndicate, amid international calls to free reporters
Egyptian police on Saturday were heavily deployed outside the journalists’ syndicate in Cairo in a bid to prevent protests from taking place, amid international criticism over the detention of the entire Matsad’ash fact-checking platform’s staff.
Security cordons were placed around the roads leading to the journalists’ syndicate, located in downtown Cairo, preventing people from passing through the area.
Police also set up security barriers to search passers-by, and asked people to show their ID to verify and confirm they were not journalists.
Dozens of cars were stopped in the area by plain-clothed soldiers who were deployed in the event of a protest breaking out.
This comes as officials in the journalist’s union council called people to attend a vigil, but warned them not to take part in any demonstrations on the union steps, in order to prevent a potential clash with police.
This comes after six journalists from the independent fact-checking platform were detained after their homes were raided on 28 September.
The journalists have been identified as Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel.
The development also comes as the journalists’ syndicate submitted two requests to the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Attorney General of the Supreme State Security Prosecution on Saturday morning, demanding answers over reports which state that the journalists have been arrested for 15 days pending investigations.
The union said in their request that five of the detained journalists were trainees, and that their primary concern is to protect media workers, whether they are registered with them, trainees, or otherwise.
They also confirmed that they have not been informed of any investigations being carried out with the detained journalists when they went to the prosecutor’s office, so reports circulating in the media had been surprising.
The case has triggered widespread concerns as the syndicate has not been notified of the charges against the journalists, the case number, their whereabouts ot if they have been interrogated.
Human Rights Watch on Friday condemned the arrests, stating that authorities in Cairo routinely flout due process protections and forcibly disappear people.
“Egyptian authorities’ simultaneous arrest of the entire newsroom at a prominent independent news platform is deeply alarming,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch.
“Dismantling an entire newsroom in a matter of hours without warning or cause sends a chilling message to all journalists working in Egypt and shows just how little space is left there for critical reporting,” Khawaja added.
Reporters Without Borders this week condemned Egyptian authorities' actions, stating: "It's a violation of the Egyptian Constitution, even though this is common practice. Journalists detained in Egypt are often forcibly disappeared for several days before being officially charged and brought before a court.”
Sara Qudah, Middle East and North Africa Regional Director for the Committee to Protect Journalists, told The New Arab earlier this week that action must be taken to find the whereabouts of the journalists and secure their release.
"CPJ is appalled by the arrests of Egyptian journalists Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud, and Mohamed Adel, effectively detaining Matsadaash investigative media platform's entire newsroom," she said.
The Matsad’ash platform was founded in 2018, with staff members working to correct misleading or inaccurate information from various sources, including from within Egypt and the broader region.

Tennessee prisons official resigns after Christa Pike’s failed US execution
Unknown

Tennessee prisons official resigns after Christa Pike’s failed US execution
The state’s governor said Frank Strada would step down as an independent review examines what went wrong.
The official in charge of the prison system in the US state of Tennessee has resigned just days after overseeing the botched execution of Christa Pike.
The state’s governor, Bill Lee, announced on Saturday that Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada would step down from his role later this month, a decision Lee described as necessary after the stunning failure.
“Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment”, Lee said in a statement. “I have accepted his decision to step down and am grateful for his commitment to ensuring a smooth leadership transition”.
A replacement for Strada was not announced.
Strada, who started his role in Tennessee three years ago, previously served as a top official in Arizona’s corrections department where multiple executions on his watch faced complications. He said he was resigning “in the best interest of Tennesseans” as an independent review examines what went wrong.
“I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred,” Strada said in a statement that defended his department’s handling of Pike’s execution.
Pike was transported from prison to hospital on Wednesday after surviving two injections of the drug pentobarbital, which Tennessee uses to execute prisoners.
Strada’s resignation was “justified”, Pike’s lawyers said in a statement. “But it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” they wrote. “We hope the Governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
In a court filing on Friday, Pike’s lawyers said she had been placed on a ventilator and intubated as medical staff worked to clear the drug from her system. They argued problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote in the filing.
Pike was 18 years old when she was sentenced to death for the torture and murder of another young woman in 1995, becoming one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Lee has suspended all executions for the remainder of the year while the state investigates.

====================================================================================================

Flydubai aircraft reached near-supersonic speeds, extreme airframe stress levels - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:24:06 UTC
02:24:06 KST

Damage to flydubai flight FZ1073’s rudder likely resulted from the extreme speeds, angles, and G-forces (gravitational acceleration) the aircraft reached during its dive and subsequent recovery amid its attempted hijacking, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
According to the report, the Boeing 737 MAX reached an estimated speed of Mach 0.96, with Mach 1.0 being the speed of sound. For comparison, such commercial aircraft cruise below the “high altitude never exceed speed (MMO)” of Mach 0.82. Speeds beyond MMO can damage the aircraft, while speeds slightly below can still cause damage if flight conditions are not smooth.
The report noted that the estimated speed and other flight parameters, sourced from Flightradar24 satellite tracking data, are less accurate than the data in the aircraft’s flight data recorder, also known as the “black box,” which investigators will rely on.
In addition, the estimations do not take into account variables, such as wind speed and direction, air temperature, and pressure levels, all of which contribute to what is known to pilots as True Airspeed (TAS), the most accurate representation of an aircraft’s speed concerning its performance and the forces acting upon it.
With this in mind, the aircraft may have reached a TAS higher than estimated, though investigators will need more time to confirm.
Aircraft fell over 17,000 feet in 92 seconds, satellite tracking data shows
What is known is that the stresses suffered by the aircraft caused a large portion of the rudder, which controls a plane’s yaw (side-to-side) movement, to break off.
The tracking data also showed that the aircraft fell about 17,400 feet over 92 seconds at a 39° nose-down attitude, far steeper than the standard descent angle of 3°.
As the aircraft was brought back under control, it sustained further stress through the return to straight-and-level flight, with the WSJ putting an emphasis on the estimated three G’s of force, three times the force of gravity.
A 737 MAX is only rated to sustain 2.5 positive G’s, according to its official limitations, which is unlikely to ever be reached in the course of a commercial flight.
The aircraft is also rated for a maximum maneuvering speed (VA) of between 210 and 230 knots, depending on configuration, meaning that beyond that speed, any abrupt or full-control movements can damage the aircraft. Mach 0.96 is well beyond that range.
Regardless of the cause, the damage to the rudder suggests a departure from the aircraft’s limitations in at least one of the areas discussed in the report.
A second pair of flydubai pilots, who took over control following the attempted hijacking, flew the damaged aircraft for over an hour before diverting to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
According to the report, the plane’s altitude fluctuated by about 500 feet (152 meters) at a time as it progressed, suggesting difficulty maintaining straight-and-level flight amid the damage.
The flydubai aircraft is still parked at Tabuk Airport as of the time of writing, where teams will examine the full extent of the damage to determine whether the plane is still airworthy after any needed repairs, the WSJ reported.
Embry-Riddle aerodynamicist: 'I’m not sure it can ever be used again'
Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University aerodynamicist Tony Farina told the WSJ that the aircraft will need, “at the very least... a complete and thorough inspection.”
“I’m not sure it can ever be used again,” Farina, who has worked with the US Air Force and NASA on aviation-related projects, said.
The fact that the Boeing managed to stay intact amid such extreme stresses marks a win for the US aircraft manufacturer, with the report noting the issues the 737 MAX has faced in recent years, ranging from physical cracks and software glitches to two separate fatal crashes resulting from a design flaw.
The WSJ reached out to Boeing, which declined to comment.
US President Donald Trump congratulated the American plane maker in a special media post on Wednesday following the incident, noting the 737 MAX aircraft’s ability to “withstand G-forces and strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do.”
Space-company TransAstra CEO and aerospace engineer Joel Sercel also commented on the security aspect of the incident, telling the WSJ that an aircraft’s good design “will not save the airplane if a qualified person on the flight deck commands a dive and the other person cannot stop him in time.”

The international slate features highly anticipated award-winners. Headline films include Markus Schleinzer’s Rose, which earned Sandra Hüller the Silver Bear at the Berlin Film Festival, and Dylan Meyer’s crime comedy The Wrong Girls, starring Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat.
Audiences can also look forward to Adam Shankman’s camp comedy Stop! That! Train! featuring RuPaul, alongside major festival favorites from Cannes and Montreal’s Fantasia.
A rich mosaic of new Israeli cinema
