Pontoon crossings coming to Kyiv following Russian strikes on key bridges, media reports
Following Russian attacks on vital bridges in central Kyiv, the capital plans to construct pontoon crossings across the Dnipro River, Ukrainian media reported on Oct. 3.
"Urgent solutions are a dam and a pontoon crossing, which are being built quickly," Ukraine's Reconstruction, Infrastructure, and Transport Minister, Mykola Kalashnyk, told Suspilny news about responding to the bridge attacks. "This work has already begun. A corresponding coordination meeting was held with the president."
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 3, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges over the Dnipro River were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid Moscow's unrelenting attacks on the civilian infrastructure across Ukraine. This week alone, the capital had 56 air raid sirens, lasting over 87 hours in total, emergency services said on Oct. 2.
Kalashnyk said that the construction of pontoon crossings could take up to three months and would help traffic move through the capital, which remains heavily restricted after the bridge attacks.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA) announced new restrictions on movements over Kyiv's bridges during air raid alerts on Oct. 3.
"On average, about 600,000 cars cross the left and right banks [of the Dnipro] during the day and the task is to maintain this throughput," Kalashnyk said. "Therefore, the locations where construction will begin have been determined accordingly."
Kalashnyk also revealed that plans for constructing underground tunnels beneath the Dnipro were being considered, though construction could "cost tens of billions of hryvnias."
Before constructing alternative crossings, Kalashnyk said that protecting the capital's existing bridges should remain the priority.
"Our first task is to provide protection from the sky, which we are doing in coordination with the military," Kalashnyk said. "The first step is to prevent strikes. The second part is to provide protection. The third is rapid recovery. And the fourth is to make decisions regarding alternative reserve crossings, i.e., the construction of new alternative bridge infrastructure facilities."
To counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.

As the march set off, Alexandre Schon, co-president of Inter-LGBT, which organises the march, said: “We are just a few months away from the presidential election, so we are calling on LGBT+ people and allies to mobilize for a future based on solidarity.”

Schon expressed worry about the future of LGBTQ+ people's rights. “We could be the next targets,” Schon added, noting that abroad, including in the United States and Senegal, the rights of LGBT+ people are “under attack.”

At least 16 Palestinians, including a woman, were injured and 55 olive trees were burned Saturday in attacks by illegal Israeli settlers on olive harvesters across the occupied West Bank, according to medical and local sources.
The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said five Palestinians were beaten by occupiers while picking up olives in a field in Sebastia, north of Nablus.
The society also said three Palestinians were injured in an illegal settler assault in Asira al-Qibliya, south of Nablus, while two others were injured after being sprayed with pepper spray in nearby Beit Imrin.
A farmer also suffered bruises after illegal settlers attacked him while he was harvesting olives in Arrabuna, east of Jenin, the same source said.
Attacks on farmers during harvest
In Rantis, northwest of Ramallah, illegal settlers attacked a man, his wife and their children with sticks, weapons and pepper spray in the village’s Al-Tin al-Shami area, injuring five family members, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The wife was also run over during the attack, according to the agency.
Meanwhile, illegal settlers burned about 55 olive trees more than 40 years old on Palestinian land in the wilderness area of Abu Dis, southeast of Jerusalem, Wafa said.
The attack took place as a Palestinian farmer was harvesting olives with his wife, children and grandchildren, the agency said.
Illegal settlers also assaulted Palestinian farmers harvesting olives east of Qalqilya in an attempt to prevent them from reaching their land and force them to leave, according to local sources.
The olive harvest typically begins in early October and continues through late November, making it one of the most important agricultural and economic seasons in Palestinian towns and villages.
Tens of thousands of trees uprooted

Figures released by the commission Friday showed that settlers carried out 647 attacks across the West Bank in September, killing three Palestinians.
About 750,000 illegal Israeli settlers live in 194 illegal settlements and 400 settlement outposts across the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, according to official Palestinian figures.

Iraq moves to restore flights to Iran after clerical appeals and public protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:29:39 UTC
01:29:39 KST

Iraq moves to restore flights to Iran after clerical appeals and public protests
TEHRAN- Baghdad secures a US sanctions exemption allowing up to 40 daily flights to and from Najaf, following appeals from senior Iraqi political and religious figures and demonstrations demanding the restoration of air links between the two neighboring countries.
Iraq has taken a significant step towards restoring air links with Iran after securing a limited exemption from US sanctions for flights to and from Najaf International Airport, following mounting political pressure, appeals from prominent Shia religious figures and protests by Iraqis demanding an end to restrictions that disrupted travel between the two neighbors.
Under an agreement announced by the Iraqi government on Friday, October 2, Iranian airlines will be permitted to operate up to 40 flights a day to and from Najaf, with the exception of Mahan Air. The arrangement followed direct discussions between Baghdad and Washington to secure an exemption from US restrictions targeting Iran s aviation sector.
The decision marks a development in efforts to restore a vital transportation link between the two countries, whose close religious, social and economic ties sustain substantial cross-border travel. It also follows growing objections in Iraq to restrictions that affected religious pilgrims, patients, students, businesspeople and other travelers.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi welcomed the US decision, describing it as a positive response to Baghdad s diplomatic efforts. He said the resumption of flights would facilitate travel, particularly for pilgrims, patients and tourists.
Air travel does not merely represent transportation between two airports, but rather a bridge of communication between peoples, al-Zaidi said.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein also welcomed the agreement, linking the resumption of flights to efforts to develop an Iraqi-US partnership based on mutual respect. He further highlighted the importance of respecting religious freedom and facilitating access to holy sites.
However, the agreement has not fully resolved the issue. While it allows Iranian carriers other than Mahan Air to operate flights to and from Najaf, the broader demand among Iraqi political figures, religious authorities and members of the public is for the restoration of regular air links between the two countries and the reopening of all Iraqi airports to Iranian flights.
 
Senior Iraqi cleric calls for all airports to reopen
Among the prominent voices calling for a broader restoration of air links is Ammar al-Hakim, the leader of Iraq s National Wisdom Movement and a senior Shia religious and political figure.
Welcoming the agreement, al-Hakim thanked Prime Minister al-Zaidi for the diplomatic efforts that led to the exemption, describing the decision as an important step towards facilitating transportation and communication between the peoples of Iran and Iraq.
He said the development demonstrated that dialogue and constructive diplomacy could resolve outstanding issues and overcome obstacles in the interests of Iraq and its people.
Al-Hakim also expressed solidarity with Iran and its people in the face of unilateral US sanctions, emphasizing the humanitarian importance of restoring air travel between the two neighboring Muslim countries.
Going beyond the limited arrangement for Najaf, he called on Iraq s civil aviation authorities to reopen all airports across the country to flights between Iran and Iraq.
His appeal reflects the wider concern that restrictions imposed in response to US sanctions could continue to disrupt travel even if a limited exemption allows some services to resume.
Najaf is a particularly important destination because of its religious significance to Shia Muslims. The city is home to the Imam Ali shrine and serves as a major gateway for Iranian pilgrims visiting Iraq s holy sites. Air links also facilitate travel by Iraqi pilgrims and other visitors heading to Iran s religious centers, including Mashhad and Qom.
For many travelers, direct flights offer a practical alternative to lengthy overland journeys. Interruptions to these services can therefore impose additional costs and logistical difficulties, particularly on patients and elderly pilgrims.
Iraqi political leadership had called for an exemption
The push to restore flights had extended beyond individual political and religious figures.
In an earlier joint statement, Iraq s senior political leadership called for Najaf International Airport to be exempted from US sanctions targeting Iran. The statement was issued by Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, President Nizar Amedi, Parliament Speaker Haibat al-Halbousi and Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zaidan.
The officials opposed the application of US restrictions to Najaf airport, emphasizing its distinctive religious status and its role in receiving millions of pilgrims.
They argued that the airport s importance to religious travel warranted an exemption from measures directed at Iran s aviation sector.
The joint appeal underscored the issue s significance within Iraq, where the consequences of sanctions extend beyond commercial aviation to religious tourism, family ties and humanitarian travel.
The subsequent agreement allowing up to 40 daily flights to and from Najaf represents a partial response to those concerns, although it falls short of the broader demand for access to all Iraqi airports.
Nujaba warns of renewed protests if restrictions continue
The campaign to restore flights has also drawn support from Iraq s resistance groups, which have strongly criticised the suspension of air links with Iran.
Akram al-Kaabi, secretary-general of Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, previously warned that the group would organize sit-ins at Iraqi airports nationwide unless normal air traffic between the two neighboring countries resumed.
The group s position was reinforced by Sheikh Nazim al-Saidi, head of Nujaba s executive council, who praised participants in a sit-in at Najaf International Airport and described their actions as an expression of commitment to Iraq s national sovereignty.
Al-Saidi said the demonstrators had shown a sense of responsibility and solidarity with those affected by the restrictions, framing support for the Iranian people as a moral, religious and humanitarian obligation.
Following the reopening of Najaf airport to eligible Iranian flights, the planned indefinite sit-in was called off. Al-Saidi nevertheless warned that continued US sanctions against Iraqi airports would provoke a renewed and potentially larger public response.
He stressed that Iraq s decisions should not be subject to external tutelage and that national sovereignty remained a fundamental principle.
The warning highlights the possibility that further restrictions on Iranian flights could reignite public opposition, particularly if travelers and religious communities conclude that the limited exemption has failed to restore normal services.
Public demonstrations add pressure on Baghdad
Public opposition has been another important element in the campaign to resume flights.
On Monday, Iraqis from different walks of life held demonstrations across the country to condemn the government s decision to suspend flights to and from Iran, according to Press TV.
The protests reflected concerns that restrictions introduced under US sanctions were directly affecting ordinary people, including pilgrims, patients, students, traders and families travelling between the two countries.
The demonstrations, alongside appeals from political leaders and religious figures, increased pressure on Baghdad to seek an arrangement that would allow air services to resume without exposing Iraqi airports and aviation service providers to US penalties.
Former Iraqi Prime Minister Adel Abdul Mahdi also criticized the suspension, describing Iran as Iraq s neighbor, ally and friend and urging the authorities to reverse the decision. He characterized the closure of air links as a major mistake.
Taken together, these reactions showed that the issue had developed beyond a dispute over airline operations into a broader debate about Iraq s sovereignty, its relations with Iran and the consequences of complying with US sanctions.
US sanctions disrupted a major regional travel corridor
The restrictions followed a new round of US measures targeting Iran s aviation sector in September. Washington threatened sanctions against companies and service providers that fueled, maintained, or otherwise assisted Iranian aircraft, including those operating outside the United States.
The measures created risks for airports, ground-handling companies, fuel suppliers and other businesses serving Iranian carriers. Concern over potential US penalties contributed to the suspension of Iranian flights at several Iraqi airports.
 
Najaf International Airport, a principal gateway for Iranian visitors to Iraq s holy cities, halted Iranian flights in late September after initially continuing to receive them. Erbil and Sulaymaniyah airports also took restrictive measures, while Kirkuk International Airport reported that it had no flights to Iran.
Iran s Foreign Ministry condemned the extraterritorial enforcement of US sanctions, arguing that the restrictions harmed ordinary travelers and interfered with legitimate economic and transport links.
Iran had also urged Baghdad to take steps to restore regular air connections, citing the difficulties faced by pilgrims, patients, students and businesspeople.
The dispute highlighted the pressure facing third countries and commercial operators whose dealings with Iranian airlines could expose them to US secondary sanctions, even when their activities take place outside American territory.
Thousands of passengers affected by the suspension
The scale of the disruption was reflected in figures previously provided by Iran s ambassador to Baghdad, Mohammad Kazem al-Sadegh.
Before the restrictions, approximately 25 Iranian flights a day arrived at Najaf and around 15 at Baghdad, according to the ambassador. He also estimated that between 12,000 and 13,000 people travelled between Iran and Iraq each day on Iranian airlines.
Those figures illustrate the importance of air links to the movement of people between the two countries and the potential consequences of prolonged interruptions.
For religious travelers, the effects are particularly significant. Najaf and Karbala are among the most important pilgrimage destinations for Shia Muslims, while Iran attracts visitors to its own major religious centers. The two countries also maintain extensive family, educational, commercial and cultural connections that generate demand for regular travel.
A limited exemption, with broader demands still outstanding
The agreement announced on October 2 offers a route towards restoring part of the disrupted air traffic, allowing eligible Iranian airlines to operate up to 40 daily flights to and from Najaf International Airport. The exclusion of Mahan Air, however, means that the arrangement does not restore access for all Iranian carriers.
Nor does the agreement, as announced, establish a blanket exemption for Iranian flights at every Iraqi airport.
Ammar al-Hakim s call for all Iraqi airports to reopen, the earlier appeal by Iraq s senior political leadership, and warnings from Nujaba indicate that pressure for a more comprehensive settlement is likely to remain an important part of the debate.
The immediate outcome is a partial restoration of air links following negotiations between Baghdad and Washington. The wider question is whether Iraq can secure arrangements that protect the operation of its airports while restoring reliable air travel with Iran.
For Baghdad, the challenge is to reconcile its diplomatic relationship with Washington with the practical needs of its own citizens and the country s longstanding connections with its eastern neighbor. For travelers, airlines and businesses, the central concern is whether the latest exemption will translate into stable, accessible and predictable services.
The resumption of eligible flights to Najaf is therefore an important step, but the broader demand voiced by Iraqi political figures, religious leaders and demonstrators remains clear: air links between Iran and Iraq should be restored on a more comprehensive and sustainable basis.

Somalia won’t accept Israeli presence ‘under any circumstances’: President
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:25:03 UTC
01:25:03 KST

Somalia won’t accept Israeli presence ‘under any circumstances’: President
In exclusive Al Jazeera interview, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud says attempts to pull Somalia into Middle East crises won’t succeed.
Somalia will not accept Israeli presence in the country “under any circumstances” and will resist any attempts to be pulled into the Middle East’s crises, its President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud tells Al Jazeera.
Speaking in an exclusive interview, Mohamud said that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, adding that its real aim was to get closer to the Gulf states and Iran.
Berbera is a port city on the Gulf of Aden coast in Somaliland – the self-declared republic in northwestern Somalia that Israel recognised last year, but which is claimed by Mogadishu.
Berbera faces Yemen across the water near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait. The Iran-aligned Houthis have previously enforced a blockade on Israel-linked ships in the area.
“We will overcome the challenges posed to our country by Israeli moves,” Mohamud said in his wide-ranging interview.
He added that the Israeli plans fall under the “Greater Israel” project – referring to a term for various proposals, often rooted in biblical interpretations, for Israeli control over territory beyond its current borders. Some versions extend from the Nile to the Euphrates.
Israel has not adopted it as official policy, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in an August 2025 interview that he felt connected to the vision, prompting condemnation from Arab governments.
The Somali president described Israel as a “destabilising force” that does not abide by international law.
He also criticised Tel Aviv’s recognition of Somaliland in December.
No country other than Israel recognises Somaliland, while the region’s own residents are completely opposed to an Israeli presence, Mohamud said.
Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and has governed itself independently for more than three decades. But it had not secured recognition from any United Nations member state until Israel’s move.
Fight against armed groups
The Somali president told Al Jazeera the United States remains his country’s strongest partner in the fight against “terrorism”, and added that al-Shabab has no presence in the major cities, leaving no possibility of the group taking control in Somalia.
Al-Shabab is a Somali armed group that emerged from the Islamic Courts Union in the mid-2000s and pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda in 2012. It has fought Somalia’s federal government for years, holds territory in parts of southern and central Somalia, and has carried out deadly attacks, including in Mogadishu and in neighbouring Kenya.
Regarding the East Africa region, Mohamud said Somalia’s relations with neighbouring Ethiopia are good, and Mogadishu does not object to Addis Ababa gaining access to the sea through a joint agreement to use Somali ports for its economic interests.
Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea became independent in 1993 and relies largely on Djibouti’s ports for trade. In January 2024, Addis Ababa signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland on sea access, which Somalia condemned as a violation of its sovereignty. Somalia and Ethiopia later agreed to ease tensions.
Houthis ‘destabilising’ region
Mohamud also accused Yemen’s Houthis of “destabilising the region” and disrupting navigation in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
His comments come as the group attempts to build on its lightning offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.
Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the front lines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.
The Houthis have also intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, but the kingdom’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has promised not to compromise on its security, saying the Yemeni rebels chose “chaos and destruction, threatening the Yemeni people and the region”.
The full interview with President Mohamud will be broadcast on Al Jazeera Arabic on Sunday.

US forces may retreat farther from Persian Gulf, IRGC deputy commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:20:22 UTC
01:20:22 KST

US forces may retreat farther from Persian Gulf, IRGC deputy commander says
TEHRAN- Major General Mostafa Izadi says US forces have moved more than 500 kilometers from regional waters, arguing that Washington’s military presence has failed to provide security for regional countries.
The United States may move its forces even farther from the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman, the deputy commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), Major General Mostafa Izadi, has said, attributing the withdrawal to Washington’s concerns over Iran’s military capabilities.
In an interview with Tasnim News Agency, Izadi said US forces had moved more than 500 kilometers away from the region’s waters, adding that the distance could increase further in light of the United States’ current predicament.
“Given the current situation of the United States, this distance may increase even further,” he said.
Izadi portrayed the repositioning as evidence of a shift in the regional security balance, arguing that the presence of US military forces had failed to deliver security and had instead contributed to regional instability.
He said countries in the region had increasingly recognized that their security could not be guaranteed by an outside military presence, stressing the importance of regional countries taking greater responsibility for their own security.
Iran says military readiness has grown through conflict
The IRGC deputy commander said successive wars and confrontations had enhanced the preparedness and vigilance of Iran’s Armed Forces, while also giving the country’s military personnel and population greater familiarity with adversaries’ tactics.
He also pointed to public mobilization as a factor in thwarting efforts to undermine Iran’s territorial integrity and gain control over its strategic resources.
“Iranian people have been present in the streets for seven months and thwarted the enemy’s plan to disintegrate our country and gain control over our oil,” Izadi said.
He added that repeated assassinations had failed to weaken Iran’s capabilities or bring the country to defeat, arguing that military pressure and targeted killings had not achieved their intended objectives.
The remarks reflect Tehran’s broader position that its military resilience rests on a combination of defense capabilities, public support and the ability to sustain pressure during prolonged confrontations.
Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab at the center of regional security
Izadi also highlighted the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, two critical maritime chokepoints connecting major shipping routes and energy markets.
“The Resistance Front has accomplished a major feat, and today the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait are in the hands of the Resistance,” he said.
The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman, is a vital route for global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments from the Persian Gulf. Bab al-Mandab, linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean, is an important passage for commercial shipping between Europe and Asia.
The two waterways occupy distinct but strategically significant positions in regional security calculations. Developments affecting either can have implications for maritime traffic, energy supply chains and shipping costs.
Izadi’s remarks linked the movement of US forces to Iran’s ballistic-missile capabilities and the broader regional influence of the Resistance Front.
“Today, the enemy has fled hundreds of kilometers away from our seas out of fear of Iran’s ballistic missiles,” he said.
The IRGC deputy commander described the developments as evidence of Iran’s strength and determination to confront its adversaries, arguing that the regional balance had entered a new phase.

Saudi Arabia launches dozens of strikes on Yemen’s capital, say Houthis

Saudi Arabia launches dozens of strikes on Yemen’s capital, say Houthis
- Saudi Arabia launched dozens of airstrikes on Yemen’s capital Sanaa, while Houthis attacked an Aramco oil facility near Riyadh, escalating the conflict between the two sides.
- The renewed fighting began in July after a fragile truce ended, leading to intensified battles, including heavy clashes in Taiz with significant casualties.
- The conflict worsens Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, with the World Food Programme warning that three-quarters of Yemenis cannot meet basic food needs amid ongoing hostilities and blockades.
AI generated
SANAA – Yemen’s Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of launching dozens of strikes on Sanaa on Oct 3, while an AFP journalist in Riyadh reported seeing flames and smoke coming from an oil facility on the outskirts of the Saudi capital.
Though Saudi officials and the Houthis have not yet commented on the refinery fire, the Iran-backed group has in recent weeks launched attacks on oil facilities in the kingdom as part of the war in Yemen, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government.
The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive.
Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that “Saudi enemy aircraft” hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting “Saudi aggression” against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles on the city.
In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on the afternoon of Oct 3 from a facility belonging to state-owned oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said, although both the Houthis and Saudi authorities had yet to comment.
The circumstances remained unclear, though the Houthis have claimed several attacks on facilities belonging to Aramco in recent months.
The journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at the refinery, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility.
Al-Masirah earlier on Oct 3 also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen’s north-western governorate of Saada, one of the group’s strongholds.
It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on the night of Oct 1 for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.
Hunger warning
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east – a region that is larger but much less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Since then, fighting has intensified, with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets, including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh, while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.
The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Oct 2 that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs.
Battle for Taiz
Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Oct 2 by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, which is Yemen’s third-largest, after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Oct 2 said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
The Saudi authorities, meanwhile, reported that a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Oct 3, US media outlet Axios reported that top Cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced. AFP

“No alien quantum modems”: 1 to 3 concealed devices in Kyiv may be why Russian drones keep hitting so precisely, Ukraine’s top tech adviser says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:14:11 UTC
01:14:11 KST

A few hidden transmitters may be sitting somewhere in Kyiv, switching on just long enough to steer Russian drones onto their targets. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, says one to three concealed enemy repeaters may be operating in the capital, giving Russia a brief online channel to guide jet-powered Gerans onto precise targets.
He calls the devices MESH repeaters, compact modems that relay a short control signal to a Geran at the moment of attack, a channel Ukraine has been testing electronic warfare against for months. As long as they operate, he warns, sealing the city with jammers will not work.
Flash makes the case
"I now insist that the enemy's MESH radio repeaters are being switched on in Kyiv, providing a temporary, short-term control channel for jet-powered Gerans to adjust strikes," Flash says.
He keeps the number low: "Maybe 1 to 3. Such repeaters are hard to find, but we have to search." As evidence, he points to the guided strike on the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service. A Russian agent, he said then, likely switched on a MESH relay within five kilometers of the target for the length of the attack.
The wreckage shows no other hidden link, he adds: "No LTE, no Rassvet, no alien quantum modems."
Jamming alone won't shield Kyiv
The stakes, in his telling, run past the bridges.
"As long as online control of the drones exists, not only the bridges but the air-defense assets on them will be under threat," Flash explains, noting that a Gepard anti-aircraft gun on a bridge crossed by tens of thousands a day cannot be hidden.
Without a stable channel right up to the impact point, he argues, a drone cannot strike a bridge pier or cable precisely. He leaves room for doubt, ending, "Let me be wrong about the repeaters." Yet in the whole war, he adds, he has "never once been wrong" in his technical reads of the enemy.

Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow’s ‘new doctrine’ of airstrikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:08:40 UTC
01:08:40 KST

Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow’s ‘new doctrine’ of air strikes
- Ukraine will intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s new doctrine targeting civilian infrastructure to force evacuations, but will avoid hitting civilian objects.
- Ukrainian forces have recaptured around 140 sq km in Donbas amid ongoing counteroffensive, while facing persistent Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv’s energy and infrastructure.
- Ukraine develops new defence systems against Russian drones, announces first use of domestic ballistic missile FP-7, and secures funding with European partners to sustain defence through 2027.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of air strikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure... logistics... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” he said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin’s desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key front-line region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Oct 3. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi”, had recaptured around 140 sq km of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, President Donald Trump’s administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe’s bloodiest since World War II.
The US leader in September urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure.
For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G-20, but he warned the US not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It’s not fair just to normalise,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said. “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the US has proposed a resumption of trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defences have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones were too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions – including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it would receive the first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defence chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%. “We’ll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we’ll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile – the FP-7, which has a range of around 250km.
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to finish quickly a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow. “I said to them, where is my FP-9?” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I’m sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine. Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine had found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on plans with European partners to plug a US$27 billion (S$34.5 billion) hole in Kyiv’s defence budget in 2026.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine’s own budget resources, bilateral assistance and using “money credits” from 2027’s portion of a €90 billion (S$130 billion) EU loan, Zelensky said. REUTERS

Ceuta support T-shirt: €10 of its €35 price goes to self-described ‘patriotic’ movement Save Europe Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:06:34 UTC
01:06:34 KST

A T-shirt bearing the slogan “We are all from Ceuta” is being sold as a show of support for Ceuta, but part of the proceeds goes to Save Europe Act, a self-described patriotic movement that advocates remigration.
Journalist and social media expert Carmela Ríos posted an investigation into the sale of the garment on X on 27 September. The T-shirt emerged following the mass entry of migrants into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Here is what lies behind the sale.
The T-shirt is being launched by Terre de France, a brand that sells a "patriotic and solidarity-based" range of products it claims are 100% French. Part of the revenue is used to support other organisations that, according to its website**,** include groups of farmers, agricultural colleges and an association for wounded French soldiers.
In this case, €10 of the garment’s €35 price goes to Save Europe Act. No money is earmarked for directly supporting people or organisations in Ceuta, while almost 28.6% of the purchase price goes directly to Save Europe Act.
The company claims that residents of Ceuta, whose nickname and popular demonym is "caballas", "are surviving a migratory invasion that threatens the very existence of their city". One X account, Damien Rieu (@DamienRieu on X), who has 325,000 followers, promoted the sale on 26 September.
The promotional image shows a person wearing the T-shirt in front of what appears to be Trampolín beach, but the image is fabricated. The tools Hive Detect, TruthScan and Sight Engine indicate that it was generated using artificial intelligence.
On its social networks, Terre de France spreads messages claiming to defend a Catholic and white France, which, according to the brand, is not represented by LGBTQ+ people. It also rejects "crousty", the fried-chicken-based fast food currently in fashion in the country, saying it is not 100% French.
Save Europe Act and remigration
Save Europe Act presents itself as a "patriotic" movement. It demands that "the political elite" "put an end to replacement immigration", that borders be protected and that the "ethnocultural identity of European nations" be defended. It proposes halting "non-Western/non-European migration routes" until "social cohesion and cultural continuity" have been restored in the member states.
It also advocates "remigration", compulsory or voluntary, of people in an irregular situation, those who have committed crimes and those "who are not integrated or constitute a significant cultural or financial burden".
The organisation is collecting signatures across Europe in a bid to reach one million and submit its proposal as a European Citizens' Initiative. That mechanism allows citizens to put forward new rules to the European Commission.
The Commission has refused to register it, considering it "manifestly contrary to the values enshrined in the Treaty and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU". The Commission also says the initiative would be used as “a vehicle for offensive or caricatural messages". According to 'Euronews', its organisers are preparing to challenge the decision in court.
Europe's far right in Ceuta and a precedent
Following Ceuta's migrant crisis, the autonomous city was visited by members of far-right organisations. Activists from Reform UK on 1 August, from Junge Tat in Switzerland on 2 August, and from Reconquista in Portugal on 4 August, as well as from Generation Identity in Germany.
Members of the neo-Nazi organisation Núcleo Nacional were expelled on 1 August when they attempted to hold a demonstration and were met with a counter-demonstration by local residents.
Among the promoters of Save Europe Act is Martin Sellner, who has almost 200,000 followers on X. On 3 August he shared videos from the city in which he called for "this ethnic replacement" to be stopped through "non-violent civil disobedience".
Its co-founder Eva Vlaardingerbroek posted on 31 July a message denouncing the "orchestrated invasion" of Ceuta, which was shared by Elon Musk. She has 1.2 million followers on X and 1.3 million on Instagram.
Ríos argues that Europe's far right sees Ceuta as a real stage "to advance its strategy". She outlines a roadmap based on "the massive use of disinformation, artificial intelligence and the whole machinery of bots, trolls and fictitious digital operations". According to the journalist, these movements rely on one another "on the basis of similar talking points and a shared technological framework".
There is a precedent. In the Torre Pacheco case in July 2025, when an attack on a local resident by a young man of Moroccan origin triggered a wave of racist unrest, the promoters of Save Europe Act and the organisation itself spread false claims.
They claimed that "Moroccan migrants" had assaulted white people for three nights in a row and that "North Africans" were arming themselves "to terrorise Spaniards". In any case, their proposal for that situation was "remigration".

ShinyHunters hacker in FBI data theft detained in Jordan, 'cooperating with bureau'
A key member of the ShinyHunters hacking group, which claims to have stolen data on every FBI employee, was detained this week in Jordan, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Two of the sources said he was cooperating with the FBI to identify his fellow hackers.
Saif al-Din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities, the three sources said. Two of them said he was brought into custody on Tuesday. Reuters’ attempts to reach Khader and members of his family over the past week and a half have been unsuccessful.
The detention of Khader — whose alleged hacker nickname is Rey — is the latest twist in the case of ShinyHunters, a motley crew believed by experts to consist mainly of young, English-speaking hackers focused on data theft and extortion.
Their theft of what they claim are mountains of data on every single FBI employee has drawn comparisons to the allegedly Chinese-linked intrusion at the US Office of Personnel Management in 2015, which compromised sensitive details on millions of Americans who had been vetted for security clearances.

Brain scans reveal hyper-connected reward networks in autistic individuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:00:10 UTC
01:00:10 KST

Autistic individuals often process social information differently, which is reflected in how various regions of the brain communicate with one another. A recent study published in Autism Research reveals that the brain’s reward center is unusually intertwined with other social processing networks in autistic people. This hyper-connectivity correlates with social communication differences and is linked to specific genetic and chemical markers in the brain.
The human brain handles social interactions through a distributed set of specialized regions known collectively as the social brain. This system includes four distinct subnetworks that govern different aspects of human connection. The reward system processes motivation and the pleasure associated with social stimuli. The face perception network supports the encoding and recognition of facial expressions.
The other two subnetworks handle more abstract social processes. The theory of mind network allows individuals to attribute mental states and intentions to themselves and others. The mirror neuron system activates both when an individual performs an action and when they observe someone else performing the same action, aiding in imitation and learning.
For social cognition to function smoothly, these four subnetworks must maintain a delicate balance. They need to operate independently to process their specific tasks efficiently, a concept known as modular segregation. At the same time, they must share information across the broader brain network to produce coherent social behaviors, a process known as modular integration.
Previous research indicates this balance is altered in autism spectrum disorder. Autistic people often exhibit differences in social motivation, facial recognition, and mimicking behaviors. Researchers Chen Yang, Ai-Ping Sun, and colleagues wanted to systematically map how these social subnetworks integrate and whether any imbalances relate to clinical social symptoms. They also aimed to investigate the underlying chemical and genetic profiles of these brain regions.
To examine these network dynamics, the researchers analyzed brain imaging data from an existing database of 646 participants, comprising 298 autistic individuals and 348 typically developing individuals. They used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, which tracks blood flow to measure brain activity while participants are awake but not engaged in a specific task. By recording how blood oxygen levels fluctuate over time, researchers can identify which brain areas activate synchronously and infer how strongly they are connected.
Using an automated process, the team isolated 102 specific brain regions that make up the four subnetworks of the social brain. They then calculated a metric called the participation coefficient for each participant. This mathematical formula quantifies how much a specific brain node communicates with outside modules compared to its own internal components. A low score indicates high segregation, while a high score indicates high integration across different networks.
The analysis showed that autistic participants exhibited increased modular integration of the reward system. Instead of remaining relatively isolated, the reward network formed an unusually high number of connections with the face perception network and the mirror neuron system. Autistic individuals also showed higher integration in the face perception network itself, though the changes in the reward system were more pronounced.
Next, the researchers investigated whether this network overlap corresponded to observable social behaviors. They compared the brain connectivity metrics against the participants’ scores on standard clinical assessments, including parental reports of social communication and motivation.
The researchers found that increased integration of the reward system correlated with higher scores on the Social Responsiveness Scale. This means that individuals with a more hyper-integrated reward network tended to experience greater challenges in social communication, social awareness, and social cognition. The team verified that this correlation was driven specifically by social functioning rather than restricted and repetitive behaviors.
To understand the chemical foundation of these brain patterns, the team compared their brain connectivity maps against established atlases of neurotransmitter distribution. Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that either stimulate or inhibit brain activity. A leading theory in neuroscience proposes that autism involves an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory signals in the brain, often stemming from alterations in how these chemicals bind to their receptors.
The regions of the reward system that were highly integrated in autistic participants physically overlapped with brain areas known to have lower densities of certain serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA, receptors. GABA is the brain’s primary inhibitory messenger. A reduction in these receptors implies a lack of inhibitory control, supporting the idea that a hyper-excitable reward network might drive the observed social differences in autism.
The researchers then explored the genetic underpinnings of this connectivity pattern using a public database of human brain tissue gene expression. They mapped thousands of gene transcripts to see if the expression levels of specific genes matched the locations where the reward system was most hyper-integrated.
This spatial analysis identified a set of genetic signatures associated with the structural development of the nervous system. The genes most correlated with the altered reward network are primarily involved in cellular proliferation, the positive regulation of cell migration, and the formation of tissues during early development. This implies that the hyper-integration seen in the adult and adolescent autistic brain may originate from foundational changes in how neurons migrate and form circuits during early development.
The team also mapped how this reward network integration changes over time and tested their findings in a second, independent dataset. Because autism is a developmental condition, the brain’s organization naturally shifts as an individual ages. The researchers used linear regression models to track age-related changes in both autistic and typically developing participants, looking for divergent or parallel growth trajectories.
The integration of the reward system increased as individuals grew older in both groups, maintaining a parallel developmental trajectory. However, the connectivity levels in autistic individuals remained consistently higher than those of their typically developing peers across all age stages. In the second dataset, the direction of the effect was similar: autistic participants showed higher reward system integration at seven of nine sites. However, the pooled effect across sites was small and not statistically significant.
While these analyses draw connections between brain activity, genetics, and behavior, they rely on chemical and genetic maps derived from healthy individuals. The study overlays these standard profiles onto the brain scans of autistic individuals to estimate molecular relationships. Because the researchers did not directly measure neurotransmitter levels or gene expression in the autistic participants themselves, the results do not definitively prove that these specific chemical deficits caused the altered brain connectivity.
Future studies will need to incorporate molecular imaging data collected directly from autistic individuals to confirm these relationships. Additionally, longitudinal tracking of the same individuals over time, rather than comparing different age groups in a single snapshot, could reveal exactly how the social brain develops and changes throughout an autistic person’s lifespan.
The study, “Disrupted Modular Integration of the Reward System Is Associated With Social Deficits in Autism Spectrum Disorder,” was authored by Chen Yang, Ai-Ping Sun, Sheng-Zhi Ma, Wen-Qiang Dong, Xiao Chen, Shuai-Yu Chen, Yuqi You, Yu-Feng Zang, and Li-Xia Yuan.

The winter war: Ukraine is prepping for another season of Russian attacks before the cold sets in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:59:11 UTC
00:59:11 KST

On Sept. 23, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov once again voiced Moscow’s rejection of a Ukrainian proposal to halt fighting along the current front line. Now Kyiv is preparing for another series of strikes on its critical infrastructure that appear intended to freeze the country during the upcoming winter and result in a humanitarian disaster. Ukraine’s military and civilian institutions have already begun preparing for what they expect to be an especially difficult Russian campaign, with energy companies inspecting equipment and stockpiling fuel while apartment associations buy up generators.
In September, air raid alerts have sounded in Kyiv every day — and almost continuously. Jet-powered Shahed drones circle over the city, disrupting the work of municipal services, shops, businesses, and public institutions. A new operating protocol took effect on Sept. 10, introducing a “yellow” alert level for Shaheds and a “red” level for missiles. Under a yellow alert, most businesses and institutions now remain open.
The changes do not apply to schools, which are still required to suspend classes during air raid alerts. Schools without underground classrooms have moved children to online learning. Across Ukraine more broadly, local authorities have been given discretion over how to respond to alerts.
In August and September, central government officials held a series of meetings with businesses. Entrepreneurs were advised to consider setting up air defenses on their own, to cooperate with existing volunteer territorial defense formations (known by the Ukrainian acronym DFTG), and to move warehouses underground.
Russian forces have been striking warehouses belonging to home improvement retailer Epicentr and delivery company Nova Poshta for years, but the logistical networks of supermarket chains recently started coming under systematic attacks for the first time. Strikes on warehouses reduced the range of goods available in stores in August, though the situation had largely stabilized by mid-September.
As fall begins, everyone in Ukraine seems to be asking the same question: how can the country make it through a winter of relentless strikes? It is already clear that the infrastructure responsible for heating and other fundamental civilian services will be among Russia’s targets.
The military shield and the front line
Ukraine needs interceptors to defend against ballistic and cruise missiles. But increasingly frequent attacks by jet-powered drones have created another challenge.
A volunteer (call sign Max) with a Kyiv Region DFTG told The Insider that his unit formed teams of interceptor-drone pilots in preparation for the winter campaign, alongside its regular gun and mobile fire teams. Training began in mid-spring, and by the end of summer, most volunteers had passed examinations and received certificates — along with combat interceptor drones.
But a problem emerged: older interceptor drones work well against conventional Shaheds traveling at speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour, but new interceptors designed to take out jet-powered Shaheds have only recently completed testing. Russia is expected to use both conventional and jet-powered Shaheds during the fall and winter, meaning crews are expected to use different interceptors depending on the target.
Volunteer formations are part of Ukraine’s Territorial Defense Forces (TDF) and their supply system tends to lag somewhat behind those of the Unmanned Systems Forces, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the National Guard. Newer technologies only reach the TDF and volunteer groups after they have been tested by regular units.
By Sept. 20, videos had emerged showing jet-powered Shaheds being intercepted by high-speed fixed-wing interceptor drones and Sting S quadcopters.
“We have to remember that there is no such thing as 100% effective air defense. Some missiles and Shaheds will get through any defenses. That is why residents should always follow the recommendations of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. New Ukrainian interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can engage targets at greater distances and altitudes than the usual weapons used by ground-based fire teams. But they cannot offer a complete guarantee either. The same applies to Russia, where they are also technologically behind. So if power stations, thermal power plants, and combined heat-and-power plants burn here this winter, there is an even greater likelihood that they will burn in Russia as well,” Max said.
Ukraine’s new interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can hit targets at greater ranges and altitudes, but they cannot provide a complete guarantee against Moscow’s aerial attacks
A Kyiv volunteer territorial defense formation commander called Asgard said his unit has gun teams equipped with a wide range of weapons “from 5.45 mm up to 23 mm,” along with interceptor-drone crews. “The biggest target was probably a cruise missile we shot down in 2024. Believe it or not, we brought it down with a 7.62 mm Maxim machine gun manufactured in 1942.” Unsurprisingly, Asgard’s unit also engages jet-powered Shaheds.
There has been no particular need for “retraining” this year, the Kyiv DFTG commander said. “Every day we face new challenges and learn. Before, they were ordinary Shaheds. Those are very easy targets for us now. We still have work to do with the jet-powered ones.”
Ukraine’s small mobile air defense units shoot down conventional Shaheds in 95% to 99% of cases, but their success rate against jet-powered versions is no more than 40% to 60%. Volunteer formations hope that rate will increase soon as interceptor-drone teams receive more high-speed drones of their own.
At the front itself, winter could provide Ukraine with some advantages, according to Silver, an FPV drone pilot who flies fiber-optic-controlled drones.
“There will be more work in winter. First, the leaves will fall, which will make things easier. Even now we manage to fly fiber-optic drones through forests, but without the ‘greenery’ [the military term for dense seasonal foliage] we will create far more problems for the Russians. Second, we will rely on skill, quality, and careful planning rather than quantity. We are changing our approach, adapting technically and improving our skills. Everyone is talking about AI-equipped drones now, but artificial intelligence will not replace the person who still decides which target to send it toward. I’ve worked with AI-assisted terminal guidance, and it works!”
Even if Russia carries out another mobilization, conditions will become harder for Russian soldiers in winter, according to a Nemesis bomber-drone pilot who has flown 1,000 combat missions over a year and a half.
“The Russian military is adapting too, changing tactics and infiltrating our lines. Maybe they have something new prepared for us. But overall, we’re ready. We’ll see how their mobilization goes and how many more targets we have along the line of contact,” the pilot said.
Front-line cities
About 127,500 people live in the Ukrainian-controlled portion of the Kherson Region — about a quarter of the prewar population. In the city of Kherson itself, 63,000 out of the prewar population of 283,000 remain — roughly 22%.
The situation there is difficult. Russian forces deliberately target energy and heat-generating facilities in an effort to deprive residents of basic services. Strikes take place around the clock, with explosions heard roughly every two minutes. Since the area was liberated in November of 2022, the regional administration has recorded 400,000 Russian attacks involving more than 900,000 munitions.
Elvina Osmanova, head of the Kherson regional administration’s domestic and information policy department, told The Insider that between three and 10 guided aerial bombs (known by the Russian and Ukrainian abbreviation KAB) are dropped on Kherson each day. “They hit infrastructure sites one after another, including the combined heat-and-power plant, and essentially everything responsible for electricity, heating, gas, and water supplies.”
Alongside guided bombs, Russian forces make extensive use of conventional drones, a particular problem for Kherson, Nikopol, and other cities within a 20-kilometer range of the front line. Osmanova lists off the drone types that most frequently attack the city: “FPV drones, Mavics, cheap Molniya kamikaze drones, and other systems. Most of them use fiber-optic control, which makes them difficult to stop. As many as 5,000 drones can be launched at Kherson in a week.”
Still, food deliveries still make it to central Kherson, Osmanova said:
“The city has a sufficient supply of food. But the Russians deliberately destroy trucks and kill drivers transporting bread and other foodstuffs, so issues with deliveries cannot be ruled out. Due to constant shelling, some parts of Kherson are already effectively dead — riverside areas such as Antonivka, Voyenne, Korabel, and several others near the Dnipro. They haven't had normal municipal services for a long time.
Last winter, there were times when people went 10 days without electricity or water. Right now, one district of the city has been without power for 14 days. In other areas, electricity has been restored through the heroic efforts of utility workers. Many have unfortunately been wounded or killed. Drones deliberately target workers while they repair infrastructure.
We understand that the Russians will only increase their attacks in the fall and winter. The number and severity of enemy attacks are increasing every day. Kherson may end up without electricity and heating not just for hours or days but for prolonged periods, and we're preparing for that. We're adapting our anti-drone system — detection systems, electronic warfare, and mobile fire teams — and increasing physical protection for important facilities.”
Shelters are another major focus. Osmanova said 307 protective structures have been repaired and 439 mobile shelters installed in crowded public areas. Protection for critical infrastructure is also being strengthened through backup power, additional physical defenses, and alternative systems intended to allow facilities to continue operating after Russian attacks.
“The Russians attack any kind of transportation with drones: mopeds, passenger cars, trucks, ambulances, municipal vehicles, and public transit,” Osmanova said. “Last week alone, about 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed. We are doing everything possible to protect the city’s supply routes, including covering roads and streets with anti-drone nets. About 270 kilometers of roads have already been protected that way.”
Zarina Zabrisky, an American journalist with Byline Times who lives in Kherson, told The Insider that residents are preparing for winter however they can. Residents with standalone, private houses were able to heat their homes with firewood in previous winters and are preparing to do so again — and many of them have generators. Zabrisky’s apartment has access to a supply of natural gas, which she used to heat her home last winter.
At the same time, the local administration is advising residents — particularly older people, those with limited mobility, and families with children — to seriously consider temporarily relocating to safer parts of Ukraine. The authorities say they are prepared to assist at every stage, including organizing evacuation, finding housing, providing humanitarian aid, and offering psychological and legal assistance.
Kyiv
Locals in Kyiv are not counting on an energy ceasefire. Instead, they are preparing for something resembling a repeat of last year. The main difference is that the upcoming winter is expected to be milder, with frequent thaws.
Vyacheslav Hryb, who heads three condominium associations in Kyiv, told The Insider how preparations are going:
“We’re buying additional inverters, checking the generators, and connecting elevators to them. If the power goes out, our calculations show the elevators can operate for five to six hours. Heating should also be fine. We have a large building and a 110-kilowatt generator that powers the cold-water supply, hot-water supply, and heating.
Last year, the unprecedented cold made everything harder, and after the strikes, many buildings had to drain water from their heating pipes. Restarting the heating at minus 22 Celsius [about negative 8 degrees Fahrenheit] was what you might call an advanced-level challenge. The instructions say it’s impossible, but we pulled together and managed to get it running.”
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult among Ukrainian cities not located near the front. Last winter, residents of several buildings on the eastern bank of the Dnipro went without centralized heating for around a month after heating pipes burst. Electricity schedules were largely maintained, with power generally available for four hours followed by four hours without it.
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult of Ukraine’s non-frontline cities
Residents are now buying batteries and inverters in order to be more self-sufficient. Buildings with condominium associations are generally better prepared, often with generators or high-capacity battery and inverter systems that can keep heat, water and elevators running during outages. But only about 2,000 of Kyiv’s more than 10,000 residential buildings have these associations.
Other buildings are serviced by municipal housing offices, commonly known by the Soviet-era abbreviation ZhEK. Their residents therefore often have to go to special “Points of Invincibility” set up by city authorities and Ukraine’s State Emergency Service to warm up and charge their devices.
The Zhytomyr phenomenon
The city of Zhytomyr is located less than 100 miles from Kyiv, but last winter it did not even suffer widespread short-term power cuts. Vitaliy, a Zhytomyr resident, told The Insider that while Kyiv spent days at a time without electricity, Zhytomyr experienced only a handful of outages, none lasting more than an hour:
“Specialists had told me before that Zhytomyr had inherited many military factories from the Soviet era. It was also an early adopter of power systems designed for wartime conditions. The city developed a distributed energy system, which is why, despite repeated attacks, we did not face major disruptions or prolonged power outages last winter or the winter before.”
In Ukrainian cities where power distribution has been managed effectively, utility services remain close to prewar levels. Residents of Kyiv — and perhaps soon Moscow and St. Petersburg — can only look with envy at Zhytomyr.
The overall state of Ukraine’s energy system
The risk of new large-scale attacks remains one of the most serious and unpredictable factors facing Ukraine this winter. DTEK, the country’s largest private energy company, is preparing for a range of possible scenarios.
“First and foremost, we are repairing and restoring thermal power plants around the clock after attacks,” the company told The Insider. “There is not a single DTEK generating unit that has not been damaged or destroyed during the years of the full-scale war, and some units have had to be rebuilt several times.”
At the same time, the company is carrying out scheduled equipment repairs in order to improve reliability during the winter. It is also stockpiling fuel and supporting the operation of mines, machine-building facilities, and repair businesses. DTEK spent more than 7.6 billion hryvnias ($170 million) on those efforts in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, it has spent more than 51 billion hryvnias ($1.2 billion) restoring thermal generation, supporting its businesses, and preparing for wartime winters.
In the first half of 2026, DTEK invested 3.3 billion hryvnias ($74 million) in repairing and modernizing power grids. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, investment in that area has exceeded 15 billion hryvnias ($335 million). The company says its central goals are to restore as much available capacity as possible, maintain sufficient supplies for emergency repairs, and be prepared to respond as quickly as possible to new attacks.
DTEK is advising Ukrainians to use electricity carefully, particularly during periods of peak demand, and says it will do everything possible to minimize the effects of attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, said the government would prepare the country’s air defense network for the winter.
“This is extremely difficult, but it has to be expanded. Absolutely everyone is working on it: the Defense Ministry, the Foreign Ministry, and the Foreign Intelligence Service. The obvious challenge, as you know, is missiles for the Patriot system. But we are working on that as well,” Zelensky told reporters Sept. 25. “Separately, we are working on our own anti-ballistic air defense system. That is the FREYJA system. We will work on all of this so there is no collapse.”
Zelensky also said Ukraine would retaliate for attacks on its energy system by striking not only Russian oil refineries — but its energy facilities as well.

Roundup: Myanmar experts stress ecosystem conservation for migratory bird habitats, flyways
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:58:07 CST
00:58:07 KST

People visit a photo exhibition marking World Migratory Bird Day in Yangon, Myanmar, Oct. 3, 2026.(Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- A series of photo exhibitions and thematic talks were held in Yangon on Saturday to mark World Migratory Bird Day, as Myanmar ornithologists and environmentalists urge global efforts to protect migratory bird habitats and migration routes increasingly threatened by human activities.
Of the world's billions of birds spanning over 10,000 species, some 18 to 20 percent are migratory, said renowned Myanmar ornithologist Thein Aung. He noted that human activities including illegal bird hunting for trade, wetland pollution, and large-scale infrastructure development near feeding grounds have posed growing risks to migratory birds along their flight paths.
This year's World Migratory Bird Day falls under the global theme "Every Bird Counts -- Your Observations Matter." Thein Aung, one of the event's organizing ornithologists, said the activity aims to disseminate popular science knowledge about migratory birds and mobilize public participation in conservation work.
During the event, Ko Phyo, a veteran bird photographer and environmental conservation practitioner as well as director of Myanmar's non-profit organization Wild Wings Group, exhibited bird photos taken across Myanmar over more than 15 years. "Bird observation requires systematic learning of bird habits, habitats, breeding grounds and chirps through both books and on-site observation," he said.
He stressed the importance of joint efforts to protect local vegetation and ecological environments. "Birds serve a vital role in ecological protection. For example, they prey on pests that damage rice and other crops, forming an interdependent ecological relationship with human agricultural production. This is why bird conservation matters greatly," he explained.
Daw Khin Khin Thaw, a Yangon-based teacher who brought nearly 50 students to the event, emphasized that bird conservation awareness should be cultivated among children from an early age. She said interactive activities such as bird observation and bird drawing based on the photo exhibition help students gradually build ecological and environmental awareness.
Thein Aung also called for strengthened international cooperation on transboundary bird conservation. He introduced that two major global migratory flyways, namely the Central Asian Flyway and the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, traverse multiple ASEAN countries.
Taking neighboring China as an example, Thein Aung said China has accumulated mature and extensive expertise in migratory bird protection. Advanced academic programs at the master's and doctoral levels in China offer valuable learning opportunities for Myanmar researchers.
He expressed the hope for future China-Myanmar cooperation, including joint research on cross-border migratory bird routes, to jointly advance regional conservation undertakings.
World Migratory Bird Day is observed twice annually, in May for spring migration departure and in October for autumn migration arrival. The official observance dates for 2026 are May 9 and Oct. 10. ■

Unidentified Object Entered Lithuanian Airspace From Belarus—Search Underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:57:27 UTC
00:57:27 KST

On the morning of October 3, Lithuania declared a yellow threat level due to an unidentified aerial object, likely a drone, that entered the country’s airspace from Belarus.
This was reported by Vilmantas Vitkauskas, Head of Threat Management and Crisis Prevention at the Prime Minister’s Office in Lithuania, according to LRT.
Due to the incident, the airspace near Vilnius Airport was temporarily closed, and operations at the airport were suspended. NATO fighter jets were scrambled.
A yellow-level alert was issued shortly before 10:00 a.m. Residents of the region received alerts on their cell phones urging them to find a safe place.
However, the aerial object could not be fully identified. According to Vitkauskas, the fighter jets took to the air and carried out the appropriate procedures.
Authorities also received reports from residents who claimed to have seen the object outside Vilnius in the direction of Jonava. However, these reports were not confirmed.
The air threat was lifted at 10:37 a.m. According to Vitkauskas, the object disappeared from the surveillance zone and no longer posed a threat. It is currently being searched for.
Vitkauskas noted that it is unknown whether the object was actually a drone. He said that certain parameters of the object indicated a speed slightly lower than what is typical for a UAV.
“If it crashed, if it was a drone, we’ll have to find it. But it wasn’t necessarily a drone,” Vilmantas Vitkauskas said.
The official also did not rule out that the observed phenomenon could have been related to an anomaly or bird migration. Lithuanian authorities are currently continuing to determine the nature of the object and the circumstances of its appearance in the vicinity of the Lithuanian capital.
As a reminder, on the morning of September 13, a drone flew from Belarus to the Kaliningrad region of the Russian Federation through Lithuanian territory. It was also initially identified as an unidentified aerial object. The UAV flew 60–70 km over Lithuania and remained in the NATO country’s airspace for about 20 minutes.
Amid the growing threat from drones in Lithuania, a pilot version of the Ukrainian SkyFortress system is being deployed, which is designed to help detect them at low altitudes using sound or radio signals.
