Spanish director Alberto Sciamma brings his allegorical film, ‘Cielo,’ to Haifa Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:08:20 UTC
00:08:20 KST

A little girl sits in front of a spectacularly beautiful lake in rural Bolivia and captures a fish, a moment that is the starting point for Alberto Sciamma’s allegorical, magical-realist film, Cielo, which just had its Israeli premiere at the 42nd Haifa International Film Festival.
From there, the movie moves in directions that no viewer could anticipate, as it tells the tale of Santa (Fernanda Gutiérrez Aranda) as she sets off, with only her fish for company, to try to find a way to visit the only place she has ever heard of that offers relief from the rural poverty in which she has grown up: Heaven.
Along the way, she comes closer to the urban reality of modern life, as savage as the wild landscape she left behind, and encounters a priest, a group of bold indigenous female wrestlers, and a lonely policeman.
Sciamma, a Spanish-born director who is now based in the UK, has a diverse filmography that includes horror films and comedies. With Cielo, he has switched gears and created a movie that is difficult to classify and which elicits strange, contradictory emotions.
In an interview in Haifa, he said he had never been to Bolivia before developing the film, but that an image in his mind inspired the story and eventually led him there.
“Seven or eight years ago, I was in Berlin with a friend of mine, who became one of the producers of the movie. He is married to Ana María Vera, a very well-known Bolivian classical pianist.
“They asked me what I wanted to do next, and I said, ‘I don’t know, but I have an image in my head.’ It was just an image of a little girl lost in the Altiplano, swallowing a fish.
“Ana María said, ‘Have you thought about Bolivia?’ I hadn’t. Then I went there and discovered it, and I started writing the script, thinking about Bolivia,” he explained.
“So, it wasn’t a story written somewhere else that we decided to take to Bolivia. The story grew out of Bolivia and out of my impressions of the country.”
Film shows realities of harsh life in Bolivia despite beautiful landscapes
While the landscapes are spectacular, the film also shows how harsh life can be there.
“When you are in El Alto and the Altiplano, you are 4,000 meters above sea level. It is really cold at night. When you first arrive, you think, Where is the oxygen? It’s gone.
“It is beautiful and majestic, with incredible light and colors, but it is also a very hard life.”
Among the locations Sciamma and his crew discovered was a church covered in vivid murals depicting scenes from Christian biblical stories.
“It is considered something like the Sistine Chapel of the Altiplano,” he said.
He soon discovered that working in Bolivia was very different from the kind of filmmaking he was used to.
“In Europe or the United States, if you need a location, a location manager shows you photographs and negotiates a price.
“In Bolivia, you may have to speak with the Aymara community, which meets in an assembly and decides collectively whether you can film on its land. If they agree, there may be a Pachamama ceremony, and you don’t necessarily pay in money.
“For one location, the production gave the community bricks because they needed them for an extension. At the church, our payment was replacing all the light bulbs that had been broken for years.”
Sciamma was especially taken with the Cholita wrestlers, a troupe of exuberant, traditionally dressed women fighters, who appear in the film.
Describing them as “an explosion of life,” he recalled that they constantly joked, sang, and laughed during the shoot. “They were so much fun, so colorful, so strong-minded,” he said, adding that their presence gave the movie a jolt of feminine power it needed.
The extraordinary performance of Fernanda Gutiérrez Aranda
Fernanda Gutiérrez Aranda, as Santa, gives an extraordinary performance.
“The first time she looks at the fish, I told Fernanda, ‘Look at it as if you had never seen a fish.’ I didn’t want judgment in her expression. I just wanted her to look....
“The movie begins in quite a violent way, but it isn’t filmed as a horror movie. It is very matter-of-fact. We needed that matter-of-factness to make her strong, almost supernatural. She has a fixation, and she needs to fulfill it.
“The whole movie has a kind of fairy-tale quality, and that could only be achieved by having the little girl alone. As soon as you introduce a mature person who reacts according to logic rather than the dreams of a child, you lose that.
“It wasn’t easy to find a child actress who could bring the child heroine to life,” he said. “We had been casting children, but by the time we were ready to shoot, the girls we had first considered had grown too old.
“Ana María Vera runs a music program for children in La Paz and said, ‘There is a little girl here you should meet because she is very clever.’
“Fernanda was seven. I realized immediately that she was extraordinarily intelligent. She was already two years ahead in school and had read all the Harry Potter books....
“Working with her was like working with an adult. She would ask me things such as, ‘Why is Santa biting the policeman? I thought Santa was good. Why is she doing that?’ And we would discuss it.”
Told that the film seems designed to be experienced more than explained, Sciamma agreed.
“Absolutely. A lot of the film is expressed visually rather than through a completely logical plot. When you stand in front of a certain landscape, you don’t start rationalizing why the tree is green. You just look at it and feel something. Cielo was constructed in the same way. It was not designed to appeal primarily to the logical brain. Hopefully, it appeals to the heart, and then people bring their own feelings and experiences to it.”
Asked how he decided to take part in a film festival in Haifa at a time when so many artists are calling for a cultural boycott of Israel, he said that when he told people he would be coming to the festival, “Some people were saying, ‘Absolutely, you should go,’ and some people were saying, ‘Are you crazy?’”
Sciamma, who left Spain at the age of 18 decades ago, was undeterred.
“Cielo is a piece of art. I don’t mean that art is necessarily a good thing – it can be bad art – but it is art. And for me, that transcends all of that. So, I didn’t listen to one side or the other. I just did what my gut was telling me to do, which was to go and share the movie.”

Disabled Ukrainian woman abducted by Russians from Oleshky care home goes missing in Russia

Disabled Ukrainian woman abducted by Russians from Oleshky care home goes missing in Russia
Relatives and acquaintances have lost contact with Anastasiia Mamotiuk, a Ukrainian citizen who was abducted by Russian forces from the Oleshky psychoneurological care home and taken to Russia.
Source: Emile Foundation, a humanitarian organisation
Details: Emile Foundation told Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) that contact with Mamotiuk was lost while arrangements were being made for her return to Ukraine.
The Russians occupied the Oleshky care home in Kherson Oblast in the very first days of the full-scale invasion and began deporting its residents in 2022. In November 2023, Anastasiia was among three adults taken to Penza, Russia.
Oleksandr Danylchuk, one of the residents who subsequently returned to Ukraine, said they were told about the relocation just one day before leaving. They were not asked whether they wanted to go to Russia.
Anastasiia and the others were moved to Novye Berega (New Shores), an assisted living facility for people with disabilities run by Sofia Lvova-Belova, the sister of Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights.
Danylchuk said he told Sofia Lvova-Belova that he wanted to return to his friends and family in Ukraine, but Russian officials publicly claimed that the abducted Ukrainians did not want to go home.
Despite being illegally taken to Russia, Anastasiia remained in contact with people in Ukraine: Viacheslav Shchyrskyi, her foster father in the House of Stefan family, whom she regarded as her own family; a former teacher at the care home; and Oleksandr Danylchuk.
Shchyrskyi had previously sought the organisation's help in securing Anastasiia's return to Ukraine. He is close to her and plans to become her legal guardian. Together with the foundation, he prepared and submitted official appeals to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and Russia's commissioner for human rights.
The Emile Foundation says Anastasiia repeatedly said she wanted to return to Ukraine and that she feared for her own safety in Russia. She cannot yet leave the country because she is waiting for the passport she needs to travel, the foundation said.
Maria Lvova-Belova released a video of the young woman on 16 September. According to the organisation, the video provides no way to assess the Ukrainian woman's health or the circumstances in which it was recorded and cannot replace direct, confidential communication with her.
Over the last few days, direct contact with her has been lost. As of 1 October, three former residents of the Oleshky care home – Anastasiia Mamotiuk, Viktoriia Markeliuk and Anastasiia Yavorska – are still in Penza, the Emile Foundation has learned.
The foundation is calling for an immediate, independent assessment of Anastasiia's safety and health, the confidentiality of communication to be ensured, direct contact to be restored, and international support to be provided for her return.
Mariam Lambert, CEO and co-founder of the Emile Foundation, says Nastia must never be used as a pawn in political bargaining. She says Nastia is a woman with a disability who has the right to safety, dignity and the freedom to make decisions about her own life.
Lambert says that, for the first time, none of those helping Nastia return to Ukraine have been able to contact her. She says an independent assessment of Nastia's condition and safety, the restoration of communication, and concrete diplomatic action to ensure her safe return to Ukraine are urgently needed.
At the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, 101 people were living at the Oleshky care home, including children and adults with various forms of disability. Most were not orphans or children deprived of parental care.
In October 2022, the Russian military began moving the residents to different institutions. In total, Russia abducted 84 people, 13 of whom their families managed to bring back.
One of the care home's residents was taken away and ended up with a Russian family – a Russian soldier who had fought against Ukraine tried to adopt her.
The foundation said that the lack of a legal mechanism for the return of adults with disabilities is one of the main obstacles to bringing them back.
According to Lambert, a permanent international humanitarian mechanism should be established to facilitate the return of adults, with the involvement of intermediary countries.
Previously: Two Russian-installed Donetsk officials are suspected of deporting 31 Ukrainian children to Russia for "medical treatment".
Lvova-Belova said a Ukrainian teenager abducted from Mariupol and "adopted" by her would become a prosecutor.

Portugal prosecutors probe legality of US use of Lajes base in Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:07:58 UTC
00:07:58 KST

Portuguese prosecutors said on Saturday they had opened a probe into the legality of the center-right government's authorisation of the United States' use of the Lajes Air Base in the Azores during the Iran conflict, following a complaint by an opposition party.
A longstanding agreement with the US allows Washington to use the base without prior authorisation during peacetime, but requires Portugal to give approval once hostilities begin.
Portugal, unlike neighboring Spain, authorized several US transit flights through the Lajes air base, a decision that drew criticism from left-wing opposition parties and triggered a political debate over Lisbon's role in operations linked to the conflict with Iran.
In a statement, the Prosecutor General's Office said "the probe was opened following a complaint filed by members of the Left Bloc party," without providing further details.
Portugal's Foreign Ministry declined to comment.
Left Bloc claims US use of base was 'gross violation of international law'
The Left Bloc asked prosecutors in April to investigate the US use of the Lajes base, arguing it amounted to a "gross violation of international law."
However, Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel has said Portugal was not involved in the conflict and that the use of the Lajes base complied with international law, having been authorized only after assurances from Washington that any operation would be defensive, necessary and proportionate, and limited to military targets.
Portugal's prosecutors are bound by the principle of legality, requiring them to investigate alleged wrongdoing when there are sufficient grounds to do so, unlike in some jurisdictions where prosecutors have broader discretion to decide whether a case should proceed.
The Lajes base, located in Portugal's Atlantic Azores archipelago, is a strategic transit hub for US forces under a bilateral defense treaty dating back to 1951 and hosts the 65th Air Base Wing of the US Air Force, providing support for US, NATO, and allied operations.

Red Sea conflicts converge as Ethiopia, Yemen, Sudan crises deepen regional instability - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:07:54 UTC
00:07:54 KST

The conflicts stretching from Yemen across the Red Sea to the Horn of Africa are increasingly becoming interconnected. Renewed fighting in Ethiopia, the rupture between Ethiopia and Eritrea, Sudan’s civil war, and tensions over Red Sea access are unfolding as Saudi Arabia faces threats from the Houthis and Washington weighs its next steps against Iran and its allies.
Reports over the weekend made it appear that Riyadh is considering backing a major offensive in Yemen. Meanwhile, the US is also looking at what may come next in Yemen.
A review of articles in Egypt’s Al-Ahram state media, Saudi Arabia’s Arab News, and the UAE’s Al-Ain presents different views on what is happening in the region. This matters to Israel as well because Israel has recognized Somaliland. A new article at Middle East Eye argued that Israel and Turkey may be competing in Somalia now. This means that what is happening in the region of the Red Sea has strategic implications far beyond the area involved.
The area is also huge. If you look at the conflicts in Sudan, Somalia, Yemen, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, it is a landmass of around 5.5 million square kilometers. This is about the size of half the continental United States.
The result is an increasingly complex strategic landscape. Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan are concerned about Ethiopia’s regional ambitions. Saudi Arabia is focused on Yemen and the Houthis across its southern border and the Red Sea. Meanwhile, the United States is considering its options in Yemen while confronting Iran elsewhere in the region.
Red Sea security crisis grows
It should be noted that the US has also increased pressure on the Sudanese army over the civil war in Sudan. The US wanted a ceasefire. It didn’t get one at the recent UN General Assembly. Other issues may be afoot, such as the conflict in Libya, amid reports that Saddam Haftar was in the UAE for meetings in September.
Ethiopia is at the center of one part of the emerging crisis. Renewed fighting involving the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and other armed groups has undermined the 2022 Pretoria agreement that ended the devastating Tigray war. The TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups shortly before the latest fighting began, according to the reports provided.
The fighting has now become entangled with Ethiopia’s deteriorating relations with its neighbors. Addis Ababa severed diplomatic relations with Eritrea after accusing Asmara of hostile activities. Eritrea rejected the allegations. Ethiopian military officials have also accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting forces fighting the federal government. All three countries deny involvement. Egypt recently expelled an Ethiopian diplomat in a tit-for-tat expulsion.
Egypt has been particularly careful to distance itself from Ethiopia’s internal conflict. An Egyptian source said to Al-Ahram that the crisis was an internal Ethiopian matter and emphasized Cairo’s stated policy of respecting sovereignty and non-interference. Cairo also rejected attempts to connect Egypt to Ethiopia's domestic turmoil. However, Egypt appears to be discussing developments with Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan.
What are the disputes between Egypt and Ethiopia?
Egypt and Ethiopia have their own longstanding strategic disputes. The Nile is one source of tension. This is linked to Egypt’s dam and the Blue Nile. Africa News notes that “the dispute is the latest in a years-long rift between the two countries over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.”
There are other old grievances. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has subsequently portrayed access to the sea as important to Ethiopia’s economic and security interests. The reports provided note that Ethiopia depends heavily on the corridor through Djibouti and that Abiy has discussed the historical loss of Ethiopia’s coastline in increasingly assertive terms.
This puts Eritrea in a particularly sensitive position. Ethiopia and Eritrea were partners against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, despite their own history of conflict. That alignment deteriorated after the Pretoria agreement, which excluded Eritrea. Ethiopia's subsequent focus on Red Sea access has intensified Asmara's concerns.
The crisis therefore cannot be viewed solely as another round of fighting inside Ethiopia. It sits at the intersection of the Nile dispute, Sudan’s war, and competition surrounding the Red Sea.
Then comes Yemen. Across the Red Sea, Yemen adds another piece to this emerging strategic picture. The Houthis have transformed themselves over the past decade from a Yemeni insurgent movement into a regional actor capable of threatening Saudi Arabia and maritime traffic at the Bab al-Mandeb. Allied with Iran, they have ballistic missiles and long range drones.
How will the US respond to Red Sea tensions?
Iran's relationship with the Houthis connects Yemen to the wider confrontation between Tehran, Washington and US regional partners. This makes developments on the African shore of the Red Sea increasingly relevant to the security environment facing Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states.
The Trump administration is now weighing its options. According to one of the reports provided to Al-Ain news, senior US officials met at Camp David on October 2 to discuss both Iran and Yemen. The meeting reportedly included Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and other senior national security officials. Yemen was specifically discussed as Washington considered whether to take further action against the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia faces a different calculation. Riyadh has sought de-escalation while making clear that attacks on the kingdom cannot continue indefinitely. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman recently reiterated Saudi Arabia's preference for diplomacy while saying the kingdom would respond to threats against its security. Former Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki al-Faisal similarly argued that restraint has historically characterized Saudi policy but has limits when Saudi sovereignty is threatened.
The historical parallel is notable. Saudi Arabia and Egypt were on opposing sides of the North Yemen Civil War in the 1960s, when Egyptian forces intervened in support of Yemen's republican government. Prince Turki specifically invoked that period while discussing the kingdom's current security calculations.
Today the alignments are different. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have shared interests in preventing further instability around the Red Sea. For Egypt, security in the Red Sea is directly connected to the approaches to the Suez Canal. For Saudi Arabia, the same maritime space includes its western coastline and the approaches to Yemen.
This is where developments in Yemen and the Horn of Africa converge. The Bab el-Mandeb is the narrow link between them. Yemen occupies its northeastern approaches, while Djibouti and Eritrea sit on the African side. Sudan lies farther north along the Red Sea, while Ethiopia's lack of a coastline drives Addis Ababa's search for more secure maritime access.
Iran and the Houthis represent only one dimension of Red Sea instability. The possibility of renewed interstate conflict in the Horn could create another. For Eritrea, the primary concern is preserving its sovereignty and coastline amid Ethiopian pressure for sea access. For Ethiopia, dependence on Djibouti creates a strategic vulnerability that Addis Ababa wants to reduce. Egypt views Ethiopia through the additional prism of the Nile dispute. Sudan is fighting its own civil war while trading accusations with Ethiopia over support for hostile forces. Saudi Arabia must contend with the Houthis and protect its Red Sea coast, while Washington is deciding how far it wants to go in confronting Iran and the Houthis. Many regional countries are potentially involved in these conflicts, including the UAE in the Horn of Africa. Turkey is also involved in Somalia.
These conflicts are not a single war, and the alliances do not line up neatly. Nevertheless, geography is increasingly tying them together. The Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb connect the Horn of Africa to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and ultimately the Mediterranean.
This means a new conflict involving Ethiopia and Eritrea would not remain merely a Horn of Africa crisis. Combined with the war in Sudan, Houthi activity in Yemen and the wider confrontation with Iran, it could add another layer of instability along one of the world's most strategically important maritime corridors.

Getting the word out: The Israeli Institute for Hebrew Literature flies the flag in Frankfurt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:07:52 UTC
00:07:52 KST

A picture may, indeed, be worth a thousand words but, as any book reader knows, there is a special magic to revealing a literary creation, page by page, as the storyline gradually unfolds. If one may be so bold as to riff on a biblical sobriquet, as the People of the Book, we tend to enjoy burying ourselves in some plot of a novel, thriller, or sci-fi tome.
Naturally, in this increasingly digital, AI-assisted/lumbered day and age, more and more of us, particularly those born into the Internet era, opt for means of momentary instant gratification via, for example, social media networks. Even so, it is fair to say we have plenty to offer the world in terms of quality literary output.
But how can that be achieved? The fruits of Israeli writers’ labors, one assumes, are not the natural go-to choice of the average reader in the US, UK, France, or Italy. And there is the small matter of political ebbs and flows, and whether literature consumers are impacted by global media anti-Israeli coverage when they possibly come to consider purchasing a translated copy of a book by any of our better-known scribes, such as Amos Oz, David Grossman, Etgar Keret, or AB Yehoshua.
Those thorny issues feature highly in the list of Sigalit Gelfand’s activities to be addressed at next week’s Frankfurt Book Fair. These days having any sort of Israeli presence at offshore events is an achievement in itself. But Gelfand, and the Israeli Institute for Hebrew Literature, which she serves as CEO, will be well and truly in the thick of things when the world’s largest literary gathering takes place in the German city Oct. 7-11.
German goodwill towards Israel
In fact, the program will be officially opened the day before as an extraordinary gesture of goodwill to the Israeli contingent. “The fair, together with the Municipality of Frankfurt, made a decision to have the first work day of the fair on Oct. 7, so that they can have the festive event of the opening on the sixth,” Gelfand explains. “They did that so that Oct. 7 will be a work day, and not a day for celebrations.” It seems the hosts are going out of their way to accommodate and salute Israel and its literary output. “I happily received a request from the director of the Mayor of Frankfurt’s Office, telling me the mayor would like to come to the Israeli pavilion at the fair on the seventh of October. That is a gesture of support for Israel.”
That is, indeed, impressive and heartwarming but Gelfand is not getting carried away by the positive stuff. “We have hired Israeli undercover security, that’s in addition to the security facilities provided by the fair management,” she notes. “That is for our safety, and the safety of visitors to our pavilion.” Not that she is exactly shivering in her boots. “The atmosphere at our pavilion last year was warm and wonderful,” she recalls. “Of course, having excellent Israeli wine on offer helps,” she laughs, “but it was a positive experience for everyone. We are not politicians. We are people of literature.” Skirting around the political minefield, if possible, is always a good idea. Let’s hope the feel-good vibes abound there this year too.
We return to the crux of the book fair, and Israel’s participation. Gelfand, who will be joined in Frankfurt by the institute’s literary editor Dr. Oded Wolkstein and content manager Dana Simhayof-Shahaf, says the institute is making great efforts to facilitate translations of Israeli works so that folks of all nationalities, cultures, and ethnic origins can gain a handle on Israeli literature, and hopefully enjoy it and come back for more.
Making Israeli literature accessible
To that end, the institute has launched the Hebrew Literature Translation Fund, which is designed to help more Israeli books reach readers worldwide. “Every contribution, at any level, can give a book the wings it needs to cross borders and expand minds. Let the world read diverse Israeli voices!” the website exclaims. There has, it seems, been some assistance available to publishers who have enthused over some Israeli book or other but balked at the cost of having it translated. “There have been funds available for that, in conjunction with the Foreign Ministry, but it hasn’t generally been adequate. Publishers around the world have told us we have great books but they previously met with someone from a different country which has grants for translations.”
That doesn’t help the Israeli global literary cause. “There are [foreign] publishers that want to work with us but that is not always the case, particularly since Oct. 7,” she adds somewhat superfluously. “Publishers also tell us that they may bring out a translation of an Israeli book but the bookstores don’t want to promote it. At the end of the day, publishing houses and stores are businesses.” Politics aside, the monetary shortfall doesn’t help matters either. The hope is the new fund, fueled by private donors, will obviate the financial obstacle to spreading the good Israeli literary word. “We want, at least, to be operating on a level playing field, so we can provide the same support as other countries,” Gelfand says.
The institute, as our national representative in Frankfurt, is pulling out all the stops to show the world there is more to this country than meets the mainstream media news-oriented eye, and that Israel has a broad, diverse sweep of voices that need to be heard. “We are taking 40 books with us to the fair,” Gelfand advises. “They are for adults and also for youth and small children.” The institute’s wares in Germany will include works by Haggai Linik, Michal Zamir, Moroccan-born writer and rabbi Moshe Suissa, and Yonatan Sagiv. The younger reader’s consignment features books written by Ruth Margalit, Nurit Zarchi, Avihai Nizri, and Hava Havushi.
Gelfand says there has been a fair amount of interest in the Israeli rollout already. “Oded and Dana already have meetings set up with publishers and agents. We have not experienced any opposition to meetings. We will show the publishers and agents the actual books, in Hebrew, and the [English-language] catalogues with all information about all the books we are taking with us.”
It is not just about the quality of the writing or the translation. “Publishers look for some added value, something special. They look for a reason why they should translate this literature. They frequently look for a certain Israeli flavor to the story in the book.” That can also provide sorely needed national PR dividends on the global stage. “That presents the world with a different face of Israel. There are so many facets to our country and literature is a means of showing that in a beautiful way.”
With over a quarter of a million visitors expected to throng the Frankfurt Book Fair next week, that sounds like just what the doctor – writer – ordered. It also suggests that, perhaps, our writers can do a better job in the global arena than our politicians.■

‘The fringe didn’t disappear’: Expert explains how to combat online threats, antisemitic propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:07:49 UTC
00:07:49 KST

Online hate is no longer confined to the darkest corners of the Internet, putting all of us at risk of encountering nefarious figures or entities from a shadowy realm we can’t see. Extremist subcultures, conspiracy networks, and foreign influence operations that were once confined to fringe message boards have broken into the mainstream and infiltrated social media platforms, reaching millions of people.
The average person never knows when a bad actor, such as a foreign agent, extremist, or impersonator, will strike in the virtual world. That’s where Alex Goldenberg, an open-source intelligence and cyber-threat analyst, comes in.
Goldenberg tracks online extremism and foreign influence operations and trains international law enforcement and intelligence agencies to identify emerging online threats, enabling them to better protect vulnerable communities.
“I frequently brief law enforcement on issues ranging from foreign influence to ghost guns created with 3D printers, to drones equipped for mass casualty attacks that are being weaponized with bombs and guns and sold to consumers,” Goldenberg explained to the Magazine.
“I also train security folks in the private sector to help them better understand threats emerging online that can have a real-world impact.”
After receiving his MA in global affairs, with a concentration in transnational security, from New York University in 2019, he worked as a director of intelligence, lead analyst, and adviser for the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI), a nonprofit research institute that analyzes threats emanating from the cyber-social domain. In 2024, he co-founded Narravance, a threat intelligence company, the same year that he testified before Congress on Chinese foreign influence operations in the US.
This past April, Goldenberg founded his own national security consulting firm, Silent Index, to help governments, institutions, and organizations mitigate the risk and potential impact of online threats. He has been a senior research fellow at the Rutgers University Miller Center for the last five years. In 2026, for the second year in a row, Goldenberg was named a Top 40 Thought Leader by Life Safety Alliance, a global nonprofit organization for the security and life safety profession.
“I think my entire career has really been about one question: How do bad actors exploit emerging technologies such as social media, artificial intelligence, and prediction markets, before the rest of us understand them?” he said.
He warns that the consequences of extremist ideologies spread through social media “are no longer virtual. Radicalized online communities have inspired real-world violence against Jews around the world.”
He became interested in the growing field of threat intelligence because of his father, Paul Goldenberg, a globally recognized police and security expert. “I was definitely influenced by him and his desire to make an impact on the world that’s positive,” he recalled. “He always said, ‘If you can change just one life in your lifetime, it will all be worth it.’ That always stuck with me.”
Due to the sensitive and confidential nature of his work, Goldenberg could not reveal specific details about his investigations, but he offered insight, observations, and advice from his unique position as a Jewish threat intelligence analyst about the climate of antisemitism online.
When did online threats toward the Jewish community start to increase? Which websites were the first to disseminate antisemitic hate and propaganda?
It has accelerated in the past 15 years. There was always a prevalence, so long as the Internet has existed, of antisemites, going back to Stormfront (launched in 1995), which was an online space for neo-Nazis to communicate with each other.
In 2003, things started to change with the advent of image boards like 4chan, which created, almost organically, what we refer to as an “Internet meme,” where you have a photo with text over it. 4chan created the Pepe the Frog meme, which is now unfortunately considered a hate symbol, but wasn’t always.
They wanted to make him unpalatable to normal people, so they started making Pepe the Frog look like Hitler. These communities started engaging in ironic hatred and ironic antisemitism – antisemitic memes and stereotypes under the guise of humor and parody in an effort to be edgy or to troll. If you get social points on your online communities for spreading this type of content, the irony fades away – it oftentimes just becomes hate.
Groypers emerged in 2019, named after a variant of Pepe the Frog, and they’re loosely defined as a set of followers of Nick Fuentes [an avowed antisemite and white nationalist]. Their goal is to show up inside broader conservative spaces and apply pressure from within. Fuentes openly tells his followers: conceal your views, get credentialed, get hired.
Why are these fringe memes, ideologies, humor, etc. gaining in popularity? How is social media helping to amplify these messages?
The hate I studied years ago (and still study today) was trafficked in tight, highly active subcultural communities like Telegram or Discord or Gab, and quarantined to message boards in the worst corners of the Internet. These still exist, and they still have millions of people in them.
But the hate, and the meme culture that carries it, has broken out of containment and gone mainstream. You see it on X, in Instagram Reels, on TikTok. The platforms’ own algorithms amplify it, and our kids are inundated with the likes of Fuentes and Candace Owens [the right-wing, anti-Israeli media personality] without ever going looking. The fringe didn’t disappear; it just stopped being fringe.
Which nefarious movements or organizations, which pose a threat on social media to young people, should parents be aware of? Do they result in violence in real life?
The Incel movement is an online movement of frustrated young men, motivated by involuntary celibacy, who are unable to find a significant other, and hold resentment against the world because of that. It has inspired countless attacks that have led to dozens of casualties. They venerate previous individuals – who have killed on behalf of this movement – as saints.
On June 22, 2026, there was a violent attack in a Montreal neighborhood with a large Jewish community that left the shooter, Seth Hatfield, a police officer, and an innocent Israeli bystander dead. Hatfield had a manifesto that promoted this Incel ideology and expressed hatred toward women, Zionists, and capitalists. He [also] hated the police.
When we think of true crime, we think of a murder mystery docu-series on Netflix. There is a more extreme segment of the True Crime Community (TCC) that is interested in mass shooters and serial killers, which some of them seek to emulate.
We’re increasingly seeing young women engage in violent attacks. A study conducted by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue reported that approximately half of those who traffic in this True Crime Community are young women.
On December 16, 2024, Natalie Rupnow, a 15-year-old girl active in the TCC, killed two people and injured six at the Abundant Life Christian School in Madison, Wisconsin. She took her own life at the scene. Her TikTok account had antisemitic and racist memes. The FBI said she was motivated by nihilistic violent extremism.
How does your organization expose the plans of these radicalized online subcultures?
For years, I’ve been briefing the International Association of Chiefs of Police and the International Association of Campus Law Enforcement Officials to raise awareness, so they can better understand these groups and potential indicators of violence. I’ve also briefed the Pentagon’s insider threat team. I can’t name them, but I’ve also worked with social media platforms.
How do you infiltrate these communities online, and what do you do once you’ve blended in?
Essentially, you create a sock puppet or an avatar account [a fake account with no personally identifiable information]. You signal in your bio that you are part of the “in” group in some of these subcultural communities.
You get invited to their Telegram or Discord channels, and essentially, you just watch. Sometimes you may catch indicators of violence, but it’s also worthwhile just monitoring for trends and narratives because it could give you potential indicators of who the targets are in these communities as well.
Is AI also playing a role in influencing the minds of young people?
There’s a loneliness epidemic. Young people have fewer close friends and fewer romantic partners than any generation before them. A lot of them are finding solace online, increasingly with AI chat interfaces.
We’re seeing people form long-term romantic relationships with AI characters. What makes that different from social media is that these systems talk back, and they are designed to agree with you. For a lonely kid, that feels like connection. For the angry and isolated, it could create a dangerous echo chamber that reinforces dangerous behaviors.
What happens when radicalized people start interacting with AI?
AI chat interfaces, like ChatGPT, are very sycophantic. They tell you exactly what you want to hear, and they reinforce your beliefs, even when those beliefs are problematic. In a few circumstances, they have assisted in the planning of mass shootings.
What can parents do to protect their children from dangerous content and predators on the Internet?
The uncomfortable truth is that filters and parental controls are largely theater at this point. What actually works is inoculation – teaching kids to recognize the tropes, the irony-as-cover, the “just asking questions” funnel before the algorithm serves it to them.
The other thing that works is simply talking about it. Ask your kids what’s in their feed. Most parents are shocked by the answer.
“Don’t talk to strangers” is an age-old saying, yet many parents are comfortable giving their teens a device that connects to billions of them. Some of them are intense and capable of doing real harm.
Parents need to be aware that their child is only a few clicks away from a digital hellscape and can end up there without looking for it. They should seriously consider limiting social media for their kids altogether.
There’s a growing movement around this called the “anxious generation,” after Jonathan Haidt’s book [on the subject], built on a few common-sense norms: no smartphones before high school, no social media before 16, and phone-free schools.
The book provides data that shows how social media is having a negative impact on youth, raising levels of anxiety, potentially raising levels of suicide, eating disorders, and the like. I think there’s a new norm now that sees social media as akin to cigarettes or alcohol, but even worse.
Networks of parents should create new norms for social media use together; they can’t do it alone, because the cost of opting out falls on the kid whose friends are all online, but when parents act together at the school or community level, it works.
The movement is gaining real momentum with phone-free school laws passing across the country. The best defense is a kid who gets involved in the community and belongs somewhere real, be it theater or the football team.
What can people do to protect themselves if they are receiving threats on social media?
If you are the subject of a coordinated doxxing campaign, I would lock down your personal exposure. It’s important to have no digital footprint, or at least a minimal footprint, so your home address, workplace, etc. is not online. You can go to data broker removal services, like Delete Me.
Typically, once these bad actors experience some friction, they go on to the next target. Turn on the strongest authentication available everywhere, starting with two-factor authentication. The more sophisticated harassment campaigns often include attempts to take over one’s account (like Gmail).
During a pile-on, oftentimes there is an instinct to respond to the trolls. Don’t – that’s exactly what they want. Most of the time, these pile-ons burn out in 24 to 48 hours.
What are social media platforms doing to combat antisemitism? People have told me that when they report antisemitic posts, they’ll often receive responses stating that the posts do not violate their community standards/guidelines.
The detection and enforcement machinery for credible threats and incitement has genuinely improved. What has not improved, and by some measures has gotten worse, is everything below that line: the dehumanization, the tropes, the conspiracy content, the “ironic” hate that primes people for violence without ever explicitly calling for it.
Meta’s January 2025 policy changes loosened its hate speech rules (what it now calls “hateful conduct”) but left the violence-and-incitement policies largely in place. They’ve gotten better on direct violence but worse on hate.
Do you have any recommendations for how Jewish organizations should combat online antisemitism?
Unfortunately, there’s what I refer to as the antisemitism attention economy right now. If you amplify antisemitism, you’re going to get views and “likes” and retweets, which means you get revenue. We need to spend money exposing these networks, both online in the real world. The cost of being an antisemite needs to be high professionally and socially.
Is there a great need for more people to go into your field, especially given the extreme rise in online antisemitism? Do you have any advice you’d like to share with prospective threat intelligence analysts?
I think our community is facing real threats that would benefit enormously from having people within our community inside disciplines that track those threats, but there are some honest caveats. This work certainly carries real personal exposure. Researchers in my field who track extremism, like myself, have gotten doxxed and harassed. I’ve been on the receiving end of death threats; some of them were legitimate.
Anyone entering this field should certainly have some operational security habits from day one. Separate your personal identity from your research identity. Use a VPN. Make sure that you don’t have any personally identifiable information attached to the accounts that you use to research these communities that I’ve been talking about.
This expertise can be extremely beneficial for those going into law enforcement, for those who want to join the Trust and Safety teams of social media companies, and community security organizations. It’s a growing field with real career paths. I do recommend it, but it’s not for the faint of heart. ■

====================================================================================================

What Remains Awake: Artist Sarah Svetlana's searching, luminous homecoming to Jaffa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:07:42 UTC
00:07:42 KST

At Mika Contemporary Art Gallery, the Los Angeles-based artist’s first solo exhibition in Israel turns memory, grief, and inherited displacement into a vivid abstract language.
In the stone-vaulted rooms of Mika Contemporary Art Gallery in Jaffa, Sarah Svetlana’s paintings arrive with the force of accumulated memory. Large, brightly colored fields are overlaid with bold, flower-like forms, polka dots, charcoal gestures, and traces of personal history.
The exhibition, What Remains Awake, is Svetlana’s first solo presentation in Israel and, for the artist born in Soviet Belarus and raised in the United States, it is also a return charged with family history, mourning, and a newly urgent question of belonging.
Born in 1985 to a Belarusian Jewish family, Svetlana left the Soviet Union as a child in 1989, shortly before its collapse. Her family, refugees at the time, had a choice between Israel and the US while passing through Rome; they ultimately settled in America.
She now lives and works in the Los Angeles area. That unchosen route to Israel has remained a quiet but persistent presence in her work.
“My work has always revolved around exile, assimilation, finding home,” Svetlana said. “It’s always been about trying to find home physically and within yourself.”
Her first visit to Israel, undertaken alone, coincides with the exhibition and gives the project its emotional center.
Svetlana's return to Israel as a full-circle moment
Svetlana described the journey as a full-circle moment: an opportunity not only to reach a place bound up with her Jewish heritage, but to bring a new body of paintings to the country.
“I’m the first person in my maternal bloodline in almost 2,000 years to come back,” she said. “To bring back basically 10 altars to lay on this soil is really beautiful.”
The timing is inseparable from the period after October 7, 2023. Svetlana said that the rupture she experienced in relationships in the US, alongside the wider atmosphere she encountered, led to a deep depression and temporarily made painting feel impossible.
This exhibition marks her return to the studio after that break. Rather than illustrating a single event, the paintings gather pain, images, memories, and the persistent work of survival into color.
“I take all of that, and I turn it into really beautiful bright colors,” she said. “Even though they come from pain, they all end up as beauty.”
The exhibition’s title names that process. For Svetlana, What Remains Awake is “what’s left after everything burns down” – memory, ash, residue, and the part of the self that persists while the world appears to be asleep.
The gallery’s presentation frames the works as deeply autobiographical without treating autobiography as a fixed archive. Names, dates, colors, household patterns, and fragments of family life emerge and recede.
What cannot be seen directly is held within the painting’s layers.
On raw canvas, Svetlana works with charcoal, acrylic, oil, and spray paint. She writes the names and birth dates of her mother and grandmother into underlayers before covering them with paint.
The act both preserves and obscures: history is present, but never completely recoverable. Her mother’s death a decade ago sharpened that inquiry.
An old, seemingly incidental flower doodle from earlier paintings has evolved into a central structural element in the new series – a dark floral form that she now understands as a frame, or even a home, holding the work together.
The Root, The Heart, The Will
The series unfolds in three movements: The Root, The Heart, and The Will.
In The Root, charcoal and translucent color evoke maternal lineage and the search for an origin. The Heart moves through deep blues and reds, making memory feel close, embodied, and almost tactile.
The Will, marked by radiant yellow, charcoal, and remnants of lived time, turns from the past toward endurance: the decision to remain present and awake.
Curator Ellada Ilana Matatoc, an Israeli who also left the former Soviet sphere as a small child, first encountered Svetlana’s work on Instagram in 2019 while working with Mika Gallery.
The two immediately recognized resonances in the artist’s visual vocabulary, particularly the polka dots that Svetlana associates with Soviet domestic culture: bright, memorable motifs in an environment she recalled as overwhelmingly gray.
A small number of paintings were shown at the gallery then, but the relationship developed gradually through shared background and Matatov’s sustained response to the work.
For Matatov, Svetlana’s self-taught position is part of what gives the paintings their particular directness.
“She is working on the edges of things,” the curator said, describing an artist whose practice is led by emotion and intuition rather than academic convention.
Yet Matatov emphasized that her task was not to impose a theme or tell Svetlana what to make: “I saw her art; I didn’t tell her what to create,” she said. “Whenever I see what she did, I’m giving my interpretation to the theory of her practice.”
That distinction matters in What Remains Awake. The title was chosen by the artist, as were the internal movements of the series.
Matatov’s curatorial work includes the installation, exhibition text, public program, and the practical care surrounding the works, but it proceeds from an effort to make room for Svetlana’s own confidence and language.
“A curator is kind of like a producer,” Matatov said, while also returning to the older meaning of the word: to care for, preserve, and tend to art.
That care is palpable in the installation, where Svetlana’s black-grounded paintings meet the warm limestone walls of the Jaffa gallery.
Their graphic, almost emblematic shapes carry the intimacy of domestic objects and family inscriptions while retaining the freedom of abstract expressionism. The works do not offer a clean resolution to displacement.
Instead, they make a place where fragments can coexist: Belarus and Los Angeles, inherited grief and present-day resilience, private memory and collective feeling.
For Svetlana, simply bringing the paintings across the ocean already counts as a success.
“The moment I shipped those paintings, I felt like I did it,” she said. “I could hear all of my maternal line, all my ancestors cheering for me.”
In Jaffa, What Remains Awake gives that feeling a physical form: 10 works made from what remains, and from the will to continue.
Exhibition details: What Remains Awake, a solo exhibition by Sarah Svetlana, opened September 24, 2026, at Mika Contemporary Art Gallery in Jaffa. Curated by Ellada Ilana Matatov.

Tens of thousands protest in Spain after failed housing reforms
Latest demonstrations deepen a days-long crisis after parliament struck down two affordable housing decrees.
Tens of thousands of people are rallying across Spain to demand affordable housing measures, the day after members of parliament rejected an emergency relief package for tenants.
Demonstrators took to the streets in the capital, Madrid, and about 50 other cities on Saturday, calling for a general strike and reforms to address the country’s increasingly expensive housing market.
On Friday, the Spanish parliament voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing government that intended to quell the crisis.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, told the Reuters news agency while protesting in Madrid. “It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.
The eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her Madrid home triggered the movement more than a week ago, as hundreds set up tents in central Madrid to push for reforms.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.
In the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police ousted them.
Protests in dozens of other cities were peaceful, as people waved signs with slogans such as “Houses to live in, a planet to inhabit” and “the right to a roof”.
Pressure on Sanchez
Friday’s vote was a blow to Spanish leader Sanchez, who heads a coalition government made up of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar.
The two measures were scrapped after the right-wing Catalan separatist party Junts voted against them, arguing they would tighten the housing market.
Junts joined the main opposition Popular Party (PP) and the far-right Vox party in downing the measures.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged Sanchez after the vote to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.
Spanish media reported on Friday that Sanchez would be watching the strength of Saturday’s protests before making a decision.
Sanchez’s office did not comment on the reports.

Poland updates nuclear strategy with delays to launch of first two plants

The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule.
The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020.
However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040.
“This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.”

Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors.
The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway.
The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030
In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025
Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned.
Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation.
Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year.
Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government.
That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications.
The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses.

The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU.
Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period.
Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).
Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty".

As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects.
SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity.

Faslane sees British and American subs arrive in one day
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:00:56 BST
00:00:56 KST

Two nuclear-powered attack submarines came in to HM Naval Base Clyde on Friday, a United States Navy Virginia-class boat arriving in the morning and the Royal Navy’s newest hunter-killer, HMS Agamemnon, following later in the day.
Neither navy has identified the American submarine, and visits of this kind are not usually announced in advance for reasons that need little explaining. American submarines call at Faslane regularly to take on stores, change crew members and rest their people, often after periods working in the North Atlantic and the waters north of Scotland.
The Virginia class is the current American attack submarine, displacing around 7,800 tonnes dived and armed with Mk 48 heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk cruise missiles, with the later blocks carrying additional vertical launch tubes. The United States Navy has more than twenty in commission and is building more at Groton in Connecticut and Newport News in Virginia, and the type is the same one Australia is due to buy under the first phase of the AUKUS agreement.
Agamemnon’s arrival was her first at the base that will be her home. The sixth Astute-class boat sailed from the BAE Systems yard at Barrow-in-Furness on 25 September for contractor sea trials, thirteen years after her keel was laid, and she completed the passage north over the following week.
Announcing the start of those trials, the First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said: “In an increasingly dangerous world, sea power remains fundamental to keeping our country and people safe. Our submarine fleet is essential to that effort, which is why I am delighted that HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of our Astute-class submarines, has now begun sea trials.
“She embodies the best of British engineering and the professionalism of our submariners and will be one of the most advanced submarines ever operated by the Royal Navy. As we continue to strengthen our warfighting readiness, HMS Agamemnon will play a central role in keeping the United Kingdom safe, contributing to NATO’s collective defence and ensuring we are ready to lead, fight and win.”
The two boats are not far apart in size or in what they are asked to do. Both are built to escort ballistic missile submarines, hunt other submarines and surface ships, put special forces ashore, gather intelligence and strike inland with cruise missiles, and British and American attack boats have operated closely together in the North Atlantic for decades.
That relationship is also being built into the next generation of hardware as the Barrow yard is constructing the four Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines using a missile compartment designed jointly with the United States for its own Columbia class, and SSN-AUKUS, the British design that will replace the Astutes, is to be built with American technology and sold to Australia as well. Faslane, meanwhile, is in the middle of a long programme of work under the Clyde Transformation Programme, including three new floating docks that the Treasury confirmed last week will be competed among British yards only.

The first Russian Rassvet communications satellite from the second batch entered its operational orbit at an altitude of approximately 500 km, 68 days after launch.
This was reported by Militarnyi, based on an analysis of data from the Satcat satellite tracking service.
The Rassvet-3 No. 29 satellite first reached its operational altitude, with an apogee of 507–508 km, on September 29, 2026, after which it stabilized at that altitude. By comparison, it took the first satellite from the first batch 78 days to reach this altitude.
The other 12 satellites from the second batch, which show no signs of problems, are also continuing their ascent at a rate of about 5–10 km per day. Starting on September 29, the satellites that reached an altitude of 480 km have stabilized at that altitude, presumably grouping together for the final maneuver to deploy into a chain at the target altitude.
The last Rassvet-3 satellite, No. 21, which shows no signs of problems, is expected to reach an altitude of 480 km in about two weeks at the current rate.
Although the Rassvet satellite deployment program cannot be considered a failure overall, a significant number of ‘teething problems’ and defects were discovered in the first two production batches.
For example, in the first batch, satellite No. 4 was definitively lost. It failed to begin its ascent and fell out of orbit on June 6. Satellites No. 11 and No. 14 continue to perform maneuvers but show no consistent trend toward gaining altitude: since mid-June, they have remained in the 340–360 km range. It is likely that they will ultimately fail to reach stable orbits and will burn up in the atmosphere over the next few years.
In the second batch, satellites No. 17 and No. 23 have the most obvious problems. They have not begun to climb since launch and are gradually descending. As of October 2, they are at an altitude of 255–260 km.
Moreover, their descent is accelerating. While their descent rate was about 0.5 km per day after launch, as of October 2 it had increased to 1 km per day. It is likely that the satellites will soon leave orbit and burn up in the atmosphere.
Satellite No. 26 is also experiencing some issues. Initially, it briefly rose to 305.8 km, then dropped back down to approximately 289 km by September 26, after which it resumed its ascent and reached an altitude of 300 km as of October 2.
This could indicate a failed attempt to begin ascent or a malfunction in the propulsion system. However, Satellite No. 10 from the previous batch was able to ascend from a lower altitude, so it is too early to say with certainty that No. 26 will inevitably fall.
It is worth noting that although the Russian Rassvet satellite constellation did not reach its planned orbit at an altitude of 800 km, satellite communication tests involving real users in the Arctic confirmed the system’s operational capability.

Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services | Phillip Inman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:00:02 UTC
00:00:02 KST

Andy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s.
Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government.
A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election.
There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost.
The economist Sir John Kay, a fellow of St John’s College, Oxford and former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, is a keen advocate of organisations that remember for whose benefit they exist. That means their primary aim should be to achieve customer satisfaction. In the private sector, profits will follow. In the public sector, there will be savings.
In his book Obliquity, Kay shows how those companies that pursued shareholder value as their primary aim failed. And those that wanted to produce the best product secured long-term success.
Just as a devotion to shareholder value – a financial metric of the benefit to investors -proved a blind alley for thousands of now-deceased companies, so the reliance on protocols in the public sector as a substitute for understanding the task in hand leads to failed outcomes and wasted money.
You can see it now in the NHS, where satisfaction levels are rising in relation to GP and hospital visits. The new system for booking appointments has its drawbacks, but people are finding doctors are available more quickly, especially for GP and outpatient appointments.
You can see the failures in the NHS from the cover-ups by maternity unit managers of rising mortality rates.
Neither the success nor the failure can be attributed to the regulation of the health service. Regulation is an extra layer of cost that has, time after time, been shown to undermine productive behaviour, either because private providers and managers find they can game the system or it stifles innovation.
Another example can be found in two unconnected government agencies. Last week, the Environment Agency said it would fund the planting of half a million trees, giving funds to councils and mayors and other government bodies to carry out the work. Surely this is a good thing?
On the other hand, you might think it a complete waste of time and money when National Highways, the main road builder in England, planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge, only to report three years later, in an internal review, that three-quarters of them had died.
These failures are about the way public sector departments and agencies go about their work. Regulation only adds to a tick-box culture that asks: “Did you follow the protocol? If so, everything’s fine.”
Eminent figures in Whitehall, from the former mandarin and Bank of England deputy governor Sir Jon Cunliffe to the House of Lords industry and regulators committee believe the answer is more intensive oversight.
Kay has many examples of companies that grew because the boardroom was dominated by people who were more obsessed about delivering the best service or product than rewarding their shareholders as the chief metric. Profits and improvements in things such as market share were not the dominant metrics in companies that expanded.
The aircraft maker Boeing succeeded before it lost its way chasing quarterly profit targets. ICI, once the UK’s largest industrial company, was broken up and faded away after a higher stock market value became the main target.
The management consultant John Seddon, whose Vanguard consulting firm has adapted the Toyota systems method, supports Kay’s studiously well-informed analysis of what it takes to make a successful organisation. Seddon puts flesh on the bones with the kind of practical systems approach that has helped Portsmouth city council’s housing department win international awards for its repairs service.
He has seen many new initiatives in public sector management from grand strategies to more prosaic schemes for benchmarking services against the private sector. All have failed to improve services.
Seddon is not in favour of ditching regulation altogether. Regulation based on how well an organisation achieves the purpose will, he says, avoid the persistent problem of regulation “running behind events, shutting the stable door after another horse has bolted”.
He adds: “Having a clear statement of purpose will enable regulators to apply sanctions immediately if and when an organisation is found to be undermining its allotted purpose.
“It is time to liberate public servants from the prison of suspicion and distrust that our current method of regulation locks them in, demeaning their professionalism and casting them as part of the problem rather than as active creators of solutions.”
Burnham’s staff should avoid letting the debate about ownership dominate – ignoring a maxim that says “private bad, public good.”. They should work more closely on how public sector organisations achieve better outcomes. The evidence is available. They don’t need to look very far.

Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:00:01 UTC
00:00:01 KST

The Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn announced last year if they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor.
Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”.
The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power.
Last October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further.
“The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department. I know there are areas that we can make savings, and that’s true of every every part of government.”
He added: “There is a moral mission to get our economy growing, give people opportunity, as well as let people keep more of what they earn. It’s pretty simple. We’re Conservative, this is what we stand for.”
A Tory spokesperson acknowledged the party was seeking to make cuts beyond what it had already announced.
“Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, the Conservatives have consistently advocated for a smaller state and a government that does fewer things but better,” the spokesperson said.
“In Birmingham, we will go further, setting out further savings to Labour’s bloated welfare bill and cracking down on wasteful spending as part of our plans to build a stronger economy and a stronger country.”
Kemi Badenoch has previously outlined how the government would cut government spending by £47bn, mainly by cutting welfare spending for all non-British or EU citizens.
The plans would also save £8bn by cutting 132,000 civil service jobs, another £1.6bn by scrapping almost all of Labour’s clean energy scheme and more than £7bn by cutting international aid.
In August she promoted Griffith, who previously worked as chief operating officer for Sky, from his role as shadow business secretary.
In government, Griffith worked in the Treasury under Kwasi Kwarteng and was one of the ministers tasked with defending the mini-budget even as the markets tanked in response.
On Friday Badenoch promised another £4bn of spending reductions, including taking another £2.5bn out of the aid budget – leaving it with just £1bn as year – as well as reducing the budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport by £1bn.
The Tory leader said she would use half of those savings to pay for an additional 50,000 prison places. She has previously promised to use half of any cuts she makes to reduce the deficit.
Griffiths’ leaked comments come as the Tories prepare to gather in Birmingham for their annual conference, with Badenoch seeking to make a virtue of the growing distance between Labour’s plans for government and her own.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised a series of potentially expensive interventions, including a new national care service and public control over utility companies, as he seeks to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”.
However, Badenoch, who has called Margaret Thatcher her hero, is attempting to gain an electoral advantage with her vision of lower taxes and a significantly smaller state.
“[Thatcher] is somebody who brought a lot of wealth and prosperity to this country,” the Tory leader told ITV Meridian on Friday.
“Privatisation was a success … I don’t think that Andy Burnham running the water companies is the answer to those problems.”
The Tories remain in third place in the polls, behind Labour and Reform UK, although Badenoch’s personal ratings have rallied over the last 12 months.

Ukraine to set up working group to identify fallen soldiers
Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council will establish a working body to consider issues related to the identification of fallen military personnel.
Source: Ihor Klymenko, Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council (NSDC), on Telegram
Quote: "For families of missing people, having to wait a long time to learn what happened to their loved ones only adds to their pain. The state must do everything it can to speed up the process and ensure that examinations are carried out properly."
Details: Klymenko said that, on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's instructions, Ukraine plans to strengthen its forensic examination system. The number of experts will be increased, and steps will be taken to improve working conditions.
In addition, specialised regional bureaus will be set up to focus solely on identifying the remains of military personnel.
Quote: "From now on, this work will be overseen by the National Security and Defence Council. The relevant working group will bring together all the state institutions involved. We need to look at the entire process as a whole: where delays occur, what decisions are still needed and who is responsible for implementing them. Families do not need explanations for why the system is slow, they need answers."
Background:
- On 2 October, a meeting of the Coordination Council on the Protection of the Rights of War Veterans and Their Family Members, Family Members of Fallen Defenders of Ukraine, Prisoners of War and Missing Persons, was held at the Office of the President.
- Following the meeting, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said the Cabinet of Ministers will adopt all the necessary regulations by mid- October to help forensic groups work faster and more effectively. "Another important issue is the approval of international agreements that will help strengthen efforts to find missing Ukrainian defenders and identify them. Our international partners are willing to actively support us in this, and we should make use of this opportunity," the prime minister added.
- Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office, previously said a significant number of the 26,000 bodies and remains brought back from Russia have yet to be identified.
- He added that Ukraine would establish an interagency group to address issues related to the identification of the fallen. The work of forensic examination bureaus is also planned to be reviewed, and "international capabilities" will be involved in identifying the dead.

BMW M has produced its millionth car — the anniversary vehicle was a striking M3 sedan
Kyiv • UNN
BMW M’s millionth anniversary car was an orange M3 sedan produced in Munich. Starting in 2027, the plant will produce only electric vehicles.
BMW M recently reached an important milestone: the company produced its one-millionth car. The event was marked by the rollout at the plant in Munich, Germany, of a special BMW M3 finished in BMW Individual Fire Orange III. This is reported by Motor1, writes UNN.
Details
The keys to the M3 were symbolically handed over by Peter Weber, head of the Munich plant, to BMW M CEO Frank van Meel during a ceremony dedicated to the brand’s history while also offering insight into its future development.
This landmark event caps more than 50 years of BMW M history.
The electric M3 will be produced in Munich
BMW’s main plant in Munich will be the production site for the next-generation fully electric BMW M3, which will become the first high-performance model featuring BMW M Neue Klasse technologies. It will be the second Neue Klasse model assembled in Munich after the electric BMW i3, effectively opening a new chapter in the history of the M model range.
The connection between the M3 and the Munich plant is not accidental.
According to Weber, the current-generation M3 began production here in 2020, creating a special bond between the car and the employees who build it. However, from 2027, BMW’s main plant will produce only electric vehicles. This transformation will be supported by total investments of around €650 million.
The work covers approximately one-third of the entire plant, including a new body shop and a modernized assembly area, as well as completely upgraded logistics infrastructure. BMW says that all the work was carried out without halting current production.
BMW is preparing for a completely different M3
According to Frank van Meel, reaching the one-million-car milestone shows that BMW M’s core philosophy — combining racetrack capability with everyday usability — continues to resonate with buyers. And this is happening exactly 40 years after the first M3 appeared.
The next generation of high-performance BMW M cars will be based on Neue Klasse technologies, while electric powertrains will play an increasingly important role.
The future electric M3 will be the clearest evidence of this transition, bringing next-generation BMW M technologies to one of the brand’s most iconic models.

A failed, incapable, vulnerable America: Scope Ratings exposes Washington’s unsustainable debt path
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
